items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: A county agricultural extension office wanted to estimate the percentage of all farmers in the county who plant cover crops. Staff surveyed 60 farmers who attended a free workshop on cover-crop methods, and 52 of them reported planting cover crops.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The only flaw is the sample size; surveying 300 workshop attendees in the same way would fix the results.
The results may be biased because farmers at a cover-crop workshop are not a random sample of all county farmers.
Because 52 of the 60 farmers plant cover crops, most farmers in the county must also plant cover crops.
The results would be representative if staff had surveyed only farmers who did not attend the workshop.
items.explanation: The office wants to learn about all farmers in the county, but it sampled only farmers who chose to attend a cover-crop workshop. Those farmers are probably more interested in cover crops than farmers in general. Because the sample was not chosen at random from the whole population, the results may be biased.

A.why: You blamed the sample size. Surveying 300 attendees still samples only people drawn to a cover-crop event, so the bias stays. A bigger biased sample is still biased.

C.why: You treated a large majority in a biased sample as proof about the whole county. A lopsided result from an unrepresentative group says nothing reliable about everyone else.

D.why: You swapped one unrepresentative group for its opposite. Farmers who skipped the workshop are not a random sample of all farmers either.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The results may be biased because drivers stuck on the bridge are not a random sample of all city residents.
The results show that $84\%$ of all city residents support spending $\$40$ million to widen the bridge.

items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: A city's water department wants to know what percent of the city's residents support a new monthly fee to pay for storm-drain upgrades. The department held an evening public meeting about street flooding at a community center in the Riverside neighborhood, which floods more often than any other part of the city. All 1,200 people who attended the meeting were surveyed, and 80% of them said they support the fee.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: With 1,200 people surveyed, the sample is large enough to show that about 80% of all city residents support the fee.
About 80% of Riverside's residents support the fee, since the survey took place inside the Riverside neighborhood.
The people surveyed chose to attend a meeting about flooding, so the results may not represent the city's residents.
Surveying an equal number of residents from neighborhoods that rarely flood would make the results represent the city.
items.explanation: The department wants to learn about all city residents, but the sample was everyone who chose to attend a flooding meeting in the neighborhood that floods most. These people have an obvious stake in the question, and they were not randomly selected from any population. Because the sample is self-selected and unrepresentative, the 80% may be biased and can't be generalized to the city.

A.why: You let the large sample size cover for a biased method. Surveying 1,200 self-selected attendees still gives a biased result. A bigger sample doesn't fix how the sample was chosen.

B.why: You narrowed the population to Riverside, but even that isn't justified. The attendees chose to come to a flooding meeting and may not all live in Riverside, so they are not a random sample of Riverside's residents either.

D.why: You accepted a fix that adds another non-random group. Combining attendees with residents of low-flood areas still doesn't produce a random sample, and the two groups wouldn't be weighted to match the city's population.

items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: A folklorist wants to estimate the proportion of adults living in a mountain region who can retell, from memory, a traditional local tale about a shepherd and a talking river. The regional storytelling society has 4,000 adult members. The folklorist randomly selected 300 of these members and asked each to retell the tale. Of the 300 members, 270, or 90%, were able to do so.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Since the 300 members were selected at random, about 90% of the region's adults can likely retell the tale.
Since all 300 people were storytelling society members, the sample likely does not represent the region's adults.
Since 300 people is a small number for a whole region, the sample likely does not represent the region's adults.
A random sample of adults who are not society members would likely represent all of the region's adults.
items.explanation: The population of interest is all adults in the region, but the sample was drawn only from storytelling society members, a group especially likely to know traditional tales. The random selection lets the folklorist generalize to society members, not to the region's adults. Because the sample comes from a special subgroup, it is unrepresentative and the 90% is likely biased upward for the region.

A.why: You saw "randomly selected" and stopped there. The members were chosen at random from the society, not from the region, so the result applies only to society members.

C.why: You blamed the sample size instead of where the sample came from. A random sample of 300 of the region's adults could support a reasonable estimate. The flaw is that only society members could be chosen.

D.why: You swapped one subgroup for its opposite. Adults outside the society leave out the members, so that sample would also be unrepresentative and would likely be biased downward.

items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: A linguist wants to estimate the percent of the country's secondary school students who use the slang word "zonked" in everyday speech. The linguist posted a poll on a popular video channel devoted to new slang, inviting viewers who are secondary school students to answer. Of the 2,000 students who answered, 1,280, or 64%, said they use the word.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Because the poll received 2,000 answers, the 64% estimate is very likely close to the true percent for the country's students.
Because the students chose to answer a poll on a slang channel, the 64% estimate may not represent the country's students.
Because most answers probably came from cities, adding more answers from rural students would make the 64% estimate representative.
Because 64% of students said they use the word, about 36% of the country's secondary school students do not use it.
items.explanation: The linguist wants to learn about all of the country's secondary school students, but the sample was made up of slang-channel viewers who chose to respond. Students who follow new slang and opt into a slang poll are probably more likely to use the word. This self-selected sample is not random, so the 64% may be biased and can't be generalized to all of the country's students.

A.why: You trusted the size of the sample instead of checking how it was chosen. Two thousand self-selected viewers still form a biased sample, and more answers of that kind don't reduce the bias.

C.why: You fixed one possible imbalance but left the main flaw in place. Rural or urban, every respondent is still a slang-channel viewer who chose to answer, so the sample is still self-selected.

D.why: You took the complement of a biased figure and applied it to every student in the country. If 64% doesn't represent the country's students, then 36% doesn't either.

items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: A county health department wants to estimate the percent of the county's adults who have received this season's flu vaccine. During one week in October, staff members stood outside the county's pharmacies and randomly selected 500 adults from the people leaving the pharmacies. Of those 500 adults, 350, or 70%, said they had received this season's flu vaccine.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Since the 500 adults were selected at random, the 70% estimate applies to all of the county's adults.
Since pharmacy visitors may be more likely to be vaccinated, the 70% estimate is likely biased.
Since 500 adults is a small sample, surveying 1,000 pharmacy visitors would remove the bias.
Since a hospital serves all kinds of adults, surveying at a hospital would remove the bias.
items.explanation: The department wants to learn about all of the county's adults, but the sample came only from people leaving pharmacies, where flu vaccines are often given. Selecting people at random from that location doesn't make them a random sample of the county. Pharmacy visitors are a convenience group that is probably more likely to be vaccinated, so the 70% estimate is likely biased upward.

A.why: You let the word "random" carry the result to the whole county. The adults were chosen at random only from pharmacy visitors, so the estimate can't be generalized beyond that group.

C.why: You blamed the sample size instead of how the sample was chosen. Doubling the number of pharmacy visitors gives a more precise estimate of the same biased group. It doesn't remove the bias.

D.why: You swapped one convenience location for another. Hospital visitors are also an unrepresentative subgroup, and their vaccination rate may differ from the county's in its own way.

items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: An agronomist wanted to estimate the mean wheat yield, in bushels per acre, for all wheat farms in a state. The agronomist randomly selected 40 farms from the membership list of the state's Irrigated Grain Growers Cooperative, which accepts only farms that irrigate their fields. The mean yield of the selected farms was 72 bushels per acre.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Because the farms were chosen at random, 72 bushels per acre is a sound estimate for all wheat farms in the state.
The only problem is size; randomly choosing 400 cooperative farms would give a sound estimate for the whole state.
The farms were chosen at random from irrigated farms only, so the estimate may be biased for all farms in the state.
Randomly choosing 40 farms that do not irrigate would give a sound estimate of the mean yield for the whole state.
items.explanation: The agronomist wants to know about all wheat farms in the state. The farms were chosen at random, but only from a cooperative that accepts irrigated farms. Random selection lets you generalize only to the group you selected from, which here is irrigated cooperative farms. Irrigated farms may yield more than farms that rely on rain, so the estimate may be biased for the state as a whole.

A.why: You saw the word 'random' and stopped there. The farms were chosen at random from irrigated cooperative farms only, so the result can't be stretched to every wheat farm in the state.

B.why: You blamed the sample size. Choosing 400 farms from the same irrigated-only list still leaves out every farm that doesn't irrigate, so the bias stays.

D.why: You swapped one subgroup for its opposite. Farms that don't irrigate are no more representative of all farms than irrigated farms are.

items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: A folklore student wanted to estimate the percentage of adults in the town of Marrow Bend who believe the legend of the Lantern Woman, a ghost said to walk the old mill road. The student set up a table at the town's yearly Lantern Night parade, which is held in honor of the legend, and asked 200 adults who stopped at the table. Of these adults, 150 said they believe the legend.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Since 150 of the 200 adults believe the legend, about 75% of the adults in Marrow Bend believe it as well.
Parade-goers who stop at a table about the legend are not a random sample of town adults, so the result may be biased.
The sample of 200 is too small; asking 2,000 adults at the next Lantern Night parade would give an accurate estimate.
Asking 200 adults who stayed home during Lantern Night would give an accurate estimate for all adults in the town.
items.explanation: The student wants to know about all adults in Marrow Bend but only asked people who came to a parade celebrating the legend and chose to stop at the table. C.why: You blamed the sample size. Asking 2,000 people at the same parade repeats the same selection problem on a larger scale.

D.why: You swapped one unrepresentative group for its opposite. Adults who stayed home that night are not a random sample of the town either.

items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: A city's public works department wanted to learn how all drivers in the city rate the condition of city streets. The department posted a rating form inside a smartphone app that residents use to report potholes. Of the 480 app users who chose to fill out the form, 360 rated the condition of city streets as poor.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Because 360 of the 480 respondents chose poor, about three-fourths of all drivers in the city rate the streets as poor.
With 480 responses the method is sound, but a larger number of responses is needed before drawing any conclusion.
Sending the form to 480 randomly chosen app users would give a reliable estimate of how all city drivers rate streets.
Respondents chose to answer and use an app for reporting potholes, so the results may not represent all city drivers.
items.explanation: The population is all drivers in the city. The respondents, though, used a pothole-reporting app and also chose to answer, so they were selected twice over. People who report potholes are likely to be the ones most bothered by bad streets. A sample like that isn't random or representative, so the results may be biased.

A.why: You turned 360 out of 480 into three-fourths and applied it to every driver. A self-selected group of pothole reporters can't stand in for all drivers.

B.why: You blamed the sample size and called the method sound. The problem is who answered, not how many, and more responses through the same app wouldn't fix it.

C.why: You fixed the self-selection but kept the wrong sampling frame. A random sample of pothole-app users lets you generalize only to app users, not to all drivers in the city.

items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: A county hydrologist wanted to estimate the percentage of all private wells in the county whose water level dropped by more than 2 meters during last summer's drought. The hydrologist measured the wells of 90 homeowners who had called a county hotline to report well problems during the drought. Of those 90 wells, 72 had dropped by more than 2 meters.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Owners who called to report well problems likely had worse-affected wells, so 80% may overstate the county percentage.
About 80% of all private wells in the county dropped by more than 2 meters, since 72 of the 90 wells measured did.
The only issue is that 90 wells is too few; measuring 900 wells of hotline callers would give an accurate estimate.
Measuring 90 wells whose owners never called the hotline would give an accurate estimate for all wells in the county.
items.explanation: First find the sample rate: 72 ÷ 90 = 80%. Then compare who was sampled with the population. The hydrologist wants all private wells in the county but measured only wells whose owners called to report problems. Those wells are more likely to have dropped, so the sample isn't representative, and 80% probably overstates the true county percentage.

B.why: You calculated the 80% correctly but treated it as the county rate. The wells came from owners who reported problems, so they can't represent every well in the county.

C.why: You blamed the sample size. Measuring 900 wells from hotline callers still samples only owners who had problems, so the bias stays.

D.why: You swapped one subgroup for its opposite. Leaving out every caller removes the wells most likely to have dropped, so this sample would be biased in the other direction.

items.subtype_name: Spot the biased sample
items.stimulus: A city planning office wanted to know whether the city's residents support replacing street parking on Elm Avenue with a protected bike lane. The office randomly selected 250 of the 1,000 business owners on Elm Avenue and asked each one for an opinion. Of those surveyed, 150 opposed the bike lane.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Because the 250 owners were chosen at random, about 60% of the city's residents oppose the proposed bike lane.
A sample of 250 is too small to support any conclusion, even about the opinions of the business owners on Elm Avenue.
The result applies to the 1,000 business owners on Elm Avenue but cannot be generalized to all city residents.
Randomly selecting 250 cyclists who ride on Elm Avenue would show whether the city's residents support the bike lane.
items.explanation: The selection was random, but only from the 1,000 Elm Avenue business owners, so the result can be generalized to that group. The office wanted to know about all city residents, though, and business owners on the street have a direct stake in losing parking. They aren't a representative sample of the city, so the result can't be extended to all residents.

A.why: You calculated 150 ÷ 250 = 60% and generalized it to the whole city because the selection was random. Random selection from business owners lets you generalize only to those business owners.

B.why: You blamed the sample size. A random sample of 250 out of 1,000 owners is plenty to say something about those owners. The problem is that they are the wrong group for a question about all residents.

D.why: You swapped one stakeholder group for another with the opposite interest. Cyclists on Elm Avenue are no more representative of all residents than the business owners are.

items.stimulus: A musicologist wanted to estimate the percentage of adults in a metropolitan area who listen to classical music at least once a week. Of those interviewed, 285 said they listen to classical music at least once a week.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

items.stimulus: A materials engineer wanted to estimate the percentage of all ceramic floor tiles a factory produced last year that would crack under a standard 500-newton load test. D.why: You swapped one unrepresentative subgroup for another. Top-grade tiles would probably crack less often than average, so this sample would be biased in the other direction.

items.stimulus: A city health department wanted to estimate how many minutes of exercise adults in the city get per week. It surveyed 600 adults as they left one of the city's gyms. The average reported was 290 minutes per week.
items.stem: Which of the following best explains why the results of the survey are unlikely to represent the population?
choices: The sample was taken only from gym visitors, so it is not representative of all city adults.
The sample of 600 adults is too small to estimate weekly exercise for an entire city.
The sample should have been taken only from adults leaving a public library instead.
An average of 290 minutes is high enough to show that most city adults exercise often.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
Versions of "The Lantern Bride," a tale about a woman who guides lost boats home, have been recorded in more than forty fishing villages along the Merrin coast. Folklorist Tomas Ehrlund notes that the versions share an unusually specific plot, and he argues that sailors carried a single original story from port to port.

Text 2
No one questions that the Merrin versions of "The Lantern Bride" are strikingly alike. Yet villages facing the same storms and the same losses at sea could simply have arrived at similar stories independently. Shared hardship, not shared sailors, may explain the resemblance.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Sailors spread one original version of the tale along the coast.
Communities facing similar dangers tend to invent similar stories.
The tale was first told in the largest Merrin fishing village.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: At the start of a hand-washing campaign, a county health office recorded 400 cases of a stomach virus. Each week after that, the number of reported cases was 20% less than the week before.
items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $C$ is the number of reported cases $t$ weeks after the start of the campaign?
items.explanation: The starting amount is 400. A 20% decrease means each week keeps 100% − 20% = 80% of the week before, so the growth factor is $1 - 0.2 = 0.8$. The model is $C = 400(0.8)^t$.

A.why: You used the rate of decrease, 0.2, as the factor. Multiplying by 0.2 keeps only 20% of the cases each week. To keep 80%, the factor must be $1 - 0.2 = 0.8$.

C.why: You added the 20% instead of subtracting it. A factor of 1.2 means the cases go up by 20% each week, but they went down.

items.stimulus: A musicologist studying tuning systems notes that, in equal temperament, the frequency of a note doubles every 12 semitones. One note has a frequency of 110 hertz.

items.stimulus: A conservator studying a seventeenth-century wool tapestry measures the saturation of its madder-red dye at 250 units. Based on samples of similar textiles, the conservator estimates that the dye loses 20% of its remaining saturation every 25 years.

items.stimulus: A new labour contract at a regional warehouse sets a starting hourly wage of $\$20.00$ for all loaders. Under the contract, the hourly wage increases by $4\%$ every $2$ years.

items.stimulus: In the tuning system used for a study of piano repertoire, the reference pitch has a frequency of $220$ hertz. Each time a note is $12$ semitones higher, its frequency doubles.

C.why: After the 6th print the score is about 53.1, which is not yet below 50. That is the last print that keeps the score above 50, not the first one that drops it below.

items.stem: Based on the model, how many more recordings were in the collection 5 years after the project began than when it began, at $t = 0$?

A.why: You used an exponent of 4 instead of 5, which gives $30 \cdot 3^{4} = 2{,}430$, and then subtracted 30. At $t = 5$ the starting amount has been tripled five times.

B.why: You took the first table row, 90, as the starting amount and subtracted it from 7,290. That row is the value at $t = 1$. At $t = 0$ the collection held $90 \div 3 = 30$ recordings.

D.why: 7,290 is the size of the collection at $t = 5$. The question asks how many more recordings there were than at the start, so you still need to subtract the original 30.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: Marine biologists are restoring a seagrass meadow in a shallow bay. They model the meadow's area with the function $A(t) = 840(1.15)^{t/4}$. Here $A(t)$ is the area, in square meters, $t$ years after the restoration began.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $1.15$ in this context?
choices: The area increases by 15% each year.
The area increases by 15% every 4 years.
The area increases by 115% every 4 years.
The area increases by 15 square meters every 4 years.
items.explanation: The base $1.15$ is the growth factor, and $1.15 = 1 + 0.15$, so each time the factor is applied, the area grows by 15%. The exponent is $\frac{t}{4}$, which goes up by 1 only when $t$ goes up by 4. So the factor is applied once every 4 years, and the area increases by 15% every 4 years.

A.why: You read the 15% correctly but missed that the exponent is $\frac{t}{4}$, not $t$. The factor of $1.15$ is applied once for every 4 years, not once a year. You forgot to divide by the step interval.

C.why: You treated the whole factor as the percent increase. Multiplying by $1.15$ means the new area is 115% of the old one, so the increase is only 15%. An increase of 115% would mean multiplying by $2.15$.

D.why: You read the change as a fixed amount added each time, which describes a linear model. A base raised to a power means a constant percentage change. So $1.15$ means 15% more each time, not 15 more square meters.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: A linguist is tracking an endangered language. She estimates its number of fluent speakers with the function $S(t) = 3{,}200(0.94)^t$. Here $S(t)$ is the estimated number of fluent speakers $t$ years after 2010.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $0.94$ in this context?
choices: Each year, the number of speakers decreases by 94%.
Each year, the number of speakers increases by 6%.
Each year, the number of speakers decreases by 6% of the 2010 total.
Each year, the number of speakers decreases by 6%.
items.explanation: The base $0.94$ is the yearly multiplier. Because $0.94 = 1 - 0.06$, each year keeps 94% of the previous year's speakers and loses 6%. The exponent is just $t$, so this happens every year. The number of speakers decreases by 6% each year.

A.why: You mixed up the share that stays with the share that is lost. Multiplying by $0.94$ keeps 94% of the speakers, so only 6% are lost each year. A 94% decrease would mean multiplying by $0.06$.

B.why: You found the 6% but got the direction wrong. A base less than 1 means decay, so the number of speakers is shrinking. A 6% increase would need a base of $1.06$.

C.why: Losing 6% of the 2010 total every year means losing the same number of speakers each year (192), which is a linear model. In this exponential model, the 6% is taken from the previous year's count, so fewer speakers are lost each year.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: After a strong earthquake, seismologists modeled the number of aftershocks recorded each day with the function $N(d) = 480\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{d/3}$. Here $N(d)$ is the number of aftershocks recorded on day $d$, and $d = 0$ is the day of the main earthquake.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $3$ in this context?
choices: The daily number of aftershocks is cut in half 3 times each day.
The daily number of aftershocks decreases by 3 every day.
The daily number of aftershocks is cut in half every 3 days.
The daily number of aftershocks is cut to one-third every day.
items.explanation: The factor $\frac{1}{2}$ means the daily count is halved each time it is applied. The exponent $\frac{d}{3}$ goes up by 1 only when $d$ goes up by 3. So the 3 is the length of each step: the daily number of aftershocks is cut in half every 3 days. For example, $N(3) = 240$ and $N(6) = 120$.

A.why: You read the exponent as $3d$ instead of $\frac{d}{3}$. Halving 3 times a day would multiply the count by $\frac{1}{8}$ each day. Dividing by 3 in the exponent stretches each halving over 3 days.

B.why: You treated the model as linear, with the same number subtracted each day. The 3 is in the exponent, so it sets how often the count is halved. It is not an amount taken away.

D.why: You swapped the roles of the two numbers and treated 3 as the decay factor. The factor is $\frac{1}{2}$, which is the base. The 3 divides $d$ in the exponent, so it is a number of days, not a fraction kept.

items.stimulus:
A paleobotanist studies a buried seed bank of an extinct pine species. In the model, the number of seeds that can still sprout drops by 25% every 4 years. The table shows the estimated number of viable seeds at two times after burial.

Viable Seeds in a Buried Seed Bank
Years after burial, $t$ | Viable seeds, $S$
4 | 1,200
8 | 900
items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $S$ is the number of viable seeds $t$ years after burial?
items.explanation: A 25% drop means you multiply by $1 - 0.25 = 0.75$, and it happens once every 4 years, so the exponent is $t/4$. The table has no row for $t = 0$, so work back one step: $1{,}200 \div 0.75 = 1{,}600$. That gives $S = 1{,}600(0.75)^{t/4}$. Check: at $t = 4$ you get $1{,}600(0.75) = 1{,}200$, and at $t = 8$ you get $1{,}600(0.75)^2 = 900$. Both rows match.

A.why: You used the first table row, 1,200, as the starting amount. That row is at $t = 4$, not $t = 0$. Put in $t = 4$ and this model gives 900, not 1,200.

B.why: You used the percent lost, 0.25, as the multiplier. After a 25% drop, 75% is left, so each step multiplies by 0.75. This model gives 400 at $t = 4$.

C.why: You multiplied by the 4-year interval instead of dividing by it. With $4t$, the decrease happens 16 times by year 4 instead of once, so the model drops far below 1,200.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: A linguist estimates that a regional language currently has 50,000 fluent speakers and that this number decreases by 8% each year.
items.stem: If this trend continues, after how many whole years will the number of fluent speakers first be less than 30,000?
items.explanation: A decrease of 8% each year means the model is $50{,}000(0.92)^t$. Solving this directly takes logarithms, so test the choices. At $t = 6$: $50{,}000(0.92)^6 \approx 30{,}318$, which is still above 30,000. At $t = 7$: $50{,}000(0.92)^7 \approx 27{,}892$, which is below. So 7 years is the first whole year below 30,000.

A.why: You took off 8% of 50,000, or 4,000 speakers, every year, which is a linear model. A percent decrease is exponential: each year's 8% comes from a smaller number, so the yearly losses get smaller. After 5 years, about 32,954 speakers remain.

B.why: You probably solved $0.92^t = 0.6$, got about 6.1, and rounded down. After 6 years there are still about 30,318 speakers, which is not less than 30,000. You have to go up to the next whole year.

D.why: You found when the number of speakers lost first passes 30,000, which happens when fewer than 20,000 remain. The question asks when the number remaining drops below 30,000.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: An immunologist models the number of B cells in a culture $d$ days after an experiment begins with the function $N(d) = 4{,}000b^d$, where $b$ is a constant. The number of B cells increases by 50% every 12 hours.
items.stem: What is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: A 50% increase means you multiply by 1.5 every 12 hours. One day has two 12-hour periods, so in one day the count is multiplied by $1.5 \times 1.5 = 2.25$. Check a choice: after 1 day there should be $4{,}000(1.5)(1.5) = 9{,}000$ cells, and $4{,}000(2.25)^1 = 9{,}000$. So $b = 2.25$.

A.why: You used the 12-hour multiplier as if it were the daily one. Because $d$ is measured in days, $b$ has to cover two 12-hour periods. If you use 1.5, the model gives only 6,000 cells after 1 day instead of 9,000.

B.why: You added the two 50% increases to get 100%, as if each were 50% of the original amount. The second increase applies to the larger count, so the multipliers combine as $1.5 \times 1.5$, not $1 + 0.5 + 0.5$.

D.why: You doubled the multiplier, $2 \times 1.5$, instead of squaring it. Repeating a growth step twice means multiplying by the factor twice: $1.5^2 = 2.25$.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus:
A survey team counted the nesting pairs of a ground-nesting plover in one coastal reserve. Over the survey period, the number of nesting pairs decreased by the same percentage every 3 years. The table shows two of the counts.

Nesting Pairs of Plovers in the Reserve
Years after 2010, $t$ | Nesting pairs, $P$
3 | 800
9 | 512
items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $P$ is the number of nesting pairs $t$ years after 2010?
items.explanation: From $t = 3$ to $t = 9$ is 6 years, which is two 3-year steps. So the 3-year factor $b$ satisfies $800b^2 = 512$. That gives $b^2 = 0.64$, so $b = 0.8$ (a 20% decrease every 3 years). The table has no row for $t = 0$, so you work back one 3-year step from $t = 3$: $800 \div 0.8 = 1{,}000$. The model is $P = 1{,}000(0.8)^{t/3}$. Check it: at $t = 3$ it gives $1{,}000(0.8) = 800$, and at $t = 9$ it gives $1{,}000(0.8)^3 = 512$.

A.why: You used the first row of the table, 800, as the starting amount. That count is from $t = 3$, not from $t = 0$. At $t = 3$ this model gives 640, not 800.

C.why: You found the ratio $512 \div 800 = 0.64$ and used it as the factor for one 3-year step. Those rows are 6 years apart, so 0.64 is the factor for two steps. The 3-year factor is $\sqrt{0.64} = 0.8$.

D.why: You found the correct factor of 0.8, but when you worked back to $t = 0$ you divided 800 by 0.64. That undoes two 3-year steps. The table starts only one step after 2010, so you divide by 0.8 once. This model gives 1,000 at $t = 3$, not 800.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: A printmaking studio etches copper plates in a ferric chloride bath. With use, the bath's concentration decreases by 10% every 6 months. Eighteen months after the bath was mixed, its concentration was 29.16 grams per liter. The concentration can be modeled by an equation of the form $S = a \cdot b^t$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants.
items.stem: Which equation gives $S$, the concentration of the bath in grams per liter, $t$ years after the bath was mixed?
items.explanation: Each 6-month period multiplies the concentration by 0.9. Eighteen months is three of those periods, so $a(0.9)^3 = 29.16$. Since $0.9^3 = 0.729$, $a = 29.16 \div 0.729 = 40$. Because $t$ is measured in years, and each year contains two 6-month periods, the yearly factor is $b = 0.9^2 = 0.81$. The model is $S = 40(0.81)^t$. Check it: at $t = 1.5$, $40(0.81)^{1.5} = 40(0.9)^3 = 29.16$.

A.why: You added the two 10% decreases to get a 20% decrease per year. Percent decreases compound: after one year 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81 of the concentration remains, not 0.80. This is a linear habit applied to a percent change.

B.why: You used 29.16 as the starting amount. That is the concentration at 18 months, not at mixing. You need to work back three 6-month periods to get $a = 40$.

D.why: You worked back correctly to $a = 40$, but you used 0.9 as the yearly factor. The factor 0.9 applies to each 6-month period, and $t$ counts years, so the yearly factor is $0.9^2 = 0.81$. This model gives about 34.2 at $t = 1.5$, not 29.16.

items.stimulus:
A marine biologist tracks the moon jellyfish polyps in an aquarium tank. The number of polyps is multiplied by the same factor every week. The table shows two of the weekly counts.

Week, t | Number of polyps

items.stem: Which function best models the number of moon jellyfish polyps, $P(t)$, in the tank $t$ weeks after the count began?
items.explanation: From week 2 to week 5 is 3 weeks, and the count goes from 96 to 768, so it was multiplied by 8. Three equal weekly factors multiply to 8, so the weekly factor is 2. D.why: You found the weekly factor of 2 but divided 96 by 2 only once. Week 2 is two steps after week 0, so you need to divide by 2 twice.

items.stimulus: A civil engineer models the compressive strength of the concrete in a bridge pier. The strength starts at 60 megapascals when the pier is built and decreases by 19% every 10 years. The model can be written as $S(t)=60b^{t/5}$, where $S(t)$ is the strength, in megapascals, $t$ years after construction and $b$ is a constant.
items.stem: What is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: A 19% decrease means the strength is multiplied by 0.81 every 10 years. In the model the exponent $t/5$ counts 5-year periods, so 10 years is 2 periods and $b^{2}=0.81$. That makes $b=0.9$. Check it: $60(0.9)^{10/5}=60(0.81)$, which is a 19% drop.

B.why: You used the rate of decrease, 0.19, as the multiplier. A 19% decrease leaves 81% of the strength, so the multiplier must be close to 1.

C.why: You halved the percent, using 9.5% per 5 years. Percent changes compound, so two decreases of 9.5% are not the same as one decrease of 19%: $0.905^{2}\approx 0.819$, not 0.81.

D.why: 0.81 is the factor for 10 years, but the exponent $t/5$ makes $b$ the factor for each 5-year period. With $b = 0.81$, the strength would fall 19% every 5 years.

items.stimulus: A seismologist models the number of aftershocks recorded on day $n$ after a main earthquake, where day 0 is the day of the main shock. In the model, the count on each day is 20% less than the count on the day before. The model gives 320 aftershocks on day 2.
items.stem: According to the model, what is the smallest whole number $n$ for which fewer than 100 aftershocks are recorded on day $n$?
items.explanation: Work back from day 2 to day 0: $320 \div 0.8^{2} = 320 \div 0.64 = 500$. The model is $A(n)=500(0.8)^{n}$. On day 7, $500(0.8)^{7}\approx 104.9$, which is still at least 100. On day 8, $500(0.8)^{8}\approx 83.9$, which is below 100. The first day under 100 is day 8.

A.why: You used a linear model and subtracted 20% of 500, which is 100 aftershocks, every day. A percent decrease shrinks by a smaller amount each day, so the count falls more slowly than that.

B.why: You treated 320 as the day-0 count. Since 320 is the count on day 2, your model runs two days early.

C.why: Day 7 is the last day with at least 100 aftershocks (about 104.9). The question asks for the first day with fewer than 100.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus:
A materials scientist loads an aluminum alloy test bar over and over and measures the length of a fatigue crack. In the model, the crack length is multiplied by the same factor every 1,000 cycles.

Fatigue Crack Length
Loading cycles | Crack length (micrometers)
2,000 | 288
4,000 | 648
items.stem: To the nearest micrometer, what crack length does the model predict after 6,000 loading cycles?
items.explanation: From 2,000 to 4,000 cycles the length is multiplied by $648/288=2.25$. That span is two 1,000-cycle steps, so each step multiplies by $\sqrt{2.25}=1.5$. From 4,000 to 6,000 cycles is two more steps: $648(1.5)^{2}=648(2.25)=1{,}458$ micrometers.

A.why: You added the same amount, 360 micrometers, for every 2,000 cycles. That is a linear model, but the crack grows by a constant factor, not a constant amount.

C.why: You split the 125% increase into two 62.5% increases. Percent changes compound, so you need to take the square root of the factor 2.25, not halve the percent.

D.why: You applied the 2,000-cycle factor of 2.25 to each 1,000 cycles. You needed to divide the cycle count by the length of the step the factor belongs to.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: A musicologist studying a historical organ finds that its pipes are tuned in equal steps: moving up one step always multiplies the frequency by the same factor, and the frequency doubles every 12 steps. The pipe at step 9 sounds at 440 hertz.
items.stem: Which function gives the frequency $f(s)$, in hertz, of the pipe at step $s$?
items.explanation: The frequency doubles every 12 steps, so the exponent on 2 must be the number of steps moved divided by 12. The only known value is at step 9, not step 0, so count steps away from 9 using $s-9$. Then $f(9)=440\cdot 2^{0}=440$ and $f(21)=440\cdot 2^{1}=880$, which is one doubling 12 steps higher.

A.why: You treated 440 Hz as the frequency at step 0. Since it belongs to step 9, this model gives about 740 Hz at step 9.

B.why: You shifted the input the wrong way. To make the exponent zero at step 9 you need $s-9$, not $s+9$.

C.why: You multiplied by 12 instead of dividing by 12. That would make the frequency double 12 times per step, rather than once every 12 steps.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: A paleobotanist dates two fossilized seeds of the same plant species. The amount of carbon-14 in a dead plant halves every 5,730 years. Seed A contains 12.5% of the carbon-14 it had when it died. Seed B contains one-fourth as much carbon-14 as Seed A.
items.stem: Assuming both seeds began with the same amount of carbon-14, about how many years older is Seed B than Seed A?
items.explanation: Seed B has $\tfrac{1}{4}$ as much carbon-14 as Seed A, and $\tfrac{1}{4}=\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}$, so B has gone through 2 more halvings than A. Two half-lives are $2(5{,}730)=11{,}460$ years. You can check with full ages: A has 12.5%, which is 3 half-lives (17,190 years). B has 3.125%, which is 5 half-lives (28,650 years). The difference is 11,460 years.

A.why: You assumed carbon-14 is lost at a constant 50 percentage points every 5,730 years. That is a linear model, but halving is exponential decay.

C.why: 17,190 years is Seed A's age. The question asks how much older Seed B is than Seed A.

D.why: 28,650 years is Seed B's full age. You still need to subtract Seed A's age to get the difference.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus:
An agricultural scientist counts aphids on soybean plants in an untreated test plot. In the model, the average number of aphids per plant is multiplied by the same factor every 4 days.

Average Aphids per Soybean Plant
Day | Aphids per plant
3 | 160
7 | 240
11 | 360
items.stem: According to the model, by what percent does the number of aphids per plant increase over any 12-day period?
items.explanation: Each 4-day step multiplies the count by $240/160=1.5$. Twelve days is 3 steps, so the count is multiplied by $1.5^{3}=3.375$. A factor of 3.375 means the new count is 337.5% of the old one, which is an increase of $337.5\%-100\%=237.5\%$.

A.why: 125% is the increase over 8 days, from 160 to 360, which are the first and last rows of the table. A 12-day period is three 4-day steps, not two.

B.why: You added the 50% increase three times. Percent increases compound, so you need to multiply the factors: $1.5^{3}$.

D.why: 337.5% is the new count as a percent of the old count, from the factor 3.375. The increase is what is left after subtracting the original 100%.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: A hydrologist monitors a retention pond during a dry season. At the start of the dry season, the pond holds 50,000 cubic meters of water. In the model, the volume decreases by 2% every 3 days.
items.stem: Which function gives the volume $V(w)$, in cubic meters, of water in the pond $w$ weeks after the start of the dry season?
items.explanation: A 2% decrease multiplies the volume by 0.98. The exponent must count 3-day periods. In $w$ weeks there are $7w$ days, which is $7w/3$ periods of 3 days. Check with $w=3$: that is 21 days, or 7 periods, and the exponent $7(3)/3$ is 7.

B.why: You divided by the 3-day step but didn't convert weeks to days. This model loses 2% every 3 weeks instead of every 3 days.

C.why: You used the rate of decrease, 0.02, as the factor. Losing 2% leaves 98% each period, so the factor is 0.98.

D.why: You turned the unit conversion upside down. One week is $7/3$ periods of 3 days, not $3/7$ of one.

items.subtype_name: Build the line, then use it
items.stimulus: A musicologist timing performances of a traditional work song models the recordings with line $t$ in the xy-plane, where $x$ is the number of verses sung and $y$ is the running time, in minutes. Line $t$ has a y-intercept of $(0, 4)$ and passes through the point $(2, 10)$.
items.stem: The point $(5, b)$ lies on line $t$. What is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: From $(0, 4)$ to $(2, 10)$, y rises 6 while x rises 2, so the slope is $3$. The y-intercept is 4, so line $t$ is $y = 3x + 4$. Substitute $x = 5$: $y = 3(5) + 4 = 19$, so $b = 19$.

A.why: You treated 5 as the y-coordinate and solved $3x + 4 = 5$ to get $x = \frac{1}{3}$. The unknown in $(5, b)$ is the y-coordinate, so you need to substitute 5 for x instead.

B.why: You multiplied the slope by 5 but dropped the y-intercept. $3(5) = 15$ is only part of $3(5) + 4$.

D.why: You used 10, the y-coordinate of the second point, as the y-intercept and wrote $y = 3x + 10$. The y-intercept is 4, from the point $(0, 4)$.

items.subtype_name: Build the line, then use it
items.stimulus: While calibrating a seismometer, a seismologist draws line $p$ in the xy-plane. Line $p$ has a y-intercept of $(0, 8)$ and passes through the point $(2, 4)$. Line $q$ is the result of shifting line $p$ down 2 units.
items.stem: What is the x-coordinate of the x-intercept of line $q$?
items.explanation: The slope of line $p$ is $\frac{4 - 8}{2 - 0} = -2$, so line $p$ is $y = -2x + 8$. Shifting it down 2 units lowers the y-intercept to 6, so line $q$ is $y = -2x + 6$. Set $y = 0$: $0 = -2x + 6$, which gives $x = 3$.

D.why: 6 is the y-intercept of line $q$. The question asks where line $q$ crosses the x-axis, so you need to set $y = 0$, not $x = 0$.

items.stimulus: Ornithologists at a bird-banding station put numbered bands on the legs of migrating warblers. Last season, the station started with 480 bands, and 6 days later 390 bands were left. items.subtype_name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
items.stimulus: Early pianos were built on wooden frames, which could not hold strings under high tension without warping. In the 1820s and 1830s, makers began adding cast-iron frames that could withstand much greater string tension. This let the strings be struck harder without going out of tune or breaking. ______ composers of the period began writing louder, more forceful passages than earlier keyboard music had allowed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The earlier sentences describe how iron frames let strings be struck harder. The last sentence gives the outcome: composers wrote louder music. You can put 'so' between them, which makes this a cause-and-effect relationship, and 'As a result' signals it.

A.why: You picked a time word, but 'previously' places the louder writing before the iron frames. The passage says the frames made that writing possible, so it must have come after.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. The composers' louder writing is not a sample of stronger frames. It is what the stronger frames led to, so the relationship is cause and effect, not example.

D.why: You read a contrast where there is none. Louder music follows naturally from strings that can be struck harder. It does not go against that point.

items.stimulus: The true brightness of a Cepheid variable star is tied to the length of its pulse: the longer a Cepheid takes to brighten and dim, the more light it actually gives off. C.why: Nothing in the final sentence goes against the earlier ones. Cepheids became standard tools because of the method just described, so a contrast word reverses the logic.

D.why: 'Meanwhile' marks two things happening at the same time. The final sentence describes a result of the method, not a separate event running alongside it.

items.stimulus: As moist air is pushed up the windward slope of a mountain range, it cools, and cooler air can hold less water vapor than warm air can. items.stimulus: Oral folktales shift slightly with each retelling: a storyteller may change a character's name, move the setting to a nearby village, or add an episode that suits a particular audience. A.why: This is the subtype's trap. Gathering dozens of versions is not a sample of tales changing. It is what folklorists do because tales change, so a cause-and-effect word fits.

C.why: 'Afterward' only orders events in time. The final sentence is not the next event in a story. It is a method that follows logically from the problem described.

items.stimulus: Concrete expands in summer heat and contracts in winter cold, and a long, unbroken slab has no room to absorb that movement. items.stimulus: Longleaf pine seedlings spend years as low tufts of needles, and during that stage they face two kinds of competitors: hardwood shrubs, which shade them from above, and dense grasses, which crowd their roots. Fire checks both, since thick sheaths of needles shield the seedlings' growing tips while the competitors burn back. ______ managers of the Corley Flats preserve set low-intensity fires every two to three years, timing most burns for early summer, when the hardwood shrubs are actively growing and least able to recover.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The sentences before the blank set out a need and a mechanism. The seedlings face competitors, and fire suppresses those competitors while sparing the seedlings. The sentence after the blank describes what managers do because of that: they burn on a regular schedule and time the fires to hit the shrubs hardest. If you put 'so' in the blank, the passage holds together. 'Hence' signals that the managers' practice is a result of the mechanism described.

A.why: The passage names two competitors, and the sentence after the blank mentions only one of them, the hardwood shrubs. That made it look as though the sentence zooms in on one member of the group. But 'Specifically' needs the next sentence to restate the previous one more precisely, and a burn schedule is not a sharper version of 'fire checks both competitors.' It is an action taken because of that fact.

B.why: 'Afterward' sets up a sequence in time, as if the managers' burns came after the fire described in the previous sentence. That sentence is not an event, though. It is a general explanation of how fire affects the plants. The burns follow from that explanation logically, not chronologically.

D.why: 'Even so' means the next sentence goes ahead despite what came before. Nothing in the passage argues against burning. The passage explains why fire helps the seedlings, so the managers' burns agree with it. You read the deliberate setting of fires as surprising, but the passage has already explained why it makes sense.

items.subtype_name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
items.stimulus: Most metals bent past their elastic limit stay bent. Nickel-titanium alloys behave differently: deformed while cool, they return to a remembered shape when warmed past a transition temperature that manufacturers can tune to just below 37°C. Designers of arterial stents faced an awkward requirement: the device had to be narrow enough to slide through a catheter yet wide enough, once placed, to brace a vessel open. ______ many stents are now made of the alloy, crimped small inside a chilled sheath and left to spring open as the patient's blood warms them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: Cover the choices and try putting 'so' in the blank. The alloy changes shape when it warms to body temperature, and the stent has to be narrow on the way in and wide once it's in place. So designers use the alloy. The last sentence describes a design decision that follows from that property and that requirement together, so you need a cause-and-effect word: 'Hence.'

A.why: You read the stent as an example of the alloy's shape memory. It isn't one more example of that behavior. It's a choice designers made because of the property and the requirement, so it's a result, not an instance.

B.why: The word 'yet' inside the requirement made you expect a contrast. The final sentence doesn't push against the requirement, though. It solves it.

D.why: 'Previously' puts the sentence in the past, but the sentence says stents are 'now' made of the alloy. The time word clashes with the sentence it opens.

items.subtype_name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
items.stimulus: Concrete shrinks as it cures, and a long slab that cannot shrink freely will crack wherever it happens to be weakest. Engineers cannot prevent the shrinkage, but they can decide where the cracks go. Saw-cut grooves about a quarter of the slab's depth, spaced at regular intervals, create planes of deliberate weakness. ______ the cracks that do form run neatly along the bottoms of the grooves, mostly hidden from view, rather than wandering across the surface.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The grooves make planes of weakness, and the passage already said a slab cracks where it's weakest. So the cracks follow the grooves. The last sentence is the outcome of that mechanism, which calls for 'As a result.' Note that the passage never says the grooves prevent cracking. It says engineers 'cannot prevent the shrinkage' and only decide where the cracks go.

B.why: You assumed the grooves were meant to stop cracks, so 'the cracks that do form' sounded like a failure. The passage says the goal was to choose where cracks happen. Cracks forming along the grooves means the plan worked, so nothing is being contradicted.

C.why: You treated the last sentence as an example of engineers deciding where cracks go. It's the one outcome the grooves produce, not a sample from a larger set. A finding that follows from a mechanism is a result, not an example.

D.why: 'Before then' puts the cracking before the grooves are cut. That reverses the order, since the grooves have to exist before cracks can follow them.

items.subtype_name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
items.stimulus: Because the influenza virus's surface proteins mutate from season to season, antibodies raised by last year's vaccine may fail to recognize this year's strain. One small region of the virus, the stalk of its hemagglutinin protein, barely changes across strains, however, since mutations there tend to leave the virus unable to enter cells. ______ several research groups have aimed experimental 'universal' vaccines at the stalk rather than at the protein's highly variable head.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The contrast in this passage happens inside the second sentence: most of the virus mutates, but the stalk doesn't. The blank connects that fact to what researchers did next. The stalk stays the same across strains, so researchers target it. That's a decision that follows from the evidence, so you need 'Therefore.'

A.why: 'Similarly' means the next sentence shows the same pattern in a new case. Researchers choosing a target isn't a parallel to the stalk staying the same. Their choice follows from it.

B.why: You carried the 'however' from the previous sentence into the blank. That contrast is already finished. Targeting the stalk agrees with the fact that it doesn't change, and 'Even so' would mean researchers acted despite it.

D.why: You read the vaccine work as an example of the stalk staying the same. The previous sentence isn't a general claim about research that this sentence could illustrate. The research is what scientists did because of that fact.

items.subtype_name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
items.stimulus: Under the city's 2019 zoning code, any lot within 400 meters of a rail station may be built to six stories without a variance. The Linden Street parcel lies about 380 meters from the Eastgate platform. ______ the developer's plan for a six-story apartment block went forward without a hearing before the zoning board, though neighbors had expected one.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: This question takes three steps. First, the rule allows six stories within 400 meters of a station. Second, the parcel is 380 meters away, which is inside that limit. Third, the plan needed no hearing. The third sentence is the conclusion you get by applying the rule to the parcel, so 'Thus' is correct. The neighbors' surprise is a side clause and doesn't change how the two main sentences connect.

B.why: The clause 'though neighbors had expected one' made the sentence sound like a reversal. The main claim, that no hearing was needed, is exactly what the rule predicts. Something surprising to the neighbors isn't a contradiction of the sentence before.

C.why: The parcel is an example of the rule, but that's the job of the second sentence. The blank sentence gives the result of applying the rule to that parcel. It's a finding, not another example.

D.why: 'Additionally' adds an unrelated fact. You missed that the 380-meter distance is the reason no hearing was needed.

items.subtype_name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
items.stimulus: Nutrition labels report a food's total iron, but the body absorbs far less of the iron in plants than of the iron in meat. Vitamin C changes that calculation: eaten in the same meal, it converts plant iron into a form the gut takes up several times more readily. ______ dietitians advising vegetarian patients often suggest pairing lentils or spinach with citrus, peppers, or tomatoes rather than simply adding more iron-rich vegetables.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: Vitamin C makes plant iron easier to absorb, so dietitians suggest pairing plant iron with vitamin C. The last sentence is advice that follows from the mechanism. 'Accordingly' means 'because of this, acting in line with it,' so it fits.

B.why: The words 'rather than' inside the sentence made you think of opposites. The contrast is between two kinds of advice within the sentence. It doesn't go against the vitamin C finding, which the advice follows.

C.why: You treated pairing lentils with citrus as an example of vitamin C converting iron. Dietitians giving advice isn't a case of a chemical reaction. It's what they recommend because of that reaction.

D.why: 'In fact' strengthens or intensifies the claim before it. The advice doesn't make the vitamin C claim stronger. It's what follows from that claim.

items.subtype_name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
items.stimulus: Beaver dams slow streams enough for sediment to settle, and over decades a chain of abandoned beaver ponds fills in to form flat, saturated meadows. Because these meadows hold water through dry summers, they halt wildfire far more reliably than the forest around them. Across much of the American West, though, trapping eliminated beavers long ago. ______ some land managers have begun installing low wooden structures that imitate beaver dams, hoping to rebuild wet valley floors where no beavers remain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: Two facts come before the blank. Wet beaver meadows stop fire, and beavers are gone from much of the West. Land managers respond by building imitation dams. Because both facts lead to that action, 'Consequently' is correct. The 'though' only connects the two facts to each other. Once you see that, the action in the last sentence follows from both of them.

A.why: You read the imitation dams as an example of beaver meadows stopping fire. They aren't a case of that principle. They're what land managers built because of it.

B.why: 'Instead' needs an option that gets replaced. The structures do stand in for beavers, but that idea is already inside the sentence ('where no beavers remain'). The link to the sentence before is cause and effect, not substitution.

D.why: You carried the 'though' forward. 'Even so' would mean managers acted despite the beavers being gone. They acted because the beavers are gone.

items.subtype_name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
items.stimulus: In many living plants, leaves grown in air richer in carbon dioxide develop fewer stomata, the pores through which they exchange gases. Paleobotanists have counted stomata on fossil ginkgo leaves preserved in rock layers of known age, and the counts drop sharply in layers from the early Eocene. ______ researchers have concluded that atmospheric carbon dioxide was unusually high during that interval.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives a rule: more carbon dioxide means fewer stomata. The second gives evidence: fossil leaves from the early Eocene have fewer stomata. The third is the conclusion you get by applying the rule to that evidence. Because of the low counts, researchers infer high carbon dioxide, so 'For this reason' is correct.

B.why: This is the classic trap. A general rule is followed by a case, so 'for example' looks right. But the case is the fossil counts in the second sentence. The blank sentence is the conclusion drawn from applying the rule, not another example of it.

C.why: 'Drop sharply' sounded like a change of direction to you. A drop in stomata is exactly what high carbon dioxide predicts, so the conclusion agrees with the evidence.

D.why: 'Similarly' would make the conclusion a parallel observation. It's an inference that depends on the two sentences before it.

items.stimulus: In etching, an artist draws through a waxy coating on a copper plate, and acid eats into the metal only where the needle has exposed it. The longer the plate sits in the acid, the deeper, and once inked the darker, a line prints. The printmaker Ilse Voorhuis wanted the foregrounds of her harbor scenes to look heavy and close while the far shoreline stayed faint. ______ she would lift the plate from the bath partway through, brush varnish over the distant lines to shield them, and return it so that only the foreground went on deepening.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: Two things set up the blank. Time in the acid controls how dark a line prints, and Voorhuis wanted dark foregrounds with faint distances. Putting those together, she protected the distant lines and let only the foreground keep etching. Her method is an action taken because of the principle and her goal, so 'Thus' is correct.

B.why: The contrast between 'heavy' and 'faint' is inside her goal. Her method doesn't go against that goal. It carries the goal out.

C.why: You read her technique as an example of how etching works. It's her deliberate use of that principle to get a particular effect, so it's a result, not an instance.

D.why: Words like 'partway through' and 'return it' made the passage feel like a sequence of steps. 'Afterward' would place her method after her wish in time, but the method is what her wish led her to do. The time order inside the sentence doesn't make the link between the sentences a time link.

items.subtype_name: Cause-and-effect logic (because / since / so / led to)
items.stimulus: Before synthetic dyes were introduced in the 1850s, many vivid colors could be produced only from rare insects, lichens, or shellfish, and thousands of shellfish might be needed to dye a single garment. Because the raw materials were so scarce, deep purple cloth was ______ and was generally worn only by royalty and the very wealthy.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The chain is simple: the dye sources were scarce and huge quantities were needed, so the cloth was expensive, which is why only the wealthy wore it. 'Costly' is the only word that follows from scarcity and explains who wore it.

A.why: You picked a word about how the color looked. The passage is about the supply of dye and who could afford the cloth, not about the quality of the color.

C.why: You chose a word that suits the topic of fabric but describes the wrong kind of effect. Scarce raw materials make cloth expensive, not long-lasting, and durability would not explain why only the wealthy wore it.

D.why: You reversed the chain. Scarce materials make a product rare, not common, and the passage says only royalty and the wealthy wore it.

items.subtype_name: Cause-and-effect logic (because / since / so / led to)
items.stimulus: When a regional hospital raised wages for its night-shift nurses by 15 percent, far fewer of them left to work for competing employers over the following year. Because experienced staff stayed longer, the hospital was able to ______ the amount it spent on recruiting and training replacements, which partly offset the cost of the raise.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Fewer nurses left, so fewer replacements were needed, so the hospital spent less on hiring and training them. 'Offset the cost of the raise' confirms that the spending went down. 'Reduce' fits the chain exactly.

B.why: You picked a verb that goes in the right general direction but acts on the wrong thing. Keeping staff changes how much the hospital spends, not whether the spending is hidden.

C.why: You picked a word from the world of budgets without checking the chain. Fewer departures lower recruiting costs. They do not give the hospital a reason for those costs.

D.why: You reversed the direction. If fewer nurses leave, the hospital needs fewer replacements, and the passage says the savings offset the raise.

items.subtype_name: Cause-and-effect logic (because / since / so / led to)
items.stimulus: Dietary fiber slows the rate at which food passes from the stomach into the small intestine, where most sugars are absorbed. For this reason, meals high in fiber tend to ______ the rise in blood sugar that follows eating, releasing glucose into the bloodstream gradually rather than all at once.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Fiber slows digestion, so sugar enters the blood more slowly, so the rise in blood sugar is gentler. The phrase 'gradually rather than all at once' tells you the rise is lessened. 'Moderate' means exactly that.

A.why: You reversed the direction. Fiber slows digestion, so it makes the rise in blood sugar slower, not faster.

B.why: You picked a verb that acts on the wrong thing. Fiber changes the size and speed of the blood-sugar rise. It does not make the rise easier to see.

D.why: You matched the scientific topic instead of the causal logic. A meal cannot measure anything. The sentence needs a word for what fiber does to the rise.

items.subtype_name: Cause-and-effect logic (because / since / so / led to)
items.stimulus: Concrete expands in summer heat and contracts in winter cold, and a long, unbroken slab can split under that repeated strain. Because these gaps give each section room to move, they ______ the cracking that would otherwise spread across the surface as the material shifts.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Concrete moves, and movement causes cracks. The joints give it room to move, so there is less cracking. 'Limit' is the word that says the joints cut down the damage.

A.why: You picked a verb that goes in the right general direction but acts on the wrong thing. The joints give the concrete room to move so that fewer cracks form. They do not just hide cracks that are already there.

B.why: You picked a word for a different kind of effect. A gap in pavement does not keep track of cracking. The passage is about how the gaps change the amount of cracking.

C.why: You got the direction backwards. The strain causes cracking, and the joints are the fix for it.

items.stimulus: Waterlogged peat bogs contain very little oxygen, and the bacteria and fungi that break down organic matter need oxygen to thrive. As a result, wooden tools, leather, and woven textiles buried in bogs are often ______ for thousands of years, allowing archaeologists to study objects that would have rotted away long ago in dry soil.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: With no oxygen, the organisms that cause decay cannot thrive, so buried objects do not rot. Objects that do not rot are 'preserved,' which also fits the contrast with things that 'would have rotted away.'

B.why: You reversed the chain. Low oxygen stops decay, so the objects survive. They are not destroyed.

C.why: You picked a word that acts on the wrong thing. Burial does keep objects out of sight, but the low oxygen explains why they do not rot, not why they cannot be seen.

D.why: You matched the museum setting instead of the causal logic. The bog's chemistry affects whether the objects decay, not whether anyone exhibits them.

items.stimulus: Distance runners who train at high altitude take in less oxygen with each breath. items.stimulus: Farmers who plant clover between cash-crop seasons are often advised to cut their fertilizer applications the following spring. items.stimulus: Older keyboard tunings made a few keys sound sweetly pure at the cost of making distant keys grate, so composers mostly avoided those distant keys. items.subtype_name: Cause-and-effect logic (because / since / so / led to)
items.stimulus: Researchers long assumed that island rails lost the power of flight simply because they had no predators to escape. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Food is scarce, so large flight muscles become an energy burden. Birds that carry less of that burden do better, and those are the ones with smaller wings. D.why: This is the trap. You saw that scarce food matters but applied it to the wrong birds. Scarcity weighs most on birds feeding large muscles, so the small-winged birds would be the last to starve.

items.stimulus: For decades, bridge decks in cold regions have been reinforced with steel bars. to corrode more quickly than the bridge's older steel bars.
to outlast every other kind of reinforcing bar now in use.

grew their own indigo plants instead of trading for the dye.
colored many of the cloth fragments they produced with indigo.

confirm the assumption that frequent job changes early on slow a worker's wage growth

does not by itself establish that a body formed beyond Neptune rather than near Saturn

Tax records show that throughout the fourteenth century, all alum reaching Serro was imported from mines in Anatolia. The dyers who colored the fragment therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: grew their madder in fields near the Anatolian alum mines
used madder because alum could not be obtained in Serro
produced a redder wool than any other medieval European dyers
combined madder with alum that had come from Anatolian mines
items.explanation: You need three facts together. Alizarin means the dyers used madder. The aluminum residue means they used alum. All alum in Serro came from Anatolia. So they combined madder with Anatolian alum. Each part of the answer comes directly from a stated fact.

A.why: You added an extra step. The passage says where the alum came from, not where the madder was grown.

B.why: The fragment contains alum residue, and the tax records show that alum reached Serro, so alum was available there.

C.why: You went past the chain to a comparison with all other European dyers. The analysis describes only one fragment.

items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: Folklorists have long assumed that Scandinavian ballads about a drowned bride began among fishing communities on the coast. Folklorist Ingrid Solheim's survey of 300 recorded versions complicates that view: every version that ends with the bride returning as a seabird was collected inland, along the Glomma river. Solheim also notes that all of the versions in the Haugen collection, one of her survey's sources, end with that seabird return. Taken together, these findings indicate that the Haugen versions ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: were collected inland rather than in coastal fishing villages.
are older than the versions recorded in coastal fishing villages.
prove that the ballad first arose along the Glomma river.
include some endings in which the bride does not return.
items.explanation: Link the two facts through the term they share, the seabird ending. Fact 1: every surveyed version with the seabird ending was collected inland. Fact 2: every Haugen version has the seabird ending, and the Haugen versions are part of the survey. Take out the shared term and you get this: the Haugen versions were collected inland. Choice A says exactly that and adds nothing else.

B.why: The passage says nothing about when any version was composed or collected. You went past the chain and added a claim about age that neither fact supports.

C.why: This is the trap for this subtype: a broader claim that goes past the chain. Knowing where some versions were collected doesn't tell you where the ballad began. Solheim's survey only 'complicates' the coastal-origin view. It doesn't settle where the ballad came from, and 'prove' is much stronger than the evidence allows.

D.why: The passage says all of the Haugen versions end with the bride returning as a seabird, so none of them can end without her return. You reversed the second fact.

items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: Many coaches assume that extra sleep only makes athletes feel more rested and does nothing measurable to their bodies. Work by sports physiologist Imani Okafor challenges that view. She found that when competitive swimmers extended their sleep to ten hours a night, the amount of glycogen stored in their muscles rose. Other studies have shown that higher muscle glycogen delays fatigue during sustained high-intensity efforts. Taken together, these findings suggest that by extending their sleep, swimmers may also be ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: delaying fatigue during sustained high-intensity efforts.
outperforming athletes in other sports who sleep less.
storing more glycogen because they already tire less.
feeling more rested without any change in their muscles.
items.explanation: The shared term is muscle glycogen. Okafor's study links extra sleep to more glycogen, and other studies link more glycogen to delayed fatigue. Remove the middle term and you get extra sleep → delayed fatigue. Choice A states that link and adds nothing else, and the passage's 'may' fits it.

B.why: You went past the chain. The passage only discusses swimmers and never compares them with athletes in other sports, so this comparison is a claim nobody established.

C.why: You reversed the chain. The passage says more glycogen leads to less fatigue. It never says less fatigue causes glycogen to build up, and in the passage the glycogen rise comes from sleep.

D.why: You picked the popular view the passage sets out to undercut. Okafor found a measurable change, higher muscle glycogen, so 'without any change in their muscles' contradicts her finding.

items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: Scholars have long assumed that the anonymous motets in the Brenner Codex were copied in Paris, where most fourteenth-century motets originated. Musicologist Tomás Lindqvist disputes this. He observes that the codex marks syncopated rhythms with a small hooked stroke. He also notes that among all surviving fourteenth-century sources, only manuscripts produced at the cathedral of Ivrea use that stroke. If Lindqvist's observations are accurate, it follows that the Brenner Codex was ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: composed by musicians who had trained at Ivrea.
produced at Ivrea rather than copied in Paris.
the first manuscript ever to use a hooked stroke.
copied in Paris by a scribe who had visited Ivrea.
items.explanation: The shared term is the hooked stroke. The Brenner Codex uses it, and only manuscripts produced at Ivrea use it. Since the codex is itself a surviving fourteenth-century source, it must be one of the Ivrea manuscripts. Choice B states that conclusion and nothing more.

A.why: You added an extra step. The evidence concerns where the manuscript was produced, not who composed the music or where they trained. Music can be composed in one place and copied in another.

C.why: You went beyond the chain. The passage says only Ivrea manuscripts use the stroke. It says nothing about which manuscript used it first, so 'first ever' is unsupported.

D.why: You held on to the older assumption. If only manuscripts produced at Ivrea use the stroke, a codex copied in Paris could not use it, whatever the scribe's travels.

items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: Researchers gave two groups of older adults identical diets, except that one group also ate a daily serving of fermented cabbage. After twelve weeks, the groups' total fiber intake did not differ, but the cabbage group had markedly higher levels of the gut bacterium Lactobacillus plantarum. Earlier work had established that L. plantarum produces butyrate, a compound that strengthens the intestinal lining. These findings imply that eating fermented cabbage ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: may increase the amount of butyrate produced in the gut.
benefits the gut mainly by raising a person's fiber intake.
strengthens the gut more than any other fermented food.
raises L. plantarum levels by first increasing butyrate.
items.explanation: The shared term is L. plantarum. Fermented cabbage raised L. plantarum levels, and L. plantarum produces butyrate. Link the two facts and you get fermented cabbage → more butyrate-producing bacteria → possibly more butyrate. Choice A states that link with 'may', which matches the passage's 'imply'.

B.why: You missed the half of the result that held steady. Fiber intake did not differ between the groups, so fiber cannot explain the difference.

C.why: You went past the chain. The study tested only fermented cabbage and compared no other fermented foods, so 'more than any other' is a claim nobody established.

D.why: You reversed the chain. The passage says L. plantarum produces butyrate. It does not say butyrate produces more L. plantarum.
