items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: Paleobotanists studying a 300-million-year-old coal seam found that fossil leaves of the seed fern Alethopteris have unusually thick cuticles, the waxy outer layer of a leaf. In living plants, thick cuticles are strongly associated with limiting water loss in dry or salty settings. Some researchers had assumed the seam formed in a uniformly wet swamp. However, Alethopteris leaves appear only in the seam's upper layers. Taken together, these findings support each of the following conclusions EXCEPT that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the seam's upper layers preserve leaves with a trait linked to limiting water loss.
the assumption that the swamp stayed uniformly wet throughout may need revision.
the seam's lower layers formed under wetter conditions than any other seam of that age.
Alethopteris may have been suited to drier or saltier conditions than a wet swamp.
items.explanation: Each layer of evidence is about this one seam: a trait (thick cuticle) goes with resisting water loss, and that trait appears only in the upper layers. Linking those facts supports A, B, and D. Nothing in the text compares this seam with any other seam of the same age, so C adds a comparison nobody established. That's the claim the evidence does not support.

A.why: You rejected this because it only restates one fact and doesn't link the two. A plain restatement is still supported. The question asks which claim is NOT supported, not which one goes furthest.

B.why: You read the 'uniformly wet' assumption as the passage's own view. The word 'However' signals that the leaf evidence undercuts it, and 'may need revision' is hedged enough for the evidence to support.

D.why: You thought this went too far because no single sentence says it. But 'thick cuticles go with dry or salty conditions' and 'Alethopteris has thick cuticles' together give you exactly this, and 'may' keeps it modest. Linking two facts this way is the inference, not an extra step.

items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: Health departments have traditionally tracked influenza through hospital admission records. Those records have two weaknesses: they include only patients sick enough to be admitted, and they typically reach officials weeks after infections occur. Wastewater testing avoids both problems. Nearly all infected people, including those with mild illness, shed viral fragments into sewage, and a sample can be analyzed within days. A city that adds wastewater testing to its surveillance could therefore reasonably expect each of the following EXCEPT to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: detect infections among residents whose illness never required hospital admission.
determine exactly how many residents are infected with influenza on a given day.
notice rising influenza activity sooner than admission records alone would allow.
receive results from a collected sewage sample within a matter of days.
items.explanation: The text says that viral fragments show up in wastewater, including from mild cases, and that results come back quickly. Connecting those facts to the weaknesses of hospital records supports A, C, and D. But knowing that fragments are present, even from nearly everyone infected, doesn't tell you an exact count of infected people. 'Exactly' goes past what the passage establishes, so B is the expectation the text does not support.

A.why: You thought this went beyond the text because it is never stated outright. Link 'records include only admitted patients' with 'mild cases shed fragments too' and this follows directly.

C.why: You saw a comparison and assumed it was unsupported. The passage gives both halves of the comparison: records arrive weeks late and samples are analyzed within days. Putting them together is the chain, not an added assumption.

D.why: You rejected this because it simply repeats a detail instead of linking facts. A repeated detail is still something the city can reasonably expect. The question asks for the claim the text fails to support.

items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: Seismologists have long treated very small earthquakes as too weak to matter for forecasting large ones. However, a team monitoring a fault in northern Chile found that clusters of tiny quakes there consistently accompanied slow slip, a gradual movement of the fault that unfolds over weeks. Earlier research had shown that slow slip on this fault adds stress to the locked segment where the region's large earthquakes begin. Taken together, these findings support all of the following EXCEPT that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: slow slip on this fault is a gradual process that can continue for weeks.
the view that tiny quakes are useless for forecasting may not hold for this fault.
clusters of tiny quakes on the fault coincide with periods of added stress on the locked segment.
every cluster of tiny quakes on the fault will be followed by a large earthquake.
items.explanation: The shared term is slow slip. Tiny-quake clusters go with slow slip, and slow slip adds stress to the locked segment, so the clusters go with periods of added stress (C). That in turn undercuts the old view (B), and A restates a given fact. But added stress is not the same as a guaranteed rupture, and nothing says 'every' cluster leads to a large quake. D turns 'adds stress' into 'will be followed by,' which the evidence does not support.

A.why: You rejected this because it uses only one fact from the passage. A choice can repeat half the evidence and still be supported. Here you needed the one claim that fails, not the one that does the least.

B.why: You read the opening view as the passage's conclusion. 'However' sets up the new findings as an undercut, and the hedge 'may not hold' keeps this claim within what those findings show.

C.why: You thought this added a step because no single sentence links tiny quakes to stress. That link comes from cutting out the shared term, slow slip. That's exactly what 'taken together' asks you to do.

items.stimulus: Many coaches assume that a pre-race warm-up helps mainly by loosening the muscles. Physiologist Rhea Tamsin argues that temperature matters more. In her trials, runners who warmed up for fifteen minutes started their races with muscle temperatures about 1.5°C higher than runners who skipped the warm-up. Separate laboratory studies have found that each degree of warming increases how quickly muscle fibers can contract. Taken together, these findings suggest that, compared with runners who skip a warm-up, runners who warm up ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: loosen their muscles more fully, the true source of the benefit.
begin their races with muscle fibers that can contract more quickly.
gain more contraction speed from each degree of muscle warming.
finish their races faster by a fixed amount for every degree.
items.explanation: Connect the two facts through the term they share, which is muscle warmth. Runners who warm up start with warmer muscles, and warmer muscle fibers contract more quickly. D.why: You went past the end of the chain. The passage stops at how fast fibers can contract. It never measures race times, and it never says the gain is a fixed amount per degree.

items.stimulus: Grammatical complexity was once thought to change at random as languages age. Linguist Oren Valdés disputes this. In his cross-language sample, languages acquired by large numbers of adult learners tended to shed their case endings, the suffixes that mark a noun's role in a sentence. Valdés also notes that a trading-port dialect of one language has been learned by far more adults than a highland dialect of the same language has. If Valdés is correct, the port dialect, compared with the highland dialect, has likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: been learned by a greater number of adult speakers.
lost all of the case endings that it once had.
lost case endings at random rather than through learners.
retained fewer of its case endings over time.
items.explanation: The shared term is learning by many adults. Languages learned by many adults tend to shed case endings, and the port dialect has had far more adult learners than the highland dialect. So the port dialect has likely kept fewer case endings. The words 'tended' and 'likely' allow a difference in degree and nothing stronger.

A.why: You repeated one of the facts instead of linking the two. The passage already states that the port dialect had more adult learners. The blank asks what follows from that about its case endings.

B.why: This is strength creep. Valdés found that such languages 'tended to shed' case endings, which supports fewer endings. It does not support losing all of them.

C.why: You picked the older view that Valdés disputes. His evidence ties the loss of case endings to adult learners, not to chance.

items.stimulus: Oysters build their shells from calcium carbonate, and the work takes more energy as seawater becomes more acidic. Ecologist Priya Nandakumar monitored two sites in a coastal bay. likely build their shells faster in warmer water.
save energy on shells whenever the pH happens to rise.
spend half as much energy forming their shells.

items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: A flat transmission spectrum, one showing no absorption features, was long read as evidence that an exoplanet lacks an atmosphere. Astronomers now recognize that a high-altitude aerosol layer, such as photochemical haze or silicate cloud, can produce the same flat spectrum by blocking starlight before it reaches the gases below. Photochemical hazes are thought to form only on planets cooler than about 850 K, while silicate clouds are thought to condense only on planets hotter than about 1,300 K. The planet Veyra-4b has a flat spectrum and a temperature of about 1,050 K, so ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: its flat spectrum is better explained by silicate clouds than by the photochemical hazes found on cooler planets.
it must lack an atmosphere, since both kinds of aerosol layer have been excluded as causes of its flat spectrum.
neither of the two aerosol layers described is a likely source of the flatness in its spectrum.
planets with temperatures between 850 K and 1,300 K are less likely than other planets to retain atmospheres.
items.explanation: You need three facts at once. At 1,050 K, Veyra-4b is above haze's ceiling of 850 K, so haze is unlikely. It is also below the 1,300 K floor for silicate clouds, so those are unlikely too. Put together, neither named layer accounts for the flat spectrum. That is as far as the chain goes. Haze and silicate cloud are given only as examples ('such as'), and the temperature limits are only 'thought' to hold. So the passage supports ruling out these two layers. It does not support any conclusion beyond that.

A.why: You used only half the chain. You saw that 1,050 K is too hot for haze and stopped there, so you never checked the silicate-cloud threshold. Those clouds condense only above 1,300 K, so the planet is too cool for them as well.

B.why: You got the key point that both layers are ruled out, then took one extra step. The passage gives haze and silicate cloud only as examples ('such as'), so other aerosols aren't excluded. The thresholds are also only 'thought' to hold, so 'must' claims more certainty than the passage gives.

D.why: You went from one planet to a claim about a whole temperature range. The passage says nothing about how often planets in that range keep their atmospheres. It doesn't even establish that Veyra-4b has lost its own.

items.stimulus: Traffic-safety campaigns usually judge a street by how often collisions occur on it. would lower trauma-ward admissions more than any other safety measure Ardell has tried.

items.subtype_name: Link the two facts (syllogism)
items.stimulus: Many folklorists assume that the longer a tale has circulated, the more versions of it collectors will find. Folklorist Ilse Hartmann challenges this view. In her survey of Baltic archives, a tale's number of recorded variants tracked the number of distinct dialect regions it had crossed, not its age. a household tale would likely have fewer recorded variants than a market tale that has circulated for a similar length of time.
every tale told mainly at seasonal markets has more recorded variants than any tale told mainly within households.
household tales gather variants more quickly than market tales do, because families retell them more often.
items.explanation: The shared term is dialect regions. Variants track dialect regions crossed, and market tales cross more regions than household tales. items.stimulus: Historians once dated medieval tapestries by their dyes. But madder and weld were in use for centuries, so a dye can place a tapestry only within a very wide span. items.stimulus: All the stars in a cluster formed at about the same time, and the more massive a star is, the sooner it uses up the hydrogen in its core and leaves the main sequence. star R is more massive than star P.
star P is more massive than star R.
every star in cluster M is more massive than star P.

D.why: You stretched one comparison to a whole cluster. Stars still on M's main sequence can be any small mass, so 'every' is not established.

items.stimulus: A county health clinic tracked flu shots. The number given in October was 15% greater than the number given in September. The number given in November was 10% less than the number given in October.
items.stem: Which expression represents the percent change in the number of flu shots given, from September to November?

D.why: You used $1.10$ for a 10% decrease. 'Less than' means the factor is $1 - 0.10 = 0.90$.

items.stimulus: A printmaker pulls three runs of the same woodcut. Run A contains 25% more prints than run B, and run B contains 20% fewer prints than run C.
items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Run A contains 5% more prints than run C.

Run B contains 25% fewer prints than run A.
Run A contains 25% more prints than run C.

D.why: You applied A's 25% to run C when it belongs to run B. The base is the quantity after "than", and in the first statement that is B. You skipped the second link in the chain.

items.stimulus: At a weather station, the rainfall recorded in July was 50% greater than the rainfall recorded in June. The rainfall recorded in August was 40% less than the rainfall recorded in July.

items.stimulus: After a storm, a hydrologist models the depth of water in a reservoir with the function $d(t) = 0.5t + 14$. Here $d(t)$ is the depth, in meters, $t$ days after the storm ends, for $0 \le t \le 20$.
items.stem: By how many meters does the water depth increase when $t$ increases by $6$?
items.explanation: The change in output equals the slope times the change in input. The slope is $0.5$ meter per day, so a 6-day increase raises the depth by $0.5 \times 6 = 3$ meters. The 14 is the starting depth, and it cancels out of any change: $d(t+6) - d(t) = 3$.

A.why: This is how much the depth rises in a single day. You found the slope but didn't multiply it by the 6-day increase.

C.why: You added the slope and the change in input ($0.5 + 6$) when you should have multiplied them.

D.why: You plugged 6 straight into the function and got $d(6) = 0.5(6) + 14 = 17$. That is the depth on day 6, which includes the starting depth of 14, so it isn't the change.

items.stimulus: A marine biologist models the length of a giant kelp frond with the equation $2y - 5x = 30$. Here $y$ is the frond length, in centimeters, $x$ days after the biologist begins measuring, for $0 \le x \le 20$.
items.stem: According to the equation, by how many centimeters does the frond length $y$ increase when $x$ increases by $4$?
items.explanation: Solve for $y$: $2y = 5x + 30$, so $y = 2.5x + 15$. The slope is $2.5$ centimeters per day, so a 4-day increase adds $2.5 \times 4 = 10$ centimeters. The constant 15 cancels out of any change.

D.why: You plugged 4 into $y = 2.5x + 15$ and got 25. That is the frond length on day 4, which includes the 15. It isn't the increase.

items.stem: According to the model, by how many grams does the bird's body mass decrease when $h$ increases by $6$?

D.why: You used $M(1) = 34.5$ as the rate and multiplied it by 6. $M(1)$ is the mass after one hour. The rate is the difference between $M(0)$ and $M(1)$.

items.stimulus: An astronomer models the surface temperature of a slowly rotating asteroid as one patch of its surface turns into sunlight. The model is $T(m) = 1.6m - 170$, where $T(m)$ is the temperature, in degrees Celsius, $m$ minutes after the patch enters sunlight, for $0 \le m \le 60$.
items.stem: According to the model, by how many degrees Celsius does the surface temperature increase as $m$ increases from $20$ to $45$?
items.explanation: The input increases by $45 - 20 = 25$ minutes. The change in output is the slope times the change in input: $1.6 \times 25 = 40$ degrees Celsius. You can check this with $T(45) - T(20) = -98 - (-138) = 40$.

D.why: You multiplied the slope by 45, the end of the interval, rather than by the 25 minutes that actually pass between $m = 20$ and $m = 45$.

items.subtype_name: How much does the output change?
items.stimulus: In a sports science lab, a runner's heart rate during a treadmill test is modeled by $H(s) = 4s + 92$, where $H(s)$ is the heart rate, in beats per minute, at a treadmill speed of $s$ kilometers per hour.
items.stem: By how many beats per minute does the model's predicted heart rate increase when the treadmill speed increases by 3 kilometers per hour?
items.explanation: The change in output equals the slope times the change in input. The slope is 4 beats per minute for each kilometer per hour, so a 3 km/h increase raises the heart rate by $4 \times 3 = 12$ beats per minute. The constant 92 is in both heart rates, so it cancels out. You can check this with any speed: $H(5) - H(2) = 112 - 100 = 12$.

B.why: 4 is the increase for a 1 km/h change, which is the slope. The question asks about a 3 km/h increase, so you still need to multiply by 3.

D.why: You put 3 straight into the function and got $H(3) = 104$. That's the heart rate at a speed of 3 km/h, not the amount it changes. It also includes the starting value of 92, which cancels when you take a difference.

items.stimulus: A linguist studying early language development uses the equation $V = 48t + 310$ to estimate the number of distinct words, $V$, that a child produces $t$ months after the child's second birthday.
items.stem: Which expression represents the increase in the predicted number of words a child produces when $t$ increases by $n$ months?
items.explanation: The coefficient 48 is the rate: 48 more words for each month. When $t$ goes up by $n$ months, the output goes up by $48 \times n = 48n$. The 310 is part of both the starting and ending values, so it cancels when you subtract: $(48(t+n) + 310) - (48t + 310) = 48n$.

C.why: You used 310 as the rate. But 310 is the starting vocabulary, the value when $t = 0$. The rate per month is the coefficient on $t$, which is 48.

D.why: You added the monthly rate to the number of months when you should have multiplied. Each of the $n$ months adds 48 words, so the total change is $48n$.

items.stimulus: A nutritionist uses the function $C(s) = 35s + 140$ to estimate $C(s)$, the total number of calories in a fruit smoothie that contains $s$ scoops of protein powder.
items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Adding 2 more scoops of protein powder increases the smoothie's estimated total by 70 calories.
Adding 2 more scoops of protein powder increases the smoothie's estimated total by 210 calories.
Adding 2 more scoops of protein powder increases the smoothie's estimated total by 280 calories.
Adding 2 more scoops of protein powder increases the smoothie's estimated total by 35 calories.
items.explanation: The question asks how much the output changes, so the change in calories is the slope times the change in input. The slope is 35 calories per scoop, and the input goes up by 2 scoops, so the total goes up by $35 \times 2 = 70$ calories. The 140 is the smoothie's calories with no protein powder. It's the same at both ends, so it cancels: $C(s+2) - C(s) = 35(s+2) + 140 - (35s + 140) = 70$.

items.subtype_name: Pick the equation that fits the scatterplot
items.stimulus: An immunologist measured the concentration of a vaccine-induced antibody, in units per milliliter, in blood samples from a volunteer. The first sample was taken on the day of vaccination, and one sample was taken each week after that for 10 weeks. In the scatterplot, $x$ is the number of weeks since vaccination and $y$ is the antibody concentration.
items.stem: Which of the following equations best models the data in the scatterplot?
items.explanation: First check the shape. The points fall quickly at first and then level off as they approach the x-axis, so the model is exponential decay, and the base must be between 0 and 1. Next check the starting value. At $x = 0$ the concentration is about 400, so $a = 400$. Last, check the rate. items.stem: The equation $y = a(b)^x$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants, models the data shown. What is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: The points curve down toward the x-axis, so the model shows exponential decay and $b$ must be between 0 and 1. In $y = a(b)^x$, $b$ is the factor that y is multiplied by each time x goes up by 1. Read two neighbouring points: from $(0, 800)$ to $(1, 400)$ the count is multiplied by $\frac{400}{800} = \frac{1}{2}$. The same holds for every step (400 to 200, 200 to 100, 100 to 50), so $b = \frac{1}{2}$. As a check, $a = 800$, which is the value at $x = 0$.

figure.caption: Conifer Pollen in a Sediment Core
figure.y_label: Pollen grains per gram of sediment
figure.alt: Scatterplot of five points: (0, 800), (1, 400), (2, 200), (3, 100), (4, 50). The values fall steeply at first and then level off toward the x-axis.

items.subtype_name: Pick the equation that fits the scatterplot
items.stimulus: A materials scientist hangs different loads from a strip of a new polymer and measures the strip's length under each load.
items.stem: The equation $y = mx + b$ models the data shown. What is the value of $m$?
items.explanation: The points lie on a straight line that rises, so $m$ is positive and equals the change in length per newton. items.subtype_name: Pick the equation that fits the scatterplot
items.stimulus: A city's planning office counts the cyclists passing an automated counter on a new bike lane. In the scatterplot, $x$ is the number of hours after 8:00 a.m. and $y$ is the number of cyclists counted in a 10-minute interval.
items.stem: The equation $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants, models the data shown. What is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: The points rise and then fall, so the model is a downward-opening parabola and $a < 0$. The point at $x = 0$ gives $c = 20$. The data are symmetric about $x = 4$, so the vertex is at $x = 4$, which means $-\frac{b}{2a} = 4$, or $b = -8a$. Substitute the vertex $(4, 100)$: $100 = 16a + 4b + 20$. Replace $b$ with $-8a$: $80 = 16a - 32a = -16a$, so $a = -5$ and $b = -8(-5) = 40$. Check: $y = -5x^2 + 40x + 20$ gives 80 at $x = 2$.

figure.caption: Cyclists on the Elm Street Bike Lane
figure.alt: Scatterplot of five points: (0, 20), (2, 80), (4, 100), (6, 80), (8, 20). The points rise to a highest value in the middle and fall again symmetrically.

items.license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

Solves correctly for the leading coefficient $a$ and reports it instead of $b$.
Gives the x-coordinate of the vertex instead of the coefficient $b$.

items.subtype_name: Pick the equation that fits the scatterplot
items.stimulus: A printmaker adds different amounts of a drying agent to six batches of relief-printing ink and records how long each batch takes to dry.
items.stem: The equation $y = mx + b$ models the data shown. What is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: The points lie on a falling line, so the slope is negative. Each step of 2 drops lowers the drying time by 3 hours, so $m = \frac{-3}{2} = -1.5$. The first point is at $x = 2$, not $x = 0$, so you can't read $b$ straight off the plot. Go back one step of 2 drops from $(2, 30)$, which raises y by 3: $b = 30 + 3 = 33$. In algebra: $30 = -1.5(2) + b$, so $b = 33$.

items.subtype_name: Pick the equation that fits the scatterplot
items.stimulus: Astronomers track a nova as it brightens. In the scatterplot, $x$ is the number of days after the nova was first detected and $y$ is its brightness, in arbitrary units.
items.stem: The equation $y = a(2)^x$, where $a$ is a positive constant, models the data shown. What is the value of $a$?
items.explanation: The brightness doubles each day, which matches the base 2 in the model. $a$ is the model's value at $x = 0$, but the first data point is at $x = 2$, so you have to work backward. Substitute $(2, 5)$: $5 = a(2)^2 = 4a$, so $a = \frac{5}{4} = 1.25$. Or halve twice going back from day 2: $5 \to 2.5 \to 1.25$.

items.stimulus: An immunologist measured the concentration of a vaccine-induced antibody in a volunteer's blood every week for 10 weeks after a booster dose. The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, where $x$ is the number of weeks after the booster and $y$ is the antibody concentration, in units per milliliter.
items.stem: Which of the following equations best models the data shown in the scatterplot?
items.explanation: The points fall quickly at first and then level off toward the x-axis, so the model is exponential decay, which needs a base between 0 and 1. The data meet the y-axis near 400, so the coefficient in front is 400. To pick the base, check a point: at $x = 5$, $400(0.8)^5 \approx 131$, which is close to the plotted value of about 135. So $y = 400(0.8)^x$ fits.

A.why: You got the decay base right but used the wrong starting value. At $x = 0$ this model gives 200, but the data start near 400. Read where the cloud meets the y-axis.

B.why: This is the trap: a base of 1.2 is greater than 1, so the model grows. Your concentrations fall every week, so the base has to be between 0 and 1.

D.why: You got the shape and intercept right but the base decays far too quickly. At $x = 5$, $400(0.4)^5 \approx 4$, but the data show about 135. Test a point to check the base.

items.stimulus: Agricultural scientists grew wheat on 11 test plots, each given a different amount of nitrogen fertilizer. The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, where $x$ is the nitrogen applied, in tens of kilograms per hectare, and $y$ is the grain yield, in hundreds of kilograms per hectare.
items.stem: Which of the following equations best models the data shown in the scatterplot?
items.explanation: The yield rises and then falls, so the model is a parabola that opens down, which needs a negative leading coefficient. The data meet the y-axis at about 30, so the constant term is 30. The peak is near $x = 5$, and for $y = -2x^2 + 20x + 30$ the vertex is at $x = -\frac{20}{2(-2)} = 5$. This equation gives 80 at $x = 5$, which matches the data.

B.why: This is the trap: the intercept is right, but a positive leading coefficient makes the parabola open up. That model has its minimum at $x = 5$, where the data have their maximum.

C.why: You got the downward opening and the intercept right but did not check the vertex. Here $-\frac{b}{2a} = -5$, so the model only decreases for $x \ge 0$. The data rise first.

D.why: You used the maximum yield, about 80, as the constant term. The constant term is the value at $x = 0$, and there the data show about 30.

items.stimulus: Nutrition researchers recorded the average daily sodium intake and the resting systolic blood pressure of 9 adult participants. The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, where $x$ is the daily sodium intake, in grams, and $y$ is the systolic blood pressure, in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg).
items.stem: Which of the following equations could be a line of best fit for the data shown in the scatterplot?
items.explanation: The points rise from left to right, so the slope is positive. If you extend the trend back to $x = 0$, it meets the y-axis at about 110 mm Hg. From $x = 0$ to $x = 7$ the pressure rises from about 110 to about 138, which is a slope of $\frac{28}{7} = 4$. So $y = 110 + 4x$.

C.why: You divided run by rise (7 ÷ 28) when slope is rise over run. A slope of 0.25 would make the line almost flat, but the data climb about 28 mm Hg across the plot.

items.stimulus: A civil engineering lab loaded a steel test beam in stages. At each stage, it recorded the load on the beam, $x$, in kilonewtons (kN), and the downward deflection at the beam's midpoint, $y$, in millimeters (mm). The scatterplot shows the 10 measurements.
items.stem: Which of the following equations could represent a line of best fit for the data?
items.explanation: The points rise in a straight pattern, so the slope is positive. Going from a load of 2 kN to 20 kN, the deflection rises from about 3 mm to about 12 mm, or about 9 mm over 18 kN. That gives a slope of about $0.5$. Extending the pattern back to $x = 0$ gives a deflection of about 2 mm. So $y = 2 + 0.5x$ fits the data.

A.why: You have the right intercept and the right size of slope, but the sign is wrong. A negative slope would make the deflection go down as the load goes up, and the points clearly go up.

C.why: You swapped the slope and the intercept. A slope of 2 would add 2 mm for every 1 kN of load, so at 20 kN this line gives about 40 mm, far above the data.

D.why: You have the right slope, but this line meets the y-axis at 6 instead of about 2. That puts the whole line about 4 mm above the points, so it doesn't run through the middle of them.

items.stimulus: A folklore archive tracks a recently emerged legend. Each year it records $y$, the number of distinct variants of the legend that collectors have documented. Here $x$ is the number of years since the legend was first reported. The scatterplot shows the results.
items.stem: Which of the following equations best models the data?
items.explanation: The points curve upward more and more steeply, so this is exponential growth and the base must be greater than 1. At $x = 0$, the count is about 5, so $a = 5$. After that the count roughly doubles each year (about 10, 20, 40, 80, 160), so $b = 2$. That gives $y = 5(2)^x$.

B.why: You swapped the starting value and the growth factor. This model starts at 2 and multiplies by 5 each year, which gives 250 by year 3. The data at year 3 is about 40.

C.why: The growth factor is right, but the starting value is wrong. At $x = 0$, this model gives 20, and it gives 640 at year 5, four times the data. You may have read the point at year 2 as the starting value.

items.stimulus: Ornithologists counted the nesting pairs of a seabird at one island colony each spring. Here $y$ is the number of nesting pairs and $x$ is the number of years since the first count. The scatterplot shows the counts.
items.stem: Which of the following equations best models the data?
items.explanation: The counts fall quickly at first and then level off toward the x-axis. That is exponential decay, so the base must be between 0 and 1. The count at $x = 0$ is about 640, so $a = 640$. Each count is about three-quarters of the year before (640, 480, 360, 270, and so on), so $b = 0.75$. That gives $y = 640(0.75)^x$.

D.why: The decay factor is right, but you used the year-1 count, about 480, as the starting value. At $x = 0$, the data are near 640, so this curve runs well below every point.

items.stimulus: A hydrologist recorded the water level of a small reservoir every two days during a 20-day period with no rainfall. The scatterplot shows the water level $y$, in meters, $x$ days after the period began.
items.stem: Which of the following equations best models the data in the scatterplot?
items.explanation: The points fall in a straight line, so you want a linear model. The level drops as days pass, so the slope is negative. The data would meet the y-axis near 40, so the intercept is 40. From about 40 m at day 0 to about 10 m at day 20, the level falls 30 m over 20 days, which gives a slope of $-30/20 = -1.5$. So the model is $y = 40 - 1.5x$.

D.why: You divided the 30-meter drop by 10 days when it happened over 20 days. A slope of $-3$ would take the level below zero by day 14.

items.stimulus: Engineers tested how a plastic used in outdoor furniture holds up under ultraviolet light. The scatterplot shows the tensile strength $y$, in megapascals, of test samples after $x$ weeks of exposure in a UV chamber.
items.stem: Which of the following equations best models the data in the scatterplot?
items.explanation: The points fall quickly at first and then level off toward the x-axis, which is exponential decay. A decay model needs a base between 0 and 1. The strength at week 0 is 80, so the starting value is 80. Between week 0 and week 1 the strength falls from 80 to about 64, so each week keeps about 80% of the last value, a base of 0.8. The model is $y = 80(0.8)^x$.

C.why: You used the share lost each week (20%) as the base. The base is the share kept, 0.8. With 0.2, the strength would drop to 16 after one week.

items.explanation: The points drop by half every 0.5 meter: 80, 40, 20, and so on. That is exponential decay. Working back half a meter from the first point at $x = 0.5$ gives the starting value: $2 \times 80 = 160$ at $x = 0$. C.why: You saw the halving pattern, but you counted each gridline step as 1 meter. The data halve every 0.5 meter, so they fall by a factor of 4 per meter. This model gives 80 at $x = 1$, but the data show 40.

items.stimulus: Two folklore archives are digitizing recorded oral tales. Archive A started with 360 digitized tales and adds 90 tales at the end of each year. Archive B started with 40 digitized tales, and at the end of each year its total grows by 100%. items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus: A meteorologist uses the function $P(h) = 1{,}000(2)^{-h/5}$ to model the atmospheric pressure P, in hectopascals, at an altitude of h kilometers above sea level, for $0 \le h \le 15$.
items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between h and P?
items.explanation: The function has the variable in the exponent, so it is exponential. Because the exponent is negative, $P(h) = 1{,}000(2)^{-h/5} = 1{,}000\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{h/5}$, so the pressure is cut in half for every 5 kilometers of altitude: 1,000, then 500, then 250, then 125. Multiplying by a constant factor less than 1 is exponential decrease.

A.why: You got both the direction and the type wrong. The variable is in the exponent, which makes the function exponential, and the negative exponent makes the pressure fall as altitude rises.

B.why: You saw a base of 2, which is greater than 1, and concluded the function grows. You missed the negative sign in the exponent $-h/5$, which flips the base to $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and makes P decrease.

C.why: This is the trap. You got the direction right but treated 'loses half every 5 km' as losing a fixed amount. The drops are 500, then 250, then 125: the same factor each time, not the same amount. That is exponential, not linear.

items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus: A textile historian models the output of two 19th-century weaving workshops. Workshop A produced $200$ bolts of cloth in year $0$, and its yearly output rose by $100$ bolts each year after that. Workshop B produced $100$ bolts in year $0$, and its yearly output rose by $50\%$ each year after that.
items.stem: Based on these models, which statement about the workshops' yearly output is true?
choices: Workshop A produces more than Workshop B in each year from year 0 to year 10.
Workshop A produces more through year 2; Workshop B produces more from year 3 on.
Workshop B produces more through year 4; Workshop A produces more from year 5 on.
Workshop A produces more through year 4; Workshop B produces more from year 5 on.
items.explanation: Workshop A grows linearly: $200 + 100t$. Workshop B grows exponentially: $100(1.5)^t$. In year $4$, A makes $600$ bolts and B makes $100(1.5)^4 = 506.25$, so A is still ahead. In year $5$, A makes $700$ and B makes $100(1.5)^5 \approx 759$, so B is now ahead. Exponential growth keeps pulling away after that.

A.why: You saw that A starts twice as high and assumed it stays ahead. Exponential growth always passes linear growth eventually. B overtakes A in year $5$, and by year $10$ B makes about $5{,}767$ bolts while A makes $1{,}200$.

B.why: You compared the yearly increases, not the outputs. B's increase first beats A's $100$ in year $3$ (it rises by $112.5$), but B's total that year is only $337.5$, while A's is $500$.

C.why: You found the right crossover year but put the workshops the wrong way around. A starts ahead because it begins at $200$. B, the exponential one, is the one that takes the lead.

items.stimulus: At the start of a drought, a reservoir held 800 million gallons of water. Each week during the drought, the reservoir lost an amount of water equal to 3% of the volume it held at the start of the drought.

items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus: A weather agency is building two networks of automatic rain gauges. Network P started in year 0 with 120 gauges and adds 30 gauges each year. Network Q started in year 0 with 40 gauges, and its number of gauges increases by 25% each year.
items.stem: Which statement best compares the number of gauges in the two networks?
choices: Network P has more gauges than Network Q in every year.
Network Q first has more gauges than Network P in year 6.
Network Q first has more gauges than Network P in year 10.
Network Q first has more gauges than Network P in year 11.
items.explanation: Network P is linear: $P(t) = 120 + 30t$. Network Q is exponential: $Q(t) = 40(1.25)^t$. Exponential growth always eventually passes linear growth, so the only question is when. Setting the two equal can't be solved with simple algebra, so test the years in the choices. In year 10, $Q = 40(1.25)^{10} \approx 372.5$ and $P = 420$, so P is still ahead. In year 11, $Q \approx 465.7$ and $P = 450$. Network Q has more gauges for the first time in year 11.

A.why: You treated 25% as 25% of the starting 40 gauges, which is a fixed 10 gauges a year. That would never catch P's 30 a year. Or you compared only the first year, when P adds 30 and Q adds 10. Q actually adds 25% of its current size, so its yearly gains keep growing until it passes P.

B.why: Year 6 is the first year Q adds more gauges than P (about 30.5 compared with 30). That compares how much each network grows in a year, not how many gauges each network has. In year 6, Q has only about 153 gauges while P has 300.

C.why: The two models are equal at about t ≈ 10.7, and you rounded down. In year 10, Q has about 372 gauges and P has 420, so Q is not ahead yet. The first whole year when Q is ahead comes after the crossover, which is year 11.

items.stimulus: A hospital offers a new technician two pay plans. Under Plan A, the starting salary is $48,000 and goes up by $2,500 at the end of each year. Under Plan B, the starting salary is $50,000 and goes up each year by 4% of the starting salary.
items.stem: Which statement best describes how the two starting salaries compare over the years?

Plan B's salary is higher before year 4, and Plan A's is higher after year 4.
Plan A's salary is higher than Plan B's in every year.
Plan A's salary is higher before year 4, and Plan B's is higher after year 4.
items.explanation: Plan B's raise is 4% of the starting salary, which is always 0.04 × 50,000 = $2,000. That is a fixed amount added each year, so Plan B is linear, just like Plan A. After t years, Plan A pays 48,000 + 2,500t and Plan B pays 50,000 + 2,000t. Plan B starts $2,000 ahead, but Plan A gains $500 on it each year, so the gap closes after 2,000 ÷ 500 = 4 years. C.why: You swapped the starting salaries and gave Plan A the $50,000. With the bigger start and the bigger raise, Plan A would lead every year. In fact Plan A starts $2,000 behind.

D.why: You found the right crossover year but had the plans the wrong way round. Plan B starts higher and Plan A, with the larger raise, pulls ahead after year 4.

items.stimulus: On day 0, the snow depth was 200 centimeters at weather Station P and 160 centimeters at weather Station Q. During a warm spell, Station P's snow depth decreased each day by an amount equal to 10% of its day 0 depth. Station Q's snow depth decreased each day by 15% of its depth at the end of the previous day. Depths are recorded at the end of each day.
items.stem: Which of the following statements is true?
choices: The depth at Station Q never exceeds the depth at Station P.
The depth at Station Q first exceeds Station P's at the end of day 7.
The depth at Station Q first exceeds Station P's at the end of day 8.
The depth at Station Q first exceeds Station P's at the end of day 10.

items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus: A materials scientist tracks the stiffness of two curing resin samples. Sample A's stiffness $t$ hours after mixing is modeled by $a(t) = 30(0.75)^{-t}$, and sample B's is modeled by $b(t) = 20(0.5)^{-t}$, both in gigapascals. The function $r$ is defined by $r(t) = \dfrac{a(t)}{b(t)}$.
items.stem: Which of the following best describes how the value of $r(t)$ changes as $t$ increases?
items.explanation: Write $r(t) = \dfrac{30}{20}\cdot\dfrac{(0.75)^{-t}}{(0.5)^{-t}} = 1.5\left(\dfrac{0.5}{0.75}\right)^{t} = 1.5\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{t}$. That is a constant multiplier of $\tfrac{2}{3}$ for each hour, so it is exponential, and because $\tfrac{2}{3} < 1$ it is decreasing. Both samples get stiffer, but B gets stiffer faster, so the ratio shrinks.

B.why: You got the direction right but called the ratio linear. $r(t)$ is multiplied by $\tfrac{2}{3}$ every hour. It does not lose a fixed amount each hour, so it is exponential.

C.why: You flipped the quotient and got $\left(\tfrac{0.75}{0.5}\right)^{t} = 1.5^{t}$, or you reasoned that two growing quantities must have a growing ratio. With the negative exponents handled correctly, the base is $\tfrac{0.5}{0.75} = \tfrac{2}{3}$, which is less than 1.

D.why: You saw that both samples get stiffer and assumed their ratio grows steadily. The ratio is neither increasing nor linear. It is multiplied by $\tfrac{2}{3}$ each hour.

items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus:
A musicologist measures $L$, the average length, in seconds, of a recurring cadenza in recordings of one concerto made $t$ decades after 1920.
Average Cadenza Length
t (decades after 1920) | L (seconds)

2 | 34
3 | 31

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between $t$ and $L$ shown in the table?
items.explanation: The $t$-values are not evenly spaced, so divide each change in $L$ by the change in $t$: $\frac{-6}{2} = -3$, $\frac{-3}{1} = -3$, $\frac{-12}{4} = -3$. $L$ falls by the same 3 seconds per decade, so the relationship is linear and decreasing: $L = 40 - 3t$.

D.why: You saw the constant rate but flipped its sign, probably by reading the table from the bottom up. $L$ drops 3 seconds per decade as $t$ increases.

items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus: In year 0, weaving workshop A produced 600 meters of cloth and workshop B produced 300 meters. Each year after that, A's output increased by 20% of its year-0 output. B's output increased by 25% of the previous year's output.
items.stem: What is the least whole number of years $n$ after year 0 for which workshop B's output is greater than workshop A's output?
items.explanation: A adds 20% of a fixed amount, which is 120 m every year, so it is linear: $A(n) = 600 + 120n$. B is exponential: $B(n) = 300(1.25)^n$. In year 7, $A = 1{,}440$ and $B \approx 1{,}430.5$, so A is still ahead. In year 8, $A = 1{,}560$ and $B \approx 1{,}788.1$. The answer is year 8.

A.why: You compared only the start. A begins higher and adds 120 m in year 1 while B adds only 75 m. But exponential growth always passes linear growth eventually, and here it happens in year 8.

B.why: You rounded $1.25^7 \approx 4.77$ up to 4.8, which gives B exactly 1,440. That ties A, it doesn't beat it. With the exact value, B is about 1,430.5, still short of A.

D.why: You treated A's 20% increase as compounding, $600(1.2)^n$. But A grows by 20% of its year-0 output, a fixed 120 m each year, so A is linear. Compared with that linear A, B pulls ahead much sooner.

items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus: Two archaeological collections of unglazed pottery are deteriorating. Collection P starts with 600 intact pieces and loses 30 pieces each decade until none remain. Collection Q starts with 900 intact pieces and loses 20% of its remaining intact pieces each decade. Use these models to predict the number of intact pieces after $n$ decades.
items.stem: Which statement correctly compares the two collections for whole numbers of decades $n$ from 0 to 25?
choices: Q has more pieces than P in every decade from 0 through 25.
Q has fewer pieces than P in every decade from 3 through 25.
Q has fewer pieces than P in every decade from 3 through 20 only.
Q has fewer pieces than P in every decade from 3 through 19 only.
items.explanation: $P(n) = 600 - 30n$ until it reaches 0 at $n = 20$, and $Q(n) = 900(0.8)^n$. At $n = 2$, $Q = 576 > 540$. At $n = 3$, $Q = 460.8 < 510$, and Q stays below P through $n = 19$, where $Q \approx 13.0 < 30$. At $n = 20$, P is 0, but exponential decay never reaches 0 ($Q \approx 10.4$), so Q has more again from decade 20 through 25.

A.why: You judged from the start, where Q has 300 more pieces. Q loses 180 pieces in the first decade, though, and it falls below P by decade 3.

B.why: You found the first switch correctly but missed the second one. P's linear loss takes it to exactly 0 at decade 20. Q only shrinks by a factor each decade, so it stays above 0 and passes P again.

C.why: You found that P reaches 0 at $n = 20$ and stopped the interval there. In decade 20 itself, P has 0 pieces and Q has about 10, so Q is already ahead in that decade.

items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus: A folklorist tracks two tales beginning in 1900. Each decade, the archive for Tale A gains new recorded variants equal to 40% of the number it held in 1900. Each decade, 40% of the people who could tell Tale B at the start of that decade stop telling it.
items.stem: Which of the following best describes how the number of recorded variants of Tale A and the number of tellers of Tale B change over time?
choices: A: increasing exponential; B: decreasing exponential
A: increasing linear; B: decreasing linear
A: increasing exponential; B: decreasing linear
A: increasing linear; B: decreasing exponential
items.explanation: For Tale A, 40% of the 1900 total is a fixed number, so the archive gains the same number of variants every decade. That makes A increasing linear. For Tale B, 40% of the tellers at the start of each decade changes as that number changes. Multiplying by 0.6 each decade makes B decreasing exponential.

B.why: You read both rules as percents of the 1900 values because both say 40%. B's percent is of the tellers at the start of each decade, so B is multiplied by 0.6 each decade.

C.why: You switched the two rules. A's 40% is taken of a fixed starting amount, which makes it linear. B's is taken of a changing amount, which makes it exponential.

items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus: In a pest-control trial, the number of aphids on a test plot $w$ weeks after the trial begins is modeled by $a(w) = 5(2)^w$, and the number of ladybugs released on the plot is modeled by $\ell(w) = 500 + 60w$.
items.stem: What is the least whole number of weeks $w$ for which $a(w) > \ell(w)$?
items.explanation: Test whole values. At $w = 7$, $a = 640$ and $\ell = 920$. At $w = 8$, $a = 1{,}280$ and $\ell = 980$. So the aphids first outnumber the ladybugs in week 8. You can also graph both functions in Desmos and find where they intersect, between 7 and 8.

A.why: You compared only the first weeks. The ladybugs start at 500 and gain 60 a week, while the aphids gain only 5 in week 1. But exponential growth always passes linear growth eventually.

B.why: You found when the aphids' weekly increase passes the ladybugs'. From week 4 to week 5 the aphids gain 80, which is more than 60. Growing faster doesn't make them more numerous yet. In week 4 there are only 80 aphids against 740 ladybugs.

D.why: You divided both sides by 5 but divided only the 500. That gave $2^w > 100 + 60w$ instead of $2^w > 100 + 12w$, which pushed the crossover too late.

items.subtype_name: Colon: complete clause, then the explanation or example
items.stimulus: In the 1990s, field linguists began recording the last fluent speakers of a small language spoken in the Andean highlands. As they transcribed hours of conversation, the researchers noticed one grammatical feature that set the language apart from its neighbors______ a set of verb endings that marked whether the speaker had personally witnessed the event being described.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words before the blank form a complete sentence that points forward to "one grammatical feature" without naming it. The words after the blank are a noun phrase that names that feature. A colon is the right mark to join a complete sentence to a phrase that explains or specifies it.

B.why: You chose the semicolon because it looks formal. A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, but "a set of verb endings..." has no main verb. It is only a noun phrase.

C.why: Adding "it was" turns the second part into a complete sentence, so a bare comma now joins two complete sentences. That is a comma splice.

D.why: A period makes "A set of verb endings that marked..." its own sentence, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

Art historian Noriko Ashdown, however, studying a set of Edo-period landscapes, argued that their most admired feature—the soft, graded blues of sky and water—owed its existence to someone far less visible ______ printer who, working without a signature, wiped each inked block by hand to produce the fading gradient known as bokashi.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Start with the words before the blank: "Art historian Noriko Ashdown... argued that their most admired feature... owed its existence to someone far less visible." That is a complete sentence, and it ends by pointing forward to an unnamed "someone." Next, look at what comes after the blank: "the printer who... wiped each inked block by hand." It contains the verb "wiped," but that verb sits inside a "who" clause, so the whole thing is a noun phrase that names the "someone." A complete sentence followed by a phrase that identifies what it set up calls for a colon.

A.why: You picked the semicolon because it looks formal. A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and "the printer who... wiped each inked block" is only a noun phrase with a relative clause attached. The verb "wiped" belongs to "who," so it can't make the phrase a sentence.

C.why: The verb "wiped" probably made the second part look like a sentence. Because it belongs to the relative clause beginning with "who," "The printer who... wiped each inked block by hand" has no main verb and would stand as a fragment after the period.

D.why: Adding "it was" turns the second part into a complete sentence, so a comma now joins two complete sentences. That is a comma splice. You need a colon here, with no new subject and verb added.

items.subtype_name: Colon: complete clause, then the explanation or example
items.stimulus: Early-twentieth-century researchers studying pellagra, a disease caused by a shortage of niacin, faced a puzzle. Poor communities in the American South that lived largely on corn were hit hard, yet in Mexico, where corn was eaten at nearly every meal, the disease was rare. The difference lay in a step that Mexican cooks had performed for ______ the kernels in limewater, a treatment that frees the niacin locked inside them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: "The difference lay in a step that Mexican cooks had performed for centuries" is complete, and it ends on a step it hasn't named yet. What follows names the step. It's a gerund phrase, "soaking the kernels in limewater," followed by an appositive. The only finite verb, "frees," sits inside the relative clause "that frees the niacin." A colon is the mark that delivers what the clause promised.

A.why: "They were soaking..." is a complete sentence, so a bare comma between it and the first clause makes a comma splice. "They" also has no clear referent.

B.why: "Soaking the kernels in limewater, a treatment that frees the niacin..." has no main verb, because "frees" belongs to the relative clause. A period leaves it standing as a fragment.

C.why: You read the verb "frees" as the main verb of a second clause and chose a semicolon because it looks formal. The words after the blank are a phrase, and a semicolon needs a complete clause on both sides.

items.stimulus: Fossil leaves from an Eocene lakebed in Wyoming have given paleobotanists an unexpected record of ancient air. Each leaf preserves a feature that shifts with the air's carbon dioxide ______ density of stomata—the tiny pores through which a plant takes in gas—on its underside, a figure that falls as carbon dioxide rises.

items.explanation: "Each leaf preserves a feature that shifts with the air's carbon dioxide level" is complete, and the noun phrase after the blank names the feature. Normally a colon or a single dash would both work here. But the explanation already contains a pair of dashes around "the tiny pores through which a plant takes in gas." Only the colon introduces the explanation and leaves that pair intact.

bound by one rule in particular: a cornice line

items.subtype_name: Add or subtract the equations to target one value
items.stimulus:
A civil engineer checking a pedestrian bridge models the forces, in kilonewtons, on two support members, $x$ and $y$, with this system:

$x + 4y = 30$
$x - 4y = 6$
items.stem: The solution to the given system of equations is $(x, y)$. What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: The $y$-terms have opposite coefficients, so add the equations as they stand: $(x + 4y) + (x - 4y) = 30 + 6$, which gives $2x = 36$. Divide by 2 to get $x = 18$. You never need to find $y$.

A.why: This is the value of $y$. You solved the whole system and then reported the other variable instead of $x$.

B.why: You subtracted the constants ($30 - 6 = 24$) when you should have added them, then divided by 2. Subtracting the equations cancels $x$, not $y$, so this number isn't $x$.

D.why: This is $2x$, the result of adding the equations. You stopped before dividing by 2.

items.stimulus:
An urban planner uses the system below to compare costs, in millions of dollars, for two kinds of street upgrades, $x$ and $y$:

$3x + 2y = 24$
$2x + y = 14$
items.stem: The solution to the given system of equations is $(x, y)$. What is the value of $x + y$?
items.explanation: The target is $x + y$, so check what subtracting does. Subtract the second equation from the first: $(3x + 2y) - (2x + y) = 24 - 14$, which gives $x + y = 10$ in one step.

A.why: This is the value of $x$ alone. You solved the system but didn't go on to find $x + y$, which the question asks for.

B.why: This is the value of $y$ alone. You reported one variable instead of the sum $x + y$.

D.why: You added the equations, which gives $5x + 3y = 38$, and took 38 as the answer. Adding doesn't produce $x + y$. Subtracting does.

items.stem:

$3x + y = 11$

$x - y = 1$

Add them together. The $y$-terms cancel. What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Adding left side to left side and right side to right side gives $(3x + x) + (y - y) = 11 + 1$, so $4x = 12$ and $x = 3$. You never need $y$. $x - 2y = 3$
items.stem: The solution to the given system of equations is $(x, y)$. Which of the following must be true?
items.explanation: The $y$-terms have opposite coefficients, $+2y$ and $-2y$. Add the equations as they stand and $y$ cancels: $4x = 44$, so $x = 11$. Only this statement has to be true.

A.why: You solved the whole system and then gave $y$'s value to $x$. Once $x = 11$, the second equation gives $y = 4$. So 4 counts the compound words, not the borrowed words.

C.why: You added the equations to get $4x = 44$ and stopped. 44 is $4x$. You still have to divide by 4.

D.why: You put $x = 11$ into $x - 2y = 3$ and got $2y = 8$, then forgot to divide by 2. The number of compound words is $y = 4$.

items.stimulus:
A contractor pays $x$ dollars for each day of regular shift work and $y$ dollars for each day of training. One worker's pay over two pay periods is described by the system below.

$5x + 3y = 710$
$3x + 2y = 440$
items.stem: The solution to the given system of equations is $(x, y)$. Which of the following must be true?
items.explanation: Before solving, check what subtracting gives. Take the second equation from the first: $(5x - 3x) + (3y - 2y) = 710 - 440$, which is $2x + y = 270$. That one subtraction tests the claim directly.

A.why: You subtracted the equations and got the sign of the $y$-term wrong. $3y - 2y$ is $+y$, not $-y$. In fact $2x - y = 130$.

B.why: You solved the whole system and then gave $y$'s value to $x$. The solution is $x = 100$ and $y = 70$, so 70 is the daily training rate, not the regular rate.

D.why: You added the equations when you needed to subtract them. Adding gives $8x + 5y = 1150$, which is not $2x + y$. Pairing 1150 with $2x + y$ gives a false statement.

items.subtype_name: Add or subtract the equations to target one value
items.stimulus: A hydrologist fills a test basin using two inflow pipes, each with a constant flow rate. Running pipe A for 5 hours and pipe B for 2 hours delivers $P$ liters. items.stem: Which expression represents the combined flow rate, in liters per hour, of pipe A and pipe B running together?
items.explanation: The combined rate is $x + y$. Add the two equations as they are: $8x + 8y = P + Q$. Divide by 8 and you get $x + y = \frac{P+Q}{8}$. You never need $x$ or $y$ on its own.

D.why: You divided the total liters by all the hours combined ($5 + 2 + 3 + 6 = 16$). After adding the equations, the coefficient on $x + y$ is 8, so 8 is the number to divide by.

items.stem: The solution to the given system of equations is $(x, y)$. What is the value of $y^2 - x^2$?
items.explanation: Write $y^2 - x^2$ as $(y + x)(y - x)$. You can get each factor in one step. Adding the equations gives $10x + 10y = 200$, so $x + y = 20$. Subtracting the first equation from the second gives $-4x + 4y = 16$, so $y - x = 4$. That makes $y^2 - x^2 = (20)(4) = 80$. You never have to find $x$ or $y$ on their own (they are 8 and 12).

A.why: You subtracted in the wrong order, second equation from the first, and got $x - y = -4$. Then you used that as the $y - x$ factor. Here $y - x = 4$, so the sign of your product came out wrong.

B.why: You added the equations and stopped at $x + y = 20$. That is only one factor of $y^2 - x^2 = (y + x)(y - x)$. You still need to multiply by $y - x = 4$.

D.why: You solved the whole system ($x = 8$, $y = 12$) and gave $y^2 = 144$. You forgot to subtract $x^2 = 64$.

items.subtype_name: Expanded circle equation: complete the square
items.stimulus:

items.explanation: Group the x terms and the y terms, then complete the square. Half of −6 is −3, and (−3)² = 9. Half of 4 is 2, and 2² = 4. Add 9 and 4 to both sides: $(x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 12 + 9 + 4 = 25$. Since $r^2 = 25$, the radius is 5.

C.why: You completed the square correctly, but 25 is $r^2$, not r. The radius is the square root, 5.

D.why: You added 9 and 4 to the left side only, so you took $r^2 = 12$ and $r = 2\sqrt{3}$. Whatever you add to complete the square on the left has to be added to the right side too.

items.stimulus: Paleobotanists working at a 50-million-year-old lakebed deposit in central Montana have catalogued an unusually varied flora. items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three finds, and the first two are already separated by a semicolon after "extinct." Each item has its own internal comma: "dawn redwood, a conifer...", "walnut relative, which..." and "palms, a group...". A list whose items contain commas needs semicolons between the items, so the blank must use the same semicolon the sentence has already used.

A.why: You treated the blank as the start of an explanation. A colon there would announce that the palm pollen explains the walnut seeds, and "and" can't follow a colon in a series. The blank only separates two items in the same list.

B.why: You ended the sentence at the blank. That leaves "And pollen from palms, a group now restricted to far warmer latitudes" standing alone, but it has no verb, so it's a fragment. It's the third item of the list and has to stay in the sentence.

D.why: You decided from the nearby words alone. The comma before "which" made a comma at the blank look natural. But the sentence already separates its items with a semicolon after "extinct." Using a comma here mixes separators, and the reader can no longer tell where the second item ends.

D.why: You multiplied by $3^3 = 27$, which is the cubic conversion for volume. Area needs the factor squared, not cubed.

items.stimulus: An ecologist monitoring a farm pond finds that a floating mat of duckweed is expanding at a constant rate of $0.45$ square meters per day. ($1$ meter $= 100$ centimeters and $1$ day $= 24$ hours.)
items.stem: At this rate, by how many square centimeters does the mat's area increase each hour?
items.explanation: Make both changes inside one chain and check that the units cancel. Square meters become square centimeters, so you apply the linear factor twice: $1\text{ m}^2 = (100\text{ cm})^2 = 10{,}000\text{ cm}^2$. Students commonly get these wrong answers: 1.875 (using 100 instead of 10,000 for the area), 4500 (converting the area but leaving the rate per day), 108000 (multiplying by 24 instead of dividing).

items.explanation: Only the time part of the unit changes, so the kilometers stay as they are. $5.4 \text{ km/s} \times \frac{3{,}600 \text{ s}}{1 \text{ h}} = 19{,}440$ km/h. The seconds cancel and you are left with kilometers per hour.

A.why: You divided by 3,600 when you should have multiplied, so the conversion factor was flipped. Write the units down: the seconds then fail to cancel.

B.why: Multiplying by 60 gives kilometers per minute, which is halfway there. You still need to multiply by 60 again to get from minutes to hours.

D.why: You converted both parts of the rate and also changed kilometers to meters. The question keeps kilometers, so only the time part should change.

items.subtype_name: Converting rates and squared/cubed units
items.stimulus: During a breeding-season survey of a salt-marsh tern colony, an ornithologist found an average density of 0.04 nests per square foot.
items.stem: Which of the following is closest to the average number of nests per square yard in the colony? (1 yard = 3 feet)
items.explanation: A square yard is $3^2 = 9$ square feet, so it holds 9 times as many nests as a square foot: $0.04 \times 9 = 0.36$ nests per square yard. You can check with units: $\frac{0.04 \text{ nests}}{1 \text{ ft}^2} \times \frac{9 \text{ ft}^2}{1 \text{ yd}^2}$, and the square feet cancel.

A.why: You divided by 9 instead of multiplying. Square yards are in the denominator, so a larger area unit means more nests per unit, not fewer.

B.why: You divided by the linear factor 3, so you made two errors: the factor is flipped, and it was used once when it should have been squared.

C.why: You multiplied by 3 only once. A square yard is 9 square feet, so the linear factor has to be squared. This is the subtype's main trap.

items.explanation: The shoot count stays the same. Only the "per square meter" part changes. One square meter is $100 \times 100 = 100^2$ square centimeters, so the same 1,200 shoots are spread over $100^2$ times as many units. That gives $\frac{1{,}200}{100^2}$ shoots per square centimeter.

A.why: You used the linear factor only once. The density is per square meter, so the factor of 100 has to be squared.

C.why: You multiplied by the conversion factor when you should have divided by it. A square centimeter is much smaller than a square meter, so it holds far fewer shoots, not more.

D.why: You cubed the factor as if the density were per cubic meter. The survey measures area on the seafloor, so the factor is squared.

items.subtype_name: Converting rates and squared/cubed units
items.stimulus: A lab is testing a thin polymer sheet. Every square centimeter of the sheet has a mass of 0.6 grams, and the mass is spread evenly across the sheet. (1 meter = 100 centimeters)
items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: A piece of the sheet measuring 1 square meter has a mass of 60 grams.
A piece of the sheet measuring 1 square meter has a mass of 6,000 grams.
A piece of the sheet measuring 1 square meter has a mass of 600,000 grams.
A piece of the sheet measuring 1 square meter has a mass of 0.00006 grams.
items.explanation: Only the area part of the unit changes, so you keep 'grams' as it is. A square meter is 100 cm by 100 cm, so $1\text{ m}^2 = 100^2 = 10{,}000\text{ cm}^2$. That gives $0.6 \tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^2} \times 10{,}000 \tfrac{\text{cm}^2}{\text{m}^2} = 6{,}000 \tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{m}^2}$.

A.why: This is the trap for this kind of question. You multiplied by the linear factor 100 once ($0.6 \times 100 = 60$). A square meter is 100 cm on each side, so you need to square the factor and multiply by 10,000.

C.why: You used the factor three times ($0.6 \times 100^3$), which is the conversion for cubic units. The sheet is measured in square units, so you square the factor, not cube it.

D.why: You divided by 10,000 instead of multiplying. A square meter is far bigger than a square centimeter, so it has to hold more mass, not less. If you write the units out, $\tfrac{\text{cm}^2}{\text{m}^2}$ only cancels when you multiply.

items.subtype_name: Converting rates and squared/cubed units
items.stimulus: A hospital IV pump is set to give a patient saline at a steady rate of 90 milliliters per hour.
items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The pump delivers saline at 15 milliliters per minute.
The pump delivers saline at 0.09 liters per minute.
The pump delivers saline at 1.5 milliliters per minute.
The pump delivers saline at 5,400 milliliters per minute.
items.explanation: All four choices are per minute, so only the time part of the unit has to change. Keep milliliters as they are and convert hours to minutes: $90 \tfrac{\text{mL}}{\text{hr}} \times \tfrac{1\text{ hr}}{60\text{ min}} = 1.5 \tfrac{\text{mL}}{\text{min}}$.

A.why: You read the rate as 900 mL per hour ($900 \div 60 = 15$), or slipped a decimal place. The rate given is 90 mL per hour.

B.why: You converted the part that should have stayed the same. You changed 90 mL into 0.09 L, then just relabeled 'per hour' as 'per minute' without dividing by 60. The correct rate in liters is 0.0015 L per minute.

D.why: This is the trap for this kind of question. You flipped the factor and multiplied by 60 ($90 \times 60$) when you should have divided. A minute is shorter than an hour, so less fluid goes in per minute, not more.

items.stimulus: On a hiking map, 1 centimeter represents 2 kilometers. On the map, a lake covers 7.5 square centimeters.

C.why: You cubed the factor ($7.5 \times 2^3$), which is the conversion for volume. An area uses the factor twice, not three times.

items.subtype_name: Converting rates and squared/cubed units
items.stem: A stream gauge records a steady discharge of 18 cubic feet of water per second. What is this discharge, in cubic yards per minute? (1 yard = 3 feet)
items.explanation: A cubic yard is $3^3 = 27$ cubic feet, so convert the volume with the cubed factor and the time with 60 seconds per minute: $18\ \frac{\text{ft}^3}{\text{s}} \times \frac{1\ \text{yd}^3}{27\ \text{ft}^3} \times \frac{60\ \text{s}}{1\ \text{min}} = \frac{18 \times 60}{27} = 40$ cubic yards per minute. Cubic feet and seconds both cancel, and only cubic yards per minute are left.

A.why: You converted cubic feet to cubic yards correctly ($18 \div 27 \approx 0.67$), but you stopped there. That number is still per second, and the question asks for per minute.

C.why: You divided by 3 instead of 27, using the linear factor once for a cubic unit: $18 \div 3 \times 60 = 360$. A cubic yard is $3 \times 3 \times 3$ cubic feet, so the factor has to be cubed.

D.why: You multiplied by 27 where you should have divided: $18 \times 27 \times 60$. A cubic yard is bigger than a cubic foot, so the same flow is fewer cubic yards. Writing the units down would have shown the cubic feet not cancelling.

items.stimulus: A printmaker's press bed has an area of 3 square feet. The linoleum block she plans to carve has an area of 360 square inches.
items.stem: How many more square inches of area does the press bed have than the linoleum block? (1 foot = 12 inches)

items.stimulus: A sports scientist records sprinter A's top speed as 8 meters per second and sprinter B's top speed as 36 kilometers per hour.

items.stimulus: An orbiting telescope's infrared camera is cooled by two liquid-helium tanks. Tank A has a volume of 2.4 cubic meters, and tank B has a volume of 600,000 cubic centimeters.

C.why: You squared the factor when it should be cubed: $2.4 \times 100^2 = 24{,}000$, and $\frac{24{,}000}{600{,}000} = 0.04$. Cubic units need the factor three times.

items.stimulus: A pipe organ's blower supplies air at a rate of 25 cubic feet per minute, but 10% of that air is lost through leaks before it reaches the pipes. While it sounds, each pipe in one rank of the organ uses 9 cubic inches of air per second. (1 foot = 12 inches)

items.stimulus: A printmaker inks a rectangular plate that measures 20 inches by 34 inches. items.stimulus: A seismologist sorts recorded earthquakes into bands by magnitude. An earthquake goes in the moderate band if its magnitude is at least 5.0 but less than 6.0.

D.why: You put the bounds the wrong way round. 6.0 is the upper limit, not the lower one, and no number can be at least 6.0 and also less than 5.0.

items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: A survey telescope's image archive held 1,200 images at the start of an observing run. On each night of the run, the telescope adds a minimum of 80 images and a maximum of 150 images to the archive. Let $T$ be the total number of images in the archive after 10 nights of the run.
items.stem: Which inequality represents this situation?
items.explanation: Over 10 nights the telescope adds at least $10(80) = 800$ and at most $10(150) = 1{,}500$ images. You add the starting 1,200 images to both ends: $1{,}200 + 800 = 2{,}000$ and $1{,}200 + 1{,}500 = 2{,}700$. 'Minimum' and 'maximum' both include their endpoints, so $2{,}000 \le T \le 2{,}700$.

D.why: You added one night's range to the starting 1,200 and never multiplied by the 10 nights. That gives the archive size after one night, not after ten.

items.stimulus: A polymer strip that is 50 millimeters long is stretched in a tensile test. To pass, the strip must stretch to more than 12 percent beyond its original length but no more than 30 percent beyond its original length. Let $L$ be the stretched length, in millimeters, of a strip that passes.
items.stem: Which inequality represents this situation?
items.explanation: 12 percent of 50 is 6 and 30 percent of 50 is 15, so the stretched length is $50 + 6 = 56$ at the low end and $50 + 15 = 65$ at the high end. D.why: You added 12 and 30 straight to 50 as if they were millimeters. You needed to take 12 percent and 30 percent of 50 first.

items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: A score marks a passage to be played at a tempo of more than 100 beats per minute but at most 120 beats per minute. The passage contains 360 beats.
items.stem: Which inequality represents the possible time $m$, in minutes, needed to play the passage?
items.explanation: Time is $m = \frac{360}{b}$, where $b$ is the tempo, so a faster tempo means a shorter time. The fastest allowed tempo, 120, is included and gives the shortest time, $\frac{360}{120} = 3$, so 3 is included. The slower end is strict ($b > 100$), so the time stays below $\frac{360}{100} = 3.6$, and 3.6 is excluded. The result is $3 \le m < 3.6$.

A.why: You kept each sign where it was in the tempo range. Dividing into 360 reverses the order, so the strict tempo bound (100) becomes the upper time bound (3.6). The strict sign belongs at the upper end.

C.why: You found both endpoints but made both inclusive. The tempo must be strictly more than 100, so a time of exactly 3.6 minutes is not possible.

D.why: This is the tempo range in beats per minute, not the time in minutes. You never converted beats into playing time.

'More than 600' is strict and 'no more than 900' is inclusive, so $600 < 200 + 20n \le 900$. Subtract 200 from all three parts to get $400 < 20n \le 700$, then divide by 20: $20 < n \le 35$.

A.why: You used the starting 240 trout and forgot the 40 that were removed. That gives $600 < 240 + 20n \le 900$, so $18 < n \le 33$. The removal happens before the deliveries, so the base is 200.

B.why: Your algebra is right, but you made the lower end inclusive. 'More than 600' is strict, so $n = 20$, which gives exactly 600 trout, does not fit. The left end needs $<$.

D.why: You divided the bounds 600 and 900 by 20 but never subtracted the 200 trout already in the pond. $600 < 20n \le 900$ counts only the delivered fish, not the total the pond holds.

items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: A warehouse employee works 5 shifts each week. Every shift lasts at least 6 hours but less than 9 hours, and the employee is paid $22 per hour. A $40 transit fee is deducted from each week's pay. Let $P$ be the employee's weekly pay after the deduction, in dollars.
items.stem: Which inequality represents this situation?
items.explanation: Weekly hours run from $5(6) = 30$, which is allowed, up to but not including $5(9) = 45$. Multiply by the wage to get $660 \le 22h < 990$. Then subtract the $40 fee from both ends: $620 \le P < 950$. The upper end stays strict because no shift can reach 9 hours.

B.why: You scaled the range correctly, but you used ≤ at the top. 'Less than 9 hours' is strict, so the weekly pay can never actually reach $950.

C.why: You added the $40 transit fee to both ends. It is a deduction, so it has to be subtracted.

D.why: You subtracted the $40 fee from the lower end only. Any amount taken off the pay has to come off both ends of the range.

items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: An excavation trench is already 40 centimeters deep. Each day, the team deepens it by at least 12 centimeters but no more than 15 centimeters. A buried floor lies 160 centimeters below the surface. Let $R$ be the distance, in centimeters, between the trench bottom and the floor after 6 more days of digging.
items.stem: Which inequality represents the possible values of $R$?
items.explanation: After 6 days the trench is between $40 + 6(12) = 112$ and $40 + 6(15) = 130$ centimeters deep. The distance left is $160$ minus the depth, so the greatest depth gives the smallest $R$: $160 - 130 = 30$ and $160 - 112 = 48$. That gives $30 \le R \le 48$.

A.why: This is the range for the trench's total depth after 6 days. The question asks how much distance is left before the floor.

C.why: You left out the 40 centimeters that had already been dug. The starting depth has to be counted at both ends.

D.why: You took the starting 40 centimeters off one end of the range but not the other. A starting amount applies to both ends.

items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: A linguist records a narrator for 12 minutes. The recording includes pauses totaling 90 seconds, during which no syllables are spoken. While speaking, the narrator's rate is more than 150 syllables per minute but no more than 190 syllables per minute.
items.stem: Which of the following could be the total number of syllables the narrator spoke during the recording?
items.explanation: The narrator speaks for $12 - 1.5 = 10.5$ minutes. Total syllables $S$ satisfy $10.5(150) < S \le 10.5(190)$, which is $1{,}575 < S \le 1{,}995$. Only 1,890 falls in that range.

D.why: You used all 12 minutes as speaking time, which gives $1{,}800 < S \le 2{,}280$. Subtract the 90 seconds of pauses first. Then the maximum is 1,995.

items.stimulus: A coach estimates an athlete's maximum heart rate as $220$ minus the athlete's age, in beats per minute. A 20-year-old's training zone is at least 60% but less than 75% of this maximum. The coach counts the athlete's heartbeats for 15 seconds. Let $c$ be a count that lies in the zone.
items.stem: Which inequality represents this situation?
items.explanation: The maximum heart rate is $220 - 20 = 200$ beats per minute. The zone is $0.60(200) \le h < 0.75(200)$, which is $120 \le h < 150$ beats per minute. A 15-second count is a quarter of that, so $30 \le c < 37.5$. The strictness at each end stays the same.

D.why: You used 220 as the maximum heart rate and never subtracted the athlete's age of 20.

items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: In a stretch of ocean, the water temperature $T$, in degrees Celsius, at a depth of $d$ meters is modeled by $T = 28 - 0.05d$. A species of sponge survives only where the temperature is at least $13^{\circ}\text{C}$ but below $18^{\circ}\text{C}$.
items.stem: Which inequality represents all depths $d$ at which this species can live?
items.explanation: Start with $13 \le 28 - 0.05d < 18$. Subtract 28 to get $-15 \le -0.05d < -10$. Divide by $-0.05$, which flips both signs: $300 \ge d > 200$. Read left to right, that is $200 < d \le 300$. Temperature 18 is excluded, and it matches depth 200, so the strict end is now on the left.

A.why: You found the right endpoints but left the strictness where it was in the temperature inequality. Dividing by a negative swaps the ends, so the strict sign moves to the 200 end.

C.why: You divided 13 and 18 by 0.05 without using the surface temperature of 28 in the model.

D.why: You added 28 to each bound instead of subtracting it. To isolate the $d$ term, subtract 28 from all three parts.
