items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: A dance piece has 96 measures with 3 beats in each measure. In performance, the first 32 measures are played twice. The ensemble's tempo is at least 64 but fewer than 96 beats per minute. Let $t$ be the length of a performance, in minutes.
items.stem: Which inequality represents this situation?
items.explanation: With the repeat, the performance has $96 + 32 = 128$ measures, or $128 \times 3 = 384$ beats. Time is beats divided by tempo, so a faster tempo gives a shorter performance. The tempo can't reach 96, so $t > 384/96 = 4$. A tempo of 64 is allowed, so $t \le 384/64 = 6$. That gives $4 < t \le 6$.

A.why: You kept the strictness in the same place as in the tempo range. Time goes down as tempo goes up, so the excluded tempo of 96 gives the excluded time of 4, on the left.

C.why: You used 96 measures and left out the 32 repeated measures. The performance actually has 384 beats, not 288.

D.why: You treated each measure as one beat. Multiply the 128 measures by 3 beats per measure before you divide by the tempo.

items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: To test a serum sample with antibody concentration $c$ units per milliliter, a technician mixes 1 part serum with 7 parts buffer. The assay adds a constant background of 3 units per milliliter to the diluted concentration. A reading is valid only if it is at least 15 but less than 60 units per milliliter.
items.stem: Which inequality represents the possible values of $c$?
items.explanation: One part in $1 + 7 = 8$ total parts is serum, so the reading is $\tfrac{c}{8} + 3$. Solve $15 \le \tfrac{c}{8} + 3 < 60$. Subtract 3 to get $12 \le \tfrac{c}{8} < 57$, then multiply by 8: $96 \le c < 456$.

A.why: You scaled the range correctly but changed the upper end to ≤. 'Less than 60' is strict, so $c$ can't equal 456.

B.why: You used 7 as the dilution factor. Mixing 1 part serum with 7 parts buffer makes 8 parts in total, so the serum is diluted by a factor of 8.

D.why: You multiplied by 8 before dealing with the background and then subtracted 3. The background is added after dilution, so remove it first and then multiply.

items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: A clinic starts Monday with 2,400 vaccine doses and receives no new supply that week. On each day from Monday through Saturday, it gives more than 250 doses but no more than 340 doses.
items.stem: Which of the following could be the number of doses remaining at the end of Saturday?
items.explanation: Monday through Saturday is 6 days. The clinic gives out more than $6(250) = 1{,}500$ doses and no more than $6(340) = 2{,}040$. The doses remaining are $2{,}400$ minus that number, so $2{,}400 - 2{,}040 \le R < 2{,}400 - 1{,}500$, which is $360 \le R < 900$. 360 is possible: it is what's left if the clinic gives 340 doses every day.

C.why: You kept 'more than 250' as the strict end. Subtracting from 2,400 reverses the order, so 900 is the excluded endpoint and 360 is included.

D.why: 1,800 is a possible number of doses given out. The question asks how many doses are left.

A.why: 3 is the median (and the mode) of this data. The 10th and 11th values in order both fall in the '3' row. The question asked for the mean, which takes every value into account.

C.why: You averaged the five numbers in the first column, $\frac{2+3+4+5+6}{5} = 4$, and ignored how many weeks each one happened. Rows with more weeks have to count more, so you need to weight each value by its frequency.

D.why: You found the weighted total of 69 correctly, then divided by 5, the number of rows in the table. The mean divides by the number of weeks, which is 20.

D.why: You took the 5th value in the order recorded instead of sorting first. A median has to come from the sorted list, and $58$ is actually the largest corrected value.

items.stimulus: Many coaches believe that static stretching before a sprint loosens the muscles and so makes athletes faster. In a recent trial with forty collegiate sprinters, the first half of that belief held up: after holding stretches for ninety seconds, the athletes rated their legs as markedly looser than on days when they skipped stretching. ______ their times over 60 meters were, on average, a few hundredths of a second slower on the days they stretched.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The coaches' belief has two parts: stretching loosens muscles, and looser muscles mean more speed. The sentence before the blank confirms only the first part. The sentence after reports the opposite of what that would lead you to expect, because the athletes felt looser and ran slower. You need a word that sets a result against what the previous sentence led you to expect, and 'Even so' does exactly that.

A.why: You saw that both sentences are about the same stretching days and assumed the second follows from the first. Feeling looser did not cause slower times. The slower times are the surprise, and 'For this reason' claims a cause the passage never gives.

B.why: You correctly saw that you needed a concession word, then chose one that belongs in the wrong spot. 'Granted' concedes a point that a later 'but' will push back on. Here the sentence after the blank is already the pushback, and no reversal follows it.

D.why: You read 'the first half of that belief held up' and expected more confirmation. 'Likewise' says the next finding points the same way, but slower times work against the belief instead of supporting it.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: Engineers designing a lighter bicycle frame hoped that packing more ceramic particles into an aluminum alloy would keep making it stronger. Early results were encouraging: at every concentration from 5 to 15 percent by volume, the reinforced alloy was both stiffer and stronger than plain aluminum. ______ at 20 percent, the reinforced alloy proved weaker than the plain metal, because the particles clumped together and cracks began at the clumps.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The engineers hoped that more particles would always mean more strength, and the 5-15 percent results supported that hope. At 20 percent the alloy became weaker than plain aluminum, which reverses the pattern. 'Yet' marks that reversal.

A.why: You treated '20 percent' as a closer look at the range you had just read. That range ended at 15 percent, and the new sentence reports a different result. 'Specifically' only restates the previous claim more precisely.

B.why: Both sentences report test results at a given concentration, so you assumed they point the same way. The first reports gains and the second reports a loss, so 'Similarly' sends the logic in the wrong direction.

C.why: The passage explains a mechanism (clumping, then cracking), so you reached for a cause word. That cause sits inside the second sentence. The encouraging results before the blank did not produce the weakness.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: Fossil plants have proved useful to scientists in many ways: they let researchers map vanished forests, date layers of volcanic ash, and trace how early farming spread across Europe. ______ the most consequential use of the fossil plant record may be one its first collectors never imagined: estimating past levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide from the density of tiny breathing pores, called stomata, on fossil leaves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence lists several respected uses. The second ranks a different use above all of them, one nobody expected, so it pivots against the list instead of adding to it. 'Still' marks that turn: despite all those uses, the most important one lies elsewhere.

A.why: You saw 'many ways' and expected the next sentence to give one of them. The carbon dioxide use is not one of the listed uses. It is ranked above them and described as unforeseen, so it is not a sample drawn from that group.

C.why: You assumed that a long list of uses leads to the conclusion that follows. Nothing in the list causes the stomata method to be the most important one. 'Accordingly' invents a cause.

D.why: This is the list trap. Both sentences are about uses of fossils, so you read the second as one more item. Because it ranks a never-imagined use above all the others, the second sentence turns against the list, which 'Similarly' cannot express.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: Because school handwashing campaigns target the germs that spread through shared food and surfaces, many health officials assume their main payoff is fewer cases of stomach illness. ______ when researchers tracked absences in 60 elementary schools for two years, absences from stomach illness fell only slightly; the much larger drop, nearly a third, came from colds and flu.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives an assumption, and the second gives the measured reality that corrects it. When a mistaken belief is followed by the true finding, 'In fact' is the natural correction word.

B.why: You saw that a correction was coming and chose a concession word, but 'Admittedly' introduces a point the writer grants before arguing against it. The study finding is the writer's main point, not something conceded.

C.why: The 'Because' in the first sentence pulled you toward a cause word. The officials' assumption did not cause the study's results, and the results contradict the assumption.

D.why: A study with specific numbers looks like an illustration, so you chose an example word. The study does not illustrate the officials' assumption. It overturns it.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: The linguist who first documented the language in the 1970s recommended writing it in the Latin alphabet, arguing that its sounds mapped neatly onto Spanish spelling. ______ the community's own writing committee, meeting a decade later, adopted a syllabary devised by a local schoolteacher, judging that it captured distinctions in vowel length that Spanish letters ignored.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives one person's recommendation, and the second reports that the community chose something else. Advice followed by a different choice is a contrast, and 'However' marks it.

A.why: You assumed the committee acted on the linguist's advice because the sentences come one after the other. The committee rejected the Latin alphabet, so 'Accordingly' says the opposite of what happened.

B.why: You may have grouped 'Of course' with the concession words, but it signals that what follows was obvious or expected. The committee's choice went against the expert's advice, so it was not the expected outcome.

D.why: 'Namely' restates the previous idea more precisely. The syllabary is not a sharper version of the linguist's recommendation. It replaces that recommendation.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: A vaccine is tested in three stages: first for safety in a few dozen volunteers, then for immune response in a few hundred, and lastly for protection in thousands. A nasal flu vaccine developed in 2021 cleared the first two stages easily, producing antibody levels higher than those of any injected vaccine it was compared with. ______ in the final stage, it protected volunteers no better than a placebo did.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: Record antibody levels lead you to expect strong protection. The final stage showed no protection at all. 'Nonetheless' marks a result that comes despite what came before.

A.why: Nothing about strong early results predicts failure. 'Predictably' calls the outcome expected when the passage presents it as a reversal.

C.why: The three-stage frame primed you for a sequence word, and 'Finally' fits the order of stages. It only marks the next step, though, and misses that the result goes against the first two stages.

D.why: You linked the high antibody levels to the final result as if one produced the other. 'Therefore' claims the early success caused the failure, and the passage makes no such link.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: The nineteenth-century luthier Ilse Varga built more than four hundred violins, trained a generation of apprentices across Central Europe, and wrote a treatise on varnish that restorers still consult. ______ the achievement she herself ranked highest was a modest one: a set of graded finger exercises that let village schoolchildren begin string lessons without a private teacher.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence lists grand achievements. The second says Varga valued a modest piece of work above all of them, which turns against the list. 'That said' marks that turn.

A.why: The list of achievements made you expect one of them next. The finger exercises are not among the listed achievements, and the sentence ranks them above everything listed.

B.why: You assumed that a long list of successes leads to a conclusion. Her violins and treatise do not explain why she valued the exercises most, so 'Thus' invents a cause.

C.why: This is the list trap. 'Indeed' intensifies the previous point, as if the next sentence named an even grander success. The sentence instead calls her favourite achievement 'modest' and ranks it above the impressive list, so it turns against the list.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: Seismologists once assumed that, during any earthquake, the buildings nearest the epicenter would always shake hardest. ______ in 1985, an earthquake centered roughly 350 kilometers from Mexico City toppled hundreds of buildings there while towns far closer to the epicenter suffered less, because the city rests on soft lakebed sediments that amplified the seismic waves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence states an old assumption. The second gives a real event that disproves it: distant buildings fell while nearer towns did better. When a mistaken belief is followed by what actually happened, 'In reality' is the correction word.

B.why: You saw a single dated event and treated it as an illustration. An example has to support the claim before it, and this event is a counterexample that disproves the assumption.

C.why: You noticed the 'because' and the cause-and-effect language about sediments and carried it back to the blank. The seismologists' assumption did not lead to the 1985 damage. The damage contradicts the assumption.

D.why: Both sentences are about how hard buildings shake, so you read them as moving in the same direction. 'Likewise' would need the second sentence to support the assumption, but it overturns it.

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability where you must build the given group
items.stimulus:
A city planning office recorded the zone and height of each of the 100 buildings that received new construction permits last year.

New Construction Permits by Zone and Height
Zone | 1 to 3 stories | 4 or more stories | Total
Residential | 30 | 10 | 40
Commercial | 14 | 6 | 20
Industrial | 25 | 15 | 40
Total | 69 | 31 | 100
items.stem: If one of the buildings that is not in the industrial zone is selected at random, what is the probability that the building has 4 or more stories?
items.explanation: "Not in the industrial zone" means the residential and commercial rows together. That makes your group $40 + 20 = 60$ buildings. Inside that group, $10 + 6 = 16$ buildings have 4 or more stories. The probability is $\frac{16}{60} = \frac{4}{15}$.

A.why: You used only the residential row, $\frac{10}{40}$. "Not industrial" also includes the commercial row, so you have to add both rows to build the group.

B.why: You found the right numerator, 16, but divided by all 100 buildings. The condition limits you to the 60 buildings outside the industrial zone, so 60 is the denominator.

D.why: You computed $\frac{15}{40}$ for the industrial row, which is the group the question excludes. You read "not in the industrial zone" as "in the industrial zone."

items.stimulus:
An astronomer catalogued 50 stars that are known to host planets. The table shows each star's type and its number of known planets.

Planet-Hosting Stars by Type and Number of Known Planets
Number of known planets | Single star | Binary system | Total
1 | 18 | 7 | 25
2 | 10 | 5 | 15
3 or more | 6 | 4 | 10
Total | 34 | 16 | 50
items.stem: If one of the stars with at least 2 known planets is selected at random, what is the probability that the star is part of a binary system?
items.explanation: "At least 2" includes the "2" row and the "3 or more" row, so your group is $15 + 10 = 25$ stars. Of these, $5 + 4 = 9$ are in binary systems. The probability is $\frac{9}{25}$.

B.why: You used only the "3 or more" row, $\frac{4}{10}$, so you treated "at least 2" as "more than 2." Stars with exactly 2 planets are part of the group too.

C.why: You divided the 9 binary stars by all 50 stars. The condition limits your world to the 25 stars with at least 2 planets.

D.why: You divided by the 16 binary stars, which reverses the fraction. That answers "Of the binary stars, what fraction have at least 2 planets?" The question's group is stars with at least 2 planets.

items.stimulus:
A linguist classified every word in a large sample of a language's written texts by word class and by origin. A word was counted as borrowed if it entered the language from another language, and as native otherwise. The table shows the proportion of all words in the sample that fall into each category.

Proportion of Words in Sample by Class and Origin
Word class | Borrowed | Native
Noun | 0.15 | 0.25
Verb | 0.05 | 0.20
Adjective | 0.10 | 0.25
items.stem: If one of the words that is not a verb is selected at random from the sample, what is the probability that the word is borrowed?
items.explanation: Treat the proportions as counts. Words that are not verbs are the nouns and adjectives: $0.40 + 0.35 = 0.75$. The borrowed words in that group make up $0.15 + 0.10 = 0.25$. The probability is $\frac{0.25}{0.75} = \frac{1}{3}$.

D.why: You used only the noun row, $\frac{0.15}{0.40}$. "Not a verb" also includes the adjectives, so you have to combine both rows.

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability where you must build the given group
items.stimulus: For a nutrition study, researchers prepared 4 trays of high-fiber meals and 5 trays of low-fiber meals. Each tray held 6 meals. Of the high-fiber meals, 10 contained legumes. None of the low-fiber meals contained legumes.
items.stem: If one of the high-fiber meals is selected at random, what is the probability that the meal contains legumes?
items.explanation: Build the group by multiplying trays by meals per tray: $4 \times 6 = 24$ high-fiber meals. Of these, 10 contain legumes. The probability is $\frac{10}{24} = \frac{5}{12}$.

C.why: You computed $\frac{24}{54}$, the probability that a randomly selected meal is high-fiber. That is the size of your group as a fraction of all meals, not the chance that a meal in the group contains legumes.

items.stimulus: A music festival has 40 performances, assigned to slots numbered 1 through 40. A performance features a string quartet if and only if its slot number is a multiple of 4.
items.stem: If one of the performances in a slot numbered greater than or equal to 25 is selected at random, what is the probability that the performance features a string quartet?
items.explanation: The slots numbered greater than or equal to 25 run from 25 through 40, which is $40 - 25 + 1 = 16$ slots. The multiples of 4 in that range are 28, 32, 36, and 40, so there are 4. The probability is $\frac{4}{16} = \frac{1}{4}$.

B.why: You counted only the slots from 26 through 40, which gives 15. "Greater than or equal to 25" includes slot 25, so the group has 16 slots.

D.why: You divided by the 10 quartet performances across the whole festival, which reverses the fraction. That answers "Of the quartet performances, what fraction are in slots 25 or higher?"

An ornithologist banded 84 warblers at a coastal station and recorded each bird's age class and wing length.

Warblers Banded, by Wing Length and Age Class
Wing length (mm) | Adult | Juvenile
50–54 | 6 | 14
55–59 | 10 | 12
60–64 | 18 | 6
65–69 | 16 | 2
items.stem: One bird with a wing length of at least 60 millimeters is selected at random from the birds in the table. Which of the following must be true?
choices: The probability that the bird is an adult is $\frac{17}{21}$.
The probability that the bird is an adult is $\frac{8}{9}$.
The probability that the bird is an adult is $\frac{17}{42}$.
The probability that the bird is an adult is $\frac{17}{25}$.
items.explanation: "At least 60 mm" covers two rows, 60–64 and 65–69, so first you rebuild that group: $18 + 6 + 16 + 2 = 42$ birds. The adults in that group number $18 + 16 = 34$. The probability is $\frac{34}{42} = \frac{17}{21}$.

B.why: You read "at least 60" as "more than 64" and used only the 65–69 row: $\frac{16}{18} = \frac{8}{9}$. The 60–64 row is part of the condition too, so you dropped the boundary bin.

C.why: You found the right numerator, 34 adults, but divided by all 84 birds. The condition means your denominator is the 42 birds with wing length of at least 60 mm, not the whole table.

D.why: You divided by all 50 adults: $\frac{34}{50} = \frac{17}{25}$. That is the probability an adult has a wing length of at least 60 mm, which is the reverse of what was asked.

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability where you must build the given group
items.stimulus:
A linguist surveyed speakers in a river valley. She grouped them by how many languages they speak, then recorded the share of each group that uses the regional dialect at home.

Survey of Valley Speakers
Language group | Share of all speakers | Share of group using dialect at home
Monolingual | 0.40 | 0.10
Bilingual | 0.40 | 0.30
Multilingual | 0.20 | 0.75
items.stem: One speaker who is not monolingual is selected at random from the survey. Which of the following must be true?
choices: The probability that the speaker uses the dialect at home is 0.27.
The probability that the speaker uses the dialect at home is 0.45.
The probability that the speaker uses the dialect at home is 0.10.
The probability that the speaker uses the dialect at home is 0.30.
items.explanation: "Not monolingual" means bilingual or multilingual, so the group is $0.40 + 0.20 = 0.60$ of all speakers. The dialect users inside it make up $0.40(0.30) + 0.20(0.75) = 0.12 + 0.15 = 0.27$ of all speakers. Treat these proportions as counts, since the scaling cancels: $\frac{0.27}{0.60} = 0.45$.

A.why: 0.27 is the share of all speakers who are not monolingual and use the dialect. You stopped before dividing by the 0.60 that makes up the given group.

C.why: You read "not monolingual" as "monolingual" and took that group's rate of 0.10. The condition leaves the monolingual row out.

D.why: You used only the bilingual row's rate of 0.30. "Not monolingual" also includes multilingual speakers, so you have to combine both rows, weighted by their shares.

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability where you must build the given group
items.stimulus:
A music library stores its classical recordings on shelves. Every shelf of a given genre holds the same number of discs.

Recording Archive Holdings
Genre | Shelves | Discs per shelf | Live recordings (total)
String quartet | 6 | 15 | 30
Symphony | 4 | 20 | 50
Opera | 5 | 12 | 24
items.stem: One disc that is not an opera recording is selected at random from the archive. Which of the following must be true?
choices: The probability that the disc is a live recording is $\frac{8}{23}$.
The probability that the disc is a live recording is $\frac{2}{5}$.
The probability that the disc is a live recording is $\frac{8}{17}$.
The probability that the disc is a live recording is $\frac{5}{8}$.
items.explanation: Build the given group by multiplying shelves by discs per shelf. There are $6 \times 15 = 90$ string quartet discs and $4 \times 20 = 80$ symphony discs, for 170 discs that are not opera. Of these, $30 + 50 = 80$ are live, so the probability is $\frac{80}{170} = \frac{8}{17}$.

A.why: You divided the 80 non-opera live discs by all 230 discs in the archive. The condition limits you to the 170 non-opera discs, so that is the denominator.

B.why: You worked with the opera row, $\frac{24}{60} = \frac{2}{5}$. That is the group the condition leaves out.

D.why: You used only the symphony row, $\frac{50}{80} = \frac{5}{8}$. "Not opera" also includes the string quartet discs, so you have to add both rows.

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability where you must build the given group
items.stimulus:
A sports science lab tracked 200 athletes for one season and recorded their weekly training hours and whether they had an overuse injury.

Athletes by Weekly Training Hours and Injury Status
Hours per week | Injured | Not injured
0–4 | 4 | 36
5–9 | 8 | 52
10–14 | 14 | 36
15 or more | 16 | 34
items.stem: An athlete will be selected at random. How much greater is the probability that the athlete was injured, given that the athlete trains at least 10 hours per week, than the probability that the athlete was injured, given that the athlete trains fewer than 10 hours per week?
items.explanation: Build each group yourself. At least 10 hours means the 10–14 and 15-or-more rows: $14+16=30$ injured out of $50+50=100$, so the probability is $0.30$. Fewer than 10 hours means the 0–4 and 5–9 rows: $4+8=12$ injured out of $40+60=100$, so the probability is $0.12$. The difference is $0.30-0.12=0.18$.

A.why: You divided both injury counts by the grand total of 200 instead of by each rebuilt group of 100: $\frac{30}{200}-\frac{12}{200}=0.09$. With 'given that', the group named is the whole denominator.

C.why: You used only the 15-or-more row for 'at least 10 hours' and dropped the 10–14 row, getting $\frac{16}{50}-0.12=0.20$. 'At least 10' includes the 10–14 row.

D.why: $0.30$ is the probability for the at-least-10-hours group alone. The question asks how much greater it is than the other group's probability, so you still have to subtract $0.12$.

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability where you must build the given group
items.stimulus: In a printmaking studio's archive, 40% of the prints are woodcuts, 30% are etchings, and 30% are screen prints. Of the woodcuts, 30% are signed by the artist. Of the etchings, 50% are signed, and of the screen prints, 70% are signed.
items.stem: A print will be selected at random from the archive. How much greater is the probability that the print is signed, given that it is not a woodcut, than the probability that the print is signed, given that it is a woodcut?
items.explanation: Treat the percentages as counts out of 100 prints. 'Not a woodcut' is the etchings and screen prints together, so $30+30=60$ prints. Of those, $0.5(30)+0.7(30)=15+21=36$ are signed, so the probability is $\frac{36}{60}=0.60$. For woodcuts it is $0.30$. The difference is $0.60-0.30=0.30$.

B.why: You used only the etchings for 'not a woodcut' ($0.50-0.30=0.20$). 'Not a woodcut' covers both the etchings and the screen prints.

D.why: $0.60$ is the probability for the prints that aren't woodcuts. You stopped before subtracting the woodcut probability of $0.30$.

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability where you must build the given group
items.stimulus:
A seismology network classified 130 recorded earthquakes by region and by focal depth.

Recorded Earthquakes by Region and Depth
Depth | Region 1 | Region 2 | Region 3
Shallow | 21 | 45 | 27
Deep | 9 | 5 | 23
items.stem: An earthquake will be selected at random from these records. The probability that it was deep, given that it was not in Region 2, is how many times the probability that it was deep, given that it was in Region 2?
items.explanation: 'Not in Region 2' means Regions 1 and 3 together: $30+50=80$ earthquakes, of which $9+23=32$ were deep, so the probability is $\frac{32}{80}=0.4$. In Region 2, $5$ of $50$ were deep, so the probability is $0.1$. Then $\frac{0.4}{0.1}=4$.

A.why: You used only Region 1 for 'not in Region 2': $\frac{9}{30}=0.3$, and $\frac{0.3}{0.1}=3$. The group has to include Region 3 as well.

C.why: You used only Region 3 for 'not in Region 2': $\frac{23}{50}=0.46$, and $\frac{0.46}{0.1}=4.6$. You need to add Region 1 and Region 3 together before you divide.

D.why: You divided both deep counts by the grand total of 130, so the ratio became $\frac{32}{5}=6.4$. The two groups have different sizes (80 and 50), so each count has to be divided by its own group.

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability where you must build the given group
items.stimulus:
A weather station classified each of 125 days by total rainfall, in millimeters (mm), and by whether a thunderstorm was recorded that day.

Days by Rainfall and Thunderstorm Activity
Rainfall (mm) | Thunderstorm | No thunderstorm
0 to 9 | 4 | 41
10 to 19 | 11 | 23
20 to 29 | 15 | 9
30 or more | 18 | 4
items.stem: If one of these days is selected at random, what is the probability that a thunderstorm was recorded, given that the day had at least 20 mm of rainfall?
items.explanation: The condition 'at least 20 mm' isn't a single row. It covers both the 20 to 29 row and the 30 or more row, so you have to build the group yourself: $15+9$ days plus $18+4$ days. Within that group, the days with a thunderstorm are $15+18$. The probability is $\frac{15+18}{15+18+9+4}$.

A.why: You read 'at least 20' as 'more than 29' and dropped the 20 to 29 row. 'At least 20' includes the boundary bin, so both the 20 to 29 row and the 30 or more row belong in the group.

C.why: You divided by every thunderstorm day. That answers a reversed question: of the thunderstorm days, what fraction had at least 20 mm of rain? The given group is the rainy days, so their total goes in the denominator.

D.why: You found the right numerator but divided by all 125 days. That ignores the 'given that' condition, which shrinks your world to only the days with at least 20 mm of rain.

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability where you must build the given group
items.stimulus:
An excavation team recovered 171 artifacts from four trenches at a site. The table shows the number of artifacts of each material found in each trench.

Artifacts Recovered by Trench and Material
Material | Trench A | Trench B | Trench C | Trench D
Pottery | 26 | 31 | 18 | 22
Bone | 9 | 14 | 12 | 7
Stone | 5 | 10 | 6 | 11
Total | 40 | 55 | 36 | 40
items.stem: If one of these artifacts is selected at random, what is the probability that it is pottery, given that it was not recovered from Trench B?
items.explanation: 'Not from Trench B' means Trenches A, C, and D together. No single printed total covers that group, so you add the column totals: $40+36+40$. The pottery inside that group is $26+18+22$. The probability is $\frac{26+18+22}{40+36+40}$.

A.why: You read 'not from Trench B' as 'from Trench B' and used only that column. The given group is every trench except B.

B.why: You divided by all 171 artifacts, so the condition did nothing. Once you're told the artifact isn't from Trench B, the Trench B artifacts leave the denominator.

C.why: You divided by all the pottery. That gives the probability that a piece of pottery came from somewhere other than Trench B, which swaps the denominator. The group after 'given that' is the artifacts outside Trench B, not the pottery.

items.stimulus:
A seismic network classified every earthquake it recorded in one year by magnitude and by focal depth. The table shows the proportion of all recorded earthquakes that fall in each category.

Depth | Under 4.0 | 4.0 to 4.9 | 5.0 to 5.9 | 6.0 or greater
Shallow | 0.42 | 0.18 | 0.07 | 0.03
Deep | 0.16 | 0.09 | 0.04 | 0.01
items.stem: If one of these earthquakes is selected at random, what is the probability that it was shallow, given that its magnitude was greater than or equal to 5.0?
items.explanation: 'Greater than or equal to 5.0' covers two columns: 5.0 to 5.9 and 6.0 or greater. Build that group by adding all four of its cells: $0.07+0.03+0.04+0.01$. The shallow part of the group is $0.07+0.03$. You can treat the proportions as counts, because the overall scale cancels when you divide. The probability is $\frac{0.07+0.03}{0.07+0.03+0.04+0.01}$.

A.why: You used only the 5.0 to 5.9 column. The condition covers both columns at or above 5.0, so the 6.0 or greater column belongs in both the numerator and the denominator.

B.why: You divided by the whole shallow row. That gives the probability that a shallow earthquake had magnitude 5.0 or greater, which reverses the question. The given group is the strong earthquakes, not the shallow ones.

D.why: You read 'greater than or equal to 5.0' as '6.0 or greater' and dropped the 5.0 to 5.9 column. The 'or equal to' brings that boundary column back into the group.

items.stimulus: A printmaking studio stores its work in a flat file with 9 numbered drawers. Drawers 1 through 4 each hold 15 prints, and all of them are linocuts. Drawers 5 through 9 each hold 12 prints: 4 linocuts and 8 etchings.
items.stem: If one of the prints in drawer 3 or higher is selected at random, what is the probability of selecting a linocut?

D.why: You counted the 50 linocuts in drawers 3 through 9 but divided by all 120 prints in the flat file. Only the 90 prints in drawer 3 or higher can be selected.

"Each capsule can rupture only once, so a region... is left defenseless against a second crack" is also a complete sentence. Two complete sentences need a strong break such as a semicolon. Next, decide which clause "however" belongs to. The contrast is between the samples regaining their strength and the capsules working only once, so "however" opens the second clause. The semicolon goes before "however," and a comma follows it.

A.why: You treated "however" like "but" and let commas join two complete sentences. "However" is not a coordinating conjunction, so this is a comma splice. The sentence that ends at "strength" needs a semicolon or a period.

B.why: There is no punctuation between "strength" and "however," so the two complete sentences run together with nothing marking where the first one ends. This is a run-on. A semicolon has to come before "however."

D.why: The semicolon is after "however" instead of before it, so the word gets attached to the first clause. That makes "regained nearly all of their original strength" contrast with the previous sentence about capsules sealing cracks, but those two ideas don't conflict. The real contrast is with the one-use limit that comes next, so "however" belongs at the start of that clause.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

items.explanation: The storm adds 0.4 inch/hour × 6 hours = 2.4 inches. The gauge already held 1.5 inches, so at the end it holds 1.5 + 2.4 = 3.9 inches.

A.why: You subtracted the starting 1.5 inches from the storm's 2.4 inches. The storm adds water to the gauge, so you should have added the two amounts.

B.why: 2.4 inches is only the rain the storm added. You stopped before adding the 1.5 inches that were already in the gauge.

D.why: You divided 6 hours by 0.4 inch per hour (getting 15) and then added 1.5. Hours ÷ (inches/hour) doesn't give inches. Rate × time does.

items.stimulus: A sports scientist mixes 4,000 milliliters of an electrolyte drink for a training session. Each athlete must receive at least 450 milliliters of the drink.
items.stem: What is the greatest number of athletes who can each receive at least 450 milliliters of the drink?
items.explanation: Number of athletes = total ÷ amount per athlete = 4,000 mL ÷ 450 mL/athlete ≈ 8.9. Only whole athletes count, and each one needs at least 450 mL, so round down to 8. Eight athletes use 3,600 mL, and a ninth would push the total past 4,000 mL.

items.stimulus: A linguist hires an annotator to tag every word of a 9,000-word corpus by part of speech. The annotator works at a constant rate of 450 words per hour and has already tagged 3,600 of the words.

items.stimulus: A seismometer records ground motion at a constant rate of 40 samples per second. During a small earthquake, the ground shook for 1 minute 15 seconds, and the seismometer recorded throughout the shaking.

At the end of the season, the worker sends all of these earnings to family abroad through a transfer service. The service converts dollars to euros at a rate of 1 euro = 1.20 dollars, then deducts a flat fee of 45 euros. There are no other deductions.
items.stem: How many euros does the worker's family receive?
items.explanation: Total earnings = $18/hour × 35 hours/week × 6 weeks = $3780. To convert, multiply by (1 euro / 1.20 dollars) so the dollars cancel: 3780 ÷ 1.20 = 3150 euros. Then take off the fee: 3150 − 45 = 3105 euros. Check the units on the conversion. Multiplying by 1.20 would leave dollars²/euro, which tells you the setup is wrong.

items.subtype_name: Constant rate: rate × time (or amount ÷ rate)
items.stimulus: A materials lab tests two alloys in a saltwater tank. Alloy A loses thickness to corrosion at a constant rate of 0.12 millimeter per year, and alloy B loses thickness at a constant rate of 0.05 millimeter per year. One plate of each alloy is placed in the tank, and each plate starts 3.0 millimeters thick.
items.stem: After 20 years, how many millimeters thicker is the alloy B plate than the alloy A plate?
items.explanation: Thickness lost = rate × time. Alloy A loses $0.12 \times 20 = 2.4$ mm, so it is $3.0 - 2.4 = 0.6$ mm thick. Alloy B loses $0.05 \times 20 = 1.0$ mm, so it is $3.0 - 1.0 = 2.0$ mm thick. The difference is $2.0 - 0.6 = 1.4$ mm.

D.why: You found how much thickness alloy A lost in 20 years. That is one plate's loss, not the difference between the two plates.

items.stimulus: An agricultural research station applies a liquid fertilizer at a rate of 2.4 gallons per acre. Its test field is divided into plots that are each 0.4 acre. The sprayer tank holds 150 gallons, and a plot counts as treated only if the entire plot receives the full application rate.
items.stem: What is the maximum number of plots that can be completely treated with one full tank?
items.explanation: Each plot needs $2.4 \text{ gal/acre} \times 0.4 \text{ acre} = 0.96$ gallon. One tank covers $150 \div 0.96 = 156.25$ plots. Only whole plots count, so round down: 156 plots.

D.why: You rounded 156.25 up. The 157th plot would get only part of its fertilizer, so it would not be completely treated.

items.subtype_name: Constant rate: rate × time (or amount ÷ rate)
items.stimulus: A public health department runs a vaccination site with 3 stations. Each station vaccinates people at a constant rate of 15 people per hour, and the site is open 8 hours each day. The department plans to vaccinate 1,620 people at this site.
items.stem: What is the minimum number of days the site needs to vaccinate all 1,620 people?
items.explanation: The site vaccinates $3 \times 15 \times 8 = 360$ people per day. Then $1{,}620 \div 360 = 4.5$ days. You can't stop partway through day 5 and count it as 4 days, so the minimum is 5 days.

D.why: You found the number of hours needed, $1{,}620 \div 45 = 36$. The question asks for days, so you still need to divide by 8 hours per day.

items.stimulus: A historian studying a 19th-century textile mill finds records showing that one of its power looms wove cloth at a constant rate of 0.75 inch per minute. The mill ran this loom for a 10-hour shift without stopping.

C.why: You divided 450 by 3. That converts feet to yards, but the 450 is in inches, so you needed to divide by 36.

items.subtype_name: Constant rate: rate × time (or amount ÷ rate)
items.stimulus: A fiber supplement powder contains 5 grams of fiber in every 12 grams of powder. A participant in a nutrition study must get at least 20 grams of fiber from the powder each day. One container holds 750 grams of the powder.
items.stem: What is the greatest number of full days the container can supply this participant?
items.explanation: First find how much fiber the container holds: $750 \text{ g powder} \times \frac{5 \text{ g fiber}}{12 \text{ g powder}} = 312.5$ grams of fiber. Then divide by the daily amount: $312.5 \text{ g fiber} \div \frac{20 \text{ g fiber}}{1 \text{ day}} = 15.625$ days. A day only counts if the participant gets at least 20 grams, so you round down. The container covers 15 full days.

B.why: You rounded 15.625 up to 16. On day 16 only 12.5 grams of fiber are left, which is less than the required 20 grams, so that day is not fully supplied. With 'at least' and 'full days', you round down.

C.why: You divided 750 grams of powder by 20 grams of fiber per day, as if the powder were all fiber. Check the units: grams of powder divided by grams of fiber per day doesn't give days. Convert powder to fiber first.

D.why: You found how many 12-gram portions of powder are in the container ($750 \div 12 = 62.5$) and stopped there. That's a count of portions, not days. You still need to convert those portions to fiber and divide by 20 grams per day.

items.explanation: The crew still has $9 - 2.4 = 6.6$ kilometers to paint. Time is distance divided by rate: $6.6 \text{ km} \div 0.6 \text{ km/day} = 11$ days. The kilometers cancel and leave days. To check, $11 \times 0.6 = 6.6$ kilometers, and $2.4 + 6.6 = 9$.

A.why: You multiplied $6.6 \times 0.6$ when you should have divided. The units would come out as km²/day, which is not a number of days.

B.why: $2.4 \div 0.6 = 4$ is the number of days the crew has already worked, not the number of days still to go.

D.why: $9 \div 0.6 = 15$ is the time for the whole lane. You didn't take off the 2.4 kilometers that are already painted.

items.stimulus: A cartography team scans paper map sheets into a digital archive at a constant rate of 12 sheets per hour. A county atlas has 150 sheets, and the team has already scanned 42 of them.

D.why: You divided the rate by the amount, $12 \div 108 = \frac{1}{9}$, instead of the amount by the rate. Write the units down: sheets/hour ÷ sheets gives 'per hour', not hours.

items.stimulus: At 9:00 p.m., a weather station recorded 4 inches of snow on the ground. Snow then fell at a constant rate of 1.5 inches per hour until 3:00 a.m., and none melted.
items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The snow depth at 3:00 a.m. was 9 inches.
The snow depth at 3:00 a.m. was 13 inches.
The snow depth at 3:00 a.m. was 8 inches.
The snow depth at 3:00 a.m. was 14.5 inches.
items.explanation: From 9:00 p.m. to 3:00 a.m. is 6 hours. New snow = rate × time = $1.5 \text{ in/hour} \times 6 \text{ hours} = 9$ inches. Add the 4 inches already on the ground: $4 + 9 = 13$ inches.

D.why: You counted 7 hours (9, 10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3) when there are only 6. That gives $4 + 1.5 \times 7 = 14.5$. Count the gaps between the times, not the clock readings.

items.stimulus: A wildlife refuge covers 128 acres. Its managers require at least 2.5 acres of habitat per deer. The refuge currently has 38 deer.
items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The refuge can take in at most 13 more deer.
The refuge can take in at most 14 more deer.
The refuge can take in at most 51 more deer.
The refuge can take in at most 282 more deer.
items.explanation: Count = total ÷ rate: $128 \text{ acres} \div 2.5 \text{ acres/deer} = 51.2$ deer. You can't have part of a deer, and 52 deer would give each one less than 2.5 acres, so round down to 51. The refuge already has 38, so it can take in $51 - 38 = 13$ more.

D.why: You multiplied, $128 \times 2.5 = 320$, and then subtracted 38. Acres × (acres per deer) gives square acres per deer, which makes no sense. Acres ÷ (acres per deer) gives deer.

items.stimulus: Six volunteers are replanting a marsh with sedge plugs. Each volunteer plants at a constant rate of 40 plugs per hour. The marsh needs 1,920 plugs. A coordinator computes $\frac{1{,}920}{6 \times 40} = 8$.
items.stem: In this context, what does 8 represent?
choices: The number of hours the six volunteers need to plant all the plugs
The number of hours one volunteer needs to plant all the plugs
The number of plugs the six volunteers plant together in one hour
The number of minutes the six volunteers need to plant all the plugs
items.explanation: The denominator, $6 \times 40 = 240$, is the team's combined rate in plugs per hour. Dividing a total by a rate gives a time: $\frac{1{,}920 \text{ plugs}}{240 \text{ plugs/hour}} = 8$ hours. C.why: You described the denominator, not the result. The team plants $6 \times 40 = 240$ plugs per hour. That is a step on the way, and the full expression goes on to divide the total by it.

D.why: You read the rate as 40 plugs per minute. It is 40 plugs per hour, so when the plugs cancel, hours are left, not minutes.

items.stimulus: A crew is paving a 12-kilometer road at a constant rate of 0.4 kilometer per day. The crew has already paved 2 kilometers. An engineer computes $\frac{12 - 2}{0.4} = 25$.
items.stem: In this context, what does 25 represent?
choices: The number of days the crew needs to pave the entire road
The number of kilometers of road the crew has left to pave
The number of days the crew needs to pave the remaining road
The number of days the crew has already spent paving the road
items.explanation: The numerator, $12 - 2 = 10$, is the distance still unpaved, in kilometers. Dividing a distance by a rate gives a time: $\frac{10 \text{ km}}{0.4 \text{ km/day}} = 25$ days. B.why: You described the numerator. The unpaved distance is $12 - 2 = 10$ kilometers. Dividing that by 0.4 kilometer per day changes the units from kilometers to days.

D.why: You reversed the timeline. The time already spent would come from the 2 kilometers already paved: $\frac{2}{0.4} = 5$ days. The expression uses the distance still left, so it gives the time ahead, not the time behind.

items.stimulus: Two tagged shorebirds each fly the same 2,700-kilometer migration route nonstop. A godwit flies at a constant speed of 60 kilometers per hour. A plover flies at a constant speed of 750 meters per minute.
items.stem: How many more hours than the godwit does the plover take to fly the route?

D.why: 900 is the difference in minutes ($3{,}600 - 2{,}700$). You worked in the plover's units and never converted back. The question asks for hours, and $900 \text{ min} \div 60 = 15$ hours.

items.stimulus: A public health clinic plans to give 200 people one 0.3-milliliter dose of a vaccine each. Each vial contains 5.0 milliliters, but 0.35 milliliter of every vial stays in the vial and cannot be drawn into a syringe. Each dose must come entirely from a single vial.

items.stimulus: A printmaker is pulling an edition of 140 relief prints. Each print uses 2.5 grams of ink. At the start of each printing session, 20 grams of ink is used to charge the roller, and no session can produce more than 40 prints. Ink is sold only in 60-gram tins.
items.stem: What is the minimum number of tins of ink the printmaker must buy to print the entire edition?
items.explanation: The edition needs $140 \div 40 = 3.5$ sessions, so the printmaker must hold 4. The ink needed is $140 \times 2.5 + 4 \times 20 = 350 + 80 = 430$ grams. Then $430 \div 60 \approx 7.17$, so the printmaker must buy 8 tins.

A.why: You counted only the ink on the prints: $350 \div 60 \approx 5.83$, rounded to 6. You left out the 20 grams used to charge the roller in each session.

B.why: You either rounded 7.17 tins down, or you used 3.5 sessions instead of 4, which gives exactly $420 \div 60 = 7$. Sessions are whole events, and a partial tin means buying another one.

D.why: You may have counted 5 sessions, adding a roller charge at the end: $350 + 100 = 450$ grams, which needs 8 tins. Or you may have rounded up twice. Four sessions and 430 grams need 8 tins, not 9.

items.stimulus: A musicologist orders scans of a baroque manuscript from a European archive that charges €3.50 per page. The musicologist has \$500. The bank first deducts a \$20 transfer fee and then converts the rest at 1 U.S. dollar = 0.80 euro.
items.stem: What is the greatest number of complete pages the musicologist can order?
items.explanation: After the fee, $500 - 20 = 480$ dollars is converted. That gives $480 \times 0.80 = 384$ euros. Then $384 \div 3.50 \approx 109.7$, so the musicologist can order 109 complete pages.

D.why: You divided by 0.80 when you should have multiplied, which turned \$480 into 600 euros. Check the units: dollars × (euros per dollar) gives euros, and a euro is worth more than a dollar, so you should get fewer euros than dollars.

items.subtype_name: Constant rate: rate × time (or amount ÷ rate)
items.stimulus: A steel test plate is 6.0 millimeters thick when installed. In a corrosive environment it loses thickness at a constant rate of 40 micrometers every 6 months ($1 \text{ millimeter} = 1{,}000 \text{ micrometers}$). The plate must be removed from service once its thickness falls below 70% of its original thickness.
items.stem: What is the greatest whole number of years the plate can remain in service?
items.explanation: The minimum allowed thickness is $0.70 \times 6.0 = 4.2$ mm, so the plate can lose $1.8$ mm, or 1,800 micrometers. The rate is 40 micrometers every half year, which is 80 micrometers per year. Then $1{,}800 \div 80 = 22.5$ years. D.why: You divided the 4.2 mm the plate must keep by the yearly loss: $4{,}200 \div 80 = 52.5$. The limit depends on the 1.8 mm the plate is allowed to lose.

items.stimulus: While the leaf fossils at the Eocene lake site are fragmentary and few, its pollen record is ______: more than two thousand grains, from at least forty plant families, preserved in a single meter of sediment. items.subtype_name: Similar / congruent figures: read off corresponding parts
items.stimulus: An agronomist marks out two triangular test plots so she can compare the yields of two fertilizer blends. Triangle $PQR$ is similar to triangle $STU$, where $P$, $Q$, and $R$ correspond to $S$, $T$, and $U$, respectively. Each side of triangle $STU$ is 3 times as long as the corresponding side of triangle $PQR$. The measure of angle $Q$ is $64^\circ$.
items.stem: What is the measure of angle $T$?
items.explanation: From the letter order, $Q$ matches $T$. In similar triangles, corresponding angles are equal, and the scale factor of 3 changes only the side lengths. So angle $T$ measures $64^\circ$.

D.why: You multiplied the angle by the scale factor, $64 \times 3 = 192$. A scale factor stretches side lengths but never changes angle measures. Also, no angle in a triangle can be more than $180^\circ$.

items.subtype_name: Similar / congruent figures: read off corresponding parts
items.stimulus: On a regional storm-tracking map, a meteorologist draws triangle $ABC$. Point $D$ lies on $\overline{AB}$ and point $E$ lies on $\overline{AC}$, and $\overline{DE}$ is parallel to $\overline{BC}$. On the map, $AD = 40$ kilometers, $AB = 120$ kilometers, and $DE = 50$ kilometers.
items.stem: What is the length, in kilometers, of $\overline{BC}$?
items.explanation: Because $\overline{DE}$ is parallel to $\overline{BC}$, triangle $ADE$ is similar to triangle $ABC$. Set up small over large on both sides: $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{DE}{BC}$, so $\frac{40}{120} = \frac{50}{BC}$. Cross-multiplying gives $40 \cdot BC = 6{,}000$, so $BC = 150$ kilometers.

C.why: You added the 80-kilometer difference between $AB$ and $AD$ to $DE$. Similar triangles scale by multiplying, not by adding.

items.stimulus: A hydrologist studies a drainage channel whose cross-section is triangle $ABC$, with the lowest point $C$ at the bottom and the rim $\overline{AB}$ at ground level. The rim is 8 meters wide, and the channel is 5 meters deep, measured along the altitude from $C$ to $\overline{AB}$. During a storm, the water surface forms segment $\overline{DE}$, with $D$ on $\overline{CA}$ and $E$ on $\overline{CB}$. $\overline{DE}$ is parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and is 6 meters wide.
items.stem: What is the depth, in meters, of the water at the center of the channel?
items.explanation: Because $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{AB}$, triangle $CDE$ is similar to triangle $CAB$, so corresponding altitudes are in the same ratio as corresponding sides. The water depth $d$ is the altitude of the small triangle, so $\frac{d}{5} = \frac{6}{8}$ and $d = \frac{30}{8} = \frac{15}{4}$ meters.

A.why: You found the height of the dry part of the channel, $5 - \frac{15}{4} = \frac{5}{4}$. The water depth is the altitude of the small triangle below the surface.

B.why: The surface is 2 meters narrower than the rim, so you subtracted 2 meters from the depth. Similar triangles shrink by a common factor, not by a common amount.

D.why: You wrote $\frac{d}{5} = \frac{8}{6}$, which puts the large triangle's width over the small one's. That gives a depth greater than the channel itself.

items.stimulus: An immunology textbook shows a four-sided outline of a cell-surface receptor, drawn as quadrilateral $ABCD$, and an enlarged copy of the same outline, quadrilateral $EFGH$. Quadrilateral $ABCD$ is similar to quadrilateral $EFGH$, where $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ correspond to $G$, $H$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Each side of $EFGH$ is $1.5$ times as long as the corresponding side of $ABCD$. In quadrilateral $ABCD$, the measure of angle $A$ is $80^\circ$, the measure of angle $B$ is $115^\circ$, and the measure of angle $C$ is $70^\circ$.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $F$?
items.explanation: The stated correspondence pairs $F$ with $D$, so angle $F$ equals angle $D$. The angles of a quadrilateral sum to $360^\circ$, so angle $D = 360 - (80 + 115 + 70) = 95^\circ$. The $1.5$ scale factor does not affect angles, so angle $F$ is $95^\circ$.

B.why: You matched $F$ with $B$ because both are the second letter in their quadrilateral's name. The stated correspondence pairs $F$ with $D$, and $115^\circ$ is the measure of angle $H$.

C.why: You found angle $D = 95^\circ$ and then multiplied it by the scale factor $1.5$. Enlarging a figure scales its sides, not its angles.

D.why: You added the three given angles to get $265^\circ$ and stopped. You still needed to subtract that total from $360^\circ$.

items.stimulus: A meteorologist marks three weather stations on a regional map, and they form triangle $KLM$. On a wall-sized display, the same three stations appear as triangle $RST$, which is a dilation of triangle $KLM$ by a scale factor of $4$. Vertices $K$, $L$, and $M$ correspond to vertices $R$, $S$, and $T$, respectively. In triangle $KLM$, the measure of angle $K$ is $34^\circ$ and the measure of angle $L$ is $90^\circ$.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $T$?
items.explanation: Match the vertices using the stated order: $K \to R$, $L \to S$, $M \to T$, so angle $T$ corresponds to angle $M$. A dilation changes side lengths but never changes angles, so you can ignore the scale factor of $4$. In triangle $KLM$, the angles add to $180^\circ$, so angle $M = 180 - 34 - 90 = 56^\circ$. Angle $T$ is therefore $56^\circ$.

items.stimulus: A printmaker carves a triangular linoleum block in the shape of triangle $ABC$. To separate two ink colors, the printmaker cuts a groove $\overline{DE}$, where point $D$ lies on $\overline{AB}$, point $E$ lies on $\overline{AC}$, and $\overline{DE}$ is parallel to $\overline{BC}$. The length of $\overline{AD}$ is $6$ centimeters, the length of $\overline{DB}$ is $9$ centimeters, and the length of $\overline{DE}$ is $8$ centimeters.
items.stem: What is the length, in centimeters, of $\overline{BC}$?
items.explanation: Because $\overline{DE}$ is parallel to $\overline{BC}$, triangle $ADE$ is similar to triangle $ABC$ (they share angle $A$, and the corresponding angles at $D$ and $B$ are equal). Pair matching sides: $\overline{AD}$ goes with the whole side $\overline{AB}$, not with $\overline{DB}$. $AB = 6 + 9 = 15$. Set up small/large = small/large: $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{DE}{BC}$, so $\frac{6}{15} = \frac{8}{BC}$. Cross-multiplying gives $6 \cdot BC = 120$, so $BC = 20$.

Each side of $QRS$ is twice the corresponding side of $KLM$. Angle $L$ is a right angle and the measure of angle $S$ is $58^\circ$. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $K$?
items.explanation: Match by letter order: $M \leftrightarrow S$, so angle $M = 58^\circ$. Angle $L = 90^\circ$, so angle $K = 180 - 90 - 58 = 32^\circ$. The scale factor of 2 has no effect on angles.

items.stem: An astronomer connects three stars on a chart to form triangle $ABC$. Triangle $DEF$ is a dilation of triangle $ABC$ by a scale factor of 3, where $A$, $B$, and $C$ correspond to $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Angle $A$ measures $48^\circ$, and angle $B$ is a right angle. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $F$?
items.explanation: Match the vertices using the letter order: $F$ corresponds to $C$. A dilation does not change angle measures, so angle $F$ equals angle $C$. The angles in triangle $ABC$ add to $180^\circ$, so angle $C = 180 - 48 - 90 = 42$. Angle $F$ measures $42^\circ$. The scale factor of 3 has no effect on any angle.

Multiplied the given 48 by the scale factor 3, treating the angle as if it scaled like a side.

items.stem: In a diagram for a labour-market report, segment $ST$ is drawn inside triangle $PQR$, with $S$ on $\overline{PQ}$, $T$ on $\overline{PR}$, and $\overline{ST} \parallel \overline{QR}$. If $PS = 6$ centimeters, $SQ = 4$ centimeters, and $ST = 9$ centimeters, what is the length, in centimeters, of $\overline{QR}$?
items.explanation: Because $ST$ is parallel to $QR$, triangle $PST$ is similar to triangle $PQR$ (AA). Corresponding sides are $PS$ with $PQ$ and $ST$ with $QR$. First find the whole side: $PQ = 6 + 4 = 10$. Then set up small over large on both sides: $\frac{6}{10} = \frac{9}{QR}$. Cross-multiply to get $6 \cdot QR = 90$, so $QR = 15$.

Set up the correct sides but flipped one ratio, 6/10 = QR/9, so QR = 5.4.

items.stem: A cartographer enlarges a region on a map shaped like quadrilateral $WXYZ$ to quadrilateral $W'X'Y'Z'$ using a scale factor of 2.5. In quadrilateral $WXYZ$, angles $W$, $X$, and $Y$ measure $80^\circ$, $95^\circ$, and $110^\circ$, respectively. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $Z'$?
items.explanation: Angle $Z'$ corresponds to angle $Z$, and enlarging a figure does not change its angles. The angles of a quadrilateral add to $360^\circ$, so angle $Z = 360 - (80 + 95 + 110) = 360 - 285 = 75$. Angle $Z'$ measures $75^\circ$. The scale factor of 2.5 doesn't affect the answer.

items.stem: On a weather map, a forecaster draws triangle $ABC$ connecting three stations. A front is shown as segment $DE$, with $D$ on $\overline{AB}$, $E$ on $\overline{AC}$, and $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$. If $AD = 8$ kilometers, $AB = 20$ kilometers, and $BC = 35$ kilometers, what is the length, in kilometers, of $\overline{DE}$?
items.explanation: Since $DE$ is parallel to $BC$, triangle $ADE$ is similar to triangle $ABC$ (AA). Pair $AD$ with $AB$ and $DE$ with $BC$, writing small over large on both sides: $\frac{8}{20} = \frac{DE}{35}$. Then $DE = \frac{8 \cdot 35}{20} = 14$.

Triangle $RST$ is similar to triangle $UVW$, with $R$, $S$, and $T$ corresponding to $U$, $V$, and $W$, respectively. Each side of $UVW$ is 1.5 times the corresponding side of $RST$. If $RS = RT$ and angle $U$ measures $40^\circ$, what is the measure, in degrees, of angle $W$?

items.stimulus: A civil engineer is designing two triangular steel brackets for a pedestrian bridge. The larger bracket is modeled by triangle $DEF$, and the smaller bracket is modeled by triangle $ABC$. Triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$, where $A$, $B$, and $C$ correspond to $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Each side of triangle $DEF$ is $3$ times as long as its corresponding side in triangle $ABC$. The measure of angle $A$ is $38^\circ$, and the measure of angle $B$ is $90^\circ$.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $F$?
items.explanation: Angle $F$ corresponds to angle $C$, and similar triangles have equal corresponding angles. The scale factor changes only the side lengths. Using the triangle sum, angle $C$ is $180^\circ - 38^\circ - 90^\circ = 52^\circ$, so angle $F$ also measures $52^\circ$.

A.why: You found the measure of angle $D$, which corresponds to angle $A$. The question asks for angle $F$, which corresponds to angle $C$.

C.why: You took the supplement of angle $A$, $180 - 38$, and forgot to subtract the right angle as well.

D.why: You multiplied the correct angle, $52^\circ$, by the scale factor $3$. A scale factor changes side lengths, but it never changes angle measures.

items.stimulus: A labour economist sketches a wage diagram. A downward-sloping labour demand line, the vertical wage axis, and a horizontal line at the current wage form triangle $RST$. Point $R$ is where the demand line meets the wage axis, $S$ is on the wage axis, and $T$ is on the demand line. To show a higher proposed wage, the economist draws a horizontal segment $\overline{UV}$ with $U$ on $\overline{RS}$ and $V$ on $\overline{RT}$, so that $\overline{UV}$ is parallel to $\overline{ST}$. On the diagram, $RU = 4$ units, $RS = 10$ units, and $ST = 15$ units.
items.stem: What is the length of $\overline{UV}$, in diagram units?
items.explanation: Since $\overline{UV}$ is parallel to $\overline{ST}$, triangle $RUV$ is similar to triangle $RST$. Setting small over large gives $\frac{UV}{ST} = \frac{RU}{RS}$, so $\frac{UV}{15} = \frac{4}{10}$. Therefore $UV = 6$ units.

D.why: You inverted the ratio and computed $15 \cdot \frac{10}{4}$. That makes the inner segment longer than the base it is parallel to.

The volunteers' records back up her observation: at Harrow Ridge, the number of broad-winged hawks counted ______

Year | Broad-winged hawks | Red-tailed hawks

2019 | 5,640 | 1,420

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

rose from 4,210 in 2016 to 5,640 in 2019 and then to 7,050 in 2022.
fell from 7,050 in 2016 to 5,640 in 2019 and then to 4,210 in 2022.
rose in every single year from 2016 to 2022, reaching 7,050 by the end.

C.why: You read the years in reverse. The 4,210 count is from 2016 and the 7,050 count is from 2022, so the numbers went up, not down.

In most metals, shrinking the crystal grains raises hardness, because the boundaries between grains block the dislocations that let a metal deform. Sample | Average grain size (nm) | Hardness (GPa)
P | 200 | 3.1
Q | 80 | 4.4
R | 35 | 5.6
S | 18 | 6.0

the sample with 18 nm grains had a hardness of 6.0 GPa, while the sample with 8 nm grains had a hardness of 5.2 GPa.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
Great tits living in cities often sing with a higher minimum pitch than rural birds. This is usually blamed on low-frequency traffic noise drowning out deep notes, but cities differ from the countryside in many other ways too. Ornithologist Ilse Varga therefore recorded males at four sites chosen so that noise level and setting would not always go together. Her results suggest that noise, not urban living as such, drives the shift. For example, ______

Minimum Song Frequency of Male Great Tits at Four Sites
Site | Setting | Traffic noise (decibels) | Minimum song frequency (kHz)
Elm Park | urban | 48 | 2.1
Harbor Road | urban | 71 | 3.0
Millbrook Farm | rural | 69 | 2.9
Ashford Wood | rural | 45 | 2.0
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: birds at Millbrook Farm, a rural site, sang at a higher minimum frequency than birds at Elm Park, an urban site.
birds at Harbor Road, an urban site, sang at a higher minimum frequency than birds at Ashford Wood, a rural site.
birds at Harbor Road, an urban site, sang at a higher minimum frequency than birds at Millbrook Farm, a rural site.
birds at Ashford Wood, a rural site, sang at a higher minimum frequency than birds at Elm Park, an urban site.

D.why: You misread the table. Ashford Wood birds sang at 2.0 kHz, which is lower than the 2.1 kHz at Elm Park, not higher.

items.stimulus:
Steel reinforcing bars inside concrete bridge decks rust when chloride from deicing salt seeps down to them, and the expanding rust then cracks the concrete around them. Epoxy coatings on the bars are meant to block the first step in that chain, but they add to construction costs. After comparing decks that had been in service for twenty years, engineer Tomás Aldana concluded that coated bars are hard to justify on bridges that never receive salt. For example, ______

Rebar Surface Area Corroded After 20 Years (%)
Deicing salt use | Uncoated rebar | Epoxy-coated rebar
Heavy | 18 | 6
None | 4 | 3
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: on decks with heavy salt use, coated rebar showed less corrosion than uncoated rebar did.
on decks with no salt use, coated and uncoated rebar showed nearly the same corrosion.
uncoated rebar showed more corrosion on decks with heavy salt use than on decks with none.
coated rebar showed less corrosion on decks with heavy salt use than on decks with none.
items.explanation: Aldana's claim covers only bridges that never receive salt, and it says the coating isn't worth the cost there. To support that, the example has to show that the coating does little where there is no salt. On no-salt decks, coated bars had 3% corrosion and uncoated bars had 4%, so the coating made almost no difference.

A.why: This is a true reading (6% against 18%), and it's the subtype's trap. It shows that coatings work where salt is used, which is the opposite case from the one Aldana is making a claim about.

C.why: This is true (18% against 4%), but it compares salt exposure for uncoated bars only. It supports the first link in the chain, that salt causes corrosion. It says nothing about whether the coating is worth it without salt.

D.why: You reversed the numbers. Coated rebar showed 6% corrosion with heavy salt and 3% with none, so it corroded more on the salted decks.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus: When cold air flows over a large lake that hasn't frozen, it picks up heat and moisture and then drops that moisture as snow once it reaches land. Because winter winds in the region blow mostly from the west, this lake-effect snow should fall on the lake's eastern side. Meteorologist Dana Okafor compared stations along an east-west line through the lake and argued that the effect reaches well inland on the downwind side, not just along the shore. For example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
choices: the station 40 km east of the lake received more than twice as much snow as the station on the west shore.
the station on the east shore received more than twice as much snow as the station on the west shore.
the station 40 km east of the lake received less snow than the station on the east shore did.
the station 20 km west of the lake received more snow than the station on the west shore did.
items.explanation: Okafor makes two points: snow is heavier on the downwind side, and the extra snow reaches well inland, not just the shore. In the 1850s, printers began electroplating engraved copper plates with a thin, hard layer of iron, a process known as steel facing, so that the soft copper would not wear away under the press. items.stimulus:
Plants tend to form fewer stomata, the pores that take in carbon dioxide, when atmospheric CO2 rises, so paleobotanists use the stomatal index of fossil leaves to estimate past CO2 levels. But shade leaves normally have a higher index than sun leaves, so if a fossil collection simply contained more shade leaves, that alone could look like a change in CO2. Sorting fossil Ginkgo leaves from below and above a rock boundary by leaf type, paleobotanist Kwame Asante concluded that the drop he found across the boundary can't be explained by such a shift. For example, ______

Stomatal Index of Fossil Ginkgo Leaves (%)
Leaf type | Below boundary | Above boundary
Sun leaves | 9 | 6
Shade leaves | 12 | 8
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?

shade leaves had a higher stomatal index than sun leaves both below and above the boundary.
shade leaves from above the boundary had a lower stomatal index than shade leaves from below it.
sun leaves from above the boundary had a higher stomatal index than sun leaves from below it.
items.explanation: To rule out a change in leaf type, the example has to hold leaf type constant and still show a drop. Shade leaves fell from 12% below the boundary to 8% above it. Both numbers come from shade leaves, so the decline can't come from a change in the mix of leaf types.

items.stimulus:
Crack Closure in Mortar Samples after 28 Days (% of crack width sealed)
Mortar type | 50% humidity | 95% humidity
Plain | 12 | 18
With bacterial spores | 15 | 71

Some engineers mix dormant bacterial spores into mortar so that the material can repair itself. When water seeps into a fresh crack, it revives the spores. The spores then turn a calcium-based nutrient packed into the mortar into calcite, which gradually fills the gap. Materials scientist Leilani Kahale and her colleagues compared plain mortar with spore-treated mortar at two humidity levels. They concluded that the advantage the spores provide depends heavily on available moisture: for example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: at 95% humidity, mortar with spores sealed 71% of its crack width, whereas plain mortar sealed only 18%.
the spores raised crack closure by 53 percentage points at 95% humidity but by only 3 points at 50% humidity.
plain mortar sealed a larger share of its crack width at 95% humidity than it did at 50% humidity.
at 50% humidity, mortar with spores sealed a smaller share of its crack width than plain mortar did.
items.explanation: The claim is about the spores' advantage, meaning how much better spore-treated mortar does than plain mortar, and says that this advantage changes with moisture. D.why: This misreads the table. At 50% humidity, mortar with spores sealed 15% of its crack width and plain mortar sealed 12%, so the spore-treated mortar did slightly better, not worse. Check the direction of each comparison against the numbers.

items.stimulus:
Raccoons climb the poles of nest boxes to take eggs and chicks, and a metal cone guard fixed to the pole stops the climb. Ornithologist Priya Raman put guards on half the tree swallow boxes at each of three sites. Raccoons were common only at the marsh edge. Tree Swallow Fledging Success (% of eggs producing fledglings)
Site | Unguarded boxes | Guarded boxes
Marsh edge | 41 | 78
Meadow | 62 | 66
Orchard | 58 | 61
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?

beat unguarded boxes by 37 percentage points at the marsh edge but by only 4 at the meadow.

Concrete hardens through hydration, a reaction between cement and water, and that reaction slows sharply in cold weather. Because hydration continues for weeks, though, engineers at a state road agency argue that cold curing delays strength gain without greatly reducing the strength concrete eventually reaches. Curing temperature | Day 7 | Day 28
5°C | 18 | 39

were stronger than 20°C cylinders at day 28 despite being weaker at day 7.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
In drypoint, an artist scratches lines straight into a copper plate. This throws up a ridge of metal, the burr, which holds extra ink and prints a soft, velvety line. Each pass through the press flattens the burr a little. Etched lines, bitten into the plate by acid, have no burr to lose. Conservator Ines Valdés argues that drypoint plates therefore wear out far sooner than etched ones. In her printing trial, ______

Line Detail Retained Compared with First Proof (%)
Impression | Drypoint plate | Etched plate
10th | 96 | 99
30th | 71 | 97
50th | 44 | 95
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: both plates kept more than 90% of their line detail through the 10th impression.
the etched plate kept 99% of its line detail at the 10th impression and 97% at the 30th.
the drypoint plate kept more detail at the 50th impression than the etched plate did at the 30th.
from the 10th to the 50th impression, the drypoint plate lost 52 points of detail and the etched plate 4.
items.explanation: Valdés claims drypoint plates wear out *far sooner* than etched ones. To show that, you need both plates' loss over the same run of impressions. Adjuvants are substances added to vaccines to strengthen the immune response. To test one adjuvant, immunologist Rana Okafor gave two groups of mice the same vaccine. items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus: Endurance athletes lose sodium in sweat, and low blood sodium can hasten fatigue. Because athletes sweat more in heat, this loss is greatest on hot days. A team of sports scientists had cyclists ride to exhaustion in a cool room and in a hot room. The cyclists drank either plain water or an otherwise identical drink with added sodium. The team concluded that the sodium drink lessened, though it did not eliminate, the toll that heat took on endurance: for example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
choices: in cool conditions, cyclists rode for 60 minutes whether they drank water or the sodium drink.
with water, cyclists rode for 60 minutes in cool conditions but only 36 minutes in hot conditions.
moving from cool to hot conditions cut riding time by 24 minutes with the sodium drink but by 12 with water.
moving from cool to hot conditions cut riding time by 12 minutes with the sodium drink but by 24 with water.
items.explanation: First work out what the sentence needs: the drop caused by heat should be smaller with the sodium drink than with water, and it still shouldn't be zero. The toll was smaller but still there, which matches both parts of the claim.

items.stimulus:
Cooking pots absorb fats from the food prepared in them, and chemical tests on these residues can show whether a household cooked fish. Researchers tested pots from two ancient villages, one on the coast and one about 40 kilometers inland. The pots were dated to before and after a stone road was built linking the two villages. The team concluded that the road changed inland diets far more than it changed coastal ones: for example, ______

Pots with Marine Food Residue (%)
Village | Before road | After road
Coastal | 70 | 72
Inland | 8 | 41
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: the coastal village had a larger share of pots with marine residue than the inland village had, both before and after the road.
after the road, the inland village's share of pots with marine residue, 41 percent, was still below the coastal village's share.
the share of pots with marine residue rose by 2 percentage points at the inland village but by 33 at the coastal village.
the share of pots with marine residue rose by 33 percentage points at the inland village but by only 2 at the coastal village.

Sports physiologist Dana Ruel tested whether a carbohydrate drink protects cyclists against fatigue. items.stimulus:
Some polymer coatings contain microscopic capsules of liquid resin. When a crack forms, it ruptures the capsules, and the released resin flows into the gap and hardens, restoring some of the coating's strength. Materials scientist Ines Varga tested identical coatings with and without capsules at two temperatures. Because the resin thickens in the cold, she concluded that the capsules' benefit depends strongly on temperature. For example, ______

Temperature | Without capsules | With capsules

−10°C | 6 | 14

Flora S (upland lake, 14°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora Q (upland lake, 18°C) did.
Flora S (upland lake, 14°C) had a higher percentage of toothed-margin species than Flora R (streamside, 14°C) did.

So the example has to compare a streamside flora with a non-streamside flora at the same temperature, and the streamside flora has to have the higher percentage. Floras P and Q were both 18°C, P is streamside, and P has 41% against Q's 27%. Setting is the only thing that differs between them, so the difference can be put down to setting.

B.why: This is the second-order trap. You saw correctly that the example needs streamside versus non-streamside, and R (55%) is higher than Q (27%). But R is also 4°C cooler than Q, and cooler climates have more toothed species anyway. The gap could come entirely from temperature, so it doesn't show what setting does when temperature is held equal.

C.why: This reading is accurate: S (38%) is higher than Q (27%). But both floras come from upland lakes. The only difference is temperature, so this shows the familiar temperature effect, not Haldane's point about streamside settings. You picked a true comparison that doesn't prove the passage's claim.
