items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus: City planners often widen sidewalks by narrowing traffic lanes, expecting the added room to draw more pedestrians. In hot months, however, unshaded concrete absorbs heat, and hot pavement discourages walking, so extra sidewalk space may attract few people unless something keeps it cool. After studying 40 downtown blocks from 2023 to 2025, urban planner Tomás Reyes-Whitfield concluded that widening sidewalks increased summer afternoon foot traffic only on blocks where street trees shaded the sidewalk. For example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
choices: widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 8% for unwidened, shaded blocks, while widened and unwidened unshaded blocks each gained 4%.
widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 4% for widened, unshaded blocks, while unwidened, shaded blocks gained just 8%.
widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 4% for unwidened, unshaded blocks, while unwidened, shaded blocks gained just 8%.
widened, shaded blocks gained 24%, versus 8% for unwidened, shaded blocks, while widened, unshaded blocks gained more than unwidened ones.
items.explanation: The word 'only' means the example has to show two things. First, among shaded blocks, widening raised foot traffic: widened blocks gained 24% and unwidened blocks gained 8%. Second, among unshaded blocks, widening made no difference: widened and unwidened blocks both gained 4%. Choice A is the only option that states both comparisons, each with shade held constant. Together they show that widening helped where there was shade and did not help where there wasn't.

B.why: These numbers are read correctly, but the main comparison (24% versus 4%) is between two widened blocks that differ in shade. That shows shade matters once a sidewalk is widened. It doesn't show what widening does on unshaded blocks, because there's no unwidened, unshaded baseline. The 4% could still be a gain caused by widening, so 'only on shaded blocks' isn't established.

C.why: Comparing widened, shaded blocks (24%) with unwidened, unshaded blocks (4%) changes two things at once. The gap could come from widening, from shade, or from both, so it can't show that widening works only where there is shade. You went with the biggest gap on the graph instead of a comparison that isolates widening.

D.why: This choice starts with the right comparison, which is why it's tempting once you've found the key idea. But it finishes by misreading the graph: widened and unwidened unshaded blocks both gained 4%, so neither gained more. And if widening had helped unshaded blocks, that would undercut the word 'only' in the claim rather than support it.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
Low-frequency traffic noise can mask birdsong, and birds in noisy places often sing with a higher minimum frequency. Because cities are noisy, it is hard to tell whether this shift responds to noise itself or to other features of urban life. After recording great tits at four sites, a research team concluded that traffic noise outweighed setting, urban or rural, in predicting a site's minimum song frequency. For example, ______

Minimum Song Frequency of Great Tits at Four Sites
Site | Setting | Traffic noise (dB) | Minimum frequency (kHz)
P | Urban | 68 | 3.4
Q | Urban | 49 | 2.6
R | Rural | 67 | 3.3
S | Rural | 47 | 2.5
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: urban site P had a higher minimum frequency than rural site S.
rural site R had a higher minimum frequency than rural site S.
rural site R had a higher minimum frequency than urban site Q.
urban site Q had a higher minimum frequency than rural site R.
items.explanation: To show that noise outweighs setting, you need a case where the two pull in opposite directions. Site R is rural but noisy (67 dB), and site Q is urban but quiet (49 dB). R's higher minimum frequency (3.3 kHz against 2.6 kHz) means noise won even though the setting pointed the other way.

A.why: This is true, but P is both urban and noisy while S is both rural and quiet. Either factor could explain the gap, so it can't show that one outweighs the other.

B.why: You saw that you needed to separate noise from setting, and this does show that noise matters when setting is held constant. But the claim is that noise outweighs setting, and only a comparison that sets the two against each other can show that.

D.why: You reversed the data. Q's minimum frequency is 2.6 kHz, which is lower than R's 3.3 kHz.

items.stimulus:
Soluble fibers such as beta-glucan thicken the contents of the small intestine, and that added viscosity slows the rate at which glucose passes into the blood. A nutrition team therefore argued that what blunts the rise in blood glucose after a meal is the viscosity a fiber creates, not simply the amount of fiber a food contains. As evidence, the team noted that ______

Blood Glucose After Eating Four Test Breads
Bread | Added fiber | Intestinal viscosity (mPa·s) | Peak glucose rise (mmol/L)
W | None | 5 | 3.2
X | 6 g cellulose | 6 | 3.1
Y | 3 g beta-glucan | 240 | 2.0
Z | 6 g beta-glucan | 410 | 1.4
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: bread Z, which contained 6 grams of added fiber, produced a smaller glucose rise than bread W, which contained none.
bread Y, which contained 3 grams of added fiber, produced a smaller glucose rise than bread X, which contained 6 grams.
bread Z, which contained 6 grams of added fiber, produced a smaller glucose rise than bread Y, which contained 3 grams.
bread X, which contained 6 grams of added fiber, produced a smaller glucose rise than bread Y, which contained 3 grams.
items.explanation: To show it is viscosity rather than amount, you need a bread with less fiber but more viscosity that still does better. Bread Y has half the fiber of bread X but far more viscosity (240 against 6), and it produced the smaller rise (2.0 against 3.1). That beats an explanation based on amount alone.

items.stimulus:
Fly ash, a by-product of burning coal, can replace part of the cement in concrete. It reacts slowly, gradually filling pores that would otherwise let chloride from road salt seep in and corrode steel reinforcement; lower penetration values indicate better resistance. Because of that slow reaction, engineers testing bridge-deck mixes argued that the standard 28-day test understates the advantage fly ash gives over plain concrete. For example, ______

Chloride Penetration of Concrete Samples (coulombs)
Curing time | Plain mix | 25% fly ash mix
28 days | 3,300 | 3,150
90 days | 2,900 | 1,250
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: the fly ash mix allowed 1,900 fewer coulombs through at 90 days than it had allowed at 28 days.
the plain mix improved by more between 28 and 90 days than the fly ash mix improved.
at 90 days, the fly ash mix allowed 1,650 fewer coulombs through than the plain mix did.
the fly ash mix's advantage over the plain mix grew from 150 coulombs to 1,650 coulombs.
items.explanation: The claim is about the advantage over plain concrete, which is a gap between the two mixes, and about how that gap looks at 28 days compared with later. A printmaker tested two inks on the same woodblock and paper. She defines an ink's clean-print rate as the number of clean prints divided by the total number of prints pulled. She claims that oil-based ink has a higher clean-print rate than water-based ink.

items.stimulus:
Winter cover crops such as cereal rye are planted after harvest and killed in spring, which leaves a layer of residue on the soil surface. That residue slows evaporation, so the soil under it holds more water into midsummer, when corn is most sensitive to moisture stress. Agronomists at a Nebraska research farm compared corn grown after rye with corn grown on bare soil over eight seasons, four wet and four dry. They concluded that a rye cover crop raises corn yields in dry seasons, when the extra stored water matters most.

Average Corn Yield (bushels per acre)
Season type | Bare soil | After rye
Wet | 182 | 176
Dry | 131 | 154
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the agronomists' conclusion?
choices: In wet seasons, corn grown on bare soil yielded 182 bushels per acre, while corn grown after rye yielded 176.
Corn grown on bare soil yielded 182 bushels per acre in wet seasons but only 131 bushels per acre in dry seasons.
In dry seasons, corn grown after rye yielded 154 bushels per acre, while corn grown on bare soil yielded 131.
Corn grown after rye yielded more per acre than corn grown on bare soil in both wet seasons and dry seasons.

B.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice holds the treatment fixed at bare soil and compares weather conditions. That shows drought lowers yield, not that rye raises it.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
When seismic waves pass from hard bedrock into the soft sediments that fill many valleys, they slow down and grow in amplitude, so the ground shakes harder. Seismologists express this as an amplification factor: peak shaking at a sediment site divided by peak shaking at a nearby bedrock site. Distant earthquakes arrive dominated by long-period waves, which sediment layers tend to resonate with. For that reason, one team hypothesized that basin sediments amplify shaking from distant earthquakes more than shaking from nearby ones.

Average Peak Ground Acceleration (cm/s²)
Earthquake distance | Bedrock sites | Sediment sites
Under 50 km | 120 | 180
Over 150 km | 20 | 50
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the team's hypothesis?
choices: For nearby earthquakes, sediment sites exceeded bedrock sites by 60 cm/s², whereas for distant ones the gap was only 30 cm/s².
Sediment sites recorded stronger shaking than bedrock sites did for both nearby earthquakes and distant earthquakes.
Shaking at sediment sites was 2.5 times that at bedrock sites for nearby earthquakes but 1.5 times for distant ones.
Shaking at sediment sites was 2.5 times that at bedrock sites for distant earthquakes but 1.5 times for nearby ones.
items.explanation: The passage defines amplification as a ratio, sediment divided by bedrock. So you have to compute it: 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 for distant earthquakes and 180 ÷ 120 = 1.5 for nearby ones. Choice D shows that distant earthquakes are amplified more, which is what the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: You used raw differences when the passage defined amplification as a ratio. The gaps are accurate, but subtraction doesn't measure the amplification factor. Measured as a ratio, the result goes the other way.

B.why: You chose a true statement that supports a broader claim, that sediments amplify shaking at all. The hypothesis is about which distance is amplified more, and this choice doesn't compare the two.

C.why: You reversed the ratios. Nearby earthquakes give 180 ÷ 120 = 1.5, and distant ones give 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5, not the other way around.

items.stimulus:
Hillshading simulates the shadows that terrain casts under light from one direction. It is often added to contour maps to make relief easier to see. Cartographer Tomasz Wierzbicki asked novice and experienced map readers to identify the easiest walking routes on contour-only or hillshaded versions of the same maps. Experienced readers can already picture terrain from contour lines alone. Wierzbicki therefore hypothesized that hillshading would improve novices' accuracy more than it would improve experienced readers' accuracy.

Route Choices Judged Correct (%)
Reader group | Contour-only map | Hillshaded map
Novice | 58 | 64
Experienced | 71 | 83
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to weaken Wierzbicki's hypothesis?

Novices chose correct routes 64% of the time with hillshaded maps and 58% of the time with contour-only maps.
Experienced readers chose correct routes more often than novices did with both contour-only and hillshaded maps.
Hillshading raised novices' accuracy by 12 percentage points but raised experienced readers' accuracy by only 6 points.

Economists who study employee turnover often find that workers leave jobs when their schedules clash with obligations outside work. Employee group | On-site | Remote-eligible

Non-caregivers | 11 | 10

items.stimulus:
Vaccine adjuvants are added to stimulate the innate immune cells that help launch an antibody response, and these cells become less responsive with age. Researchers gave younger and older adults a flu vaccine with or without an experimental adjuvant. They measured antibody titers before vaccination and four weeks after. Because baseline titers differ by age, they compared groups using the fold rise: the post-vaccination titer divided by the pre-vaccination titer. They hypothesized that the adjuvant would benefit older adults more than younger adults.

Mean Antibody Titer
Group | Pre-vaccination | Post-vaccination
Younger, standard vaccine | 50 | 400
Younger, with adjuvant | 50 | 500
Older, standard vaccine | 10 | 30
Older, with adjuvant | 10 | 90
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: The adjuvant raised younger adults' post-vaccination titer by 100, compared with a rise of only 60 for older adults.
The adjuvant raised older adults' fold rise from 3 to 9 but raised younger adults' fold rise only from 8 to 10.
Older adults given the adjuvant reached a titer of 90, three times the 30 reached with the standard vaccine.
Older adults given the adjuvant showed a larger fold rise than younger adults given the same adjuvant did.
items.explanation: The researchers measure benefit using fold rise, so you have to compute it for all four rows. For older adults, fold rise went from 3 (30 ÷ 10) to 9 (90 ÷ 10). For younger adults, it went from 8 (400 ÷ 50) to 10 (500 ÷ 50). Older adults gained far more, as the hypothesis predicts.

D.why: You misread the adjuvant rows. With the adjuvant, older adults' fold rise was 9 and younger adults' was 10, so older adults' fold rise was not larger. The hypothesis concerns the size of the gain, not the final fold rise.

Adding clay platelets a few nanometers thick to a polymer can stiffen it by restricting how freely its molecular chains slide past one another. Test temperature | Without nanoclay | With nanoclay

120°C | 0.6 | 1.4

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
In many songbirds, both parents carry insects to the nest, and a larger brood means more hungry mouths per trip. Ecologists watching blue tit nests counted parents' feeding visits per hour at broods of three and of six chicks. They made counts in a year when caterpillars were plentiful and in a year when a late frost made them scarce. They measured provisioning as visits per chick: hourly visits divided by brood size. They concluded that when food is scarce, chicks in large broods are fed less often than chicks in small broods.

Parental Feeding Visits per Hour
Year | Brood of three | Brood of six
Plentiful caterpillars | 12 | 24
Scarce caterpillars | 12 | 15
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the ecologists' conclusion?
choices: In the scarce year, parents of six-chick broods made 15 visits per hour, more than the 12 made by parents of three-chick broods.
In the scarce year, chicks in broods of six received 2.5 visits each per hour, while chicks in broods of three received 4.
In the plentiful year, parents of six-chick broods made 24 visits per hour, twice the 12 made by parents of three-chick broods.
In the plentiful year, chicks in broods of six received fewer visits each per hour than chicks in broods of three did.
items.explanation: The conclusion applies to the scarce year and depends on visits per chick, so you have to divide. In the scarce year, 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5 visits per chick in large broods and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 in small broods. Chicks in large broods were fed less often, as the ecologists concluded.

items.stimulus:
Cyclist Ridership and Injuries by Corridor Type
Corridor type | Period | Daily cyclists | Annual cyclist injuries

Protected lanes | After | 5,000 | 20
Painted lanes | Before | 2,000 | 14
Painted lanes | After | 2,500 | 20

When a city separates bike lanes from traffic with curbs or planters, ridership on those streets often climbs, so total crash counts can rise even if each trip becomes safer. items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: on protected-lane corridors, annual injuries rose from 16 to 20, matching the final total recorded on painted-lane corridors.
on protected-lane corridors, the injury rate fell from 8 to 4 per 1,000 daily cyclists but rose from 7 to 8 on painted-lane ones.
on protected-lane corridors, daily cyclists rose from 2,000 to 5,000, a far larger gain than painted-lane corridors experienced.
on painted-lane corridors, the injury rate fell from 8 to 7 per 1,000 daily cyclists, a smaller drop than protected lanes saw.

items.stimulus:
Many songbirds sing at dawn, when the air is still and sound carries far. Ornithologist Talia Brenner noticed that house wrens nesting along a commuter highway in Ohio seemed to start singing unusually early, possibly to finish before the morning traffic peaks. Traffic on that highway is far lighter on weekends. Brenner therefore reasoned that if traffic, rather than some other feature of roadside habitat, causes the early start, the shift should shrink on weekends. Her data support this hypothesis: ______

Mean Start of Dawn Song (minutes before sunrise)
Nest location | Weekdays | Weekends
Roadside | 52 | 38
Forest interior | 36 | 35
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

roadside wrens began singing 52 minutes before sunrise on weekdays but only 38 minutes before on weekends, while forest-interior wrens shifted by just 1 minute.

items.stimulus:
In many shrublands, rodents eat or store a large share of the seeds that fall to the ground. Ecologist Amaka Okafor suspected that fire alters this pattern. Burning clears the low cover that rodents use to hide from owls and foxes, so it should make them less willing to linger over large seeds, which take a long time to husk. Their harvest of small, quickly eaten seeds should stay largely unchanged. Because the burned plots were smaller, Okafor set out fewer seeds in them.

Seeds Removed by Rodents After 10 Days
Plot type | Seed size | Seeds set out | Seeds removed
Unburned | Large | 400 | 240
Burned | Large | 200 | 60
Unburned | Small | 400 | 100
Burned | Small | 200 | 50
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Okafor's hypothesis?
choices: Rodents removed 240 of 400 large seeds from unburned plots but 60 of 200 from burned plots, and one-fourth of the small seeds in each plot type.
Rodents removed 240 large seeds from unburned plots but only 60 from burned plots, and 100 small seeds from unburned plots but only 50 from burned plots.
In burned plots, rodents removed 60 large seeds and 50 small seeds, so they took only slightly more large seeds than small seeds there.
In burned plots, rodents removed a smaller proportion of the large seeds set out than of the small seeds set out in those same plots.
items.explanation: Burned plots received half as many seeds, so raw counts can't be compared. You have to compare proportions. For large seeds, removal fell from 60% (240 of 400) to 30% (60 of 200). items.stimulus:
When an athlete's core body temperature climbs toward about 40°C, the brain reduces muscle activation, and the athlete slows or stops. items.stimulus:
Folklorists have long noted that children who hear a familiar tale often object if a teller strays from the expected wording. Community | Told to children | Told to adults
With printed collections | 81 | 77

The team then measured each rider's body mass and sustained power. The coaches claim that interval training produced the better climbers, even though it yielded lower total power.

Mean Results After Ten Weeks
Training group | Body mass (kg) | Sustained power (watts)
Heavy resistance | 80 | 320
Intense intervals | 60 | 270
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the coaches' claim?
choices: The interval group averaged 4.5 watts per kilogram, compared with 4.0 watts per kilogram for the resistance group.
The resistance group sustained an average of 320 watts, which is 50 watts more than the interval group sustained.
The interval group's riders weighed an average of 20 kilograms less than the resistance group's riders weighed.
The resistance group averaged more watts per kilogram of body mass than the interval group averaged after training.
items.explanation: The passage says climbing depends on watts per kilogram, so you have to compute that ratio for each group: 270 ÷ 60 = 4.5 for intervals and 320 ÷ 80 = 4.0 for resistance. The interval group comes out ahead on the measure that predicts climbing, even with lower raw power, which matches the claim.

B.why: This is accurate, but it uses raw power. The passage says raw power is not what decides climbing, and the claim expects the interval group to have less of it. You read the raw values instead of computing the ratio the passage defined.

C.why: Body mass is only half of the ratio. A lighter rider climbs better only if their power doesn't drop too much. You stopped after one part of the calculation.

D.why: The resistance group averaged 4.0 W/kg, which is lower than the interval group's 4.5. You may have assumed that more total watts means more watts per kilogram.

items.stimulus:
In many maritime and farming traditions, work songs use call-and-response: a leader sings a line and the group answers. Ethnomusicologist Adaeze Okafor examined 400 transcribed work songs. She sorted them by the size of the crew that sang them and by whether the task they accompanied, such as hauling a rope, required workers to move in unison. Okafor concludes that larger crews favored call-and-response, but only for tasks that demanded synchronized movement.

Share of Song Lines in Call-and-Response Form (%)
Crew size | Synchronized tasks | Unsynchronized tasks
Small (2–4 workers) | 30 | 25
Large (10 or more workers) | 70 | 27
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Okafor's conclusion?
choices: Large crews doing synchronized tasks used call-and-response in 70% of lines, the highest share of any group.
For both synchronized and unsynchronized tasks, large crews used call-and-response far more than small crews.
Small crews used call-and-response at similar rates for synchronized and unsynchronized tasks, 30% and 25%.
For synchronized tasks, the share rose from 30% to 70% with crew size; for other tasks, it barely changed.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus: Folklorists have long debated why oral tales become more uniform over time. Rhea Castellanos studied one widespread tale, counting how many distinct endings appeared among variants collected in coastal and inland villages in the 1880s and in the 1950s. Printed tale collections reached the coastal villages around 1900 but did not circulate inland until the 1970s. Castellanos hypothesizes that printed collections reduced the variety of endings by giving tellers a single fixed version to imitate.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Castellanos's hypothesis?
choices: In the 1880s, coastal and inland villages had the same number of distinct endings, with 12 recorded in each.
Coastal villages fell from 12 distinct endings to 4, while inland villages fell only from 12 to 10.
Inland villages had fewer distinct endings in the 1950s than in the 1880s, dropping from 12 to 10.
Coastal villages had more distinct endings in the 1950s than inland villages had in the 1950s.
items.explanation: Use the passage to decide the direction first. Between the 1880s and the 1950s, only the coastal villages had print, so if print reduced variety, endings should drop sharply on the coast and change little inland. The coast falls from 12 to 4, while inland falls only from 12 to 10. That contrast links the decline to print.

D.why: In the 1950s, coastal villages had 4 distinct endings and inland villages had 10, so the coast had fewer, not more. You reversed the comparison.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Adjuvants are substances added to vaccines to provoke a stronger immune reaction. Because the immune system weakens with age, older animals often respond poorly to a vaccine given alone. Immunologist Rana Okafor and colleagues vaccinated young and old mice, either with or without an adjuvant, and four weeks later measured antibody levels in the animals' blood. The researchers hypothesized that the adjuvant would increase antibody levels by a greater amount in old mice than in young mice.

Mean Antibody Level Four Weeks After Vaccination (units per milliliter)
Age group | Without adjuvant | With adjuvant
Young | 40 | 60
Old | 15 | 45
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: Among mice given the adjuvant, young mice had antibody levels 15 units higher than old mice did.
The adjuvant raised antibody levels by 30 units in old mice but by only 20 units in young mice.
The adjuvant raised antibody levels by 30 units in young mice but by only 20 units in old mice.
The adjuvant raised old mice's antibody levels by 30 units, to match young mice given the adjuvant.
items.explanation: The hypothesis is about the size of the adjuvant's effect in each age group, so you need two gaps. For each row, subtract the 'without' number from the 'with' number. For old mice the gap is 45 − 15 = 30. For young mice it is 60 − 40 = 20. A gain of 30 is bigger than a gain of 20, which is exactly what the hypothesis predicts, so this choice supports it.

A.why: The number is right (60 − 45 = 15), but you compared the wrong cells. This compares the two age groups within one column. The hypothesis is about how much the adjuvant changes each group's level, so you need the gap within each row.

C.why: You worked out the right two gaps but gave them to the wrong groups. The table shows a 20-unit gain for young mice and a 30-unit gain for old mice, not the other way around.

D.why: The 30-unit gain is correct, but the choice claims more than the table shows. Old mice given the adjuvant reached 45 units, still well below the 60 units of young mice given the adjuvant, so the two groups did not match.

items.stimulus:
Folklorists have long asked whether printed collections flatten regional folktales. When a tale passes by word of mouth, tellers tend to tie it to nearby places, a habit that may fade once a standard printed version circulates. Folklorist Ines Varga recorded tellings of one legend across a mountain region, noting where each teller lived, how the teller had learned the tale, and whether the telling named a local landmark. Varga concluded that how a tale is learned makes a bigger difference to landmark mentions in villages than in towns.

Tellings That Name a Local Landmark (%)
Where teller lives | Learned orally | Learned from print
Village | 72 | 30
Town | 48 | 40
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Varga's conclusion?
choices: Among tellers who learned the tale orally, village tellings named a landmark 24 percentage points more often than town tellings did.
Orally learned tellings named a landmark 8 percentage points more often than print-learned ones in villages and 42 points more often in towns.
In both villages and towns, orally learned tellings named a landmark at least 40 percentage points more often than print-learned ones did.
Orally learned tellings named a landmark 42 percentage points more often than print-learned ones in villages but only 8 points more often in towns.
items.explanation: Varga's claim compares how much the way a tale is learned matters in two places. That means two gaps, one for each row. In villages, oral minus print is 72 − 30 = 42 points. In towns it is 48 − 40 = 8 points. The gap is far wider in villages, so this choice makes the comparison the conclusion needs.

A.why: The number is right (72 − 48 = 24), but you compared the wrong cells. This compares villages with towns among oral learners only. The conclusion is about the gap between oral and print learners within each place.

B.why: You found the right two gaps but swapped them. The 42-point gap belongs to villages and the 8-point gap belongs to towns, so this version turns the finding around.

C.why: You took the village result and applied it to towns too. The town gap is only 48 − 40 = 8 points, nowhere near 40.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Most printed maps put north at the top, so a traveler heading south must mentally rotate the map to decide which way to turn. Some navigation displays instead rotate the map so that the traveler's direction always points up. Cartographer Tomas Lindqvist suspected that the burden of mental rotation grows with the number of possible turns. His team had participants walk unfamiliar routes with one kind of map or the other and counted wrong turns. The researchers concluded that heading-up maps reduce errors chiefly at complex intersections.

Mean Wrong Turns per Route
Intersection type | North-up map | Heading-up map
Simple | 1.2 | 1.0
Complex | 4.6 | 2.2
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?
choices: At complex intersections, heading-up map users made 2.4 fewer wrong turns than north-up users did, compared with 0.2 fewer at simple intersections.
At simple intersections, heading-up map users made 2.4 fewer wrong turns than north-up users did, compared with 0.2 fewer at complex intersections.
North-up map users made 3.4 more wrong turns at complex intersections than they made at simple intersections, on average, across the routes.
Heading-up map users made fewer than half as many wrong turns as north-up users did at both simple and complex intersections.
items.explanation: The conclusion says the heading-up map's advantage shows up mainly at complex intersections. So you need the map gap within each row. At complex intersections it is 4.6 − 2.2 = 2.4 fewer wrong turns. At simple intersections it is 1.2 − 1.0 = 0.2. Nearly all the benefit falls at complex intersections, which is what 'chiefly' requires.

B.why: You calculated both gaps correctly but gave them to the wrong intersection types. The 2.4 reduction happens at complex intersections, not simple ones.

C.why: The number is right (4.6 − 1.2 = 3.4), but it comes from the north-up column only. It shows that complex intersections cause more errors, but it says nothing about whether heading-up maps cut those errors. The conclusion depends on comparing the two maps.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Living woody plants in cool climates tend to have leaves with toothed edges, while those in warm climates more often have smooth edges. Paleobotanists therefore use the share of toothed species in a fossil flora to estimate past temperatures. Studying four fossil sites that span a regional cooling event, Anika Rautio and colleagues hypothesized that the cooling raised the share of toothed species at inland sites but barely changed it at coastal sites, where the nearby ocean kept temperatures steady.

Share of Fossil Species with Toothed Leaf Margins (%)
Site | Before cooling | After cooling
Inland site 1 | 30 | 48
Inland site 2 | 26 | 41
Coastal site 1 | 33 | 34
Coastal site 2 | 29 | 30
items.stem: Which choice does NOT effectively use data from the table to support Rautio and colleagues' hypothesis?
choices: Inland site 1 rose from 30% to 48% toothed species, while coastal site 1 rose only from 33% to 34%.
Inland site 2 gained 15 percentage points of toothed species, while coastal site 2 gained just 1 point.
After cooling, both inland sites topped 40%, while each coastal site ended within 1 point of where it began.
Before cooling, coastal site 1 had a larger share of toothed species (33%) than inland site 1 did (30%).
items.explanation: The hypothesis is about change over time: inland sites should rise a lot from before to after the cooling, and coastal sites should barely move. To support it, a choice has to compare before and after for both kinds of site. Choice D reads the table correctly, but it uses only the 'Before cooling' column and compares two sites at a single moment. It says nothing about what the cooling did, so it does not support the hypothesis.

A.why: This choice gives both the before and after values for an inland site and a coastal site, and the inland site rises 18 points while the coastal site rises 1. That is exactly the contrast the hypothesis predicts. If you rejected it, you may have thought one pair of sites was too little evidence, but the question asks whether the choice uses the data to support the claim, and it does.

B.why: You have to do the subtraction yourself here: 41 − 26 = 15 and 30 − 29 = 1. Both are correct, and a large inland gain next to a tiny coastal gain supports the hypothesis. If you picked this, you probably made an arithmetic slip or expected raw table values and distrusted a computed difference.

C.why: This one looks as if it reads only the 'After cooling' column, which is the subtype's usual trap. It doesn't. 'Within 1 point of where it began' compares each coastal site with its earlier value, and both inland sites started below 30% before ending above 40%, so the before-and-after contrast is all there. You fell for the look of a single-column comparison without checking what the wording actually compares.

items.stimulus:
After harvest, nitrate fertilizer left in a field can wash down past the roots and into groundwater. Because water drains quickly through the large pores of sandy soil, these losses tend to be greatest there. A winter cover crop such as cereal rye can absorb leftover nitrate before it drains away. Agronomist Tomás Ferreira therefore hypothesized that a rye cover crop would sharply reduce nitrate leaching in sandy soil but would have little effect in loam or clay.

Nitrate Lost to Leaching (kilograms per hectare)
Soil type | No cover crop | Rye cover crop
Sandy | 48 | 21
Loam | 19 | 17
Clay | 12 | 11
items.stem: Which choice does NOT effectively use data from the table to support Ferreira's hypothesis?
choices: Plots with rye lost less nitrate than plots without rye in sandy, loam, and clay soil alike.
In sandy soil, rye cut nitrate loss from 48 to 21 kg per hectare, but in loam only from 19 to 17.
Rye reduced nitrate loss by 27 kg per hectare in sandy soil but by just 1 kg per hectare in clay.
Sandy plots lost over twice as much nitrate without rye as with it, while clay plots lost about the same either way.

That supports a broader claim, 'rye reduces leaching', and ignores the sandy-versus-finer-soil contrast the hypothesis is about, so it does not support it.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Giant planets are thought to begin as rocky cores that must grow large enough to capture gas before a young star's disk disperses. Metal-rich disks supply more solid material, so cores grow faster. Red dwarfs have small disks that sit near the limit for forming giant planets at all. Astronomer Leila Haddad therefore hypothesized that metal richness raises giant-planet rates proportionally more for red dwarfs than for Sun-like stars, as measured by each type's boost ratio: the rate among metal-rich stars divided by the rate among metal-poor stars.

Stars Hosting at Least One Giant Planet (%)
Star type | Metal-poor | Metal-rich
Sun-like | 4 | 12
Red dwarf | 1 | 5
items.stem: Which choice does NOT effectively use data from the table to support Haddad's hypothesis?
choices: Metal-poor red dwarfs host giant planets at 1% and metal-rich ones at 5%, a boost ratio above that of Sun-like stars.
Metal richness raised the Sun-like rate by 8 percentage points but raised the red dwarf rate by only 4 points.
Metal richness made red dwarfs five times as likely to host giant planets but Sun-like stars only three times as likely.
Sun-like stars outpace red dwarfs fourfold among metal-poor stars but only 2.4-fold among metal-rich stars.
items.explanation: The passage defines the comparison as a ratio, so first work out each boost ratio: red dwarfs 5 ÷ 1 = 5, Sun-like stars 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The hypothesis needs the red dwarf ratio to be larger, and it is. Choice B uses raw percentage-point gains instead. Those numbers are accurate, but they make the Sun-like stars look more affected (8 points against 4), so B does not support the hypothesis. It is the raw-values trap the passage set up by defining a ratio.

A.why: This choice states the red dwarf values (1% and 5%, a ratio of 5) and says that ratio is higher than the Sun-like ratio (12 ÷ 4 = 3), which is true. If you rejected it because it gives no number for the Sun-like ratio, you needed only to check that the comparison holds, and it does.

C.why: 'Five times as likely' and 'three times as likely' are the boost ratios in plain words: 5 ÷ 1 and 12 ÷ 4. If you picked this, you probably compared raw gains (4 points against 8) and decided the choice reversed the table. The passage asks for a ratio, and by that measure this choice is right.

D.why: This looks like the subtype's wrong-series trap, because it compares the two star types instead of the two metallicity groups. But 4 ÷ 1 = 4 and 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4. If the Sun-like advantage shrinks as metallicity rises, red dwarfs must gain proportionally more, which is Haddad's hypothesis. You rejected a valid comparison because of how it was framed, without checking what it implies.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Drinking an ice slurry before exercise, known as precooling, lowers an athlete's starting core temperature. This delays the point at which overheating forces the athlete to stop. Researchers divided 40 cyclists into four groups by two factors: whether they were acclimatized to heat and whether they precooled. Each group then rode to exhaustion once at 20°C and once at 35°C. The groups differed in baseline fitness, so the team compared each group's heat penalty: the percentage by which its hot-ride time fell short of its temperate-ride time. The researchers hypothesize that precooling reduces the heat penalty only for cyclists who are not acclimatized to heat.

Average Time to Exhaustion (minutes)
Cyclist group | Precooling | Temperate ride | Hot ride

items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: Precooling raised hot-ride time by 18 minutes for non-acclimatized cyclists but by only 16 minutes for acclimatized cyclists.
Precooling cut the heat penalty from 40% to 20% for non-acclimatized cyclists but left it at 20% for acclimatized cyclists.
Without precooling, the heat penalty was 40% for non-acclimatized cyclists but only 20% for acclimatized cyclists.
Precooling cut the heat penalty from 40% to 20% for non-acclimatized cyclists and from 20% to 10% for acclimatized cyclists.
items.explanation: The hypothesis has two parts, and both are about the heat penalty, not raw times. Non-acclimatized: (50 − 30)/50 = 40% without precooling and (60 − 48)/60 = 20% with it. Acclimatized: (40 − 32)/40 = 20% without and (60 − 48)/60 = 20% with. The numbers are correct, but raw gains mix precooling's effect with each group's baseline. items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
A city's heat island intensity is the temperature at an urban site minus the temperature at a nearby rural site, both measured at the same time. One proposed mechanism holds that asphalt and concrete absorb sunlight by day, store it as heat, and release it after sunset. This keeps cities warm while the countryside cools. Meteorologist Ana Okafor recorded temperatures at paired sites through one summer. Clouds limit how much sunlight pavement can absorb, so she reasoned that the mechanism makes a firm prediction only for clear days. She hypothesizes that on clear days, heat island intensity is greater at night than in the afternoon.

Average Summer Temperatures (°C) at Paired Sites
Sky | Time | Urban site | Rural site
Clear | Afternoon | 31 | 26
Clear | Night | 21 | 18
Cloudy | Afternoon | 25 | 22
Cloudy | Night | 19 | 17
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that weaken Okafor's hypothesis?
choices: On clear days, the urban site cooled from 31°C in the afternoon to 21°C at night.
On cloudy days, the heat island intensity was 3°C in the afternoon and 2°C at night.
On clear days, the heat island intensity was 5°C in the afternoon and 3°C at night.
At night, the heat island intensity was 3°C on clear days and 2°C on cloudy days.
items.explanation: Start by writing down the prediction: on clear days, urban minus rural should be larger at night than in the afternoon. To weaken it, the data must show the clear-day intensity at night is the same as or smaller than in the afternoon. Clear afternoon: 31 − 26 = 5°C. Clear night: 21 − 18 = 3°C. The intensity shrinks after dark, which is the opposite of what Okafor predicts, and choice C reports exactly that comparison.

A.why: You read a raw urban temperature when the hypothesis is about a difference that the passage defines. A city that cools by 10°C at night tells you nothing about heat island intensity until you know how much the rural site cooled. If the rural site had cooled more, this same fact would fit Okafor's hypothesis.

B.why: You correctly calculated intensities and found a drop from afternoon to night, but you did it under the wrong condition. Okafor says her prediction applies only to clear days, because clouds limit how much heat pavement stores. A cloudy-day result is outside the claim, so it cannot weaken it.

D.why: You compared clear and cloudy nights instead of afternoon and night on clear days. The hypothesis says nothing about how the two sky conditions compare. If anything, a stronger heat island on clear nights fits the pavement mechanism, so this choice does not weaken the claim.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Public health researchers sent text-message reminders to some patients due for the second dose of a two-dose vaccine and compared their completion rates with those of patients who received no reminder. Because missed doses were far more common among patients living far from the clinic, the team judged a reminder's effectiveness by the share of otherwise-missed doses it recovered, not by the raw gain in completion. They hypothesized that, by this measure, reminders would be most effective for the most distant patients. The data, however, do not support this hypothesis: ______

Second-Dose Completion Rate (%)
Distance from clinic | No reminder | Reminder
Under 5 km | 80 | 90
5–15 km | 60 | 78
Over 15 km | 40 | 64
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: reminders raised completion by 24 percentage points for patients over 15 km away but by only 10 points for those under 5 km away.
reminders recovered half of the otherwise-missed doses for patients under 5 km away but only two-fifths for those over 15 km away.
reminders recovered a smaller share of otherwise-missed doses for patients 5–15 km away than for those over 15 km away.
patients over 15 km away who received reminders completed the series at a lower rate than patients under 5 km away who received none.
items.explanation: The passage sets the measure: the share of otherwise-missed doses that reminders recovered. That is the drop in missed doses divided by the missed-dose rate without reminders. Under 5 km, 20% of doses were missed without reminders and reminders recovered 10 points, so 10/20 = one-half. Over 15 km, 60% were missed and reminders recovered 24 points, so 24/60 = two-fifths. The share falls as distance grows, which is the opposite of the hypothesis. That is the result the statement needs.

A.why: Your numbers are right, but you used the raw gain in percentage points, which is the measure the passage tells you the team rejected. On raw gain the hypothesis even looks supported, so this choice can't finish a sentence saying the data do not support it.

C.why: Do the calculation for the middle row: reminders recovered 18 of 40 missed points, or 45%. That is more than the 40% recovered for the over-15 km group, not less.

D.why: This comparison is accurate, but it sets a reminder group against a no-reminder group at a different distance. It says nothing about how effective reminders were within any distance band, which is what the hypothesis is about.

items.stimulus:
Stars rich in heavy elements, or metals, host giant planets more often than metal-poor stars do. The usual explanation is that metal-rich disks of gas and dust build planetary cores faster. Low-mass stars, however, have thin disks that may disperse before any core, however quickly it forms, can grow into a giant. After surveying stars in three mass ranges, astronomers hypothesized that high metallicity raises giant-planet occurrence only for stars of at least 0.7 solar masses.

Stars Hosting a Giant Planet (%)
Stellar mass (solar masses) | Low metallicity | High metallicity
Below 0.7 | 2 | 2
0.7 to 1.2 | 3 | 11
Above 1.2 | 5 | 16
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the astronomers' hypothesis?
choices: High metallicity raised occurrence from 5% to 16% for stars above 1.2 solar masses, more than tripling the rate.
Among high-metallicity stars, occurrence rose from 2% to 16% as stellar mass increased across the three ranges.
High metallicity raised occurrence from 3% to 11% for stars of 0.7 to 1.2 solar masses but not at all below 0.7.
High metallicity raised occurrence in all three mass ranges, though least for stars below 0.7 solar masses.
items.explanation: The hypothesis has two parts, signalled by 'only': metallicity should matter at or above 0.7 solar masses and should not matter below it. To support it, you need a metallicity comparison at both ends of that boundary. C shows a rise from 3% to 11% just above the boundary and no change (2% and 2%) below it.

A.why: You found the right comparison, low against high metallicity, but you stopped after half the claim. The word 'only' means the evidence must also show no effect below 0.7 solar masses, and this choice never looks there.

B.why: This is accurate, but it compares rows within the high-metallicity column, so it shows an effect of stellar mass. The hypothesis is about metallicity's effect within each mass range.

D.why: Below 0.7 solar masses, occurrence is 2% at both metallicities, so high metallicity raised nothing there. This choice describes a small effect that the table doesn't show.

items.stimulus:
Between 1830 and 1880, minor-key hymns were becoming scarcer in churches across one region. A musicologist traces part of this shift to the pipe organ: organists favored the keys that sounded best on the instrument, mostly major ones, and congregations sang what their organists chose. Congregations that bought organs in the 1850s, however, were already using fewer minor-key hymns than other congregations beforehand. The musicologist hypothesizes that acquiring an organ made the existing decline steeper.

Minor-Key Hymns in Congregational Hymnals (% of hymns)
Congregations | 1830–1849 | 1860–1879
Acquired an organ in the 1850s | 26 | 12
Never acquired an organ | 34 | 30
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the musicologist's hypothesis?
choices: In congregations that acquired organs, the minor-key share of hymns fell by more than half, from 26% to 12%.
By 1860–1879, organ congregations' minor-key share (12%) was less than half that of other congregations (30%).
The minor-key share fell by 14 percentage points with organs but by only 4 points in congregations without them.
The minor-key share fell by more in congregations that never acquired organs than in those that did.
items.explanation: The claim is about a steeper decline in congregations with organs, set against a decline that was happening everywhere. You therefore need to compare the size of the drop in each row. The organ congregations fell 14 points (26 to 12) and the others fell 4 points (34 to 30), so the decline was steeper with organs.

A.why: You correctly looked at change over time, but in only one row. The passage says minor-key hymns were declining everywhere, so a drop in organ congregations shows the decline was steeper only when you set it beside the drop in congregations without organs.

D.why: Congregations without organs fell 4 points and organ congregations fell 14, so you have the direction reversed.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
A drainage layer beneath a road is meant to keep water out of the soil that supports the pavement, because saturated soil deforms under traffic and leaves ruts. Engineers built road sections with and without such a layer at wet and dry sites and measured them after five years. They hypothesized that the layer reduces rutting only where it substantially lowers soil moisture, so it should make little difference at dry sites.

Test Section Results After Five Years
Site | Drainage layer | Soil moisture (%) | Rut depth (mm)
Wet | Absent | 24 | 18
Wet | Present | 15 | 9
Dry | Absent | 12 | 8
Dry | Present | 11 | 8
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the engineers' hypothesis?
choices: The layer halved rut depth at wet sites, from 18 mm to 9 mm, showing that it works where the soil is saturated.
The layer cut wet-site moisture by 9 points and halved rutting, but cut dry-site moisture by 1 point and left rutting unchanged.
Dry sections without the layer rutted less than wet sections with the layer did, 8 mm compared with 9 mm.
The layer lowered soil moisture about as much at dry sites as at wet sites but reduced rutting only at wet sites.
items.explanation: The hypothesis ties rutting to moisture and includes the condition 'only where it substantially lowers soil moisture'. Supporting it takes both columns at both kinds of site. At wet sites the layer lowers moisture a lot (24 to 15) and rutting drops (18 to 9). At dry sites moisture barely changes (12 to 11) and rutting stays at 8 mm.

A.why: This is accurate, but it uses only the wet-site rows and only the rut column. It never checks the moisture link the hypothesis depends on, and it never shows that the layer makes little difference at dry sites.

C.why: Both numbers are right, but this compares a dry section without the layer to a wet section with it. Two things differ at once, so the comparison can't isolate what the layer does.

D.why: The layer cut moisture by 9 points at wet sites and by only 1 point at dry sites, so it did not lower moisture about as much at both. If this were true, it would weaken the hypothesis rather than support it.

When a city adds a bike lane, the number of cyclists on that street usually rises, whatever kind of lane it is. Planners in one city cared about something narrower: who rides. Surveys suggest that many women avoid cycling in traffic unless they are physically separated from cars. The planners therefore hypothesized that protected lanes, unlike painted ones, would increase the proportion of cyclists who are women. Counts taken on both kinds of street support this hypothesis: ______

Average Daily Cyclists Counted
Street | Period | Women | Men
Protected lane | Before | 60 | 240
Protected lane | After | 150 | 350
Painted lane | Before | 50 | 200

women's share of cyclists rose from 20% to 30% on protected-lane streets but stayed at 20% on painted-lane streets.
after the lanes were added, protected-lane streets drew more women per day (150) than painted-lane streets did (100).
women's share of cyclists fell on painted-lane streets while it rose on protected-lane streets.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus: Habitual caffeine users often gain less from a pre-race dose of caffeine than people who rarely consume it. Some scientists attribute this to tolerance, which should fade with abstinence. Others suspect that habitual users simply differ from nonusers in some lasting way. Runners completed a 3 km time trial after taking caffeine and, on another day, after taking a placebo. Habitual users were tested twice: once on their usual routine and again after seven days without caffeine. The researchers concluded that tolerance, not a lasting difference, explains the smaller benefit.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researchers' conclusion?
choices: On their usual routine, habitual users ran 4 seconds faster with caffeine than with placebo, while nonusers ran 12 seconds faster.
After abstaining, habitual users ran 12 seconds faster with caffeine than with placebo, the same gain that nonusers showed.
After abstaining, habitual users' caffeine time (640 seconds) was slower than their caffeine time on their usual routine (636 seconds).
After abstaining, habitual users gained less from caffeine than they had gained on their usual routine.
items.explanation: The benefit is each group's placebo time minus its caffeine time, so you have to compute it rather than read single bars. The conclusion picks tolerance over a lasting difference, so the evidence must show that abstinence brings the benefit back. After abstaining, habitual users gained 652 − 640 = 12 seconds, which matches nonusers' 660 − 648 = 12. If habitual users differed in some lasting way, the gap would have stayed.

A.why: You computed the benefits correctly, but this only confirms what the passage already accepts: habitual users gain less. Both explanations predict that, so it can't separate tolerance from a lasting difference.

C.why: This compares raw caffeine-trial times across two test periods. It ignores the placebo baseline, which also moved, so it says nothing about how much caffeine helped.

D.why: After abstaining, the benefit was 12 seconds. On the usual routine it was 4 seconds. The gain grew rather than shrank.

figure.alt: Bar graph of average 3 km times: nonusers 660 s with placebo and 648 s with caffeine; habitual users on their usual routine 640 s with placebo and 636 s with caffeine; habitual users after abstaining 652 s with placebo and 640 s with caffeine.

In one region, a common folktale ends in one of two ways: the trickster either escapes or is punished. From about 1850, local presses printed cheap chapbook versions of the tale, nearly all with the punishment ending. A folklorist hypothesizes that this ending spread mainly through the chapbooks rather than by word of mouth. If so, tellers who could read should favor it over tellers who could not, but only in towns where chapbooks were printed and sold.

Recorded Versions Ending in Punishment (%)
Town | Tellers who could read | Tellers who could not read
With a print shop | 70 | 35
Without a print shop | 30 | 28
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the folklorist's hypothesis?

Tellers who could not read used the punishment ending more often in print-shop towns than in other towns.
Readers used the ending 35 points more often than nonreaders in print-shop towns but only 2 points more often elsewhere.
In towns without a print shop, tellers who could not read used the punishment ending more often than readers did.

So you compare the reader–nonreader difference in each row. It is large in print-shop towns (70 − 35 = 35 points) and almost nothing in other towns (30 − 28 = 2 points).

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus: Older mice produce far fewer antibodies after vaccination than young mice do. Immunologists tested an adjuvant, an additive meant to strengthen the immune response, by vaccinating young and old mice with and without it. Because old mice start from such a low level, the team measured the age deficit as young mice's antibody level divided by old mice's, rather than as the difference between them. They hypothesized that the adjuvant shrinks the age deficit by this measure.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the immunologists' hypothesis?
choices: Young mice's antibody levels were four times old mice's without the adjuvant but only twice old mice's with it.
The adjuvant raised antibody levels by 400 units in young mice and by the same 400 units in old mice.
Old mice given the adjuvant still had lower antibody levels than young mice given no adjuvant.
The adjuvant multiplied young mice's antibody levels by a larger factor than it multiplied old mice's.
items.explanation: The passage defines the deficit as a ratio: young level divided by old level. Without the adjuvant it is 800/200 = 4. With the adjuvant it is 1,200/600 = 2. The deficit halves, so it shrinks just as the hypothesis predicts.

B.why: Both gains really are 400 units, but that is the difference measure the team set aside. On differences the adjuvant looks equally helpful at both ages, so you'd miss that the ratio deficit shrank.

items.stimulus: A music conservatory keeps its collection of $4{,}800$ handwritten opera scores in a climate-controlled vault. The vault has a floor area of $60$ square meters.
items.stem: What is the density of manuscripts in the vault, in manuscripts per square meter?
items.explanation: Density is the amount divided by the space: $\frac{4{,}800 \text{ manuscripts}}{60 \text{ m}^2} = 80$ manuscripts per square meter. The units read manuscripts per square meter, which is what the question asks for.

D.why: You multiplied the manuscripts by the area. That gives manuscript-square-meters, which is not a density. Density is a quotient, amount ÷ space.

items.stimulus: A public health department is planning vaccination clinics for a district with 120,000 residents. The district covers 50 square miles, and 10 of those square miles are water.
items.stem: What is the population density, in people per square mile of land, of the district?
items.explanation: First find the land area: $50 - 10 = 40$ square miles. Then divide the population by the land area: $\frac{120,000}{40} = 3,000$ people per square mile of land.

A.why: You added the water area to the total instead of subtracting it, $\frac{120,000}{60} = 2,000$. The land area is the total area minus the water area.

D.why: You divided by the water area, $\frac{120,000}{10} = 12,000$. People live on the land, so the denominator should be the 40 square miles of land.

D.why: You added the two numbers. A density always comes from dividing one quantity by another, never from adding them.

items.stimulus: A sports scientist estimates an athlete's body composition by underwater weighing. The athlete has a mass of 78 kilograms. items.stem: Which of the following is closest to the athlete's body density, in kilograms per liter?

items.stimulus: A planetary scientist cuts a solid cube from an iron meteorite to study under a microscope. The meteorite has a density of $8$ grams per cubic centimeter, and the cube has a mass of $1.728$ kilograms.

D.why: You divided area by count, $\frac{800\pi}{1{,}200}$. That gives square kilometers per aftershock, the flipped quotient.

The higher wage likely helped them staff night shifts they had been unable to fill.
They raised pay above the new minimum to compete with employers in nearby towns.
Their experience shows that higher minimum wages increase hiring in most regions.

items.stimulus: Legume cover crops such as clover and vetch are usually planted in autumn and add nitrogen to the soil only after farmers till them under in spring. Agronomist Lena Okafor's field trials with a cowpea line called Ridgeback, however, point to a different path. Ridgeback is sown in late summer, fixes nitrogen through the fall, and is killed by the first hard frost. Its residue then breaks down on the surface over winter, releasing nitrogen for a spring crop without any tilling at all.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Unlike many legume cover crops, Ridgeback can supply nitrogen to a later crop without being tilled into the soil.
Legume cover crops such as clover and vetch must be tilled under in spring before they release any nitrogen.
Ridgeback survives winter frost, so it can keep fixing nitrogen until farmers till it under in the spring.
Ridgeback fixes more nitrogen than clover or vetch, so farmers are replacing those crops with the new cowpea.
items.explanation: Collect every sentence about Ridgeback: it is sown in late summer, a frost kills it, and its residue releases nitrogen 'without any tilling at all.' Now set that against the group in the first sentence, whose members release nitrogen only after they are tilled under. Put together, those sentences say Ridgeback feeds a later crop without tilling, and the whole passage is built to show that. Choice A says exactly that and nothing more.

B.why: You described the group instead of the exception. The first sentence does say this about clover and vetch, but it only sets up the contrast. The passage is about Ridgeback, so this choice is too narrow to be the main idea.

C.why: You got Ridgeback's key fact backwards. The text says the first hard frost kills Ridgeback and that it needs no tilling. This choice has it surviving the frost and being tilled, which is how the group behaves, not Ridgeback.

D.why: The passage never compares how much nitrogen each crop fixes, and it never says farmers are switching. This sounds like a reasonable scientific claim, but you can't point to any line that supports it.

items.stimulus: Static stretching just before exercise has repeatedly been found to reduce jump height. Kinesiologist Mara Lindqvist suspected that the effect depends on habit. items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Static stretching before exercise lowers jump height in athletes regardless of how often they usually stretch.
Recreational runners in Lindqvist's study jumped about 4 percent lower after holding static stretches.
Lindqvist's study shows that daily stretching raises the jump height of trained athletes in every sport.
items.explanation: The general finding comes first, and then the passage turns to the gymnasts, who are the exception: they 'jumped no lower after stretching.' items.stimulus: Most of the world's languages mark grammatical tense, signaling on the verb whether an event is past, present, or future. Mandarin Chinese, however, generally does not. Instead, its speakers use aspect markers, short words that show whether an action is finished or still ongoing, and leave the timing of an event to context. Linguist Wen Liu argues that this does not make Mandarin less precise; it simply moves the work of placing events in time from the verb to the surrounding conversation.
items.stem: Based on the text, which choice does NOT accurately describe Mandarin Chinese?
choices: It uses short words to show whether an action has been completed.
It usually marks on the verb whether an event is past or future.
It relies on context to convey when an event takes place.
It is not made less precise by the way it handles time.
items.explanation: Marking past, present, or future on the verb is what the text says *most* languages do. It then says Mandarin, 'however, generally does not.' So B describes the group, not the exception, and it is the one statement the text contradicts. Each of the other three matches a sentence about Mandarin that you can point to.

A.why: You mixed up aspect and tense. Showing whether an action is finished is aspect, and the text says that is exactly what Mandarin's aspect markers do. This is the category confusion the passage is built around, and it made a true statement look false.

C.why: You suspected that 'relies on context' says more than the passage does. But the text states that speakers 'leave the timing of an event to context,' so the choice simply restates the text.

D.why: You treated this as an unsupported judgment. The last sentence reports Liu's view that the system 'does not make Mandarin less precise,' so the statement is backed directly by the text.

items.stem: Based on the text, which choice does NOT accurately describe grocery retail in Okafor's study?

Its total hours fell by about as much as in other sectors.

D.why: You treated this as a stretch beyond the data. To get there, though, you only combine the two facts about grocers, as the method asks: hours per worker fell, so total hours fell 'by roughly as much as elsewhere,' which the text states outright.

items.explanation: The pivot word "However" brings in the heat-trained group, and the last sentence sums up what the passage is about: heat training shrinks the slowdown (2 percent instead of 6) but doesn't eliminate it. items.stimulus: Agronomists comparing a new sorghum line, DR-7, with a standard variety over six growing seasons found that DR-7's roots reached nearly twice as deep. In the three dry seasons, that depth let DR-7 draw on moisture the standard variety could not reach, and it outyielded the standard by about a quarter. In the one unusually wet season, however, DR-7's deep roots sat in waterlogged soil, and it yielded less than the standard. The same trait, the researchers conclude, was both DR-7's advantage and its weakness.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: DR-7's deeper roots gave it higher yields than the standard variety in dry seasons but lower yields than the standard in a very wet one.
In each of the three dry seasons in the trial, DR-7 outyielded the standard sorghum variety by about a quarter of the standard's yield.
DR-7 outyielded the standard variety in every season of the trial because its roots reached nearly twice as deep into the soil.
Farmers should replace standard sorghum with DR-7 in any region where dry growing seasons are more common than unusually wet ones.
items.explanation: The final sentence puts the middle details together: one trait, deep roots, helped DR-7 in dry seasons and hurt it in the wet one. Choice A gives the gap in both directions, ahead of the standard variety when it's dry and behind it when it's wet, and ties both to the roots.

items.stimulus: During a 2021 drought, ecologists tracked brook trout in twelve beaver ponds in a Montana watershed. In eleven of them, the shallow water warmed past what trout can tolerate, and most of the fish died. The twelfth pond is fed by an underground spring. It stayed cool, and its trout survived. However, that spring water carries little dissolved oxygen. When winter ice sealed the ponds off from the air, only the spring-fed pond suffered a mass trout die-off. The researchers note that the other ponds were spared largely because the drought had already left them with few trout to lose.
items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the spring-fed pond?
choices: Like most of the ponds in the survey, it lost much of its trout population when the drought warmed its water.
The water source that kept its trout alive through the drought also contributed to their deaths the following winter.
Its spring kept it cool during the drought, which caused it to freeze over earlier than the other ponds that winter.
Over the full year, it lost more trout than any of the other ponds that the ecologists surveyed in the watershed.
items.explanation: Gather every sentence about the spring-fed pond and put them together. The spring kept the pond cool, so its trout survived the drought. The same spring water is low in oxygen, and once ice cut the pond off from the air, its trout died off. One feature, the spring, both protected the fish and later exposed them. That is what B says, and it claims nothing the text doesn't support.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. The other eleven ponds lost their trout in the drought. The spring-fed pond is the one whose trout survived it.

C.why: You spotted that the spring both helped and hurt, then finished the thought with the wrong cause. The first half is right. But the text never says the pond froze earlier. The winter problem was low oxygen once the ice sealed off every pond, not the timing of the freeze. Read every choice to the end.

D.why: The last sentence says the other ponds had few trout left, and you turned that into a ranking. The text gives no counts, so you can't say which pond lost the most fish over the year.

items.subtype_name: Which choice best describes X / what does the text indicate about X
items.stimulus: In a study of six leafy vegetables, nutrition researchers measured two things: how much calcium each vegetable contained, and what fraction of that calcium participants' bodies absorbed. For five of the vegetables, the fraction absorbed varied little, so the ones richest in calcium delivered the most usable calcium. Spinach did not fit this pattern. It contained more calcium than any other vegetable tested, yet participants absorbed a far smaller fraction of it. The researchers attribute this to oxalate, a compound in spinach that binds calcium in the gut.
items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes spinach in the study?
choices: As with the other vegetables tested, its calcium content was a dependable guide to how much usable calcium it delivered.
It contained the most calcium of the vegetables tested, but oxalate reduced how much calcium its leaves actually held.
Unlike the other vegetables tested, its calcium content was not a dependable guide to how much usable calcium it delivered.
It delivered less usable calcium than any other vegetable tested, even though it contained the most calcium of all.
items.explanation: For the other five vegetables, the absorbed fraction barely changed, so calcium content alone told you which ones gave the most usable calcium. Spinach broke that link. Its content was the highest, but its absorbed fraction was much lower, so its content no longer predicts what the body gets. C states exactly that. It doesn't go further and claim how much usable calcium spinach gave compared with the others, which the text never says.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Content predicted usable calcium for the other five vegetables. The text says spinach 'did not fit this pattern.'

B.why: You put oxalate in the wrong place. The text says oxalate binds calcium in the gut, which lowers absorption. It doesn't lower the calcium in the leaves. In fact, spinach had the highest calcium content of the six.

D.why: You saw that spinach's absorbed fraction was low and treated that as a low total. Usable calcium depends on both the content and the fraction absorbed. Spinach had the most calcium, and the text gives no numbers, so you can't say it delivered less usable calcium than every other vegetable.

items.stimulus: In the peat bogs of the Halvard Plateau, nearly all sundews flower in midsummer, once their sticky leaves have trapped enough insects that year to pay for seed production. items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Drosera tardiva?
choices: It relies less on trapped insects than the other sundews of the plateau do.
It flowers earlier than its neighbors and therefore produces fewer seeds.
It pays for its flowers with insects captured before the year it blooms.
It traps the insects that fund its seeds in early spring, before midsummer.
items.explanation: Put two sentences together. D. tardiva flowers before its leaves unfold, so it cannot have caught any insects yet that year. Aston says its flowers are funded by nutrients stored during the previous summer's hunting. So the insects that pay for its flowers were caught in an earlier year.

A.why: You saw that it doesn't use this year's insects and decided it needs insects less. The text says only that it uses insects from an earlier year. It never says it depends on them any less than the other sundews do.

B.why: The first half is right and the second half is wrong. The text says its seed counts match those of its neighbors, so it does not produce fewer seeds.

D.why: You described the group's habit, catching insects in the year of flowering, and gave it to the exception. In early spring its leaves haven't unfolded, so it can't be trapping insects then.

items.stimulus: In a study of 40 regional labor markets, economists Tobias Renn and Ama Owusu found that a rise in the minimum wage was followed, in almost every market, by a drop in the hours offered to teenage workers. The exception was Kessler County, where teenage hours rose. However, Kessler's wage increase coincided with the opening of a distribution center that hired heavily from all age groups, and teenage hours there rose by less than adult hours did. The researchers therefore treat Kessler as a market where the expected effect was likely masked.
items.stem: Based on the text, what do Renn and Owusu indicate about Kessler County?
choices: It shows that a minimum wage increase need not reduce teenage hours.
Its rise in teenage hours probably fits, rather than defies, the wider pattern.
Its wage increase cut teenage hours more sharply than in the other markets.
Its teenage hours rose because the new distribution center hired mostly teenagers.
items.explanation: The researchers call the expected effect 'masked'. That means they think it was still there, just hidden by the hiring boom. Teenage hours rising by less than adult hours supports this. So the researchers read Kessler as consistent with the pattern, not as an exception to it.

A.why: This is the face-value reading of 'teenage hours rose'. The researchers reject it. The 'However' sentence and the word 'masked' tell you they don't treat Kessler as counterevidence.

C.why: You correctly saw that the effect was probably present, then took it further. The text never compares the size of Kessler's hidden effect with the effect in the other markets.

D.why: The center hired heavily from all age groups, not mostly teenagers. Teenage hours also rose by less than adult hours, which points the other way.

items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the marsh warbler?
choices: It is among the few valley migrants that depart at an unusual time of year.
It departs when most valley migrants do but follows a different route south.
It takes a longer route that brings it to its wintering grounds sooner.
It follows the river south before turning east toward richer feeding grounds.

D.why: This reverses the order. The warbler flies east first and turns south afterward. It does not follow the river at all.

items.stimulus: When the Orlen Viaduct was built in 1911, its engineers set its piers on timber piles driven into waterlogged clay, a common practice because wood that stays submerged resists rot. items.stem: Based on the text, what is true about the groundwater around the Orlen Viaduct's piles?
choices: It once preserved the piles entirely but now leaves their upper parts exposed to rot.
Its drop in 2009 has caused the piles to decay along their entire length.
It was lowered in 2009 to protect the viaduct from flooding along the river.
It had been slowly weakening the piles for a century before the drainage project.
items.explanation: Submerged wood resists rot, and for a century the piles held, so the groundwater kept them preserved. Once the water table dropped, only the upper portions began to decay. The same water that protected the piles now leaves their upper parts exposed.

C.why: The text never gives a reason for the drainage project. Flood protection is an invented purpose that only sounds plausible.

D.why: The text says the piles held for a century and that submerged wood resists rot. The groundwater protected the piles before 2009. It did not weaken them.

items.stem: Based on the text, what does Petrosyan indicate about the black-burnished ware?
choices: It was likely brought from elsewhere, since none appears in the settlement.
It was likely used in homes for food before being placed in graves.
It was likely prized above every other kind of pottery the community made.
It was likely made from local clay specifically for use in burials.

B.why: No food or oil residue was found, and Petrosyan says the ware was not borrowed from household use. This is the view she argues against.

C.why: Pottery made for burial may sound special, but the text never ranks it against the community's other pottery.

items.stimulus: Records of the Lennart weavers' guild show that, between 1620 and 1680, members were fined whenever inspectors found cloth dyed with logwood, a cheap dye that faded quickly. Hanne Bjerke was the only member never fined, though her account books show steady purchases of logwood throughout those years. Historian Paul Ivers notes that the same books record large purchases of alum, which fixes logwood's color, and suggests that inspectors, who judged cloth by how it held its color, may have been unable to detect logwood in cloth treated this way.
items.stem: Based on the text, what does Ivers suggest about Hanne Bjerke?
choices: She escaped fines by never selling the logwood-dyed cloth she produced.
She deliberately used alum to deceive the guild's inspectors about her dyes.
She may have sold logwood-dyed cloth that inspectors failed to recognize.
She, like other members, was fined less often after she began buying alum.
items.explanation: Inspectors judged cloth by whether its color held. Alum fixes logwood's color, and Bjerke bought both. Ivers suggests inspectors 'may have been unable to detect' logwood in her cloth. This choice keeps his hedge ('may') and makes no claim about her intent.

A.why: Ivers's point is that she probably did use logwood and simply wasn't caught. Saying she never sold it reverses his explanation.

B.why: You got the alum insight right and then went further. Ivers says only that inspectors 'may have been unable' to detect the logwood. He says nothing about her intent, and his hedge rules out certainty.

D.why: You described her as part of the group. She was the only member never fined, so she couldn't have been fined 'less often'.

items.stimulus: The ballad "The Miller's Grey Mare" has long been credited to collector Edwin Hale, who printed it in 1874 as a song he had taken down from a Dorset farmhand. However, folklorist Ruth Okafor has located a broadside of the ballad, printed in Bristol in 1852, with nearly identical wording. Okafor does not accuse Hale of inventing his singer.
