items.stem: Based on the text, what does Okafor indicate about Hale's 1874 version of the ballad?
choices: It probably came from a real singer whose own source was a printed text.
It was probably copied by Hale himself from the 1852 Bristol broadside.
It shows that most songs Hale collected in Dorset came from printed sheets.
It differs enough from the 1852 broadside to show decades of oral change.
items.explanation: Okafor accepts that Hale had a real singer. She argues that the farmhand probably learned the song from print. So Hale's version came from a living singer, but the song had passed through print before it reached that singer.

B.why: You found the broadside and jumped to the obvious conclusion, that Hale copied it. Okafor explicitly says she does not accuse Hale. She places the printed source with the farmhand, not with Hale.

C.why: Okafor's argument is about one ballad. Extending it to most of Hale's collection goes beyond what she says.

D.why: The text says the broadside has nearly identical wording, so the two versions don't differ enough to show oral change.

• Cover crops are planted between cash-crop seasons to protect bare soil.
• Agronomist Dalia Fenwick asked whether a winter cover of crimson clover affects spring weed growth in squash fields.
• Her team sowed clover in half of 24 test plots and left the other half bare over the winter.
• Each spring week for six weeks, the team counted the weed seedlings in every plot.
• Clover plots had 40 percent fewer weed seedlings than bare plots.
• Fenwick concluded that clover may reduce growers' reliance on herbicides.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the methods Fenwick's team used in the study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Fenwick's team found that the plots sown with crimson clover had 40 percent fewer weed seedlings than the bare plots had.
Fenwick wanted to learn whether a winter cover of crimson clover would change the amount of spring weed growth in squash fields.
Fenwick's team sowed clover in 12 of 24 plots, left the rest bare, and counted weed seedlings weekly for six weeks.
Fenwick's clover study shows that a winter cover crop can eliminate squash growers' need to apply any herbicides at all.
items.explanation: The notes follow research order: background, aim, method, result, conclusion. The goal asks only for the method. Choice C describes what the team did: it planted clover in half of the 24 plots (12), left the rest bare, and counted seedlings every week for six weeks. Every other choice is taken from a different stage of the study.

A.why: This is the result, the stage that comes after the method. You probably chose it because it sounds like the main news of the study. The goal asks how the team did the work, not what they found.

B.why: This is the study's aim, the question Fenwick asked before any work began. It names the right study and the right crop, but it describes the wrong stage.

D.why: Fenwick said clover 'may reduce' reliance on herbicides. This choice turns that into 'eliminate' any need for them, and it reports a conclusion even though the goal asks for the method.

items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Lake Verrin is a 300-hectare lake surrounded by farmland.
• Until 2004, fertilizer runoff from nearby farms fed algae blooms that left much of the lake murky every summer.
• In 2004, a restoration program planted buffer strips of native grasses along the lake's shores.
• By 2015, the lake's water clarity had doubled, and submerged plants had returned to its shallows.
• Ecologist Teodor Vance has monitored the lake since 2009.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the condition of Lake Verrin before the restoration program began. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: By 2015, the water clarity of Lake Verrin had doubled, and submerged plants had returned to the lake's shallows.
Before 2004, buffer strips of native grasses kept fertilizer runoff from reaching the murky waters of Lake Verrin.
In 2004, a restoration program planted buffer strips of native grasses along the shores of Lake Verrin.
Before 2004, runoff from nearby farms fed algae blooms that left much of Lake Verrin murky each summer.
items.explanation: The goal limits you to one period, before the restoration began, and to one aspect, the lake's condition. Choice D is the only one that describes the lake during that period: runoff fed algae blooms, and the water turned murky every summer. The other choices describe the restoration itself, the lake after it, or a version of events the notes contradict.

A.why: This is the lake's condition, but from the wrong period. 2015 comes after the restoration. You matched 'condition of Lake Verrin' and skipped the word 'before' in the goal.

B.why: The buffer strips were planted in 2004, as part of the restoration. Before then, runoff was reaching the lake. This choice puts the remedy in the period before it existed.

C.why: This describes the program, not the lake. It names the right lake and the right year, but its subject is the planting. It says nothing about what the water was like.

items.subtype_name: Zoom in on one named detail
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Engineers at the Halvorsen Materials Lab, led by Hanne Østby, developed three self-healing concretes.
• One of them, Calcara, contains dormant bacterial spores sealed inside tiny clay capsules.
• When a crack lets water into Calcara, the spores become active.
• The active bacteria produce limestone, which gradually fills the crack.
• In testing, Calcara sealed cracks up to 0.8 millimeters wide within 28 days.
• Another of the concretes, Fibrel, uses polymer fibers that swell when wet.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the process by which Calcara repairs cracks. Which choice does NOT effectively use relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: In Calcara, water entering a crack activates dormant bacterial spores, and the bacteria then produce limestone that gradually fills the gap.
Calcara repairs itself when seeping water wakes bacterial spores held in clay capsules, prompting them to generate limestone that seals the crack.
Calcara, one of three self-healing concretes from Hanne Østby's team, sealed cracks up to 0.8 millimeters wide within 28 days of testing.
Calcara's spores, kept dormant inside clay capsules, become active once a crack admits water and begin producing limestone to fill the opening.
items.explanation: The goal asks for the process: how Calcara repairs a crack. Choice C names Calcara and is accurate, but its main clause gives a test result (how wide a crack it sealed and how fast). It never says what happens inside the concrete. Choices A, B and D each walk through the mechanism: water gets in, the spores wake up, and the bacteria produce limestone. So C is the only one that fails the goal.

A.why: You may have thought this choice was too bare because it leaves out the clay capsules. A process description doesn't need every note, though. It goes from water to active spores to limestone, and that is exactly how Calcara repairs a crack.

B.why: You may have read 'wakes' and 'seals' as claims the notes never make. They are paraphrases of 'become active' and 'fills the crack.' The sentence stays true to the notes and describes the repair process step by step.

D.why: This choice opens with the spores instead of with Calcara's name, and you may have taken that as drifting from the topic. The spores are part of Calcara, and the sentence traces the full repair sequence, so it accomplishes the goal.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Between 1971 and 1974, folklorist Marisol Quintero-Bray recorded 46 tales in the coastal villages of the Varela Peninsula.
• She published them in 1980 as The Salt Ledger.
• One tale, "The Lantern Ferryman," takes place at a fog-bound river crossing in the estuary below the town of Puerto Calma.
• Its events unfold on the one night each year when the tide reaches the old ferry steps.
• Another tale, "The Weaver's Debt," is set in a mountain market town.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the setting of "The Lantern Ferryman." Which choice does NOT effectively use relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: "The Lantern Ferryman" takes place at a fog-bound river crossing in the estuary below Puerto Calma, on the night the tide reaches the ferry steps.
"The Lantern Ferryman" is one of the 46 tales that Marisol Quintero-Bray recorded in the coastal villages of the Varela Peninsula.
Set on the one night each year when the tide reaches the old ferry steps, "The Lantern Ferryman" unfolds at a foggy estuary crossing.
The fog-bound crossing in the estuary below Puerto Calma, where the tide climbs the old ferry steps, is the setting of "The Lantern Ferryman."
items.explanation: The goal names one tale and one feature of it: its setting, meaning where and when the story happens. Choice B names the tale, and it does mention a place. But that place, the coastal villages of the Varela Peninsula, is where Quintero-Bray collected the tales, not where this story's events happen. Choices A, C and D each give the tale's actual setting: the fog-bound estuary crossing below Puerto Calma, the night the tide reaches the ferry steps, or both.

A.why: You may have rejected this choice because it gives two setting details, a place and a time, and seemed to do too much. Both details belong to the setting of this one tale, so the sentence stays on target.

C.why: The opening phrase gives a time, not a place, and you may have taken that as off topic. A setting covers when a story happens as well as where, and the sentence also names the estuary crossing. It accomplishes the goal.

D.why: The tale's title doesn't appear until the end of this sentence, so you may have thought it wasn't really about the tale. The sentence's whole job is to name the setting of "The Lantern Ferryman," which is exactly what the goal asks for.

items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Halvorsen-3 is a short-period comet first observed in 1987.
• Its icy nucleus measures about 3 kilometers across.
• Before 2011, the comet took 6.2 years to complete one orbit around the Sun.
• In 2011, the comet passed unusually close to Jupiter.
• Jupiter's gravity stretched the comet's path, and Halvorsen-3 now takes 7.9 years to orbit the Sun.
items.stem: The student wants to specify how much longer the comet's orbit has taken since its 2011 encounter with Jupiter. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Halvorsen-3, a short-period comet with a nucleus about 3 kilometers across, was first observed in 1987 and passed close to Jupiter in 2011.
Since passing close to Jupiter in 2011, Halvorsen-3 has taken 7.9 years to orbit the Sun, 1.7 years longer than its earlier 6.2-year orbit.
Since passing close to Jupiter in 2011, Halvorsen-3 has needed a full 7.9 years to complete each of its orbits around the distant Sun.
When Halvorsen-3 passed close to Jupiter in 2011, the giant planet's gravity stretched the comet's path and lengthened its orbit around the Sun.
items.explanation: The goal asks for one specific detail: HOW MUCH LONGER the orbit has become since 2011. That is a gap between two numbers, so you need both the old period (6.2 years) and the new one (7.9 years), or the difference between them. Choice B gives the new period and says outright that it is 1.7 years longer than the old one, so it does exactly what the goal asks.

A.why: You picked a sentence that names the right comet and the 2011 encounter, but it tells you about the comet's size and when it was discovered. It says nothing about how long its orbit takes.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. It gives you the new orbital period, but only one of the two numbers. 'How much longer' asks for the difference, and nothing here compares 7.9 years with the old 6.2-year period.

D.why: You chose the sentence that explains why the orbit changed. It tells you the orbit got longer but never says by how much, and the amount is the detail the goal names.

Sayegh's team found that Tell Qarsa's lower hearth was about 5,200 years old, older than earlier estimates had suggested.
Sayegh's team dated Tell Qarsa's lower hearth by measuring the light released by heated quartz grains from its clay.

There is no question that power looms outpaced handlooms. But weavers' wages were already falling in the 1810s, when few power looms were running. A more likely cause is that thousands of new workers, drawn by earlier high pay, had crowded into the trade.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The power loom was the main cause of handloom weavers' poverty.
Weavers' wages fell because too many workers entered the trade.
Power looms could produce cloth faster than handlooms could.
Few power looms were operating in England before the 1830s.
items.explanation: Text 1 says the power loom produced several times as much cloth per worker. Text 2 opens by granting that point: "There is no question that power looms outpaced handlooms." The authors disagree about why wages fell, but both accept that power looms were faster. That shared ground is choice C.

A.why: You took Text 1's conclusion and assumed both authors hold it. Text 2 argues against it and blames an oversupply of workers instead. You got one text's role right and the other's wrong.

B.why: You took Text 2's explanation and gave it to both authors. Text 1 blames the machine, not the number of workers, so its author would not agree.

D.why: Text 2 only says few power looms were running in the 1810s. Neither text says anything about the 1830s, so you stretched a claim about one decade to cover a later one.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Over the past four decades, weather forecasts have grown steadily more accurate. Satellites now track moisture and wind over oceans that once went unobserved, feeding richer data into forecasting models. A forecaster can therefore now plan a full week ahead with confidence.

Text 2
Gains in forecasting are real, but they are uneven. Individual thunderstorms form within hours from small pockets of rising air, too small for most models to capture. For a town wondering whether a storm will strike tomorrow afternoon, a forecast is still little more than an estimate of the odds.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Weather forecasts have become more accurate in recent decades.
Forecasts are now dependable a week ahead for any kind of weather.
Satellite data has done little to improve forecasting models.
Thunderstorms have become harder to predict than they once were.
items.explanation: Text 1 describes forecasts growing steadily more accurate. Text 2 begins "Gains in forecasting are real" before limiting the claim to exclude thunderstorms. Text 2 narrows Text 1 without rejecting it, so both authors accept that forecasting has improved.

B.why: This is a stronger form of Text 1's final sentence, and it is exactly the claim Text 2 limits. Text 2 shows that storms still can't be predicted with confidence even a day ahead, so its author would reject "any kind of weather."

C.why: Text 1 credits satellite data with the improvement, and Text 2 does not dispute it. This choice reverses what Text 1 says.

D.why: Text 2 says thunderstorms are still hard to predict, not that they have become harder. Neither text compares storm forecasts now with those of the past.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
In a survey of 3,000 adults, researchers found that people who ate breakfast every day weighed less, on average, than people who regularly skipped it. The team concluded that a morning meal helps regulate appetite, keeping people from overeating later in the day.

Text 2

Breakfast eaters weigh less mainly because they exercise more.
Body weight in the survey was unrelated to breakfast habits.
People who ate breakfast daily tended to weigh less on average.

Long static stretches can briefly reduce a muscle's force.
Flexibility matters more than power in most sports.
Static stretching before competition helps sprinters perform.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
In early 2020, the red star Betelgeuse faded to less than half its usual brightness, a larger drop than any recorded in a century of observation. Text 2

choices: Betelgeuse's fading showed that it was about to become a supernova.
Dust shed by Betelgeuse has blocked its light many times before.
Betelgeuse grew noticeably fainter than usual in early 2020.
Betelgeuse's brightness in 2020 stayed within its usual range.
items.explanation: Text 2 begins by granting Text 1's observation: the dimming "was real and remarkable." It then offers dust as another explanation. The texts disagree about the cause, but both accept that Betelgeuse faded noticeably in early 2020.

A.why: This is the supernova idea from the end of Text 1, and Text 2 was written to question it. You read the concession as agreement and missed the turn at "but."

B.why: Text 2 says only that dust could have dimmed the star this time. Nothing in either text says this has happened "many times before."

D.why: Text 1 calls the drop the largest in a century, and Text 2 calls it remarkable. Both describe a change far outside the star's usual range.

Text 1
Divers surveying Caribbean reefs counted far more parrotfish inside no-fishing zones than in nearby fished waters. Because parrotfish graze the algae that smother young coral, the researchers concluded that banning fishing is enough to bring a damaged reef back.

Text 2

items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

No-fishing zones tend to contain more parrotfish than fished waters.
Water temperature matters more to reefs than fishing does.
Parrotfish are the most important animals living on a reef.
items.explanation: Text 2 begins by granting Text 1's finding: 'While no-fishing zones clearly hold more parrotfish.' Text 1 reports that finding directly, so both authors accept it. items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
At a coastal settlement, archaeologists uncovered several thin layers of charcoal mixed with burned seeds. The team concluded that the inhabitants regularly set fires to clear land for planting crops.

Text 2

items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The inhabitants grew crops on land they had cleared by burning.
Lightning was the most likely cause of the fires at the site.
The seeds at the site came from plants that grew in the wild.
The settlement contains layers of material that had been burned.
items.explanation: Text 2 says outright that 'no one disputes' the burned layers, and Text 1 is the source of that observation. The two authors agree on what was found and disagree about what caused it. This is the 'same observation, different explanation' pattern. Being able to separate the shared observation from the disputed explanation is what lets you choose 'offers an alternative explanation' on a real relationship question.

C.why: Neither author says where the seeds came from. You latched on to a detail that appears in Text 1, the seeds, and attached a claim that neither text makes.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Pavement and buildings absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly, so cities are usually warmer than the countryside around them. Meteorologists call this pattern the urban heat island.

Text 2

items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Most cities are warmer than the countryside that surrounds them.
Every city stays warmer than its surroundings at all hours.
Desert cities are cooler than their surroundings at noon.
Shade trees are the best way to cool down a crowded city.
items.explanation: Text 2 opens with 'Although most cities are indeed warmer than their surroundings,' which concedes Text 1's main point. It then names one group of cities and one time of day where the pattern breaks down. That narrows Text 1's claim without rejecting it. When a relationship question asks what Text 2 does, the answer here would be that it limits Text 1's claim, not that it disagrees with Text 1.

B.why: Text 1 says cities are 'usually' warmer. It doesn't say every city at all hours. Text 2 is responding to a stronger claim than the one Text 1 makes.

C.why: This is Text 2's own point, and it's limited to 'some' desert cities. Text 1 never mentions deserts, so you can't treat this as something the two authors share.

D.why: Text 2 says shade trees help cool some desert cities. It never calls them the best method, and Text 1 doesn't discuss ways to cool a city.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In warm climates, many trees have leaves with smooth edges, while in cool climates, more trees have toothed edges. By counting smooth-edged fossil leaves at an ancient site, paleobotanists estimated its past temperature and concluded the site was once tropical.

Text 2
Leaf edges are certainly a useful clue to past climate. Yet plants growing beside streams often have toothed leaves no matter how warm the air is, so fossils from old riverbanks may make a site seem cooler than it was.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The ancient site described in Text 1 was once a tropical place.
Fossils from riverbanks should not be used to study past climate.
The shape of leaf edges can give information about past climate.
Trees with toothed leaves grow only in places with cool climates.
items.explanation: Text 1 relies on leaf edges to estimate temperature, and Text 2 begins by calling leaf edges 'certainly a useful clue to past climate.' Both authors accept the method. Text 2 then adds a warning about one kind of site. Identifying this shared ground is the first step in recognizing that Text 2 qualifies Text 1 rather than rejecting it.

A.why: This is Text 1's final conclusion. Text 2 never confirms it, and its warning about riverbank fossils raises doubts about this kind of estimate. You applied Text 1's view to both authors.

B.why: Text 2 says riverbank fossils may make a site 'seem cooler.' That is a caution, not a ban. Text 1 doesn't mention riverbanks at all.

D.why: Text 1 says only that toothed edges are more common in cool climates. Text 2 directly contradicts this choice by saying toothed leaves appear beside streams 'no matter how warm the air is.'

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Woolen cloth fragments found at a fourteenth-century Baltic trading post contain red dye from a variety of madder that grew only far to the south. Historian Ilse Varga concludes that the post therefore imported its finished cloth from southern workshops rather than weaving its own.

Text 2
The dye evidence is sound, but dyestuffs were trade goods in their own right: light, durable, and valuable. Bundles of dried madder root could have reached the post as easily as bolts of cloth, and local weavers could simply have dyed their own wool with it. The loom weights recovered at the site make that possibility difficult to exclude.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 presents new chemical evidence that the dye discussed in Text 1 came from a plant grown locally.
Text 2 rejects the dye evidence in Text 1 as unreliable and concludes the post imported no cloth at all.
Text 2 accepts the evidence that Text 1 relies on but suggests another process that could have produced it.
Text 2 offers further evidence for Text 1's view that the post obtained finished cloth from southern workshops.
items.explanation: Text 1 uses the southern madder in the fragments to conclude that the cloth was imported finished. Text 2 opens by granting that the dye evidence is sound, then offers a second route: the post could have imported the raw dye and done the weaving and dyeing itself. Same observation, different explanation, so Text 2 accepts the evidence and proposes another process behind it.

A.why: You credited Text 2 with disputing where the dye came from. Text 2 accepts that the madder was southern and calls the dye evidence sound. It disputes only what Varga infers from that evidence.

B.why: You took a hedged alternative and turned it into flat disagreement. Text 2 calls the evidence sound and says only that local dyeing 'could have' happened. It never says the post imported no cloth.

D.why: This is the trap of getting one text's role right and the other's wrong. Text 1's view is described correctly, but Text 2 does not support it. The loom weights point toward local weaving, which works against Varga's conclusion.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In listening studies with Western concert audiences, participants consistently rate passages in a minor key as sadder than the same passages in a major key. Musicologist Paulo Brandt argues that the link between minor mode and sadness is therefore a universal feature of human music perception.

Researchers played the same passages to listeners in a remote highland community with little exposure to Western recordings. These listeners rated the minor and major versions as equally sad, although they readily judged fast passages as happier than slow ones.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 describes listeners for whom a pattern that Text 1 treats as universal did not appear.
Text 2 argues that tempo rather than mode conveys sadness to all listeners, including those in Text 1.

Text 2 supports Text 1's conclusion by showing that highland listeners also hear emotion in music.

C.why: You had Text 2 attack the wrong part of Text 1. Text 2 leaves the concert-audience finding alone and challenges only the leap from that finding to 'universal'.

D.why: You fixed on the fact that the highland listeners heard some emotion in music. That isn't the point. On the specific link Brandt calls universal, minor mode and sadness, they did not show the pattern, so Text 2 works against his conclusion.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Self-healing concrete contains dormant bacterial spores that, when a crack lets in water, become active and produce limestone that seals the gap. In laboratory trials, cracks up to 0.8 millimeters wide closed within four weeks, and engineer Rosa Achterberg argues the material could sharply reduce maintenance costs for bridges and tunnels.

Text 2
Although the laboratory results are impressive, the spores in those trials were tested within months of mixing. Bridges and tunnels are built to last for decades, and no one yet knows whether the spores remain viable that long inside hardened concrete. Until long-term data exist, the cost savings remain a projection.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 provides evidence that the bacteria in Text 1 stop working after several years inside concrete.
Text 2 disputes the laboratory results in Text 1, arguing that the trials were too brief to be trusted.
Text 2 explains the chemical process by which the bacteria described in Text 1 produce limestone.
Text 2 accepts the trial results in Text 1 but notes an untested condition on which its projection depends.
items.explanation: Text 2 begins with a concession ('Although the laboratory results are impressive'), then turns. Achterberg's predicted savings depend on the spores staying viable for decades, and that has not been tested. Text 2 accepts the results and points out the untested condition the projection relies on.

A.why: You read uncertainty as a negative finding. Text 2 says 'no one yet knows' whether the spores survive. It gives no evidence that they fail.

B.why: You got Text 2's role half right. It does raise the short testing period, but to question the long-term projection, not the lab results, which it calls 'impressive'.

C.why: You picked a detail from Text 1. Text 1, not Text 2, describes how the bacteria make limestone, and this choice says nothing about how the two texts relate.

Text 1

Text 1
Researchers studying a coastal fishing village found that younger residents had largely stopped using a regional vowel sound that their grandparents used. Teenagers in the village regularly hear the standard dialect through media.
Broadcast media is the most likely cause of the regional vowel's decline.
A change in how a community speaks can be traced to a social cause.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
Agronomist Lena Fairweather tracked corn yields on 40 Iowa farms over six seasons. In dry years, fields that had carried a winter cover of cereal rye far outyielded bare fields, apparently because the rye's leftover residue slowed evaporation from the soil. Fairweather concluded that rye's advantage grows as rainfall shrinks.

Text 2
Fairweather's findings on soil moisture are persuasive. Yet in her wet seasons, rye fields barely outyielded bare ones, and on some farms they fell behind, likely because decomposing rye briefly locks up nitrogen that young corn needs. Rye, then, is less a universal booster than a hedge against drought.

The yield gap between rye-covered and bare fields was wider in dry seasons than in wet ones.
Rye cover raises corn yields enough to justify planting it on every farm in every season.
Decomposing rye reduces corn yields by locking up nitrogen that young plants need to grow.
items.explanation: Write the two sentences first. Author 1 thinks rye helps most when rainfall is low. Author 2 accepts the moisture finding but adds that rye barely helps, and sometimes hurts, in wet seasons. Text 2 qualifies Text 1; it doesn't reject it. Both authors therefore accept that the difference between rye and bare fields is larger in dry years than in wet years. Notice that the question is about the gap between two kinds of season, not about either season alone.

Text 1
After the city of Harlow Falls raised its minimum wage by 18 percent, economist Dalia Osei tracked staffing at 240 local restaurants. Eighteen months later, payroll head counts were essentially unchanged. Osei concluded that the higher wage floor had not reduced restaurants' use of low-wage labor.

Text 2
Osei's head counts are careful, and the restaurants did keep about as many people on staff. But a payroll lists a worker scheduled for twelve hours a week the same way it lists one scheduled for thirty, and the restaurants' time sheets show average weekly hours per employee falling by roughly a tenth.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The wage increase did little to change how much low-wage labor the restaurants used.
The restaurants employed about as many workers after the increase as they had before it.
Payroll head counts cannot reveal how the restaurants adjusted to the higher wage.
Raising a city's minimum wage does not, in general, cause employers to cut jobs.
items.explanation: Text 1 sets up a finding (head counts stayed the same) and then draws a conclusion from it (the restaurants used no less labor). Text 2 opens by granting the finding ('the restaurants did keep about as many people on staff'). It then disputes only the conclusion, because hours per worker fell. So Text 2 qualifies Text 1. It accepts the observation and rejects the inference. The only thing both authors would accept is the observation itself: the restaurants employed about as many workers as before.

A.why: This is Text 1's final conclusion, and it is exactly what Text 2 was written to challenge. Fewer hours per worker means the restaurants used less labor even with the same head count. You saw that Text 2 concedes something, but you picked the claim it rejects instead of the one it concedes.

C.why: This gets Text 2's position right but not Text 1's. Osei relied on head counts as her evidence, so she would not accept that they miss how the restaurants adjusted. A statement that only one author holds cannot be something both would agree with.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In the eleven days before a magnitude 5.4 earthquake struck the Vessel Ridge fault, seismometers recorded over 300 small tremors clustered near the eventual rupture. Geophysicist Tomas Reyna concludes that the tremors marked slow, silent slip that loaded the fault until it failed, and thus that swarms there may warn of larger shocks.

Text 2
The timing and placement of the Vessel Ridge tremors are hard to dismiss as chance. Yet fluid rising through fractured rock can raise pressure enough to set off a swarm and, days later, a larger rupture, and it is difficult to exclude that sequence. If fluid was responsible, a swarm need not reflect slow slip.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The tremors reveal that slow slip was loading the fault before it ruptured.
Swarms on the Vessel Ridge fault reliably signal that a larger quake will follow.
The tremors were most likely connected to whatever produced the mainshock.
Rising fluid is the likelier source of the tremors recorded before the mainshock.
items.explanation: Text 1 gives an observation (a swarm of tremors just before and near the mainshock) and an explanation for it (slow slip loaded the fault). Text 2 offers a different explanation for the same observation: rising fluid could have caused both the swarm and the rupture. Text 2 does not deny the link between the swarm and the mainshock. It says the link is 'hard to dismiss as chance'. Reyna's account also ties the two together, through slow slip. The authors disagree about what the connecting cause was, but both treat the tremors as connected to the cause of the mainshock.

A.why: This is Reyna's explanation, and it is the very claim Text 2 targets. Text 2 says that if fluid was responsible, the swarm 'need not reflect slow slip.' You found the claim under attack but treated it as common ground.

B.why: This turns Text 1's claim into a stronger one than it makes. Reyna says swarms 'may warn' of larger shocks, not that they reliably do. Text 2's account suggests a swarm might show only that fluid is moving. Neither author makes a claim this strong.

D.why: This gets one text's role right and the other's wrong. Text 2 only says the fluid sequence is 'difficult to exclude'. It never says fluid is the likelier cause, and Reyna would reject the idea outright. Agreeing with a hedged alternative is different from both authors endorsing it.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Indigo-dyed cotton in the Varenna valley has long been credited to merchants who settled there in the 1680s. But textile historian Ilse Marchetti found indigo in cloth fragments radiocarbon-dated to the 1620s, and she concluded that valley weavers were dyeing with indigo decades before the merchants arrived.

Text 2
Marchetti's dates are secure, and the early fragments do carry indigo. Yet a residue shows where cloth was used, not where it was dyed. Valley households in the 1620s bought finished cloth from coastal ports, and no dye vats from that period have been found in Varenna.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Weavers in the Varenna valley were dyeing cotton with indigo before the 1680s.
Indigo-dyed cloth was present in the Varenna valley before the merchants settled there.
Radiocarbon dating cannot establish when the Varenna cloth fragments were made.
The merchants who arrived in the 1680s had no part in spreading indigo dyeing.
items.explanation: Text 2 accepts Marchetti's dates and the indigo, then disputes only where the dyeing happened. What both texts accept, then, is that indigo cloth was already in the valley before the 1680s. Text 1 also says the cloth was dyed locally, and Text 2 rejects that part.

A.why: You picked Text 1's conclusion and assumed Text 2 shares it because Text 2 opens by agreeing. Text 2's turn ('Yet...') is aimed at exactly this claim: the cloth could have been dyed on the coast and bought ready-made.

C.why: You assumed Text 2 attacks the dating. It says the opposite ('Marchetti's dates are secure'), and Text 1 depends on those dates.

D.why: You went further than either text. Text 1 says only that the merchants did not introduce indigo first, and Text 2 says nothing about their later role.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Over three decades, thunderstorms formed 30 percent more often east of Harlow, downwind of the city, than west of it. Meteorologist Dana Okafor attributes the gap to the city's heat: pavement and roofs warm the air above them, and the rising plume, carried east by prevailing winds, seeds storms.

Text 2
Okafor's comparison is careful, and regional weather alone cannot explain the gap. But a city is also an obstacle. Dense blocks of tall buildings force incoming air upward and split approaching storm cells, which could produce the same eastern excess without any added warmth.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Heat rising from Harlow's pavement and roofs is what seeds the additional storms east of it.
Some feature of Harlow itself, not regional weather, accounts for the additional storms east of it.
Tall buildings split storms that would otherwise have passed directly over Harlow's center.
Thirty years of records are too few to show a reliable difference in storm frequency.
items.explanation: Text 2 offers a different explanation for the same result. Okafor blames the city's heat, and Text 2 blames the city's shape. Both blame the city, though, and Text 2 says outright that regional weather cannot explain the gap. The statement both accept is that something about Harlow itself causes the extra storms.

A.why: You saw that Text 2 agrees with Okafor's comparison and assumed it also agrees with her cause. Text 2 offers buildings as a cause that works 'without any added warmth', so it does not accept heat as the cause.

C.why: This is Text 2's mechanism only. Text 1 never mentions buildings or split storm cells, so you can't say its author would agree.

D.why: Neither author questions the record. Text 1 builds on it, and Text 2 calls the comparison careful.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In a study of 1,400 recreational runners, those assigned to stretch statically before each run reported injuries at the same rate over twelve weeks as those who did not. The researchers concluded that pre-run static stretching does nothing to protect runners from injury.

Text 2
For joggers, who make up most such samples, that conclusion is probably right: their typical injuries come from repeated impact, which stretching does not address. Sprinters are another matter. Their most common injury, the hamstring strain, occurs when a muscle is rapidly lengthened, and in trials with competitive sprinters, stretching has reduced such strains.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Static stretching before a run does not lower the injury rate of runners in general.
Pre-run static stretching is unlikely to reduce injuries among recreational joggers.
Static stretching before a run reduces hamstring strains in competitive sprinters.
Joggers and sprinters tend to suffer their injuries through the same mechanism.
items.explanation: Text 2 narrows the claim without rejecting it. It accepts the finding for joggers ('probably right') and makes an exception for sprinters. Both authors therefore agree that stretching before a run does little for recreational joggers.

A.why: You read Text 2's opening agreement as accepting Text 1's whole conclusion. Text 1 says 'runners', and Text 2 rejects it for sprinters, who are runners too. Text 2 accepts only the narrower version of the claim.

C.why: Only Text 2 makes this claim. Text 1's own conclusion says stretching protects runners from nothing, so its author would not agree.

D.why: Text 2's argument depends on the two groups being injured differently: joggers through repeated impact, sprinters through rapid lengthening of a muscle.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Every 212 days, the star KX-17 dims by about 4 percent for nine days. Because the dimming repeats so regularly, a team led by astronomer Rafael Ostby concluded that a giant planet encircled by a broad ring system is crossing in front of the star.

Text 2
The regularity does rule out spots or flares on the star itself, which come and go on no fixed schedule. But a ringed planet at that orbital distance would cross the star in under two days. A diffuse band of dust strung out along a single orbit could block light for nine.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The dimming of KX-17 results from orbiting material passing in front of the star.
A giant planet with broad rings is responsible for the regular dimming of KX-17.
The dimming of KX-17 is most likely caused by activity on the star's own surface.
Bands of dust orbiting stars commonly gather to form the rings of giant planets.
items.explanation: Text 2 grants Ostby's main inference, that the regular schedule means something is orbiting the star and not changing on its surface. It disputes only what that object is. A ringed planet and a band of dust are both orbiting material, so both authors accept this choice.

B.why: You took Text 1's specific conclusion as shared ground. Text 2 rejects the ringed planet because its crossing would last under two days, not nine.

C.why: Both authors reject this. Text 1 relies on the regular timing, and Text 2 says that timing rules out spots and flares on the star.

D.why: You combined the two texts' objects into a general claim about how rings form. Neither text discusses where rings come from.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Folklorist Mara Lindqvist collected forty versions of the tale of the drowned bell from villages along the Selm River. Versions told near the river's source are brief, while those told near its mouth add names, places, and a second bell. She concludes that the tale began upstream and gathered detail as it traveled downriver.

Text 2
The pattern Lindqvist documents is real, but the towns near the Selm's mouth were also the largest, and they supported paid storytellers who lengthened every tale they performed. Elaboration there may reflect who told the story, not how far it had traveled.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: A folktale's content can change as it is retold by different communities of tellers.
The tale of the drowned bell originated in villages near the Selm River's source.
Paid storytellers in the river-mouth towns first invented the tale of the drowned bell.
The most elaborate versions of the tale were collected near the Selm River's source.
items.explanation: Both texts explain the same pattern of variation differently. Lindqvist says the tale gained detail as it traveled, and Text 2 says storytellers lengthened it in performance. Either way, the tale changes when it is retold, and that is the point both authors share.

B.why: This is the claim Text 1 ends on, and Text 2 is written to challenge it. If the detail reflects who told the story, the detail is no longer evidence that the tale started upstream.

C.why: You made Text 2's point stronger than it is. Text 2 says the storytellers lengthened tales, not that they created this one, and Text 1 would reject the idea.

D.why: This reverses the pattern both texts accept. The fuller versions come from near the mouth, not the source.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Teodor Vasko's admirers described him writing whole quartets in an afternoon. His manuscripts tell a different story: nearly every page is crowded with cancellations and inserted passages. Musicologist Aiko Brandt concludes that Vasko composed slowly, reworking each piece at length before it could be performed.

Text 2
Brandt is right that the revisions are extensive. But the inks used for them did not exist until the 1840s, years after the pieces premiered, when Vasko was preparing them for print. The drafts beneath the corrections are fluent and may well have been written quickly.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Vasko made extensive changes to his manuscripts after first writing out his works.
Vasko reworked each of his pieces at length before it was first performed.
Vasko's admirers were accurate in claiming he wrote whole quartets in an afternoon.
Vasko's printed scores are nearly identical to the drafts beneath his corrections.
items.explanation: Text 2 accepts that the revisions are extensive and disputes only when they were made. Both authors therefore agree that Vasko heavily revised his works after the first draft. They disagree about whether that happened before the premieres or decades later.

B.why: You saw that both texts agree about the revisions and carried that agreement over to their timing. The ink dates in Text 2 place the revisions after the premieres, which goes directly against this claim.

C.why: Text 2 says only that the drafts 'may well' have been written quickly, which is not the same as confirming the legend. Text 1 explicitly rejects the legend.

D.why: Text 2 says the corrections were made to prepare the pieces for print, so the printed scores would differ from the drafts.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
After a wetland was restored upstream of Corbin in 2009, hydrologists compared fifteen storms from before and after the restoration. For storms of similar size, peak river flow at Corbin fell by an average of 20 percent. The team concluded that the wetland is an effective defense against flooding in the town.

Text 2
For storms like those fifteen, the wetland clearly helps. But none approached the size of Corbin's most destructive floods. In those, days of rain saturate the wetland before the peak arrives, leaving it little capacity to absorb more water.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The restored wetland lowered peak river flow at Corbin during storms like those studied.
The restored wetland is an effective defense against all of the flooding Corbin experiences.
The fifteen storms studied included several of the largest floods in Corbin's history.
Wetlands upstream of a town become saturated during most heavy rainstorms.
items.explanation: Text 2 limits Text 1's claim to a smaller range of storms. It accepts the result for storms like the fifteen studied ('clearly helps') and denies it only for the largest floods. Both authors agree that the wetland reduced peak flow in storms of the kind that were measured.

B.why: You stretched Text 1's conclusion until it covered every flood. Text 2 says the wetland does little in the most destructive floods, so its author would reject this.

C.why: Text 2 says none of the fifteen storms approached the size of Corbin's worst floods.

D.why: Text 2 describes saturation only during the largest, multi-day storms. It does not say this happens in most heavy storms, and Text 1 never mentions saturation.

Text 1
During a 2021 marine heat wave, corals in Tavu Lagoon, where water temperatures swing by up to 6°C each day, bleached far less than corals on the nearby outer reef. items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

Individual corals grow more heat tolerant through daily exposure to temperature swings.
Outer-reef corals moved into Tavu Lagoon would gain little resistance to heat.
Lagoon corals and outer-reef corals bleached at similar rates during the heat wave.
items.explanation: Text 2 offers a different explanation for the same result, but both explanations depend on the temperature swings. In Text 1, the swings condition each coral. In Text 2, they remove sensitive corals over generations. Either way, the swings help explain the lagoon corals' tolerance.

C.why: This is the prediction from Text 2's view. Text 1's conditioning explanation suggests a moved coral would gain tolerance, so its author would not agree.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Ines, a visiting birdwatcher, has just told her uncle Tomas that the swallows nesting in his barn are a nuisance and should be driven off.

TOMAS: A nuisance? Each of those birds eats hundreds of flies a day. Before they came, my cows were tormented from June to September. Drive the swallows off, and the flies will be back before summer ends. I would sooner lose the barn roof than lose those birds.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines argues that the swallows in the barn are a nuisance and should be removed.
Tomas argues that the swallows are valuable because they keep flies away from his cows.
Tomas worries that the swallows nesting in the barn will soon damage its roof.
Tomas claims that swallows eat more flies than any other bird in the region.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you Tomas is answering Ines's complaint. In plain English, his lines say the swallows eat the flies that used to bother his cows, and the flies will come back if the birds leave. His last line, which says he would rather lose the roof than the birds, sums up that view: the swallows are worth keeping.

A.why: You summarized the other character. The introduction gives Ines's view, but the question is about Tomas's speech, and he argues against her.

C.why: You read 'I would sooner lose the barn roof' literally. Tomas isn't predicting damage. He is saying how much more he values the birds than the roof.

D.why: Tomas says each swallow eats hundreds of flies, but he never compares swallows with other birds. You added a claim the text doesn't make.

Hannah is unsure whether machine-made cloth keeps its pattern after many washings.
Hannah argues that her handwoven cloth is better made, even if machines are faster.
Hannah explains that her customers are wealthy women who buy linen from her.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. A student has just called the speech of a coastal fishing village "bad English." Her professor responds.

"Bad? Listen to how the fishermen say 'I be mending' for work they do every day and 'I'm mending' for a single job. That is not carelessness, my dear. It marks a difference standard English cannot show in so few words. Their grammar is not broken; it is simply different from ours."
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The professor argues that the village speech follows consistent rules of its own.
The student argues that the village speech is a careless form of standard English.
The professor argues that standard English is less expressive than any dialect.
The professor notes that the fishermen mostly discuss mending their nets and boats.
items.explanation: The professor rejects the word 'bad' and gives an example: the fishermen use 'I be' and 'I'm' to mark two different meanings. His conclusion is in the last line: their grammar 'is not broken; it is simply different.' The dialect has its own system.

B.why: This is the student's view from the introduction, and it's the view the professor is arguing against. You matched the wrong speaker.

C.why: The professor says standard English can't make this one distinction as briefly. He never claims it is less expressive than every dialect.

D.why: 'Mending' appears only in the professor's example. You picked a detail from the illustration instead of the point it illustrates.

The following text is from a play set at a rural experiment station. Halloway, a farmer, has asked the station chemist, Pryce, why his wheat yields keep falling.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Halloway insists that his poor harvests must come from faulty seed, since he has manured the field faithfully.
Pryce contends that changing the seed will raise the yield only if it is done many times over several seasons.
Pryce contends that the falling yields come from years of wheat draining the soil rather than from the seed.
Pryce contends that manure has done the field no good and that wheat should be abandoned there permanently.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you Pryce is answering Halloway's question, so Pryce's reply carries the point. B.why: You read 'a dozen times' literally. Pryce means that no amount of seed-changing will help ('still the yield will fall'). He isn't telling Halloway to do it more often.

The following text is from a play. After a month of small tremors, the town's mayor, Fenwick, speaks with a visiting geologist, Dr. Asante.
FENWICK: Forty little shakes, and not one cracked a cup. Surely the ground is letting off its pressure gently, a bit at a time.
ASANTE: I wish it worked so. But a fault that slips by inches has not paid down a debt of yards. Swarms like this have come before large earthquakes about as often as they have simply faded. They may mean nothing, but they are no reason to stop inspecting the school.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Asante argues that the small tremors offer no assurance of safety, so precautions should continue.
Fenwick suggests that the frequent small tremors are harmlessly releasing the fault's pressure.
Asante argues that the small tremors show a large earthquake will certainly strike the town soon.
Asante argues that the small tremors have already released most of the strain stored in the fault.
items.explanation: Asante's 'But' rejects Fenwick's comforting idea. Small slips don't relieve much of the stored strain, and swarms like this one are as likely to come before a large earthquake as to fade away. Her hedge, 'They may mean nothing,' leads into her real point: keep the precautions going. Choice A fits both her doubt and her caution.

B.why: This is Fenwick's hope, which Asante rejects ('I wish it worked so'). You matched the wrong speaker.

C.why: You ignored Asante's hedge. She says swarms come before large earthquakes about as often as they fade, and that they 'may mean nothing.' That rules out 'certainly.'

D.why: Asante says the opposite: inches of slip haven't 'paid down a debt of yards,' so most of the strain is still there.

The following text is from a play set aboard a whaling ship in the 1840s. The cook, Pell, is defending the crew's diet to the ship's surgeon, Haddon.
PELL: Salt pork fills a man's belly, and a full belly never yet went sick. Give them enough of it and they'll want for nothing.
HADDON: Enough of it? They've had their fill every day since we left port, and still their gums bleed. A belly may be full and the body starve all the same. 'Tis not how much they eat but what. Put the limes back on the table.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Haddon argues that the crew's illness stems from what their diet lacks, not how much they eat.
Haddon argues that the crew has been underfed and needs larger daily portions of salt pork.

items.explanation: Haddon's key sentence is 'Tis not how much they eat but what.' The crew have eaten their fill and are still sick, so something is missing from their food, and the limes should come back. Choice B states that point.

C.why: Haddon says the crew have 'had their fill every day.' Quantity isn't the problem, so more pork isn't his fix.

D.why: Haddon blames what the diet is missing, not anything harmful in the pork. Calling it poisonous claims more than he says.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a 1904 play. Mr. Pell, an amateur bird collector, has just shown his niece Agnes a drawer of mounted warblers.
PELL: There, every one labeled. Thou canst not know a bird till thou hast it in hand.
AGNES: And what hast thou learned of it, Uncle, save the colour of its coat? This one sang at dawn from the alder, I'd wager, and fed its young on midges. If the drawer holds only feathers, then all the bird's life went out of it with its breath. Ere you take another, sit an hour by the marsh and watch.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Agnes argues that a mounted specimen shows how a bird looked but reveals little about how it lived.
Agnes comes to accept that a bird must be collected and labeled before it can be properly studied.
Agnes asks her uncle to explain what the warblers' feathers have taught him about their coloring.
Agnes argues that collecting warblers should be forbidden because it threatens the marsh's birds.
items.explanation: Put Agnes's lines into plain English: a drawer of skins tells you only the bird's color, while its singing, feeding and raising of young are lost when it dies. Her conditional ('If the drawer holds only feathers, then...') and her advice to watch living birds both make one point: specimens show appearance, not behavior. That claim covers everything she says.

C.why: You read 'what hast thou learned of it' as a real question. It is rhetorical: Agnes means he has learned almost nothing, so she is not actually asking for an explanation.

D.why: Agnes asks her uncle to watch before he collects again. She never calls for a ban or says the marsh's birds are under threat, so this choice claims more than the text supports.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in an English weaving village in 1822. Mr. Cartwell, a mill owner, has told the hand weaver Hannah Doyle that his new power looms will free weavers from their toil.
HANNAH: Free us, sir? Aye, free us of our bread. If your engine weaves in a day what I weave in a week, then who will pay me for the other six days? You call it relief. But a weaver relieved of her loom is only a woman with empty hands and a hungry family.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hannah argues that power looms will strip hand weavers of their income instead of easing their labor.
Hannah agrees that power looms will spare hand weavers the long hours their work currently demands.
Hannah asks Cartwell to explain how he plans to pay weavers for the days the new looms stand idle.
Hannah argues that power looms will ruin the mill because machine-woven cloth is poorer than hers.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you Hannah is answering Cartwell's claim that the looms will free weavers. Her conditional ('If your engine weaves in a day what I weave in a week, then who will pay me...') and the 'But' sentence turn that claim around: the looms will take away weavers' livelihood rather than bring them relief.

B.why: This summarizes Cartwell's claim, which the introduction reports. Hannah mocks 'Free us, sir?' and rejects it, so this choice gets her position backward.

C.why: You took 'who will pay me for the other six days?' literally. Her point is that nobody will pay her. She is not asking about a payment plan, and the looms would not be the ones standing idle.

D.why: Hannah says nothing about the quality of machine-made cloth or about the mill failing. You added an argument the text never makes.

The following text is adapted from an English translation of a nineteenth-century dialogue. A professor has just told his student Lena that regional dialects are corruptions of the standard language.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Lena argues that the standard language owes its status to political circumstance, not superior grammar.
Lena agrees that regional dialects are flawed versions of a standard language that is more correct.

Lena argues that schools should teach regional dialects in place of the standard form of the language.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play set aboard a trawler in 1958. The captain, Ewan Muir, has dismissed a young biologist's worry about his catch by remarking that the sea is too big to empty.
DR. SORENSEN: So said the men who fished the old cod banks, Captain. The sea is wide, I grant you, but a shoal is not. Your nets go where the fish gather to spawn. If you take them before they breed, then it matters little how many miles of water lie beyond your boat.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Sorensen argues that the ocean's size cannot protect a fish population that is caught before it breeds.
Sorensen accepts that the ocean is too vast for fishing to seriously reduce the number of its fish.
Sorensen recounts how fishermen on the old cod banks once boasted about the size of their catches.
Sorensen argues that commercial fishing should be stopped until all of the cod banks have recovered.
items.explanation: Sorensen grants a small concession ('The sea is wide, I grant you') and then moves to her real point with 'but a shoal is not.' C.why: The cod-bank fishermen come up in one clause, as a warning example that they once said what Muir says now. The text never mentions them boasting about catches, and the example is not her main point.

D.why: Sorensen warns about catching fish before they breed but never proposes stopping commercial fishing. This choice is a stronger claim than she makes.

The following text is from a play set on a merchant ship in 1912. Captain Rourke has insisted that his crew is well fed, since the men have all the salted beef and ship's biscuit they want and none ever goes hungry.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Dr. Abara argues that eating enough food does not ensure a person is getting the nourishment the body needs.
Dr. Abara agrees that the crew is healthy because the men have as much beef and biscuit as they want.

The following text is from a 1911 play. Margery Thorne, who owns a country estate, plans to drain the marsh that borders it. Her steward, Hollis, responds.

MARGERY: The marsh yields nothing. Drain it, and we shall have forty acres of good wheat by the harvest after next.
HOLLIS: Nothing, ma'am? And where do you suppose the herons feed, or the pike breed that your tenants take from the river each spring? Drain the marsh, and the river grows poorer, and so do they. Wheat you may have, but you will pay for it in fish.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hollis believes the marsh is unproductive land that would be better used for growing wheat.
Hollis argues that the marsh supports wildlife and food that the tenants depend on, so draining it has a cost.
Hollis admits he does not know where the herons feed and asks Margery to find out before she acts.
Hollis insists that wheat will not grow on the drained marsh, so the plan to plant it there will fail.
items.explanation: Put Hollis's lines into plain English. His question 'Nothing, ma'am?' rejects Margery's claim that the marsh yields nothing. He then points out that the marsh feeds herons and is where the pike breed, and that the tenants rely on those fish. His last sentence sums it up: she can have her wheat, but she will lose the fish. So his point is that draining the marsh has a real cost.

A.why: You summarised Margery's line, not Hollis's. She is the one who calls the marsh useless. Hollis speaks to argue against her.

C.why: You read a rhetorical question as a real one. Hollis knows perfectly well where the herons feed. He asks the question to show Margery that the marsh is not worthless.

D.why: Hollis says the opposite: 'Wheat you may have.' He agrees the wheat will grow. His objection is about what it will cost.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a 1903 novel. Captain Hale has just returned from charting a stretch of northern coast. The mapmaker Lindqvist plans to fill in the parts Hale could not survey.

LINDQVIST: Buyers will not pay for a chart with holes in it. I shall sketch in the inlets as they likely run.
HALE: And when some master steers by your sketch into an inlet that runs only in your imagination? A blank tells him to go carefully; a guess tells him he may go boldly. I had rather sell an honest hole than a handsome lie.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hale agrees that buyers will not pay for charts that leave parts of the coastline blank.
Hale argues that blank areas on a chart keep sailors safer than guesses that look reliable.
Hale asks Lindqvist which ship captains have already steered by the charts he has sold.
Hale insists that no chart should be sold until every part of its coast has been surveyed.
items.explanation: Hale's question describes a danger: a captain trusting a guessed inlet that does not exist. He then contrasts the two options. A blank makes a sailor careful, while a guess makes him confident. His last line says he would rather leave an honest gap. So his point is that blanks are safer than guesses that look trustworthy.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a 1923 play. Professor Hale, a scholar of regional dialects, is answering her student Tobias, who has complained that the villagers they are recording "speak English badly."

TOBIAS: They drop half their consonants, ma'am, and say "I be" for "I am." Surely that is mere carelessness.
HALE: Carelessness? If a whole parish drops the same consonants in the same places, generation after generation, is that the work of careless tongues? A careless man errs at random. These people err by rule, and a rule kept by thousands is no error at all. It is a grammar.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Tobias argues that the villagers' speech is a careless departure from correct English.
Hale points out that the villagers drop the same consonants their parents dropped.
Hale argues that the villagers' speech follows consistent rules and so forms a grammar.
Hale claims that village dialects are older and more correct than standard English.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you Hale is answering Tobias's complaint, so her lines carry the point. Put them into plain English: careless mistakes happen at random, but the villagers make the same changes in the same places, generation after generation. A pattern kept by thousands of speakers is a rule, and a set of rules is a grammar. Her opening 'Carelessness?' is a rhetorical question that rejects Tobias's word. Choice C states her claim.

A.why: You summarised the wrong character. This is Tobias's view, and the whole exchange exists so that Hale can reject it. You may also have read her 'Carelessness?' literally, as if she were agreeing.

B.why: You picked a true detail that is too narrow. Hale brings up the repeated consonants only as evidence. Her point is what that consistency proves: the speech is rule-governed and counts as a grammar.

D.why: You went past the text. Hale says the dialect is a grammar and not an error. She never says it is older than standard English or more correct.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from an 1890 play. Captain Rowe intends to sail before noon. Agnes, who keeps the harbor's weather station, has been reading her barometer.

ROWE: The sky is clear as glass, woman. Not a cloud from here to the cape.
AGNES: Thou mayst trust the sky if it please thee. But the glass in my parlor has fallen since dawn, and it fell so before the gale of '78, under a sky as fair as this. Ere noon the clouds will come to match it. The sky tells thee what is; the glass tells thee what is coming.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Agnes argues that the falling barometer forecasts the weather better than the clear sky does.
Rowe argues that the cloudless sky shows it is safe for his ship to sail this morning.
Agnes recalls that the gale of '78 arrived under a sky just as clear as the present one.
Agnes claims that a clear sky is usually a sign that a severe storm is on its way.
items.explanation: The introduction sets up the disagreement: Rowe is relying on the sky, and Agnes is relying on her barometer (the 'glass'). In modern English she says, 'Trust the sky if you like, but my barometer has been falling, and the clouds will come before noon.' Her last line sums up her point: the sky shows present conditions, and the barometer shows what is coming. Choice A states that.

B.why: You summarised the other character. Rowe makes this point, and Agnes's whole speech answers it. Her 'Thou mayst trust the sky' is a concession that leads into 'But,' not an agreement.

C.why: You picked a true detail that is too narrow. Agnes mentions the gale of '78 only as an example of the barometer warning under a fair sky. It supports her point but is not the point itself.

D.why: You turned one case into a general rule Agnes never states. She says the falling barometer signals a storm. She does not say a clear sky usually means bad weather.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a translation of a 1911 play. Bram, a fisherman, is speaking with Ilse, a naturalist who has spent several seasons studying the eels of his harbor.

BRAM: You count the eels and measure them and write it all down. Why trouble? The sea holds eels enough to feed us forever.
ILSE: Forever, you say? Then tell me why your father's nets came up heavy and yours come up light. If the sea held an endless store, would each year's catch be smaller than the last? I write it down because the numbers remember what men forget.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Bram insists that the sea holds enough eels to supply his village for all time.
Ilse argues that shrinking catches show the eels are limited, as her records reveal.
Ilse notes that fishermen of Bram's generation use lighter nets than their fathers did.
Ilse warns that the harbor's eels will vanish entirely within the next few years.
items.explanation: Ilse answers Bram with questions, but they are not real requests for information. 'Tell me why your father's nets came up heavy and yours come up light' means 'catches are falling.' 'Would each year's catch be smaller?' means 'an endless supply would not shrink.' Her last line explains why she keeps records: they preserve a decline people would otherwise forget. Choice B states both parts of her point.

A.why: You summarised the wrong character. This is Bram's belief, and Ilse's questions are built to refute it. If you took 'Forever, you say?' as agreement, you read a rhetorical question literally.

C.why: You misread the detail. The nets 'come up light' because they hold fewer eels, not because the nets themselves are lighter. Even read correctly, this detail is only her evidence, not her point.

D.why: You claimed more than Ilse does. She says the supply is shrinking and is not endless. She makes no prediction that the eels will disappear, and she gives no timeline.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from an original play set in a cotton mill. The overseer has just announced that the spinners' wages will rise by a penny a day. Agnes, a spinner, replies.

AGNES: A penny more, you say, and we are to thank you for it. But the loaf in Fenwick's window has gone up threepence since Lady Day. If a penny comes in at the door while threepence goes out at the window, then tell me, sir, which way is the household moving? You have raised our wages and left us poorer.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Agnes argues that the wage increase is smaller than the rise in bread prices, so the spinners are worse off than before.
Agnes agrees that the spinners should thank the overseer for raising their wages by a penny each day.
Agnes points out that the price of a loaf in Fenwick's window has risen by threepence since Lady Day.
Agnes argues that mill wages across the country have failed to keep pace with prices for many decades.
items.explanation: Put Agnes's conditional into plain English: if a penny comes in and threepence goes out, the household is going backward. Her last line says so directly: the raise has 'left us poorer.' Her point is about the gap between the two amounts. The raise is twopence smaller than the price rise, so the spinners lose ground. Choice A states that claim and covers everything she says.

B.why: You took the overseer's framing, that the spinners should be grateful, and gave it to Agnes. 'We are to thank you for it' is sarcasm, and her rhetorical question exists to reject that gratitude, not to offer it.

C.why: This is true, but it covers only one of the two amounts Agnes compares. Her point is the gap between the penny and the threepence. The bread price on its own is evidence for her point, not the point itself.

D.why: Agnes is talking about one raise, one loaf and one household since Lady Day. Nothing in her lines reaches to the whole country or to decades of wages.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from an original play set in an engraving workshop. Teodor, an apprentice, has proudly told his master, Ilse, that he cut a woodblock in two days. Cutting one usually takes six.

ILSE: Two days, and thou wouldst have me praise the speed? Pull a hundred sheets from it, then. Thy lines are cut so shallow that the ink will choke them ere the fortieth. Mine took six days and gives a thousand clean prints. Count it out, boy: which block has truly cost less labour for each sheet it yields?
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ilse argues that Teodor's quicker block will give far fewer prints and so costs more labour per sheet than hers.
Ilse praises Teodor for finishing his block in two days, a third of the time her own block required.
Ilse notes that a block with shallow lines will fill with ink after it has been printed many times.
Ilse insists that apprentices should never be allowed to cut a woodblock without a master's supervision.
items.explanation: Translate Ilse clause by clause. Teodor's block clogs before 40 prints, and hers gives 1,000. She ends with a question that is really a claim: once you count labour per print, the six-day block is the cheaper one. Her point is the gap in output between the two blocks, which outweighs the four days he saved. Choice A states that.

B.why: You read her opening question literally. 'Thou wouldst have me praise the speed?' is a challenge, not praise. The rest of the speech argues that the speed was a false saving.

C.why: This is the reason Teodor's block fails. It is not the point Ilse is making. She uses the shallow lines to set up the comparison of 40 prints against 1,000, so this choice is too narrow.

D.why: Ilse judges one block against another. She never lays down a rule about what apprentices may do, so this claims more than her lines support.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from an original play set during an 1850s fever outbreak. A councilman has just credited the town's lime-washing of houses with keeping deaths down. Dr. Marlowe answers him.

MARLOWE: On Tanner's Lane every house was washed white, and twelve were buried. On Mill Row not one wall saw lime, yet the Row draws from the new well and lost but two. If thy whitewash saved them, sir, why did it spare the street that had none of it? Look to the water.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Marlowe argues that the gap in deaths between the two streets points to the water supply rather than to lime-washing.
Marlowe agrees with the councilman that lime-washing the houses is what kept the town's deaths low.
Marlowe reports that twelve people died on Tanner's Lane even though every house there was washed.
Marlowe declares that the new well has ended the fever and that the town needs no further measures.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you Marlowe is answering the councilman's claim about lime-washing. He compares two streets. The washed street lost twelve and the unwashed street lost two, and the unwashed street is the one with the new well. His rhetorical question means that whitewash cannot explain why the street without it did better. 'Look to the water' names the real cause. Choice A captures that comparison and his conclusion.

B.why: This summarises the councilman's view, not Marlowe's. You may have taken 'If thy whitewash saved them' as agreement. It is the start of a rhetorical question built to knock that view down.

C.why: This is accurate, but it gives you only one side of Marlowe's comparison. His point depends on setting Tanner's Lane against Mill Row, so this choice is too narrow.

D.why: Marlowe says only that the water deserves the credit. He never says the fever is over or that nothing more should be done, and Mill Row still lost two people.
