items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
In this scene from a play set in 1721, the physician Thomas Ware urges Ann Lisle to let him inoculate her son against smallpox.

LISLE: You would put into him the very sickness I pray he never meets.

WARE: A little of it, madam, given in a quiet house, that he may be spared the whole of it in a crowded street. Mark me, I promise no miracle; a few so treated do fall gravely ill. But of a hundred children who wait, how many more shall I bury?
items.stem: Based on the text, which of the following is NOT a point Ware makes?
choices: A mild infection given under care can protect against a severe one.
Some children who are inoculated go on to become seriously ill.
Inoculation is certain to leave every treated child unharmed.
More children are likely to die if they are left uninoculated.
items.explanation: Ware says outright, "I promise no miracle; a few so treated do fall gravely ill." He never claims inoculation is certain to leave every child unharmed. He admits the opposite. Choice C is the one point he does not make. Each of the other three can be traced to a clause in his speech.

A.why: You read "a little of it... that he may be spared the whole of it" as Lisle's fear rather than Ware's argument. Put that clause into plain English and Ware is saying a small, controlled dose protects against the full disease, so this is a point he makes.

B.why: You may have rejected this because it seems to work against Ware's case. But he concedes it himself in "a few so treated do fall gravely ill." A speaker can grant a weakness and still argue his side, so this is a point he makes.

D.why: You took "how many more shall I bury?" as a real question Ware cannot answer. It is rhetorical. He means that more children who wait will die. This is the subtype's trap: the question form hides a plain claim, and this choice states that claim.

items.stimulus:
In this scene from a play set in an 1890s textile town, the weaver Edith Marsh answers the mill owner Samuel Crane, who has refused a wage increase.

CRANE: Raise wages, and I must raise prices; raise prices, and the buyers go to Leeds.

MARSH: Then how came you by six new looms this spring, sir, if there's no money in the till? I'll grant a mill must sell cheap. But a girl who leaves takes her skill to Leeds as surely as your buyers would.
items.stem: Based on the text, which of the following is NOT a point Marsh makes?
choices: The mill recently found money to spend on new equipment.
Higher wages would push up prices and drive buyers away.
A mill has to keep the price of its cloth low to compete.
Workers who leave carry their skills to competing mills.
items.explanation: The claim that higher wages would push up prices and lose buyers belongs to Crane. It is his "if... then" chain in the first speech. Marsh is answering that argument, not making it, so B is not a point Marsh makes. The other three choices each paraphrase a sentence of her reply.

A.why: You took "how came you by six new looms...?" as a sincere request for information. It is rhetorical. Marsh is pointing out that the mill did have money to spend. This is the subtype's trap: a question that is really a claim.

C.why: You assumed that only the owner would say a mill must sell cheap, so you credited this line to Crane. Marsh concedes it herself in "I'll grant a mill must sell cheap" before she turns with "But." A concession is still a point the speaker makes.

D.why: You may have read "Leeds" as part of Crane's worry about buyers and stopped there. Marsh turns his own image around: a worker who leaves takes her skill to Leeds just as the buyers would. This is a point she makes.

items.stimulus:
In this scene from a play, the city planner Rosa Imari responds to Councilman Lyle Brandt, who supports building a highway through the Eastgate district.

BRANDT: The road will carry forty thousand cars a day. That is progress you can count.

IMARI: Count them, then. But count too the shops whose doors will face a wall, and the children who must cross six lanes to reach school. I do not say the city needs no road. I say that if we measure progress only in cars, we will build a city easy to drive through and hard to live in.
items.stem: Based on the text, which of the following is NOT a point Imari makes?
choices: The road would harm the shops that sit along its route.
The road would make some children's walk to school riskier.
Judging the road only by its traffic would mislead the city.
The city should abandon its plan to build any new road.
items.explanation: Imari states directly, "I do not say the city needs no road." Her objection is to measuring progress only by traffic. She is not objecting to roads in general. Choice D credits her with a position she explicitly rejects, so it is the one point she does not make.

A.why: You read "shops whose doors will face a wall" as background description rather than as part of her argument. In plain English she is saying the road would cut those shops off. That is a cost she wants counted, so this is a point she makes.

B.why: You may have tied the six lanes to Brandt's traffic figures and treated this as his detail. Imari is the one who raises the children crossing six lanes to reach school. She uses it as a danger the road would create, so this is a point she makes.

C.why: You skipped the conditional that carries her claim: "if we measure progress only in cars, we will build a city... hard to live in." This is the subtype's trap: older-sounding "if... then" phrasing hiding a simple point. This choice states that point.

items.stimulus:
A materials scientist is cutting square test samples from a sheet of a new ceramic composite. The side length $x$, in centimeters, of one sample satisfies the equation below.

$4x^2 = 100$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: First get $x^2$ by itself: divide both sides by 4 to get $x^2 = 25$. Then take the square root of both sides: $x = 5$ or $x = -5$. The positive solution is $5$. You can check it: $4(5)^2 = 4(25) = 100$.

D.why: You subtracted 4 from 100 when you should have divided. The 4 multiplies $x^2$, so you undo it by dividing both sides by 4.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
While fitting a model to the dive path of an osprey, an ornithologist arrives at the equation below.

$x^2 - 3x - 28 = 0$
items.stem: Which of the following is a solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Look for two numbers that multiply to $-28$ and add to $-3$. Those are $-7$ and $4$, so the equation factors as $(x - 7)(x + 4) = 0$. The solutions are $x = 7$ and $x = -4$, and only $7$ is among the choices. Check: $49 - 21 - 28 = 0$.

A.why: You flipped the sign when turning the factor $(x - 7)$ into a solution. Setting $x - 7 = 0$ gives $x = 7$, not $-7$. The value $-7$ solves $x^2 + 3x - 28 = 0$, which has the sign of the middle term reversed.

D.why: 28 is the constant term in the equation, not a root. The constant is the product of the factor numbers, so it doesn't tell you a value of $x$ directly.

items.stem: Which of the following is a solution to the given equation?

items.stem: What is the positive solution to the equation?
items.explanation: The zero-product property only works when one side is 0, so you can't set each factor equal to 20. Distribute and move everything to one side: $6x^2 + 7x - 20 = 0$. This factors as $(3x - 4)(2x + 5) = 0$, so $x = \frac{4}{3}$ or $x = -\frac{5}{2}$. The positive solution is $\frac{4}{3}$. You can also use the quadratic formula: the discriminant is $49 + 480 = 529 = 23^2$, so $x = \frac{-7 \pm 23}{12}$, which gives $\frac{16}{12} = \frac{4}{3}$. To check in Desmos, graph $y = x(6x+7)$ and $y = 20$ and click the intersection on the right.

You flipped the signs when factoring, $(3x + 4)(2x - 5) = 0$, or used $+b$ in the quadratic formula. Either way you got the positive root of the sign-flipped equation, $\frac{5}{2}$ (2.5).
You factored correctly to $3x - 4 = 0$ but forgot to divide by the coefficient 3.
In the quadratic formula you divided by $a = 6$ instead of $2a = 12$, getting $\frac{-7 + 23}{6} = \frac{8}{3}$ (2.666 or 2.667).

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
A linguist fitting a model of vowel-length variation obtains the following equation.

$9(x + 1)^2 = 64$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the equation?
items.explanation: There's no separate $x$ term, so isolate the square and take both roots. Divide by 9 to get $(x + 1)^2 = \frac{64}{9}$. Then $x + 1 = \frac{8}{3}$ or $x + 1 = -\frac{8}{3}$, so $x = \frac{5}{3}$ or $x = -\frac{11}{3}$. The positive solution is $\frac{5}{3}$. To check in Desmos, graph $y = 9(x+1)^2$ and $y = 64$. The crossing on the right is at about $x = 1.667$.

You stopped at $x + 1 = \frac{8}{3}$ and forgot to subtract 1 (2.666 or 2.667).

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
A marine biologist analyzing kelp-forest growth data arrives at the following equation.

$\frac{1}{2}x^2 - 3x = 8$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the equation?
items.explanation: Multiply every term on both sides by 2 to clear the fraction: $x^2 - 6x = 16$. Write it in standard form, $x^2 - 6x - 16 = 0$, and factor: $(x - 8)(x + 2) = 0$. So $x = 8$ or $x = -2$, and the positive solution is 8. If you'd rather keep the fraction, use the quadratic formula with $a = \frac{1}{2}$, $b = -3$, $c = -8$. Then $b^2 - 4ac = 9 + 16 = 25$ and $2a = 1$, so $x = \frac{3 \pm 5}{1}$, which gives 8. To check in Desmos, graph $y = \frac{1}{2}x^2 - 3x - 8$ and click the x-intercept on the right.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
While checking a pressure-correction step, a meteorology student arrives at the equation below.

$\frac{1}{2}(x+3)^2 - 8 = 10$
items.stem: What are the solutions to the given equation?
items.explanation: Add 8 to both sides to get $\frac{1}{2}(x+3)^2 = 18$. Multiply by 2 to get $(x+3)^2 = 36$. Then $x+3 = 6$ or $x+3 = -6$, so $x = 3$ or $x = -9$.

A.why: You took only the positive square root, $x+3 = 6$. You forgot that $x+3 = -6$ also works, which gives the second solution, $x = -9$.

B.why: You divided 18 by 2 when you should have multiplied, so you got $(x+3)^2 = 9$. That gives $x+3 = \pm 3$, so $x = 0$ or $x = -6$.

D.why: You found $x+3 = \pm 6$ correctly but flipped the sign of 3 when you isolated $x$. You wrote $x = 3 \pm 6$ when it should be $x = -3 \pm 6$.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
An ecologist modelling how a pond's algae cover recovers after treatment reduces one step to the equation below.

$x^2 = 6x + 11$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Rewrite the equation in standard form as $x^2 - 6x - 11 = 0$. The quadratic formula gives $x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36+44}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm 4\sqrt{5}}{2} = 3 \pm 2\sqrt{5}$. Since $2\sqrt{5} \approx 4.47$, only $3+2\sqrt{5}$ is positive.

A.why: You kept the sign of $6x$ when you moved it to the left side, so you solved $x^2 + 6x - 11 = 0$. The roots of that equation are $-3 \pm 2\sqrt{5}$, which is a different equation.

B.why: This is a root of the equation, but $2\sqrt{5} \approx 4.47$ is larger than 3, so $3-2\sqrt{5}$ is negative. The question asks for the positive solution.

C.why: You divided only the radical part of $\frac{6+4\sqrt{5}}{2}$ by 2. The 6 has to be divided by 2 as well, which gives 3.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
A folklore scholar tallying repeated motifs across versions of a tale sets up the equation below.

$4(x^2 - 5) = x^2 + 7$
items.stem: Which of the following is a solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Distribute the 4 to get $4x^2 - 20 = x^2 + 7$. Then $3x^2 = 27$, so $x^2 = 9$ and $x = \pm 3$. The positive root, 3, isn't among the choices, but $-3$ is. Check it: $4(9-5) = 16$ and $9+7 = 16$.

A.why: You multiplied only $x^2$ by 4 and left $-5$ unchanged, so you got $4x^2 - 5 = x^2 + 7$. That leads to $x^2 = 4$.

C.why: You reached $3x^2 = 27$ but never divided by 3. You took the square root of 27 when you should have taken the square root of 9.

D.why: 9 is the value of $x^2$. You stopped before taking the square root to find $x$.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
An astronomy student calibrating the spacing of marks on a star-tracking scale writes the equation below.

$(x-4)(x+2) = 2x + 7$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Expand the left side to get $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 2x + 7$, which becomes $x^2 - 4x - 15 = 0$. The quadratic formula gives $x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16+60}}{2} = 2 \pm \sqrt{19}$. Only $2+\sqrt{19}$ is positive.

A.why: You expanded the middle term as $+2x$ when it should be $-2x$. The $x$ terms then cancelled and you were left with $x^2 = 15$.

B.why: You added 7 when you moved it to the left side, so you solved $x^2 - 4x - 1 = 0$. The correct step subtracts 7, which gives $-15$.

D.why: You divided only the radical in $\frac{4 \pm \sqrt{76}}{2}$ by 2. The 4 has to be divided by 2 as well, which gives 2.

items.stimulus:
A sports scientist analysing sprint-start data reduces a calculation to the equation below.

$2x^2 - 9 = 63$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Add 9 to both sides to get $2x^2 = 72$. Divide by 2 to get $x^2 = 36$, so $x = \pm 6$. The positive solution is 6.

A.why: You took the square root before isolating $x^2$. You wrote $\sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}$ and then divided by 2, but you have to divide by 2 first.

D.why: You left the coefficient 2 in place and took the square root of 72. You need to divide by 2 first to get $x^2 = 36$.

A textile historian estimating the thread count of a woven fragment arrives at the equation below.

$\frac{1}{4}x^2 - x = 3$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Multiply every term by 4 to get $x^2 - 4x = 12$, which becomes $x^2 - 4x - 12 = 0$. This factors as $(x-6)(x+2) = 0$, so $x = 6$ or $x = -2$. The positive solution is 6.

C.why: You multiplied $\frac{1}{4}x^2$ and 3 by 4 but not $-x$, so you solved $x^2 - x - 12 = 0$. Its positive root is 4.

A.why: $-9$ really is a solution, but it is the negative one. The question asks for the positive solution.

C.why: You ignored the $5x$ term and took the square root of 36. Because the equation has an $x$ term, you have to move everything to one side and factor.

D.why: You got the signs in the factors backwards and wrote $(x - 9)(x + 4)$. That gives the positive root of $x^2 - 5x - 36 = 0$, not of the given equation.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
In a model of how an antibody concentration changes after a booster dose, an immunologist arrives at the equation below.

$x^2 - 6x + 4 = 0$
items.stem: What are the solutions to the given equation?
items.explanation: This does not factor over the integers, so use the quadratic formula: $x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 16}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm 2\sqrt{5}}{2} = 3 \pm \sqrt{5}$.

A.why: You used $b$ instead of $-b$ in the quadratic formula. That gives the roots of $x^2 + 6x + 4 = 0$, the same equation with the sign of the $x$ term flipped.

B.why: When you completed the square you added 4 to 9 instead of subtracting it. The correct step is $(x - 3)^2 = 9 - 4 = 5$, not 13.

C.why: You simplified $\sqrt{20}$ to $2\sqrt{5}$ but divided only the 6 by 2. Both parts of the numerator have to be divided by 2.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
A cartographer checking the scale of a square map inset writes the equation below.

$4x^2 - 9 = 27$
items.stem: Which of the following is a solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Add 9 to both sides to get $4x^2 = 36$, then divide by 4 to get $x^2 = 9$. So $x = 3$ or $x = -3$. Only $-3$ is among the choices. Check: $4(9) - 9 = 27$.

B.why: You solved $4x^2 - 9 = 0$ as if the right side were 0. The right side is 27, so you have to add 9 to 27 first.

C.why: You never divided by the coefficient 4. You treated $4x^2 = 36$ as $x^2 = 36$ and took the positive root.

D.why: You stopped at $x^2 = 9$. That is $x^2$, not $x$. Take the square root, and remember the negative root.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
An agricultural scientist sizing rectangular test plots for a fertilizer trial gets the equation below.

$x(x - 2) = 3(x + 8)$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Expand both sides: $x^2 - 2x = 3x + 24$. Put it in standard form: $x^2 - 5x - 24 = 0$. This factors as $(x - 8)(x + 3) = 0$, so $x = 8$ or $x = -3$. The positive solution is $8$.

C.why: You reversed the signs when factoring and wrote $(x + 8)(x - 3)$. That gives the positive root of $x^2 + 5x - 24 = 0$, not of the given equation.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
A linguist modeling how a vowel's length changes across a set of dialect recordings reduces the model to the equation below.

$(2x + 1)^2 = 49$
items.stem: What are the solutions to the given equation?
items.explanation: Take the square root of both sides: $2x + 1 = 7$ or $2x + 1 = -7$. Then $2x = 6$ or $2x = -8$, so $x = 3$ or $x = -4$.

B.why: You added 1 to both sides where you should have subtracted it. That solves $(2x - 1)^2 = 49$, the same equation with the sign flipped.

C.why: You never took the square root. You set $2x + 1$ equal to $\pm 49$ when it should be $\pm 7$.

D.why: You divided $\pm 7$ by 2 but never subtracted the 1. Isolate $2x$ before you divide.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
An archaeologist estimating how far a buried wall extends from a marker stake obtains the given equation, where $x$ is a signed distance in meters.

$2x^2 - 7 = 43$
items.stem: Which of the following statements about the solutions to the given equation must be true?
items.explanation: First add 7 to both sides to get $2x^2 = 50$. Then divide by 2 to get $x^2 = 25$. Taking the square root of both sides gives $x = 5$ or $x = -5$, because both $5^2$ and $(-5)^2$ equal 25. If you graph $y = 2x^2 - 7$ and $y = 43$, they cross at $x = -5$ and $x = 5$.

A.why: You took only the positive square root of 25. $(-5)^2 = 25$ as well, so $x = -5$ also satisfies the equation, and the equation has two solutions, not one.

B.why: You added 7 correctly to get $2x^2 = 50$, but then took the square root of 50 without first dividing by the coefficient 2. Isolate $x^2$ completely before taking the root.

D.why: You subtracted 7 from 43 instead of adding it, which gives $2x^2 = 36$ and $x^2 = 18$. To undo $-7$ you add 7 to both sides.

C.why: You solved $x^2 - 4x = 0$ and dropped the 21 on the right side. Factoring $x(x - 4)$ only works when the other side is zero, so you have to move 21 over first.

D.why: You kept only the $+$ branch of the $\pm$. The value $3 - \sqrt{5}$, about 0.76, also satisfies the equation, so there are two solutions.

items.stem: Which of the following is a solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: First get everything on one side: $2x^2 - 12x + 8 = 0$. Dividing by 2 gives $x^2 - 6x + 4 = 0$. items.stem: What is the negative solution to the given equation?

items.stem: The equation $x^2 + 6x = 4$ is rewritten in the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$. What is the value of $c$?
items.explanation: To get 0 on the right, subtract 4 from both sides: $x^2 + 6x - 4 = 0$. The constant term is now $-4$, so $c = -4$. This is the first move in every "find the constant from the number of solutions" question. The discriminant only works once the equation reads $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, and the sign of $c$ has to come across correctly.

B.why: You read the 4 straight off the right side without changing its sign. Moving a term to the other side of the equals sign flips its sign, so $c$ is $-4$, not 4. This is the most common way to get the discriminant wrong on the real question.

C.why: 6 is the coefficient of $x$, so it is $b$. The question asks for the constant term, $c$.

D.why: 1 is the coefficient of $x^2$, so it is $a$. The question asks for the constant term, $c$.

items.stem: The discriminant of a quadratic equation is $-12$. How many real solutions does the equation have?
items.explanation: A negative discriminant means the parabola never crosses the x-axis, so the equation has no real solutions. D.why: "Infinitely many" describes an equation that is true for every $x$, such as two identical lines. A quadratic with a nonzero $x^2$ term never has infinitely many solutions.

items.subtype_name: Find the constant from the number of solutions
items.stem: In the equation $x^2 + 6x + k = 0$, $k$ is a constant. If the equation has exactly one real solution, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: The equation is already in the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, with $a = 1$, $b = 6$ and $c = k$. A quadratic has exactly one real solution when its discriminant is zero, so set $b^2 - 4ac = 0$: $6^2 - 4(1)(k) = 0$, which gives $36 - 4k = 0$, so $k = 9$. As a check, $x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2$, which equals zero only at $x = -3$. This is the basic move behind every SAT question that tells you how many solutions a quadratic has and asks for the unknown constant. Harder versions also make you rearrange the equation into standard form first, or use $< 0$ or $> 0$ in place of $= 0$.

A.why: You wrote the discriminant as $b^2 + 4ac$, which dropped the minus sign. That gave $36 + 4k = 0$ and $k = -9$. The formula is $b^2 - 4ac$. Losing that minus sign is the most common slip in these questions.

B.why: You halved $b$ and got $3$, then stopped. That is the first step of completing the square. The constant term has to be that half squared, $3^2 = 9$, for the equation to become a perfect square with only one solution.

D.why: You worked out $b^2 = 36$ and gave that as $k$. You still have to set $36 - 4k = 0$ and divide by $4$, which gives $k = 9$.

items.stem: In the given equation, $c$ is an integer constant. The equation has no real solutions. What is the least possible value of $c$?

D.why: You never subtracted $2x$ from both sides and kept $b = 6$. That gives $36 < 4(c + 5)$, or $c > 4$, and $5$ is the least integer in that range. With the correct $b = 4$, smaller values also work.

D.why: You found $a = 12$ correctly but gave it as the answer. The question asks how much greater $a$ is than $b$, so you still need to subtract $b = 10$.

A paleobotanist checking a growth model for fossil fern fronds arrives at the following equation.

$2x^2 - kx = 3x - 8$
items.stem: In the equation above, $k$ is a positive constant. If the equation has exactly one real solution, what is the value of $k$?

D.why: You picked the first integer outside the boundary $k = 7.5$. When $k = 8$, the discriminant is $49 - 36 = 13 > 0$, so the equation has two real solutions, not none.

items.stimulus: A folklorist counted the number of distinct versions of a trickster tale recorded in each of 11 villages. The 11 counts have a mean of 16 and a median of 14. The folklorist then adds a twelfth village, where 60 versions of the tale were recorded.
items.stem:
Which of the following must be true?

I. The mean of the 12 counts is greater than 16.
II. The median of the 12 counts is greater than 14.
III. The median of the 12 counts is not less than 14.
items.explanation: The original total is $11 \times 16 = 176$. Adding 60 gives 236, and $236 \div 12 \approx 19.7$, which is greater than 16. So statement I must be true. Before the twelfth village, the median, 14, was the 6th of 11 sorted values. The new value goes at the top of the list, so the new median is the average of 14 and the old 7th value. That 7th value is at least 14, so the median can't drop below 14 (III must be true). However, the 7th value could equal 14, which would leave the median at exactly 14, so II need not be true.

A.why: You treated the median as completely unknown after the change. The new value sits above every old value, so the new median is the average of 14 and a value that is at least 14. It can't fall below 14.

C.why: You assumed the median must rise because the mean does. That's possible, but if the 7th sorted value is also 14, the median stays at 14. 'Must be true' rules out claims that are only possible.

D.why: You swapped the roles of the two measures and treated the mean as the resistant one. A value of 60, far above the mean of 16, must pull the mean up.

items.stimulus:

C.why: You overlooked the range. The new sample is the new maximum and the minimum is unchanged, so the range has to increase.

D.why: You rejected I. A value larger than every existing value is also larger than their mean, and adding a value above the mean always raises it.

items.stimulus: An ecologist measured water depth, in centimeters, at 20 stations in a wetland, and no two stations had the same depth. After a storm, the depth at each of the 10 deepest stations increased by exactly 6 centimeters, and the depth at each of the other 10 stations did not change.

D.why: You took the median to be the 11th value alone. With an even count, the median is the average of the 10th and 11th, so it rises by half of 6.

items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the achievement of Reyna's footbridge. All of the following choices use relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal EXCEPT:

items.explanation: Choice D explains how the concrete works, with the bacteria, the limestone and the rainwater. It never says what the bridge achieved. items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Kelp forests can collapse when sea urchins overgraze them, leaving bare areas called urchin barrens.
• Researchers had long assumed that kelp returns to a barren only if urchin densities fall below about 2 per square meter.
• Marine ecologist Tomás Ibarra monitored 12 barrens off the coast of Chile for three years.
• In four barrens, kelp regrew even though urchin densities stayed above 6 per square meter.
• In those four barrens, urchins mostly sheltered in crevices and ate drifting kelp rather than grazing attached kelp.
• Ibarra concluded that urchin behavior, not just urchin numbers, can determine whether kelp recovers.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Ibarra's findings in relation to what researchers had previously assumed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Over three years, Ibarra monitored 12 urchin barrens off the coast of Chile, tracking urchin densities and recording where and how the urchins fed.
In four of the barrens Ibarra monitored, kelp regrew while urchin densities stayed above 6 per square meter and the urchins ate mostly drifting kelp.
Kelp regrew in four barrens with more than 6 urchins per square meter, well above the long-assumed threshold of 2, showing that urchin numbers play no role in recovery.
Kelp regrew in four barrens with more than 6 urchins per square meter, well above the long-assumed threshold of 2, suggesting that urchin behavior also shapes recovery.
items.explanation: The goal ties the findings to an earlier assumption, so the answer has to include that assumption. Regrowth at more than 6 urchins per square meter only matters because researchers expected kelp to return only below 2. Choice D sets the finding against that threshold and then states Ibarra's conclusion accurately: behavior matters as well as numbers.

A.why: You picked a description of the study's method: where Ibarra worked, for how long, and what he measured. It reports no finding and never mentions the earlier assumption, so it can't show why the results matter.

B.why: You found the key result, but here it is a bare fact. 'Above 6 per square meter' only shows significance next to the long-assumed threshold of 2, and this choice leaves that threshold out, so a reader can't tell the result overturned anything.

C.why: You correctly set the finding against the old threshold, then accepted a conclusion that goes too far. Ibarra concluded that behavior, 'not just urchin numbers,' matters. That means numbers still count. Saying they play 'no role' turns his conclusion into a stronger claim than he made.

items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $f(x)$. Function $f$ is linear. Which equation defines $f$?

D.why: You used the change from 14 to 20 as the slope without dividing by the 2 weeks it took. This equation fits the first row, but at $x = 2$ it gives 26, not 20.

items.stimulus: A textile historian rebuilds an eighteenth-century hand loom and records how much cloth it produces after a new warp is set. Line $\ell$ models the total length $y$, in meters, of cloth woven $x$ days after the warp was set.
items.stem: In the xy-plane, line $\ell$ has a slope of 4 and passes through the point $(3, 21)$. Which equation defines line $\ell$?
items.explanation: Substitute the point into $y = 4x + b$: $21 = 4(3) + b$, so $21 = 12 + b$ and $b = 9$. The line is $y = 4x + 9$.

D.why: You found the correct intercept, 9, but then put it in the slope's place. The slope is given as 4, so it multiplies $x$. Also, $9(3) + 4 = 31$, so this line misses $(3, 21)$.

items.stem: In the xy-plane, line $k$ has a slope of $4$ and passes through the point $(0, -9)$. Which equation defines line $k$?
items.explanation: A point with an x-coordinate of $0$ lies on the y-axis, so $(0, -9)$ is the y-intercept and $b = -9$. You were given the slope directly, so $m = 4$. When you're given two points or a table, you first work out the slope, and then you're in exactly this position: you have m and b, and you need to put each in its correct place. Cartographers use the same idea when they lay a straight route on a map grid: the route starts where it crosses the y-axis and climbs at a steady rate.

items.stimulus: A seismologist models the time $T$, in seconds after a recorder was started, at which a shear wave from a small earthquake reaches a station $d$ kilometers from the source. items.stem: According to the model, at what distance from the source, in kilometers, does the shear wave reach a station 50 seconds after the recorder started?

A.why: You used the 16-beat jump as the slope without dividing by the 2-unit change in $x$. This equation fits the first row, since $16(2) + 78 = 110$, but it fails the other two, because $16(4) + 78 = 142$, not 126.

C.why: You worked out the slope as change in $x$ over change in $f(x)$, $\frac{2}{16}$, so the rate is upside down. Slope is always the change in output divided by the change in input.

D.why: You took 110 as the y-intercept, but 110 is the value when $x = 2$, not when $x = 0$. To get the intercept, go back one step of 2 from the first row: $110 - 16 = 94$.

items.subtype_name: Build the line from two points, a table, or slope plus a point
items.stimulus: A civil engineer models the elevation of a drainage culvert's floor, in centimeters above a fixed reference mark, with the linear function $g$, where $x$ is the distance in meters along the culvert from its inlet.
items.stem: The graph of the linear function $g$ in the xy-plane passes through the points $(4, 23)$ and $(10, 8)$. Which equation defines $g$?
items.explanation: The slope is $\frac{8 - 23}{10 - 4} = \frac{-15}{6} = -\frac{5}{2}$. Substitute $(4, 23)$: $23 = -\frac{5}{2}(4) + b = -10 + b$, so $b = 33$. That gives $g(x) = -\frac{5}{2}x + 33$. The elevation drops along the culvert, so a negative slope makes sense.

A.why: You mismatched the subtraction order, taking $8 - 23$ over $4 - 10$ in effect, and got a positive slope. The output falls from 23 to 8 as $x$ rises, so the slope has to be negative.

B.why: You used the y-coordinate of $(4, 23)$ as the y-intercept. The intercept is the value when $x = 0$, and this point has $x = 4$.

D.why: You found the slope as change in $x$ over change in $y$, $\frac{6}{-15}$, and then solved for $b$ from one point. The line goes through $(4, 23)$ but misses $(10, 8)$.

items.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. The graph of $y = f(x)$ in the xy-plane has a slope of 6 and passes through the point $(5, 47)$. What is the value of $a + b$?

D.why: You added 30 to 47 when solving for $b$ instead of subtracting it, which gave $b = 77$ and $a + b = 83$. From $47 = 30 + b$, you get $b = 17$.

items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $h(x)$, where $h$ is a linear function. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Going from $x = 1$ to $x = 3$, the elevation rises 36 meters, so the slope is $\frac{36}{2} = 18$ meters per kilometer. Going from $x = 3$ to $x = 7$ is 4 more kilometers, so $k = 448 + 18(4) = 520$.

D.why: You treated 412 as the elevation at $x = 0$ and calculated $412 + 18(7)$. But 412 is the elevation at $x = 1$.

items.stem: The graph of the linear function $L$ in the xy-plane passes through the points $(20, 1004)$ and $(80, 1016)$. Which equation defines $L$?
items.explanation: The slope is $\frac{1016 - 1004}{80 - 20} = \frac{12}{60} = 0.2$ millimeters per degree. Substitute $(20, 1004)$: $1004 = 0.2(20) + b = 4 + b$, so $b = 1000$. That gives $L(T) = 0.2T + 1000$.

C.why: You used 1004 as the intercept. But 1004 is the length at $20^\circ$C, not at $0^\circ$C.

items.stimulus: At an excavation site, an archaeologist uses a linear function $A$ to model the age of the soil. Here $A(d)$ is the estimated age, in years, of soil at a depth of $d$ centimeters. Soil at a depth of $40$ centimeters is estimated to be $1{,}300$ years old, and soil at a depth of $90$ centimeters is estimated to be $2{,}800$ years old.
items.stem: According to the model, how many years older is soil at a depth of $150$ centimeters than soil at a depth of $60$ centimeters?
items.explanation: The two data points are $(40, 1300)$ and $(90, 2800)$. The slope is $\frac{2800 - 1300}{90 - 40} = \frac{1500}{50} = 30$ years per centimeter. Moving from $60$ cm down to $150$ cm adds $90$ cm of depth, so the age goes up by $30 \times 90 = 2{,}700$ years. To check, $A(d) = 30d + 100$, which gives $A(150) - A(60) = 4600 - 1900 = 2700$.

A.why: You divided the change in depth by the change in age, $\frac{50}{1500} = \frac{1}{30}$, which flips the slope. Then $\frac{1}{30} \times 90 = 3$. Slope is the change in output over the change in input.

B.why: $1{,}900$ is $A(60)$, the age of the shallower soil by itself. The question asks for the difference between the two ages.

D.why: $4{,}600$ is $A(150)$, the age of the deeper soil by itself. You still need to subtract the age at $60$ cm to get the difference.

items.stem: According to the models, how many more miles of bike lanes did District B have than District A in 2020?

D.why: $27$ is District B's length in 2020. You found one of the two quantities but didn't subtract District A's $17$ miles to get the difference.

items.stimulus:
A battery powers a remote seismometer. The function $f$ gives the battery's charge, as a percentage of full charge, $x$ days after the seismometer was deployed. The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $f(x)$.

Seismometer Battery Charge
$x$ (days) | $f(x)$ (percent)
4 | 85
10 | 67
16 | 49
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of the slope of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in this context?
choices: The battery's charge decreases by 18 percentage points each day.
The battery's charge decreases by 3 percentage points each day.
The battery's charge decreases by $\frac{1}{3}$ percentage point each day.
The battery's charge decreases by 97 percentage points each day.
items.explanation: The slope is the change in output divided by the change in input. Between the first two rows, $f(x)$ goes from 85 to 67, a change of $-18$, while $x$ goes from 4 to 10, a change of 6. So the slope is $\frac{-18}{6} = -3$, and the units are percentage points per day. The third row checks out too: $67 - 3(6) = 49$. In this context, the charge drops by 3 percentage points each day.

A.why: 18 is the change in charge between two rows that are 6 days apart. You stopped before dividing by the 6 days, so you have the drop over six days, not the drop per day.

C.why: You divided the change in days by the change in charge, $\frac{6}{18}$, which flips the slope. Slope is the change in output over the change in input, so the charge goes on top.

D.why: 97 is the y-intercept: substituting $(4, 85)$ into $y = -3x + b$ gives $b = 97$, the charge on the day of deployment. It's a starting amount in percent, not a rate in percentage points per day.

items.stimulus: An agricultural scientist uses the linear model $y = mx + b$ to estimate the corn yield $y$, in bushels per acre, of a test plot when $x$ pounds of nitrogen fertilizer per acre are applied. The graph of the model in the xy-plane passes through the points $(20, 52)$ and $(50, 64)$.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of the y-intercept of the graph in this context?
choices: The estimated yield is 2 bushels per acre when no nitrogen is applied.
The estimated yield is 0.4 bushels per acre when no nitrogen is applied.
The estimated yield is 44 bushels per acre when no nitrogen is applied.
The estimated yield is 52 bushels per acre when no nitrogen is applied.
items.explanation: First find the slope: $m = \frac{64 - 52}{50 - 20} = \frac{12}{30} = 0.4$ bushel per acre for each pound of nitrogen. Then put $(20, 52)$ into $y = 0.4x + b$: $52 = 8 + b$, so $b = 44$. The y-intercept is the yield when $x = 0$, so with no nitrogen applied the model estimates 44 bushels per acre.

A.why: You found the slope as change in $x$ over change in $y$, $\frac{30}{12} = 2.5$, and then solved $52 = 2.5(20) + b$ to get 2. The slope has to be change in yield over change in nitrogen.

B.why: 0.4 is the slope, the extra yield for each additional pound of nitrogen. You calculated it correctly but reported it as the starting amount instead of going on to find $b$.

D.why: 52 is the yield at the given point where $x = 20$, not at $x = 0$. The y-intercept is where nitrogen is zero, so you have to work back 20 pounds using the slope.

items.stimulus: A linguist models the number of fluent speakers of a regional language with the function $f(t) = mt + b$, where $t$ is the number of years after 2000 and $m$ and $b$ are constants. According to the model, $f(4) = 2{,}860$ and $f(10) = 2{,}500$.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $b$ in this context?

The model estimates that there were 3,100 fluent speakers in 2000.
items.explanation: The slope is $m = \frac{2{,}500 - 2{,}860}{10 - 4} = \frac{-360}{6} = -60$, so the model loses 60 speakers per year. A materials engineer models the hardness $H(t)$ of an aluminum alloy sample, in Vickers hardness units, as a linear function of the annealing temperature $t$, in degrees Celsius.

items.stem: The function $H$ is defined by $H(t) = at + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. The table shows three values of $t$ and their corresponding values of $H(t)$. What is the value of $a + b$?

Using $(150, 312)$ and $(310, 248)$: $a = \frac{248 - 312}{310 - 150} = \frac{-64}{160} = -0.4$. Check with the third row: $\frac{212 - 312}{400 - 150} = \frac{-100}{250} = -0.4$. items.stimulus: At a seismic monitoring station, the S-wave from an earthquake arrives after the P-wave. A seismologist models this lag time $L(d)$, in seconds, as a linear function of the station's distance $d$ from the earthquake's epicenter, in kilometers.
items.stem: For the linear function $L$, $L(80) = 14$ and $L(240) = 34$. For what value of $d$ does $L(d) = 49$?
items.explanation: The slope is the change in output over the change in input: $\frac{34 - 14}{240 - 80} = \frac{20}{160} = \frac{1}{8}$ second per kilometer. Substitute $(80, 14)$ into $L(d) = \frac{1}{8}d + b$: $14 = 10 + b$, so $b = 4$. Now set $\frac{1}{8}d + 4 = 49$. That gives $\frac{1}{8}d = 45$, so $d = 360$. Check: $L(360) = 45 + 4 = 49$.

A.why: You treated lag time as proportional to distance, using $\frac{14}{80} = \frac{7}{40}$ second per kilometer from the first point alone, and solved $\frac{7}{40}d = 49$. That line passes through $(80, 14)$ but gives $L(240) = 42$, not $34$, so it fails the second condition.

C.why: You found the correct slope, $\frac{1}{8}$, but left out the intercept and solved $\frac{1}{8}d = 49$. The line has $b = 4$, so you have to subtract it from $49$ before multiplying by $8$.

D.why: You found $b = 4$ but moved it to the wrong side with the wrong sign and solved $\frac{1}{8}d = 49 + 4$. To isolate $\frac{1}{8}d$, subtract $4$ from both sides, which gives $45$, not $53$.

items.stimulus: An immunologist counts antibody-producing cells $y$, in thousands per millilitre, in blood samples from a volunteer. A booster dose was given on day 3 of the study. items.stem: Which equation models $y$ in terms of $x$, the number of days since the booster dose?
items.explanation: Measure time from the booster. Day 9 is 6 days after it and day 18 is 15 days after it, so the points are $(6, 14)$ and $(15, 26)$. The slope is $\frac{26 - 14}{15 - 6} = \frac{4}{3}$. Substitute $(6, 14)$: $14 = 8 + b$, so $b = 6$.

D.why: You subtracted the counts in one order and the days in the other, which gave a negative slope. The count rose, so the slope must be positive.

items.stem: Which table gives three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $y$ for the given equation?
items.explanation: Substitute each x-value into $3x - 4y = 24$. When $x = 0$, $-4y = 24$, so $y = -6$. When $x = 4$, $12 - 4y = 24$, so $y = -3$. When $x = 8$, $24 - 4y = 24$, so $y = 0$. Only this table works for all three rows.

B.why: This table gets the signs of the y-intercept and the slope wrong. It does share the x-intercept $(8, 0)$, so it looks right if you check only that row. At $x = 0$, though, $3(0) - 4(6) = -24$, not 24.

C.why: You divided 24 by 3 instead of by 4 when you found the y-intercept, which gave $-8$. The slope of $\frac{3}{4}$ is right, but $3(0) - 4(-8) = 32$, not 24.

D.why: The first two rows fit the equation, but at $x = 8$ you get $24 - 4(-1) = 28$, not 24. You have to check every row before you choose a table.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus:
A materials scientist heats an alloy rod and records its length. In the table, $x$ is the increase in the rod's temperature, in degrees Celsius, and $y$ is the length of the rod, in millimeters.

Alloy Rod Length During Heating
Temperature increase, $x$ (°C) | Length, $y$ (mm)
20 | $k + 1$
60 | $k + 3$
100 | $k + 5$
items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $y$, where $k$ is a positive constant. Which equation represents the linear relationship between $x$ and $y$?
items.explanation: The slope is $\frac{(k + 3) - (k + 1)}{60 - 20} = \frac{2}{40} = \frac{1}{20}$. Substitute $(20, k + 1)$ into $y = \frac{1}{20}x + b$: $k + 1 = 1 + b$, so $b = k$. Check $x = 100$: $5 + k$. The equation is $y = \frac{1}{20}x + k$.

A.why: You calculated the slope as run over rise, $\frac{40}{2} = 20$. At $x = 20$ this equation gives $400 + k$, not $k + 1$.

B.why: You put $k$ inside the parentheses, which divides it by 20 as well. At $x = 20$ this gives $1 + \frac{k}{20}$, which equals $k + 1$ only if $k = 0$, and $k$ is positive.

C.why: You took $k + 1$, the length in the first row, as the y-intercept. That length is for $x = 20$, not $x = 0$. At $x = 20$ this equation gives $k + 2$.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus:
A paleobotanist analyzing a lake-sediment core estimated the percentage of fossil pollen grains that came from conifers. In the table, $x$ is the age of a sediment sample, in thousands of years, and $y$ is the percentage of conifer pollen in that sample.

Conifer Pollen in Sediment Samples
Age, $x$ (thousands of years) | Conifer pollen, $y$ (%)
6 | 41
9 | 35
15 | 23
items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $y$. Which equation represents the linear relationship between $x$ and $y$?
items.explanation: The slope is $\frac{35 - 41}{9 - 6} = \frac{-6}{3} = -2$. The rows are not evenly spaced, so check the next pair as well: $\frac{23 - 35}{15 - 9} = -2$. Substitute $(6, 41)$: $41 = -12 + b$, so $b = 53$. The equation is $y = -2x + 53$.

A.why: This line has the wrong sign of slope. It passes through $(6, 41)$, but y decreases as x increases. At $x = 9$ this equation gives 47, not 35.

C.why: You calculated the slope as run over rise, $\frac{3}{-6} = -\frac{1}{2}$, then forced the line through $(6, 41)$. At $x = 9$ it gives 39.5, not 35.

D.why: You used 41, the y-value in the first row, as the y-intercept. That row has $x = 6$, not $x = 0$, so this line misses every point in the table.

items.stimulus: A nutrition researcher models the protein in a lunch plan made of a fixed base meal plus $x$ servings of a protein bar. The total protein in the lunch, $y$, in grams, is given by the equation $y - 30 = 8(x - 2)$.
items.stem: Which table gives three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $y$ for the given equation?
items.explanation: The point-slope form tells you directly that the line passes through $(2, 30)$ and has a slope of 8. Expanding gives $y = 8x - 16 + 30 = 8x + 14$. So $x = 0, 2, 4$ give $y = 14, 30, 46$.

A.why: You distributed 8 to $x$ but not to $-2$, which gives $y = 8x - 2 + 30 = 8x + 28$. At $x = 2$ this gives 44, but the equation requires 30.

B.why: You treated the 30 in the equation as the y-intercept. In this form, 30 is the y-value when $x = 2$, not when $x = 0$. This table has the right numbers paired with the wrong x-values.

D.why: This table has a slope of 8, but the intercept has the wrong sign: $-14$ instead of 14. You moved a term to the wrong side when you solved for $y$. At $x = 2$ it gives 2, not 30.

items.stimulus: During the rising phase of an immune response, a researcher measured the concentration of a specific antibody in a patient's blood. The graph shows the linear relationship between $x$, the number of days after vaccination, and $y$, the antibody concentration, in units per milliliter.
items.stem: Which equation represents the linear relationship between $x$ and $y$?
items.explanation: Between $(4, 10)$ and $(8, 16)$, the slope is $\frac{16 - 10}{8 - 4} = \frac{6}{4} = \frac{3}{2}$. Substitute $(4, 10)$: $10 = 6 + b$, so $b = 4$. Check $(16, 28)$: $24 + 4 = 28$. The equation is $y = \frac{3}{2}x + 4$.

B.why: You calculated the slope as run over rise, $\frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$. The intercept matches, but at $x = 4$ this equation gives about 6.7, not 10.

C.why: This line passes through $(4, 10)$, but you counted the 2 gridline intervals between $x = 4$ and $x = 8$ instead of the 4 days they represent, which doubled the slope. At $x = 8$ it gives 22, not 16.

D.why: You used 10, the y-value of the first plotted point, as the y-intercept. That point is at $x = 4$, not $x = 0$. At $x = 4$ this equation gives 16.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus:
At a warehouse, part-time workers earn a fixed hourly wage, and the same weekly equipment fee is deducted from every paycheck. In the table, $x$ is the number of hours a worker worked in a week, and $y$ is the worker's net pay for that week, in dollars.

Net Weekly Pay
Hours worked, $x$ | Net pay, $y$ (dollars)
10 | 120
25 | 345
40 | 570
items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $y$. Which equation represents the linear relationship between $x$ and $y$?

A.why: This is $y = 15x + 30$, so the intercept has the wrong sign. The fee is subtracted from pay, not added. At $x = 10$ this gives 180, not 120.

B.why: This equation gives 120 at $x = 10$, so it passes the first row. At $x = 25$ it gives 420, not 345. Check at least two rows before you choose.

C.why: You found the intercept, $-30$, and then put it inside the parentheses. Factoring 15 out of $15x - 30$ leaves $x - 2$, not $x - 30$. At $x = 10$ this equation gives $-300$.

items.stem: The relationship between $x$ and $y$ is linear and can be written as $y = mx + b$, where $m$ and $b$ are constants. What is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: Start with two rows to find the slope. From $(2, 14)$ to $(5, 23)$, $y$ goes up 9 while $x$ goes up 3, so $m = \frac{9}{3} = 3$. The table has no row where $x = 0$, so you have to work backward to the intercept. Substitute one point into $y = 3x + b$: $14 = 3(2) + b$, so $b = 14 - 6 = 8$. Check it with another row: $3(8) + 8 = 32$. Wrong answers you might get: 14 if you take the first $y$-value in the table as the intercept even though that row has $x = 2$, not $x = 0$; 3 if you report the slope instead of $b$; 20 if you add $3 \cdot 2$ instead of subtracting it; and $\frac{40}{3}$ if you find the slope as run over rise ($\frac{3}{9} = \frac{1}{3}$) and then solve for $b$.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus: A marine biologist seals several small reef fish in a respirometry chamber of seawater and records the dissolved oxygen level $y$, in milligrams per liter, $x$ hours after sealing. The graph models the relationship.
items.stem: The line shown is the graph of $ax + 2y = 24$, where $a$ is a constant. What is the value of $a$?
items.explanation: Read two clear points off the graph. The intercepts work well: $(0, 12)$ and $(8, 0)$. The equation is in standard form, and standard form is quickest with intercepts. Substitute the $x$-intercept $(8, 0)$: $8a + 2(0) = 24$, so $a = 3$. The $y$-intercept checks out: $3(0) + 2(12) = 24$. Using the slope gives the same result: $m = \frac{0 - 12}{8 - 0} = -\frac{3}{2}$, so $y = -\frac{3}{2}x + 12$. Multiplying by 2 gives $3x + 2y = 24$. Wrong answers you might get: $\frac{4}{3}$ if you find the slope as run over rise; $\frac{3}{2}$ if you find the slope's size but don't multiply by 2 to match the $2y$; and $-3$ if you move the $x$-term across without changing its sign.

figure.alt: A line decreasing from (0, 12) to (8, 0), passing through (2, 9), (4, 6), and (6, 3).

Rewrites y = −(3/2)x + 12 as 2y = −3x + 24 and keeps −3 without moving the x-term across, so the sign is wrong.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus:
A dietitian is planning menus that each give a patient exactly the same total amount of protein from two foods. The table shows three menus, where $x$ is the number of servings of cooked lentils and $y$ is the number of servings of Greek yogurt. The relationship between $x$ and $y$ is linear.

Protein-Matched Menus
Lentil servings, $x$ | Yogurt servings, $y$
0 | 12
4 | 9
8 | 6
items.stem: The relationship between $x$ and $y$ can be represented by the equation $px + 12y = 144$, where $p$ is a constant. What is the value of $p$?
items.explanation: The fastest way is to substitute a row into the equation you are given. With $(4, 9)$: $4p + 12(9) = 144$, so $4p = 36$ and $p = 9$. Check with $(8, 6)$: $9(8) + 12(6) = 72 + 72 = 144$. The slope gives the same answer: $m = \frac{9 - 12}{4 - 0} = -\frac{3}{4}$ and the $y$-intercept is 12, so $y = -\frac{3}{4}x + 12$. Multiply by 12 to get $9x + 12y = 144$. Wrong answers you might get: 16 if you find the slope as run over rise; 3 if you write $3x + 4y = 48$ but don't scale it to match the $12y$ in the given equation; and $\frac{3}{4}$ if you report the slope's size as $p$.

Finds the slope −3/4 and reports its size as p, which treats the slope as the x-coefficient.

items.stem: The relationship between $x$ and $y$ is linear and can be written as $y = mx + b$, where $m$ and $b$ are constants. What is the value of $m$?
items.explanation: Pick two rows and divide the change in $y$ by the change in $x$. From $(3, 41)$ to $(7, 69)$: $m = \frac{69 - 41}{7 - 3} = \frac{28}{4} = 7$. Check with the next pair of rows: $\frac{97 - 69}{11 - 7} = \frac{28}{4} = 7$. The $x$-values go up by 4, not 1, so you have to divide by 4. Wrong answers you might get: 28 if you use only the change in $y$; $\frac{1}{7}$ if you divide run by rise; and $\frac{41}{3}$ (or 13.67) if you divide a single $y$-value by its $x$-value, which assumes the line passes through the origin when the cloth beam actually started with cloth already on it.

items.explanation: The line crosses the $y$-axis at $(0, 12)$, so $b = 12$. From $(0, 12)$ to $(2, 15)$, $y$ goes up by 3 while $x$ goes up by 2, so the slope is $\frac{3}{2}$. The equation is $y = \frac{3}{2}x + 12$.

A.why: You divided run by rise, getting $\frac{2}{3}$. Slope is the change in $y$ divided by the change in $x$: $\frac{3}{2}$.

C.why: You used the rise of 3 as the slope without dividing by the run of 2 weeks between the points.

D.why: You switched the slope and the intercept. The 12 is where the line crosses the $y$-axis, so it is $b$, not the coefficient of $x$.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus: On a coordinate grid laid over a survey map, a cartographer draws a straight boundary line for a protected wetland. Every point $(x, y)$ on the boundary satisfies the equation $2x + 3y = 36$, where $x$ and $y$ are measured in grid units.
items.stem: Which table gives three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $y$ for the given equation?
items.explanation: Substitute each value of $x$. When $x = 0$, $3y = 36$, so $y = 12$. When $x = 3$, $6 + 3y = 36$, so $y = 10$. When $x = 6$, $12 + 3y = 36$, so $y = 8$. Only this table has all three pairs.

A.why: These $y$-values go up as $x$ goes up, so the slope is positive. Rearranging gives $y = -\frac{2}{3}x + 12$, so $y$ has to go down.

B.why: To find $y$ at $x = 0$, you divided 36 by 2 (the coefficient of $x$) when you should have divided by 3 (the coefficient of $y$). Every row is 6 too high as a result.

C.why: $(0, 12)$ is on the line, but $(3, 9)$ is not: $2(3) + 3(9) = 33$, not 36. A table has to work for every row, not only the first.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus:
A materials scientist hangs loads on a polymer strip and measures how far it stretches. The relationship between the load $x$, in newtons, and the strip's length $y$, in millimetres, is linear.

Polymer Strip Length Under Load
Load, $x$ (N) | Length, $y$ (mm)
0 | 60
4 | 66
8 | 72
12 | 78
items.stem: Which equation represents the relationship between $x$ and $y$?
items.explanation: The slope is $\frac{66 - 60}{4 - 0} = \frac{3}{2}$ and the $y$-intercept is 60, so $y = \frac{3}{2}x + 60$. Multiply by 2 to get $2y = 3x + 120$, then rearrange to $3x - 2y = -120$. Check with $(8, 72)$: $24 - 144 = -120$.

A.why: This rearranges to $y = \frac{3}{2}x - 60$, so the intercept has the wrong sign. When you moved 120 to the other side, the sign did not change.

B.why: This passes through $(0, 60)$, but its slope is $\frac{2}{3}$ because you divided run by rise. At $(4, 66)$ it gives $8 - 198 = -190$, not $-180$.

D.why: This passes through $(0, 60)$, but its slope is $-\frac{3}{2}$. The strip gets longer as the load increases, so the slope has to be positive.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus:
A paleobotany lab is cataloguing fossil seeds from a new core sample. Some seeds were already catalogued when the session began, and the lab then catalogues seeds at a constant rate. The table shows $y$, the total number of seeds catalogued, $x$ hours into the session, where $k$ is a positive constant.

items.stem: Which equation represents the relationship between $x$ and $y$?
items.explanation: When $x = 0$, $y = k$, so the $y$-intercept is $k$. From $x = 0$ to $x = 2$, $y$ goes up by 10, so the slope is $\frac{10}{2} = 5$. The equation is $y = 5x + k$. Check $x = 5$: $5(5) + k = k + 25$.

A.why: You switched the slope and the intercept. $k$ is the starting total (the value at $x = 0$), so it is the constant term, and 5 is the rate that multiplies $x$.

C.why: You dropped $k$ as if the lab started with no seeds. The table shows $y = k$ at $x = 0$, so the intercept is $k$, not 0.

D.why: You divided run by rise and got $\frac{2}{10}$. The slope is the change in $y$ over the change in $x$: $\frac{10}{2} = 5$.

items.stimulus: A nutrition researcher tracks how much of a participant's 32-gram daily fibre target is still left after eating servings of a high-fibre cereal. items.stem: Which equation represents the relationship between $x$ and $y$?
items.explanation: At $x = 0$, $y = 32$, so $b = 32$. From $(0, 32)$ to $(2, 24)$, $y$ goes down by 8 while $x$ goes up by 2, so the slope is $\frac{-8}{2} = -4$. The equation is $y = -4x + 32$.

B.why: You used 8 as the intercept. The equation needs the $y$-intercept, which is 32, the amount needed before any servings.

C.why: This passes through $(0, 32)$, but at $x = 2$ it gives 16, not 24. You used the drop of 8 over 2 servings as the slope without dividing by 2.

items.stem: Which equation represents the relationship between $x$ and $y$?

D.why: You used 13, the $y$-value in the second row, as the y-intercept. The y-intercept is the $y$-value when $x = 0$, which is 7.

items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $y$. Which equation represents the linear relationship between $x$ and $y$?

D.why: You used 13, the first $y$-value in the table, as the y-intercept. That value goes with $x = 2$, not $x = 0$, so it isn't the intercept.

A dietitian adds scoops of protein powder to a fruit smoothie. The table shows three values of $x$, the number of scoops added, and their corresponding values of $y$, the total protein in the smoothie, in grams.

Scoops, $x$ | Total protein (grams), $y$

items.stem: There is a linear relationship between $x$ and $y$. Which of the following equations represents this relationship?
items.explanation: Use two rows to find the slope: $\frac{50 - 26}{3 - 1} = \frac{24}{2} = 12$ grams per scoop. Substitute $(1, 26)$: $26 = 12(1) + b$, so $b = 14$, which is the protein in the smoothie before any powder goes in. The equation $y = 12x + 14$ also works for $(5, 74)$, since $12(5) + 14 = 74$.

A.why: You swapped the slope and the intercept. The protein added per scoop is 12 grams and the starting amount is 14 grams, not the other way round. Check $(3, 50)$: $14(3) + 12 = 54$, not 50.

C.why: This equation works for $(1, 26)$, since $13 + 13 = 26$, but you didn't check the other rows. At $x = 3$ it gives $13(3) + 13 = 52$, not 50. The equation has to fit every point in the table.

D.why: You took the $y$-value in the first row as the starting amount. That row is for 1 scoop, not 0 scoops, so 26 grams already includes one scoop of powder. The $y$-intercept is the value when $x = 0$, which is 14.

D.why: You divided $330$ by $10$ and used only the first row. $y = 33x$ fits $(10, 330)$, but at $x = 20$ it gives $660$, not $510$. Any choice you pick has to fit every row.

items.explanation: Put 9 in for $t$: $d(9) = 120 - 3(9) = 120 - 27 = 93$. The pond is 93 centimeters deep 9 days after the rainfall.

A.why: You solved $120 - 3t = 9$ and got $t = 37$. That finds the day when the depth is 9 centimeters. The question asks for $d(9)$, which is the depth on day 9, so 9 is the input, not the output.

C.why: You subtracted 9 from 120 and dropped the coefficient 3. The depth falls 3 centimeters per day, so after 9 days it has fallen $3(9) = 27$ centimeters, not 9.

D.why: You added $3(9)$ to 120 when you should have subtracted it. The minus sign means the pond loses 27 centimeters, so the depth has to be less than 120.

items.stimulus: The function $c$ is defined by $c(x) = 4x + 60$, where $c(x)$ is the total number of calories in a fruit smoothie with $x$ grams of protein powder blended in.
items.stem: What is the value of $c(80)$?
items.explanation: Put 80 in for $x$: $c(80) = 4(80) + 60 = 320 + 60 = 380$. A smoothie with 80 grams of protein powder has 380 calories.

A.why: You solved $4x + 60 = 80$ and got $x = 5$. That finds how many grams of powder give an 80-calorie smoothie. The question asks for $c(80)$, the calories when 80 grams of powder are added.

B.why: You found $4(80) = 320$, which is only the calories from the protein powder, and then stopped. You still need to add the 60 calories the smoothie has with no powder.

D.why: You added 80 and 60 first and then multiplied by 4, which gives $4(140) = 560$. Order of operations says you multiply $4 \cdot 80$ first and then add 60.

items.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = 4x + 1$. What is the value of $f(5)$?
items.explanation: Put 5 in for $x$: $f(5) = 4(5) + 1 = 20 + 1 = 21$. This one step comes up in every SAT question that defines a function and then asks for its value at a given input, including the word-problem versions where the input is a number of hours or items.

A.why: You solved $4x + 1 = 5$ and got $x = 1$. That finds the input that gives an output of 5. The question asks for the output when the input is 5. $f(5)$ means put 5 in for $x$, not set the function equal to 5.

B.why: You worked out $4(5) = 20$ and stopped there. You still need to add the constant: $20 + 1 = 21$.

D.why: You added before you multiplied and worked out $4(5 + 1) = 24$. Order of operations says multiply first: $4 \cdot 5 = 20$, then add 1.

items.stem: The function $g$ is defined by $g(x) = 3x + 8$. What is the value of $g(-2)$?
items.explanation: Put $-2$ in for $x$, with parentheses around it: $g(-2) = 3(-2) + 8 = -6 + 8 = 2$. Keeping parentheses around a negative input stops you from losing the sign. That matters in harder questions too, where a negative input is often the whole trap.

A.why: You got $-6$ for $3(-2)$ but then treated the $+8$ as $-8$ as well, which gave $-6 - 8 = -14$. Only the input is negative. The constant stays $+8$.

D.why: You dropped the negative sign and worked out $3(2) + 8 = 14$. Put the input in exactly as given: $3(-2) = -6$.

items.stem: The function $p$ is defined by $p(x) = \frac{1}{2}x - 3$. What is the value of $p(10)$?
items.explanation: Put 10 in for $x$: $p(10) = \frac{1}{2}(10) - 3 = 5 - 3 = 2$. Fractional coefficients come up often on the SAT. Choosing inputs that cancel the fraction cleanly, as 10 does here, is a skill you will use again when you check answer choices against a function.

D.why: You solved $\frac{1}{2}x - 3 = 10$ and got $x = 26$. That is the input that gives an output of 10. $p(10)$ asks for the output when the input is 10.

items.stem: If $f(x) = -3x + 4$, what is the value of $f(-2)$?
items.explanation: Put $-2$ in for $x$ and keep the parentheses: $f(-2) = -3(-2) + 4 = 6 + 4 = 10$. A negative times a negative is positive, so the first term is $+6$. This is the move behind every 'plug in and evaluate' question. Later you will meet it inside a model such as an archaeologist's formula for the depth of a dig after a given number of hours. C.why: You solved $-3x + 4 = -2$ and got $x = 2$. That answers the reverse question: which input gives an output of $-2$. The question asks for the output when the input is $-2$.

items.stem: According to the model, what is the air temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, at an altitude of 6,400 feet?

items.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = -\frac{2}{3}(x - 9) + 5$. What is the value of $f(-6)$?
items.explanation: Put $-6$ in for $x$ and keep it in parentheses: $f(-6) = -\frac{2}{3}(-6 - 9) + 5 = -\frac{2}{3}(-15) + 5 = 10 + 5 = 15$. A negative times a negative is positive, so the product is $+10$.

D.why: You solved $f(x) = -6$ and got $x = \frac{51}{2}$. The question asks for $f(-6)$, the output when the input is $-6$. It does not ask which input gives an output of $-6$.

items.explanation: Keep the negative input in parentheses: $g(-2) = -4(-2) + 15 = 8 + 15 = 23$. Then $g(3) = -4(3) + 15 = -12 + 15 = 3$. The gap is $23 - 3 = 20$ meters.

A.why: You calculated $g(3) - g(-2) = 3 - 23$. That's the reverse subtraction. The question asks how much greater $g(-2)$ is, so $g(-2)$ comes first.

B.why: You dropped the negative when you substituted and wrote $-4(-2)$ as $-8$, which gives $g(-2) = 7$ and a gap of $7 - 3 = 4$. A negative times a negative is positive.

D.why: You found $g(-2) = 23$ but never subtracted $g(3) = 3$. The question asks for the difference between the two elevations.

items.stimulus: A marine biologist uses the function $p(x) = \frac{3}{4}x + 6$ to estimate the length, in centimeters, of a juvenile reef fish $x$ weeks after it was tagged.
items.stem: According to the model, how many centimeters longer is a fish 12 weeks after tagging than 4 weeks after tagging?
items.explanation: Evaluate at each input: $p(12) = \frac{3}{4}(12) + 6 = 9 + 6 = 15$ and $p(4) = \frac{3}{4}(4) + 6 = 3 + 6 = 9$. The fish is $15 - 9 = 6$ centimeters longer.

D.why: You found $p(12) = 15$, the fish's length at 12 weeks, and stopped. You still need to subtract its length at 4 weeks, which is 9 centimeters.

choices: $48$; the mass the chick gains, in grams, in its first 12 days
$86$; the chick's mass, in grams, 12 days after hatching
$86$; the number of days it takes the chick to reach 12 grams
$4$; the mass the chick gains, in grams, during each day
items.explanation: Put 12 in for $d$: $M(12) = 4(12) + 38 = 48 + 38 = 86$. The input $d = 12$ is the number of days, and the output of $M$ is always a mass in grams. So $M(12) = 86$ means the chick weighs 86 grams 12 days after hatching.

C.why: You got the number right but swapped input and output. The 12 in $M(12)$ is a number of days that goes in, and 86 is the mass in grams that comes out. Finding when the chick reaches 12 grams would mean solving $M(d) = 12$, which is a different question.

D.why: You read off the slope instead of evaluating the function. The 4 is the rate in grams per day. The question asks for the output when $d = 12$.

items.stem: The function $T$ is defined by $T(h) = 18 - 3h$, where $T(h)$ is the temperature, in degrees Celsius, of an observatory telescope's mirror $h$ hours after the dome is opened for the night. What is the value of $T(4)$, and what does it represent?
choices: $30$; the mirror's temperature, in °C, 4 hours after the dome opens
$12$; the drop in the mirror's temperature, in °C, over 4 hours
$6$; the number of hours until the mirror's temperature is 4 °C
$6$; the mirror's temperature, in °C, 4 hours after the dome opens
items.explanation: Put 4 in for $h$: $T(4) = 18 - 3(4) = 18 - 12 = 6$. The input is time in hours and the output is temperature in °C, so $T(4) = 6$ means the mirror is at 6 °C 4 hours after the dome opens. The answer also fits the story: the mirror is cooling, so its temperature should be lower than the starting 18 °C.

A.why: You lost the negative sign and added $3(4)$ to 18 instead of subtracting it. The mirror is cooling, so its temperature has to go down from 18, not up.

B.why: You found $3(4) = 12$, which is how much the temperature has fallen, and stopped there. $T(4)$ is the temperature itself, so you still need $18 - 12$.

C.why: You got the number right but read it the wrong way round. In $T(4)$, the 4 is hours going in and the 6 is degrees coming out. The time it takes to reach 4 °C would come from solving $T(h) = 4$, and that does not give 6.

C.why: You stopped at $24(3) = 72$ without adding the starting height of 50 cm. The 72 cm is the growth since tagging, not the height.

D.why: You swapped input and output. The 3 in $K(3)$ is a number of weeks going in, and 122 is the height in centimeters coming out. Finding when the frond is 3 cm tall would mean solving $K(w) = 3$.

items.stimulus: A historian models the price, in pence, of one pound of a certain cotton yarn sold by a Lancashire spinning mill with the function $p(t) = 38 - \frac{5}{2}(t - 4)$, where $t$ is the number of years after 1800 and $0 \le t \le 12$.
items.stem: According to the model, what was the price, in pence, of one pound of this yarn in 1810?
items.explanation: 1810 is 10 years after 1800, so the input is $t = 10$. Don't subtract the 4 yourself. The function does that. Substitute: $p(10) = 38 - \frac{5}{2}(10 - 4) = 38 - \frac{5}{2}(6) = 38 - 15 = 23$. The output is a price in pence, which is what the question asks for, so the answer is 23.

A.why: You distributed the $-\frac{5}{2}$ only to $t$ and then subtracted 4, giving $38 - 25 - 4$ or $38 - 25 + 4$. Correct distribution gives $-\frac{5}{2}t + 10$, so $p(10) = 38 - 25 + 10 = 23$.

C.why: You found how much the price fell between 1800 and 1810. The price in 1800 is $p(0) = 38 + 10 = 48$, not 38, and $48 - 23 = 25$. The question asks for the 1810 price itself, not the drop.

D.why: You treated $t$ as years after 1804 and used $t = 6$, which subtracts the 4 twice: $38 - \frac{5}{2}(2) = 33$. Since $t$ counts years after 1800, the input for 1810 is $t = 10$.

items.stem: According to the model, how many measures of the gigue remain 3 minutes 55 seconds after the start of the recording?
items.explanation: The input $t$ is measured from the start of the gigue, not from the start of the recording. Convert both times to seconds: 3 min 55 s = 235 s and 2 min 40 s = 160 s. So $t = 235 - 160 = 75$. Then $R(75) = 96 - \frac{3}{5}(75) = 96 - 45 = 51$ measures remain.

B.why: You solved $R(t) = 75$ instead of finding $R(75)$: $96 - \frac{3}{5}t = 75$ gives $t = 35$. The 75 is the input, so substitute it for $t$.

C.why: 45 is $\frac{3}{5}(75)$, the number of measures already played. The function gives the measures remaining, so subtract that from 96.

items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

D.why: "Celebrate" is approving, as if the study praised the coaches' view. The slower times work against that view, so the sentence calls for disagreement, not praise.

Traffic counts taken one year after the lanes opened ______ that expectation, showing that daily bike trips on the redesigned streets had more than doubled.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The planners expected more cycling, and the counts show bike trips more than doubled. The evidence shows the expectation was correct, so the counts "validated" it.

A.why: You reversed the evidence. A doubling of bike trips is what the planners expected, so the counts back up the expectation. They don't overturn it.

C.why: You picked a neutral word that sounds like research. Planners survey streets and riders, but counts don't "survey" an expectation. The word also doesn't say whether the numbers matched what the planners predicted.

D.why: "Regretted" expresses an attitude that only people can have, and it is a negative one. The data can't regret anything, and the outcome was good for the planners' expectation.

items.subtype_name: How findings relate to a claim (support / undermine / question)
items.stimulus: When ecologist Ana Ruiz proposed that wolves returning to a mountain valley would help its streamside willow trees recover, many of her colleagues were ______: they doubted that a predator could influence plant life so directly. A decade of field surveys has since shown willow cover along the valley's streams nearly tripling as wolves kept browsing elk on the move.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The blank describes the colleagues, and the text after the colon defines it: they "doubted" Ruiz's idea. People who doubt a claim are "skeptical."

A.why: You mixed up who held which view. The later surveys support Ruiz, but at the time her colleagues doubted her. That is the opposite of being convinced.

B.why: You picked a word that fits the topic, since field ecologists are observant. But the text after the colon is about the colleagues' reaction to Ruiz's idea, which was doubt, and "observant" says nothing about that.

C.why: "Grateful" is a positive attitude toward the proposal. The colon explains that the colleagues doubted it, so the sentence calls for a doubting attitude, not an appreciative one.

items.subtype_name: How findings relate to a claim (support / undermine / question)
items.stimulus: Marine biologists long held that brittle stars living in cold, deep water regrow lost arms far more slowly than their shallow-water relatives. To test this view, biologist Imani Okafor's team measured arm regrowth in both groups over six months. The deep-water animals regrew their arms nearly as fast as the shallow-water ones, a finding that ______ the long-held view.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The long-held view said deep-water brittle stars regrow arms much more slowly. Okafor's team found that they regrow arms nearly as fast. That finding goes against the earlier view, so the blank needs a word that means weakening a claim. "Undermines" does exactly that.

A.why: You reversed the relationship. The view predicted much slower regrowth, but the study found nearly the same speed. That result works against the view instead of backing it up.

B.why: You chose a neutral, research-sounding verb. A finding doesn't "record" an earlier belief, and the word says nothing about whether the new evidence agrees or disagrees. The question turns on that relationship.

D.why: To repeat the view, the finding would have to say the same thing as the view. Here it says something different: the deep-water animals were nearly as fast, not far slower.

items.subtype_name: How findings relate to a claim (support / undermine / question)
items.stimulus: For decades, seismologists ______ that the Varden Fault was fully locked, storing strain silently between large earthquakes. That view seemed safe, since no tremors had ever been recorded there. But when a dense network of new sensors was installed along the fault in 2019, it detected thousands of tiny slips every year.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The blank describes what the seismologists themselves believed. The next sentence calls it a view that "seemed safe," so they held it. Then "But" brings in the new sensor data that overturns it. "Assumed" fits a belief that people accepted without proof and that later turned out to be wrong.

A.why: You mixed up who did what. The new sensor data challenges the view, but the seismologists in the blank held it. The text says the view "seemed safe" to them, so they didn't doubt it.

D.why: To demonstrate something is to prove it true. The seismologists had no recorded evidence for the view, just an absence of tremors, and the new data shows the view was false. Nobody could have proved it.

items.subtype_name: How findings relate to a claim (support / undermine / question)
items.stimulus: For years, many people assumed that drinking cold water right after a meal slows digestion. To test this belief, a team of nutrition researchers timed digestion in 120 adults who drank either cold or warm water after eating. The two groups digested their meals at the same rate. The results ______ the popular belief.
items.stem: Does the new finding agree with the earlier belief or go against it? Choose the word that shows that relationship.
items.explanation: Start by asking whether the finding agrees with the belief or goes against it. The belief says cold water slows digestion, but the study found no difference between the groups, so the finding goes against the belief. 'Challenged' is the word for evidence that goes against a view. This is the first step in every Words in Context question that sets up a belief and then brings in a study: decide whether the evidence agrees or disagrees before you look at the choices.

A.why: You reversed the relationship. For the study to confirm the belief, the cold-water group would have needed slower digestion. The two groups digested at the same rate, so the evidence goes against the belief.

C.why: You chose a word that sounds like research. A study can reveal facts, but 'revealed the popular belief' would mean the study uncovered the belief itself. The blank needs a word that says whether the evidence agrees or disagrees, and 'revealed' does neither.

D.why: You picked a neutral research verb. The researchers inspected their data, but saying the results 'inspected' the belief doesn't make sense, and the word doesn't say whether the evidence supports or opposes the belief.

items.stimulus: Vegetable growers in the region had long ______ that planting beans in a field one season leads to a bigger corn harvest there the next season. items.stimulus: When a city replaced the steel cables on an old footbridge with a lighter synthetic material, some engineers worried that the new cables would stretch in freezing weather and let the deck sag. Over two winters of testing, the cables kept their original length within a fraction of a millimeter. These measurements ______ the engineers' concern.
items.stem: Does the new finding agree with the earlier concern or go against it? Choose the word that shows that relationship.
items.explanation: The concern was that the cables would stretch in the cold. The tests showed they didn't, so the evidence goes against the concern. 'Dispelled' means made a worry go away, which is what evidence against a concern does. Words in Context questions often build a passage this way: a worry or belief, then a 'but actually' finding. A.why: You reversed the relationship. The measurements would justify the concern only if the cables had stretched. They kept their length, so the evidence goes against the worry.

D.why: You confused the people with the evidence. The engineers held the concern, but the measurements came later and showed the concern was wrong, so the measurements didn't 'expect' anything.

items.subtype_name: How findings relate to a claim (support / undermine / question)
items.stimulus: Ecologists predicted that removing an invasive grass from a small meadow plot would allow native wildflowers to return. The team cleared the grass and checked the plot each spring. After three years, native wildflowers covered most of the ground where the grass had been. This result ______ the ecologists' prediction.
items.stem: Does the new finding agree with the earlier prediction or go against it? Choose the word that shows that relationship.
items.explanation: The ecologists predicted that wildflowers would return, and they did, so the evidence agrees with the prediction. 'Confirmed' means showed a prediction to be correct. Notice that it is a measured word: one plot over three years supports the prediction without settling it everywhere. D.why: You picked a word that is too strong. One small plot over three years can confirm a prediction, but it cannot guarantee the same thing will happen in other meadows or future years. Choose the word the evidence can actually support.
