items.subtype_name: Which finding would weaken or challenge the claim
items.stimulus: Concrete bridge decks often fail from the inside. De-icing salt dissolves in meltwater and seeps down through the concrete to the steel reinforcing bars. As the bars rust, they swell and crack the concrete above them. After surveying 40 bridge decks in Vermont, a team of engineers found that decks built with zinc-coated bars showed far less surface cracking after twenty years than decks built with bare bars. The engineers concluded that the zinc coating reduces cracking by slowing the rusting of the bars.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the engineers' claim?
choices: Bars taken from the zinc-coated decks showed much less rust than bars taken from the decks built with bare bars.
Most zinc-coated decks were on rural roads treated with far less de-icing salt than the roads carrying the bare-bar decks.
Zinc-coated bars cost more to produce than bare bars, so few states have used them in new bridge decks.
Salt-laden meltwater reached the bars in both groups of decks at about the same rate over the twenty years.
items.explanation: The engineers credit the coating for the difference in cracking. That only holds if the two groups of decks were otherwise alike, and above all if they got similar amounts of salt. If the zinc-coated decks mostly sat on lightly salted rural roads, less salt is a better explanation for the lower cracking, and the coating may have done nothing.

A.why: This is the trap for this kind of question: you answered the opposite question. Less rust on the coated bars is just what the engineers predicted, so this finding supports their claim.

C.why: You picked a true-sounding fact about zinc-coated bars that has nothing to do with whether the coating reduces cracking. Cost doesn't make the claim more or less likely to be true.

D.why: You misread where the coating acts in the chain. The engineers say it slows rusting, not the seeping of salt. Equal salt exposure actually makes the two groups a fairer comparison, so this finding strengthens the claim.

items.subtype_name: Which finding would weaken or challenge the claim
items.stimulus: Many etchings printed in the 1800s show faint brown halos around their inked lines. Art historians have long said the halos come from linseed oil in the ink: the oil slowly spread outward into the paper and darkened as it aged. Conservator Inés Valdés doubts this account. Printers of the period usually dampened their paper with well water before printing. Valdés suspects that iron dissolved in that water caused the stains, not the oil.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the art historians' claim?
choices: Etchings printed on dampened paper with an oil-free ink show halos as often as those printed with linseed-oil ink.
Halos are wider in etchings whose ink held a large share of linseed oil than in those whose ink held little.
Printers of the period dampened their paper mainly so that it would press more fully into the plate's grooves.
Iron is present in small amounts in nearly all paper made in the 1800s, whether or not it was dampened.
items.explanation: The historians' claim needs the oil to be the cause, so halos should form only where there is oil. Etchings that contain no oil but still get halos just as often show that the oil isn't needed. That points to something else, such as the dampening water.

B.why: This is the trap for this kind of question: you sided with the experts being challenged. If more oil gives wider halos, that supports the historians' claim instead of weakening it.

C.why: You chose a detail about why paper was dampened. The reason for dampening says nothing about whether the oil or the water caused the halos.

D.why: You mixed up whose claim is under attack. Iron being in all paper, dampened or not, undercuts Valdés's explanation that iron came from the dampening water. It doesn't undercut the historians'.

items.subtype_name: Which finding would weaken or challenge the claim
items.stimulus: During heat waves, older adults who live alone face special risk. Many don't notice the early signs of heat illness until they need emergency care. In 2023, health officials in Tucson began phoning every registered resident over 70 who lived alone on days above 105°F, reminding them to drink water and visit a cooling center. Heat-related emergency visits in that group fell by a third compared with 2022. The officials concluded that the calls caused the decline.

choices: Residents who answered the calls needed emergency care less often than registered residents who never answered them.

items.subtype_name: Which finding would weaken or challenge the claim
items.stimulus: Along one stretch of rocky coast, kelp forests are much denser in coves where sea otters forage than in nearby coves where otters are absent. Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins graze on kelp. On that basis, marine ecologist Ines Varga hypothesizes that the gap in kelp density between the two kinds of cove exists mainly because otters reduce the number of urchins in the coves where they forage.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Varga's hypothesis?
choices: Coves with otters had far fewer urchins than coves without otters, and their kelp was correspondingly denser.
Sea otters eat more urchins than any other predator living in the coves along that stretch of coast.
Coves with otters had about as many urchins as coves without otters, yet their kelp was still much denser.
Kelp in both kinds of cove grew fastest in summer, when the coastal water reached its highest temperatures.
items.explanation: Varga's hypothesis is a chain: otters reduce urchin numbers, fewer urchins means less grazing, and less grazing means denser kelp. For the chain to explain the gap, coves with otters must have fewer urchins. If urchin numbers are about the same in both kinds of cove and the kelp gap is still there, that middle link is gone. Something other than urchin numbers must be causing the difference, so this finding weakens the hypothesis directly.

A.why: You answered the opposite question. This finding confirms each link in Varga's chain, so it strengthens her hypothesis. It feels like the best fit because it lines up so closely with the passage, but the question asks what would weaken it.

B.why: You treated a general fact about otters as evidence about the gap. Knowing that otters are the main urchin predator says nothing about whether urchin numbers actually differ between the two kinds of cove. If anything, it leans toward supporting Varga.

D.why: You chose a true-sounding detail about kelp growth. The pattern is the same in both kinds of cove, so it doesn't address the difference between them or why it exists.

items.subtype_name: Which finding would weaken or challenge the claim
items.stimulus: In a study of 80 warehouses owned by one retailer, half began posting shift schedules two weeks in advance. The other half were matched to them for size and wages and kept posting schedules two days ahead. After one year, annual worker turnover was 9 percentage points lower at the advance-notice warehouses. Economist Dara Okafor claims that this gap arose mainly because early schedules let workers with young children arrange child care.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Okafor's claim?
choices: At the advance-notice warehouses, turnover fell most sharply among workers who needed child care for young children.
The turnover gap between the two groups of warehouses was about as large for workers without children as for parents.
Several warehouses owned by other retailers began posting shift schedules two weeks in advance the following year.
Turnover at the advance-notice warehouses ended the year lower than the national average for warehouse workers.
items.explanation: Okafor's claim depends on the word "mainly" and on one group, parents of young children. If the gap comes mainly from parents being able to arrange child care, it should be much larger for parents than for workers without children. A gap of about the same size in both groups means child care can't be the main reason. Something that affects all workers is more likely behind it.

A.why: You picked the finding that supports Okafor instead of the one that weakens her claim. If turnover fell most among parents who needed child care, that is exactly what her explanation predicts. Check the direction word in the question before you choose.

C.why: You read other retailers adopting the policy as evidence about why it worked. That they copied it says nothing about which workers stayed, or why, at the warehouses in this study.

D.why: You compared one group with an outside benchmark instead of looking at the gap between the two matched groups. Okafor's claim is about why the two groups differ, and this finding doesn't address that.

items.subtype_name: Which finding would weaken or challenge the claim
items.stimulus: Two surviving impressions of an eighteenth-century woodblock print of a river crossing differ in one noticeable way. The fine lines of a boatman's rain cape are crisp in the Leiden impression but blurred in the Boston impression. Carved blocks wear down with each printing, and damage such as a crack appears in every impression pulled after it occurs. Citing the difference in sharpness, art historian Kenji Mori concluded that the Boston impression was printed later than the Leiden impression.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Mori's conclusion?
choices: A crack in the block's border appears in the Boston impression but is absent from the Leiden impression.
Both impressions were printed on paper from a single mill that operated for roughly twenty-five years.
Other prints from the same publisher show blurred fine lines in impressions known to have been printed later.
A crack in the block's border appears in the Leiden impression but is absent from the Boston impression.
items.explanation: Mori's conclusion only holds if the blurring comes from later wear, which would make Boston the later impression. According to the passage, a crack shows up in every impression printed after it forms. If the Leiden impression has a crack that the Boston one lacks, Leiden must have been printed later. In that case the sharper impression is the later one, so the blurring in Boston can't be from wear, and Mori's dating is undercut.

A.why: You reversed the direction. A crack that appears in Boston but not Leiden would mean Boston was printed later, which strengthens Mori's conclusion. Before reading the choices, work out which order the crack would have to show to weaken it.

B.why: You focused on a shared feature of the two impressions. Paper from the same mill, made over a twenty-five-year span, doesn't tell you which impression came first, so it can't weaken Mori's conclusion.

C.why: You took a general pattern from other prints as a verdict on these two impressions. At most, the pattern makes Mori's reasoning look plausible. It gives no evidence against his dating of the Leiden and Boston impressions.

items.subtype_name: Which finding would weaken or challenge the claim
items.stimulus: Along the Varn River, villages tell a tale of a church bell that sank during a flood and can still be heard ringing beneath the water. The versions share a plot but differ in local details, such as the saint to whom the bell was dedicated. Earlier scholars credited peddlers who walked the valley roads with spreading the tale. Folklorist Ines Marlowe, however, concludes that the tale was carried downstream by the river's boatmen.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would NOT weaken the folklorist's conclusion?
choices: Versions collected in inland villages along the peddlers' roads closely match those collected in riverside villages.
The tale is absent from several riverside villages where boatmen regularly stopped to trade their cargo.
The earliest recorded version of the tale comes from a village at the river's mouth, its farthest point downstream.
Riverside versions share local details with versions from upstream villages more often than with nearby inland versions.
items.explanation: Marlowe's claim is that the tale moved down the river with boatmen rather than over land with peddlers. If riverside versions share details with versions upstream more than with nearby inland versions, the tale's family resemblances follow the river and not the roads. That fits her conclusion, so it is the one finding that does not weaken it. Each of the other three choices does weaken it.

A.why: You probably assumed boatmen could also have carried the tale inland, but the passage never says so. Close matches in inland villages on the peddlers' roads point to the peddlers, which is the explanation Marlowe rejects. So this choice does weaken her conclusion.

B.why: You probably treated a choice about where the tale is missing as beside the point. If boatmen spread the tale, it should turn up where they regularly stopped. Its absence there removes a condition Marlowe's claim depends on.

C.why: You probably saw 'river' and read this choice as support. A tale that moved downstream should appear first upstream. An oldest version at the river's mouth runs the wrong direction for Marlowe's account.

items.subtype_name: Which finding would weaken or challenge the claim
items.stimulus: Some engineers add capsules containing dormant bacterial spores and calcium lactate, a nutrient, to concrete. When a crack lets in water, the spores revive, feed on the lactate, and release calcite, a mineral that can fill the crack. To test this, a team cast two sets of slabs that were identical except that one set contained the capsules. After all slabs were cracked and kept wet, only the capsule slabs' cracks sealed. The team concluded that the bacteria's activity sealed those cracks.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would NOT weaken the team's conclusion?
choices: Capsule slabs whose spores had been killed by heat before mixing sealed their cracks as quickly as the other capsule slabs did.
Cracks in capsule slabs that were kept completely dry sealed as fully as cracks in capsule slabs that were kept wet.
Calcium lactate mixed into concrete without any spores reacts with the cement to form calcite that fills cracks.
Calcite was found only in cracks in capsule slabs where living bacteria were also detected along the crack walls.
items.explanation: The team's claim depends on a chain: water revives the spores, and the living bacteria produce the calcite that seals the crack. If calcite appears only where living bacteria are present, the sealing tracks the bacteria, which is what the conclusion needs. This finding supports the claim, so it does not weaken it. Each of the other three choices breaks a link in the chain or offers another cause.

A.why: You probably read 'sealed as quickly' as good news for the capsules. If dead spores work just as well, living bacteria are not what seals the cracks. That reverses the team's conclusion.

B.why: You probably treated keeping the slabs wet as a minor test detail. The passage says water is what revives the spores. If dry cracks seal just as well, the bacteria cannot be the cause.

C.why: You probably saw the nutrient as incidental, but only the capsule slabs contained it. If the lactate forms calcite without any bacteria, it explains the result just as well as the bacteria do.

items.subtype_name: Which finding would weaken or challenge the claim
items.stimulus: A 1630 chart of the island of Kessra by mapmaker Joan Ruys contains a distinctive error: a deep bay drawn on the island's northern coast where none exists. The same bay appears on a 1652 chart of Kessra by Pieter Haelst. Shared mistakes are a common clue that one map was copied from another. Historian Mara Lindqvist claims that Haelst copied the northern coastline from Ruys's chart rather than surveying that coast himself.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would NOT weaken the historian's claim?
choices: Haelst's logbooks record that he personally surveyed the northern coast of Kessra in 1648.
A 1625 chart that Ruys worked from shows the same false bay and was in Haelst's possession.
Haelst's northern coastline departs from Ruys's in most other features and matches the real coast more closely.
Haelst's southern coastline differs considerably from Ruys's southern coastline in shape and in place names.
items.explanation: Lindqvist's claim is limited to the northern coastline. How Haelst drew the southern coast has no bearing on whether he copied the north from Ruys, because a mapmaker could copy one coast and survey another. This finding leaves her claim intact. Each of the other choices challenges the claim about the north directly.

A.why: You probably read a survey record as consistent with the claim. Lindqvist says Haelst did not survey that coast himself, and a record that he did contradicts her directly.

B.why: You probably treated a third chart as outside the comparison. If Haelst owned the earlier chart that also shows the false bay, he could have copied the error from it rather than from Ruys. That is a competing explanation.

C.why: You probably took one shared error as proof of copying regardless of everything else. If most of Haelst's northern coast differs from Ruys's and is more accurate, the evidence points toward his own survey and away from copying.

items.stimulus: A nutrition scientist is working out how much seed coating each cracker in a test batch carries per unit of surface. Each cracker is a square with a side length of 6 centimeters.
items.stem: What is the area, in square centimeters, of one cracker?
items.explanation: The area of a square is $A = s^2$. With $s = 6$, $A = 6^2 = 36$ square centimeters.

B.why: You took half of $6^2$, which uses the triangle formula's $\frac{1}{2}$. A square's area is $s^2$ with nothing taken off.

C.why: You found the perimeter, $4 \times 6 = 24$ centimeters. The question asks for area, so you need $s^2$, not $4s$.

items.stimulus: A labor economist is studying a small manufacturer that plans to build a staff break area on a lot shaped like a right triangle. The two legs of the lot are 12 meters and 16 meters, and the side opposite the right angle is 20 meters.
items.stem: What is the area, in square meters, of the lot?
items.explanation: In a right triangle, the two legs are the base and the height. $A = \frac{1}{2}bh = \frac{1}{2}(12)(16) = 96$ square meters. The 20-meter side is the hypotenuse, so it is not used here.

C.why: You used the hypotenuse as one of the dimensions, $\frac{1}{2}(16)(20) = 160$. The height has to be perpendicular to the base, so use the two legs, 12 and 16.

D.why: You multiplied the legs, $12 \times 16 = 192$, and did not take half. A triangle's area is $\frac{1}{2}bh$.

items.stimulus: A city planner's design for a new neighborhood park is a rectangle 90 meters long and 60 meters wide. A rectangular paved plaza 20 meters long and 15 meters wide sits inside the park, and the rest of the park will be lawn.

items.explanation: The perimeter gives $2(l + w) = 34$, so $l + w = 17$. The area gives $lw = 60$. Test the choices: if the longer side is 12, the shorter side is $17 - 12 = 5$. Then $12 \times 5 = 60$ and $2(12 + 5) = 34$, so both conditions hold. The longer side is 12 meters.

A.why: 5 is the length of the shorter side. The question asks for the longer side.

B.why: A 6-by-10 rectangle does have an area of 60 square meters. But its perimeter is $2(6 + 10) = 32$ meters, not 34. You checked the area and skipped the perimeter.

D.why: 17 is $l + w$, the sum of the two sides, which you get by halving the perimeter. It is a step along the way, not the length of either side.

items.subtype_name: 2D area or perimeter: plug in and combine
items.stimulus: An immunologist cuts a test strip shaped like a right triangle from a sheet of antibody-coated membrane. The two shorter sides are 9 millimeters and 12 millimeters long, and the longest side is 15 millimeters. To find how much coated surface the strip has, the immunologist computes $\frac{1}{2}(9)(12) = 54$.
items.stem: Which of the following best describes what 54 represents in this situation?
choices: The perimeter of the strip, in millimeters
The area of the strip, in square millimeters
The area of the strip, in millimeters
Twice the area of the strip, in square millimeters
items.explanation: In a right triangle, the two shorter sides (the legs) are the base and the height, so $\frac{1}{2}bh = \frac{1}{2}(9)(12) = 54$ is the triangle's area. Area is measured in square units, so 54 is the area of the strip in square millimeters.

A.why: You mixed up area and perimeter. The perimeter is the sum of all three sides, $9 + 12 + 15 = 36$ millimeters, not 54. The expression $\frac{1}{2}bh$ gives area.

C.why: You have the right quantity but the wrong units. Multiplying millimeters by millimeters gives square millimeters, so an area can't be measured in plain millimeters.

D.why: You treated $9 \times 12$ as the triangle's area and read the $\frac{1}{2}$ as halving it. In fact $9 \times 12 = 108$ is the area of a rectangle. The $\frac{1}{2}$ is part of the triangle formula, so 54 is the area itself.

items.stimulus: A paleobotanist is digging for fossil leaves in a rectangular plot 8 meters long and 5 meters wide. A square patch 3 meters on a side, inside the plot, lies under a boulder and will not be dug. The paleobotanist computes $8(5) - 3^2 = 31$.
items.stem: Which of the following best describes what 31 represents in this situation?
choices: The area of the whole plot, in square meters
The area under the boulder, in square meters
The perimeter of the excavated region, in meters
The area of the excavated region, in square meters
items.explanation: The term $8(5) = 40$ is the area of the whole rectangular plot, and $3^2 = 9$ is the area of the square patch under the boulder. Subtracting the cut-out from the big shape leaves $40 - 9 = 31$ square meters, which is the area that will actually be dug.

A.why: You stopped at the first part of the calculation. The whole plot is $8(5) = 40$ square meters. The value 31 comes after the boulder's patch has been subtracted.

B.why: You chose the piece that was removed instead of the piece that is left. The area under the boulder is $3^2 = 9$ square meters, and 31 is what remains after you take it away.

C.why: You mixed up area and perimeter. Products like $8(5)$ and $3^2$ measure area in square meters. They are not side lengths added together.

items.subtype_name: 2D area or perimeter: plug in and combine
items.stimulus: A seismology team monitors a rectangular zone that measures 40 kilometers by 24 kilometers. The team drops one corner of the zone from monitoring. The dropped part is a right triangle whose two legs lie along the two sides of the rectangle that meet at that corner. The leg along the 40-kilometer side is 15 kilometers long, and the dropped triangle has an area of 60 square kilometers.
items.stem: What is the perimeter, in kilometers, of the remaining monitoring zone?
items.explanation: First find the missing leg. The triangle's area is $\frac{1}{2}(15)(b) = 60$, so $b = 8$ km. The legs are 15 and 8, so the hypotenuse, which is the new boundary, is $\sqrt{15^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{289} = 17$ km. The rectangle's perimeter was $2(40 + 24) = 128$ km. Cutting off the corner removes 15 km and 8 km of the old edges and adds the 17 km hypotenuse: $128 - 15 - 8 + 17 = 122$ km.

A.why: You took the 15 km and 8 km of edge away from the original 128 km, which leaves 105 km, but you forgot that the cut adds a new 17 km side along the hypotenuse. The region is still closed, so that side belongs in its perimeter.

C.why: This is the perimeter of the whole rectangle, $2(40 + 24) = 128$. You never accounted for the dropped corner. The boundary changes when the triangle is removed, because two leg-length stretches are swapped for one hypotenuse.

D.why: You found the area of the remaining zone, $40 \cdot 24 - 60 = 900$ square kilometers, but the question asks for the perimeter. You've swapped area for perimeter, which is the trap this kind of question is built to catch.

items.stimulus: A printmaker pulls an etching on a rectangular sheet of paper. The sheet's length is 3 times its width, and its perimeter is 96 centimeters. The printed image is a rectangle centered on the sheet. It leaves a blank margin exactly 3 centimeters wide along all four edges.
items.stem: What is the area, in square centimeters, of the margin?
items.explanation: Start with the sheet: $2(w + 3w) = 96$, so $8w = 96$, which gives $w = 12$ cm and a length of 36 cm. The sheet's area is $36 \cdot 12 = 432$ square cm. The margin takes 3 cm off both ends of each dimension, so the image measures $(36 - 6)$ by $(12 - 6)$, or 30 cm by 6 cm, for an area of 180 square cm. The margin is the sheet minus the image: $432 - 180 = 252$ square centimeters.

A.why: You took the 3 cm margin off each dimension only once, which makes the image 33 cm by 9 cm and gives $432 - 297 = 135$. The margin runs along both ends of the length and both ends of the width, so each dimension shrinks by 6 cm.

B.why: This is the area of the printed image, $30 \cdot 6 = 180$. That is the part inside the margin. The question asks for the blank border, so you still need to subtract this from the sheet's area.

D.why: You multiplied the sheet's perimeter by the margin's width, $96 \cdot 3 = 288$, as if the border were one straight strip. Using the perimeter to stand in for an area is the trap here. It counts each $3 \times 3$ corner square twice, so it overshoots by $4 \cdot 9 = 36$.

items.stem: What is the perimeter, in meters, of the work area?
items.explanation: The work area is $2x \cdot x - \frac{1}{2}x \cdot x = \frac{3}{2}x^2 = 54$, so $x^2 = 36$ and $x = 6$. The floor is 12 meters by 6 meters. Its perimeter is $12 + 6 + 6 + 6\sqrt{2} = 24 + 6\sqrt{2}$ meters.

D.why: You added the hypotenuse to the rectangle's perimeter but did not remove the two 6-meter legs, which are no longer part of the work area's boundary.

Any athlete who tapers for two weeks will improve performance by at least 2 percent.
items.explanation: Choice C is about "most athletes" across several sports, and no single study or group is its subject. That makes it a claim about tapering in general. In 2019, economist Rania Delacroix studied wage records from 1,200 grocery stores following a state minimum-wage increase.
items.explanation: A generalization makes a claim about the whole phenomenon without making any single case its subject. Choice A describes what usually happens when minimum wages rise and why employers do it, which is a broad claim about spillover effects.

C.why: You went for a broad-sounding claim that goes too far. The notes say workers slightly above the minimum 'often' get raises. They never say every worker does, and the 4 percent figure comes from a single study.

items.subtype_name: Write a function for a geometric quantity
items.stimulus: A rectangular solar panel on a small research satellite has a length that is 4 meters greater than its width. The length of the panel is $x$ meters.
items.stem: Which function $A$ gives the area of the panel, in square meters, in terms of $x$?
items.explanation: The length is $x$, and the width is 4 meters less than the length, so the width is $x - 4$. The area is length times width: $x(x - 4) = x^2 - 4x$.

B.why: You wrote the width as $x + 4$, as if $x$ were the width. Here $x$ is the length, so the width is the smaller dimension, $x - 4$, and the sign of the offset flips.

C.why: You added the two dimensions, $x + (x - 4)$, when you should have multiplied them to get the area.

D.why: You multiplied $x$ by $x$ but did not multiply $x$ by $-4$. Distributing fully gives $x^2 - 4x$.

items.subtype_name: Write a function for a geometric quantity
items.stimulus: A marine biologist builds a rectangular holding tank for juvenile sea turtles. The tank has a height of 2 feet, and its length is 3 feet greater than its width. The width of the tank is $w$ feet.
items.stem: Which function $V$ gives the volume of the tank, in cubic feet, in terms of $w$?
items.explanation: The width is $w$ and the length is $w + 3$. Volume is length times width times height: $2 \cdot w(w + 3) = 2w^2 + 6w$.

A.why: You found the area of the base, $w(w + 3)$, but forgot to multiply by the 2-foot height.

B.why: You wrote the length as $w - 3$. The length is 3 feet greater than the width, so it is $w + 3$.

D.why: You multiplied $w^2$ by 2 but not the $3w$ term. The height multiplies the whole product, giving $2w^2 + 6w$.

items.stimulus: At an excavation site, archaeologists uncover an ancient grain-storage pit shaped like a right circular cylinder. The depth of the pit is 4 feet more than its radius.

items.explanation: The variable is the depth, $h$. The depth is 4 more than the radius, so the radius is $h - 4$. A cylinder's volume is $\pi r^2 h$, so $V(h) = \pi (h - 4)^2 h = \pi h(h - 4)^2$. Check with $h = 6$: the radius is 2, so the volume is $\pi(4)(6) = 24\pi$, and $\pi(6)(2)^2 = 24\pi$.

items.stem: Which function $V$ gives the volume, in cubic meters, of the trench in terms of its length $L$, in meters?

items.stimulus: The cross section of a drainage channel is an isosceles trapezoid. The bottom of the channel is as wide as the channel is deep, and the top of the channel is 6 feet wider than the bottom.
items.stem: Which function $A$ gives the area, in square feet, of the cross section in terms of the channel's top width $t$, in feet?
items.explanation: The bottom width is $t - 6$, and the depth equals the bottom width, so the depth is also $t - 6$. A trapezoid's area is the average of its parallel sides times its height: $\frac{1}{2}(t + t - 6)(t - 6) = (t - 3)(t - 6)$.

D.why: You added the two parallel sides but left out the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$, so your area is twice the true area.

items.stem: Which equation represents the line shown in the graph?
items.explanation: The line crosses the vertical axis at $(0, 8)$, so the y-intercept is $8$. From $(0, 8)$ to $(1, 6)$ the line drops $2$ for every $1$ it moves right, so the slope is $-2$. That gives $y = -2x + 8$. This is the reading you need when a question shows two graphed lines and asks which pair of equations they could be: you do this for each line, then keep only the choice that matches both.

A.why: You read the steepness correctly but missed the direction. The line goes down from left to right, so its slope is negative. Mixing up whether a line rises or falls is the most common mistake when matching graphed lines to equations.

C.why: You used where the line meets the horizontal axis, at $x = 4$, as $b$. In $y = mx + b$, $b$ is where the line crosses the vertical axis, which is $8$.

D.why: You found the slope as run over rise. Slope is rise over run: the line falls $2$ for every $1$ to the right, so the slope is $-2$, not $-\frac{1}{2}$.

The first line slants up from left to right and passes through the points $(0, -2)$, $(2, 1)$, and $(4, 4)$. The second line slants down from left to right and passes through the points $(-2, 3)$, $(0, 2)$, and $(4, 0)$.
items.stem: One of the two graphed equations is $3x + ky = 12$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: First work out which line $3x + ky = 12$ can be. Solving for $y$ gives $y = -\frac{3}{k}x + \frac{12}{k}$. For the rising line you would need $-\frac{3}{k} = \frac{3}{2}$, so $k = -2$, and also $\frac{12}{k} = -2$, so $k = -6$. Those two values disagree, so the equation has to be the falling line. That line passes through $(0, 2)$. Substitute: $3(0) + k(2) = 12$, so $k = 6$. Check it with the slope: $-\frac{3}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}$. That matches the falling line, which drops 2 over a run of 4, from $(0, 2)$ to $(4, 0)$.

You set $-\frac{3}{k}$ equal to the rising line's slope, $\frac{3}{2}$. You paired the equation with the line that increases.
You read the x-intercept $(4, 0)$ as $(0, 4)$ and substituted it: $4k = 12$.
You substituted $(4, 4)$. That point is on the rising line only, so it does not have to satisfy this equation.
You took the slope of $3x + ky = 12$ to be $-\frac{k}{3}$ instead of $-\frac{3}{k}$, and solved $-\frac{k}{3} = -\frac{1}{2}$. 1.5 is the same error.
This is $\frac{3}{2}$ as a decimal. It comes from flipping the slope of $3x + ky = 12$ to $-\frac{k}{3}$.

items.subtype_name: Read or match the solution on a graph
items.stimulus: A linguist modeled the number of entries, $y$, in two regional dialect dictionaries $x$ years after both projects began. Each model is linear, and both models are graphed in the $xy$-plane. The graph of the model for the Coastal dictionary passes through the points $(0, 200)$, $(10, 700)$, and $(20, 1{,}200)$. The graph of the model for the Upland dictionary passes through the points $(0, 500)$, $(10, 800)$, and $(20, 1{,}100)$.
items.stem: The solution to the system is the point where the two models predict the same number of entries. How many entries does each model predict at that point?
items.explanation: The Coastal line rises 500 entries every 10 years, so $y = 50x + 200$. The Upland line rises 300 entries every 10 years, so $y = 30x + 500$. The lines cross where $50x + 200 = 30x + 500$. That gives $20x = 300$, so $x = 15$. Substitute back: $y = 50(15) + 200 = 950$. Check it with the other model: $30(15) + 500 = 950$. Both models predict 950 entries.

items.subtype_name: Read or match the solution on a graph
items.stimulus: A nutrition science researcher graphed a system of two linear equations in the $xy$-plane while comparing two fiber-intake models. The first line slants up from left to right and passes through the points $(0, -1)$, $(3, 3)$, and $(6, 7)$. The second line slants down from left to right and passes through the points $(0, 4)$, $(3, 2)$, and $(6, 0)$.
items.stem: If $(x, y)$ is the solution to the system, what is the value of $x + y$?
items.explanation: The lines do not cross at a lattice point, so write each equation from two clear points. The first line rises 4 over a run of 3 from $(0, -1)$, so $y = \frac{4}{3}x - 1$. The second line falls 2 over a run of 3 from $(0, 4)$, so $y = -\frac{2}{3}x + 4$. Set them equal: $\frac{4}{3}x - 1 = -\frac{2}{3}x + 4$. That gives $2x = 5$, so $x = \frac{5}{2}$. Then $y = -\frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{2} + 4 = \frac{7}{3}$. Add the two: $x + y = \frac{5}{2} + \frac{7}{3} = \frac{29}{6}$.

items.subtype_name: Read or match the solution on a graph
items.stimulus: A cartographer plotted two straight roads on a coordinate grid of a city map. For the first line in the system, the line slants up from left to right and passes through the following points: $(1, -1)$ and $(6, 9)$. For the second line in the system, the line slants down from left to right and passes through the following points: $(-2, 8)$ and $(8, 3)$.
items.stem: The graph of a system of linear equations is shown. What is the solution $(x, y)$ to the system?
items.explanation: Line 1 has slope $\frac{9 - (-1)}{6 - 1} = 2$, so $y = 2x - 3$. Line 2 has slope $\frac{3 - 8}{8 - (-2)} = -\frac{1}{2}$, so $y = -\frac{1}{2}x + 7$. Setting them equal gives $2x - 3 = -\frac{1}{2}x + 7$, so $\frac{5}{2}x = 10$ and $x = 4$. Then $y = 2(4) - 3 = 5$. The lines cross at $(4, 5)$.

A.why: You found the crossing point but wrote it as $(y, x)$. The x-coordinate is $4$ and the y-coordinate is $5$.

B.why: $(0, 7)$ is the y-intercept of the second line only. The first line is at $y = -3$ when $x = 0$, so this point fails the first equation.

C.why: $(2, 6)$ is on the second line, but the first line is at $y = 1$ when $x = 2$. A solution has to lie on both lines.

items.subtype_name: Read or match the solution on a graph
items.stimulus: A labour economist compared two pay plans for warehouse workers. In the $xy$-plane, $x$ is the number of hours worked in a week and $y$ is the weekly pay, in dollars. For the first line in the system, the line slants up from left to right and passes through the following points: $(0, 200)$ and $(30, 500)$. For the second line in the system, the line slants up more steeply from left to right and passes through the following points: $(0, 0)$ and $(30, 600)$.
items.stem: The graph of a system of linear equations is shown. What is the solution $(x, y)$ to the system?
items.explanation: The first line has slope $\frac{500 - 200}{30} = 10$, so $y = 10x + 200$. The second line has slope $\frac{600}{30} = 20$, so $y = 20x$. Setting them equal gives $20x = 10x + 200$, so $x = 20$. Then $y = 20(20) = 400$. The lines cross at $(20, 400)$.

A.why: $(0, 200)$ is the y-intercept of the first line only. The second line passes through $(0, 0)$, so this point fails the second equation.

C.why: You found the crossing point but wrote it as $(y, x)$. The hours, $20$, come first and the pay, $400$, comes second.

D.why: $(30, 500)$ is one of the listed points on the first line. The second line is at $y = 600$ when $x = 30$, so this point is not on both lines.

items.subtype_name: Read or match the solution on a graph
items.stimulus: An immunologist compares two groups of volunteers. Group A received a new vaccine and their antibody levels are rising. Group B has antibodies from an earlier infection, and their levels are slowly falling.
items.stem: The graph shows Group A's antibody concentration $y$, in units per milliliter, $t$ weeks after a vaccine dose. Group B's concentration is modeled by $y = 70 - 5t$. If $(t, y)$ is the solution to the system made up of the graphed line and Group B's equation, what is the value of $y$?
items.explanation: Only one line is drawn, so first read its equation off the graph. It crosses the y-axis at 10 and rises 10 units for every 2 weeks, so its slope is 5 and the line is $y = 5t + 10$. The solution is the point that lies on both lines, so set the two equal: $5t + 10 = 70 - 5t$. That gives $10t = 60$, so $t = 6$. Substitute to get $y = 5(6) + 10 = 40$. Check it in Group B's equation: $70 - 5(6) = 40$.

figure.caption: Group A Antibody Concentration
figure.alt: A straight increasing line passing through (0, 10), (2, 20), (4, 30), (6, 40), (8, 50), and (10, 60).

items.stimulus: A sports scientist records two athletes' heart rates during a treadmill test in which the speed is raised step by step.
items.stem: The graph shows Athlete A's heart rate $y$, in beats per minute, when running at a treadmill speed of $x$ kilometers per hour. Athlete B's heart rate is modeled by $y = 15x + 40$. items.stem: The graph shows the number of sea urchins $y$ per square meter on Reef P, $t$ months after sea otters returned. On Reef Q, $y = 2t + 6$. If $(t, y)$ is the solution to the system of the graphed line and Reef Q's equation, what is the value of $y$?

items.stem: Which system of equations could be represented by the lines shown?
items.explanation: The rising line passes through $(0, 4)$ and $(2, 7)$, so its slope is $\frac{3}{2}$. At $x = 4$ it is at 10, which gives $y - 10 = \frac{3}{2}(x - 4)$. The falling line passes through $(0, 11)$ and $(2, 7)$, so its slope is $-2$. At $x = 4$ it is at 3, which gives $y - 3 = -2(x - 4)$. Neither choice is written at the crossing point $(2, 7)$, so you have to check which line each point $(4, 10)$ and $(4, 3)$ lies on.

A.why: You flipped the signs in point-slope form. $y + 10 = \frac{3}{2}(x + 4)$ passes through $(-4, -10)$, not $(4, 10)$, so neither equation matches its line.

C.why: You have the right two points and the right two slopes, but paired them wrongly. The slope $-2$ is attached to the point $(4, 10)$ on the rising line, and $\frac{3}{2}$ to $(4, 3)$ on the falling line.

D.why: You took run over rise for each slope. That gives $\frac{2}{3}$ and $-\frac{1}{2}$ instead of $\frac{3}{2}$ and $-2$. The points are right but both lines are too flat.

figure.caption: Two features of learner speech
figure.alt: Two straight lines drawn as rows of dots: one rising and one falling. They cross once.

items.subtype_name: Read or match the solution on a graph
items.stimulus: An agronomist modeled the height $y$, in centimeters, of two seedling varieties $x$ days after transplanting. The graph shows the two linear models.
items.stem: What is the solution $(x, y)$ to the system of equations represented by the lines?
items.explanation: The lines are nearly parallel, so where they cross is hard to see. Work it out from lattice points instead. One line passes through $(0, 4)$ and $(4, 8)$, so $y = x + 4$. The other passes through $(0, 2)$ and $(4, 7)$, so $y = \frac{5}{4}x + 2$. Setting them equal gives $\frac{1}{4}x = 2$, so $x = 8$ and $y = 12$.

A.why: $(7, 11)$ is a gridline point on $y = x + 4$ where the lines look like they touch. The other line is at 10.75 there, so this point lies on only one line.

B.why: You found the right crossing point but wrote it as $(y, x)$. The days go first.

C.why: You added the constants instead of subtracting them, getting $\frac{1}{4}x = 6$. From $x + 4 = \frac{5}{4}x + 2$, the correct step is $\frac{1}{4}x = 4 - 2 = 2$.

figure.alt: Two rising straight lines drawn as rows of dots. They have nearly the same steepness and run very close together across the middle of the graph.

items.subtype_name: Read or match the solution on a graph
items.stimulus: A paleobotanist modeled the percent $y$ of pine pollen and of oak pollen in lake sediment laid down $x$ thousand years after a glacial period ended. The graph shows both models for $2 \le x \le 10$.
items.stem: Which system of equations could be represented by the lines shown?
items.explanation: The horizontal axis starts at 2, so neither y-intercept is shown. The falling line passes through $(2, 17)$ and $(4, 14)$, so its slope is $-1.5$. Going back 2 units from $(2, 17)$ gives a y-intercept of $17 + 3 = 20$. The rising line passes through $(2, 5)$ and $(4, 6)$, so its slope is $0.5$ and its y-intercept is $5 - 1 = 4$. As a check, both lines pass through $(8, 8)$.

A.why: You read the y-intercepts at the left edge of the graph, but that edge is $x = 2$, not $x = 0$. The slopes are right, but these lines are 3 units and 1 unit off from the graph.

C.why: You put each slope on the wrong line. The falling line drops 1.5 per unit and the rising line climbs 0.5, not the other way around.

D.why: You took run over rise for each slope, getting $-\frac{2}{3}$ and $2$ instead of $-\frac{3}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$. The intercepts are right but the slopes are not.

figure.x_label: Thousands of years after glacial period
figure.alt: Two straight lines drawn as rows of dots for x from 2 to 10: one falling and one rising. They cross once.

items.subtype_name: Read or match the solution on a graph
items.stimulus: A folklorist modeled the number $y$ of new recordings collected per year for two folktales $x$ years after an archive opened. The graph shows both linear models.
items.stem: Which system of equations could be represented by the lines shown?
items.explanation: The two axes use different scales: 2 units per gridline across and 5 units per gridline up. The falling line passes through $(0, 30)$ and $(4, 20)$, so $y = -\frac{5}{2}x + 30$, which is $5x + 2y = 60$. The rising line passes through $(0, 10)$ and $(4, 20)$, so $y = \frac{5}{2}x + 10$, which is $5x - 2y = -20$. Both pass through $(4, 20)$.

A.why: You counted gridlines instead of units. Each line moves 2 gridlines up or down for every 2 gridlines across, which looks like a slope of 1. But 2 gridlines across is 4 years and 2 gridlines up is 10 recordings, so the slopes are $\pm\frac{5}{2}$.

B.why: These lines have the right y-intercepts, 30 and 10, but slopes of $\mp\frac{2}{5}$. You took run over rise.

C.why: You have the right slopes but swapped the intercepts. $5x + 2y = 20$ falls from 10, and $5x - 2y = -60$ rises from 30. On the graph, the falling line starts at 30 and the rising line at 10.

items.stimulus: An immunology student models antibody data with a linear function $f$ and graphs $y = f(x)$ in the $xy$-plane. From left to right, the line passes through the following points: $(-4, 0)$, $(0, 6)$, and $(2, 9)$.
items.stem: What is the $y$-intercept of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the $xy$-plane?
items.explanation: The $y$-intercept is the point where the line crosses the $y$-axis, which is where $x = 0$. The listed point with $x = 0$ is $(0, 6)$.

B.why: This is where the line crosses the $x$-axis, because $y = 0$ there. You gave the $x$-intercept, but the question asked for the $y$-intercept.

C.why: You found the right number but put the coordinates in the wrong order. $(6, 0)$ lies on the $x$-axis, not the $y$-axis.

D.why: You took $-4$, the $x$-value where the line crosses the $x$-axis, and put it in the $y$-intercept's place. On this line, $x = 0$ goes with $y = 6$.

items.subtype_name: Read a feature off the graph, or match an equation to its graph
items.stimulus: A sports scientist uses the equation $y = -2x + 8$ to model a sprinter's recovery data.
items.stem: Which of the following describes the graph of $y = -2x + 8$ in the $xy$-plane?
items.explanation: The constant term gives the $y$-intercept $(0, 8)$. The slope is $-2$, so the line falls 2 units for every 1 unit to the right and reaches $y = 0$ when $x = 4$. That gives $(4, 0)$.

B.why: The $y$-intercept is right, but a line from $(-4, 0)$ to $(0, 8)$ rises, so its slope is $+2$. You missed the negative sign on the slope.

C.why: You swapped the intercepts. This line crosses the $y$-axis at 4, but the equation's constant term says it crosses at 8.

D.why: You read the coefficient $-2$ as the $y$-intercept. The coefficient is the slope, and the constant 8 is where the line crosses the $y$-axis.

items.subtype_name: Read a feature off the graph, or match an equation to its graph
items.stimulus: The graph shows part of the linear function $f$. An agricultural science lab used it as a model.
items.stem: What is the $y$-intercept of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the $xy$-plane?
items.explanation: The line is not drawn as far as the $y$-axis, so you have to extend it yourself. Use two lattice points, $(2, 12)$ and $(6, 6)$. The slope is $\frac{6 - 12}{6 - 2} = -\frac{3}{2}$. Going 2 units left from $x = 2$ to $x = 0$ raises $y$ by $2 \cdot \frac{3}{2} = 3$, so $y = 12 + 3 = 15$. The $y$-intercept is $(0, 15)$, and $f(x) = -\frac{3}{2}x + 15$.

B.why: $(2, 12)$ is the leftmost point drawn, but it is not on the $y$-axis. You took its $y$-value as the intercept without extending the line from $x = 2$ back to $x = 0$, where it rises 3 more units.

C.why: This is where the line crosses the $x$-axis. It is the $x$-intercept, not the $y$-intercept. The $y$-intercept is the point where $x = 0$.

D.why: You got the right value, 15, but put it in the wrong coordinate. A $y$-intercept always has $x = 0$, so it is $(0, 15)$, not $(15, 0)$.

items.stimulus: A printmaker uses a linear relationship to set the angle of a cut across a woodblock grid. The graph of this relationship is shown in the $xy$-plane.
items.stem: Which equation represents the line shown?
items.explanation: Read the intercepts off the graph: the line crosses the $x$-axis at $(-4, 0)$ and the $y$-axis at $(0, -6)$. The slope is $\frac{-6 - 0}{0 - (-4)} = -\frac{3}{2}$, so $y = -\frac{3}{2}x - 6$. Multiply by 2 and rearrange to get $3x + 2y = -12$. Check: $(-4, 0)$ gives $-12$ and $(0, -6)$ gives $-12$.

B.why: This equation is $y = \frac{3}{2}x - 6$. It has the correct $y$-intercept, $(0, -6)$, but a positive slope, so its line rises. The line in the graph falls. You stopped checking once the $y$-intercept matched and never checked the sign of the slope.

C.why: This line crosses the axes at $(-6, 0)$ and $(0, -4)$. You swapped the two intercepts, which gives a slope of $-\frac{2}{3}$ instead of $-\frac{3}{2}$. Substitute $(0, -6)$: you get $-18$, not $-12$.

D.why: You lost a negative sign while clearing the fractions from $y = -\frac{3}{2}x - 6$. This line has the right slope, but it crosses the axes at $(4, 0)$ and $(0, 6)$, which is the mirror image of the graph through the origin.

D.why: You used the x-intercept, $-6$, for $b$. But $b$ is where the line crosses the y-axis, which is $-4$.

items.explanation: The graph shown is $y = f(x) + 4$, and it crosses the y-axis at $(0, 1)$, so $f(0) + 4 = 1$. That gives $f(0) = -3$, so the graph of $y = f(x)$ has its y-intercept at $(0, -3)$.

B.why: You saw that the graph was shifted but added 4 to the shown intercept instead of subtracting it, so you moved further from $f$, not back to it.

C.why: You read the y-intercept straight off the picture, but the picture is $y = f(x) + 4$, not $y = f(x)$.

D.why: You found $-3$ correctly but wrote the point with its coordinates reversed. That point is on the x-axis, not the y-axis.

items.stimulus: A cartographer graphed a linear function $f$ for only part of its domain.
items.stem: Part of the graph of the linear function $y = f(x)$ is shown. What is the x-intercept of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the xy-plane?
items.explanation: From $(-8, 9)$ to $(-4, 6)$ the line falls 3 over a run of 4, so the slope is $-\tfrac{3}{4}$. Starting at $(-4, 6)$, the line has to fall 6 more to reach $y = 0$, which takes a run of 8. So $x = -4 + 8 = 4$, and the x-intercept is $(4, 0)$.

B.why: You extended the line correctly but stopped at the y-axis. $(0, 3)$ is the y-intercept, and the question asked where the line crosses the x-axis.

C.why: You found 4 but wrote the point with its coordinates reversed, which puts it on the y-axis.

D.why: You took the slope as $+\tfrac{3}{4}$ and extended the line the wrong way. The segment falls left to right, so it reaches $y = 0$ to the right.

items.stem: The graph of $y = f(x)$ is shown, where $f$ is a linear function. What is the x-intercept of the graph of $y = f(x - 3)$ in the xy-plane?

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: Marine biologists surveying a coral reef found that the number of parrotfish on the reef increased by $30\%$ from 2020 to 2024. In 2020, the biologists counted $p$ parrotfish on the reef.
items.stem: Which expression represents the number of parrotfish counted on the reef in 2024?
items.explanation: An increase of $30\%$ means you keep all of the original amount, $1p$, and add $30\%$ of it, $0.30p$. So the 2024 count is $p + 0.30p = 1.30p$. The multiplier for a $30\%$ increase is $1 + \frac{30}{100} = 1.30$.

A.why: $0.30p$ is only the number of parrotfish added to the population. You wrote the rate as the multiplier and forgot to add the increase to the original $p$ fish.

B.why: $0.70p$ is what you get after a $30\%$ decrease. The population went up, so you need $1 + 0.30$, not $1 - 0.30$.

D.why: You used the percent as a whole number. $30\%$ is $\frac{30}{100} = 0.30$, not $30$. Multiplying by $30$ would make the population 30 times as large.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: After a 12-week endurance training program, a cyclist's resting heart rate was $15\%$ lower than it was before the program. The cyclist's resting heart rate after the program was $k$ times the resting heart rate before the program.
items.stem: What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: A decrease of $15\%$ leaves $100\% - 15\% = 85\%$ of the original rate. As a multiplier, that is $1 - \frac{15}{100} = 0.85$, so $k = 0.85$.

A.why: $0.15$ is how much the heart rate dropped, written as a decimal. It is not what is left. You needed to subtract it from 1.

C.why: $1.15$ is the multiplier for a $15\%$ increase. The heart rate went down, so you subtract the rate from 1 instead of adding it.

D.why: You wrote the percent as a whole number. $15\%$ is $0.15$, and even then you would still need to subtract it from 1 to get a multiplier for a decrease.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A food company changed the recipe for one of its breakfast cereals. Nutrition scientists found that one serving of the new cereal contains $50\%$ more dietary fiber than one serving of the original cereal. One serving of the original cereal contains $f$ grams of dietary fiber.
items.stem: Which expression represents the number of grams of dietary fiber in one serving of the new cereal?
items.explanation: Fifty percent more means the original amount plus half of it: $f + 0.5f = 1.5f$. The multiplier for a $50\%$ increase is $1 + \frac{50}{100} = 1.5$.

A.why: You converted $50\%$ to $0.05$ instead of $0.5$. You also left out the original $f$ grams. $0.05f$ would be only a small part of the fiber that was added.

C.why: You added 1 correctly but converted $50\%$ to $0.05$ instead of $0.5$. $1.05f$ is a $5\%$ increase, not a $50\%$ increase.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A county health department reported that the number of residents who got a seasonal flu vaccine increased by $8\%$ from one year to the next. The number of residents vaccinated in the second year is equal to the product of $n$ and $r$, where $n$ is the number of residents vaccinated in the first year and $r$ is a constant.
items.stem: What is the value of $r$?
items.explanation: An $8\%$ increase means the second-year count is the first-year count plus $8\%$ of it: $n + 0.08n = 1.08n$. Since this equals $nr$, $r = 1 + \frac{8}{100} = 1.08$.

A.why: $0.08$ is only the rate of increase. $0.08n$ is the number of new vaccinated residents, not the total for the second year. You needed to add 1.

B.why: $0.92$ is the multiplier for an $8\%$ decrease. Vaccinations went up, so you add $0.08$ to 1 instead of subtracting it.

D.why: You converted $8\%$ to $0.8$ instead of $0.08$. $1.8$ is the multiplier for an $80\%$ increase.

items.stem: A field produces $y$ bushels of wheat. Next season the yield decreases by $15\%$. Which expression gives the new yield, in bushels?
items.explanation: A $15\%$ decrease leaves $100\% - 15\% = 85\%$ of the yield. So the new yield is $(1 - 0.15)y = 0.85y$. This is the step behind SAT questions that ask which expression shows a quantity after a percent decrease: the answer is always $1 - \frac{p}{100}$ times the quantity.

A.why: $0.15y$ is the number of bushels lost, not the number left. The yield that remains is $y - 0.15y$, which is $0.85y$.

B.why: $1.15y$ is the yield after a $15\%$ increase. The question says the yield decreases, so subtract the rate from 1 instead of adding it.

C.why: You subtracted $0.15$ from $y$, which takes away $0.15$ of a bushel instead of $15\%$ of the yield. The amount taken away depends on $y$: it is $0.15y$, not $0.15$.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A linguist tracking a regional dialect found that its number of fluent speakers fell by 15% from 2000 to 2010. From 2010 to 2020, the number of fluent speakers rose by 20%.
items.stem: The number of speakers in 2020 was $k$ times the number of speakers in 2000. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Turn each percent change into a multiplier. A 15% decrease means multiplying by $1 - 0.15 = 0.85$. A 20% increase means multiplying by $1 + 0.20 = 1.2$. items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A cartographer changes the scale of a digital map so that every distance shown on the screen is 40% shorter than it was on the original display.
items.stem: The cartographer wants to multiply each displayed distance by a number $k$ so that every distance returns to its length on the original display. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: First write the change as a multiplier. A 40% decrease multiplies each original distance $d$ by $1 - 0.40 = 0.6$, so the new distance is $0.6d$. items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A marine biologist tracks the area of a kelp forest off a rocky coastline. During the first year, a sea urchin outbreak caused the forest's area to decrease by $25\%$. During the second year, after sea otters returned to the area, the forest's area increased by $40\%$ from its area at the end of the first year.
items.stem: The area of the kelp forest at the end of the second year was $k$ times its area at the start of the first year. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: A $25\%$ decrease means you multiply by $1 - 0.25 = 0.75$. A $40\%$ increase means you multiply by $1 + 0.40 = 1.40$. The second change applies to the area left after the first year, so you multiply the two: $(0.75)(1.40) = 1.05$. The final area is $1.05$ times the original area, so $k = 1.05$. You can check this with a starting area of $100$: it drops to $75$, and $75 \times 1.4 = 105$, which is $1.05$ times $100$.

A.why: You found the net change correctly, a $5\%$ increase, but then gave the rate $0.05$ as your answer. The question asks for the number you multiply the original area by, and that is $1 + 0.05 = 1.05$. A forest that ended up at $0.05$ times its original size would have lost $95\%$ of its area.

items.stimulus: An ecologist counts the frogs in a restored wetland each spring. From 2023 to 2024 the population increased by 35%. From 2024 to 2025 the population decreased by 20%.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: In a soil trial, the barley yield of an untreated plot was 25% less than the regional average yield of $a$ kilograms. The yield of a plot treated with compost was $p\%$ greater than the yield of the untreated plot, where $p > 0$.
items.stem: Which expression represents the yield of the treated plot, in kilograms, in terms of $a$ and $p$?
items.explanation: A yield 25% less than $a$ is $(1 - 0.25)a = 0.75a$. A yield $p\%$ greater than that multiplies it by $1 + \frac{p}{100}$. The treated yield is $0.75a\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)$.

B.why: You used the percent $p$ as a whole number in the multiplier. An increase of $p\%$ is $1 + \frac{p}{100}$, not $1 + p$. If $p = 10$, this choice would multiply the yield by 11.

C.why: You used $1.25$, which makes the untreated plot 25% more than the average. The untreated yield is 25% less, so its multiplier is $0.75$.

D.why: You used $0.25a$, which is the amount by which the untreated yield falls short of the average, not the untreated yield itself. What remains after a 25% decrease is $0.75a$.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A city has $L$ kilometers of protected bike lanes. A planning board approves a plan that increases the total length of protected bike lanes by 12.5% each year for 2 years.
items.stem: After 2 years, the length of protected bike lanes is the product of $L$ and $r$. What is the value of $r$?
items.explanation: An increase of 12.5% is $1 + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{9}{8}$ each year. Two years of growth multiply: $r = \frac{9}{8} \times \frac{9}{8} = \frac{81}{64}$.

A.why: $\frac{9}{8}$ is the multiplier for one year only. The plan runs for 2 years, so you have to apply the multiplier twice.

B.why: You added the two 12.5% increases to get 25%, which gives $\frac{5}{4}$. The second year's increase is taken on the already larger length, so the multipliers have to be multiplied, not added.

D.why: You used the decrease multiplier $1 - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{7}{8}$ for both years. The plan increases the length, so each year's multiplier is $\frac{9}{8}$.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A cartographer prints a smaller copy of a rectangular trail map for a pocket guide. Each length on the copy is 40% shorter than the matching length on the original map.
items.stem: The area of the reduced map is $k$ times the area of the original map. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: A 40% decrease in length multiplies every length by $1 - 0.40 = 0.60$. Area uses two lengths, so the area is multiplied by $0.60 \times 0.60 = 0.36$.

D.why: $0.64$ is the share of the area that was lost ($1 - 0.36$), not the share that remains. The reduced map keeps $0.36$ of the original area.

items.stimulus: A printmaking studio sells a linocut print for $x$ dollars. The studio raises the price of the print by 25%. A member then gets a 20% discount on the raised price.

items.stimulus: From 2020 to 2030, the number of residents in a city district increased by 26%. Over the same period, the number of housing units in the district increased from 2,000 to 2,800.
items.stem: The average number of residents per housing unit in the district in 2030 is $k$ times the average number in 2020. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Residents per housing unit is the number of residents divided by the number of units. The residents are multiplied by $1.26$. items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: An ecologist counts a population of tree frogs in a restored wetland. Over the first year, the population increases by $40\%$. Over the second year, the population decreases by $25\%$. At the end of the second year, the population is $k$ times the population at the start of the first year.
items.stem: What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: A $40\%$ increase means you multiply by $1.40$. A $25\%$ decrease means you multiply by $0.75$. Successive changes multiply, so $k = (1.40)(0.75) = 1.05$.

A.why: You found the net change correctly but gave only the rate, $0.05$. You left off the 1 that keeps the original population. $k$ is the whole multiplier, $1 + 0.05$.

D.why: You multiplied $1.40$ by $0.25$, which is the share that was lost. A $25\%$ decrease leaves $75\%$, so the factor is $0.75$.

items.stem: What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Let plot B's yield be $b$. Then plot A's yield is $1.25b$. Solve for $b$ in terms of A's yield: $b = \frac{1}{1.25}(1.25b) = 0.8(1.25b)$. So $k = \frac{1}{1.25} = \frac{4}{5} = 0.80$.

items.stimulus: A town's population density is its population divided by its land area. Over a decade, the town's population increases by $20\%$. items.stem: What is the value of $k$?

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: An athlete's $\text{VO}_2$ max is $v$. After a training block, it increases by $p\%$. After a later injury, the new value decreases by $p\%$, where $0 < p < 100$.
items.stem: Which of the following expressions represents the athlete's final $\text{VO}_2$ max?
items.explanation: The increase multiplies by $\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)$ and the decrease multiplies by $\left(1 - \frac{p}{100}\right)$. Their product is a difference of squares: $1 - \left(\frac{p}{100}\right)^2 = 1 - \frac{p^2}{10{,}000}$. So the final value is $v\left(1 - \frac{p^2}{10{,}000}\right)$.

B.why: You set up the product correctly but squared only $p$, not $\frac{p}{100}$. The denominator has to become $100^2 = 10{,}000$.

C.why: You got the sign of the cross term wrong. $\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\left(1 - \frac{p}{100}\right)$ subtracts the square, so the final value is less than $v$.

items.stimulus: A printmaker prices each linocut so that its price is $60\%$ more than the cost of making it. At a studio sale, every price is reduced by $25\%$. The sale price of a linocut is the product of its cost and $r$.

items.subtype_name: Advanced-vocabulary choices with close meanings
items.stimulus: In eighteenth-century Kashmir, a single luxury shawl could pass through the hands of two weavers for more than a year. Working from a coded pattern, they interlocked hundreds of small bobbins of dyed wool one thread at a time, joining each patch of color to the next so that no seam was visible on either face of the cloth. This ______ technique left no room for error, since a single misplaced thread would show in the finished design.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The passage describes slow, thread-by-thread work in which one misplaced thread would ruin the design. "This ______ technique" refers back to that description, so the blank has to mean demanding great precision and care. "Exacting" means exactly that.

A.why: "Perfunctory" means done quickly and with little care. That is the opposite of a technique that takes more than a year and allows no errors.

C.why: You matched the topic (luxury shawls) instead of what the blank has to do. "Ostentatious" means showy, and it would describe how the finished shawl looks. The blank describes how hard the technique is to carry out.

D.why: "Exorbitant" looks and sounds like "exacting," but it means excessively expensive. It is used for prices, not methods, and the passage says nothing about cost.

items.stimulus: Many sprint coaches still treat a long session of static stretching before a race as ______, a routine that shields muscles from strains and tears before they can occur. items.subtype_name: Advanced-vocabulary choices with close meanings
items.stimulus: After a congested highway was widened from four lanes to six, rush-hour travel times fell for about two years and then returned to their former levels: the added capacity had drawn drivers who previously avoided the route. items.explanation: The widening relieved the symptom (travel times) temporarily without touching the cause (demand). "Palliative" means relieving symptoms without curing the underlying problem, which is exactly the distinction the "since" clause draws.

items.subtype_name: Advanced-vocabulary choices with close meanings
items.stimulus: After wolves returned to the valley, streamside willows that had been browsed nearly to the ground began to recover. The study's authors note, however, that the same decade brought unusually wet summers, which also favor willow growth. Their conclusion is accordingly ______: wolves were probably one cause of the recovery, though not necessarily the main one.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: "Accordingly" links the conclusion to the authors' caution about a second possible cause. The colon then shows the conclusion: a real claim ("probably one cause") with careful limits. "Circumspect" means cautious and attentive to the full circumstances, which describes a conclusion that commits to something while hedging it carefully.

C.why: "Tendentious" means slanted to promote a particular view. Raising a rival explanation against their own finding is the opposite of slanted.

items.stimulus: Cut off from imported indigo during the war, dyers in the region turned to woad, a locally grown plant that yields a paler and less colorfast blue. items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Mice raised in completely germ-free cages develop severe allergic reactions to harmless pollen far more often than mice raised in ordinary cages. Because the two groups of mice differ only in their contact with microbes, immunologist Rhea Kandel and her team hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: early contact with microbes helps the immune system learn to tolerate harmless substances.
pollen carries harmful microbes that directly provoke allergic reactions in exposed mice.
mice in ordinary cages encounter more pollen overall than germ-free mice encounter.
all mice exposed to microbes early in life will remain free of allergies permanently.
items.explanation: The surprise is that the mice with no microbes have more allergies. The text says the only difference between the groups is contact with microbes, so the explanation has to involve microbes helping in some way. If early microbial contact teaches the immune system not to overreact, then the germ-free mice, which missed that contact, would overreact to pollen. That is exactly what the text reports.

B.why: This explanation sounds scientific, but it gets the direction wrong. If microbes caused the allergies, the germ-free mice would have fewer of them, not more. You fell into the subtype's trap by ignoring which group reacted.

C.why: The text says the groups differ only in their contact with microbes. A difference in pollen exposure is ruled out by that detail, so you skipped the comparison the passage sets up.

D.why: Look at 'all' and 'permanently.' The text shows only that allergies are less common in mice raised with microbes. That doesn't mean every such mouse stays allergy-free forever. This is strength creep.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a hilltop village 300 kilometers from the nearest coast were surprised to find hundreds of beads carved from marine shells. The site contains no fishing gear or remains of boats, yet its pottery closely resembles pottery from coastal settlements of the same period. The team therefore hypothesizes that the villagers ______

carved the beads from freshwater shells collected in streams near the hilltop.
obtained the shells through exchange with communities living along the coast.
taught coastal communities to make pottery in the hilltop village's style.
items.explanation: The puzzle is how marine shells reached a village far inland. The text gives you two clues. The villagers had no fishing gear or boats, so they probably didn't harvest the shells themselves. Their pottery also matches coastal pottery, which points to contact with coastal people. Trade with coastal communities accounts for both details.

B.why: The text says the beads were carved from marine shells. If they came from freshwater streams, there would be no puzzle, so this choice contradicts the passage.

D.why: Similar pottery suggests contact between the two groups, but nothing says which group influenced the other. This choice also skips the real puzzle, which is the shells.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: In earlier studies, adults who ate a high-fiber breakfast felt full longer than adults who ate a low-fiber breakfast. Nutrition researcher Tomás Ibarra suspected that this effect comes only from fiber that thickens into a gel in the stomach. He therefore served high-fiber breakfasts made with fiber that does not thicken and anticipated that, compared with a low-fiber breakfast, these breakfasts would ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: keep participants feeling full for noticeably longer than the low-fiber breakfast.
make little or no difference in how long participants felt full afterward.
make participants feel hungry much sooner than the low-fiber breakfast did.
lead participants to eat larger portions of food at breakfast than usual.
items.explanation: Ibarra thinks the feeling of fullness comes only from fiber that thickens. His test breakfasts use fiber that doesn't thicken, which removes the cause he suspects. If he's right, the usual effect should disappear, so he would expect little or no difference from the low-fiber breakfast.

A.why: This is the original finding from earlier studies. Ibarra's setup takes away the ingredient he thinks causes it. You picked the original effect instead of the expected change, which is the subtype's trap.

C.why: Removing the cause would make the benefit disappear. It wouldn't create the opposite effect. Nothing in the text suggests that fiber which doesn't thicken makes people hungrier.

D.why: The study measures how long participants feel full after eating. Portion size at breakfast is never discussed, so this choice answers a different question.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Inspectors have long checked steel bridges by tapping beams with hammers and listening for a dull sound. However, this method reveals a crack only after it has grown large enough to change the sound a beam makes. A civil engineering team installing small sensors that continuously record each beam's vibrations hypothesizes that the sensors will ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: detect cracks only once they grow large enough to alter a beam's sound.
prevent cracks from ever forming in the steel beams of older bridges.
reduce the amount of noise that passing traffic produces on bridges.
reveal cracks at an earlier stage than inspectors tapping beams can.
items.explanation: The text names the flaw in the old method: tapping finds a crack only after it has grown large. A new method is worth testing because it might fix that flaw. Sensors that record vibrations all the time could pick up a crack before it becomes big enough to change the sound.

items.stimulus: After a large earthquake, aftershocks typically become weaker and less frequent as time passes. Seismologists studying the volcano hypothesize that ______

choices: the original earthquake was much stronger than seismologists first estimated.
movement of molten rock beneath the volcano was producing the added quakes.
aftershocks everywhere tend to grow more frequent in the weeks after a quake.
molten rock beneath every volcano will cause aftershocks to grow more frequent.
items.explanation: The surprise is that aftershocks increased when they would normally fade. The key detail is where the increase happened: only above the chamber of molten rock. An explanation tied to the molten rock accounts for both the timing and the location.

items.stimulus: Ornithologists noticed something odd about great tits living in a large city: their songs were higher in pitch than the songs of great tits in nearby forests. The researchers also measured the background sound in both places. Most city noise, such as the rumble of traffic, is low in pitch. The forests were quiet. The team hypothesizes that city birds sing higher because ______

choices: higher-pitched songs are easier to hear over the low rumble of traffic.
forest birds sing at a higher pitch than city birds do.
every bird species in the city has raised the pitch of its song.
city birds sing more at night, when the traffic is quietest.
items.explanation: The puzzle is the higher pitch in the city. The passage gives you one detail that explains it: city noise is low-pitched. A song pitched above that noise stands out from it, so this explanation uses both the observation and the measurement. You will use this same move on harder 'the team hypothesizes that' questions: find the detail the passage put there on purpose, and choose the answer that connects it to the puzzle.

started in the village and later spread to the fishing town.
began when villagers saw a large creature in a mountain lake.
shows that all mountain folktales first came from the sea.

the factory pays them less than other factories in the region.
the higher pay lets the factory require rotating night shifts.
no worker will ever accept rotating shifts, whatever the pay.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the popular view, that pay drives quitting, and then undercuts it: this factory pays the most and still loses the most workers. items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Air usually gets colder as you climb a mountain, so the bottom of a valley is normally warmer than the slopes above it. On calm winter nights in one mountain valley, though, meteorologists found the opposite: the valley floor was several degrees colder than the slopes. Cold air is denser, and therefore heavier, than warm air. The meteorologists hypothesize that on calm nights, ______
items.stem: Which choice best completes the researchers' explanation?
choices: cold air sinks down the slopes and collects on the valley floor.
the air on the slopes is colder than the air on the valley floor.
the valley floor is colder than the slopes on every night of the year.
strong winds carry snow down from the slopes to the valley floor.
items.explanation: The usual pattern flips: the valley floor is colder, not warmer. The passage gives you the reason in its last fact. Cold air is heavy, so when there is no wind it slides downhill and pools at the bottom. This is the 'effect flips' version of a hypothesis question. Once the passage tells you the pattern reversed, your answer has to explain the reversal, not the usual pattern.

B.why: This is the usual pattern, which the passage says reversed on these nights. This is the trap for flipped-effect questions: choosing the original effect instead of its reverse.

C.why: The finding applies only to calm winter nights. 'Every night of the year' is strength creep that the passage does not support.

D.why: The passage says the nights were calm, so strong winds do not fit. This explanation also ignores the clue about dense, heavy cold air.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Palms are sensitive to cold: today they grow only in places where the ground rarely or never freezes. Many people would therefore be surprised to learn that paleobotanists have found fossilized palm fronds in 50-million-year-old rocks on an island off the coast of Antarctica. That island is now covered in ice for most of the year. To explain why palm fossils appear in such an unlikely place, the researchers hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: palms living in the distant past could survive in places that stayed frozen for most of the year.
the island had a warm climate with little or no frost during the time when the palms were growing there.
the island was already covered in ice for most of the year during the time when the palms were growing there.
palms first appeared on this island and only later spread from there to warmer regions on other continents.
items.explanation: Start with the surprise: palms need ground that rarely or never freezes, yet their fossils turn up on an island that is icy today. Only one explanation fits every detail. When the palms were alive, the island must have been warm enough for them, so its climate has changed since then. This is the basic move behind every 'the researchers hypothesize that' question. items.stimulus: Curators have long blamed the uneven fading of blue pigment in Edo-period woodblock prints on uneven exposure to light. a heavier coating of starch sizing helps shield the blue pigment from whatever causes it to fade.
the edges of the Kisaragi prints received more light than their centers did while on display.
starch sizing speeds the fading of the blue pigment wherever it has been applied most heavily.
