items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Folklorists often assume that a tale is best preserved near the place where it began. Yet the story of the Drowned Ferryman, which is set on the Varna River and is thought to have originated there, survives in mountain villages some 300 kilometers away but not in the villages along the river itself. Parish records show that the mountain villages were founded in the 1700s by families who fled the river valley after a series of floods, and that the valley was later resettled by migrants from the coast. These facts suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the tale began in the mountain villages and was later adapted to fit a setting on the Varna River.
the coastal migrants brought their own version of the tale with them when they resettled the valley.
tales are generally best preserved in places that lie far from where they first emerged.
the families who fled the floods carried the tale away with them, leaving no one in the valley to tell it.
items.explanation: The puzzle is that a river tale survives far from the river but not beside it. The records explain it. The valley's original people, who presumably told the tale, moved to the mountains, and the people who replaced them came from the coast. If the tale traveled with the displaced families, it would turn up in the mountains and be missing from the resettled valley, which is exactly what the passage describes.

A.why: This reverses where the tale came from. The tale is set on the Varna, and the mountain villages were founded by people from the valley, so every detail points to a valley origin. You explained the puzzle by ignoring the migration record.

B.why: The passage says the tale does not survive in the river villages, so the coastal migrants could not have planted a lasting version there. You overlooked the detail that the tale is missing from the valley.

C.why: One tale with an unusual history can't support a rule about tales in general. This choice flips the folklorists' generalization into an equally broad opposite one. The passage only explains this one case.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: At most Bronze Age settlements in the Harrow Basin, the proportion of sheep bones to cattle bones rises during droughts, since sheep need far less water and forage than cattle do. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the marsh let Tell Omran keep cattle at a time when drought made them hard to keep elsewhere.
the drought around 1900 BCE was far less severe in the basin than the pollen records indicate.
sheep in the Harrow Basin needed more water and forage than researchers have usually assumed.
Tell Omran's residents hunted wild cattle more often than residents of other settlements did.
items.explanation: Normally drought shifts herds toward sheep, because cattle need more water and forage. Tell Omran went the other way. The one thing that sets it apart is a marsh that stayed wet through the drought. A reliable source of water and grazing explains why cattle could still be kept there, and even thrive, while the rest of the basin lost them.

B.why: The passage states that the pollen records show a severe drought. Doubting that evidence ignores the detail that makes Tell Omran unusual, the marsh that stayed wet. This is the trap of an explanation that sounds scientific but skips the setting.

C.why: The passage states that sheep need far less water and forage than cattle, and that the sheep-heavy pattern holds at most sites. This choice goes against that premise and still doesn't explain why Tell Omran differs.

D.why: Nothing in the passage mentions hunting or wild animals. You invented a new factor and ignored the marsh, which is the one local difference the passage points out.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: In most corn-growing regions, planting a winter rye cover crop raises the yield of the corn that follows, largely because rye residue holds moisture in the soil through early summer. Agronomists studying the Lowmoor district, where spring rains are unusually heavy, expected this benefit to reverse there: the extra moisture held by rye residue, they reasoned, would keep already saturated fields waterlogged and force farmers to delay planting. They therefore anticipated that in Lowmoor, corn planted after rye would ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: yield more than corn planted in Lowmoor fields where no rye cover crop had been grown.
grow in soil that dried out faster than the soil of Lowmoor fields left bare over winter.
yield less than corn planted in Lowmoor fields where no rye cover crop had been grown.
yield less than corn planted without rye in every region, regardless of spring rainfall.
items.explanation: The passage tells you the usual benefit will reverse in Lowmoor. Usually, corn after rye yields more than corn without rye. Flipped, corn after rye in Lowmoor yields less than corn without rye in Lowmoor. The reasoning given (waterlogged fields and delayed planting) supports a lower yield, and the comparison stays within Lowmoor.

A.why: This is the usual effect, not the reversed one. The agronomists expected the benefit to reverse in Lowmoor, and you kept the original direction.

B.why: The agronomists' reasoning is that rye residue holds extra moisture, so soil after rye should stay wetter, not dry out faster. This choice reverses the mechanism the passage relies on.

D.why: The reversal is predicted only for Lowmoor, because of its heavy spring rains. The passage says rye raises yields in most regions, so 'every region, regardless of spring rainfall' goes far beyond what was expected. Watch for words like 'every' and 'regardless.'

items.stimulus: Inspectors of the Carrow Viaduct found that the steel expansion joints at its north end had rusted through in half the time expected, while identical joints at the south end, installed the same year and carrying the same traffic, showed little rust. prolonged contact with salty meltwater caused the north joints to corrode more quickly.
the north joints were made from a lower grade of steel than the joints at the south end.
direct sunlight at the south end slowly damaged its joints as well, though less visibly.

items.stimulus: A team testing a new self-healing polymer found that cracks near the surface of a sample sealed within a day, while cracks deep inside the same sample were still open a week later. the healing agent had settled toward the surface of the sample before the polymer hardened.
water vapor in the air slows the healing reaction, so cracks near the surface should close last.
moisture from the surrounding air drives the healing reaction that seals the surface cracks.
items.explanation: Two possible causes are ruled out: the agent was spread evenly, and the temperature was held constant. If moisture from the air drives the reaction, surface cracks should heal quickly and deep cracks slowly, which is what the team saw.

B.why: The passage says the healing agent was distributed evenly throughout the polymer. This choice depends on the agent being concentrated at the surface, which the setup rules out.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Thick leaf cuticles, waxy coatings that limit water loss, are usually read as a sign that a plant grew in a dry climate. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the regional climate was dry when Salicornites lived, even though the shrub grew in a swamp.
Salicornites leaves were carried into the swamp from drier upland areas after they had fallen.
thick cuticles helped Salicornites hold on to water that its roots could take up only poorly.
all plants that grew in salty coastal swamps developed thick cuticles like those of Salicornites.
items.explanation: The key detail is the comparison group. Plants in the same deposits have thin cuticles, so the climate as a whole wasn't dry. What set Salicornites apart was salty water, and the passage says roots struggle to draw water from salty soil. A plant that can't take up water easily would benefit from losing less of it, which explains the thick cuticles without needing a dry climate.

A.why: This is the usual reading that the passage undercuts. Plants in the same deposits have thin cuticles, which wouldn't fit a dry regional climate. You applied the rule of thumb and ignored the comparison group.

B.why: The fossils were found rooted in growth position, so Salicornites grew where it was preserved. It wasn't washed in from somewhere else.

D.why: The passage describes one shrub in one swamp. Stretching that to 'all plants' in every salty swamp is strength creep that the evidence can't support.

items.stimulus: Roads usually lower the nesting success of forest songbirds, because the open edges they create draw nest predators such as crows. road edges in the Elden Forest draw ratsnakes, which then raid the thrush nests nearby.
thrushes nesting near roads find more insects for their young than thrushes elsewhere do.
roads raise the nesting success of every songbird species that breeds in the Elden Forest.

D.why: The finding is about wood thrush nests only. 'Every songbird species' stretches one species' result to a whole community, which is strength creep the passage can't support.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: For decades, historians blamed the errors in a 1740s chart of the Breton coast on careless copying from older charts. Copying mistakes, however, tend to fall at random. the headlands farthest from Brest have eroded eastward in the centuries since the chart was drawn.
a small, consistent error in the maker's measurements built up as positions were plotted outward from Brest.
the chart's maker deliberately misplaced the distant headlands in order to mislead rival navigators.
items.explanation: The surprise is that the errors are not random. They all point the same way (east), and they get bigger the farther a headland is from Brest. It also explains why Morvan rejects the copying explanation, since copying would scatter errors at random.

water in shaded pavement freezes and thaws repeatedly, producing the additional potholes on those streets.
shade protects pavement against potholes in cold regions much as it protects against rutting in warm ones.
shaded streets in any climate will develop more potholes than comparable streets left in full sun.

items.stimulus: Agronomists often credit legume cover crops such as hairy vetch with improving soil structure, a benefit that should help any crop planted afterward. choices: vetch's improvements to soil structure are enough to raise yields of any crop that follows it.
vetch benefited corn mainly by supplying nitrogen, which soybeans largely obtain on their own.
soybeans gain more than corn does from the improvements to soil structure that vetch provides.
corn yields after vetch would continue to rise if the trial were extended for several more years.
items.explanation: The puzzle is that vetch helped corn but not soybeans, even though better soil structure should help both. The passage gives you the detail that explains the split: vetch adds nitrogen, and soybeans already make much of their own. items.stimulus: In lowland populations of a certain meadow wildflower, plants secrete most of their nectar between late morning and midafternoon, when the bees that pollinate them forage most actively. Because producing nectar draws heavily on a plant's limited energy, ecologists anticipated that, compared with lowland plants, high-elevation plants would ______

secrete a greater total volume of nectar over a full day and night.
receive a larger share of their visits from daytime-foraging bees.
release most of their nectar during the hours after dark.
items.explanation: In the lowlands, nectar timing follows the pollinator: it peaks when bees are active. At high elevation the pollinators are moths that feed only after dark, and nectar is costly to make, so the expected pattern reverses. The plants should save their nectar for the hours when their actual pollinators are feeding, which means after dark.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: In a survey of twelve villages in a rural district, childhood asthma rates generally rose with proximity to the district's only highway. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: smoke from household cooking fires is responsible for much of the excess among young children.
exhaust from the highway reaches the village in concentrations high enough to harm young children.
the school in the neighboring town has features that protect older children from asthma.
distance from the highway has little relationship to childhood asthma rates in the district.
items.explanation: The surprise is a very high asthma rate in a village far from the highway. items.stimulus: A tale about a church bell that sank and still rings beneath the waves is widespread in fishing villages along one stretch of Atlantic coast but nearly absent from the interior. There, the bell lies in a lake rather than the sea, yet tellers still call the water "the salt." choices: the tale arose in the mountain parish and was later carried by travelers to the coast.
the parish's tellers invented the tale on their own, inspired by the lake near their homes.
settlers from the coast brought the tale inland and adapted its setting to their new surroundings.
most of the parish's traditional tales originated in the coastal villages its settlers left.
items.explanation: The puzzle is a coastal tale turning up far inland. Two details settle it. Coastal families moved into the parish in the 1840s, and inland tellers still call a freshwater lake "the salt," a leftover from a sea version. A tale carried in by coastal settlers, with its setting swapped from sea to lake, explains every detail the passage gives.

A.why: This reverses the direction of spread. The tale is widespread on the coast, and the inland version keeps a sea word ("the salt") for a lake. Both details point to the coast as the source, not the destination.

D.why: The passage discusses only one tale. Concluding that most of the parish's tales came from the coast stretches a single case into a broad generalization.

the composer left the court copies bare because he expected the organist to add ornaments himself.
the court copies were made late in the composer's life, after his taste in ornamentation had changed.
the students' copies record exactly the ornaments that the court organist played in performance.

items.stimulus: Oral vaccines often produce weaker immune responses in children in some low-income regions than in children elsewhere, a gap long blamed on poor nutrition. intestinal infections, rather than poor diet, weaken children's responses to oral vaccines.
children in these regions are born with immune systems that respond weakly to vaccines.
oral vaccines would outperform injected vaccines if intestinal infections were treated first.
items.explanation: The surprise is that good nutrition did not close the gap, but treating intestinal infections did. whole sea bream were carried to Tell Varesh and cleaned at the site.

the lentil group will absorb none of the iron contained in its meal.

rainfall triggers earthquakes in every region far from a plate boundary.

de-icing salt is the only cause of cracking in concrete overpasses that are exposed to winter weather.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Collectors have long regarded certain impressions of Dutch printmaker Aleida Voss's 1652 etching River Mill as forgeries, because the finest lines (the ripples on the water, the grain of the wooden wheel) appear faint or are missing entirely. He also notes that copper plates lose their shallowest grooves first as they wear down with use. Langeveld therefore hypothesizes that the faint impressions ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: were printed from a careful copy of Voss's plate that a later forger had engraved by hand.
were printed from Voss's original plate after it had already been used for many printings.
were made by Voss herself, who wanted the water and the wheel to look softer than before.
are now valued by collectors about as highly as the crisp impressions of River Mill are.
items.explanation: The shared accidental scratch shows that both sets of impressions came from the same plate. The fact that copper plates lose their shallowest grooves first explains why only the finest lines faded. Together, these details point to the original plate, printed after it had worn down. That is the corrected view, which replaces the collectors' belief that the faint impressions are forgeries.

A.why: You finished the popular view instead of the corrected one. The word "however" brings in evidence against forgery: a hand-made copy wouldn't reproduce an accidental scratch in exactly the same spot. It also leaves the detail about plate wear unexplained.

C.why: Nothing in the passage mentions Voss's intentions. This choice adds an assumption the text never gives you, and it ignores the detail about worn grooves, which explains the faint lines without any deliberate choice by the artist.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Traffic engineers have long assumed that when a road is closed, the vehicles that used it simply move onto nearby streets. But when the city of Marlow shut a riverside avenue that had carried about 30,000 vehicles a day, counts on the parallel streets rose by only about 9,000 vehicles a day, and bus and rail ridership along the corridor barely changed. Planner Ines Okafor hypothesizes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: most of the avenue's former traffic was absorbed by the buses and trains serving the corridor.
many trips once made on the avenue stopped being made rather than shifting to other routes.
the parallel streets took on nearly all of the vehicles that had once used the closed avenue.
closing any major road in any city will reduce the total amount of traffic in that city.
items.explanation: The puzzle is the missing traffic. About 30,000 vehicles a day lost their road, yet the parallel streets gained only about 9,000, and transit ridership barely moved. The 'But' tells you the engineers' assumption is being undercut. The one explanation that fits both details is that many of those trips weren't rerouted at all and simply stopped being made.

C.why: You chose the popular view the passage sets up to knock down. The parallel streets gained only about 9,000 of the 30,000 vehicles, which is nowhere near all of them.

D.why: You generalized one closure in one city to every major road everywhere, and turned a hypothesis into a certainty ('will'). Nothing in the passage supports that reach.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Mice given a course of antibiotics, which clears most bacteria from the gut, produced far fewer antibodies after swallowing a vaccine against rotavirus than untreated mice did. Yet when the same vaccine was injected into muscle instead, the antibiotic-treated mice and the untreated mice produced similar levels of antibodies. Based on these results, the research team hypothesizes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: antibiotics directly impair the antibody-producing cells found throughout a mouse's body.
gut bacteria suppress the immune system's response to vaccines that are taken by mouth.
gut bacteria help the immune system respond to vaccines that enter through the digestive tract.
injected vaccines produce stronger antibody responses than oral vaccines do in all mammals.
items.explanation: One result changed and one held steady. Clearing the gut bacteria weakened the response to the swallowed vaccine but made no difference to the injected one. The explanation that fits both results is that gut bacteria help the immune system respond specifically to vaccines that arrive through the gut, so losing them matters only for the oral route.

A.why: This sounds scientific but ignores the comparison group. If antibiotics damaged antibody-producing cells throughout the body, the injected vaccine would also have produced fewer antibodies, and it didn't.

B.why: You reversed the direction of the effect. Removing the bacteria lowered the oral-vaccine response, so the bacteria were helping that response, not holding it back.

D.why: The study compares antibiotic-treated mice with untreated mice, not injection with oral delivery across all mammals. You stretched one mouse experiment into a claim about every mammal.

items.stimulus: At a fossil site in Wyoming, paleobotanists compared leaves preserved in two rock layers. In the older layer, about 40 percent of the leaves bear holes and chew marks left by insects; in the younger layer, only about 10 percent do. The same few tree species dominate both layers, but chemical clues in the sediment indicate that the younger layer formed during a markedly cooler interval. The researchers therefore hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: a cooler climate reduced the number or activity of leaf-eating insects in the region.
the trees in the younger layer were species that insects could not easily digest.
leaf-eating insects grew more numerous in the region as its climate became cooler.
falling temperatures caused leaf-eating insects to vanish from the entire planet.
items.explanation: The surprise is the drop in insect damage from 40 percent to 10 percent. The passage rules out a change in the trees, since the same species dominate both layers, and it points to one difference: the younger layer formed when the climate was cooler. A cooler climate cutting back the leaf-eating insects explains the drop using only those details.

B.why: This ignores a key detail. The passage says the same tree species dominate both layers, so a change to less edible species can't explain the drop.

C.why: You flipped the direction of the effect. Insect damage fell in the cooler layer, which points to fewer or less active insects, not more.

D.why: One site still shows insect damage on 10 percent of leaves, so the insects didn't vanish even there. Extending that to the whole planet goes far beyond what this site can support.

the oaks in the delta grew under drier conditions than the oaks on the ridge did.
the oaks on the ridge belonged to a separate species suited to upland ground.
every oak species of that period grew smaller leaves at higher elevations.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Athletes often sit in ice baths after strength training because cold water reduces next-day muscle soreness. However, sports scientist Tomasz Wierzba notes that the inflammation cold water suppresses is also one of the signals that tells muscle to rebuild larger. To test this, his team had two groups lift weights for twelve weeks: one group took ice baths after every session, while the other cycled lightly instead. Wierzba anticipated that, compared with the cycling group, the ice-bath group would ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: report less soreness after sessions but gain less muscle over the twelve weeks.
report less soreness after sessions and gain more muscle over the twelve weeks.
report more soreness after sessions and gain less muscle over the twelve weeks.
report less soreness after sessions and gain no muscle over the twelve weeks.
items.explanation: The passage gives you two effects of cold water that point in opposite directions. It reduces soreness, and it also suppresses a signal that helps muscle grow. So compared with the cyclists, the ice-bath group should feel less sore but build less muscle. Your answer has to describe both halves of that gap.

B.why: This is the popular view that the passage sets up and then undercuts. You assumed less soreness means better recovery and more growth. Wierzba's point is that the same suppressed inflammation should mean less growth.

C.why: The first sentence establishes that cold water reduces soreness. Saying the ice-bath group would be more sore reverses the one effect the passage treats as settled.

D.why: The passage says inflammation is one of the signals for muscle growth, not the only one. Removing part of the signal supports less growth, not no growth at all. 'No muscle' is stronger than the evidence allows.

items.stimulus: Engineers testing a polymer roof coating expected it to wear out fastest in Arizona, where ultraviolet light is far more intense than on the cloudy Oregon coast. choices: constant swelling and shrinking did more harm to the coating than Arizona's stronger sunlight did.
the Oregon panels received more ultraviolet light than the Arizona panels received over the test.
Arizona's stronger sunlight did more harm to the coating than constant swelling and shrinking did.
repeated wetting and drying will crack any roof coating faster than intense sunlight can.
items.explanation: The surprise is that the site with weaker sunlight produced the faster cracking. The one detail that sets Oregon apart is the near-daily cycle of swelling and shrinking. If that cycle damages the coating more than Arizona's extra UV does, every detail in the passage makes sense, including the twofold gap.

B.why: This ignores the setting. The passage says UV is far more intense in Arizona than on the cloudy Oregon coast, so you can't explain Oregon's faster cracking with more UV.

C.why: This is the engineers' original expectation, the one the results overturned. If sunlight were the bigger threat, the Arizona panels would have cracked faster, but the Oregon panels did.

D.why: The test covered one coating, which is described as absorbing water. Extending the result to any roof coating, and saying it will always happen, claims more than one test can support.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Standard models predict that raising a wage floor reduces employment, since some jobs stop being worth their cost to employers. Studying one statewide increase, economist Lena Ostrowski compared towns where a single firm hires most local workers with towns where many firms compete for staff. Employment dipped slightly in the competitive towns but rose in the single-firm towns, and nearly all the added workers there were longtime residents who had not been seeking work, not newcomers. Ostrowski hypothesizes that before the increase, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the dominant firms had offered too few openings to employ every resident who wanted a job
firms in both kinds of towns had paid workers less than their labor was worth to the firm
the dominant firms had kept pay low enough that many residents judged a job not worth taking
residents of the competitive towns had been willing to relocate to wherever pay was rising
items.explanation: The puzzle is that a higher wage floor raised employment, but only in single-firm towns, and the new workers were local residents who had not been looking for work. One explanation fits all three details. Where one firm dominates, it can set pay low because workers have nowhere else to go, and at that low pay some residents decide a job isn't worth taking. When the floor forces pay up, those residents start working. In competitive towns, competition had already pushed pay up, so the floor only raised costs, and employment dipped as the standard model predicts.

A.why: You saw that the new workers were people who hadn't been working, but you blamed a shortage of jobs instead of a shortage of willing workers. If the firms had too few openings, making each worker more expensive would lead them to cut jobs, not add them. This choice predicts employment falling in single-firm towns, which is the opposite of what the passage reports.

B.why: You spotted the underpayment explanation but applied it to every town. If firms in competitive towns had also been underpaying, the floor should have raised employment there too. Instead it dipped, so this choice ignores the comparison group, which is the key detail.

D.why: Migration would explain a rise in one place and a dip in another, but the passage says the added workers were longtime residents, not newcomers. This choice explains the pattern by assuming something the passage rules out.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Most algae-eating reef fish feed in sunlit shallows, where algae grow fastest. Divers were therefore surprised to find juveniles of one such goby clustered on deep, dim ledges where algae are sparse, while adults stayed in the shallows. Juveniles on the ledges grew more slowly than juveniles kept in shallow pens that excluded predators, yet they outlived unprotected juveniles released on shallow reefs from which all adults had been removed. The team hypothesizes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: adult gobies defend the shallow feeding areas and force the juveniles down to the ledges
for juveniles, the safety of the ledges outweighs the faster growth the shallows would allow
for juveniles, the faster growth the shallows allow outweighs the danger of feeding there
predators in the shallows will kill any juvenile goby that does not shelter on the ledges
items.explanation: The surprise is that juveniles live where food is poor. The two comparisons give both sides of a trade-off. Juveniles in the shallows grow faster when protected from predators, so the shallows offer better food. Unprotected juveniles in the shallows die sooner than juveniles on the ledges, even with no adults around, so the shallows are more dangerous. Juveniles choose the ledges anyway, so the hypothesis has to be that, for them, safety matters more than faster growth.

A.why: Competition with adults sounds scientific, but you ignored a key detail of the setup. The unprotected juveniles were released on reefs where all the adults had been removed, and they still did worse than juveniles on the ledges. Adults can't be what drives the pattern.

C.why: You identified the trade-off correctly but settled it in the wrong direction. If faster growth outweighed the danger, juveniles would gather in the shallows. The passage says they gather on the ledges, so this choice describes the opposite of what the gobies actually do.

D.why: You saw that predation drives the pattern, then made the claim stronger than the evidence allows. The passage says ledge juveniles outlived unprotected ones. It doesn't say every unsheltered juvenile dies. 'Any' and 'will' go beyond that evidence.

items.stimulus: Because circulating memory T cells travel throughout the body, immunologists long assumed that how quickly a person clears a repeat skin infection depends mainly on these cells. some other immune cells remain in skin that was once infected and speed clearance there.
the number of circulating memory T cells in a forearm determines how fast it clears the pathogen.
repeat infections are cleared faster in the skin than in any other tissue of the body.

items.stimulus: Permeable pavement reduces stormwater runoff by letting rain pass through its pores into a gravel base and then into the soil below. Over time, fine sediment clogs the pores, and engineers have generally blamed declining performance on this clogging. In a five-year trial, however, sections built over clay soil and sections built over sandy soil lost surface infiltration at the same rate, yet by the end the clay sections were reducing runoff far less than the sandy ones. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

clogging of the pores has no effect on how much runoff permeable pavement prevents.
clearing sediment from the clay sections' pores would bring them up to the sandy sections' level.
the clay sections fall short because water drains slowly from their gravel base into the soil.
items.explanation: Surface clogging was the same for both soils, so it can't explain why the clay sections did worse. The only difference left is what lies beneath the base: clay or sand. C.why: You fell back on the popular view that the passage undercuts. Both sections clogged equally, so clearing the pores would leave the clay sections' drainage problem, and the gap, where it was.

the aquifer, lighter in late summer, presses less firmly on the faults and lets them slip.

items.stimulus: Copper etching plates wear with each printing, so fine lines grow fainter in later impressions; if a plate cracks, the crack appears in every impression printed afterward. the two impressions were pulled from separate plates that Varn etched at different times.
the uncracked impression's faint lines came from light inking rather than from a worn plate.

items.stimulus: In single-meal tests, adding vitamin C to a plant-based meal sharply increases how much iron the body absorbs from that meal. iron-deficient people can absorb iron from plant foods only when vitamin C is present.
eight weeks is too short a period for vitamin C's effect on iron stores to appear.
the body cuts its iron absorption once stores are adequate, offsetting vitamin C's boost.
items.explanation: Two results have to fit together. Over eight weeks, vitamin C did almost nothing for most people but did help those who started out deficient. If the body limits absorption once its stores are adequate, the boost would fade for people with enough iron and last for people who were short.

C.why: You ignored the comparison group. The iron-deficient participants did gain iron within the same eight weeks, so the trial was long enough for an effect to appear.

items.stimulus: Hand-hygiene compliance at Linden Hospital rose from 60 percent to 90 percent after gel dispensers were installed beside every bed, according to audits in which trained observers stood on the ward. the observers miscounted how often staff cleaned their hands while the audits were underway.
staff cleaned their hands far more often while being watched than at other times of day.
cleaning hands more often does little to reduce the infections patients acquire in hospitals.
items.explanation: The hidden counters are the key. Staff didn't know about them, and they show heavy use only while observers were present. items.stimulus: Removing trees from a watershed usually increases streamflow, since fewer trees are drawing water from the soil and releasing it through their needles or leaves. the snow melted earlier and reached the stream before the season when flow was measured.
removing trees from a watershed reduces streamflow in most forested valleys.

items.stimulus: Paleobotanists studying a 50-million-year-old lake bed found that most of its fossil leaves have smooth edges rather than toothed ones. Fossil pollen from the same layer comes from plants that today grow only in warm regions.
Fossil pollen from the same layer comes from plants that today grow only in cold regions.
The same lake bed also holds fossil leaves from several different species of fern.
items.explanation: The claim in your own words: it was warm around this lake when the leaves fell. The key term is "warm." items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Many schools place hand-sanitizer stations at cafeteria entrances, hoping to slow the spread of colds and flu. Not every school can afford them, so the stations are found in some buildings but not in others. A public health researcher claims that putting sanitizer stations at cafeteria entrances reduces the number of days students miss school because of illness.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's claim?
choices: Students at schools with the stations missed fewer days for illness than students at similar schools without them.
Most students at schools with the stations said in a survey that they liked having sanitizer near the cafeteria.
Laboratory tests show that alcohol-based sanitizer kills many common germs within thirty seconds of being applied.
Students at schools with the stations missed about as many days for illness as students at similar schools without them.
items.explanation: First put the claim in one sentence: the stations lead to fewer sick days. The key term is 'fewer sick days', so the finding you need has to compare sick days with and without the stations. Choice A does exactly that. Schools that are alike except for the stations, and the schools with stations have fewer absences. If A were true, you would believe the claim more. This is the basic move behind every 'which finding, if true, would support' question: find the claim's key term, then pick the finding that speaks to that term directly.

Killing germs in a lab doesn't show that students actually use the stations or end up missing less school. You picked a fact that sounds like it leads to the claim but doesn't establish it.

D.why: This is the right kind of comparison pointing the wrong way. If sick days were the same with and without the stations, that would weaken the claim. Before you read the choices, decide which way the result has to go: fewer sick days with the stations.

items.stimulus: Obsidian blades are abundant at Ravna Kosa, a hilltop settlement occupied around 3000 BCE, yet the nearest obsidian source is a volcanic field some 300 kilometers away. Archaeologist Mira Sotelo hypothesizes that the settlement's residents did not make the blades themselves but instead received them as finished tools.

Excavations across the settlement have recovered very few of the small obsidian flakes and chips produced during blade making.
Microscopic wear on the blades' edges indicates that most of them were used to cut plant fibers rather than meat.
Several large, partially worked obsidian cores have been recovered from the floors of houses at the settlement.
items.explanation: The claim's key term is 'finished tools': the blades were not made at Ravna Kosa. The passage tells you that making blades leaves heaps of flakes wherever the work happens. items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Many coral larvae settle preferentially on crustose coralline algae, a pink alga that coats reef rock. The algae offer both a distinctive rough surface and chemical compounds released by living cells. To separate these factors, a team placed larvae in two tanks. One held tiles coated with live algae; the other held tiles bearing algae that had been killed and bleached, which kept the same rough surface but released no compounds. The team hypothesized that chemical cues, not surface texture, drive the larvae's preference.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's hypothesis?
choices: Larvae settled at much higher rates on tiles coated with live algae than on smooth tiles that had no algae at all.
Larvae that settled on tiles coated with live algae grew faster during their first month than larvae on other surfaces.
Larvae settled at similar rates on tiles coated with live algae and on tiles bearing algae that had been killed and bleached.
Larvae settled at much higher rates on tiles coated with live algae than on tiles bearing algae that had been killed and bleached.
items.explanation: The two tanks match on texture and differ only in chemical cues. If the hypothesis is right, larvae should strongly prefer the live-algae tiles over the dead-algae tiles, even though both surfaces are equally rough. That is exactly what this choice reports.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Some self-healing plastics contain tiny capsules of liquid healing agent scattered among particles of a catalyst. When a crack forms, it ruptures nearby capsules; the released liquid flows into the crack, where contact with the catalyst makes it harden and bond the crack shut. choices: In cracked cold samples, the capsules along the crack were broken and empty, but the liquid inside the crack had not hardened.
Cracked cold samples recovered less than a third of their original strength, while room-temperature samples recovered nearly all of it.
In cracked cold samples, most of the capsules along the crack were still intact and full of liquid healing agent.
At room temperature, samples containing more capsules recovered more strength than samples containing fewer capsules.

C.why: Intact capsules would mean the cold stopped them from breaking. That is the very explanation Anand rejects.

D.why: You picked a fact about how many capsules there are, and only at room temperature. It says nothing about what the cold does to the process.

items.stimulus: In many cities, songbirds sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in the countryside, a shift that may help their songs carry over low-frequency traffic noise. Songbirds living in cities were found to begin singing earlier each morning than songbirds living in the countryside.
The same individual birds sang at a higher pitch during weekday rush hours than during quiet weekend mornings.
Chicks of urban birds raised in quiet aviaries developed the same high-pitched songs as their parents.

On unusually cool summer days, the downwind increase in storms was as large as on the hottest days of the season.

items.stimulus: Permeable pavement is full of tiny pores that let water drain straight through to the gravel below. In a three-winter study, parking lots surfaced with a dark permeable asphalt formed less surface ice than lots made of conventional light-gray concrete. Lots of dark permeable asphalt formed less surface ice than lots of conventional light-gray concrete in each of the three study winters.

Lots of dark permeable asphalt formed less surface ice than lots of conventional asphalt of the same dark color during the same winters.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: In 1794 the Swedish composer Johan Edvard Brandt revised the slow movement of his Symphony in E-flat. He removed a divided viola part and gave several sustained string passages to the woodwinds. Many scholars have read these changes as a sign that Brandt's taste had shifted toward a lighter, wind-colored sound. Musicologist Karin Lindqvist disagrees. She claims that Brandt revised the movement only to accommodate the small string section of a court orchestra in Uppsala, not because his artistic preferences had changed.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's claim?
choices: Reviews of the Uppsala court orchestra's 1794 concerts praised the revised slow movement for its clarity and its unusually prominent woodwinds.
Letters Brandt wrote in 1794 describe his growing frustration with the heavy, string-dominated texture of the original slow movement.
Concert programs show that Brandt kept conducting the original slow movement with larger orchestras in the years after the 1794 revision.
Manuscripts show that Brandt revised many of his works during the 1790s, frequently trimming their string parts and adding wind parts.
items.explanation: Lindqvist's claim has two parts: the revision suited one small orchestra, and Brandt's taste had not changed. If Brandt kept choosing the original version whenever he had a larger orchestra, the revision was a practical fix for one ensemble and not a new preference. Choice C supports both parts at once.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's an appealing fact about the revised movement and the Uppsala orchestra, but audience praise says nothing about why Brandt made the changes.

B.why: Frustration with the original string-heavy texture is evidence that Brandt's taste did shift. That supports the scholars Lindqvist argues against, not Lindqvist herself.

D.why: A habit of trimming strings across many works points toward a general change in Brandt's style. It doesn't tie this revision to one orchestra's limits, and it actually fits the view Lindqvist rejects better.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: In 2019, a city school district installed chilled drinking-water fountains in half of its elementary schools. Over the next three years, students at those schools developed fewer new cavities than students at schools without the fountains. Because the city's tap water is fluoridated, some district officials credited the improvement to students taking in more fluoride. A team of dental researchers disagrees. They claim that the fountains reduced cavities mainly by leading students to drink fewer sugar-sweetened beverages during the school day.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' claim?
choices: Students at schools with the fountains said they preferred the chilled water to the room-temperature water that had been available before.
Across many studies, children who regularly consume sugar-sweetened beverages tend to develop more cavities than children who rarely consume such beverages do.
Students at schools with the fountains had higher levels of fluoride in their tooth enamel than students at schools without the fountains did.
When a nearby city without fluoridated tap water installed identical fountains in its schools, students' new cavities declined by a similar amount.
items.explanation: Start by restating the researchers' claim: the fountains cut cavities through fewer sugary drinks, not through extra fluoride. The key word is 'mainly', which sets the researchers' explanation against the officials' fluoride explanation. Choice D is the only finding that separates the two. In a city where the fountain water carries no added fluoride, the same fountains produced the same drop in cavities. The fluoride explanation can't account for that, so the researchers' explanation becomes more likely. If D were true, you would believe the claim more.

C.why: You mixed up the two positions in the passage. More fluoride in the students' teeth supports the officials' explanation, the one the researchers reject. A finding that makes fluoride look like the cause weakens the researchers' claim.

items.stimulus: When the city of Marlow replaced curbside parking with protected bike lanes on six commercial blocks, retail sales on those blocks rose 14 percent over the next two years, while sales on comparable blocks without new lanes stayed flat. Several other cities that added protected bike lanes also saw retail sales rise on the blocks that got them.
items.explanation: Lindqvist's claim is narrower than 'the lanes raised sales.' items.stimulus: To separate the effects of altitude from the effects of training, sports scientists had twenty runners follow an identical six-week program at sea level. Ten slept each night in tents that simulated the thin air of high elevations, and ten slept normally. Afterward, the tent group had cut more time from its 5,000-meter races. Runners who live and train at high elevations all year typically have more hemoglobin than sea-level runners.
Runners in the tent group reported sleeping more deeply during the study than they had before the study began.
items.explanation: Ibarra's claim runs as a chain: thin air raises hemoglobin mass, and the extra hemoglobin makes the runners faster. If the runners with the largest hemoglobin gains also improved the most, the middle link of that chain is tied to the result Ibarra is trying to explain.

Far more vessels made from Tel Varossa clay have been found at distant sites than in the village's own houses.

items.stimulus: Engineers testing whether small amounts of graphene can toughen concrete prepared two sets of beams from the same mix, adding graphene flakes to only one set. Under repeated loading, the graphene beams cracked later and less extensively. One possible explanation is that graphene fills tiny pores and makes the concrete denser. Microscope images of the graphene beams show flakes spanning small cracks, which are narrowest where flakes cross.
The graphene beams were measurably denser and had fewer pores than the plain beams made from the same mix.
By weight, graphene is many times stronger than the steel commonly used to reinforce concrete beams.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Wheat fields bordered by hedgerows often have less aphid damage than fields bordered by open fencing. Hedgerows slow the wind that carries aphids into crops, and they also shelter ground beetles that crawl out at night and eat aphids on nearby wheat. Ecologist Nadia Ferreira claims that hedgerows reduce aphid damage mainly because they shelter beetles, not because they block wind.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's claim?
choices: Hedgerows that were fenced off at ground level to keep beetles from leaving had almost no effect on aphid damage in neighboring wheat.
Wheat fields bordered by hedgerows had lower aphid damage on average than wheat fields of the same size bordered by open fencing.
Wheat fields sheltered from wind by tall stone walls had as little aphid damage as wheat fields bordered by hedgerows.
Hedgerows bordering wheat fields shelter many kinds of insects, including bees that pollinate wildflowers growing nearby.
items.explanation: Ferreira's claim is about which mechanism matters: beetles rather than blocked wind. A barrier that keeps beetles in removes only the beetle effect and leaves the wind effect in place. If aphid damage then goes back up, the beetles must have been doing most of the work. That is the exact claim.

B.why: This is on topic and true, but the passage already says hedgerows reduce damage. Ferreira's claim is about why they do. This finding fits the beetle explanation and the wind explanation equally well, so it can't tell you which one matters more.

C.why: Stone walls block wind but don't shelter beetles. If walls protect wheat as well as hedgerows do, then blocking wind is enough on its own. That points to wind, which is the reverse of Ferreira's claim.

D.why: This is an accurate fact about hedgerows, but bees and wildflowers have nothing to do with aphids or beetles. It leaves the claim untouched.

Cooking pots matching the village's in shape and thickness were found in older layers at a coastal site 200 kilometers away.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: When a city raised its minimum wage from $12 to $15 an hour, economists compared fast-food restaurants inside the city limits with similar restaurants just outside them, where the wage floor stayed at $12. Turnover fell by about the same amount at restaurants just outside the city as it did at restaurants inside the city.
Raising a minimum wage lowers worker turnover in every industry and region where such an increase has been put in place.

D.why: This is a much broader claim than the economists made. Even if it were true, it wouldn't show that the drop in this city was concentrated among workers whose pay rose.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: When a regional grocery chain raised its starting wage from $14 to $17 an hour at half of its stores, economist Lena Okafor compared those stores with the chain's otherwise similar stores that kept the old wage. Higher pay, she reasoned, makes a job costlier to lose, so fewer workers quit, and a store that loses fewer workers has fewer replacements to train. Over the next year, the higher-wage stores lost fewer workers and spent less on training per store than the other stores did.
Both groups of stores lost similar numbers of workers that year, but the higher-wage stores drew more applicants per opening.

If C were true, you would believe the claim more.

items.stimulus: Vaccines tend to work less well in older animals, partly because their dendritic cells, which show vaccine material to other immune cells, mature slowly. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?

Without the adjuvant, old mice made about a third as many antibodies as young mice; with it, about four-fifths as many.
Dendritic cells from old mice matured more slowly than those of young mice, whether or not the adjuvant was given.
Old mice given the adjuvant stayed protected against infection longer than young mice vaccinated without it did.
items.explanation: The hypothesis is about a gap, the difference between old and young mice, and it predicts that the gap shrinks when the adjuvant is added. Choice B gives the old-to-young ratio under both conditions: it rises from about one-third to about four-fifths. That is the gap narrowing, which is exactly what the researchers predicted.

In each of three recent earthquakes, basin-floor instruments recorded about three times the peak ground motion of hillside ones.

items.stimulus: At Tell Varek, a Bronze Age village in present-day Turkey, archaeologists recovered dozens of basalt grinding stones from the floors of houses. Storage pits inside the houses held whole wheat kernels but contained no traces of already milled flour.
Grinding stones found in the larger nearby towns were cut from the same type of basalt as those at Tell Varek.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Many galaxies eventually stop forming new stars, a change astronomers call quenching. Stars form only when cold gas collapses, so anything that either removes a galaxy's gas or heats that gas can halt star formation. A galaxy's central black hole, when it is actively feeding, can do both: its energetic outflows may blow gas out of the galaxy entirely or merely warm the gas that remains. Astrophysicist Leilani Kahale argues that in dwarf galaxies, active black holes quench star formation chiefly by heating gas rather than by expelling it.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kahale's argument?
choices: Quenched dwarf galaxies are about three times as likely as star-forming dwarf galaxies of similar mass to have a central black hole that is actively feeding.
Quenched dwarf galaxies with active black holes hold about as much total gas as star-forming dwarf galaxies of similar mass, but far less of that gas is cold.
Quenched massive galaxies with active black holes hold about as much total gas as star-forming massive galaxies of similar mass, but far less of that gas is cold.
Quenched dwarf galaxies with active black holes hold far less total gas than star-forming dwarf galaxies of similar mass, and almost none of that gas is cold.
items.explanation: Kahale's claim has three parts: it is about dwarf galaxies, it says active black holes cause the quenching, and it says they do it by heating gas rather than by expelling it. If they were heating it, the gas would still be there but would no longer be cold. Choice B describes the second case: the total amount of gas matches that of star-forming dwarfs, but little of it is cold. That fits heating and rules out expulsion, in the right kind of galaxy.

A black hole that blew the gas out would produce exactly the same pattern, so this choice leaves the key part of her claim untouched. It is on topic but off claim.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Farmers in semi-arid regions often cover their fields with wheat straw. The straw slows evaporation, keeping more water in the soil for crops. But as soil microbes break the straw down, they absorb nitrogen from the soil, leaving less for the crop. In one field trial, maize grown under straw yielded no more than maize grown on bare soil, even though the straw-covered plots stayed wetter. Agronomist Tomás Ferreira concluded that the straw's moisture benefit was real but was cancelled out by the nitrogen the microbes consumed.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's conclusion?
choices: In a second trial in which only the straw-covered plots received extra nitrogen fertilizer, maize under straw yielded more than maize on bare soil.
In a second trial in which both straw-covered and bare plots received extra nitrogen fertilizer, maize under straw and on bare soil yielded about the same.
In a second trial in which both straw-covered and bare plots received extra nitrogen fertilizer, maize under straw yielded more than maize on bare soil.
In a second trial with no added fertilizer, the straw-covered plots again stayed wetter than the bare plots in both the driest and wettest months.
items.explanation: Ferreira says two things at once. First, the straw really does help through moisture. Second, that help was hidden because the microbes used up nitrogen. If both are true, then removing the nitrogen shortage should reveal the moisture benefit. The test only works if both kinds of plot get the same extra nitrogen, so that straw is the only difference between them. Choice C reports exactly that: with nitrogen added to every plot, maize under straw outyields maize on bare soil.

A.why: You had the right idea: add nitrogen and see whether the straw's benefit appears. But here only the straw plots were fertilized, so they differ from the bare plots in two ways, straw and fertilizer. The extra nitrogen alone could explain the higher yield, so this result says nothing about whether the moisture benefit is real. You read more into the result than the setup allows.

B.why: This is the right experiment, with nitrogen added to both groups, but you missed which way the result had to go. If the yields are still equal once the nitrogen shortage is gone, the straw's moisture gave no yield benefit. That is the opposite of the 'benefit was real' half of Ferreira's conclusion, so this finding would weaken it.

D.why: This choice is on topic and true to the passage, since the straw plots do stay wetter. But it repeats something the passage already established and says nothing about yield or nitrogen. It doesn't show that the extra moisture helps the crop, or that nitrogen loss cancelled that help, and those are the two points Ferreira actually concluded.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: In 2022 the city of Marrow Falls turned one car lane on Halvorsen Avenue into a protected bike lane. Over the following year, weekday car counts on the avenue fell by about 4,000. Some residents said the new lane had persuaded commuters to start cycling. Urban planner Ines Okafor disagrees. She claims that most of the decline reflects drivers moving to nearby routes, not drivers giving up their cars.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor's claim?
choices: Weekday bicycle trips on Halvorsen Avenue rose by about 3,800 after the lane opened, mostly by people who used to drive.
Weekday car counts on Halvorsen Avenue had fallen by a similar amount in the year before the bike lane was installed.
Drivers who still use Halvorsen Avenue reported in a survey that their trips have become noticeably slower since the lane opened.
Weekday car counts on the two streets running parallel to Halvorsen Avenue rose by a combined 3,500 over the same year.
items.explanation: Okafor's claim has two parts: the cars went somewhere else, and that accounts for most of the drop. If the parallel streets gained 3,500 cars while Halvorsen lost about 4,000, most of the missing traffic shows up on nearby routes. That is exactly what 'moving to nearby routes' predicts.

A.why: You matched the topic and missed the direction. A rise in cycling about as large as the drop in cars, mostly by former drivers, is the residents' explanation, the one Okafor rejects. If this were true, it would weaken her claim.

B.why: This questions whether the lane caused the decline at all. Okafor's claim is about where the drivers went, and a decline that was already happening says nothing about whether they rerouted.

C.why: This is the trap that survives the first insight. Slower trips give drivers a reason to reroute, so it feels like support. But a motive to switch routes doesn't show that anyone actually switched, let alone enough people to cover most of the 4,000-car drop.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Under a 'live high, train low' program, endurance athletes sleep at high altitude but train near sea level. They often race faster afterward. The thin air at altitude is known to trigger the production of extra red blood cells, which carry oxygen to muscles. Physiologist Tomas Reyes hypothesizes that the faster times come from this rise in red blood cells, not from the confidence athletes gain from an intensive training camp.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Reyes's hypothesis?
choices: Athletes who slept at altitude had higher red blood cell counts at the end of the program than they had at the start.
Elite endurance athletes generally have higher red blood cell counts than recreational endurance athletes have.
Among athletes in the program, those whose red blood cell counts rose the most also improved their race times the most.
Athletes in the program reported feeling more confident before races than they had felt before the camp began.
items.explanation: The hypothesis is a chain: altitude raises red blood cell counts, and that rise produces faster times. The passage already gives the first link. What needs support is the second link, from red blood cells to race times. If the athletes with the biggest gains in red blood cells also had the biggest gains in speed, the improvement follows the red blood cells and not the camp, which every athlete attended.

A.why: You saw that red blood cells were the key term and stopped there. This confirms only the link the passage already states, from altitude to red blood cells. It says nothing about whether those cells made anyone faster, and that is the link Reyes is hypothesizing.

B.why: This is a general fact about athletes, not about the program. A difference between elite and recreational athletes can't show what caused the improvement in these athletes.

D.why: A boost in confidence is the rival explanation Reyes rules out. Evidence that athletes gained confidence makes that rival more believable, so it works against his hypothesis.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Excavations at Tell Varin, a Bronze Age farming village, have produced thousands of pottery fragments. Many vessels look like wares from the coastal city of Ashkel, about 90 kilometers away, and scholars have long assumed that the village got most of its pottery by trading with Ashkel. Archaeologist Mira Haddad contends that Varin's cooking pots, whatever their style, were made in the village itself.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's claim?
choices: The clay in Varin's cooking pots matches a riverbank deposit beside the village and no deposit near Ashkel.
Varin's cooking pots share their shape and rim design with cooking pots excavated at Ashkel.
The clay in Varin's painted serving bowls matches a deposit found only in the hills near Ashkel.
A kiln full of broken cooking pots has been found at a village 30 kilometers from Varin.
items.explanation: Haddad's claim has two limits: it covers cooking pots only, and it places their production in 'the village itself.' Clay that matches a deposit right beside Varin and nothing near Ashkel ties those pots to the village's own ground and rules out Ashkel as the source.

B.why: Haddad says 'whatever their style,' so she has already set appearance aside. Pots that look like Ashkel's fit the scholars' trade view better than hers. This choice either says nothing about her claim or works against it.

C.why: This is about the right site and the right kind of evidence, but the wrong vessels. Haddad makes no claim about serving bowls, so their source neither supports nor weakens what she says about cooking pots.

D.why: You noticed that local production matters but skipped the scope words 'the village itself.' A kiln at a different village 30 kilometers away shows cooking pots were made somewhere nearby, not in Varin.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: A coating developed for car paint closes fine scratches within a day at room temperature. Two features could explain this. The coating holds microcapsules of liquid resin that burst when scratched and seep into the gap, and its polymer chains can slowly flow across a scratch on their own. Materials scientist Priya Natarajan hypothesizes that the flowing chains do most of the repair and that the resin plays at most a minor role.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Natarajan's hypothesis?
choices: Samples made without microcapsules closed scratches, but only about half as completely as standard samples did.
Samples made without microcapsules closed scratches almost as completely as standard samples did.
Standard samples closed shallow scratches and deep scratches equally completely within a day.
Polymer chains that flow at room temperature are also found in several other self-healing coatings.
items.explanation: Work out the direction first. If the resin plays at most a minor role, then removing the microcapsules should barely change how well scratches close. Samples that heal almost as completely without capsules show the chains doing nearly all the work, which is what Natarajan predicts.

A.why: This is the second-order trap. Seeing that the chains heal scratches on their own feels like support, but read the size of the effect. If removing the resin cuts healing in half, the resin is doing about half the repair. That is not a minor role, so this weakens the hypothesis.

C.why: This is an accurate-sounding fact about how well the coating heals. It does nothing to separate the chains' contribution from the resin's, and that split is the whole hypothesis.

D.why: Finding similar chains in other coatings says nothing about how much they do in this coating compared with the resin.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Paleobotanists often estimate past temperatures from fossil leaves, because woody plants in cool climates tend to have toothed leaf edges and those in warm climates tend to have smooth ones. Plants growing along streambanks, however, often have toothed leaves regardless of climate. In a two-million-year sequence of lake sediments, the share of toothed leaves falls steadily from the lower layers to the upper ones. Paleobotanist Lena Brandt concludes that this pattern reflects regional warming rather than a loss of streamside habitat around the lake.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brandt's conclusion?
choices: Smooth-edged leaves in the upper layers are larger, on average, than smooth-edged leaves in the lower layers.
Sediments in the upper layers show that the lake's feeding streams gradually dried up over the period.
Modern woody plants in cool regions around the world more often have toothed leaves than smooth ones.
Pollen in the same layers shows that streamside tree species were about as common at the top as at the bottom.
items.explanation: Brandt's conclusion has two halves: warming caused the pattern, and loss of streamside habitat did not. The passage itself raises the streambank problem. If streamside trees were just as common in the upper layers as in the lower ones, the habitat explanation fails, and the drop in toothed leaves points to climate.

A.why: Leaf size is a different trait from leaf edges. This is a true-sounding detail about the same fossils that leaves the conclusion untouched.

B.why: Streams drying up means streamside habitat shrinking, which is the explanation Brandt rejects. This would weaken her conclusion.

C.why: This just repeats the general principle the passage starts from. Brandt's conclusion is about why this particular sequence changed, and the principle can't tell warming apart from habitat loss.

items.stimulus: At dusk, many wrasses bury themselves in sand and stay there until morning. Burial is thought to offer two kinds of protection: it hides the fish from night-hunting moray eels, and it may block gnathiid isopods, tiny blood-feeding parasites that are active at night. Marine biologist Kai Moana hypothesizes that, at least on reefs where both threats are common, avoiding isopods is the more important benefit of burial.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Moana's hypothesis?
choices: On reefs that have no moray eels, wrasses kept from burying themselves received far more isopod bites than buried wrasses did.
On reefs with both threats, wrasses kept from burying themselves received far more isopod bites but no more eel attacks than buried wrasses did.
On reefs with both threats, wrasses kept from burying themselves suffered far more eel attacks but no more isopod bites than buried wrasses did.
On reefs with both threats, gnathiid isopods also feed on many fish species that never bury themselves in sand at night.
items.explanation: The hypothesis compares two benefits and limits itself to reefs where both threats are common. items.stimulus: Before the 1770s, English weavers making 'cottons' usually ran lengthwise threads of linen through their looms, because hand-spun cotton was too weak to bear the loom's tension. Machine-spun cotton thread became widely available to weavers across much of England during the 1770s and 1780s.

items.stimulus: Agnes Lindqvist's Second Symphony survives in two versions: the 1904 original and a 1907 revision in which the slow movement is shortened and several long-held brass chords are cut. Lindqvist marked the brass chords for cutting in a draft dated 1905, two years before the Stockholm hall opened.

Several composers of the period are known to have revised their works to suit the acoustics of particular halls.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: For decades, relief printmakers have cleaned ink from their carved blocks with mineral spirits, a solvent that removes oil-based ink quickly. Printmaker Ana Ruiz, however, now tells students in her workshops to use vegetable oil followed by soap and water. She notes that fumes from mineral spirits can linger for hours in small studios with little ventilation. Ruiz's recommendation suggests that, in her view, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: vegetable oil leaves behind stronger and longer-lasting fumes than mineral spirits do.
mineral spirits have a drawback in some studios that the oil-and-soap method avoids.
mineral spirits should be banned from every printmaking studio regardless of its size.
students should give up relief printing in favor of techniques that use no ink at all.
items.explanation: Ruiz recommends a new cleaning method and gives one reason: mineral spirit fumes linger in small, poorly ventilated studios. To recommend the switch for that reason, she has to believe that mineral spirits have this drawback in some settings and that the oil-and-soap method avoids it. That is the smallest belief her advice depends on.

A.why: This reverses the comparison. Ruiz recommends vegetable oil because mineral spirits cause the fume problem, so she can't think the oil gives off worse fumes.

C.why: You took the claim too far. Ruiz says the problem is fumes in small studios with poor ventilation. That gives no support for banning the solvent everywhere, including large, well-ventilated studios.

D.why: Ruiz's advice is about how to clean blocks, not whether to keep printing. Nothing in the text suggests she wants students to stop using ink.

weather balloons are of no use at all for forecasting thunderstorms.
thunderstorms form far more often now than they did decades ago.

the symphony is the most important work Lindqvist ever composed.
the printed edition might not match exactly what Lindqvist had written.
every note in the printed edition had been changed by its engravers.

radiocarbon dating cannot produce a trustworthy age for any material recovered from a hearth.

the ground stations had been recording humidity incorrectly on evenings when fog formed.

readings taken near the surface explain valley fog better than readings taken higher up.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Manufacturers usually rate a new polymer adhesive by its strength immediately after curing. an adhesive's strength after humid storage is best predicted by its strength right after curing.
strength right after curing is an unreliable guide to how an adhesive will perform when damp.
humidity weakens every polymer adhesive by roughly half within the first six months of use.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Many conservation groups judge the success of a wetland restoration by counting the plant species that return to it. restored marshes with more plant species remove less nitrogen than those with fewer species.
water sampling reveals less about a restoration's success than a survey of vegetation does.
plant species counts alone cannot show whether a restored marsh filters runoff as intended.

hospital test counts should no longer be used to monitor influenza within the region.
people with mild flu are more likely than severe cases to appear in hospital test data.
influenza now spreads through the region more quickly than it did in earlier seasons.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Engineers have long inspected steel highway bridges by eye, looking for cracks and rust during scheduled visits every two years. welded joints are a less likely site of fatigue cracking than exposed steel surfaces.
visual inspections can fail to detect fatigue cracks while those cracks are still small.
bridges over rivers develop fatigue cracks faster than bridges built over dry land.

items.stimulus: Many soybean growers decide when to add nitrogen fertilizer by checking leaf color, treating pale, yellowish leaves as a sign of nitrogen shortage. pale leaves can sometimes appear on soybean plants that already have enough nitrogen.
most pale soybean leaves are caused by something other than a lack of nitrogen.
leaf color gives growers no useful information about the nitrogen levels in a field.

the current stations detect pressure jumps less reliably near towns than in rural areas.

the existing surface stations should be replaced by sensors mounted on cell towers.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Most studies of minimum-wage increases measure their effect by counting how many people are employed before and after the change. This design suggests that Haddad thought ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: employers would certainly respond to the increase by trimming workers' hours rather than by reducing staff.
counts of employed people reveal nothing useful about how a minimum-wage increase affects workers.
changes in weekly hours are a less sensitive measure of an increase's effects than changes in headcount.
employers might respond to the increase by trimming workers' hours rather than by reducing their staff.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: City traffic engineers have traditionally graded streets using "level of service," a score based on how long drivers wait at intersections. a grade based only on drivers' waiting times to give an incomplete account of how well a street works.
the existing grade to capture travel on foot and by bus more fully than the proposed measure would.
the streets that move the most people per hour to be the ones where drivers wait the longest.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Many growers decide when to irrigate by checking a single moisture sensor buried a few centimeters below the soil surface. the cost of extra sensors is the main reason growers have not adopted them.
surface readings alone can misrepresent the water available to deep roots.
deep-rooted crops need less frequent irrigation than shallow-rooted crops do.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: For decades, a regional weather office published a single predicted snowfall total before each winter storm. When staff reviewed ten years of these forecasts, they found that actual totals often differed sharply from predictions for storms tracking near the rain-snow line, where small temperature shifts decide whether precipitation falls as rain or snow. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: single totals had been inaccurate for every type of storm the office forecast.
storms well inland were harder to forecast than storms near the rain-snow line.
storms near the rain-snow line had become more frequent over the past decade.
a single total implied more certainty than storms near the rain-snow line allowed.
items.explanation: The office switched to ranges only for storms near the rain-snow line, which are the storms where its review found large misses. Keeping single totals for inland storms shows the staff didn't have the same doubt about those storms.

B.why: You reversed the comparison. The office treats storms near the rain-snow line as the harder case. That's why only those storms now get a range.

C.why: You credited the staff with a belief the change doesn't need. The review was about forecast accuracy, not how often these storms happen, and nothing suggests their frequency changed.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Most clinics in Harlow County remind patients about overdue vaccinations by sending a mailed postcard, a practice that has gone largely unchanged for years. The county health department has now funded a six-month trial in which half of the clinics switch to text-message reminders while the other half continue mailing postcards. By funding this trial, the department indicates that in its view, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: postcards have already been shown to work less well than text messages.
mailed postcards may not be the most effective reminder clinics could use.
text-message reminders would cost clinics more to send than postcards.
all clinics should stop mailing postcards before the trial has concluded.
items.explanation: Nobody pays for a head-to-head trial of an old method against a new one unless they think the old method might not be the best option. The trial is meant to find out, so the department's belief can only be that postcards may not be the most effective reminder. It can't be that postcards are known to be worse.

C.why: You credited the department with a belief the trial never depends on. The passage says nothing about cost, and funding the trial doesn't require any view about which method is cheaper.

D.why: You missed the trial's design. Half the clinics keep mailing postcards so there's something to compare against. Stopping postcards everywhere would wreck the trial the department is funding.
