items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Surveys of marsh birds have traditionally relied on observers who stand at fixed points and record every bird they see or hear. Ornithologist Dev Rao notes, however, that secretive species such as rails rarely call when people are close by. For his survey of a Louisiana marsh, Rao placed automated recorders at the usual survey points and left them unattended overnight. Rao's approach suggests that he thought ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: rails call more often when observers are present than when they are absent.
automated recorders detect every marsh species more accurately than people do.
marsh birds are more numerous at night than they are during the day.
the presence of observers can cause some species to be undercounted.
items.explanation: Rao points to one problem: rails go quiet when people are nearby. He then takes the people out and leaves recorders. That only makes sense if he thinks a human observer can reduce how many of these birds are detected. In other words, the observer's presence can lead to some species being undercounted.

B.why: You let 'some species' grow into 'every species.' Rao's reasoning is about secretive birds like rails. Nothing suggests he thinks recorders do better for all birds.

C.why: You read too much into the word 'overnight.' Leaving the recorders unattended takes people away from the birds. It doesn't require Rao to believe bird numbers change between day and night.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Folklorists have often assumed that a tale found in many villages spread outward from one original version, and they have arranged variants into family trees tracing each back to that source. In cataloging 140 versions of a Baltic tale about a bargaining fox, however, Ilse Varga built no such tree. She grouped the versions by region and by the occasions on which they were told. Varga's choice suggests that she ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: considered the regional versions too alike to be worth telling apart.
believed the tale was first told in a single village that could be identified.
questioned whether descent from one source was a sound way to organize them.
regarded earlier folklorists' catalogs as containing no useful information.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the usual method, which is a family tree going back to one source, and then says Varga set it aside on purpose. A scholar drops the standard approach and organizes by region and occasion when she doubts the standard approach fits the material. So her choice suggests she questioned whether descent from one original was a sound way to organize the versions.

A.why: You missed what her grouping implies. Sorting the versions by region only makes sense if she thinks regional differences are worth showing. That's the opposite of finding the versions too alike.

B.why: You attributed the old view to the person who turned away from it. Believing in one identifiable source village is the assumption behind the family tree she chose not to build.

D.why: You turned a difference in method into a total rejection. Varga declined one way of organizing the material. That doesn't mean she thinks earlier catalogs are worthless.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Vaccine protection is commonly judged by the level of antibodies in the blood, and those levels typically fall in the months after a dose. Immunologist Rana Okafor, however, recruited volunteers whose antibody levels had already dropped below the threshold usually treated as protective, then tested whether their memory T cells still responded to the virus. Okafor's choice of participants suggests that in Okafor's view, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: a drop in antibody levels does not necessarily mean that a person's protection has been lost.
memory T cells, rather than antibodies, are the only source of lasting protection against the virus.
antibody levels are a more dependable measure of protection than memory T-cell responses are.
vaccine doses should be given more often so that antibody levels stay above the usual threshold.
items.explanation: Ask why Okafor would deliberately study people whose antibodies had fallen below the protective threshold. That study only makes sense if Okafor suspected those people might still be protected in another way, through memory T cells. So Okafor must doubt that low antibodies alone mean protection is gone. Choice A states that assumption and nothing more.

B.why: You went from 'antibodies may not tell the whole story' to 'T cells are the ONLY source of protection.' Okafor's study requires only that T cells might add something, not that antibodies contribute nothing. Watch for 'only.'

C.why: This reverses the comparison. Okafor looked past antibody levels to T cells, which suggests Okafor thinks antibody levels miss something. That is the opposite of trusting them more.

D.why: This assumes Okafor treats the antibody threshold as the thing that matters. The study questions that threshold, and nothing in the passage is about dosing schedules.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Many nineteenth-century folktale collections were assembled by editors who rewrote what they heard into polished literary prose, trimming repetitions and replacing regional expressions with standard ones. Folklorist Tomas Ilves has urged scholars who trace how particular tales shifted from one generation of tellers to the next to rely instead on audio recordings of storytellers made since the 1930s. Ilves's recommendation implies that, in Ilves's view, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: printed nineteenth-century collections have no value for any kind of folklore research.
nineteenth-century editors preserved tellers' exact wording more closely than recordings do.
editorial rewriting in the printed collections hides details needed to track how tales changed.
storytellers recorded since the 1930s performed tales more skillfully than earlier tellers did.
items.explanation: Ilves recommends recordings for one task: tracing how tales shifted between generations. The passage names the flaw in the printed collections. Editors smoothed away repetitions and regional wording, and those small variations are exactly what you would compare across generations. The recommendation therefore depends on the belief that the rewriting hides those details, which is what choice C says.

B.why: This reverses the comparison. The passage says editors changed tellers' wording, and Ilves prefers recordings for that reason. Ilves can't believe the printed versions are more faithful.

D.why: Ilves cares about how accurately a performance was captured, not how good it was. The recommendation doesn't depend on any view of the tellers' skill.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Ecologists have long surveyed forest birds using point counts, in which an observer stands at a fixed spot and records every bird seen or heard. Because most birds in dense forest are detected by their calls, such counts tend to miss species that seldom vocalize. In a recent survey of a cloud forest, ecologist Mei Tanaka supplemented point counts with motion-triggered cameras mounted near the forest floor. Tanaka's approach suggests that Tanaka thought ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: point counts give inaccurate results for every bird species that lives in cloud forests.
the forest might hold quiet ground-dwelling birds that point counts alone would undercount.
ground-dwelling birds in cloud forests call more often than birds in the canopy do.
cloud forests support more bird species than any other type of forest habitat does.
items.explanation: The passage states the flaw in point counts: they miss birds that rarely call. items.stimulus: Aluminum ship hulls are commonly protected with chromate coatings, which resist corrosion well but release toxic compounds into the water as they wear. the environmental benefit of the cerium coating outweighs its small shortfall in protection.
chromate coatings offer too little corrosion protection to be worth applying to hulls.
the cerium coating is suitable for all hull applications now using chromate, without exception.

items.stimulus: Many forest managers blame the poor survival of oak seedlings in eastern North America chiefly on browsing by white-tailed deer, and fencing is the standard remedy. shade could account for part of the seedling loss usually blamed on deer.
seedlings survive better beneath a dense canopy than beneath a thinned one.
shade causes far more seedling loss among oaks than deer browsing does.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Forecasters estimate hail size largely from radar, which measures how strongly a storm reflects microwave signals high in the atmosphere. Hailstones, however, can melt substantially as they fall through warm air near the ground. After reviewing a season of storms in which radar estimates and ground reports differed, meteorologist Ama Owusu recommended that her agency recruit volunteers to measure hailstones on the ground in low-lying, warmer regions. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: radar tends to overestimate the size of hail reaching the ground in warm areas.
radar tends to underestimate the size of hail reaching the ground in warm areas.
radar estimates of hail size are unreliable in every region the agency covers.
melting hail adds significantly to rainfall totals in low-lying, warmer regions.
items.explanation: Radar measures hail high in the storm, and hail shrinks as it melts in warm air near the ground. Owusu asks for ground measurements specifically in warm, low-lying places. That choice only makes sense if she thinks the hail that lands there is smaller than radar indicates, meaning radar overestimates it. Choice A states this.

D.why: You picked up an incidental detail. Melting is mentioned to explain why hail size changes, not to make a point about rainfall. Her recommendation is about measuring hail size, and this choice never touches that.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: For decades, a regional weather office based its fog warnings on readings from a single station at the county airport. In 2023, forecaster Lena Ortiz recommended adding a network of low-cost visibility sensors along the river valley. She noted that fog in the valley often forms hours before it drifts toward the airport. Ortiz's recommendation suggests that she did NOT believe that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: fog conditions in the valley can differ from conditions measured at the airport.
the airport station's readings were enough on their own to warn valley residents.
detecting valley fog earlier would help the office issue more timely warnings.
inexpensive sensors could supply visibility readings useful to forecasters.
items.explanation: Ask why Ortiz would recommend new sensors at all. Her recommendation only makes sense if she thought the single airport station fell short, since fog forms in the valley hours before it reaches the airport. So she did NOT believe the airport readings were enough on their own. The other three choices are all things she had to believe for her recommendation to make sense. The blank asks for the one she rejected.

A.why: This is the belief her whole recommendation rests on. She says valley fog forms before it reaches the airport, so she clearly thinks the two locations can differ. You found a true statement about her view and missed the NOT in the blank.

C.why: She points out that the fog forms 'hours before' it reaches the airport, and that point only matters if catching it earlier helps. She held this belief, so it can't be the one she did NOT hold.

D.why: You latched onto the detail that the sensors are cheap and read it as a doubt about their quality. Nobody recommends a sensor network they think will give useless readings, so she did believe this.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Many conservation groups judge the health of a seabird colony by counting its nesting pairs each spring. Ecologist Tomás Reyna's team, however, spent three seasons also weighing chicks just before they fledged. The researchers argued that a colony can hold its nest count steady even as food shortages leave young birds too light to survive their first winter. The team's approach suggests that the researchers did NOT assume that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: a chick's weight at fledging can affect its chances of surviving the winter.
the food available to a colony can influence how its chicks develop.
a colony's health can decline without any change in its nest count.
a steady number of nesting pairs reliably shows that a colony is thriving.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the popular method of counting nests and then undercuts it. Reyna's team added chick weights because they believed nest counts can stay level while the colony is in trouble. A team with that view could not assume that a steady nest count reliably shows a thriving colony. The other three choices are assumptions the team needed to justify weighing chicks.

A.why: The team says chicks can be 'too light to survive their first winter', which is exactly this belief. You picked a statement the researchers did hold and overlooked the NOT.

B.why: The researchers name food shortages as the reason chicks end up too light, so they clearly believed food affects how chicks develop. This assumption supports their method. It is not one they rejected.

C.why: This is the researchers' central argument, nearly word for word. You may have read it as the 'corrected view' and picked it, but the blank asks for the view they did NOT hold.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Hikers in the Vellan Range have long relied on a 1960s survey map with contour lines spaced at 50-meter intervals. When the park service commissioned a replacement, cartographer Ines Halvorsen insisted on 10-meter contours for the steep eastern trails. On the gentle western plateau, however, she kept the original 50-meter spacing. Halvorsen's decision implies that she did NOT think that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: 50-meter contours were too coarse for every part of the range.
finer contours would reveal detail that matters on the eastern trails.
50-meter contours were adequate for mapping the western plateau.
the old map's spacing hid terrain features that matter on some trails.
items.explanation: Halvorsen changed the spacing in one place and kept it in another. That split tells you she thought the old 50-meter contours were limited, not useless. She kept them for the western plateau, so she could not have thought they were too coarse for every part of the range. This choice goes too far, and that is why it is the belief she did NOT hold.

B.why: She insisted on 10-meter contours for the eastern trails, and that only makes sense if she thought the finer spacing showed detail that mattered there. She held this belief.

C.why: She deliberately kept the 50-meter spacing on the plateau, which shows she thought it was good enough there. You may have assumed a new map rejects everything about the old one, but the passage says otherwise.

D.why: Replacing the eastern contours implies she thought the old spacing hid something that mattered there. The word 'some' keeps this claim modest enough to match her view, so it is a belief she held.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Observational studies have long linked higher blood levels of vitamin D to fewer bone fractures, yet several large trials that gave vitamin D supplements to broad samples of adults found no reduction in fractures. Rather than conclude that the supplements are ineffective, nutrition scientist Priya Raman designed a new trial that enrolled only adults whose blood vitamin D fell below the deficiency threshold at the outset. Raman's design suggests that, in her view, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: vitamin D supplements cannot reduce fracture risk in adults whose blood levels are already above the deficiency threshold.
the link found in observational studies reflects other habits of adults with high vitamin D rather than the vitamin itself.
the earlier trials may have included too many adults who had little to gain from taking additional vitamin D.
the earlier trials demonstrated that supplements reduce fractures only in adults whose blood vitamin D was initially deficient.
items.explanation: Start with why Raman would run the trial this way. She refuses to read the earlier null results as proof that supplements fail, and she then enrols only deficient adults. That choice only makes sense if she thinks any benefit shows up mainly in deficient people, so a broad sample full of people who already had enough vitamin D could have hidden a real effect. Choice C states that belief. Its 'may' also fits the evidence: she is testing an explanation, not asserting one she has already proven.

A.why: You saw the key point, that the benefit is concentrated in deficient adults, and then took it one step too far. Raman's design only needs her to think adequate-level adults gain less, so including them would weaken the signal. It doesn't need her to think they gain nothing. 'Cannot' is strength creep.

B.why: You gave Raman a belief that her own action argues against. If she thought the observational link came from other habits and not from vitamin D, she would have no reason to run another supplement trial. The passage also says she specifically declined to conclude that the supplements are ineffective.

D.why: You turned Raman's hypothesis into a finding of the earlier trials. Those trials found no reduction in fractures, and nothing says they compared deficient and non-deficient adults. The idea that deficiency matters belongs to Raman's new design, not to their results.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Print historians have often ordered the undated impressions of a single etched plate by the sharpness of their lines: because each pass through the press wears the copper slightly, crisper impressions were assumed to be earlier. Studying the etchings of the nineteenth-century printmaker Odile Ferrant, historian Ana Kovač noted that Ferrant's workshop periodically re-bit worn plates in acid, deepening their lines. Kovač therefore set line sharpness aside and ordered Ferrant's impressions by the dated watermarks in their paper. Kovač's approach suggests that she regarded ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the dated watermarks as a less dependable guide than line sharpness to the order of Ferrant's impressions.
a crisp impression from one of Ferrant's plates as possibly later than a faint impression from that plate.
impressions pulled after one of Ferrant's plates was re-bitten as crisper than those pulled when it was new.
line sharpness as uninformative about the order of the impressions from any etched plate of the nineteenth century.
items.explanation: Ask why Kovač dropped line sharpness. The old method depends on lines only ever getting fainter over time. Re-biting deepens worn lines, so an impression pulled after re-biting can look crisp even though it came late. For that reason Kovač can't trust 'crisper means earlier' for Ferrant's plates, which means she must accept that a crisp impression might come after a faint one. Choice B says exactly that, and 'possibly' keeps it as strong as the passage allows and no stronger.

A.why: You reversed the comparison. Kovač gave up line sharpness and used watermarks instead, so she must think watermarks are the more dependable guide for Ferrant's work, not the less dependable one.

C.why: You understood that re-biting restores crispness, then added a step the passage never takes. 'Deepening their lines' only means re-bitten plates are crisper than they were when worn. Nothing says they become crisper than the plate was when new, and Kovač's method doesn't depend on that comparison.

D.why: You stretched one workshop's practice into a rule about every plate. Kovač's reason for dropping line sharpness is specific to Ferrant, whose workshop re-bit its plates. Her approach says nothing about plates that were never re-bitten, and 'any' goes well past what she needs to believe.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Some ecologists credit the return of wolves to a western valley with the recovery of its streamside willows, reasoning that wolves deter elk from browsing there. Ecologist Hana Ostrowski fenced willow plots to exclude elk entirely. Fenced willows outgrew unfenced ones overall, but at sites where the stream had cut a deep channel, fenced willows grew far less than fenced willows elsewhere. Ostrowski then began measuring groundwater depth at every site, suggesting she suspected that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: elk browsing had little effect on willows at deep-channel sites, where a shortage of water was the only factor limiting their growth.
elk avoided browsing at the deep-channel sites because the willows growing there had already been weakened by low groundwater.
the return of wolves had done nothing to aid willow recovery in the valley, whatever the depth of its stream channels.
keeping elk away might not be enough to restore willows where channel cutting had lowered the water available to their roots.
items.explanation: Hold two results together. First, fencing helped willows overall, so browsing matters. Second, fenced willows at deep-channel sites still grew poorly, so removing elk wasn't enough there. Measuring groundwater shows that Ostrowski suspected water as the other limit. D keeps both results: excluding elk 'might not be enough' at those sites. It doesn't say elk don't matter.

A.why: You noticed water and dropped elk. The data compare fenced plots with other fenced plots, not fenced with unfenced plots at deep-channel sites. Nothing shows that browsing had little effect there or that water was the 'only' factor.

B.why: This makes up a link between groundwater and how elk behave. The fences kept elk out entirely, so the poor growth inside them can't be explained by where elk chose to feed.

C.why: This goes much too far. Fenced willows outgrew unfenced ones, so reducing browsing does help, and that is the very mechanism the wolf explanation depends on. Her follow-up adds a second factor. It doesn't throw out the first.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Editors of Antonín Halbich's Second Quartet have long printed the pencil revisions in his autograph score as his final intentions, since the score remained in his possession until his death. Musicologist Irena Vos compared the handwriting of each revision both with samples from Halbich's letters and with pages known to be written by the copyist who lived in his household during his last years. Vos's method suggests that in her view ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the score's remaining in Halbich's possession did not guarantee that every revision in it was written in his own hand.
the copyist had altered the quartet without Halbich's knowledge during the years the two shared a household.
even revisions in Halbich's own hand should be treated as less authoritative than the original ink text of the score.
the handwriting in Halbich's letters was too inconsistent to serve as a reliable basis for any comparison.
items.explanation: The editors reason that because Halbich kept the score, the revisions are his. Vos checks each revision against two hands, his and the copyist's. She would only do that if keeping the score didn't settle who wrote in it. A states that assumption. It claims nothing about whether any revision is actually the copyist's or whether the copyist acted against Halbich's wishes.

B.why: Even if the copyist wrote some revisions, they might have been taking Halbich's dictation. Handwriting can show who held the pencil, not whether Halbich knew. You gave her a belief that her method couldn't test and didn't need.

C.why: Vos questions who wrote the revisions, not whether Halbich's own changes count. If a revision is in his hand, nothing in her method would downgrade it.

D.why: She used the letters as her sample of Halbich's handwriting. She could only do that if she trusted them, so this choice reverses her reasoning.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: A regional museum attributes nine nineteenth-century quilts to a single maker because all nine contain the same printed cottons. Textile historian Joan Pell, noting that quilters in the region routinely traded fabric scraps, has recommended that the attribution be reassessed using measurements of stitch length and thread tension instead. Pell's recommendation implies that she believes ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the nine quilts were in fact made by several different quilters who had traded scraps of the same printed cottons.
the fabrics in a quilt are more likely than its stitching to reveal which quilter in the region made it.
a maker's stitching is more likely than a quilt's fabrics to distinguish that maker's work from the work of others nearby.
stitch length and thread tension remain identical across every quilt that a single maker ever produces.
items.explanation: Pell gives a reason why shared fabric is weak evidence: fabric moved between quilters. Then she proposes stitching instead. That recommendation only makes sense if she thinks stitching tells makers apart better than fabric does. C states that comparison in the right direction and doesn't claim that stitching is a perfect fingerprint.

A.why: You correctly saw that she distrusts the evidence, then treated that as her verdict. She asked for the quilts to be reassessed, which means she thinks the attribution is unproven, not that it's wrong.

B.why: This turns her comparison around. She is replacing fabric evidence with stitch evidence, so she must rank stitching higher.

D.why: Look at 'identical' and 'every.' Her method only needs one maker's stitches to vary less than different makers' stitches do. Perfect consistency is far more than she needs to assume.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Because a tale about a drowned church bell is told in nearly identical form in dozens of Baltic coastal villages, folklorists long assumed that its versions descend through oral retelling from a single medieval original. When folklorist Aino Repo recorded the tale in 2019, she asked each teller not only from whom they had learned it but also whether they had ever read it in an 1871 anthology once sold widely along that coast. Repo's questions suggest that she thought ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the tale had not been told in the coastal villages at all before the 1871 anthology carried it into wide circulation.
the close agreement among the villages' versions might stem partly from a shared printed source, not from oral descent alone.
the anthology's compiler had probably assembled the printed text from versions told in those same coastal villages.
tellers who had read the anthology would tell the tale less faithfully than those who learned it only by ear.
items.explanation: The old view uses the near-identical versions as evidence of oral descent from one original. Repo asks about a widely sold book, which matters only if the book could explain some of that sameness. B gives that possibility with the right limits: 'might,' 'partly,' and 'not from oral descent alone.' It doesn't deny that the tale was ever passed on orally.

A.why: You took 'the book may have spread it' and turned it into 'the book started it.' She also asked whom each teller learned it from, which shows she still expected some oral transmission.

C.why: This turns the direction of influence around. Her question tests whether the book shaped the tellers, not whether the tellers shaped the book. If the book only copied village versions, asking about it wouldn't challenge the older view.

D.why: Her questions are about where the shared form came from, not about which tellers are more faithful. 'Faithful' to what? The passage gives you no standard for making that comparison.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: The seismic hazard map for the city of Tarvel is based on the 150 years of earthquakes recorded by instruments and in written accounts, none stronger than magnitude 5.8. Seismologist Delia Moretti has recommended that the map be revised to incorporate excavations across the region's faults, where layers of offset sediment preserve evidence of ruptures thousands of years old. Moretti's recommendation implies that she believes ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the 150-year record exaggerates Tarvel's hazard by including moderate earthquakes that the prehistoric ruptures show to be rare.
an earthquake stronger than magnitude 5.8 is likely to strike Tarvel sooner than the current hazard map would predict.
the instrument records and written accounts are too unreliable to contribute anything to an accurate hazard map.
the region's largest earthquakes may occur too rarely to appear in 150 years of records, so the map could understate the hazard.
items.explanation: Why would anyone add evidence thousands of years old to a map built on 150 years? Because some events may happen less often than once in 150 years, so the current record could miss them. The record tops out at 5.8, so missing those events would make the map too low. D gives that reason and keeps the hedges 'may' and 'could.'

A.why: This reverses the direction of the error. She is reaching back in time for events the recent record leaves out, which would raise the estimated hazard, not lower it.

B.why: You correctly read 'the map may be too low' and then added timing. A longer record tells you what is possible, not when it will happen. Nothing she recommends predicts that a large earthquake is coming soon.

C.why: She asked for the excavations to be incorporated, meaning added to the existing record, not substituted for it. She thinks the record is too short, not that it is worthless.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: At the Neolithic site of Kerem Tal, flint sickle blades become roughly four times as common in layers dated after 7000 BCE, a change often cited as the start of intensive cereal farming there. Yet charred cereal grains in those same layers occur no more often than before. Archaeologist Ruth Adeyemi has begun examining the blades under a microscope for wear patterns that indicate which kinds of plants they cut, suggesting that in her view ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the rise in sickle blades might reflect more cutting of plants other than cereals rather than more cereal harvesting.
the blades were used chiefly for cutting reeds and wild grasses, so cereal farming at the site remained minor.
the charred grains preserved in those layers probably undercount how much cereal the site's residents ate.
a rise in cereal farming at the site after 7000 BCE led its residents to need many more flint blades.
items.explanation: The evidence splits: sickles rose, but cereal grains stayed flat. Adeyemi chose to check what the sickles cut. That makes sense only if she thought the blades might have been used on something besides cereal. A states that possibility and keeps it a possibility.

B.why: You found the right suspicion and then answered it before she did. She has just begun examining the blades, so she is testing whether they cut other plants. She hasn't concluded that they mostly did, or that farming was minor.

C.why: This would explain the split in a different way, but her action doesn't depend on it. If she thought the grain counts were the problem, she would study how grain is preserved, not wear on the blades.

D.why: This is the popular view that the flat grain counts undercut. Her test exists because she doubts that more sickles means more cereal farming, so choosing it gives her the opposite of her view.

items.subtype_name: The logical upshot (Ultimately / Then / In the end)
items.stimulus: In Edo-period Japan, a woodblock print passed through three specialists before it was sold. A designer drew the image in ink on thin paper. A carver pasted that drawing onto a cherry block and cut away everything but the lines, making a separate block for each color. items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A musicologist compares two tuning schemes for a set of bell chimes. In the system below, $x$ is the number of chimes tuned by the first scheme and $y$ is the number tuned by the second.

$3x + 2y = 10$
$6x + 4y = k$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: For infinitely many solutions, the second equation must be a constant multiple of the first. The $x$-coefficient goes from $3$ to $6$ and the $y$-coefficient goes from $2$ to $4$, so every term is multiplied by $2$. The constant has to double as well: $k = 2(10) = 20$. That makes both equations describe the same line.

A.why: You saw that the factor is $2$ but divided $10$ by $2$ instead of multiplying. With $k = 5$ the lines are parallel, not the same line.

B.why: You matched the slopes and left the constant at $10$. The constant has to scale by $2$ too. With $k = 10$, the system $6x + 4y = 10$ is parallel to the first line, so it has no solution.

C.why: You added $3$ to the constant because $6 - 3 = 3$. Equivalent equations come from multiplying every term by the same number, not adding to it.

items.stimulus:
A nutrition scientist designs a snack mix from two ingredients. In the system below, $x$ and $y$ are the grams of each ingredient, and each equation tracks grams of fiber.

$4x + 6y = 18$
$2x + 3y = k$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: The $x$-coefficient goes from $4$ to $2$ and the $y$-coefficient goes from $6$ to $3$, so every term is divided by $2$. The constant also has to be halved: $k = \frac{18}{2} = 9$. Then both equations describe the same line.

A.why: You divided $18$ by $3$, the $y$-coefficient of the second equation, instead of by the scale factor $2$. With $k = 6$, the lines are parallel.

C.why: You saw that the slopes match and kept the constant at $18$. The constant must be halved like the coefficients. With $k = 18$, the lines are parallel and the system has no solution.

D.why: You multiplied $18$ by $2$ instead of dividing. The coefficients get smaller from the first equation to the second, so the constant has to get smaller too.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A civil engineer checking the load on a footbridge beam writes this system, where $x$ and $y$ are forces in kilonewtons.
$3x + 2y = 12$
$6x + 4y = k$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: For infinitely many solutions, the second equation has to be a constant multiple of the first. The x-coefficient goes from 3 to 6 and the y-coefficient goes from 2 to 4, so the multiplier is 2. The constant has to double as well: $k = 2 \times 12 = 24$. Then $6x + 4y = 24$ is the same line as $3x + 2y = 12$.

A.why: You found the multiplier, 2, and stopped there. You still have to apply it to the constant 12 to get k.

B.why: You matched the coefficients but left the constant at 12. The line $6x + 4y = 12$ has the same slope with a different intercept, so the lines are parallel and the system has no solution.

D.why: You multiplied 12 by the y-coefficient 4 instead of by the ratio between the two equations, which is 2.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
An archaeologist models the relationship between two layers of finds at a dig site with this system.
$y = 4x + 5$
$2y = 8x + c$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $c$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $c$?
items.explanation: Multiply the first equation by 2 and you get $2y = 8x + 10$. The second equation is the same line only if its constant is also 10, so $c = 10$.

A.why: You doubled the 5 but flipped its sign along the way. Doubling $+5$ gives $+10$.

B.why: You saw that the slopes already match and copied the constant without doubling it. The line $2y = 8x + 5$ is $y = 4x + 2.5$, which runs parallel to the first line, so the system has no solution.

C.why: You picked the x-coefficient of the second equation. The question asks for the constant term c.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus: A linguist relates two counts from a sample of recorded speech with the equation $x + 3y = 7$.
items.stem: Which equation, together with the given equation, forms a system of two linear equations that has infinitely many solutions?
items.explanation: Infinitely many solutions means both equations describe the same line, so every term has to be multiplied by the same number. Multiply $x + 3y = 7$ by 2 and you get $2x + 6y = 14$.

A.why: You doubled the x- and y-coefficients but not the constant. This line has the same slope and a different intercept, so it is parallel to the given line and the system has no solution.

C.why: You swapped the two coefficients and then scaled the constant. The slope is now $-3$ instead of $-\frac{1}{3}$, so the lines cross at exactly one point.

D.why: Changing the sign of the y-term changes the sign of the slope. The two lines cross at one point and are not the same line.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus: A public health analyst links two measures from a vaccination survey with the equation $2x - y = 5$.
items.stem: Which equation, together with the given equation, forms a system of two linear equations that has at least one solution?
items.explanation: "At least one solution" includes lines that cross, not only lines that are the same. The given line is $y = 2x - 5$, with slope 2. The line $x + y = 4$ has slope $-1$, so the two lines cross. They meet at $(3, 1)$. Every other choice has slope 2 and a different intercept, which makes it parallel.

A.why: This line has the same slope, 2, but its intercept is $-1$, not $-5$. Parallel lines never meet, so the system has no solution.

B.why: You doubled the x- and y-coefficients but not the constant. That gives a parallel line, not the same line. You may also have ruled out $x + y = 4$ because you thought only an identical line counts.

D.why: You changed the sign of the left side but not the right. This is $y = 2x + 5$, which is parallel to $y = 2x - 5$, so the system has no solution.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A textile historian compares the thread counts of two woven fragments using this system.
$y = 3x + 2$
$6x - 2y = c$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $c$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $c$?
items.explanation: Write the first equation in the same form as the second: $3x - y = -2$. Multiply by 2 to match the x-coefficient 6, which gives $6x - 2y = -4$. For the two to be the same line, $c = -4$.

B.why: You copied the intercept 2 as the constant without rearranging or scaling. That gives $y = 3x - 1$, a parallel line, so the system has no solution.

C.why: You scaled correctly but lost the negative sign when you moved $y$ to the left side. $3x - y = -2$, so the doubled constant is $-4$.

D.why: You picked the x-coefficient of the second equation. The question asks for its constant term.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stem: Which equation has the same graph as $2x + 3y = 7$?
items.explanation: Two equations give the same line when one is the other multiplied by a single number. Multiply every term of $2x + 3y = 7$ by 2: $4x + 6y = 14$. The $x$-coefficient, the $y$-coefficient and the constant are all doubled, so the ratio is the same everywhere. This is the check you need on SAT questions that say a system has infinitely many solutions: two equations that are really one line.

B.why: You doubled the $x$ and $y$ coefficients but left the constant at 7. The slopes match, but the intercepts don't, so this is a parallel line that never meets the first. That gives no solution, not infinitely many.

C.why: You swapped the coefficients of $x$ and $y$. That changes the slope from $-\tfrac{2}{3}$ to $-\tfrac{3}{2}$, so it is a different line that crosses the first one.

D.why: You multiplied the coefficients by 3 but the constant by 2. Every term has to be multiplied by the same number, or you get a different line.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stem: The equations $3x + 2y = 5$ and $6x + 4y = c$ have the same graph. What is the value of $c$?
items.explanation: Compare the coefficients: $6 \div 3 = 2$ and $4 \div 2 = 2$, so the second equation is the first multiplied by 2. The constant must also be multiplied by 2: $c = 5 \times 2 = 10$. Finding a missing constant like this is the main step in SAT questions that say a system has infinitely many solutions and ask for a value.

B.why: You saw the coefficients already matched in ratio and kept the constant as it was. With $c = 5$ the slopes are equal but the lines are parallel. That is no solution, not the same line.

C.why: 2 is the multiplier, not the constant. You found the scale factor and stopped before applying it to the 5.

D.why: You multiplied the constant by 3, maybe because 3 was the first coefficient you saw. The scale factor between the equations is 2, so $5 \times 2 = 10$.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stem: Which system of equations has infinitely many solutions?
items.explanation: In $2x + 4y = 8$, each term is twice the matching term in $x + 2y = 4$: $2 = 2 \times 1$, $4 = 2 \times 2$, $8 = 2 \times 4$. Both equations describe the same line, so every point on it is a solution. Checking whether all three ratios agree is the step that opens up SAT questions about infinitely many solutions.

B.why: Both coefficients are doubled but the constant is not, so the slopes match and the intercepts don't. These are parallel lines with no solution.

C.why: Only the $x$-coefficient and the constant are doubled. The $y$-coefficient stays at 2, so the slopes differ and the lines cross at exactly one point.

D.why: The $x$-coefficient was multiplied by 4 and the $y$-coefficient by 1, so the terms got mixed up. The ratios don't agree, so these lines cross once.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A nutrition scientist writes two equations relating $x$, the grams of carbohydrate in a snack bar, and $y$, the grams of fiber. The equations are

$\frac{3}{4}x - \frac{1}{2}y = 6$

$ax - 4y = b$

In this system, $a$ and $b$ are constants. The system has infinitely many solutions.
items.stem: What is the value of $a + b$?
items.explanation: If the system has infinitely many solutions, the two equations describe the same line. That means the second equation is a constant multiple of the first. Compare the $y$-coefficients: $-\frac{1}{2}$ becomes $-4$ when you multiply by 8. Multiply the whole first equation by 8, including the constant: $6x - 4y = 48$. So $a = 6$ and $b = 48$, and $a + b = 54$. You can check this in Desmos: graph both equations with sliders for $a$ and $b$, and the lines lie on top of each other only when $a = 6$ and $b = 48$.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
For a folklore studies project, a student builds a model of how often two motifs appear across a collection of tales. The model uses this system of equations, where $k$ is a constant:

$kx + 6y = 15$

$2x + (k - 4)y = 5$

The system has infinitely many solutions.
items.stem: What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Infinitely many solutions means one equation is a constant multiple of the other. The $x$-coefficients, the $y$-coefficients and the constants must all be in the same ratio. The constants are fully known, so start there: $\frac{15}{5} = 3$. Then $\frac{k}{2} = 3$ gives $k = 6$. Check the $y$-coefficients: $\frac{6}{k - 4} = \frac{6}{2} = 3$. That matches. If you match only the slopes by solving $\frac{k}{2} = \frac{6}{k-4}$, you get $k^2 - 4k - 12 = 0$, so $k = 6$ or $k = -2$. But $k = -2$ gives $-2x + 6y = 15$ and $2x - 6y = 5$. Their coefficients are in the ratio $-1$ and their constants are in the ratio $3$, so those lines are parallel and have no solution. In Desmos, put a slider on $k$: at $k = -2$ the lines are parallel, and at $k = 6$ they coincide.

items.stimulus:
A linguist models a relationship between $x$, the number of loanwords, and $y$, the number of native words, in a set of short text samples. Two different methods give these equations, where $c$ is a constant:

$\frac{x}{3} + \frac{y}{4} = c$

$8x + 6y = 36$

items.stem: What is the value of $c$?
items.explanation: For infinitely many solutions, the first equation must be a constant multiple of the second. Multiply the whole first equation by 24, constant included: $8x + 6y = 24c$. Set this equal to the second equation's constant: $24c = 36$, so $c = \frac{3}{2}$. Be careful: clearing fractions with the least common denominator, 12, gives $4x + 3y = 12c$. That is only half of the second equation, not the same equation.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A printmaker mixes $x$ ounces of black ink and $y$ ounces of extender for a relief print. Two recipe constraints are written as the following system, where $a$ and $b$ are constants:

$(a - 3)x + 15y = 30$

$2x + by = 6$

The system has infinitely many solutions.
items.stem: What is the value of $a + b$?
items.explanation: Infinitely many solutions means the first equation is a constant multiple of the second, so every pair of matching terms is in the same ratio. The constants are both known: $\frac{30}{6} = 5$. So the first equation is 5 times the second. From the $y$-terms, $15 = 5b$, so $b = 3$. From the $x$-terms, $a - 3 = 5 \cdot 2 = 10$, so $a = 13$. Then $a + b = 16$. Check: $10x + 15y = 30$ is exactly 5 times $2x + 3y = 6$. Same line does not mean equal coefficients. It means proportional coefficients and a proportional constant.

Found $a - 3 = 10$ but reported $a = 10$ by dropping the $-3$, then added $b = 3$.
Stopped at $a - 3 = 10$ and entered 10.
Entered the scale factor 5 between the equations instead of finishing for $a$ and $b$.

C.why: You answered the opposite question, which values of $k$ give no solution. No value does, but this question asks when there is at least one solution, and that is true for every $k$.

items.stimulus:
A musicologist relates $x$, the number of bars in a passage, and $y$, its tempo marking, using two equations taken from separate catalogues of the same composer's work.

items.stem:
In the given system of equations, $p$, $q$, and $r$ are constants. If the system has infinitely many solutions, which of the following must be true?

I. $q = -\frac{p}{3}$
II. $r = 4$
items.explanation: Infinitely many solutions means the second equation is the first multiplied by some nonzero number $t$. So $p = 3t$, $q = -t$, and $r = 4t$. Statement I always holds, because $-\frac{p}{3} = -t = q$. Statement II holds only when $t = 1$. For example, $6x - 2y = 8$ is the same line with $r = 8$. Only statement I must be true.

B.why: You made a sign error with the slope. The line $3x - y = 4$ has slope $3$, and matching that requires $q = -\frac{p}{3}$, not $q = \frac{p}{3}$. Statement I is true, and statement II is not required.

C.why: You assumed the second equation must have the same constant as the first. The constants only need to be in the same ratio as the coefficients, so $r = 4t$ for any nonzero $t$, not necessarily $4$.

D.why: You treated infinitely many solutions as two lines crossing, so you expected different slopes and rejected I. Identical lines must have the same slope, which is exactly what statement I says.

Compare the x-coefficients: $\frac{10}{4} = \frac{5}{2}$. The y-coefficients agree, because $6 \cdot \frac{5}{2} = 15$. The constant must be scaled by the same factor, so $c = 10 \cdot \frac{5}{2} = 25$. To check, divide $10x + 15y = 25$ by $\frac{5}{2}$ and you get $4x + 6y = 10$, the first equation.

A.why: You correctly found that the second equation is $\frac{5}{2}$ times the first, then stopped and gave that scale factor as your answer. You still have to multiply the constant 10 by $\frac{5}{2}$ to get $c$.

B.why: You saw that the slopes already match and kept the constant at 10. With $c = 10$ the lines are parallel and separate, so the system has no solution. For the lines to be identical, the constants must be in the same $\frac{5}{2}$ ratio as the coefficients.

C.why: You noticed the x-coefficient went from 4 to 10, so you added 6 to the constant: $10 + 6 = 16$. The coefficients are related by multiplication, not addition, so the constant must also be multiplied by $\frac{5}{2}$.

items.stimulus:
A marine biologist feeds a rescued seal $x$ buckets of herring and $y$ buckets of mackerel. A bucket of herring holds 2 kilograms and a bucket of mackerel holds 3 kilograms. The day's feeding totals 18 kilograms. An assistant logs the same feeding in grams.

$2x + 3y = 18$
$2{,}000x + 3{,}000y = k$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: For infinitely many solutions, the second equation has to be a constant multiple of the first. Here every term is multiplied by the same number. The $x$-coefficient goes from 2 to 2,000, so the multiplier is 1,000. The constant must also be multiplied by 1,000, so $k = 18 \times 1{,}000 = 18{,}000$. In the story, $k$ is the same 18 kilograms written as grams.

A.why: You matched the coefficients but left the constant unscaled. With $k = 18$, the lines have the same slope and different intercepts, so they are parallel and the system has no solution. In the story, that is the right total in the wrong units.

B.why: 1,000 is the multiplier between the two equations. You found it, but you still needed to apply it to the constant 18.

C.why: You multiplied 18 by 100 instead of by 1,000. Compare the $x$-coefficients again: 2 becomes 2,000, so the factor is 1,000.

An immunology lab runs $x$ antibody assays of type A and $y$ assays of type B. Each type A assay uses 4 microliters of serum, and each type B assay uses 6 microliters. The lab uses 120 microliters in total. A technician records the same serum budget using a different measuring unit.

items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: For infinitely many solutions, the $x$-coefficients, the $y$-coefficients, and the constants must all be in the same ratio. Both $\frac{10}{4}$ and $\frac{300}{120}$ equal 2.5, so the $y$-coefficient must also be multiplied by 2.5. That gives $k = 6 \times 2.5 = 15$.

B.why: You copied the $y$-coefficient without scaling it. With $k = 6$, the slopes are different, so the lines cross at exactly one point instead of being the same line.

D.why: You multiplied 6 by the $x$-coefficient 4 instead of by the ratio $\frac{10}{4} = 2.5$.

A textile historian studies an 18th-century weaver's ledger. In the ledger, $x$ is the number of yards of linen and $y$ is the number of yards of wool bought at a market. Linen cost 3 shillings per yard, wool cost 4 shillings per yard, and the purchase came to 24 shillings.

items.stem: One of the two equations in a system of linear equations is given. The system has infinitely many solutions. Which of the following could be the second equation in this system?
items.explanation: A system has infinitely many solutions when the second equation is the first one multiplied by a constant. Multiplying every term of $3x + 4y = 24$ by 2 gives $6x + 8y = 48$, which is the same line. You can check this in Desmos: graph both equations and they sit exactly on top of each other.

A.why: You doubled the coefficients but not the constant. This line has the same slope and a different intercept, so it is parallel to the given line and the system has no solution.

B.why: You swapped the linen and wool prices, which attaches the coefficients to the wrong variables. This line has a different slope, so it crosses the given line at only one point.

D.why: You changed the sign of the $y$-term, which flips the sign of the slope. The two lines then cross at exactly one point instead of coinciding.

items.stimulus:
A meteorologist relates rainfall $x$, in millimeters, at one station to rainfall $y$, in millimeters, at a second station using two models.

$3x - 2y = 8$
$ax - 6y = b$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $a$ and $b$ are constants. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $b - a$?
items.explanation: If there are infinitely many solutions, the second equation is a constant multiple of the first. The $y$-coefficients are $-2$ and $-6$, so the multiplier is $3$. The second equation must be $9x - 6y = 24$, which gives $a = 9$ and $b = 24$. So $b - a = 24 - 9 = 15$.

A.why: You multiplied the $x$-coefficient by 3 to get $a = 9$ but left the constant at 8, so you found $8 - 9 = -1$. With $b = 8$ the lines are parallel, not the same line. The constant has to be multiplied by 3 as well.

C.why: You found $b = 24$ correctly and stopped there. The question asks how much greater $b$ is than $a$, so you still have to subtract $a = 9$.

D.why: You found $a = 9$ and $b = 24$ correctly but added them instead of subtracting. $b - a$ is the difference, $24 - 9$.

items.stimulus:
A linguist relates $x$, the number of syllables in a word, to $y$, the time in tenths of a second needed to say it, in two ways.

items.stem: In the given system of equations, $p$ and $c$ are constants. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $p - c$?
items.explanation: Put the first equation in the same form as the second: $4x - y = -5$. Infinitely many solutions means the second equation is a multiple of this one. The $y$-coefficients go from $-1$ to $-3$, so multiply everything by 3: $12x - 3y = -15$. That gives $p = 12$ and $c = -15$, so $p - c = 12 - (-15) = 27$.

A.why: When you moved the terms to get $4x - y = -5$, you kept the constant positive and wrote $4x - y = 5$. That made $c = 15$, and $12 - 15 = -3$. Moving $5$ across the equals sign changes its sign.

B.why: You found $p = 12$ and gave that as the answer. The question asks for the gap $p - c$, so you also need $c = -15$.

C.why: You multiplied the coefficients by 3 but left the constant as $-5$, so you got $12 - (-5) = 17$. Those lines have the same slope but different intercepts, which means they are parallel. The constant has to be multiplied by 3 too.

A marine biologist mixes $x$ grams of brine shrimp and $y$ grams of mysis shrimp to feed captive seahorses. She records two conditions on the mix.

items.explanation: Infinitely many solutions means the two equations describe the same line, so one must be a constant multiple of the other. Multiplying the first equation by $12$ turns $\frac{3}{4}x$ into $9x$ and $\frac{5}{6}y$ into $10y$. The constant has to be multiplied by $12$ too, so $k = 12 \cdot 7 = 84$. A.why: You saw that the slopes already match and kept the constant at $7$. With $k = 7$ the second equation becomes $\frac{3}{4}x + \frac{5}{6}y = \frac{7}{12}$, which has the same slope but a different intercept. The lines are parallel, so the system has no solution, not infinitely many.

B.why: $12$ is the number you multiply the first equation by to get the second equation's coefficients. The question asks for the new constant, which is $12 \cdot 7$, not the multiplier itself.

C.why: You cleared the fractions with $6$ instead of $12$. Multiplying by $6$ gives $\frac{9}{2}x + 5y = 42$, and those coefficients don't match $9x + 10y$. You need to multiply everything, including the constant, by $12$.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A marine biologist uses the system below to relate two measurements, $x$ and $y$, taken at a coral reef monitoring site.

$kx + 4y = 6$
$x + ky = k + 1$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Infinitely many solutions means the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. The x-coefficients, the y-coefficients and the constants must all be in the same ratio: $\frac{k}{1} = \frac{4}{k} = \frac{6}{k+1}$. The first two parts give $k^2 = 4$, so $k = 2$ or $k = -2$. Now test each value against the constants. If $k = 2$, the second equation is $x + 2y = 3$, and multiplying it by 2 gives $2x + 4y = 6$, which is the first equation, so the two equations describe the same line. If $k = -2$, the second equation is $x - 2y = -1$, and multiplying it by $-2$ gives $-2x + 4y = 2$. The first equation is $-2x + 4y = 6$, so the lines are parallel and there is no solution. The only value is $k = 2$.

A.why: You set the constant ratio equal to the x-coefficient ratio, $\frac{6}{k+1} = k$, which gives $k^2 + k - 6 = 0$ and so $k = 2$ or $k = -3$. Then you kept $-3$ without checking the slopes. When $k = -3$ the slopes are $\frac{3}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{3}$, so the lines cross at exactly one point.

B.why: You matched the slopes ($k^2 = 4$) but never checked the constants. When $k = -2$ the equations become $-2x + 4y = 6$ and $-2x + 4y = 2$. Those lines have the same slope but different intercepts, so they are parallel and the system has no solution.

D.why: You set up $\frac{k}{1} = \frac{4}{k}$ but solved it as $k = 4$ instead of cross-multiplying to get $k^2 = 4$. When $k = 4$ the slopes are $-1$ and $-\frac{1}{4}$, so the lines intersect once.

items.stimulus:
A textile historian models the weekly output of a nineteenth-century mill, where $x$ is the number of bolts of linen and $y$ is the number of bolts of cotton.

$2x - 5y = 10$
$px - 10y = q$
items.stem:
In the given system of equations, $p$ and $q$ are constants. If the system has at least one solution, which of the following must be true?

I. $p = 4$
II. If $p = 4$, then $q = 20$.
items.explanation: Multiply the first equation by 2 so that the y-coefficients match: $4x - 10y = 20$. If $p \neq 4$, the slopes are different, so the lines cross and the system has exactly one solution, which counts as at least one. That means $p$ does not have to be 4, so statement I is false. If $p = 4$, the slopes are equal, so the system has a solution only if the lines are the same line. That requires the constants to be in the same ratio, so $q = 20$. Statement II must be true. Only II must be true.

A.why: You treated matching slopes as enough, so you required $p = 4$ and assumed $q$ could be anything. Same slope with a different constant gives parallel lines and no solution, so when $p = 4$ the value of $q$ is forced. You also missed that a different slope, which gives intersecting lines, also counts as at least one solution.

C.why: You assumed that at least one solution means the two equations must be the same line, so you decided $p$ has to be 4. Any $p \neq 4$ gives lines that cross at one point, and that is also at least one solution.

D.why: You correctly saw that intersecting lines count, which rules out I. But you matched the slopes without scaling the constant, and decided $q$ should be 10. That made statement II look false. Doubling the whole first equation turns 10 into 20, so II is true.

items.stem: In the given system of equations, $a$ and $b$ are constants. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $a + b$?

I. If $c = 24$, the system has at least one solution for every value of $k$.
II. If $k = -2$, the system has at least one solution for every value of $c$.
items.explanation: Statement I: when $c = 24$, the second equation divided by 2 is $3x - 2y = 12$. If $k = -2$, the two equations are identical, so there are infinitely many solutions. If $k \neq -2$, the slopes are different, so the lines cross once. Either way there is at least one solution, so I is true. Statement II: when $k = -2$, the slopes match. But if $c \neq 24$, the constants are out of ratio, so the lines are parallel and there is no solution. II is false.

B.why: You reversed the two cases. Fixing $k = -2$ only fixes the slope, which still allows parallel lines. Fixing $c = 24$ guarantees that every $k$ gives either the same line or a crossing line.

C.why: For II, you saw that $k = -2$ makes the slopes equal and assumed the lines coincide. Equal slopes with $c \neq 24$ give parallel lines and no solution.

D.why: You ruled out I because only $k = -2$ makes the lines identical. 'At least one solution' also counts a single crossing point, which every other $k$ gives.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A linguist models the relationship between two word-frequency measures with the equation below.
$3(y + 4) = 2x$
items.stem: One of the two equations in a linear system is given. The system has infinitely many solutions. Which of the following could be the second equation in this system?
items.explanation: Expand to get $3y + 12 = 2x$, so the given line is $2x - 3y = 12$. A second equation gives infinitely many solutions only if it is a constant multiple of this one. Multiplying by 3 gives $6x - 9y = 36$, so the two equations describe the same line.

A.why: You saw the slope $\frac{2}{3}$ and the intercept $-4$, then wrote $2x - 3y = 4$. This line has the right slope but its constant is not in the same ratio, so it is parallel to the given line and the system has no solution.

C.why: You flipped the sign of the constant when you moved 12 across. This line, $y = \frac{2}{3}x + 4$, is parallel to the given line and never meets it.

D.why: You swapped the $x$- and $y$-coefficients. This line has slope $\frac{3}{2}$, not $\frac{2}{3}$, so it crosses the given line at exactly one point.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A public health analyst compares two clinic staffing plans using the system below.
$kx + 4y = 8$
$9x + ky = 12$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: The coefficients must be proportional, so $\frac{k}{9} = \frac{4}{k}$. That gives $k^2 = 36$, so $k = 6$ or $k = -6$. The constants must also be in the same ratio, $\frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}$. For $k = 6$: $\frac{6}{9} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$, which works. For $k = -6$: $\frac{-6}{9} = -\frac{2}{3}$, which doesn't match the constant ratio. Only $k = 6$ works.

A.why: $-6$ makes the coefficients proportional, but the coefficient ratio becomes $-\frac{2}{3}$ while the constant ratio is $\frac{2}{3}$. The lines are parallel, so there is no solution. You needed to check the constants as well.

C.why: You set $\frac{k}{9}$ equal to $\frac{12}{8}$, the constant ratio turned upside down. The ratio has to compare the first equation to the second: $\frac{8}{12}$.

D.why: $36$ is $k^2$. You stopped before taking the square root and checking which root also fits the constants.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A meteorologist relates two pressure readings with the system below.
$3x + ky = 10$
$-6x + 10y = c$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ and $c$ are constants. If the system has infinitely many solutions, which of the following ordered pairs $(x, y)$ is a solution to the system for each real number $t$?
items.explanation: The second equation must be $-2$ times the first. From the $x$-coefficients, $3 \times -2 = -6$. From the $y$-coefficients, $k \times -2 = 10$, so $k = -5$. The constants then give $c = -20$. The shared line is $3x - 5y = 10$, which rearranges to $y = \frac{3x - 10}{5}$. Put in $x = t$: the pair $\left(t, \frac{3t - 10}{5}\right)$ satisfies both equations for every $t$.

A.why: This pair lies on $3x - 5y = -10$. That line has the right slope but the wrong constant, so it is parallel to the shared line and never on it.

B.why: You got the sign of $k$ wrong and used $k = 5$. The line $3x + 5y = 10$ has the opposite slope, so it meets the shared line only once.

C.why: You set $k$ equal to the second equation's $y$-coefficient, 10, instead of scaling by $-2$. The line $3x - 10y = 10$ is not the line given by the second equation.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus: A textile historian studies a workshop ledger in which $x$ is the number of linen bolts woven and $y$ is the number of wool bolts woven. Each linen bolt took 4 days and each wool bolt took 5 days, for 100 days in total. A second record gives $ax + 20y = b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants.
items.stem: If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $a + b$?
items.explanation: Name the variables first: $x$ is linen bolts and $y$ is wool bolts. The time total gives $4x + 5y = 100$. For infinitely many solutions, the second equation must be a multiple of this one. Since $20 \div 5 = 4$, multiply every term by 4: $16x + 20y = 400$. So $a = 16$, $b = 400$, and $a + b = 416$.

A.why: You scaled the coefficient to get $a = 16$ but left the total at 100. The equation $16x + 20y = 100$ is parallel to the first line, so the system would have no solution. The constant must also be multiplied by 4.

B.why: $400$ is $b$ alone. You still needed to add $a = 16$.

D.why: You attached 5 days to linen and 4 days to wool, which gives $5x + 4y = 100$. Then the factor is 5, so $a = 25$ and $b = 500$. Each number belongs to the variable it describes.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
An ecologist relates the populations of two plant species in a meadow with the system below.
$ax + 3y = 7$
$6y = 14 - 4x$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $a$ is a constant. Which of the following statements is true?
choices: There is exactly one value of $a$ for which the system has no solution.
The system has exactly one solution for every value of $a$.
The system has at least one solution only when $a = 2$.
The system has at least one solution for every value of $a$.
items.explanation: Rearrange the second equation to $4x + 6y = 14$, then divide by 2: $2x + 3y = 7$. When $a = 2$, the two equations are identical, so the system has infinitely many solutions. For any other $a$, the slopes differ, so the lines cross at exactly one point. No value of $a$ makes the lines parallel, so the system always has at least one solution.

A.why: You saw that $a = 2$ gives equal slopes and decided the lines are parallel. Both lines also have the same $y$-intercept, $\frac{7}{3}$, so they are the same line, not parallel.

B.why: This misses $a = 2$. At that value the two equations describe one line, so there are infinitely many solutions, not exactly one.

C.why: You counted only the identical-line case. Every other $a$ gives intersecting lines, which still means at least one solution.

items.stimulus:
A labor economist relates weekly overtime hours, $x$, and training hours, $y$, with the system below.
$\frac{x}{3} - \frac{y}{2} = k$
$4x - 6y = k + 33$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Multiply the first equation by 6 to clear the fractions: $2x - 3y = 6k$. The second equation is exactly twice this on the left side, so its constant must be twice $6k$: $12k = k + 33$. That gives $11k = 33$, so $k = 3$. Check: the first equation becomes $2x - 3y = 18$, and the second becomes $4x - 6y = 36$, which is the same line.

B.why: You treated $\frac{x}{3}$ as if its coefficient were 1. That gave a factor of 4 and the equation $4k = k + 33$. With that factor, the $y$-coefficients don't match, which would have shown the mistake.

C.why: You cleared the fractions on the left but didn't multiply $k$ by 6. That gave $2k = k + 33$. With $k = 33$, the constants are out of ratio and the lines are parallel, so there is no solution.

D.why: $36$ is the value of $k + 33$, the second equation's constant. The question asks for $k$.

items.explanation: Each coefficient is the price of one unit of the item its variable counts. One linocut print costs $12 dollars and one etching costs $19 dollars. To find how much more an etching costs, subtract in the order the question asks: $19 - 12 = 7$ dollars. You don't need to solve for $x$ or $y$.

C.why: You added the two prices, $12 + 19 = 31$. That is the cost of one of each. A 'how many more' question needs the difference, not the sum.

D.why: $380$ is the constant on the right side, so it is the weekend's total sales. It is not the price of any single print.

items.stimulus: A seismology team spent 72 hours installing sensors near a fault line. The equation $4x + 9y = 72$ represents this situation, where $x$ is the number of surface sensors installed and $y$ is the number of borehole sensors installed.
items.stem: How many more hours does it take to install one borehole sensor than one surface sensor?
items.explanation: Each coefficient is the number of hours needed to install one sensor of that type. A surface sensor takes $4$ hours and a borehole sensor takes $9$ hours. items.stimulus: A health department loads a truck with $x$ boxes of masks and $y$ boxes of gloves. The equation $3x + 5y = 120$ gives the total weight of the boxes, in kilograms.
items.stem: How many more kilograms does one box of gloves weigh than one box of masks?
items.explanation: Each coefficient is the weight of one box of the item its variable counts. A box of masks weighs 3 kilograms and a box of gloves weighs 5 kilograms. The question asks how much more the gloves weigh, so you subtract: $5 - 3 = 2$ kilograms. You don't need to solve for $x$ or $y$. This is the basic step behind every SAT question that asks what a number in a context equation means or how much more one item is worth than another.

B.why: 5 is the weight of one box of gloves on its own. The question asks how much more it weighs than a box of masks, so you still need to subtract the 3.

C.why: You added the two coefficients instead of subtracting them. $3 + 5$ is the weight of one box of each, not the difference between them.

D.why: 120 is the total weight of everything on the truck. The number on the other side of the equals sign is the total, not a per-box amount.

items.stimulus: An engineering lab buys $x$ kilograms of steel and $y$ kilograms of aluminum. The equation $7x + 4y = 280$ gives the total cost, in dollars.
items.stem: How many more dollars does 1 kilogram of steel cost than 1 kilogram of aluminum?
items.explanation: Each coefficient is the price of 1 kilogram of the metal its variable counts. Steel costs \$7 per kilogram and aluminum costs \$4 per kilogram. The question asks how much more steel costs, so you subtract: $7 - 4 = 3$ dollars. Being able to read the coefficients like this is what lets you answer SAT questions about what a number in a cost equation means.

B.why: 7 is the price of 1 kilogram of steel on its own. The question asks how much more it costs than aluminum, so you still need to subtract the 4.

C.why: You added $7 + 4$. That is the cost of 1 kilogram of each metal, not how much more one costs than the other.

D.why: You tried to solve the equation. You set $y = 0$ and found $x = 280 \div 7 = 40$, which is the number of kilograms of steel the budget could buy with no aluminum. The question never asked you to solve anything.

items.stem: What does the number 12 represent in this equation?

The number of type A racks in the freezer
The number of vials in one type B rack
The total number of vials in the freezer
items.explanation: A coefficient is the amount for one unit of the item its variable counts. The 12 multiplies $x$, and $x$ counts type A racks, so 12 is the number of vials in one type A rack. D.why: The total number of vials is 300, the constant on the other side of the equals sign. A coefficient is always a per-unit amount, never the total.

items.stimulus: A marine biologist counts $x$ octopuses and $y$ starfish in a tide pool. The equation $8x + 5y = 64$ gives the total number of arms counted.
items.stem: How many fewer arms does one starfish have than one octopus?
items.explanation: Each coefficient is the number of arms on one animal of the kind its variable counts. An octopus has 8 arms and a starfish has 5. A starfish has $8 - 5 = 3$ fewer arms. 'How many fewer' asks for a positive difference, so you subtract the smaller number from the larger one. You will need this step whenever an SAT question asks how much more or less one item is worth than another in an equation like $ax + by = c$.

B.why: You subtracted in the wrong order, $5 - 8$. The question already says 'fewer', so the answer is the positive gap, 3.

C.why: You added the coefficients. $8 + 5$ is the number of arms on one octopus and one starfish together, not the difference between them.

D.why: 64 is the total number of arms counted in the pool. The constant is the total, not an amount for one animal.

items.subtype_name: What does the coefficient mean
items.stimulus: At an excavation site, a volunteer pushes buckets of excavated soil through a mesh screen to recover small artifacts. Every bucket is either clay-rich or sandy. All clay-rich buckets take the same amount of time to screen, and so do all sandy buckets. The equation $\frac{x}{4} + \frac{y}{6} = 9$ models one week of the volunteer's work, where $x$ is the number of clay-rich buckets screened, $y$ is the number of sandy buckets screened, and 9 is the total number of hours spent screening.
items.stem: According to the equation, how many more hours does it take to screen one bucket of clay-rich soil than one bucket of sandy soil?
items.explanation: Rewrite each term so you can see its coefficient: $\frac{x}{4} = \frac{1}{4}x$ and $\frac{y}{6} = \frac{1}{6}y$. The coefficient is the hours needed for one bucket, so a clay-rich bucket takes $\frac{1}{4}$ hour and a sandy bucket takes $\frac{1}{6}$ hour. A larger denominator means less time, so the clay-rich bucket is the slower one. Subtract clay-rich minus sandy: $\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{3}{12} - \frac{2}{12} = \frac{1}{12}$ hour. The 9 is the week's total time, not a per-bucket amount.

items.stimulus: An ecologist studying seed dispersal in an oak woodland watches jays and squirrels bury acorns over one autumn. The equation $2(9x + 14y) = 1{,}260$ represents the situation, where $x$ is the number of jays observed, $y$ is the number of squirrels observed, and 1,260 is the total number of acorns cached by these animals.
items.stem: According to the equation, how many more acorns does one squirrel cache than one jay?
items.explanation: Distribute the 2 so each coefficient sits directly on its variable: $18x + 28y = 1{,}260$. One jay caches 18 acorns and one squirrel caches 28 acorns. So one squirrel caches $28 - 18 = 10$ more acorns than one jay.

items.stimulus: A wetland restoration crew has 30 hours of labor to spend planting native shrubs and tree saplings. items.stem: According to the equation, how many more minutes of labor does planting one sapling require than planting one shrub?
items.explanation: Each coefficient is the labor for one plant, in hours. A sapling takes 1.5 hours and a shrub takes 0.4 hours, so a sapling takes $1.5 - 0.4 = 1.1$ hours more. The question asks for minutes: $1.1 \times 60 = 66$ minutes.

items.subtype_name: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
items.stimulus: An astronomy student selected 60 asteroids at random from a catalog of 1,500 main-belt asteroids and looked up the diameter of each one. Based on the sample, the student estimated that the mean diameter of the asteroids in the catalog is 14 kilometers, with an associated margin of error of 3 kilometers.
items.stem: Based on these results, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: It is plausible that the mean diameter of all 1,500 asteroids in the catalog is between 11 and 17 kilometers.
It is plausible that every asteroid in the catalog has a diameter between 11 and 17 kilometers.
The mean diameter of all 1,500 asteroids in the catalog is exactly 14 kilometers.
The margin of error means the mean diameter of the 60 sampled asteroids could be anywhere from 11 to 17 kilometers.
items.explanation: You compute 14 − 3 = 11 and 14 + 3 = 17. The margin of error describes where the mean of the whole catalog plausibly falls, so a mean diameter between 11 and 17 kilometers for all 1,500 asteroids is the supported conclusion.

B.why: You applied the interval to individual asteroids. The margin of error is about the mean diameter, and single asteroids can be much larger or smaller than 11 to 17 kilometers.

C.why: You treated the estimate as exact. A margin of error of 3 kilometers means the true mean is uncertain, so 'exactly 14' claims more than the sample can show.

D.why: You applied the interval to the sample. The sample's mean is known: it is 14 kilometers. The interval estimates the mean of the whole catalog.

choices: Exactly 35% of all trees in the reserve have bark beetle damage.

It is plausible that between 31% and 39% of all trees in the state's forests have bark beetle damage.
items.explanation: You compute 35% − 4% = 31% and 35% + 4% = 39%. Because the trees were sampled only from the reserve, the supported conclusion is that between 31% and 39% of the reserve's trees plausibly have damage.

B.why: You read the margin of error as the share of trees that were misclassified. It actually measures the uncertainty from using a sample to estimate the percent for the whole reserve.

D.why: You extended the result beyond the population that was sampled. Only trees in the reserve were sampled, so the conclusion can't cover every forest in the state.
