items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: After a city banned smoking in restaurants and bars, emergency room visits for asthma attacks fell by 18 percent the following year, and city officials credited the ban. But three urgent care clinics opened in the city that same year. Clinics of this kind treat many mild asthma attacks that would otherwise be seen in emergency rooms. The drop in emergency room visits therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: proves that the clinics, not the ban, led residents to have fewer asthma attacks.
shows that the smoking ban had no measurable effect on residents' asthma rates.
might not mean that asthma attacks themselves became less common in the city.
indicates that the new clinics turned away residents who were having asthma attacks.
items.explanation: The complication is that the clinics may have drawn asthma patients away from emergency rooms. Fewer emergency room visits could mean the same number of attacks treated somewhere else. The passage only undermines the link between what was measured (emergency room visits) and what officials concluded (fewer attacks). The careful 'might not mean' is the only choice the passage supports.

A.why: You treated the clinics as a proven cause of fewer attacks. The passage says only that clinics change where attacks are treated, not how many happen, and it never rules the ban in or out.

B.why: You went from 'uncertain' to 'no effect.' The clinics make the evidence for the ban inconclusive, but they don't show that the ban did nothing.

D.why: The passage says the clinics treat many mild asthma attacks, which is the opposite of turning those patients away.

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: Some historians have used a 1760s survey map to argue that a coastal lagoon was once far smaller than it is now, because the map shows it covering only about a third of its present area. However, the surveyors charted this coast from a ship anchored well offshore. From that distance, the lagoon's shallow outer reaches would have been hard to see. The lagoon's size on the map therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: shows that the lagoon has grown to about three times its size in the 1760s.
suggests that the surveyors charted the shallow outer reaches with special care.
indicates that the lagoon was actually larger in the 1760s than it is today.
may not accurately reflect how large the lagoon really was in the 1760s.
items.explanation: The flaw is the viewing position. Surveyors on a ship far offshore could easily have missed the lagoon's shallow edges. That makes the map's outline unreliable as a record of the lagoon's real size in the 1760s. It doesn't establish a new size in either direction, so the cautious 'may not accurately reflect' is the supported completion.

A.why: This is the historians' original claim, and you took it at face value. The passage brings in the offshore viewpoint specifically to cast doubt on reading the map's outline as the true size.

B.why: The passage says the shallow outer reaches would have been hard to see from the ship, which is the opposite of charting them carefully.

C.why: You swapped one firm claim for its opposite. The map may have undercounted the lagoon's area, but nothing shows it was bigger than it is today.

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: Many ecologists credit sea otters with protecting kelp forests, because otters eat the sea urchins that graze on kelp. When otters returned to one Pacific reef, divers recorded a 60 percent drop in urchin numbers within a year. However, a marine heatwave struck the same coast that year, and such heatwaves are known to kill urchin larvae. No nearby reef without otters was surveyed for comparison. The divers' counts could therefore support each of the following claims EXCEPT that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: otters may have contributed to the reef's decline in urchins.
the heatwave, not the otters, caused the decline in urchins.
the decline cannot be credited to otters with full confidence.
urchin numbers on the reef fell over the period surveyed.
items.explanation: The heatwave is a second possible cause, and there was no reef without otters to compare against. That makes the cause of the decline uncertain. It doesn't show that the heatwave was the cause. Choice B swaps one firm cause for another, so it is the one claim the counts cannot support.

A.why: This claim is supported. Otters eat urchins, and the urchins declined after otters returned, so a contribution is possible. You found a true statement, but the question asks for the one the counts do NOT support.

C.why: 'Cannot' sounds absolute, so you may have marked it as going too far. But it only denies certainty, and the uncontrolled heatwave plus the missing comparison reef do exactly that. It stays within the evidence.

D.why: The divers directly recorded a 60 percent drop, so this is the most secure claim in the passage. It is supported, which makes it wrong for an EXCEPT question.

items.stimulus: A coastal chart drawn in 1794 shows a sandbar island about 2 kilometers long, and some historians cite it as proof that the island, now roughly 600 meters long, has shrunk dramatically. The surveyor's own notes, however, state that the island was sketched from the deck of a passing ship rather than measured on foot. Two centuries of storms have also reshaped the shoreline the chart used as its reference. The chart could therefore support each of the following claims EXCEPT that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: an island stood at roughly that location when the chart was drawn.
the island was once more than three times its present length.
the chart's figure of 2 kilometers may not reflect a true measurement.
how much the island has changed in size remains an open question.
items.explanation: The island was sketched from a ship, not measured, and the reference shoreline has since moved. Both facts make the 2-kilometer figure unreliable. Choice B treats that figure as exact (2 km is more than three times 600 m), so it states a firm fact the flawed chart can't support.

D.why: You may have read this as dismissing the historians too strongly. But the sketching method and the storm-altered shoreline do leave the size change unsettled, so the claim is supported.

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: Officials in a river town credit its new permeable pavement, which lets rainwater soak into the ground, with ending chronic street flooding. Reports of flooded streets fell by half in the two years after the pavement was installed. Those two years, however, brought below-average rainfall, and during the same period the town also cleared its long-clogged storm drains. The flood reports could therefore support each of the following claims EXCEPT that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the pavement may have played some part in the drop in reports.
lighter rainfall could account for some of the drop in reports.
fewer flooded streets were reported after the pavement went in.
clearing the storm drains did nothing to reduce street flooding.
items.explanation: Lighter rain and the cleared drains are two confounds, and both make the pavement's role uncertain. Nothing in the reports isolates the effect of the drains, so saying they had no effect is a firm claim the evidence can't support. Remember that a confound takes away certainty in both directions.

A.why: The confounds don't rule the pavement out. They only keep it from being proven. 'May have played some part' is supported, so it isn't the EXCEPT answer.

B.why: This can look like you're blaming the weather without evidence. But 'could account for some' is hedged, and the passage says rainfall was below average, so the claim is supported.

C.why: The passage says flood reports fell by half after installation. This is what was directly measured, so it is supported and can't be the answer.

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: In 2019 the town of Marlow raised its minimum wage, and neighbouring Ashby did not. Over the next year, restaurant employment fell by 1 percent in Marlow and by 6 percent in Ashby. Some economists said this gap showed that the higher wage had protected restaurant jobs. That same year, however, a large warehouse opened in Ashby. It paid well above either town's minimum wage and hired hundreds of workers away from local restaurants. The gap between the two towns' employment changes therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: may overstate how much the wage increase itself helped restaurant employment in Marlow.
shows that the wage increase had no effect at all on restaurant employment in Marlow.
indicates that restaurant employment fell more sharply in Marlow than it did in Ashby.
suggests that the warehouse's high wages were what led Marlow to raise its own minimum.
items.explanation: The problem here is a confound: the warehouse pulled workers out of Ashby's restaurants. That made Ashby's 6 percent drop bigger for a reason unrelated to Marlow's wage, which made the gap between the towns look bigger too. So the gap may make the wage increase look more helpful than it really was. That is the most the passage supports, and this choice says only that much.

B.why: You took a complication that removes certainty and treated it as proof of the opposite. The warehouse makes the comparison unreliable. It doesn't show that the wage had zero effect.

C.why: You mixed up the two towns. Marlow's employment fell by 1 percent and Ashby's by 6 percent, so the larger drop was in Ashby.

D.why: You latched onto the warehouse detail and invented a reason for Marlow's policy. The blank asks what the employment gap can show, not why Marlow raised its wage, and the warehouse opened the same year as the raise.

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: In a study of a new booster vaccine, participants who received the booster had, on average, four times the antibody levels of participants who did not. Most of the boosted participants, however, were hospital nurses who had volunteered through their workplace, and most of the unboosted participants were office workers. Repeated contact with infected patients can raise a person's antibody levels on its own. The fourfold difference between the two groups therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: demonstrates that the booster produced no measurable rise in participants' antibody levels.
indicates that the unboosted participants had higher average antibody levels than the boosted.
may not accurately reflect how much the booster alone raised participants' antibody levels.
confirms that the booster raises antibody levels by a factor of four in any adult who gets it.
items.explanation: The flaw is that the two groups differ in more than the booster. The nurses also had more contact with infected patients, and that contact can raise antibody levels by itself. So part of the fourfold gap could come from that exposure and not from the booster. The passage can only support saying the gap may not show the booster's own effect.

A.why: You swung from 'confounded' to 'disproved.' Patient contact might explain some of the gap, but nothing in the passage shows that the booster did nothing.

B.why: You reversed the comparison. The passage says the boosted participants had four times the antibody levels of the unboosted ones.

D.why: You accepted the result at face value and then applied it to every adult. The confound means the 'four times' figure is uncertain even for this sample, so it can't be extended to everyone.

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: Some music historians claim that the pianist Lena Haupt played Chopin's Berceuse about 20 percent faster in 1905 than in 1935. They base this on a comparison of her 1905 wax-cylinder recording with her 1935 disc. Cylinder machines of the early 1900s, however, ran at no standard speed, and no record survives of the speed at which Haupt's cylinder was made. Playing it back faster or slower than it was recorded changes the apparent tempo. The 20 percent difference between the two recordings therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: shows that Haupt actually played the piece more slowly in 1905 than she did in 1935.
might not reflect a real change in how quickly Haupt played the piece over those years.
proves that Haupt's interpretation of the piece changed greatly between 1905 and 1935.
suggests that disc recordings had largely replaced wax cylinders by the mid-1930s.
items.explanation: The complication is that nobody knows how fast the cylinder was turning when it was recorded, and playback speed changes the tempo you hear. The 1905 tempo can't be measured reliably, so the 20 percent gap could come from the machine and not from Haupt. The passage doesn't say which direction the error goes. All it supports is that the gap might not be real.

A.why: You treated the uncertainty as evidence for the opposite result. An unknown recording speed means the 1905 tempo is uncertain in both directions. It doesn't show that she played more slowly.

C.why: You accepted the historians' measurement, which is exactly what the passage casts doubt on. Then you added a claim about her interpretation that the passage never makes.

D.why: You picked up the incidental detail about recording formats. The blank asks what the tempo gap can show, and nothing in the passage is about whether discs replaced cylinders.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A field linguist uses the equation $T = 6r + 2g$ to estimate the total number of minutes, $T$, needed to process a recording of an endangered language. Here $r$ is the number of minutes of recorded speech and $g$ is the number of example sentences that must be glossed word by word.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $r$, and $g$. Which equation correctly expresses $g$ in terms of $T$ and $r$?
items.explanation: To get $g$ alone, first subtract $6r$ from both sides: $T - 6r = 2g$. Then divide the whole left side by 2: $g = \frac{T - 6r}{2}$.

A.why: You moved $6r$ to the other side but kept it positive. Taking $6r$ away from the right side means subtracting it from $T$, not adding it. This is the sign slip that this kind of rearranging is designed to catch.

B.why: You divided only $T$ by 2 and left $6r$ as it was. When you divide $T - 6r$ by 2, both terms get divided.

D.why: You swapped the two coefficients, as if the equation said $T = 2r + 6g$. In the given equation, $r$ is multiplied by 6 and $g$ is multiplied by 2.

items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $t$, $d$, $s$, and $w$. Which equation correctly expresses $d$ in terms of $t$, $s$, and $w$?
items.explanation: First subtract $w$ from both sides so the fraction is alone: $t - w = \frac{d}{s}$. Then multiply both sides by $s$ to clear the denominator: $d = s(t - w)$.

D.why: You divided by $s$ when you should have multiplied. Since $d$ is divided by $s$ in the equation, you undo that by multiplying both sides by $s$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A sports science lab screening rowers records each athlete's body mass index using $B = \frac{m}{h^2}$, where $m$ is the athlete's mass in kilograms and $h$ is the athlete's height in meters.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $B$, $m$, and $h$. Which equation correctly expresses $h$ in terms of $B$ and $m$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $h^2$ to get $Bh^2 = m$, then divide by $B$ to get $h^2 = \frac{m}{B}$. Because $h$ is positive, take the positive square root: $h = \sqrt{\frac{m}{B}}$.

A.why: You flipped the fraction the wrong way. From $Bh^2 = m$, you divide $m$ by $B$, so $m$ goes on top. You are solving for $h^2$ itself, not for its reciprocal.

C.why: You treated the exponent as multiplication by 2, as if $h^2$ meant $2h$. To undo a square, you take a square root. Dividing by 2 does not undo it.

items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $F$ in terms of $D$ and $h$?
items.explanation: First subtract 3 from both sides to get $D - 3 = \frac{F}{h}$. Then multiply both sides by $h$ to clear the fraction, which gives $F = h(D - 3)$. Check it with numbers: if $F = 20$ and $h = 5$, then $D = 4 + 3 = 7$, and $5(7 - 3) = 20$.

C.why: You subtracted 3 correctly, but then you divided by $h$ when you should have multiplied. $F$ is being divided by $h$, so you undo that by multiplying.

D.why: You lost the sign of the 3 while isolating. To undo $+3$ you subtract 3 from $D$. You don't add it.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: Ecologists estimate the number of salamanders, $N$, in a wetland with the equation $N = \frac{MC}{R}$. Here $M$ is the number marked in a first survey, $C$ is the number caught in a second survey, and $R$ is the number of marked salamanders recaught.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $R$ in terms of $N$, $M$, and $C$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $R$ to clear the denominator, which gives $NR = MC$. Then divide both sides by $N$ to get $R = \frac{MC}{N}$. Check it with numbers: if $M = 40$, $C = 30$, and $R = 6$, then $N = 200$, and $\frac{40 \cdot 30}{200} = 6$.

A.why: You flipped the whole right side upside down without flipping the left side to match. That gives $\frac{1}{R}$ in terms of the other letters, not $R$.

B.why: You moved $R$ out of the denominator and then multiplied $N$ by $MC$. Once you have $NR = MC$, you divide by $N$. You don't multiply.

C.why: You mixed up which letters sit in the numerator. After you clear the fraction, $M$ and $C$ stay multiplied together on one side and $N$ is the only letter you divide by.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: In a lab model, $\frac{1}{t} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$ gives the time $t$, in hours, for two types of white blood cells working together to clear a bacterial sample. The values $a$ and $b$ are the times each cell type would take alone.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $t$ in terms of $a$ and $b$?
items.explanation: Add the fractions on the right using the common denominator $ab$, which gives $\frac{1}{t} = \frac{b + a}{ab}$. Then take the reciprocal of both sides to get $t = \frac{ab}{a + b}$. Check it with numbers: if $a = 3$ and $b = 6$, then $\frac{1}{t} = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$, so $t = 2$, and $\frac{18}{9} = 2$.

B.why: You flipped each fraction on its own, turning $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$ into $a + b$. The reciprocal of a sum is not the sum of the reciprocals, so you have to combine the fractions first.

C.why: This is $\frac{1}{t}$, not $t$. You combined the fractions correctly but skipped the last step, which is taking the reciprocal.

D.why: You added the fractions by adding their denominators. Fractions add only over a common denominator, which here is $ab$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A marine biologist models the area of seafloor, $S$, in square centimeters, that a sea star covers as $S = kL^2$. Here $L$ is the length of one arm, in centimeters, and $k$ is a positive constant. Assume $L > 0$.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $L$ in terms of $S$ and $k$?
items.explanation: Divide both sides by $k$ to get $L^2 = \frac{S}{k}$. Then take the square root. Since $L > 0$, you keep only the positive root, so $L = \sqrt{\frac{S}{k}}$. Check it with numbers: if $k = 2$ and $L = 5$, then $S = 50$, and $\sqrt{\frac{50}{2}} = 5$.

D.why: This is $L^2$, not $L$. You divided by $k$ correctly but stopped before taking the square root.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A street-planning formula relates the spacing $s$ between streetlights, the number of lights $n$, and the length of the road $L$: $\frac{1}{s} = \frac{n}{L}$, where $s$, $n$ and $L$ are positive.
items.stem: Solve the equation for $s$.
items.explanation: The equation gives you $\frac{1}{s}$, not $s$. To get $s$, take the reciprocal of both sides, which flips $\frac{n}{L}$ into $\frac{L}{n}$. So $s = \frac{L}{n}$. This is the last step of many 'which equation expresses X in terms of...' questions: once you have solved for $\frac{1}{X}$, you still have to flip it to get $X$.

C.why: You multiplied $n$ and $L$ together instead of flipping the fraction. Taking a reciprocal turns $\frac{n}{L}$ into $\frac{L}{n}$. It does not turn it into a product.

D.why: You replaced the division with a subtraction. The two sides are linked by division, and you undo that by taking reciprocals, not by subtracting one letter from the other.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A civil engineer uses $L = L_0 + L_0 a T$ to find the length $L$ of a steel beam after heating. Here $L_0$ is the beam's original length, $a$ is a positive constant and $T$ is the temperature rise.
items.stem: Solve the equation for $L_0$.
items.explanation: $L_0$ appears twice, so factor it out first: $L = L_0(1 + aT)$. Then divide both sides by $(1 + aT)$ to get $L_0 = \frac{L}{1 + aT}$. Factoring out a variable that appears twice is a step that many harder 'which equation expresses X in terms of...' questions depend on.

D.why: You tried to undo the terms one at a time before collecting $L_0$, and you treated $aT$ as something to subtract. Collect every $L_0$ term and factor before you divide.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: In a model of fossil pollen in lake mud, $N = C - kt$. Here $N$ is the pollen count at depth $t$, $C$ is the count at the surface and $k$ is a positive constant.
items.stem: Solve the equation for $t$.
items.explanation: Add $kt$ to both sides and subtract $N$ from both sides to get $kt = C - N$. Then divide by $k$: $t = \frac{C - N}{k}$. Keeping track of the minus sign while you isolate a variable is the step these formula-rearranging questions most often test.

A.why: You dropped the minus sign in front of $kt$. If you subtract $C$ from both sides, you get $-kt = N - C$. You then have to divide by $-k$, not $k$, which gives $\frac{C - N}{k}$.

B.why: You divided before you had $t$ on its own. Dividing only $N$ by $k$ leaves $C$ untouched. Isolate $kt$ first, then divide the whole other side by $k$.

D.why: When you moved $N$ across the equals sign, you added it instead of subtracting it. Moving a term to the other side changes its sign.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: In ecology, the population density of a species in a habitat is given by $D = \dfrac{N}{A}$, where $D$ is the population density, $N$ is the number of individuals, and $A$ is the area of the habitat. $D$, $N$, and $A$ are all positive.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $A$ in terms of $D$ and $N$?
items.explanation: $A$ is in the denominator, so first multiply both sides by $A$ to clear the fraction: $DA = N$. Now $A$ is multiplied by $D$, so divide both sides by $D$: $A = \dfrac{N}{D}$. Check with numbers: if $N = 60$ and $A = 20$, then $D = 3$, and $\dfrac{60}{3} = 20$ gives back $A$. Clearing a denominator and then isolating the letter you want is the first move in every 'which equation correctly expresses ... in terms of ...' question, including the harder ones with reciprocals and squared variables.

A.why: You flipped the fraction so $A$ went from the bottom to the top, but you didn't apply that to the whole equation. Taking reciprocals of both sides gives $\dfrac{1}{D} = \dfrac{A}{N}$, and you'd still need to multiply by $N$. Try numbers: with $D = 3$ and $N = 60$, $\dfrac{3}{60}$ is nowhere near an area of 20.

B.why: You multiplied $D$ by $N$ when you should have divided. To get $A$ out of the denominator, multiply both sides by $A$ to get $DA = N$, then divide by $D$. Multiplying $D$ and $N$ together doesn't undo anything in the original equation.

D.why: You undid the division with subtraction. The original equation divides $N$ by $A$, so getting $A$ on its own takes multiplication and division, not subtraction. With $N = 60$ and $D = 3$, $60 - 3 = 57$, not 20.

items.stem: The equation can be rewritten as $w = \frac{kdh}{2h - d}$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?

items.stimulus: An ecologist models how often a predator catches a prey species using $\frac{1}{P} = \frac{1}{Q} + \frac{9}{Qm^2}$. items.stimulus: A cartographer measures how much a map projection stretches shapes near its edge with $E = \frac{3r + 2d}{r - d}$. items.stimulus: An immunologist describes how long it takes the body to clear a vaccine antigen using $\frac{4}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{3}{b}$. Here $T$ is the overall clearance time, $a$ is the clearance time due to antibodies alone, and $b$ is the clearance time due to immune cells alone. All three are positive and measured in days.
items.stem: If $b = 3T$, then $a = kT$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Solve for $a$ by isolating its term: $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{4}{T} - \frac{3}{b}$. Substitute $b = 3T$, so that $\frac{3}{b} = \frac{3}{3T} = \frac{1}{T}$. Flipping each fraction separately, as in $\frac{T}{4} = a + \frac{b}{3}$, is not a valid step.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A printmaking studio has two etching presses. Working alone, the older press finishes a run of posters in $a$ hours and the newer press finishes the same run in $b$ hours. Working together, they finish the run in $T$ hours, where $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $a$, and $b$. Which equation correctly expresses $a$ in terms of $T$ and $b$?
items.explanation: First isolate the reciprocal: $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b}$. Over the common denominator $Tb$ this is $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{b - T}{Tb}$. Then take reciprocals of both sides to get $a = \frac{Tb}{b - T}$. As a check, with $T = 2$ and $b = 3$ the original equation gives $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{6}$, so $a = 6$, and $\frac{2 \cdot 3}{3 - 2} = 6$.

A.why: You flipped each fraction separately, turning $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$ into $T = a + b$. You can't undo a sum of reciprocals one term at a time.

B.why: This is $\frac{1}{a}$, not $a$. You combined the fractions correctly but skipped the last step of taking the reciprocal.

D.why: You reversed the subtraction when combining $\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b}$. The numerator should be $b - T$. Your version gives a negative time, because two presses together finish faster than either press alone, so $T < b$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A meteorologist estimates the total pressure $P$ on a weather-station sensor using $P = \frac{d v^2}{2} + s$. Here $d$ is the air density, $v$ is the wind speed, and $s$ is the static air pressure.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $P$, $d$, $v$, and $s$. Which equation correctly expresses $v$ in terms of $P$, $d$, and $s$?
items.explanation: First subtract $s$ to get $P - s = \frac{d v^2}{2}$. Multiply both sides by $2$ and divide by $d$: $v^2 = \frac{2(P - s)}{d}$. Because $v$ is positive, keep the positive square root: $v = \sqrt{\frac{2(P - s)}{d}}$.

B.why: You multiplied by $\frac{2}{d}$ before moving $s$, so $\frac{2}{d}$ never reached $s$. Move $s$ first, then undo the coefficient on $v^2$, so that it applies to the whole of $P - s$.

C.why: You divided by 2 when you should have multiplied. Because $v^2$ is divided by 2, the 2 has to go into the numerator on the other side.

D.why: This is $v^2$, not $v$. You isolated the squared term correctly but left out the final square root.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A linguist compares a bilingual corpus in which $w$ sentences are in Welsh and $n$ sentences are in English, where $w > n$. The linguist measures the corpus's imbalance with the index $R = \frac{w - n}{w + n}$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $R$, $w$, and $n$. Which equation correctly expresses $w$ in terms of $R$ and $n$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $w + n$ to get $Rw + Rn = w - n$. Collect the $w$ terms on one side: $Rn + n = w - Rw$. Factor both sides: $n(1 + R) = w(1 - R)$. Divide by $1 - R$: $w = \frac{n(1 + R)}{1 - R}$. As a check, with $n = 1$ and $R = \frac{1}{2}$ this gives $w = 3$, and $\frac{3 - 1}{3 + 1} = \frac{1}{2}$.

A.why: You mixed up the signs when collecting terms, so the numerator and denominator traded places. Test $n = 1$ and $R = \frac{1}{2}$: this choice gives $w = \frac{1}{3}$, which is smaller than $n$.

B.why: You moved $Rw$ but then treated $w - Rw$ as just $w$. Because $w$ appears in two terms, you have to factor it out as $w(1 - R)$ and divide by $1 - R$.

C.why: You dropped a sign when you moved $Rw$ across. Since $R < 1$, the denominator $R - 1$ is negative, so this choice makes $w$ negative, which breaks the condition that $w$ is positive.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: An agricultural scientist blends $x$ kilograms of fertilizer that is $a$ percent nitrogen with $y$ kilograms of fertilizer that is $b$ percent nitrogen, where $b < a$. The blend is $C$ percent nitrogen, where $b < C < a$ and $C = \frac{ax + by}{x + y}$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $C$, $a$, $b$, $x$, and $y$. Which equation correctly expresses $x$ in terms of $C$, $a$, $b$, and $y$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $x + y$ to get $Cx + Cy = ax + by$. Collect the $x$ terms on one side: $Cy - by = ax - Cx$. Factor both sides: $y(C - b) = x(a - C)$. Divide by $a - C$: $x = \frac{y(C - b)}{a - C}$. As a check, with $a = 10$, $b = 2$, $C = 6$ and $y = 1$ this gives $x = 1$, and $\frac{10 + 2}{2} = 6$.

C.why: You flipped the fraction in the last step. From $y(C - b) = x(a - C)$, dividing by $a - C$ puts $C - b$ in the numerator.

D.why: You dropped the factor $y$. This choice is $\frac{x}{y}$, the ratio of the two amounts, not $x$ itself.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: An ecologist models how quickly a pond alga absorbs phosphate. The uptake rate is $U = \frac{Vs}{K + s}$, where $s$ is the phosphate concentration, $V$ is the maximum possible uptake rate, and $K$ is a constant for the species. The uptake rate $U$ is always less than $V$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $U$, $V$, $s$, and $K$. Which equation correctly expresses $s$ in terms of $U$, $V$, and $K$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $K + s$ to get $UK + Us = Vs$. Collect the $s$ terms on one side: $UK = Vs - Us = s(V - U)$. Divide by $V - U$: $s = \frac{UK}{V - U}$. This is positive because $U < V$.

D.why: This expression is $K$ with $s$ written in place of $K$. Solving the equation for $K$ gives $K = \frac{s(V - U)}{U}$, and this choice is that result with the two letters swapped, so you answered for the wrong variable.

items.stimulus: A folklorist builds a spread index $d$ for a trickster tale. It combines $p$, the number of villages where the tale was recorded in spoken form, and $q$, the number of villages where it appears in written collections, using $\frac{1}{d^2} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q}$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $d$, $p$, and $q$. Which equation correctly expresses $d$ in terms of $p$ and $q$?
items.explanation: Combine the right side over the common denominator $pq$: $\frac{1}{d^2} = \frac{p + q}{pq}$. Take reciprocals to get $d^2 = \frac{pq}{p + q}$. Because $d$ is positive, keep the positive root: $d = \sqrt{\frac{pq}{p + q}}$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: An urban planner studies a bus route. Buses travel outbound at an average speed of $a$ kilometers per hour and return along the same streets at $b$ kilometers per hour. The average speed for the whole round trip is $S = \frac{2ab}{a + b}$ kilometers per hour.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $S$, $a$, and $b$. Which equation correctly expresses $a$ in terms of $S$ and $b$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $a + b$ to get $Sa + Sb = 2ab$. Collect the $a$ terms on one side: $Sb = 2ab - Sa = a(2b - S)$. Divide by $2b - S$: $a = \frac{Sb}{2b - S}$. As a check, with $a = 2$ and $b = 6$ the formula gives $S = 3$, and $\frac{3 \cdot 6}{12 - 3} = 2$.

C.why: You dropped the minus sign when you moved $Sa$ to the side with $2ab$. The factored form is $a(2b - S)$.

D.why: You flipped the fraction when you divided. This choice is $\frac{1}{a}$, not $a$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: An archaeologist excavates the ring-shaped floor of a round house, between an outer wall of radius $R$ meters and a central hearth of radius $r$ meters, where $r < R$. The area of the excavated ring, in square meters, is $M = \pi(R^2 - r^2)$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $M$, $R$, and $r$. Which equation correctly expresses $r$ in terms of $M$ and $R$?
items.explanation: Divide both sides by $\pi$ to get $\frac{M}{\pi} = R^2 - r^2$. Rearrange: $r^2 = R^2 - \frac{M}{\pi}$. Because $r$ is positive, keep the positive root: $r = \sqrt{R^2 - \frac{M}{\pi}}$.

D.why: You rearranged before dividing by $\pi$, as if $\pi$ multiplied only $r^2$. Because $\pi$ multiplies all of $R^2 - r^2$, you have to divide $M$ by $\pi$ first.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A linguist models how a second-language learner's reading vocabulary grows with exposure. In the model, $T$ is the number of words the learner recognizes after $w$ hours of reading, $p$ is the greatest number of words the learner could eventually recognize from the reading material, and $k$ is a constant that depends on the material.

$T = \dfrac{pw}{w + k}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $p$, $w$, and $k$. Which equation correctly expresses $w$ in terms of $T$, $p$, and $k$?
items.explanation: First multiply both sides by $w + k$ to clear the fraction: $Tw + Tk = pw$. The target $w$ now shows up in two terms, so you collect them on one side before you divide: $Tk = pw - Tw$. Then factor out $w$: $Tk = w(p - T)$. Dividing by $p - T$ gives $w = \dfrac{Tk}{p - T}$. To check, try $w = 15$, $k = 5$, $p = 8$. Then $T = \dfrac{120}{20} = 6$, and $\dfrac{6 \cdot 5}{8 - 6} = 15$.

A.why: You probably split the equation into $\dfrac{p}{T} = 1 + \dfrac{k}{w}$ and got as far as $\dfrac{k}{w} = \dfrac{p - T}{T}$, which is right. But you then solved as though the equation said $\dfrac{w}{k}$, so you never took the reciprocal. The correct result is $w = \dfrac{Tk}{p - T}$, not $w = \dfrac{k(p - T)}{T}$.

B.why: You cleared the fraction correctly to get $Tw + Tk = pw$. Then, when you moved $Tw$ across the equals sign, you kept it positive, which turned $p - T$ into $p + T$. Subtracting $Tw$ from both sides gives $Tk = w(p - T)$.

D.why: You reached $Tk = w(p - T)$ and then flipped the result upside down, so the factor you should divide by ended up in the numerator. To isolate $w$, divide both sides by $p - T$. That leaves $Tk$ in the numerator.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A city planner estimates the peak pedestrian capacity $P$, in people per minute, of a downtown corridor. Two things limit that capacity: the crosswalk signal, which allows at most $L$ people per minute, and the sidewalk, which allows $kw^2$ people per minute. Here $w$ is the sidewalk width, in meters, and $k$ is a constant.

$\dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{L} + \dfrac{1}{kw^2}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $P$, $L$, $k$, and $w$. Which equation correctly expresses $w$ in terms of $P$, $L$, and $k$?
items.explanation: Get the term with $w$ by itself: $\dfrac{1}{kw^2} = \dfrac{1}{P} - \dfrac{1}{L}$. Over the common denominator $PL$, the right side is $\dfrac{L - P}{PL}$. Take reciprocals of both sides: $kw^2 = \dfrac{PL}{L - P}$. Divide by $k$, then take the square root. Because $w$ is positive, keep only the positive root: $w = \sqrt{\dfrac{PL}{k(L - P)}}$. To check, try $k = 2$, $w = 3$, $L = 9$. Then $\dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{9} + \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{1}{6}$, so $P = 6$, and $\sqrt{\dfrac{54}{2 \cdot 3}} = 3$.

B.why: You flipped each fraction separately and rewrote the equation as $P = L + kw^2$. A sum of reciprocals can't be undone one term at a time. You can also see that this choice can't be right: $P$ is always less than $L$, so $P - L$ is negative and the square root isn't a real number.

C.why: You found $\dfrac{1}{kw^2} = \dfrac{L - P}{PL}$ correctly, but you then treated it as $kw^2 = \dfrac{L - P}{PL}$ and skipped the reciprocal step. Flip both sides before you divide by $k$ and take the square root.

D.why: When you combined $\dfrac{1}{P} - \dfrac{1}{L}$, you added instead of subtracting and wrote the numerator as $L + P$. Over the common denominator $PL$, the difference is $\dfrac{L - P}{PL}$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: An orchard fills its irrigation reservoir using one main pump and two identical auxiliary pumps. When all three pumps run together, the reservoir fills in $T$ hours, where $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{2}{q}$. Here $p$ is the time, in hours, the main pump needs alone, and $q$ is the time, in hours, one auxiliary pump needs alone, with $p > T > 0$.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $q$ in terms of $p$ and $T$?
items.explanation: First isolate the term that contains $q$: $\frac{2}{q} = \frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{p}$. Put the right side over the common denominator $pT$ to get $\frac{2}{q} = \frac{p - T}{pT}$. Take reciprocals of both sides: $\frac{q}{2} = \frac{pT}{p - T}$. Then multiply by 2: $q = \frac{2pT}{p - T}$. To check, let $p = 6$ and $T = 3$. Then $\frac{2}{q} = \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{6}$, so $q = 12$, and $\frac{2(6)(3)}{6 - 3} = 12$. Because $p > T$, this value is positive, as a pumping time has to be.

C.why: You solved for $\frac{1}{q}$ and stopped there, so you skipped the final reciprocal step. $\frac{p - T}{2pT}$ is the value of $\frac{1}{q}$, not $q$. With $p = 6$ and $T = 3$, it gives $\frac{1}{12}$ instead of $12$.

D.why: You reached $\frac{2}{q} = \frac{p - T}{pT}$ and then divided by 2 instead of multiplying by 2 when you flipped. The 2 is in the numerator with $q$'s reciprocal, so it stays a factor of 2 in $q$. With $p = 6$ and $T = 3$, your expression gives $3$ instead of $12$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: An astronomer uses the equation $F = \frac{L}{4\pi d^2}$ to relate the flux $F$ of light from a star received on Earth to the star's luminosity $L$ and its distance $d$ from Earth. In this equation, $F$, $L$, and $d$ are all positive.
items.stem: The equation can be rewritten as $d = k\sqrt{\frac{L}{\pi F}}$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Start by clearing the fraction. Multiply both sides by $4\pi d^2$ to get $4\pi d^2 F = L$. Then divide by $4\pi F$: $d^2 = \frac{L}{4\pi F}$. The original equation gives $d^2 = 4$, so $d = 2$, and $\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{16} = 2$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A sports scientist finds a sprinter's average speed $v$ over two legs of equal length with the formula $v = \frac{2ab}{a+b}$. In this formula, $a$ and $b$ are the sprinter's speeds, in meters per second, on the first and second legs. In one trial, $v = 8$ and $a = 10$.
items.stem: What is the speed $b$, in meters per second, on the second leg?

items.stimulus: Linguists sometimes measure the variety of a speaker's vocabulary with Guiraud's index, $R = \frac{V}{\sqrt{N}}$, where $V$ is the number of distinct words in a transcript and $N$ is the total number of words in it, with $N > 0$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A bridge girder rests on two rubber bearing pads stacked one on top of the other. The combined stiffness $k$ of the stack is given by $k = \frac{ab}{a + b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are the stiffnesses of the two pads.

items.explanation: Clear the fraction by multiplying both sides by $a + b$: $ka + kb = ab$. Move every term that contains $b$ to one side: $ka = ab - kb$. Factor out $b$: $ka = b(a - k)$. items.stimulus:
In a kelp-forest study, a marine biologist finds that one urchin population would clear a test plot of kelp in $a$ days on its own and a second population would clear it in $b$ days. Together they clear it in $T$ days, where $T < b$.

$\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $a$, and $b$. Which equation correctly expresses $a$ in terms of $T$ and $b$?
items.explanation: Isolate the reciprocal: $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b} = \frac{b - T}{bT}$. Take reciprocals of both sides: $a = \frac{bT}{b - T}$. Check: with $a = 6$ and $b = 3$, $T = 2$, and $\frac{3 \cdot 2}{3 - 2} = 6$.

items.stimulus:
A public health team models the concentration $C$ of an airborne irritant at a distance of $d$ meters from a source that releases it at a rate $Q$. The constant $k$ depends on ventilation in the room.

items.stimulus:
A folklorist cataloguing versions of a trickster tale records $n$ versions collected from oral storytellers and $m$ versions found in printed collections. The fraction of all recorded versions that are oral is $V$, where $V < 1$.

C.why: You set up $n(1 - V) = Vm$ correctly but divided the wrong way round. That flips the expression you need.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
An agricultural scientist measures the moisture content $M$ of harvested grain on a dry basis. A sample weighs $W$ grams when freshly harvested and $D$ grams after oven drying.

items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $M$, $W$, and $D$. Which equation correctly expresses $D$ in terms of $M$ and $W$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $D$: $MD = W - D$. Add $D$ to both sides so every $D$ term is on one side: $MD + D = W$, so $D(M + 1) = W$. Divide: $D = \frac{W}{M + 1}$. Check: with $W = 150$ and $D = 100$, $M = 0.5$, and $\frac{150}{1.5} = 100$.

D.why: You reached $D(M + 1) = W$ and then multiplied by $M + 1$ when you should have divided by it. This would make the dry weight bigger than the wet weight.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: An astronomer focusing a refracting telescope uses the lens equation $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}$, where $f$ is the focal length of the objective lens, $d_o$ is the distance from the lens to the object, and $d_i$ is the distance from the lens to the image, all in centimeters, with $d_o > f > 0$.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $d_i$ in terms of $f$ and $d_o$?
items.explanation: Subtract $\frac{1}{d_o}$ from both sides to get $\frac{1}{d_i} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{d_o}$. Over the common denominator $f d_o$, that is $\frac{1}{d_i} = \frac{d_o - f}{f d_o}$. Take reciprocals of both sides and you get $d_i = \frac{f d_o}{d_o - f}$. items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A printmaker estimates the volume of ink $V$, in milliliters, needed to print a square woodblock with side length $s$ centimeters in $k$ layers using the formula $V = \frac{k s^2}{50} + 2$, where $s > 0$ and $k > 0$.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $s$ in terms of $V$ and $k$?
items.explanation: Subtract 2 from both sides to get $V - 2 = \frac{k s^2}{50}$. Multiply by 50 and divide by $k$: $s^2 = \frac{50(V - 2)}{k}$. Since $s > 0$, keep only the positive square root, which gives $s = \sqrt{\frac{50(V - 2)}{k}}$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A city planning office models projected daily cyclists $P$, in thousands, on a downtown network with $n$ protected bike lanes as $P = \frac{a n}{n + b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants and $0 < P < a$.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $n$ in terms of $P$, $a$, and $b$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $n + b$ to get $Pn + Pb = an$. Move every term with $n$ to one side: $Pb = an - Pn$. Factor out $n$ to get $Pb = n(a - P)$, then divide: $n = \frac{P b}{a - P}$. Because $P < a$, this value is positive, as a number of lanes must be.

D.why: You divided by $a$ before collecting the $n$ terms, so $n$ is still on the right side. That's a rearranged step, not an expression of $n$ in terms of the other letters.

items.stimulus: Two crews are clearing soil from an excavation trench at an archaeological site. Working alone, the first crew would need $p$ hours and the second crew would need $q$ hours. Working together, they need $T$ hours, where $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q}$ and $p > T$.

items.stimulus: Meteorologists sometimes model a hurricane as a heat engine. Its efficiency $E$ is given by $E = \frac{S - W}{S}$, where $S$ is the sea-surface temperature and $W$ is the temperature of the air flowing out at the top of the storm, both in kelvins, and $0 < E < 1$.

items.stimulus:
An earthquake sends out a fast P-wave and a slower S-wave. A seismograph station that is $d$ kilometers from the source records the S-wave arriving $t$ seconds after the P-wave, where

$t = \frac{d}{s} - \frac{d}{p}$

and $p$ and $s$ are the speeds, in kilometers per second, of the P-wave and S-wave.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $t$, $d$, $p$, and $s$, where $p > s$. Which equation correctly expresses $d$ in terms of $t$, $p$, and $s$?
items.explanation: Factor out $d$: $t = d\left(\frac{1}{s} - \frac{1}{p}\right)$. Combine the fractions over the common denominator $ps$: $\frac{1}{s} - \frac{1}{p} = \frac{p - s}{ps}$, so $t = \frac{d(p - s)}{ps}$. Multiply both sides by $ps$ to get $tps = d(p - s)$, then divide by $p - s$: $d = \frac{tps}{p - s}$. Because $p > s$, this value of $d$ is positive, as a distance has to be.

D.why: You treated the gap between the two arrival times as a sum and used $p + s$ in place of $p - s$. The equation subtracts $\frac{d}{p}$, so the combined numerator is $p - s$.

items.stimulus:
A tagged tern flies $d$ kilometers straight into a steady wind and then flies the same distance back with the wind behind it. Its airspeed is $v$ kilometers per hour, and the wind speed is $w$ kilometers per hour. The headwind leg takes $T$ hours longer than the tailwind leg, where

$T = \frac{d}{v - w} - \frac{d}{v + w}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $d$, $v$, and $w$, where $v > w$. Which equation correctly expresses $d$ in terms of $T$, $v$, and $w$?
items.explanation: Use the common denominator $(v - w)(v + w) = v^2 - w^2$: $T = \frac{d(v + w) - d(v - w)}{v^2 - w^2} = \frac{2dw}{v^2 - w^2}$. Multiply both sides by $v^2 - w^2$ to get $T(v^2 - w^2) = 2dw$, then divide by $2w$: $d = \frac{T(v^2 - w^2)}{2w}$.

D.why: You multiplied $(v - w)(v + w)$ incorrectly. That product is $v^2 - w^2$, not $v^2 + w^2$, because the middle terms cancel and the last term is negative.

items.stimulus: An ecologist models the feeding rate of a predator, $E$, in prey eaten per hour, using the equation $\frac{1}{E} = \frac{1}{m} + \frac{h}{mN^2}$, where $N$ is the density of prey, in prey per square meter, and $m$ and $h$ are positive constants. In this model, $N > 0$.

Its total flight time $T$, in hours, is given by $T = \frac{d}{v - w} + \frac{d}{v + w}$, where $v$ is the tern's airspeed and $w$ is the wind speed, both in kilometers per hour, and $0 < w < v$.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $w$ in terms of $T$, $d$, and $v$?
items.explanation: Combine the fractions over $(v - w)(v + w) = v^2 - w^2$. The numerator is $d(v + w) + d(v - w) = 2dv$, so $T = \frac{2dv}{v^2 - w^2}$. Multiply both sides by $v^2 - w^2$ to get $T(v^2 - w^2) = 2dv$, then divide by $T$: $v^2 - w^2 = \frac{2dv}{T}$. Isolate $w^2$: $w^2 = v^2 - \frac{2dv}{T}$. Since $w > 0$, $w = \sqrt{v^2 - \frac{2dv}{T}}$. Check with numbers: if $d = 12$, $v = 10$, and $w = 2$, then $T = \frac{12}{8} + \frac{12}{12} = 2.5$, and $\sqrt{100 - \frac{240}{2.5}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.

A.why: You flipped the wrong fraction. From $T = \frac{2dv}{v^2 - w^2}$, you need $v^2 - w^2 = \frac{2dv}{T}$. Writing $\frac{T}{2dv}$ is what you get when you take the reciprocal of one side but not the other.

B.why: You lost a sign when you moved terms to isolate $w^2$. From $v^2 - w^2 = \frac{2dv}{T}$, you get $w^2 = v^2 - \frac{2dv}{T}$, not $\frac{2dv}{T} - v^2$. Since $T > \frac{2d}{v}$, your expression is negative, so it can't be under a square root.

D.why: You dropped the factor of 2 when you combined the fractions. The numerator $d(v + w) + d(v - w)$ simplifies to $2dv$, not $dv$, because the two $d \cdot v$ terms add together.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: An agronomist models the yield $Y$ of a wheat plot, in bushels per acre, as a function of the nitrogen applied, $N$, in pounds per acre: $\frac{1}{Y} = \frac{1}{m} + \frac{c}{N^2}$. In this model, $m$ is the largest yield the plot could reach and $c$ is a constant for the soil type.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $Y$, $m$, $c$, and $N$, where $Y < m$. Which equation correctly expresses $N$ in terms of $Y$, $m$, and $c$?
items.explanation: Subtract $\frac{1}{m}$ from both sides: $\frac{c}{N^2} = \frac{1}{Y} - \frac{1}{m} = \frac{m - Y}{mY}$. Take reciprocals of both sides to get $\frac{N^2}{c} = \frac{mY}{m - Y}$, so $N^2 = \frac{cmY}{m - Y}$. Because $N$ is positive, $N = \sqrt{\frac{cmY}{m - Y}}$.

A.why: You isolated $\frac{c}{N^2}$ correctly, but then you multiplied by $c$ without taking the reciprocal. That expression is $\frac{c}{N}$ under a square root, not $N$.

C.why: This is $N^2$. You stopped before taking the square root.

D.why: You flipped each fraction separately, turning the equation into $Y = m + \frac{N^2}{c}$. You can't undo a sum of reciprocals one term at a time. The expression is also undefined here, because $Y < m$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: Ecologists studying a dragonfly nymph that hunts mosquito larvae model its consumption rate, $C$ (larvae per hour), as $C = \frac{aN}{1 + ahN}$. Here $N$ is the larval density, $a$ is the attack rate, and $h$ is the handling time per larva.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $C$, $a$, $h$, and $N$, where $Ch < 1$. Which equation correctly expresses $N$ in terms of $C$, $a$, and $h$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $1 + ahN$ to get $C + aChN = aN$. Move every term with $N$ to one side: $C = aN - aChN = aN(1 - Ch)$. Divide to get $N = \frac{C}{a(1 - Ch)}$.

A.why: When you moved $aChN$ across the equals sign, you kept it positive. The factor should be $1 - Ch$, not $1 + Ch$.

B.why: You collected the $N$ terms correctly, but you lost the $a$ in $aChN$ when you factored. The coefficient of $N$ is $a - aCh$, not $a - Ch$.

C.why: You rewrote the equation as $\frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{aN} + h$ and then flipped each term separately. You can't undo a sum of fractions one term at a time.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: In a model of antibody binding, the fraction $\theta$ of receptor sites on a B cell that are occupied by antigen is $\theta = \frac{L^2}{L^2 + K^2}$. Here $L$ is the antigen concentration and $K$ is a dissociation constant, both in nanomolar.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $\theta$, $L$, and $K$, where $\theta < 1$. Which equation correctly expresses $L$ in terms of $\theta$ and $K$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $L^2 + K^2$ to get $\theta L^2 + \theta K^2 = L^2$. Collect the $L^2$ terms: $\theta K^2 = L^2(1 - \theta)$, so $L^2 = \frac{K^2\theta}{1 - \theta}$. Because $L$ is positive, $L = K\sqrt{\frac{\theta}{1 - \theta}}$.

B.why: This expression equals $\frac{K^2}{L}$, not $L$. You turned the ratio upside down, probably by solving for $\frac{K^2}{L^2}$ and forgetting to take the reciprocal.

C.why: You took the square root of $K^2$ but not of $\frac{\theta}{1 - \theta}$. The root applies to the whole of $L^2$.

D.why: When you moved $\theta L^2$ to the other side, you added it instead of subtracting it. That made the factor $1 + \theta$ instead of $1 - \theta$.

items.stimulus: A tagged sea turtle swims a distance $d$ kilometers against a current and then the same distance back with it. Its speed in still water is $v$ kilometers per hour, and the current's speed is $u$ kilometers per hour. The total time, $T$ hours, satisfies $T = \frac{d}{v - u} + \frac{d}{v + u}$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $d$, $v$, and $u$, where $u < v$. Which equation correctly expresses $d$ in terms of $T$, $v$, and $u$?
items.explanation: Write both fractions over the common denominator $v^2 - u^2$: $T = \frac{d(v + u) + d(v - u)}{v^2 - u^2} = \frac{2vd}{v^2 - u^2}$. Then multiply both sides by $v^2 - u^2$ and divide by $2v$ to get $d = \frac{T(v^2 - u^2)}{2v}$.

D.why: When you added $d(v + u) + d(v - u)$, you got $vd$ instead of $2vd$. That drops a factor of 2.

items.stimulus: A corpus linguist models the number of distinct words, $V$, found in a sample of $N$ running words from a language's texts as $\frac{1}{V} = \frac{1}{aN} + \frac{1}{M}$. Here $M$ is the size of the full vocabulary and $a$ is a constant for the genre.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $V$, $a$, $N$, and $M$, where $V < M$. Which equation correctly expresses $N$ in terms of $V$, $a$, and $M$?

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Readers have long treated Agnes Marlowe's 1911 novel The Lexicographer's Daughter as a gentle family comedy. Its scenes of a father and daughter quarreling over word definitions are, in this view, light domestic sketches meant chiefly to amuse.

Text 2
Marlowe's novel is certainly funny. But its quarrels over definitions track a real debate of the period: whether dictionaries should record how people actually speak or dictate how they ought to. Beneath the comedy lies a serious argument about language.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The novel's dinner-table setting is its most carefully described location.
The novel's quarrels over word definitions are presented with humor.
The novel is meant mainly to amuse rather than to make an argument.
The novel takes part in a debate over the proper role of dictionaries.
items.explanation: Text 1 calls the novel a comedy whose quarrels are meant to amuse, and Text 2 opens by granting that the novel 'is certainly funny.' That concession is the shared ground: both authors see the quarrels as humorous. They split over whether anything serious lies underneath.

A.why: You went to a detail from the novel itself instead of the critics' claims about it. Neither author says anything about how carefully any setting is described.

C.why: This is Text 1's view only. Text 2 rejects it and says the comedy covers a serious argument about language.

D.why: This is Text 2's thesis. Text 1 describes the scenes as light sketches and never connects them to a debate about dictionaries.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Hester Crane's 1894 poem cycle Loom Songs is usually read as a lament. Its speakers, young women in a cotton mill, describe the shuttle's clatter and the endless hours, and critics have taken the poems as straightforward protests against factory labor.

Text 2
Although Loom Songs plainly records the hardship of mill work, its speakers also take pride in their skill, boasting of cloth woven without a single flaw. Crane portrays the weavers as craftswomen, not merely as victims.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Loom Songs presents its weavers as skilled workers proud of their cloth.
Loom Songs is best understood as a simple protest against factory labor.
Loom Songs builds its strongest effects around the sound of the shuttle.
Loom Songs depicts the difficulties of working in a cotton mill.
items.explanation: Text 1 describes the poems as a lament about the shuttle's clatter and the endless hours. Text 2's concessive clause, 'Although Loom Songs plainly records the hardship of mill work,' accepts the same point. Both agree that the cycle depicts how hard mill work is.

A.why: This is Text 2's new claim. Text 1 reads the poems only as laments and protests and says nothing about pride in skill.

B.why: This is Text 1's reading, and Text 2 argues against it by saying the weavers are more than victims.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Ruth Ansel's 1928 poem "The Coal Fern" describes a fossil frond found in a lump of coal. It is often read as a meditation on mortality, with the ancient plant serving as a reminder that every living thing passes away.

Text 2
Death is undeniably present in "The Coal Fern." But Ansel had studied fossil plants at university, and her poem dwells on how precisely the frond's veins survive in stone. For her, the fossil is less a symbol of loss than a record of endurance.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The fossil in the poem chiefly symbolizes the passing of all living things.
The poem's precise detail reflects Ansel's university study of fossil plants.
The poem engages with the theme of death in some way.
The frond's delicate veins are the most striking image in the poem.
items.explanation: Text 1 reads the poem as a meditation on mortality. Text 2 concedes that 'Death is undeniably present' before making its own argument. So both critics agree that death is one of the poem's themes.

Mara Ellison's 1926 novel *The Calorie Table* follows a young wife who weighs every portion by the new nutrition science. Most critics read it as satire: the heroine's scales and charts are comic, and her husband's secret trips to the bakery suggest that Ellison found dietary science absurd.

Text 2
Ellison does mock her heroine's obsessive weighing. But the satire's target is narrower than critics claim. The novel's one physician, who quietly cures a child's rickets with cod-liver oil, is drawn with complete respect. Ellison ridicules the fad, not the science.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Ellison's novel makes fun of the heroine's habit of weighing her food.
Ellison regarded the nutrition science of her own day as absurd.
The husband's bakery trips reveal a marriage that is quietly failing.
Ellison portrays the novel's physician as a wholly admirable figure.
items.explanation: Text 1 calls the heroine's scales and charts 'comic,' and Text 2 grants that 'Ellison does mock her heroine's obsessive weighing.' Text 2 narrows what the satire targets, but it agrees the satire exists and that the weighing is part of it.

B.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, and it's exactly what Text 2 narrows: 'Ellison ridicules the fad, not the science.' Author 2 would reject it.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's your own reading of a detail from the novel. Text 1 uses the bakery trips only as evidence of satire, and Text 2 ignores them, so neither critic makes this claim.

D.why: Only Text 2 discusses the physician. Text 1 says Ellison found dietary science absurd, which doesn't fit an admiring portrait of a doctor who heals through nutrition.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Theo Nakashima's poem "Coal Measures" (1971) describes a fossil fern pressed into a lump of coal, "a green hand / closed three hundred million years." Reviewers called the poem a meditation on loss, noting that it ends with the coal burning in a kitchen stove.

Text 2
The poem does end in the stove. But Nakashima, who studied paleobotany before turning to verse, chose that ending with care: as the coal burns, the speaker says the fern's stored sunlight is "paid back" as warmth. The poem concerns not loss but energy returning to use.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The poem is above all a meditation on what time has taken away.
The "green hand" image suggests the fern is reaching out to the reader.
The poem ends with the coal holding the fossil fern burning in a stove.
The burning coal represents ancient sunlight being returned as warmth.
items.explanation: Text 1 says the poem 'ends with the coal burning in a kitchen stove,' and Text 2 concedes it: 'The poem does end in the stove.' The critics disagree about what that ending means, not about the fact that the poem ends there.

A.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 rejects it directly: 'The poem concerns not loss but energy returning to use.'

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's a vivid reading of the quoted image, but neither critic interprets the 'green hand' this way. You read the poem yourself instead of looking for what the critics share.

D.why: This is Text 2's interpretation. Text 1 reads the burning as loss, not as energy being returned, so Author 1 would not agree.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Rafael Okonjo's 1934 novel *Day Wages* builds to a dockworkers' walkout, rendered in stirring pages of men locking arms along the wharf. Critics have therefore read the book as a celebration of collective action.

Text 2
The walkout is indeed the novel's climax. Yet a brief final chapter, often overlooked, shows the strikers' wage gains eroding within a year as shipping firms hire casual laborers from neighboring ports. Okonjo admired solidarity but doubted it could hold wages up when so many workers stood ready to replace the strikers.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Okonjo's novel is ultimately a celebration of collective action by workers.
The dockworkers' walkout serves as the climactic event of Okonjo's novel.
Okonjo believed that strikes could never improve the conditions of workers.
The wharf setting stresses how cut off the dockworkers are from the city.
items.explanation: Text 1 says the novel 'builds to' the walkout, and Text 2 grants that 'the walkout is indeed the novel's climax' before raising the overlooked final chapter. Both authors accept that the walkout is the novel's climax.

A.why: This is Text 1's conclusion. Text 2 qualifies it: the final chapter shows Okonjo doubting that solidarity can last against a surplus of labor. Author 2 would not call the book 'ultimately' a celebration.

C.why: This is a stronger version of Text 2's claim. Author 2 says Okonjo 'admired solidarity' and doubted it could hold wages up in one market condition, not that strikes could never help. Text 1 would reject it outright.

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's your own interpretation of the setting, and neither critic says anything about the dockworkers being isolated from the city.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
Edith Corran's poem sequence *Night Watches* (1893) is usually read as an expression of religious awe. Its speaker, observing from a city rooftop, calls the Milky Way "a spilled and holy milk," and readers have taken her stars as signs of divine order.

Text 2
Corran's speaker is certainly awed. But Corran was an amateur observer who corresponded with astronomers, and her poems record precise details: the star Algol dimming every few days, a comet's tail lengthening night by night. Her wonder is grounded in measurement rather than faith.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The speaker of Night Watches responds to the night sky with awe.
Corran presents the stars as signs of an order established by God.
The rooftop setting conveys the speaker's isolation from the city below.
The wonder in Corran's poems stems from precise observation of the sky.
items.explanation: Text 1 describes the sequence as an expression of 'religious awe,' and Text 2 concedes that 'Corran's speaker is certainly awed.' They disagree about where the awe comes from, faith or measurement, but both say it's there.

B.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 rejects it, saying Corran's wonder is 'grounded in measurement rather than faith.'

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. You built a plausible reading of the rooftop setting, but Text 1 mentions the rooftop only in passing and neither critic interprets it.

D.why: This is Text 2's thesis. Text 1 traces the poems' awe to religious feeling, so Author 1 would not agree that it comes from careful measurement.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Critics have read Lena Dubrow's 1962 novel *Grid*, set in a newly built planned city, as an attack on modernist urban design. Its residents wander identical boulevards, lose their way among matching towers, and long for the crooked lanes of the old town.

Text 2
Dubrow's residents are indeed disoriented by the new city's sameness. Yet later chapters show them adapting: they paint their doors, plant gardens on median strips, and nickname the towers. Dubrow's subject is not the failure of planning but the way inhabitants remake planned spaces as their own.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Dubrow wrote Grid chiefly as a critique of modernist urban design.
The crooked lanes of the old town stand for the residents' lost youth.
Grid depicts residents gradually making the planned city their own.
Residents in Grid find the uniformity of the new city disorienting.
items.explanation: Text 1 describes residents losing their way among 'identical boulevards' and 'matching towers.' Text 2 concedes that they 'are indeed disoriented by the new city's sameness' before turning to how they adapt. Both authors accept the disorientation.

A.why: This is Text 1's thesis. Text 2 denies it: Dubrow's subject is 'not the failure of planning.'

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's a symbolic reading of an image from the novel that neither critic offers. You interpreted the novel yourself instead of finding the critics' common ground.

C.why: This is what Text 2 argues. Text 1 mentions only the residents' disorientation and longing, never any adapting, so you can't credit this to Author 1.

Text 1
Arno Velasquez's 1979 novel *Backwater* depicts a valley drowned by a new reservoir. Reviewers called it a protest against dam building, citing above all its most affecting scene, in which a farmer watches his orchard vanish beneath the rising water.

Text 2
That scene is the novel's emotional center, written with real grief. But Velasquez also gives sympathetic voice to a downstream town that the dam spares from yearly floods. Rather than simply condemning the project, the novel weighs the valley's loss against the town's safety.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Backwater is best understood as a protest against the building of dams.
The rising water symbolizes the farmer's lack of control over his fate.
The scene of the farmer's flooded orchard is the novel's most moving.
Velasquez balances the valley's loss against the benefits of the dam.
items.explanation: Text 1 calls the orchard scene the novel's 'most affecting,' and Text 2 grants that it is 'the novel's emotional center, written with real grief.' The critics differ over the novel's overall stance, but they agree about the power of this scene.

A.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 says the novel does not 'simply' condemn the dam but weighs costs against benefits, so Author 2 would not agree.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's a reasonable symbolic reading of the scene, but neither critic interprets the rising water this way. You answered from your own reading of the novel instead of the texts.

D.why: This is Text 2's thesis. Text 1 reads the novel as a protest against dams, which conflicts with the idea that it balances the dam's benefits against its costs.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
The following text is adapted from Martha Greaves's 1861 novel The Thorne Inheritance. A surgeon is inoculating Mrs. Thorne's son against smallpox.
Mrs. Thorne watched the surgeon lay the infected thread in the shallow cut on her son's arm. The village called it tempting Providence. Still she held the boy steady, reasoning that a small fever, chosen, was kinder than a great one left to chance.

Text 2
Critics often read Greaves's inoculation scenes as simple celebrations of medical progress. The novel certainly admires the procedure, but its mothers do not trust science blindly. They weigh one harm against another, and the book's real subject is the burden of choosing a lesser danger.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Mrs. Thorne knowingly accepts a smaller danger to protect her son from a greater one.
The scene mainly shows how skillfully the surgeon carries out a delicate procedure.
The novel is best read as a straightforward celebration of medical progress.
The novel finally condemns inoculation as a risk that no parent should take.
items.explanation: Start with the critic's thesis in Text 2: the novel is about the burden of choosing a lesser danger. Then find the feature in Text 1 that fits it: Mrs. Thorne reasons that 'a small fever, chosen, was kinder than a great one left to chance.' The excerpt shows her making exactly the weighing the critic describes, so both authors would agree with this statement.

B.why: You read the excerpt on its own terms and fixed on the surgeon's action, which is vividly described. The critic, though, cares about the mother's choice, not the surgeon's technique, and Text 1 never says the procedure is skillful. Neither author supports this as the scene's main point.

C.why: This is the common reading that Text 2 brings up only to push back on. The critic grants that the novel admires inoculation but says its real subject is the burden of choosing harm. The critic would reject calling the novel a 'straightforward' celebration.

D.why: You went too far with the villagers' 'tempting Providence.' Mrs. Thorne goes ahead with the inoculation anyway, and the critic says outright that the novel admires the procedure. Neither text says the novel condemns it.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
The following text is from Agnes Tolliver's 1894 poem "Heron at Low Water."
The heron stands where the shallows thin,
A gray thought in the gray of the morning,
Patient as stone till the fish slides in—
Then the strike, and no warning.

Text 2
Tolliver's heron is usually taken as a portrait of serenity, a bird at rest in a quiet dawn. That calm is real, but it is never idle. Each still line leans toward the closing strike, so that the bird's patience becomes a kind of menace and its waiting turns out to be the hunt itself.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The heron's stillness is directed toward a sudden act of catching prey.
The poem's main interest is the gray color shared by the bird and dawn.
The heron is best understood as a symbol of untroubled, restful peace.
The poem shows that Tolliver admired hunting birds above all others.
items.explanation: The critic's thesis in Text 2 is that the heron's calm is 'never idle': its patience leads to the strike and is part of the hunt. Text 1 shows this. The bird is 'patient as stone till the fish slides in— / Then the strike.' Both texts tie the heron's stillness to a sudden attack on prey, so both authors would agree.

B.why: This is the bait: you paraphrased a striking image from the poem ('a gray thought in the gray of the morning') instead of reading through the critic's lens. Text 2 never mentions color, and the poem uses the gray image as one detail, not its main interest.

C.why: This is the usual reading that Text 2 corrects. The critic grants that the calm is real but argues it is 'never idle' and amounts to 'a kind of menace,' so the critic would not accept 'untroubled' peace.

D.why: Neither text compares herons with other birds or says what Tolliver preferred. You stretched one poem about one heron into a claim about the poet's views on all birds.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
The following text is adapted from Hester Vane's 1884 novel The Valley Bell.
When the shaking stopped, the people of Arnsby gathered in the churchyard, certain that heaven had spoken against them. Only old Tobias, the surveyor, walked out past the mill. He knelt beside each new crack in the road and marked it with a stake, and by evening his stakes ran in one straight line toward the hills.

Text 2
Critics have long treated The Valley Bell as a pious melodrama. Its crowd scenes certainly invite that reading, but Vane gives the chapter's final image to Tobias, whose patient measurements trace what geologists would later call a fault. The novel, I think, quietly favors observation over omen.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Tobias responds to the earthquake differently from most of Arnsby's residents.
The townspeople are mocked as foolish for gathering in the churchyard.
The Valley Bell is best understood as a pious melodrama about divine anger.
The churchyard gathering shows the comfort Arnsby finds in shared faith.
items.explanation: Text 1 sets Tobias apart: everyone else gathers in the churchyard, but he alone walks out to stake the cracks. Text 2 builds its whole reading on that contrast, calling his measurements the novel's real emphasis. Both texts treat Tobias's response as different from the crowd's.

B.why: You made the critic's claim stronger than it is. Text 2 says the novel 'quietly favors' observation, not that it mocks anyone, and Text 1 describes the townspeople without ridicule.

C.why: This is the very view Text 2 sets out to challenge. The critic grants that the crowd scenes invite it, then argues against it.

D.why: You read Text 1 on your own instead of through the critic's lens. Neither text says the gathering brings comfort, and the critic's point is about Tobias, not the crowd.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
The following text is adapted from Ada Marlow's 1909 poem "Shuttle Song."
My shuttle runs like a swallow, / back and over, back and over; / the cloth grows under my hands / as a meadow greens in April. / Twelve strokes, and the bell; / twelve strokes, and the bell.

Text 2
"Shuttle Song" is often anthologized as a cheerful hymn to the loom, and its swallows and meadows do lend it a pastoral sweetness. Yet Marlow closes on a counted refrain tied to the mill bell. Beneath the borrowed countryside, the poem records labor measured out by someone else's clock.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The poem openly protests the harsh conditions of early mill labor.
The speaker describes her weaving with images taken from the countryside.
The poem is chiefly a cheerful celebration of working at the loom.
The speaker's pride in her cloth shows that weaving is fulfilling work.
items.explanation: Text 1 compares the shuttle to a swallow and the growing cloth to a meadow in April. Text 2 grants exactly this ('its swallows and meadows do lend it a pastoral sweetness') before it turns to the bell. Both authors accept that the poem uses countryside imagery for the work.

A.why: The critic finds the regimentation 'beneath' the imagery, which means it is hidden, not openly protested. The poem itself never complains.

C.why: Text 2 names this as the common reading and then disputes it, arguing that the bell refrain undercuts the cheer.

D.why: This is your own reading of the imagery, and the critic would not accept it. Text 2 argues that the sweetness hides labor controlled by 'someone else's clock.'

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
The following text is adapted from Josiah Penrose's 1806 novel The Surgeon's House.
Dr. Lyle laid out his tables of cases, but Mrs. Hart only drew her son closer. Then Clara, the doctor's daughter, rolled back her sleeve, took the lancet, and made the small scratch herself. "It is no worse than a briar," she said. Mrs. Hart watched the girl's steady hand, then held out the boy's arm.

Text 2
Clara is usually celebrated as a heroine of the new science of vaccination. She is brave, certainly, but notice what actually moves Mrs. Hart: not the doctor's tables, which she ignores, but the sight of another person accepting the risk first. Penrose understood that trust, more than data, wins converts.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The novel suggests that medical evidence plays no part in medicine.
Mrs. Hart is persuaded mainly by the figures in Dr. Lyle's tables.
Mrs. Hart lets her son be vaccinated after watching Clara's act.
Mrs. Hart's hesitation is portrayed as a foolish superstition.
items.explanation: In Text 1, Mrs. Hart holds out her son's arm only after she watches Clara scratch her own. Text 2 points to the same moment as the thing that 'actually moves Mrs. Hart.' Both authors tie her decision to Clara's example.

A.why: You stretched the critic's 'more than data' into 'no part at all.' Text 2 ranks trust above evidence. It does not throw evidence out.

B.why: Both texts say the reverse: Mrs. Hart draws her son closer while the tables are laid out, and the critic says she ignores them.

D.why: You read Text 1 your own way instead of through the critic's frame. Neither text calls her caution foolish, and the critic treats it as something to win over with trust.
