items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Ilse Marrow's Garden Suite (1894) is a set of parlor confections: seven brief pieces of pleasant melody, written for amateur pianists to play after dinner. Nothing in them asks to be remembered the next morning, and their very brevity shows that Marrow aimed only to charm her listeners.

Text 2
Granted, Marrow wrote the seven brief pieces of the Garden Suite for amateurs to play at home, and their melodies are easy to love. Yet nearly every piece ends on an unresolved chord, so the suite never comes to rest. That refusal quietly unsettles the very parlor the music was written to entertain.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT which statement?
choices: The suite was composed for amateur performers in a home setting.
The melodies in the suite are appealing to listeners.
The suite's only purpose is to charm and entertain its listeners.
The suite is made up of several short pieces.
items.explanation: Text 1 ends on the claim that Marrow 'aimed only to charm,' and that last claim is what Text 2 answers. Text 2 grants that the suite was written for amateurs, that it has appealing melodies, and that its pieces are short. Then it turns: the unresolved endings 'unsettle' the parlor, so charm is not the suite's only purpose. Text 2's critic would reject this statement, so it is the one both authors would NOT agree with.

A.why: You may have read Text 2's 'Yet' as rejecting everything before it. But Text 2 opens with 'Granted, Marrow wrote... for amateurs to play at home,' so it accepts this point outright. Both authors agree with it.

B.why: You may have reasoned that a critic who finds the suite unsettling can't think it is pleasant. That comes from your own reading of the music, not from Text 2. Text 2 calls the melodies 'easy to love' and argues that the unease comes from the endings, not the tunes.

D.why: Both texts describe the suite as 'seven brief pieces.' Text 2 never disputes the brevity. It disputes only what Text 1 concludes from it.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Thomas Reeve's long poem The Husbandman's Year (1801) is, above all, a manual. Its twelve books follow the farming calendar month by month, and its advice on rotating turnips with barley is as sound as any treatise of the day. Scenes of village life lend color, but Reeve wrote in verse chiefly so that farmers would remember his lessons.

Text 2
Few would deny that the farming advice in The Husbandman's Year is accurate, or that its structure mirrors the agricultural calendar. Yet every book closes on a scene of open village fields that, by 1801, enclosure was fencing off. The poem is less a manual than a lament for a disappearing way of farming.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT which statement?
choices: The poem's main purpose is to teach farmers practical methods.
The poem's advice about farming is accurate.
The poem includes scenes of village life as well as instruction.
The poem's structure follows the cycle of the farming year.
items.explanation: Text 2 begins with a concession ('Few would deny') that the advice is accurate and that the poem follows the calendar. It also builds its own argument on the poem's village scenes. Its main clause then rejects Text 1's central claim: the poem is 'less a manual than a lament.' The view that the poem's main purpose is instruction belongs to Text 1 alone, so it is the statement both authors would NOT agree with.

B.why: You may have assumed that a critic who calls the poem a lament must doubt its farming advice. Text 2 says outright that 'few would deny' the advice is accurate, so both authors accept this.

C.why: You may have dismissed this because Text 1 treats the village scenes as mere 'color.' The question asks only whether both authors would agree that the scenes are in the poem. They do agree, and in fact Text 2's whole reading depends on them.

D.why: Text 1 says the books 'follow the farming calendar month by month,' and Text 2 grants that the structure 'mirrors the agricultural calendar.' This is shared ground, not the point of disagreement.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Hana Ostrow's woodcut series Harbor Hours (1927) documents working life on the Baltic docks. Its twenty prints show stevedores hauling nets, coiling rope, and mending hulls, and every winch and cleat is cut with an engineer's precision. Ostrow plainly set out to preserve a faithful record of the dockworkers' labor.

Text 2
Certainly the tackle in Harbor Hours is cut with exacting care, and the series never leaves the docks. But Ostrow printed each block repeatedly, carving more away between printings, so that in the final impressions the workers sink into solid black. Read as a whole, the series records less the labor itself than its vanishing from view.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT which statement?
choices: The series depicts people performing work at the docks.
Ostrow cut the equipment in the prints with great precision.
The series keeps its focus on the docks rather than elsewhere.
Ostrow's chief aim was to preserve a faithful record of dock labor.
items.explanation: Text 1 ends with the claim that Ostrow 'set out to preserve a faithful record,' and Text 2 is written to answer that sentence. Text 2 concedes the precise tackle and the dockside setting, and its own argument assumes the prints show workers. It then argues that the series records the labor's 'vanishing from view,' not the labor itself. A faithful record as Ostrow's chief aim is Text 1's view only, so it is the statement both authors would NOT agree with.

A.why: You may have focused on the image of workers sinking into black and decided Text 2 denies that the prints show labor. But figures can only disappear from prints that show them in the first place. Both authors agree that the series depicts dockworkers.

B.why: Text 2's 'Certainly the tackle... is cut with exacting care' grants this point. The 'But' that follows challenges what the series means, not how carefully it was cut.

C.why: Text 1 sets every print on the docks, and Text 2 says the series 'never leaves the docks.' Both authors agree on this.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: The Gauge at Pell Point is an 1894 novel by Harriet Coyle. Its main character, Nell Ambry, lives in a lighthouse on a rocky coast and keeps the daily weather log that her father began decades earlier. The log records rainfall, wind direction and air pressure for passing ships. Most of the novel takes place over one harsh winter. In an essay on the book, a literary critic claims that Nell keeps her weather records faithfully even when the conditions make the work unpleasant.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Gauge at Pell Point most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Nell loved the quiet hour after a storm, when the clouds broke apart and the harbor lay still and silver beneath them."
"Her father had kept the logbook for thirty years, and its pages had gone brown and soft from the damp of the tower."
"Though the sleet stung her cheeks and numbed her fingers, Nell climbed to the gauge at dawn and wrote down every figure."
"On mild mornings Nell would linger beside the barometer, idly tapping its glass and humming quietly to herself."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Nell keeps her records faithfully, and she does so even when conditions are unpleasant. In this line the sleet stings and numbs her (unpleasant conditions), yet she climbs to the gauge and records every figure (faithful record-keeping). It is the only choice that shows both parts.

A.why: This line has the right setting and a strong feeling about the weather, but Nell isn't recording anything, and the moment is calm rather than unpleasant. You were drawn by the matching mood and topic, but the line shows neither part of the claim.

B.why: This line describes the logbook and her father's history with it. It is about the right object, but it says nothing about Nell's own diligence or about hard conditions.

D.why: Nell is near the instruments here, but the mornings are mild and she is idling, not recording. This shows only half the claim at most and leaves out the unpleasant conditions entirely.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: The Valley Songbook is a 1931 novel by Tomas Varga. It follows Anselm Reiter, a musicologist who spends years collecting folk ballads from mountain villages before they are forgotten. Other scholars in the novel compete to publish first and to have collections named after themselves. Reiter is different. According to one reviewer, Reiter cares more about keeping the songs alive than about receiving credit for collecting them.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Valley Songbook most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: Reiter spent whole winters traveling from village to village, his notebook tucked inside his coat against the cold.
"I do not mind if no one recalls who wrote these tunes down," Reiter said, "so long as someone is still singing them."
Reiter was delighted when the city paper printed his portrait above a long article praising his new collection.
The oldest singer in the valley knew forty ballads, each of which she had learned as a girl from her own grandmother.
items.explanation: The claim compares two things: Reiter values the songs surviving more than he values getting credit. In this line he says he doesn't mind being forgotten (credit doesn't matter) as long as people keep singing the songs (survival matters). That puts both halves of the comparison in one line.

D.why: This line describes a singer and how the songs were passed down. It has the right subject, folk ballads, but tells you nothing about Reiter's attitude.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: On the Training of Runners is a 1908 book by the track coach Walter Prentiss. At the time, many coaches assumed that athletes improved simply by running as many miles as possible. Prentiss took a different view. Historians of sports science note that he argued rest was just as necessary for a runner's improvement as hard training.
items.stem: Which quotation from On the Training of Runners most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The runner should eat plain food, take very little sugar, and avoid all rich sauces in the days before a contest."
"No athlete ever won a race by training only when the mood suited him; the work must be done daily, in all weather."
"Sleep is a pleasant indulgence for the idle, but it does nothing to build the strength that a racer truly needs."
"The hard mile and the long sleep are partners in the making of a runner; neglect either one, and he will not improve."
items.explanation: The claim puts rest and hard training on equal footing as needs for improvement. This line calls the hard mile and the long sleep "partners" and says neglecting either one stops improvement. That shows both elements and their equal importance.

A.why: Diet is related to preparing for a race, but the line mentions neither rest nor training. It is on topic but doesn't address the claim.

B.why: This line stresses daily hard training, which is only one half of the claim. It leaves out rest completely. A quotation that matches part of the claim isn't enough.

C.why: This line says sleep does nothing to build strength, which is the opposite of the view the passage gives Prentiss.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: The Pump on Carrow Street is a 1952 play by Muriel Ostrander. It is set in a crowded city neighborhood during a cholera outbreak. The town physician, Dr. Imogen Hale, suspects that a shared public water pump is spreading the disease. The residents distrust her and keep using it. A theater scholar argues that the play presents Hale as someone who keeps warning the public even though her warnings are repeatedly ignored.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Pump on Carrow Street most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: HALE: "Every morning I post the notice on the pump, and every afternoon I find it torn down. Tomorrow I will post it again."
HALE: "The water from the northern spring runs clear and cold; I have tested it three times now and found nothing amiss."
HALE: "I have warned them quite enough. If they will not listen to reason, then let them drink whatever they please."
HALE: "Half the families on this street are sick now, and it is the youngest children who are suffering the worst."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Hale's warnings are ignored, and she keeps warning anyway. Her notice is torn down every day (ignored), and she says she will post it again tomorrow (she persists). This line shows both.

B.why: This line is about testing water, so it fits the public-health subject. But it describes a different water source and involves no warnings or resistance from the residents.

C.why: Here Hale gives up on warning people, which is the opposite of the persistence the claim describes.

D.why: This line comes from the right situation and has the urgent tone you might expect, but it only describes the outbreak. It shows no warning and no one ignoring her, so it misses both parts of the claim.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: "The Surveyor's Confession" is an 1887 poem by Edwin Marlowe. Its speaker is an aging mapmaker who has spent his life charting a small coastal town. Looking over his finished map, the speaker reflects on what his careful work achieved. In a study of Victorian poetry, one critic claims that the speaker regrets that his map, though accurate, cannot capture the life of the town.
items.stem: Which quotation from "The Surveyor's Confession" most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "My ink was black, my paper smooth and fine, / And I worked by candle long into the night."
"I drew each river's bend and every hill, / But not the voices calling down the lane."
"The finished chart held all the town contained— / Its songs, its fires, the faces at the door."
"Beyond the hills there lay a land unknown, / Whose roads no surveyor ever walked."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: the map is accurate, and it still fails to capture the town's life. In the first half of the line he drew every bend and hill (accuracy). In the second half he admits the voices in the lane are missing (the life left out). This line shows the full contrast.

A.why: This line shows the speaker working hard on the map, which fits the scene. But it says nothing about what the map leaves out, so the regret half of the claim is missing.

C.why: This line says the map captured everything, including songs and faces. That reverses the claim that the map cannot capture the town's life.

D.why: This line is about unmapped land beyond the town. That is a different limitation, not the one in the claim, which is the map's failure to capture the town's own life.

items.stimulus: The Millrace is a 1928 novel by Clara Dunmore. It is set in a river valley during a spring when heavy snowmelt swells the stream that drives the local grain mill. The mill's owner, Ezra Pell, knows that the stream can overflow its banks within hours once the thaw begins. Literary critics have noted that in the novel's early chapters, Ezra keeps a close watch on the rising water even while he is busy with his ordinary work: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Millrace most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Ezra had always loved the low sound of the stream, which seemed to him the oldest and steadiest voice in the whole valley."
"Even as he stacked the grain sacks, Ezra glanced every few minutes at the notched post by the millrace, noting how far the water had climbed."
"When the spring water rose, the neighbors down the lane carried their chairs and quilts to the upper rooms and waited for it to fall."
"Ezra finished hauling the grain sacks early that evening and sat out on the porch steps, his mind drifting far from the mill."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Ezra watches the rising water closely, and he does it while busy with his ordinary work. In choice B he is stacking grain sacks (ordinary work) and checking the marked post every few minutes to see how high the water has risen (close watch). It is the only quotation that shows both parts.

A.why: You went with the right mood and vocabulary. Ezra cares about the stream here, but the line shows neither part of the claim. He isn't tracking the water's rise, and he isn't working. Feeling something about the river is a related idea. It isn't the claim.

C.why: You picked a line from the right scene, the rising spring water, but it describes the neighbors. Ezra isn't in it. The claim is about what Ezra does, so a line about other people can't illustrate it.

D.why: You matched only half the claim. Ezra is doing his ordinary work, but then his mind drifts "far from the mill." That is the opposite of keeping a close watch on the water. The line works against the claim instead of supporting it.

items.stimulus: The Coal Leaves is a 1911 novel by Harriet Vossler. It follows Ada Kemble, a schoolteacher who spends her summers splitting shale at an abandoned quarry, looking for the imprints of ancient plants. The work is slow, and most slabs hold nothing at all. "Her back ached from the long hours bent over the bench, but she reached for another slab and lifted her hammer again."
"By evening she had set down her tools at last, too weary to lift even the smallest of her chisels."
"Ada loved the smell of the quarry in the early morning, when the wet shale glistened in the low sun."

D.why: You were drawn by the quarry setting and the warm tone. The line is about Ada enjoying the place, though. It shows neither fatigue nor persistence.

items.stimulus: "Plate and Acid" is a 1934 poem by Ines Harrow, who worked as an etcher. "The slip the acid kept, I keep as well; / by morning it is what the print is for."
"The stray scratch deepened overnight; I scraped / the copper smooth and started it again."
"No stroke, once bitten, ever can be called back; / the plate remembers what the hand forgot."

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. "What the hand forgot" does suggest an accident made permanent, so the line gets the first half right. But it says nothing about the speaker valuing the mark, and the claim needs both.

"Let the mills now have the market; I am glad / To lay my shuttle down and rest at last."

items.stimulus: Harlan Vosk's 1931 play The Tally Room is set in a fish cannery where workers are paid according to the total number of cans their whole line produces, not by individual output. choices: "Hurry yourself along, Tom, or the whole lot of us will be stuck here long past the evening whistle again."
"The bosses count the cans at the end of the line, and they pay the whole line together, not the single girl."
"I'll work at whatever pace suits me, Tom; my wage is my own affair and nobody else's business at all."
"Pick it up, Tom. Every can you miss on this line comes out of my pay envelope as well as out of yours."
items.explanation: The claim has a chain: Nell understands that pay is shared across the line, and that is why she pushes coworkers. items.stimulus: The Glass Meridian is a 1911 novel by Leonora Vance. Its central character, Professor Aldous Wren, spends decades at a small hilltop observatory tracking the motions of stars across the sky. "He hurried through each night's readings so that he might post them to the journal by the first morning mail."

"He cared little for the society's medals and twice that winter declined its invitation to lecture in the city."
items.explanation: The claim needs two things at once: Wren is exacting in his records, and he doesn't care whether anyone reads them. Choice C shows both. Timing transits "to the tenth of a second" is exactness, and shelving the ledgers where no colleague would look is indifference to readers.

B.why: Hurrying through readings is the opposite of exacting, and rushing to send them to a journal shows he wants them read. This line goes against both parts of the claim.

D.why: Turning down medals and lectures shows indifference to honors, which sounds close to the claim. But it isn't about whether his records get read, and it says nothing about how exact he is. You matched the tone, not the claim.

items.stimulus: Tobias Wren's 1874 memoir Gauge and Current recounts the eleven years he spent recording water levels on a lowland river for a canal company. "On the night of the great flood I read the post by lantern every hour, and by morning the water stood a full yard above the highest mark."
"My wife called the ledger my penance, for its columns rarely varied by an inch; still I kept it, rain or drought, until my hand could no longer hold a pen."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts. Wren finds the measuring monotonous, and he will not give it up anyway. per_choice.B: You may have stopped at 'nothing duller' and read the line as Wren disliking the work enough to quit. The second half reverses that: he would rather rise at dawn to read that board than do anything else. The line shows tedium and devotion together.

items.stimulus: Clara Weston's 1908 novel The Pump on Ashby Street follows Dr. Tobias Hale, a physician in a mill town where cases of cholera cluster around a single public well. Hale traces the illness to the well and asks local officials to close it. Weston portrays a widening gap between Hale and the town council: Hale treats the danger as urgent, while the council regards it as a minor matter, not worth the cost of acting.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Pump on Ashby Street most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Hale stood at the council table and named each child he had buried that week, but the aldermen asked only whether a new well would raise the tax rate."
"Hale had not slept in three nights; he walked from house to house with his bag, counting fevers and marking each stricken door in chalk."
"The aldermen listened gravely to Hale's report and voted that same evening, without a single dissent, to chain the pump handle shut."
"The mayor waved the matter aside at supper, remarking to his guests that the town had drunk from that pump for forty years."

C.why: Here the council takes Hale seriously and acts at once, which is the reverse of the claim. You may have chosen it because Hale and the council appear together in the same scene.

D.why: The mayor's remark does show officials brushing the danger aside, but Hale and his urgency are missing, and so is any mention of cost. You matched the dismissive tone and missed the other half of the gap.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: Forty Seasons on the Creek is an 1874 memoir by Elias Brandt, a Minnesota farmer who planted trial rows of unfamiliar wheat varieties beside his ordinary crop. His neighbor Sorensen planted only the seed his family had always used. Historians of agriculture often cite the memoir because Brandt presents his trials as worthwhile even in years when they produced a smaller harvest than his neighbor's fields.
items.stem: Which quotation from Forty Seasons on the Creek most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The new wheat outgrew every field along the creek that year, and Sorensen walked over twice to beg a sack of my seed for spring."
"I kept a ledger of every trial row, noting the day of sowing, the week's rainfall, and the height the stalks had reached each Sunday."
"My trial rows gave barely half what Sorensen reaped across the fence, and still I counted that summer well spent, for I learned what the soil refused."
"I have never trusted a man who will not try a new seed, and Sorensen would plant nothing that his grandfather had not planted first."
items.explanation: Narrow the claim to its two required parts: the trial crop yielded less than the neighbor's, and Brandt still valued the trial. In choice C, "barely half what Sorensen reaped" sets up the gap in the right direction, and "counted that summer well spent" shows that Brandt still valued the trial. The words "even in years when" in the claim mean the line has to show both parts at once.

A.why: In this line Brandt's wheat outyields his neighbor's, so the gap runs the wrong way. The claim is about valuing the trials when they did worse, not when they succeeded.

B.why: This line shows Brandt carefully running his trials, but it says nothing about a smaller harvest or about whether he felt the work was worthwhile. It is on topic but doesn't illustrate the claim.

D.why: This line contrasts Brandt's attitude with Sorensen's, which is a related point. It never compares their harvests or says the trials were worth a poorer yield. You picked up on the two men being set against each other and missed what the claim actually requires.

items.stimulus: In Marguerite Osei's 1923 novel The Tidewater Notebooks, Ada Lisle and her older brother, Tom, spend a summer on a rocky stretch of the Maine coast. Tom hopes to spot whales and seals offshore, while Ada is drawn to the small animals of the tide pools. One critic argues that Osei builds the novel on this contrast: Ada finds the tide pools far more absorbing than the large animals that fascinate her brother.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Tidewater Notebooks most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Ada could name every periwinkle and barnacle in the cove, and she kept their names in a notebook that she had bound with twine."
"Tom shouted that a seal had hauled out on the rocks, and Ada dropped her jar and ran to see it before it slipped back into the sea."
"Tom had read every book on whales in the village library and could recite the weight of a blue whale's heart to anyone who asked."
"While Tom scanned the horizon all morning for a whale's spout, Ada lay above a single pool, watching an anemone close around a shrimp."
items.explanation: The claim compares two things: Ada's interest in the tide pools and her lack of interest in the large animals that hold Tom's attention. Choice D shows both. C.why: This line shows Tom's interest in large animals, but Ada and the tide pools are missing. It covers one side of the contrast and leaves out the side the claim is mainly about.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: In Margaret Ilsley's 1894 novel The Glass at Ferrow Head, Hester Quayle keeps the weather records at her father's lighthouse on a stormy northern coast. The village fishermen forecast by signs, such as the color of the dawn or the behavior of gulls, while Hester's notebooks are filled with barometer readings. One critic argues that Ilsley presents Hester as relying on her instrument rather than on local lore even when its readings contradict what the sky itself appears to show: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Glass at Ferrow Head most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The sky over the harbor was cloudless, and old Tobin swore by his knee that no blow was coming; but the glass had dropped since noon, and Hester went down to keep the boats in."
"Hester had learned to read the barometer before she could read her primer, and she put more faith in its needle than in any saying the fishermen had about gulls or red mornings."
"Black clouds were piling over Ferrow Head, yet the glass held perfectly steady, and Hester stood at the window a long while, unable to say whether she believed the needle or her eyes."
"The fishermen laughed at the brass barometer in the keeper's window, calling it the lady's clock and declaring that no needle ever made had smelled a storm before a gull did."
items.explanation: The claim has three parts that must all hold: Hester (1) acts on the barometer (2) instead of local lore, (3) even when the barometer conflicts with what the sky shows. Put choice A in plain words: the sky is clear and a fisherman's sore knee says no storm is coming, but the barometer is falling, so Hester tells the boats to stay in. The clear sky conflicts with the falling barometer, Tobin's knee stands for the lore, and Hester acts on the instrument. All three parts are there.

B.why: You matched the first half of the claim. Hester does trust the needle over the fishermen's sayings, but nothing in this line puts the barometer in conflict with what the sky looks like. You took the 'instrument over lore' part as the whole claim and dropped 'even when it contradicts the sky.'

C.why: You spotted the conflict between the sky and the barometer, which is the hard part of the claim, and stopped there. But in this line Hester can't decide which to believe. That works against a claim that she relies on her instrument. Finding the conflict isn't enough; she also has to act on the barometer.

D.why: This line comes from the right scene, with the barometer up against fishermen's lore, but it describes the fishermen's scorn, not anything Hester believes or does. The claim is about Hester, and she doesn't appear in this line.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: Walter Brisco's 1923 novel The Furrow Year follows Ada Lunn, who takes over her late father's wheat farm and, on the advice of a county agent, begins planting clover in alternate years. Clover adds nitrogen to the soil, and the wheat sown in that field the following year draws on the stored nitrogen. A reviewer observed that over the course of the novel, Ada comes to value clover not for its own sake but for what it does for the wheat that follows it: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Furrow Year most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Ada, who had once thought clover a waste of good ground, came to love that acre for its purple heads and humming bees, though she knew it would never fill a single sack."
"Her father had called a clover field a field on holiday, and for years Ada had agreed with him, begrudging every acre she was obliged to leave out of wheat."
"The acre she had once grudged to clover now gave her the heaviest wheat on the farm, and Ada began to speak of the clover as if it were the first half of the wheat crop."
"The wheat on the east field came up thick and dark that June, taller than any Ada had ever grown, and the neighbors slowed their wagons at the fence to stare at it."
items.explanation: Break the claim into parts: Ada's view of clover (1) changes ('comes to value'), (2) she values it because of what it does for the next wheat crop, and (3) she does not value it for itself. In plain words, choice C says that the field Ada once resented losing to clover now grows her best wheat, and she starts treating the clover as part of the wheat crop. 'Once grudged' shows the change. Treating clover as 'the first half of the wheat crop' shows she values it only for what it does for the wheat. All three parts are there.

A.why: You saw that the claim describes a change of mind, and this line does show one. But Ada comes to love the clover for its flowers and bees, which is valuing it 'for its own sake,' the very reason the claim rules out. It even says the clover will never 'fill a sack,' so no crop benefit is involved. The tone fits; the reason is the opposite of the claim's.

B.why: This line shows only Ada's earlier view, when she resented clover as lost wheat ground. It is the starting point the claim describes moving away from. Nothing here shows her coming to value clover at all.

D.why: You brought the passage's nitrogen chain into the line. The wheat is impressive, but the quotation never mentions clover or what Ada thinks of it. It's the clover-to-wheat link and Ada's changed view that the claim needs, and you had to add both yourself.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: In Hester Calloway's 1911 novel The Fern Ledger, Agnes Ware spends her summers splitting shale along a Welsh riverbank, looking for fossil plants. Most of what she finds is fragmentary: the tip of a frond, half a stem, a leaf with no plant to belong to. Critic Lionel Dray argues that Agnes recognizes how incomplete her collection is but treats its gaps as a reason to keep searching rather than as a cause for regret: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Fern Ledger most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Every slab I split is a page torn from a book whose other pages the river carried off long before I was born."
"What the shale withholds from me I have simply not earned yet, so tomorrow I try the upper bank."
"I rose before the lark and worked the quarry face until my hands and sleeves were grey with dust."
"The professor says my ferns are common ones, but I would not trade them for all the orchids at Kew."
items.explanation: Break Dray's claim into its parts: Agnes (1) sees that her collection is incomplete, (2) responds by searching more, and (3) does not respond with regret. In B she names what the shale "withholds," which is the gap. She calls it something she has "not earned yet," so she isn't mourning it, and "tomorrow I try the upper bank" is the further search. All three parts are there.

A.why: You saw incompleteness, the first idea in the claim, and stopped. The torn page and the lost pages do show the gaps, but the tone is loss, which is the regret Dray says Agnes avoids, and nothing in the line has her searching again. This is the half-the-claim trap.

C.why: You matched hard work to "keep searching." The line shows effort, but it says nothing about gaps in the collection, and without the gaps there is nothing for her effort to be a response to.

D.why: You picked the line that shows how attached Agnes is to her fossils. Valuing ordinary specimens is a separate point from seeing the collection's gaps and digging further because of them.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: Oriel Mabry's 1928 play The Tuning Fork follows Bertram Hale, a collector who travels through mining villages writing down folk songs in standard musical notation. Hale is no naive enthusiast. As one theater historian notes, he believes that putting a song on paper changes it, yet he keeps transcribing because he judges an altered song to be better than one that disappears unrecorded: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Tuning Fork most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Put it on the staff and you've pinned a moth to a card. It's still a moth, but it will never fly again."
"Old Maddock sings it different every Sunday, and every Sunday, mind you, it's exactly the right way."
"I know my notation flattens her singing, but a flattened song outlives a song that nobody kept."
"When these singers are gone, their songs go with them, and no one in the city will even notice."
items.explanation: The claim has three parts: (1) writing a song down changes it, (2) Hale keeps doing it anyway, and (3) his reason is that an altered song is better than a lost one. In C, "my notation flattens her singing" is the change, and "a flattened song outlives a song that nobody kept" weighs the altered version against loss and prefers it. The present-tense "I know... but" shows him carrying on.

A.why: The pinned moth is a strong picture of notation changing a song, so it matches the first part. It gives no reason for continuing, and taken alone it sounds like a case against transcribing. This is the half-the-claim trap.

B.why: The line is about how a song varies from one performance to the next, which is the same general topic. It doesn't say that writing the song down changes it, and it gives no reason to keep transcribing.

D.why: You found the fear of loss, which is Hale's motive, and stopped there. The line never admits that notation changes a song, so the trade-off at the center of the claim is missing.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: In Notes from the Water Ward (1874), physician Edwin Strachan recounts tracing a cholera outbreak in a crowded district of Leeds to a single contaminated pump. The book is unusual among medical memoirs of its period. Strachan credits a resident, rather than his own training, with first identifying the source, and he admits that he had initially dismissed what she told him: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from Notes from the Water Ward most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "In March a laundress told me the pump water smelled of the drain; I noted her down as a gossip, and she was right."
"Kell Street knew its own water better than any physician did, and in time I learned to ask before I sampled it."
"Once the pump handle was taken off, the cases fell away within the week, just as my own figures had predicted."
"The families there received me kindly, though they had little reason to trust a stranger in a frock coat."
items.explanation: Three things have to hold: (1) a resident identified the source, (2) Strachan gives her the credit, and (3) he had first dismissed her. In A, the laundress connects the pump to the drain, which is the source. "I noted her down as a gossip" is the dismissal, and "she was right" gives her the credit. No other choice includes the dismissal.

B.why: This line does credit the residents over physicians, which is the claim's main attitude, so it survives a first check. It speaks about the street in general, though. No resident identifies the pump, and "in time I learned" isn't the same as admitting he dismissed something specific he was told. You read more into it than it says.

C.why: This is the right scene, since the pump is the source, but the credit goes to the wrong person. "Just as my own figures had predicted" credits Strachan's own calculations, the opposite of what the claim says.

D.why: The line is about how the residents treated Strachan, not about who found the source of the outbreak. It's on topic but has nothing to do with the claim.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: Clara Densmore's 1902 poem "Warp and Weft" is spoken by a woman who works a loom in a Lancashire cotton mill. Many mill poems of the era protest the anonymity of factory labor. Densmore's speaker, one critic observes, also recognizes that the cloth she makes will reach strangers who will never know who made it, but she finds that anonymity consoling rather than bitter: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from "Warp and Weft" most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The shuttle's click is all my song from lamplight unto lamp; / my fingers know the threads by heart, though cold and stiff and damp."
"Some merchant sells the bolt I wove and pockets what I'm owed; / my name goes nowhere with the cloth along the river road."
"I pray the cloth will keep her warm, whoever she may be, / and wonder if by firelight she ever thinks of me."
"Some woman in a distant town will wear my Tuesday on her sleeve; / she'll never learn who made it, and I find I do not grieve."
items.explanation: The claim needs (1) cloth reaching strangers, (2) the maker staying unknown, and (3) the speaker being at peace with that. In D, the "woman in a distant town" is the stranger, "she'll never learn who made it" is the anonymity, and "I find I do not grieve" is the consolation. Only this line has all three.

A.why: The line shows the speaker's labor and skill, but nothing travels to a stranger and the question of being known never comes up. It gets the setting right and says nothing about the claim.

B.why: Here the cloth does travel and her name doesn't go with it, so the anonymity is there. The feeling is resentment over pay withheld, which is the bitterness the claim says she avoids. This is the half-the-claim trap: the right situation with the opposite attitude.

C.why: The warm tone and the unknown wearer make this look right. But wondering whether the wearer "ever thinks of me" shows a wish to be known, so she hasn't accepted the anonymity. You caught the tone and missed the attitude.

items.stimulus: Darnell Okafor's 1957 novel The Marsh Census centers on Ruth Pell, a warden who counts birds on a coastal reserve that a county council plans partly to drain. items.stimulus: In Imelda Rusk's 1966 short story "The Second Trench," archaeologist Nathaniel Abara directs a dig whose sponsors expect treasure. Abara's own interests lie elsewhere. One reviewer argues that Abara values the plain evidence of ordinary life above spectacular finds, while recognizing that it is the spectacular finds that keep his excavation funded: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from "The Second Trench" most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The museum men want a gold cup for their cases, and they'll pay for next season only if we hand them one."
"Give me a midden full of fish bones over a king's tomb any day, but it's the tomb that pays for the shovels."
"A broken cooking pot will tell you more about how these people lived than any crown ever could."
"We found the gold cup on a Tuesday, and by Friday every newspaper in the capital had sent a man."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: (1) Abara prefers ordinary evidence to spectacular finds, and (2) he knows the spectacular finds pay for the dig. In B, "a midden full of fish bones over a king's tomb" is the preference, and "it's the tomb that pays for the shovels" is the funding. Only B has both.

A.why: You found the funding half: sponsors pay only for treasure. The line never shows Abara preferring ordinary evidence, so his own values are missing.

D.why: Newspaper attention is connected to spectacular finds, but it isn't funding, and Abara's own preference never appears. This is a detail from the right scene that doesn't support the claim.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: Ambrose Feld's 1934 novel The Span follows Clara Voss, a young engineer overseeing a steel bridge across a tidal river. Her superiors urge her to rely on the load tables published by the national Ministry of Works. Voss's habit of mind, as the novel presents it, is precise: she will not accept a load figure simply because an authority has published it, but she will accept one once her own tests have produced it more than once: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Span most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The Ministry's tables say the girder will hold, and the Ministry has been wrong before, so we test it."
"I loaded the girder three times and got the same sag each time; that is a number I can build on."
"The Ministry says it will hold. I'll say so too, once my third loading agrees with my first two."
"My father built bridges by feel and memory, and not one of them has fallen in forty years."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: (1) a published figure isn't enough for Voss by itself, and (2) she accepts a figure after her own tests have produced it more than once. A.why: This line refuses to take the Ministry on trust and calls for testing, so it holds up after your first good observation. It never says how many tests, though, and the claim depends on "more than once." Taking "we test it" as repeated testing reads in something the line doesn't contain.

B.why: You have the repeated-test half: three loadings, the same result, and a number she accepts. No authority appears, so the line can't show her refusing to accept a published figure.

D.why: Building by feel and memory goes against Voss's reliance on measurement. The line also comes from her father, not her, so it shows nothing about her habit of mind.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: In The Diet Kitchen (1923), dietitian Marguerite Lowell draws on two decades of running a children's convalescent home. The book was written partly to correct the nutrition pamphlets of the day, which relied on explaining to children why certain foods were healthful. Lowell holds that children come to eat a food by watching adults enjoy it, not by hearing that it is good for them: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Diet Kitchen most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Tell a child that spinach builds the blood and he will believe every word of it, and leave it on his plate."
"A child will copy the adult who feeds him in nearly everything, from how he holds a fork to when he sleeps."
"Children who were allowed to choose their own vegetables at market ate more of them at supper that night."
"One boy ate turnips for a month because I ate them in front of him, plainly and with relish, and said nothing."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: (1) children take up a food by watching an adult enjoy it, and (2) not through being told it is healthful. In D, the boy eats turnips "because I ate them in front of him," which is the watching. "With relish" is the enjoyment, and "said nothing" rules out telling. All of it is shown in one line.

A.why: This line shows that telling fails, which is the second half of the claim, and its wry tone sounds like Lowell. It never shows what does work: no adult eats anything, and no child takes up a food. This is the half-the-claim trap.

B.why: This is imitation in general, applied to forks and bedtimes. The claim is narrower: watching an adult enjoy a particular food. A broad statement about copying doesn't show that narrower point, and it leaves out the contrast with telling.

C.why: This credits choosing for oneself, which is a different explanation for why children eat a food. No adult is shown eating anything, so the line doesn't support Lowell's claim.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists have long assumed that raising the minimum wage pushes employers to cut jobs. However, a growing body of research suggests that the effect may be smaller than predicted. In a study of restaurants on either side of a state border, economist Lena Okafor found that employment in the state that raised its wage grew at nearly the same rate as employment in the neighboring state that did not. Okafor argues that employers often absorb higher wages through lower staff turnover rather than through layoffs.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor's study confirmed the long-held assumption that higher minimum wages lead employers to cut jobs.
Restaurants in the state that raised its minimum wage saw their employment grow during the study.
Research suggests that raising the minimum wage may reduce employment less than economists have expected.
Raising the minimum wage reliably increases employment because workers leave their jobs less often.
items.explanation: The word 'However' marks the turn in this passage. The old assumption is set up so it can be questioned, and Okafor's border study is the evidence for the newer view. Choice C covers the assumption, the challenge to it and the study, and it keeps the passage's hedge ('may').

A.why: You took the assumption in the first sentence for the conclusion. Okafor's findings challenge that assumption. They don't confirm it.

B.why: You picked a detail from the study that is roughly accurate. It describes one result, but it leaves out the passage's point that this result challenges a long-held assumption.

D.why: You stretched the claim too far. The passage says job losses may be smaller than expected. It never says higher wages reliably increase employment.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Many endurance athletes believe that stretching before a race helps prevent injury. Researchers at a Norwegian sports institute tested this belief by assigning 300 recreational runners to either a stretching routine or a light jogging warm-up for twelve weeks. The two groups reported almost identical numbers of injuries. The researchers concluded that pre-race stretching, though popular, appears to offer little protection against injury.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The runners in the study followed their assigned warm-up routines for a period of twelve weeks.
A study found that stretching before running does little to prevent injury, despite a common belief.
Light jogging is the most effective warm-up for runners who want to avoid injury before a race.
Most endurance athletes have stopped stretching before races because they doubt it prevents injury.
items.explanation: The last sentence sums up the passage: stretching before a race, though popular, offers little protection against injury. Choice B covers both the common belief and the study's finding that undercuts it.

A.why: You chose a true detail about how the study was set up. The length of the study isn't what the passage is trying to show.

C.why: You went beyond the evidence. The two groups had about the same number of injuries, so the study doesn't show that jogging works better than stretching, let alone that it's the most effective warm-up.

D.why: You reversed what the passage says about athletes. It says many of them believe stretching prevents injury, not that they have stopped doing it.

items.stimulus: For decades, archaeologists credited the stone terraces at a hillside site in the Andes to the Inca, who controlled the region in the fifteenth century. However, recent radiocarbon dating of charcoal buried beneath the lowest terrace walls indicates that the terraces were built roughly three hundred years before the Inca arrived. items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Inca controlled the Andean region where the stone terraces are found during the fifteenth century.
Radiocarbon dating shows that the Inca borrowed their farming methods from earlier Andean communities.
Recent evidence confirms that the Inca built the terraces soon after they arrived in the region.
New dating evidence suggests that the terraces were built by a community that predated the Inca.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the old view that the Inca built the terraces, then turns with 'However' to the dating evidence. What comes after the turn is the author's point: an earlier community probably built them. Choice D says this and keeps the hedge ('suggests').

A.why: You picked background from the first sentence. It's accurate, but the passage mentions it only to set up the older view that the new evidence corrects.

B.why: You added a claim the passage never makes. The dating shows when the terraces were built, not whether the Inca borrowed anyone's farming methods.

C.why: You stopped at the older view. The dating places the terraces about three hundred years before the Inca arrived, so it undercuts that view.

Shredded plastic is now the standard ingredient in asphalt roads throughout the Netherlands.
The Dutch test road was two kilometers long and carried heavy truck traffic for three years.
Roads made with recycled plastic cracked more often than conventional roads but cost less to build.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Fermented foods such as yogurt and kimchi contain live bacteria, and some researchers have proposed that eating them may strengthen the immune system. In a small trial, adults who ate several servings of fermented foods daily for ten weeks showed lower levels of certain inflammation markers than adults who did not. The researchers caution, however, that the trial was brief and that larger studies are needed before such foods can be recommended for immune health.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Yogurt and kimchi are among the fermented foods that researchers say contain live bacteria.
Eating fermented foods daily has been proven to protect adults from illnesses linked to inflammation.
A small trial offers early support for fermented foods aiding immunity, but more research is needed.
The trial found that fermented foods had no measurable effect on the inflammation levels of adults.
items.explanation: The hedge words ('may', 'small', 'brief', 'larger studies are needed') limit how strong the claim can be. The passage reports a promising result and then warns that it isn't conclusive. Choice C includes both the promise and the warning.

A.why: You picked a background fact from the first sentence. It names the foods but says nothing about the trial or the researchers' caution.

B.why: You ignored the hedges. The researchers say more studies are needed, so nothing has been 'proven', and the trial measured inflammation markers, not illnesses.

D.why: You reversed the result. Adults who ate fermented foods had lower levels of some inflammation markers, which is a measurable effect.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Immunologists have long assumed that innate immune cells such as macrophages, unlike T cells and B cells, keep no memory of past infections. Recent work suggests that this view is incomplete. In a study led by immunologist Rafaela Okonjo, mice whose macrophages had been exposed to a harmless fungal compound responded more quickly to an unrelated bacterial infection weeks later. The macrophages appeared to keep a kind of readiness from their earlier encounter, an effect researchers now call "trained immunity."
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okonjo's study found that macrophages lose any readiness from an earlier encounter within a few weeks.
Research suggests that innate immune cells may keep a form of memory, which challenges a long-held assumption.
In Okonjo's study, the macrophages of mice were exposed to a harmless compound taken from a fungus.
Trained immunity makes innate immune cells just as effective as T cells and B cells at fighting infections.
items.explanation: The passage sets up an old assumption (innate cells have no memory), says it is incomplete, and then gives Okonjo's study as evidence that macrophages can keep a kind of readiness. Choice B covers both parts: the evidence and the assumption it challenges. Its hedge ('suggests', 'may') matches the passage's 'suggests' and 'appeared to'.

A.why: You reversed the finding. The macrophages responded more quickly weeks later, so they kept their readiness rather than losing it.

C.why: This detail is accurate, but it only describes how the study was set up. It leaves out what the study found and why that finding matters, so it is too narrow to be the main idea.

D.why: The passage never compares how effective innate cells are with T cells and B cells. You stretched 'a kind of readiness' into a much bigger claim than the text supports.

A songbook printed in a distant port city during the 1790s included a number of popular dance tunes.
Most folk music traditions that seem local actually began as tunes printed in city songbooks.
Evidence suggests that the Ardel Valley's fiddle tunes likely drew in part on music from outside the region.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the 1850s, surveyor Ines Calloway set out to map the Merrow River delta, a maze of channels that changed shape from year to year. She measured channel depths by hand, recorded which channels shifted after floods, and asked local boat pilots about routes that opened and closed with the seasons. Because she documented how the delta moved rather than fixing it at a single moment, her map stayed useful to navigators for decades after other maps of the delta had gone out of date.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Calloway's map stayed useful for decades because it recorded how the delta changed over time.
Calloway asked local boat pilots about routes that opened and closed with the seasons.
Calloway's methods became the standard for mapmakers of river deltas around the world.
Calloway's map soon went out of date because the delta's channels shifted after floods.
items.explanation: The middle sentence lists Calloway's methods, and the last sentence sums them up: because she recorded how the delta moved, her map stayed useful for decades. Choice A states that verdict and the reason for it, so it covers the whole passage.

B.why: This is true, but it is only one of the three methods in the middle sentence. It leaves out the result the passage builds toward, so it is too narrow.

C.why: The passage says only that her map stayed useful to navigators of this one delta. It never says that other mapmakers anywhere adopted her methods.

D.why: You reversed the outcome. Other maps went out of date, but Calloway's stayed useful because she accounted for the shifting channels.

items.stimulus: Linguists have long observed that words people use often tend to grow shorter over time. A study by linguist Mireille Danso offers a clear case. Danso recorded fish sellers in a coastal market who name one particular species dozens of times each day. Danso's study shows that coastal speakers shorten nearly all of their words more than inland speakers do.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim: words used often tend to get shorter. Everything after it is one example, introduced as 'a clear case.' The sellers say the fish's name constantly and use a short form, and the villagers rarely say it and keep the long form. Choice C covers both the general claim and the study that supports it, and it doesn't claim more than the text does.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: For decades, engineers designing pedestrian bridges in the city of Varn concentrated on the strength of the main beams, assuming those beams would need the most repair over a bridge's life. However, a 2019 survey of the city's forty footbridges found that most repairs had involved something else: the small joints that let each bridge's deck expand in summer heat. Inspectors now check these joints first.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: A survey confirmed that the main beams were the footbridge parts that most often needed repair, as engineers expected.
A survey revealed that expansion joints, rather than main beams, were the footbridge parts most often needing repair.
Footbridge decks in Varn expand during summer heat, so they are built with small joints that allow them to move.
A survey showed that expansion joints cause most of the repairs needed by bridges of every type around the world.
items.explanation: The passage first describes what engineers expected: the main beams would need the most repair. Then 'However' introduces what the survey actually found, which was that the expansion joints needed most of the repairs. The final sentence describes what changed as a result. Choice B states this correction, and it stays within the forty footbridges that were surveyed.

A.why: This repeats the engineers' old assumption as if the survey had confirmed it. The word 'However' signals that the survey found the opposite. You read the setup and missed the turn.

C.why: The text does say the joints let the deck expand in heat, but that's only background to explain what the joints are. It doesn't mention the expectation, the survey, or the finding. You chose a true detail instead of the main point.

D.why: The survey covered forty footbridges in one city. Nothing in the text supports a claim about 'bridges of every type around the world.' You started with the right finding and then stretched it far beyond the evidence.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Many cities are replacing parking spaces with small public seating areas. In one riverside neighborhood, planners converted twelve curbside spaces into benches and planters. Within a year, nearby cafés reported more customers, and residents said the street felt safer at night. The project suggests that giving up a few parking spaces can make a street more useful to the people who walk along it.
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
choices: Nearby cafés gained customers after twelve parking spaces were removed.
Turning some parking into seating can make a street more useful to people.
Cities should remove all their parking to make streets safer at night.
Residents objected when planners replaced parking with benches and planters.
items.explanation: The first sentence names a trend, the middle sentences give one example, and the last sentence says what the example shows. Choice B is the only one that covers all of that: some parking becomes seating, and the street works better for people. This scope check (does the choice cover every sentence?) is the first step on every SAT main-idea question about an informational passage.

A.why: This is true, but it comes from one sentence in the middle. You picked a correct detail that is only part of the point. The passage uses the cafés as evidence for a larger claim.

D.why: The passage reports good results: more customers, and a street that felt safer. It mentions no objections. Go back to the passage before you accept a choice.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Woodcut printing is often thought of as a crude method suited only to bold, simple images. However, some eighteenth-century Japanese printers used it to produce remarkably subtle work. By carving a separate block for each color and aligning the paper with small notches, they layered as many as twenty colors into a single print with soft, precise shading.
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
choices: Some printers carved small notches into their blocks to help align the paper.
Woodcut is a crude method that is best suited to bold and simple images.
Woodcut printing, often seen as crude, could produce very subtle images.
Japanese woodcuts were the most technically advanced prints ever made.
items.explanation: The passage opens with a common view and then turns at 'However.' What comes after the turn is what the author believes: woodcut could be subtle. The last sentence explains how that was done. Choice C covers the view, the correction, and the evidence. The SAT often builds main-idea passages around a 'However' turn, and this habit helps with those.

A.why: The notches are a real detail, but they are only one part of how the printers worked. You picked an accurate piece of the final sentence instead of the point it supports.

B.why: This is the view the passage sets up only to correct. You stopped reading before 'However,' which is the word that tells you the author disagrees.

D.why: The passage says some printers did remarkably subtle work. It never compares them with every print ever made. 'Most advanced ever' is a much bigger claim than the text supports.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Medieval music manuscripts rarely record how fast a piece should be sung, so some musicologists look to other kinds of evidence. One researcher noticed that a monastery's daily schedule set aside only about ten minutes for a certain chant. If the monks kept to that schedule, the chant was likely sung much faster than it is usually performed today.
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
choices: A monastery's daily schedule set aside about ten minutes for one chant.
Medieval manuscripts give exact singing speeds for most of their chants.
Modern singers perform every medieval chant far more slowly than they should.
A monastery schedule points to one chant once being sung faster than today.
items.explanation: The passage goes from a problem (no tempo markings) to a clue (the schedule) to a careful conclusion about one chant ('if,' 'likely'). Choice D covers all three and makes the claim no stronger than the text does. Matching a choice's strength to hedge words like 'likely' is something you will need on real main-idea questions.

A.why: The passage does say this, but it is the clue and not the conclusion. You picked the most vivid fact, the ten minutes, instead of what the passage uses that fact to show.

B.why: The first sentence says manuscripts 'rarely record' speed. This choice says the opposite.

C.why: The passage is about one chant, and it hedges with 'if' and 'likely.' This choice covers every chant and sounds certain. It claims far more than the evidence allows.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Engineers inspecting an old stone bridge found that its arches had shifted only a few millimeters in a century. Its foundations rested on bedrock rather than soft clay. Its builders had also left channels that let floodwater pass beneath the road instead of pushing against it. Together, these features explain why the bridge has outlasted many newer ones nearby.
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
choices: Several features of its design explain why the old bridge has lasted so long.
The bridge's foundations were built on bedrock rather than on soft clay.
Floodwater has slowly weakened the arches of the old stone bridge over time.
Stone bridges always last longer than bridges made from newer materials.
items.explanation: The middle sentences list separate facts, and the last sentence ('Together...') combines them into one conclusion. Choice A is that conclusion. When a passage ends by adding up its details, the main idea is usually the sum and not any single item. You will see this pattern on SAT main-idea questions.

B.why: This is accurate, but it is one of the features, not the point they add up to. You chose a single correct sentence when the passage is doing more than that.

C.why: The passage says the channels let floodwater pass beneath the bridge, and that the arches barely moved. It does not say the arches were weakened.

D.why: The passage is about one bridge and the newer bridges near it. 'Always' and 'stone bridges' in general go well beyond what it says.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Fossil leaves can tell scientists about climates of the distant past. Living plants with smooth-edged leaves are more common in warm regions, while plants with toothed leaf edges are more common in cool regions. By counting the share of smooth-edged fossil leaves found at a site, researchers can estimate how warm that area was millions of years ago.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Plants with toothed leaf edges tend to be more common in cool regions than in warm ones.
Fossil leaves allow scientists to know the exact daily weather of any ancient landscape.
The edges of fossil leaves can help scientists estimate how warm a place once was.
A high share of smooth-edged fossil leaves shows that a site was once quite cool.
items.explanation: Before reading the choices, sum up what the whole passage builds toward: the first sentence says fossil leaves reveal past climates, the second explains the link between leaf edges and temperature, and the last says this lets researchers estimate ancient warmth. Choice C covers all three sentences and claims no more than the text does ('estimate', not 'know exactly'). This is the scope test you'll use on every main-idea question: the right answer covers the whole passage and nothing outside it.

A.why: This statement is true, but it repeats only the second sentence. You picked a detail you could check against the text and stopped there. The passage does more than this: it uses that pattern to estimate ancient temperatures. Ask whether the passage does more than the choice says. Here it does, so the choice is too narrow.

B.why: You stretched the topic past what the text says. The passage says researchers can estimate how warm an area was. It never says they can know the exact daily weather, and it never says this works for any landscape. Words like 'exact' and 'any' make the claim too broad.

D.why: This reverses the passage. Smooth-edged leaves are linked to warm regions, so a high share of them points to a warm site, not a cool one. You probably mixed up which leaf edge goes with which climate. Go back and find the line before you trust your memory of it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Seismologists have generally regarded slow slip events, in which a fault creeps for weeks without producing noticeable shaking, as a kind of safety valve: by releasing built-up stress gradually, they were thought to lower the odds of a large earthquake. However, seismologist Mereana Tuhi's analysis of the Hikurangi margin off New Zealand found that several slow slip events shifted stress onto neighboring locked sections of the fault, where swarms of small earthquakes followed. Tuhi notes that her data cannot show whether major quakes become more likely, but she argues that slow slip should no longer be viewed simply as a release of danger.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Swarms of small earthquakes occurred on locked sections of the Hikurangi margin after several slow slip events.
Slow slip events release stress so gradually that small earthquakes seldom follow them along the Hikurangi margin.
Evidence that slow slip events can shift stress to nearby fault sections challenges the view that they simply reduce earthquake risk.
Tuhi's analysis demonstrates that slow slip events make major earthquakes more likely on neighboring fault sections.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the accepted view that slow slip is a safety valve. After 'However,' it brings in Tuhi's finding that slow slip can move stress onto neighboring sections, and it ends with her argument that the old view is too simple. Choice C covers the expected view, the finding and the conclusion without claiming more than Tuhi does.

A.why: You picked a detail that is accurate but only one step in the argument. The swarms are evidence. The passage uses them to challenge an assumption, and this choice leaves that challenge out.

B.why: You probably recognised 'release stress' from the opening and stopped reading. The passage says swarms of small earthquakes did follow slow slip, which is the opposite of 'seldom follow.'

D.why: You missed the hedge. Tuhi explicitly says her data cannot show whether major quakes become more likely, so 'demonstrates' claims something she refuses to claim.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Fossil leaves record not only which plants once grew in a place but also the climate they grew in. Among living woody plants, species with smooth leaf edges are more common in warm regions, while toothed edges predominate in cool ones. For example, when paleobotanist Ines Varga examined a 52-million-year-old leaf bed in the Dunmore Formation, she found that only about a fifth of its species had toothed edges, pointing to a warm climate. That estimate closely matched temperatures inferred independently from chemical signatures in nearby marine sediments.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Only about a fifth of the species in the Dunmore Formation leaf bed had leaves with toothed edges.
The shapes of fossil leaves can provide evidence about ancient climates, as Varga's study of one leaf bed illustrates.
Leaf shape gives more accurate estimates of ancient temperatures than chemical signatures in marine sediments do.
Fossil leaf beds reveal much about which plants once grew in a place but little about the climates of the past.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes the general claim that fossil leaves record climate. Everything after 'For example' is one case that supports it. Choice B states the general claim and ties Varga's study to it, so it covers the whole passage.

A.why: You chose a statistic from the example. It is correct, but it is there only to support the opening claim about what fossil leaves can reveal.

C.why: You read a ranking into the passage. The two estimates 'closely matched,' and the text never says leaf shape is more accurate than the sediment chemistry.

D.why: The first half of this choice matches the opening, but the second half reverses it. The passage's point is that fossil leaves reveal climate as well as plants.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Immunologists have traditionally divided the immune system into two branches: an adaptive branch that remembers specific pathogens and an innate branch that responds to every threat as if meeting it for the first time. Recent studies suggest this division may be too tidy. After people receive certain vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine for tuberculosis, their monocytes, a type of innate immune cell, can respond more vigorously to unrelated microbes for several months. The effect appears briefer and far less targeted than adaptive memory, but it suggests the innate branch may be capable of a limited kind of memory.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: After BCG vaccination, monocytes can respond more vigorously to unrelated microbes for several months.
Innate immune cells appear to remember specific pathogens as durably and precisely as adaptive cells do.
Vaccines such as BCG can protect people against nearly any microbe by strengthening their innate immune cells.
The innate immune branch, long thought to lack memory, may possess a limited and less targeted form of it.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the traditional split, says it 'may be too tidy,' gives the BCG evidence, and ends with a hedged conclusion that innate cells may have a limited memory. Choice D keeps both the claim and its limits: 'may' and 'limited and less targeted.'

A.why: You chose the evidence instead of what it shows. The monocyte finding is accurate, but the passage uses it to question how immunologists divide the immune system.

B.why: You kept 'innate cells remember' and dropped the qualification. The passage says the effect is briefer and far less targeted than adaptive memory, not equally durable and precise.

C.why: You stretched the finding into a big claim about protection. The text reports stronger responses to some unrelated microbes for months. It never says people are protected against nearly any microbe.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Print collectors have long prized the earliest impressions from a run, assuming that later ones show a block worn down by repeated pressing. The linocuts of Hedda Lorne, a printmaker active in the 1920s, complicate that assumption. Lorne regularly recut her blocks between printings, adding figures and deepening shadows, and she adjusted her inks from one batch to the next. In letters, she called her late impressions 'the finished picture.' For Lorne's work, then, a later impression may be not a degraded copy but the version she most intended.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: For Lorne's linocuts, later impressions may represent the artist's intended work rather than inferior copies.
Lorne adjusted the inks she used for her linocuts from one batch of impressions to the next.
Later impressions of prints are generally more valuable than early ones, as Lorne's letters demonstrate.
Lorne's linocuts confirm that early impressions preserve details that are lost as a block wears down.

B.why: You picked one of the supporting facts. It is true, but it is only one piece of evidence behind the conclusion in the last sentence.

C.why: You widened a claim about one artist to prints in general and added a claim about value that the passage never makes.

D.why: This repeats the collectors' assumption that the passage says Lorne's work complicates. Her prints challenge that view instead of confirming it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Dietary guidelines usually treat fiber as a single nutrient, recommending a daily total in grams. However, research led by nutrition scientist Priya Anand suggests that total may be only part of the story. Different fibers feed different gut bacteria, and in Anand's trial, an inulin supplement sharply raised levels of beneficial Bifidobacterium in most participants but barely changed them in others, depending on which microbes each person already carried. Anand concludes that fiber's effects likely depend on both the kind of fiber and the eater's existing gut community.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: In Anand's trial, an inulin supplement raised levels of Bifidobacterium in most of the participants.
Fiber supplements do not benefit people whose gut bacteria differ from those of most other people.
Fiber's effects may depend on the type of fiber and a person's gut microbes, not only on the total eaten.
Anand's research confirms that all types of fiber affect the gut's bacteria in much the same way.
items.explanation: After 'However,' the passage argues that a daily total is only part of the story, and Anand's conclusion names the two factors that also matter. Choice C gives both factors, contrasts them with the single-total view, and keeps the hedge.

A.why: You chose half of one trial result. It leaves out the participants who barely changed, and that variation is the point the passage is making.

B.why: You turned 'barely changed' Bifidobacterium levels in some people into 'no benefit' for a whole group. The passage never measures overall benefit and never makes that claim.

D.why: The passage says different fibers feed different bacteria. That is the opposite of claiming all fibers act in much the same way.
