items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the decade after beavers were reintroduced to a river in the Scottish Borders, surveys recorded a marked rise in the number of dragonfly species along its banks. Ecologist Callum Reid considers it plausible that the beavers were responsible, since their dams create the still, plant-rich ponds in which many dragonfly larvae thrive. But the same decade also brought new limits on fertilizer runoff from nearby farms, which may have improved water quality. Establishing the beavers' role, Reid argues, will require comparing this river with similar ones where beavers are absent.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The reintroduction of beavers caused the number of dragonfly species along the river to rise.
Beavers may explain the river's rise in dragonfly species, but confirming this requires further comparison.
New limits on fertilizer runoff from nearby farms took effect during the decade after beavers returned.
Reid argues that reduced fertilizer runoff, not beaver ponds, explains the rise in dragonfly species.
items.explanation: Reid grants that the beaver explanation is plausible, points out a competing cause, and says more comparison is needed. Choice B matches that structure: a limited concession ('may') followed by the call for more evidence.

A.why: You treated 'plausible' as proven. The passage raises another possible cause and says the beavers' role has not yet been established.

C.why: You picked a detail from the middle of the passage. The runoff limits matter only because they complicate the beaver explanation, and this choice leaves that out.

D.why: You misattributed a conclusion to Reid. He says the runoff limits 'may have' mattered but does not rule out the beavers. He argues that the question is still open.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Refuse heaps, or middens, were once excavated mainly for the intact objects that might be buried in them. Archaeologists now increasingly read middens as records of changing everyday choices. At the site of Tel Harun, for instance, Sana Idris's team found that across roughly a century of deposits, deer bones gradually gave way to sheep bones while broken loom weights, used to tension threads on a weaving frame, became more common. Idris argues that the layers trace households shifting from hunting toward herding, likely in part to supply wool.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Sheep bones gradually replaced deer bones over about a century of deposits at Tel Harun.
Middens reveal more about ancient societies than any other kind of archaeological evidence does.
Middens are valued by archaeologists mainly because they preserve intact objects such as loom weights.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The 1914 anthology Songs of the Northern Dales has always been credited to the collector Albert Fenwick, whose name alone appears on its title page. However, Fenwick's field notebooks, recently catalogued by musicologist Dana Okafor, tell a different story. Most of the transcriptions in them are in the hand of his assistant, Mabel Hurst, and notes in the margins show Hurst insisting on preserving singers' irregular rhythms, which Fenwick had wanted to smooth out. Okafor argues that the anthology's distinctive character owes as much to Hurst as to Fenwick.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Hurst insisted on preserving the irregular rhythms of singers, which Fenwick had wanted to smooth out.
Fenwick's notebooks show that he transcribed most of the songs himself before later crediting Hurst.
Most early folk-song anthologies were largely compiled by assistants whose work went uncredited.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the official credit to Fenwick. After 'However,' the notebooks show Hurst's hand and her editorial choices, and Okafor concludes that Hurst shaped the anthology as much as Fenwick did. Choice A captures that correction to the credit.

B.why: You chose the most vivid detail. It is accurate, but it is one piece of evidence for the larger claim about who deserves credit for the anthology.

C.why: You probably saw 'Fenwick's notebooks' and stopped reading. The passage says most transcriptions are in Hurst's hand, and only Fenwick's name appears on the title page.

D.why: You generalized from one anthology to most anthologies of the period. The passage discusses only Songs of the Northern Dales.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Linguists studying whistled languages, in which speakers turn speech into whistles so they can talk across valleys, have often assumed that these systems can carry only simple, predictable messages. Fieldwork by linguist Ana Ribeiro-Coll in a mountain village complicates that view. Whistlers there exchanged unscripted questions about prices, directions, and absent neighbors, and listeners decoded most of them correctly on first hearing. Ribeiro-Coll cautions, however, that the whistlers she studied were lifelong practitioners, so her results may not describe communities where the practice is fading.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ribeiro-Coll's fieldwork confirms the assumption that whistled languages are suited mainly to short, simple, and predictable messages.
Listeners in one mountain village correctly decoded most of the unscripted whistled questions about prices, directions, and neighbors.
Ribeiro-Coll's fieldwork suggests that whistled languages, at least among skilled users, can carry more complex messages than expected.
Ribeiro-Coll's fieldwork shows that whistled languages can express anything spoken languages can, whatever the whistlers' experience.
items.explanation: The passage sets up an assumption (whistled languages carry only simple messages), and then Ribeiro-Coll's fieldwork 'complicates that view.' The last sentence limits the finding to lifelong practitioners. Choice C covers both parts: it gives the challenge to the assumption and keeps the limit ('at least among skilled users'). It also claims no more than the text does.

A.why: You probably recognised the assumption from the first sentence and missed the turn. The passage says the fieldwork 'complicates that view,' so it challenges the assumption rather than confirming it.

B.why: Every word of this is true, which is why it's tempting. But it only repeats the evidence from the third sentence. It leaves out what that evidence means for the linguists' assumption, and it drops Ribeiro-Coll's caution. It is too narrow.

D.why: The opening matches the passage, but the second half doesn't. The text never compares whistled languages with spoken ones. Ribeiro-Coll also warns that her results may not hold for less experienced whistlers, so 'whatever the whistlers' experience' says the opposite of her hedge.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Engineers have often hesitated to use permeable pavement in cold regions, reasoning that water trapped in its pores would freeze, expand, and crack the surface. A six-winter trial on a municipal parking lot in northern Minnesota tested that concern. The porous asphalt drained meltwater quickly enough that little remained to freeze, and it showed less cracking than the conventional asphalt beside it. Because water drained instead of pooling, the lot also needed about a third less road salt. Taken together, the results suggest that cold climates may be less of an obstacle to permeable pavement than engineers had assumed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: A trial found that a porous asphalt parking lot in northern Minnesota needed about a third less road salt than usual.
A trial suggests that permeable pavement may hold up in cold regions better than engineers had expected it would.
A trial suggests that permeable pavement performs well in cold regions only when road salt use is sharply reduced.
A trial shows that permeable pavement should replace conventional asphalt in parking lots throughout cold regions.
items.explanation: The last sentence adds up the passage: the trial's results suggest cold climates 'may be less of an obstacle' than engineers assumed. The drainage, the reduced cracking and the salt savings are all evidence for that verdict. Choice B states it with the same level of certainty ('suggests,' 'may').

A.why: This is accurate, but it's one supporting detail from the fourth sentence. The passage does more than this: it uses the salt savings, along with the drainage and cracking results, to answer engineers' worry about freezing. It is too narrow.

C.why: The start is right, but the end reverses the cause and effect. The passage says less salt was needed because water drained away. It never says the pavement worked because salt was reduced. You took a result and read it as a condition.

D.why: One parking lot and a hedged conclusion ('suggest,' 'may') can't support a recommendation to replace conventional asphalt across every cold region. This choice is much broader and more certain than the text.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: For decades, the stone farming terraces on the slopes of Cerro Alto were credited to the Inka, who expanded into the region in the fifteenth century and built similar terraces elsewhere in their empire. However, archaeologist Tomás Quilla dated charcoal and pollen preserved in the terrace soils and found that farmers were growing maize on several of the terraces at least three centuries before the Inka arrived. Quilla argues that the Inka likely repaired and enlarged an existing terrace system rather than constructing it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Quilla's dating indicates that the terraces were built by the Inka, who then grew maize on them for three centuries.
Quilla's dating indicates that the terraces predate the Inka, who likely expanded rather than built the system there.
Quilla's dating indicates that the Inka learned how to build terraces from earlier farmers living near Cerro Alto.
The Inka built stone terraces like those at Cerro Alto in several other regions that they brought under their control.
items.explanation: The passage starts with the old credit (the Inka built the terraces), and then 'However' brings in Quilla's evidence that the terraces were farmed centuries before the Inka arrived. The last sentence gives his conclusion that the Inka likely enlarged an existing system. Choice B covers the correction and that conclusion, and it keeps the hedge 'likely.'

A.why: You may have stopped at the old credit in the first sentence. Quilla's evidence shows the terraces were farmed three centuries before the Inka arrived. That contradicts the claim that the Inka built them.

C.why: This starts with the right topic and then adds a claim the passage never makes. The text says the Inka built terraces elsewhere. It never says they learned the technique from Cerro Alto's farmers. This adds a cause the text doesn't state.

D.why: This repeats background from the first sentence, and that background explains why the Inka were originally credited. It says nothing about Quilla's finding, which is what the passage is building toward.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: For decades, sprint coaches prescribed long, held stretches before races, reasoning that looser muscles would move faster. Physiologist Dana Okafor tested that reasoning with thirty collegiate sprinters, who ran 40-meter dashes after either five minutes of held stretches or five minutes of leg swings and skips. The results, however, ran counter to the coaches' expectation: the sprinters were, on average, slightly slower after the held stretches. Okafor suggests that holding a stretch may briefly reduce a muscle's springiness, the very quality a sprint start depends on.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor's study compared two five-minute warm-up routines, using thirty collegiate sprinters as its participants.
A study suggests that the held stretches coaches long recommended before sprints may slightly slow sprinters down.
Okafor's study shows that athletes should remove stretching of every kind from their training programs.
Okafor found that held stretches improved sprint times by making the sprinters' leg muscles springier.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the coaches' long-held belief, then uses 'however' to bring in the real finding: held stretches were followed by slightly slower sprints, possibly because they reduce springiness. Choice B covers both the belief and the finding that corrects it, and it keeps the text's hedge ('may').

A.why: This accurately describes how the study was set up, but it leaves out what the study found. You picked a true detail from the middle of the passage instead of the point the whole passage is building toward.

C.why: The study only compared held stretches with leg swings and skips before sprints. It says nothing about getting rid of all stretching, and leg swings are themselves a kind of dynamic stretching. You stretched a narrow finding into a sweeping rule.

D.why: The sprinters were slower after held stretches, and Okafor suggests that stretching reduces springiness. This choice turns both parts of the finding around, so you may have taken the coaches' expectation for the result.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Leaves and wood fossilize only under unusual conditions, so many ancient plants are missing from the record of large fossils. Pollen grains, by contrast, have tough outer walls that survive in ordinary lake mud. At the Harlow Basin site, for instance, paleobotanist Mei Tanaka found abundant pollen from a flowering shrub in 52-million-year-old sediments, though not a single leaf of that shrub has been found anywhere in the basin. For Tanaka, the pollen fills a gap that the larger fossils leave open.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Tanaka found pollen from a flowering shrub in 52-million-year-old sediments at the Harlow Basin site.
Pollen analysis has made the study of fossil leaves and wood unnecessary for understanding ancient plants.
Pollen grains are fragile, so they survive only in the unusual conditions that also preserve fossil leaves.
Because pollen survives more readily than leaves and wood, it can reveal ancient plants that large fossils miss.
items.explanation: The first two sentences make a general claim: large plant fossils are rare, but pollen survives well. The Harlow Basin case is an example of that claim, and the final sentence says the pollen fills the gap. Choice D states the general claim that the example supports.

A.why: This repeats the Harlow Basin example correctly, but that example only supports the passage's broader point about pollen and the fossil record. You chose the vivid case instead of the claim it illustrates.

B.why: The passage says pollen fills a gap that larger fossils leave. It never says leaves and wood are no longer worth studying. You turned 'adds to' into 'replaces'.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Some meteorologists have proposed that the heat radiating from large cities may trigger summer thunderstorms downwind. Radar records from the city of Aldermoor appear to fit this idea: storms form noticeably more often just east of the city than to its west. Meteorologist Priya Venkatesan cautions, however, that the prevailing winds also carry moisture from nearby Lake Tessel over the same eastern area. The lake, rather than the city's heat, could therefore account for the pattern, and separating the two influences will require further study.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Radar records fit the idea that city heat triggers storms downwind, but moisture from a lake could also explain them.
Radar records prove that Aldermoor's heat is the main reason summer storms form more often east of the city.
Prevailing summer winds near Aldermoor carry moisture from Lake Tessel over the area east of the city.
Venkatesan rejects the heat hypothesis because storms east of Aldermoor are no more common than elsewhere.
items.explanation: The passage gives a hypothesis and some evidence that fits it, then uses 'however' to bring in a second possible explanation, and ends by saying more study is needed. Choice A covers both the fit and the doubt, and like the text it does not claim certainty.

B.why: The passage says the records 'appear to fit' the idea, and then raises a competing explanation. 'Prove' and 'main reason' are much stronger than the text allows. You missed the hedge words.

C.why: This detail is accurate, but it is only one step in the passage's argument. It does not mention the heat hypothesis or the uncertainty the passage is really about.

D.why: The records show storms do form more often east of the city. Venkatesan does not reject the hypothesis either. She only says another cause is possible.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists generally expect a large new employer to push up wages in a small town by competing for workers. Examining warehouse openings in forty rural counties, economist Luis Ferreira found that hourly pay at nearby retailers did rise, by about 4 percent in the first year. Many retail workers soon moved to the warehouses, though, and retailers responded by cutting staff and hours rather than raising pay further. Within three years, retail wages had drifted back close to their earlier levels. Taken together, Ferreira's findings suggest that the wage boost from a new large employer may be real but short-lived.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: In the first year after a warehouse opened nearby, hourly pay at local retailers rose by about 4 percent.
Opening a large warehouse is the most effective way for a rural county to raise its long-term wages.
Research suggests that a large new employer may raise local wages at first, but the increase may not last.
Retail wages kept climbing for three years after the warehouses opened, as competition for workers grew.
items.explanation: The middle sentences give separate facts: an early rise, workers leaving retail jobs, and wages falling back. The last sentence adds them up: the boost is 'real but short-lived.' Choice C restates that conclusion and keeps its hedge.

B.why: The passage finds that the wage gain faded, and it never compares warehouses with other ways of raising wages. 'Most effective' and 'long-term' are claims the text does not support.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Farmers across the Venn Plateau widely credit a drought-tolerant maize variety, introduced in 2015, for the sharp rise in local yields since then. However, when agronomist Hana Brisco compared records from 300 farms, she found that yields rose just as much on farms that kept planting older varieties. The rise instead tracked the spread of no-till planting, a practice that leaves crop residue on fields and helps soil hold moisture. Brisco concludes that soil management, not seed choice, likely drove most of the gains.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The yield rise widely credited to a new maize variety was likely driven more by a change in soil management.
Farms on the Venn Plateau that kept planting older maize varieties also saw their yields rise after 2015.
The drought-tolerant variety performs worse than older varieties, so farmers should stop planting it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The loss of a single predator can reshape an entire ecosystem. Consider Lake Corvin, where heavy angling during the 1990s removed most of the largemouth bass. items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Histories of the Marren Valley's choral festivals have long credited conductor Elsa Varga with founding the tradition when she organized a gathering of choirs in 1869. items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Immunologists have long described the thymus as an organ that matters mainly in childhood. It trains young T cells to recognize threats, then shrinks steadily after puberty, and by middle age much of it has been replaced by fat. However, a study led by immunologist Rania Okafor suggests that the adult thymus may not be idle. Tracking newly made T cells in 140 adults aged 40 to 70, Okafor's team found that the thymus was still producing them in every participant. Output was lower than in children, and it rose briefly after infections.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: After puberty, the thymus steadily shrinks, and much of it is eventually replaced by fat tissue.
Okafor's team found that the adult thymus produces new T cells only for a short time after infections.
Although the adult thymus has been considered largely idle, it may continue producing new T cells later in life.
Okafor's research shows that the adult thymus is the main source of the T cells that fight infections.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the traditional view that the thymus matters mainly in childhood. Then 'However' brings in Okafor's study, which suggests the adult thymus keeps making T cells. Choice C covers both halves: the old view and the finding that corrects it. It also keeps the passage's hedge ('suggests', 'may') by saying 'may continue' rather than claiming more than the study shows.

A.why: You picked a true statement, but it only repeats the setup before 'However.' The passage gives the shrinking thymus as the expected view so it can challenge that view. The finding that the adult thymus is still active is left out completely.

B.why: You stopped at 'rose briefly after infections' and missed that the thymus was producing T cells in every participant all along. Infections raised output for a while. They were not the only time it happened. The word 'only' reverses what the passage says.

D.why: You went further than the study does. The passage says the adult thymus still makes some T cells, at lower rates than in children. It never compares the thymus with other sources of T cells or calls it the main source. The passage also hedges with 'suggests' and 'may,' and 'shows' drops that caution.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Farmers who rotate soybeans with corn have long credited the nitrogen in soybean residue, the stems and leaves left on the field after harvest, with boosting the next year's corn crop. A 2023 field trial complicates that account. In plots where all soybean residue was removed after harvest, the following corn crop still gained most of the yield advantage that rotation usually provides. The benefit, the researchers concluded, likely comes less from the residue than from changes soybean roots make to soil microbes during the growing season.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: A field trial suggests that rotation's benefit to corn may come mainly from soybean roots' effects on soil microbes rather than from residue.
In a 2023 field trial, researchers removed all of the soybean residue from some of their plots once the harvest was finished.
A field trial showed that soybean residue gives corn no benefit at all and should therefore be cleared from fields after harvest.
A field trial confirmed that nitrogen in soybean residue is the main reason corn grows better in fields previously planted with soybeans.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the usual explanation (residue nitrogen), then uses the trial to correct it: removing residue barely reduced the benefit, so the researchers credit root effects on soil microbes instead. Choice A covers both the old view and the correction, and it keeps the passage's hedge ('likely') as 'may.'

B.why: This is true, but it only describes how the trial was set up. You picked a detail without the finding it was there to produce. The passage does more than this.

C.why: The corn kept 'most' of the advantage, not all of it, so residue may still help a little. The passage also never tells farmers to clear their fields. You stretched the finding past what was stated.

D.why: This is the view the trial 'complicates.' You took the expected view set up in the first sentence for the author's conclusion and missed the turn that follows it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Seismometers are not the only instruments capable of recording earthquakes. Fiber-optic cables laid for telecommunications can also register ground motion, because tiny shifts in a cable change how pulses of light scatter as they travel along it. In 2024, researchers used a 40-kilometer stretch of unused cable beneath a coastal city to detect more than 800 small tremors, many too faint for the region's sparse seismometer network to have recorded. Existing cables may therefore offer an inexpensive way to monitor seismic activity where conventional instruments are few.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Pulses of light traveling along a fiber-optic cable scatter differently when the cable is shifted slightly by motion in the ground.
Fiber-optic cables detect earthquakes more accurately than seismometers do and are likely to replace them in most regions.
Fiber-optic cables laid for telecommunications may offer a low-cost way to detect earthquakes in places where seismometers are scarce.
Fiber-optic cables can register strong earthquakes, but they miss the faint tremors that a network of seismometers is able to record.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a broad claim, the 2024 study is the single example supporting it, and the last sentence draws the conclusion: existing cables may be a cheap way to monitor earthquakes where seismometers are sparse. Choice C covers that whole arc and keeps the hedge 'may.'

A.why: This accurately restates the mechanism in the second sentence, but it says nothing about earthquake monitoring, the study, or the conclusion. You picked one true detail instead of the point it supports.

B.why: The passage never compares accuracy and never predicts that cables will replace seismometers. It presents cables as an addition where instruments are few. You went past what the text claims.

D.why: The passage says the reverse: the cable caught faint tremors that the sparse seismometer network missed. You swapped which instrument picked up the small events.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Engineers have mixed dormant bacterial spores into concrete so that when cracks let in water, the bacteria revive and produce limestone that seals the gaps. In laboratory tests, cracks up to 0.8 millimeter wide closed within three weeks. But the spores must survive the concrete's highly alkaline interior for decades, and the nutrients added to feed them can weaken the material when mixed in at high levels. Bacterial concrete is promising, then, but its value in real structures over long periods remains unproven.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Bacteria-laced concrete has sealed small cracks in lab tests, but obstacles leave its long-term value in real structures uncertain.
Dormant bacteria mixed into concrete revive and produce limestone when water seeps in through cracks that have newly formed.
Bacteria-laced concrete will be able to repair itself for decades once engineers improve the nutrients that are added to it.
Bacteria-laced concrete has sealed small cracks in lab tests, but the nutrients that feed its bacteria weaken it at any level.
items.explanation: The passage gives a lab success and then two obstacles (spore survival and nutrient weakening), and the final sentence sums them up: promising, but unproven over the long term in real structures. Choice A includes both the promise and the uncertainty that the last sentence combines.

B.why: This accurately describes how the concrete works, from the first sentence, but it leaves out the obstacles and the verdict. The passage does more than explain the mechanism.

C.why: The passage says long-term value 'remains unproven.' It never promises decades of self-repair, and it never says better nutrients would solve the spore-survival problem. You turned a hedge into a prediction.

D.why: The first half is right, but the second half is wrong. The passage says nutrients weaken concrete 'when mixed in at high levels,' not at any level. Read each choice to the end before you pick it.

items.stimulus: Engineers have long treated cracking in concrete as inevitable, patching damage only after it appears. Materials scientist Ilse Varga and her colleagues tested an alternative: mixing dormant bacterial spores and calcium lactate into fresh concrete. When water seeped into a crack, the spores revived and produced limestone that sealed gaps up to 0.6 millimeters wide within four weeks. The team cautions, however, that wider cracks remained open, so the approach may supplement rather than replace conventional repair.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Varga's team found that bacteria embedded in concrete revive when water enters a crack, which is what triggers limestone production.
Varga's team found that bacteria embedded in concrete can seal small cracks on their own, though the method may only add to existing repair.
Varga's team found that bacteria embedded in concrete let it repair cracks of any size, ending the need for conventional patching.
Varga's team found that bacteria embedded in concrete seal wide cracks well but leave narrow ones open, which limits their usefulness.
items.explanation: The passage introduces a new approach, reports that it sealed small cracks, and then uses 'however' to limit the claim: wider cracks stayed open, so the method may only supplement standard repair. items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists have often assumed that raising the minimum wage leads employers to cut jobs. A study by economist Tomás Reyna of grocery chains in two neighboring regions complicates that view. After one region raised its wage floor, chains there kept staffing levels steady but saw lower turnover: workers stayed an average of five months longer. Because hiring and training replacements is costly, Reyna suggests, the savings from lower turnover may have offset much of the higher wage bill.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Reyna's study shows that raising the minimum wage always pays for itself, so employers in every industry end up gaining from it.
Reyna's study found that after a wage increase, grocery workers in one region stayed in their jobs about five months longer.
Reyna's study suggests that a higher minimum wage need not cost jobs, possibly because lower turnover offsets the added expense.
Reyna's study found that grocery chains cut staff after a wage increase, then recovered the cost through lower turnover.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the common assumption that wage increases cost jobs, then presents Reyna's study as complicating it: staffing held steady, and lower turnover may have offset the cost. Choice C covers both parts and keeps the passage's hedge ('may', 'suggests') with the word 'possibly'.

A.why: You generalized one study of grocery chains to every industry, and you turned 'may have offset much of' into 'always pays for itself'. The passage makes neither claim.

B.why: This detail is accurate, but it is only the evidence. It leaves out the claim that the evidence supports: a higher minimum wage did not reduce staffing, which challenges the common assumption.

D.why: The passage says the chains kept staffing levels steady. They did not cut staff, so this choice reverses the central finding.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Floods in river towns are usually blamed on heavy rainfall upstream. However, hydrologist Hana Okafor's analysis of the Carrow River basin points to a second cause. Over three decades, wetlands along the river's tributaries were drained for farmland, and those wetlands had once held back storm water and released it slowly. Comparing storms of similar size, Okafor found that downstream peak flows now arrive about nine hours sooner and run 30 percent higher than before the draining.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor's analysis shows that the Carrow's tributary wetlands were drained over three decades to make way for new farmland.
Okafor's analysis shows that rainfall plays no part in Carrow floods, which are caused entirely by the loss of wetlands.
Okafor's analysis shows that storms in the Carrow basin have grown larger, producing faster and higher flood peaks downstream.
Okafor's analysis shows that lost wetlands, not only upstream rain, have made Carrow floods arrive faster and run higher.
items.explanation: After 'However', the passage names its real point: draining wetlands is a second cause of flooding on the Carrow, alongside rainfall. The rest of the passage explains how wetlands slowed storm water and gives the evidence for faster, higher peaks. Choice D covers all of this.

A.why: This is true, but it is only background. It describes what happened to the wetlands and leaves out Okafor's finding about how their loss changed the floods.

B.why: The passage calls wetland loss a 'second cause', which means rainfall still matters. Saying the floods are caused entirely by wetland loss goes further than the text does.

C.why: Okafor compared storms of similar size so that storm size could be ruled out. This choice credits the change to bigger storms, which reverses the logic of the study.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists have often assumed that when a large employer closes, its former workers soon find comparable jobs and recover their lost income. However, economist Maren Okafor tracked 4,000 workers laid off from shuttered textile mills and compared them with similar workers who kept their jobs. Most of the laid-off workers were reemployed within two years, yet they still earned about 15 percent less than the comparison group, and that gap had barely narrowed a decade later.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor found that laid-off mill workers kept earning less than comparable workers who stayed employed, even after finding new jobs.
Okafor found that most of the workers laid off from the textile mills had been reemployed within two years of the closures.
Okafor found that the earnings gap between laid-off and retained mill workers had largely disappeared within a decade.

items.explanation: The passage sets up the expected view (displaced workers recover), then 'However' brings in Okafor's finding: the laid-off workers found jobs but still earned about 15 percent less than similar workers, and the gap barely shrank in ten years. D.why: Okafor studied laid-off workers from textile mills and compared them with similar workers. Nothing in the study covers 'any large employer' or 'every worker' in a town, and 'permanently' goes further than a ten-year follow-up can show.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Historians have often credited the spread of Gerardus Mercator's 1569 world map projection to its usefulness at sea: on it, a course of constant compass bearing appears as a straight line. Historian Lieve Marten, however, notes that surviving Dutch ship logs from before 1700 rarely mention Mercator charts; most navigators recorded using simpler plane charts. Marten contends that the projection's early reach owed more to atlas publishers, whose rectangular pages suited its tidy grid of parallels and meridians. Sailors may well have embraced it later, she allows, but they were not what first carried it across Europe.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Choice C covers the usual view, the evidence and Marten's alternative. It also keeps her concession intact, because she claims nothing about what happened later.

She never says publishers caused that later adoption or that it happened 'only after' them. You turned a hedged aside into a cause-and-effect claim the text never makes.
per_choice.B: This is accurate, and you can find it in the second sentence. But it is just the evidence Marten uses. The passage uses the logs to support a bigger claim about who actually spread the projection. The choice is true but too narrow, because it leaves out Marten's argument.
per_choice.D: This reverses the order Marten gives. She says publishers carried the projection first and sailors may have taken it up later. You probably remembered that the passage mentions both groups and 'later', but attached 'later' to the wrong group.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Nutrition researchers have long focused on what people eat, but a growing number suspect that when people eat may also shape how the body handles food. In a study led by nutritionist Amara Okafor, twelve adults ate identical meals for four weeks within an eight-hour window ending at 3 p.m., then for four weeks within one ending at 8 p.m. Their blood sugar after meals was lower on the early schedule. Because participants also slept longer on that schedule, however, Okafor cautions that the result is consistent with a timing effect but does not yet isolate one.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor's participants had lower blood sugar after meals when they stopped eating by 3 p.m. rather than by 8 p.m.
A small study lends some support to the idea that meal timing affects metabolism, but it cannot rule out another cause.
A small study suggests that longer sleep, not the timing of meals, explains why participants' blood sugar was lower.
Nutrition researchers now agree that when people eat matters as much as what they eat, as a recent study confirms.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces a hypothesis: meal timing may matter. The study is the example, and the last sentence weighs it. The result fits the timing idea, but the longer sleep means the study 'does not yet isolate' a timing effect. Choice B covers both halves of that verdict. It gives support without proof and leaves another possible cause open, which matches the hedged certainty of the text.

A.why: This repeats the study's result accurately, which is why it is tempting. But the passage does more than report the result. It places the result inside a broader hypothesis and then limits what the result can show. A choice about one sentence is too narrow for the whole text.

C.why: You noticed Okafor's caution, which was the key step, and then went too far with it. She says sleep is a confound that the study cannot separate from timing. She does not say sleep is the real explanation. 'Cannot rule out' is not the same as 'is the cause.'

D.why: The passage says only that 'a growing number' of researchers 'suspect' timing matters, and Okafor says her study does not isolate the effect. 'Now agree' and 'confirms' contradict both points. You read the topic correctly but missed how uncertain the passage is about it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Linguists have often read the disappearance of a grammatical ending as evidence that a language is becoming simpler. Studying a coastal dialect of Tamberan, a language spoken in a handful of villages, linguist Rhea Ostrander found that speakers under forty no longer used the ending that marks a noun as referring to exactly two things. Yet these speakers routinely placed one of two new particles before such nouns, and children began producing the particles at about the age their grandparents had acquired the ending. Ostrander concludes that, at least in this dialect, the distinction has changed address rather than been lost.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Younger speakers of the coastal dialect have stopped using the ending for pairs, which shows that the dialect is gradually becoming simpler.
Children in the coastal dialect learn the new particles at about the same age that earlier generations learned the ending for pairs.
Ostrander's study suggests that a dialect losing a grammatical ending may keep the meaning that ending carried by marking it another way.
Ostrander's study shows that when languages lose grammatical endings, they replace them with particles that children learn just as easily.
items.explanation: The passage starts with the usual view (a lost ending means simplification) and then gives one case that pushes against it. The case has three facts: the ending is gone, new particles do the same job, and children learn the particles at the usual age. The last sentence sums it up: the distinction has moved, not disappeared. Choice C covers all of that. It also keeps the author's limit, 'at least in this dialect', by saying 'may'.

A.why: This is the half-right answer. The first half is accurate: younger speakers did drop the ending. The second half then gives the conclusion the passage argues against. You recognised the opening and stopped reading before the claim it attaches.

B.why: This is true, and you can point to the line that says it. But it is one piece of supporting evidence. The passage uses it to back up Ostrander's conclusion, and this choice leaves the conclusion out. It is too narrow.

D.why: You saw the main point (the meaning moved elsewhere) and then stretched one dialect into a rule for all languages. Ostrander limits her claim with 'at least in this dialect'. Nothing in the passage says every language replaces lost endings with particles.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: When the Harlow Street Bridge reopened after a 2019 retrofit, city officials credited the new carbon-fiber wraps on its support columns with allowing the bridge to carry heavier trucks. Engineer Tomás Velde, who reviewed the project, agrees that the wraps strengthen the columns against earthquakes. However, his load calculations show that the added truck capacity came almost entirely from replacing the old deck with a lighter one, which reduced the weight the columns had to bear in the first place.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Velde's analysis indicates that the bridge's higher truck capacity owes more to its lighter deck than to the column wraps officials credited.
Velde's analysis indicates that the column wraps officials credited added little to the bridge, since its strength came mainly from a lighter deck.
Velde's review confirms that the carbon-fiber wraps on the bridge's support columns make those columns more resistant to earthquakes.
Velde's analysis shows that lightening a bridge deck is a more effective way to raise truck capacity than strengthening its columns.
items.explanation: The passage gives the official credit first, then a concession, then the 'However' turn. What comes after 'However' is the real point: the extra truck capacity came from the lighter deck, not the wraps. Choice A says that. It stays inside the question of truck capacity, so it does not deny the earthquake benefit that Velde accepts.

B.why: You correctly saw that the deck, not the wraps, explains the extra truck capacity. Then you took it one step too far and said the wraps 'added little to the bridge'. Velde says they strengthen the columns against earthquakes. That concession limits his claim, and this choice ignores it.

C.why: The passage does say this, but only as a concession before 'However'. The main point comes after the pivot and is about where the truck capacity came from. This choice leaves that out completely.

D.why: Velde's calculations cover one bridge. This choice turns that result into a general engineering rule about bridges, which the passage never states.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Excavators at Tel Varon found charred barley in a storage pit beneath a house floor, and some have proposed that the site's residents farmed barley as early as 7000 BCE. Archaeobotanist Mira Halloway grants that the grains are that old, since radiocarbon dates taken from the grains themselves confirm it. But she points out that the grains are uniformly small and lack the tough stalk joint that marks domesticated barley, so they could easily have been gathered from wild stands. Cultivation at that date is possible, she writes, but the pit alone cannot establish it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Halloway argues that the barley from the storage pit is younger than 7000 BCE and so cannot show early farming at Tel Varon.
Halloway argues that the residents of Tel Varon gathered their barley from wild stands rather than farming it around 7000 BCE.
Halloway notes that the barley grains from the pit are small and lack the stalk joint typical of domesticated barley.
Halloway accepts the early date of the barley but argues that it does not by itself show the grain was farmed at that time.
items.explanation: Halloway makes a limited concession (the date is right) and then an objection (the grains do not prove farming). Her hedges set how strong the claim is: the grains 'could' be wild, and cultivation is 'possible'. Choice D keeps both halves and matches that level of certainty.

A.why: Halloway accepts the date. She says the radiocarbon results confirm it. Her doubt is about whether the barley was cultivated, not how old it is. This choice puts her objection in the wrong place.

B.why: You noticed that Halloway is skeptical, but you missed her hedges. She says the grains 'could easily' be wild and that farming is 'possible'. She does not say the residents did not farm. This choice turns 'not proven' into 'disproven'.

C.why: This is accurate, but it is only her evidence. It leaves out both her concession about the date and her conclusion about what the pit can and cannot prove. It is too narrow.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Studies of the etcher Henrik Saal usually treat the faint gray tone in his skies as the result of careless wiping of the plate. Conservator Lena Achterberg examined forty impressions of his 1871 harbor view and found the tone in the same position in every one. She also located a notebook entry in which Saal describes a tool for leaving a thin film of ink on chosen areas, and she observed that the tone appears only in prints Saal pulled himself, not in later editions printed by others. Taken together, Achterberg argues, the evidence indicates the tone was deliberate.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Achterberg found that the gray tone appears in the same position in all forty impressions of Saal's 1871 harbor view that she examined.
Achterberg combines several kinds of evidence to argue that a tone usually seen as accidental in Saal's skies was in fact intended.
Achterberg's examination confirms the usual view that the gray tone in Saal's skies resulted from his wiping the plate unevenly.
Achterberg argues that Saal intended the gray tone in his skies, so the later editions printed by others misrepresent his work.
items.explanation: The middle sentences list three separate findings: the tone is in the same place every time, there is a notebook entry, and the tone appears only in Saal's own printings. The last sentence combines them into one verdict that overturns the usual view. Choice B covers both the combining and the verdict.

A.why: This is accurate, but it is only one of the three findings. It leaves out the conclusion they support. This is the vivid-detail trap: true, and too narrow.

C.why: This turns the passage around. The careless-wiping explanation is the view Achterberg argues against, not one she confirms.

D.why: The first half matches her conclusion. The second half adds a judgment she never makes. The passage uses the later editions only as evidence. It never says they misrepresent Saal. Read every choice to the end.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Planners often assume that new bike lanes draw their riders mainly from people who previously drove. A 2022 study of the city of Velmora suggests a more complicated picture. After the city opened twelve kilometers of protected lanes, cycling on the affected streets rose by 40 percent. But surveys of the new riders found that most had previously taken the bus or walked, and car traffic on parallel routes was essentially unchanged.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Velmora study shows that protected bike lanes can increase cycling but cannot reduce car traffic in any city that builds them.
After Velmora opened twelve kilometers of protected bike lanes, cycling on the affected streets increased by about 40 percent.
The Velmora study suggests that new bike lanes may increase cycling without drawing many of their new riders away from cars.
The Velmora study suggests that new bike lanes draw riders away from buses, which planners should count as a cost of the lanes.
items.explanation: The passage sets up an assumption and then tests it with one case. The 'But' sentence is the finding: cycling rose, but the new riders mostly came from buses and walking, and car traffic stayed the same. Choice C covers both the rise and where the riders came from. Its 'suggests' and 'may' match the passage's 'suggests a more complicated picture'.

A.why: One city's study cannot support 'cannot' and 'any city'. You got the direction right and then made it absolute.

B.why: This is the 40 percent figure, which is accurate and easy to remember. But it leaves out the 'But' sentence, and that sentence is what makes the picture 'more complicated'.

D.why: The first half is supported: most new riders came from buses or walking. The second half adds a policy judgment that the passage never makes. Nothing in the text calls the shift a cost.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Hydrologists estimating how much water a watershed can supply have traditionally relied on rain and stream gauges. Priya Ndlovu and colleagues compared such estimates for the Kessel Basin with measurements from satellites that detect changes in the mass of water stored underground. The gauges had indicated that the basin's supply was stable from 2005 to 2020, but the satellite data showed groundwater declining steadily over the same period, a loss the gauges, which record only surface flows, were never designed to detect.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ndlovu's team found that the Kessel Basin was losing groundwater that gauge-based estimates, limited to surface water, had missed.
Ndlovu's team found that the Kessel Basin's gauges had been malfunctioning, which made the basin's water supply appear stable.
Ndlovu's team found that satellites should replace rain and stream gauges as hydrologists' main tool for estimating water supply.
Ndlovu's team found that gauge-based estimates indicated the Kessel Basin's water supply remained stable from 2005 to 2020.
items.explanation: The passage builds to the 'but' clause: the satellites showed a groundwater loss that the gauges could not record, because the gauges measure only surface flow. Choice A gives the finding and the reason the gauges missed it. It also stays inside the one basin that was studied.

B.why: You saw that the gauges got the answer wrong and assumed they were broken. The passage says they were 'never designed to detect' groundwater. The gauges worked as intended. They just measure something else.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap: it treats a new tool as doing more than the passage describes. The study found one gap in one basin. It never says satellites should replace gauges.

D.why: This is true, but it is the expected view the passage sets up before the 'but'. It leaves out what the satellites showed.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Intercropping, or growing two crops in the same field, has been promoted as a way to cut fertilizer use, because legumes such as beans add nitrogen to the soil. In a three-year trial in Tamsey County, agronomist Felix Brannigan found that maize grown alongside beans needed about a quarter less nitrogen fertilizer than maize grown alone, with no loss in yield. Brannigan cautions, however, that the trial years brought unusually heavy rainfall, which favors bean growth, and that savings in drier years are likely to be smaller.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Brannigan's trial shows that intercropping maize with beans cuts fertilizer needs by about a quarter, whatever the rainfall.
Brannigan's trial found that maize grown alongside beans produced as large a harvest as maize grown on its own.
Brannigan's trial suggests that intercropping is unlikely to reduce fertilizer use at all in years with ordinary rainfall.
Brannigan's trial supports the fertilizer savings of intercropping, but he expects those savings to shrink in drier years.
items.explanation: The trial supports the claim made at the start, and then 'however' limits it: the wet years probably made the savings look bigger. 'Likely to be smaller' is the hedge you need to keep. Choice D keeps both the support and the limit, at the same strength the passage uses.

A.why: This repeats the trial's result and drops the 'however'. 'Whatever the rainfall' is the opposite of Brannigan's warning that rainfall probably increased the savings.

B.why: 'No loss in yield' is in the passage, but it is a side detail of the trial. This choice says nothing about fertilizer or about Brannigan's warning.

C.why: You caught the warning and then made it too strong. Brannigan says savings in drier years are 'likely to be smaller', not that they disappear. Going from 'smaller' to 'none at all' goes past the hedge.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Forecasters have generally credited the improved accuracy of five-day hurricane track forecasts since the 1990s to faster supercomputers that run models at finer resolution. Meteorologist Celia Varga tested this by rerunning older forecast models on modern computers. The reruns improved only modestly; most of the gain appeared only when the models were also fed today's denser observations from aircraft and satellites. Varga does not dismiss computing power, but she concludes that better data has done more of the work than is usually acknowledged.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Varga's analysis shows that faster supercomputers have done little to improve five-day hurricane track forecasts since the 1990s.
Varga's analysis indicates that denser observations account for more of the gain in track forecasts than faster computing does.
Varga's analysis shows that older forecast models improve only modestly when they are rerun on modern computers.
Varga's analysis indicates that forecasts of all kinds now depend more on observational data than on computing power.
items.explanation: The passage gives the usual credit, a test of it, and a conclusion after 'but'. That conclusion is that data did more of the work than computing, and Varga 'does not dismiss computing power'. Choice B is a comparison ('more of the gain'), which matches her conclusion. It does not drop computing, and it stays with hurricane track forecasts.

A.why: You saw that data mattered more and assumed computing mattered very little. The reruns did improve, modestly, and Varga explicitly does not dismiss computing power. 'Done little' contradicts that.

C.why: This is the result of one step in Varga's test. It leaves out the observations, and they are the point of her conclusion. It is too narrow.

D.why: Varga studied five-day hurricane track forecasts. This choice stretches her finding to 'forecasts of all kinds', which the passage never claims.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Marisol Ekwueme's 2019 novel The Long Rows. Ines, an agricultural researcher, is visiting her test fields after a summer without rain.

Ines had driven out expecting to find nothing. The neighboring farms were brown to the fence line, their corn folded over like paper. But at the edge of her plots she stopped. The wheat she had spent six years crossing and recrossing stood upright, thin but green, its heads already filling. She knelt and pressed a stalk between her fingers, as if to be sure it was real, and found that she was laughing.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines is relieved to discover that the wheat she developed has survived the drought.
Ines is discouraged to find that her test plots fared no better than nearby farms.
Ines worries that her neighbors will resent the success of her experimental crop.
Ines notices that the corn on neighboring farms has been damaged by the dry summer.
items.explanation: You follow Ines from expecting to find nothing to kneeling in disbelief and laughing. The turn at 'But' shows her wheat has survived when everything around it died, and her laughter shows relief and joy. Choice A matches both the situation and that emotional direction.

B.why: You reversed the tone. Ines expected failure, but the text says her wheat 'stood upright' and green while the nearby farms were brown. Her laughing shows the opposite of discouragement.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Nothing suggests Ines is thinking about her neighbors' feelings. Their farms appear only as a contrast to her surviving wheat.

D.why: You picked a true detail from the second sentence, but it is too narrow. The dead corn is background that sets up the real focus: Ines's reaction to her own wheat.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Tomasz Reyna's 2008 poem "Proof." The speaker is a printmaker.

All morning I cut the block by feel,
gouging the pale wood toward a shape
I carried backward in my head.
I rolled the ink, black and slow as tar,
laid the paper, leaned my weight on it.
Only when I peeled the sheet away
did I see what my hands had meant—
the heron, facing the right way at last,
more certain than I ever was.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the tools and materials needed to cut and ink a woodblock.
The speaker is frustrated that the finished print differs from the image planned.
The speaker works without fully seeing the image until the finished print reveals it.
The speaker regrets choosing a medium that offers so little certainty to the artist.
items.explanation: In plain English: the speaker carves 'by feel' with the image held 'backward' in mind, and 'only when' the paper comes off does the heron appear clearly, 'more certain' than the speaker felt. The poem moves from working half-blind to seeing the image revealed, and choice C covers both parts.

A.why: You described only the images from the first lines (the block, the ink, the paper) and missed the turn at 'Only when,' where the poem arrives at its point.

B.why: You reversed the tone. The heron faces 'the right way at last.' The print shows what the speaker's hands 'had meant,' so it matches the speaker's intention rather than disappointing it.

D.why: You added a regret the poem never states. The speaker admits to uncertainty but never wishes for a different medium. The ending sounds like wonder, not regret.

Walter is anxious that the aging bridge may no longer be safe for drivers to cross.

A white point, steady over the garden wall,

C.why: You read the wrong tone. The speaker calls the star a small 'white point' but is not let down by it. The speaker stands there absorbed, 'reading' the light like a letter.

The following text is from an original short story. Nell keeps the wage ledger at a small shoe factory.

items.stem: Follow Nell's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how it changes?

At the end, she 'found that she was smiling' after the new contract raised every rate. So her feeling goes from dread to relief. The following text is from an original memoir. The narrator is a marine biologist returning to a coral reef two years after a heat wave bleached it white.

I dropped into the water expecting a graveyard. Two years earlier the reef had been bone-white from end to end, and I had stopped telling people I studied it. However, near the base of the old brain corals, I found small brown knobs, new polyps, no bigger than my thumbnail. I counted forty before my air ran low. I surfaced laughing into my mask, already planning the next dive.
items.stem: Follow the narrator's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how it changes?
choices: The narrator expects to find a recovering reef but is let down by its damage.
The narrator dives on a reef that was bleached white by a heat wave long ago.
The narrator concludes that the reef has fully healed and needs no more study.
The narrator expects to find a dead reef but grows hopeful on seeing regrowth.
items.explanation: The word 'However' marks the turn. Before it, the narrator expects 'a graveyard.' After it, the narrator finds new polyps and surfaces 'laughing,' already planning to come back. So the feeling goes from expecting the worst to feeling hopeful. On the Easy main-idea question about memoirs and stories, the answer usually follows whatever comes after a pivot like this one.

A.why: This swaps the expectation and the outcome. The narrator expected damage and found regrowth, not the other way around. Check which side of 'However' each feeling is on.

B.why: This comes from the italic introduction and the first two sentences only. It sets the scene, but it leaves out the change of feeling, which is the point of the passage.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a short story about Ines, who has just finished her first week of work at a textile mill.

At the gate, the foreman handed Ines a brown envelope. She did not open it on the tram. At home she set it on the kitchen table and counted the coins twice, lining them up by size. Six days of threading bobbins, and here they were, small and solid. She sat back and smiled, feeling for the first time that her work was worth something.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines feels proud when she receives the wages from her first week of work.
Ines feels let down by how small the wages from her first week of work are.
Ines keeps her first week's wages hidden so that no one else can take them.
Ines notices that the coins in her pay envelope come in different sizes.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you who Ines is and what is happening: she has just finished her first week at the mill. Now follow her feelings from start to end. She counts the coins carefully, she smiles, and the last sentence names the feeling directly: her work is 'worth something.' That is pride, and choice A covers both the situation (her first wages) and where her emotion ends up. This is the basic move behind every literary main-idea question: work out the situation, then follow the character's feeling to the end.

B.why: You took the word 'small' as a complaint and flipped the tone. The coins are 'small and solid,' and Ines smiles. Nothing in the text shows disappointment. Choices that reverse the character's feeling are the most common trap in this kind of question.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Ines waits to open the envelope until she gets home, but the passage never says she is hiding it or worried that someone will take it. If you can't point to a line that states the motive, the choice is adding something the text doesn't say.

D.why: This is true, since she lines the coins up by size, but it describes only one small action. The passage is about what the wages mean to her. A choice can be accurate and still be too narrow to be the main idea.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Ines, a nutrition scientist, is visiting her grandmother.

Ines had spent a decade counting grams of sodium for strangers, and she arrived at her grandmother's kitchen braced to disapprove. The stew was dark with salted pork; the bread had been fried in lard. She opened her mouth to say something about arteries. But her grandmother was humming as she ladled, and the neighbors crowding the table were laughing over one another, and Ines found that the lecture she had rehearsed on the train no longer seemed to belong in the room. She took a second bowl and said nothing.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines, prepared to criticize the meal, decides that the nutritional advice she has given for years is mistaken.
Ines, prepared to criticize the meal, sets aside her objections once she experiences the warmth of the gathering.
Ines notices that her grandmother's stew and bread are made with salted pork and fried in lard.
Ines grows irritated by the noisy neighbors and decides to leave before the meal is over.
items.explanation: Follow Ines from start to end: she arrives 'braced to disapprove,' but after 'But' the humming grandmother and laughing neighbors make her lecture feel out of place, and she quietly takes a second bowl. Choice B gets both halves right: the situation (ready to criticize) and the direction her feeling takes (she lets the objection go because of the warmth in the room).

A.why: This is the half-right answer. The first half is accurate, but the text never says Ines thinks her science is wrong. She only decides this isn't the moment for a lecture. You stopped reading once you recognized the opening words.

C.why: This is true, but it covers just one sentence. It leaves out Ines's change of heart, which is what the whole passage builds toward. It is too narrow.

D.why: This gets the tone backwards. The laughter wins Ines over rather than annoying her, and she stays for a second bowl instead of leaving.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker, a sports scientist, is timing a young runner on a track.

The stopwatch knows her by hundredths: / stride length, ground contact, the angle / of a knee at the moment of push. / I have charted her for three seasons, / every figure tidier than the last. / Yet this morning, when she crossed the line / and threw her head back, laughing, into the wind, / I looked down and found I had forgotten / to press the button at all.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the precise measurements used to track the runner's stride and form.
The speaker, who has measured the runner for years, regrets an error that spoiled a season of data.
The speaker grows frustrated that the runner's times have stopped improving after three seasons.
The speaker, who has measured the runner for years, is so moved by her joy that the timing is forgotten.
items.explanation: Put the poem into plain English. For three seasons the speaker has recorded this runner in exact detail. Then 'Yet' brings the turn: the runner crosses the line laughing, and the speaker is so caught up in the moment that they never stop the watch. Choice D covers the years of measuring and the turn at the end.

A.why: This only describes the images in the opening lines. It skips the turn after 'Yet,' which is what the poem is really about. That is the usual poetry trap.

B.why: The first half is right, but nothing in the poem suggests regret or lost data. It misses one timing on one morning, and the tone is wonder, not dismay. Read every choice to the end.

C.why: The poem says each figure was 'tidier than the last,' so the runner is getting better, and the speaker shows delight, not frustration.

The following text is from a short story. Priya, a public health officer, is writing the final report on a clean-water campaign she led.

The report was due Friday, and Priya had the numbers: cholera admissions down by two thirds, the new pumps working in eleven of twelve villages. The minister's office would want a photograph. Although the campaign largely succeeded, Priya worries that the minister will blame her for the broken pump.
Priya records that the new pumps are working in eleven of the twelve villages in the campaign.
Priya is pleased that her report will present the campaign to the minister as a complete success.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a memoir. The author, a musicologist, describes transcribing old field recordings of folk songs.

For the first month I transcribed the tapes as I had been trained to: pitch, rhythm, the placement of each ornament, all of it pinned to the staff. The singers were long dead, and the hiss of the old reels made them sound farther away still. Then, on a recording from 1958, a woman stopped mid-verse to scold a child, laughed, and began the line again a half step higher. I did not notate the change. I rewound the tape and listened to her laugh, and then I listened again.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The author grows impatient with interruptions that make the old recordings difficult to transcribe.
The author's routine technical work gives way to a decision to abandon formal notation entirely.
The author's routine technical work gives way to fascination with a singer as a real person.
The author explains that one singer resumed her verse a half step higher than she began it.
items.explanation: Follow how the author feels over time. At first the work is mechanical and the singers seem far away. Then one woman's unplanned moment pulls the author in, and they stop notating and replay her laugh. Choice C describes that move from routine to fascination.

A.why: This gets the tone backwards. The interruption fascinates the author, who rewinds to hear it again rather than getting annoyed.

B.why: The first half is right, but the author skips notating one change on one tape. Nothing says they give up notation altogether. You stopped reading once you recognized the opening words.

D.why: This is accurate but covers only one detail. It leaves out the author's reaction, which is what the passage is building to.

A student uncovers a roof tile bearing a dog's paw print that was pressed in before the clay was fired.
The students remain bored with the excavation even after a discovery is made on the final afternoon.
Halloran, though familiar with such finds, chooses not to spoil the students' newly awakened wonder.

The following text is from a poem. The speaker, an immunologist, is looking at blood cells under a microscope.

Under the lens they are only shapes: / the macrophage slumped like a sack of grain, / the lymphocytes small and round as seeds. / I have named them all a thousand times. / But tonight, my own blood on the slide, / I watched one cell reach out and swallow / a thing that would have harmed me, / and I thanked it, aloud, alone in the lab, / as if it could hear.

choices: The speaker compares the shapes of familiar blood cells to everyday objects such as grain and seeds.
Seeing their own cells at work turns the speaker's routine observation into personal gratitude.
Seeing their own cells at work, the speaker fears that their immune system is beginning to fail.
The speaker concludes that immunologists should study patients' feelings as well as their cells.
items.explanation: Put the poem into plain English. The speaker has looked at these cells so often that they are 'only shapes.' Then 'But' brings the turn: it's the speaker's own blood, a cell destroys something harmful, and the speaker thanks it out loud. Choice B covers the routine and the gratitude it turns into.

A.why: This only describes the comparisons in the opening lines. It skips the turn after 'But,' which is where the poem's meaning is. That is the usual poetry trap.

C.why: The first half is right, but the cell is doing its job by destroying 'a thing that would have harmed me.' The speaker feels grateful, not afraid.

D.why: This turns a private moment into a lesson for the whole field. The poem never makes that claim.

Agnes, who expected to dismiss a plain quilt quickly, decides the rest of the catalog is also wrong.
Agnes observes that the quilt's cotton prints are inexpensive and have faded unevenly over time.

C.why: This is a true detail from one sentence, but it is too narrow. It leaves out the discovery and Agnes's absorption, which the passage is about.

As an adult, rereading the list, the speaker sees that it holds only labels and no record of what they actually saw, so tonight they go out 'with no name in my head, and look.' I had expected the work to feel like science: tidy, numbered, remote. For the first weeks it did. I weighed each warbler in a plastic tube, read its wing length off a steel rule, and called the numbers to Dov, who wrote them down. However, one morning a chickadee I was holding stopped struggling and simply looked at me, its heart going so fast against my fingers that I lost count of it. I released it and forgot to call the weight. Dov said nothing, but after that he let me hold each bird a moment longer before I spoke.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: An encounter with one bird changes the author's sense of banding from detached measurement into something more personal and felt.
An encounter with one bird changes the author's sense of banding, leading her to doubt that its measurements are worth recording.
The author becomes so distracted by a chickadee's rapid heartbeat that she forgets to call out the bird's weight to Dov.
Dov begins letting the author hold each bird longer so that she will stop making careless mistakes in her recording.
items.explanation: The passage sets up an expectation ('tidy, numbered, remote') and then turns on 'However.' The chickadee's gaze and racing heart break that detachment, and Dov quietly makes room for the new feeling. Choice A names both the starting view and what it changes into, which is the arc of the whole passage.

B.why: The first half is correct, so it is easy to accept the whole choice. But the author never questions whether the data matter. Forgetting one weight is a lapse in a moving moment, not a judgment that measuring is pointless.

C.why: This is true, but it is a single incident. It leaves out the author's earlier expectations and the lasting change afterward, so it is too narrow for the main idea.

D.why: This gives Dov a motive the text never states. He 'said nothing' and let her hold each bird longer, which reads as respect for what she felt. Nothing suggests he was correcting her carelessness.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a short story. Marguerite, an archaeologist near the end of her career, is excavating an ancient well.

For thirty seasons Marguerite had wanted the great find: a hoard, an inscription, anything the journals would print. The well gave her potsherds, a bent nail, the jaw of a goat. On the last afternoon her trowel turned up a clay cup with a thumbprint pressed into the rim, small, perhaps a child's, set there before the clay was fired. She sat back on her heels for a long while. The journals would not want it. She wrapped it more carefully than anything she had ever found.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Though her final dig yields nothing of the importance she long sought, Marguerite is deeply moved by a humble cup bearing one person's mark.
Though her final dig yields nothing of the importance she long sought, Marguerite expects the thumbprinted cup to finally win her recognition.
Marguerite is disappointed that her final excavation turns up only a clay cup, a bent nail, and other ordinary objects.
A small thumbprint pressed into a clay cup's rim suggests that the vessel may have been handled by a child before firing.
items.explanation: The opening establishes Marguerite's lifelong wish for a find the journals would print, and the well gives her nothing of the kind. The last sentences add it all up: she knows 'the journals would not want it,' yet she wraps the cup 'more carefully than anything she had ever found.' Choice A captures both the unmet ambition and what she feels about the cup.

B.why: The first half is right, but the second half contradicts the text, which says outright that 'the journals would not want it.' Marguerite treasures the cup for personal reasons, not for recognition.

C.why: This reverses the emotional direction of the ending. The cup does not disappoint her. She sits with it 'for a long while' and wraps it with more care than any other find.

D.why: This restates a detail about the cup accurately, but it leaves Marguerite out entirely. The passage is about what the cup means to her, so a statement about the object alone is too narrow.
