items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Corinne Abaya's 2021 novel The Drained Country. Decades earlier, Teodora, now a retired engineer, helped design the canals that drained a wetland so it could be farmed.

When the county flooded the old fields to bring back the marsh, Teodora told anyone who would listen that it was sentimental waste. She drove out on the first warm morning, intending to be proved right. However, the canal she had once measured to the inch was now choked with sedge, and a heron stood in it as though it had always owned the place. Frogs she could not name were calling from the stubble. She stayed until the light changed, and on the drive home she found that she no longer had her argument ready.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Teodora hides her change of mind from the county officials who chose to restore the marsh.
Teodora notices that a heron has settled in a canal she once measured with great precision.
Teodora, who had dismissed the marsh restoration, finds her opposition weakening as she watches it.
Teodora is pleased to see that the restored marsh has confirmed her earlier warnings about it.
items.explanation: Follow Teodora from start to end. She first calls the restoration 'sentimental waste' and comes to be 'proved right.' Then 'However' turns the passage: the sedge, the heron and the frogs hold her there 'until the light changed,' and by the end she 'no longer had her argument ready.' Choice C covers both her starting position and the way her opposition gives way.

A.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Teodora loses her argument, but nothing says she conceals that from anyone, county officials included.

B.why: The heron is in the passage, but it is one image. This choice is too narrow because it leaves out Teodora's skepticism and how her view changes, which is what the whole passage is about.

D.why: This reverses the tone. Teodora wanted to be proved right, but after the 'However' she sees the marsh thriving and loses her argument. Nothing she warned about comes true.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Ruth Penhallow's poem "Winter Count." The speaker is volunteering in an annual bird survey.

I stood at the frozen pond with clipboard and pencil,
ticking off the mallards, two coots, the jay that scolded me—
seventeen species by noon, the numbers neatly columned.
Then a wren dropped to the reeds an arm's length from my boot
and looked at me as if I were the one being counted,
and only then did I lower the pencil and simply watch.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker loses interest in the survey and leaves the pond before the count is finished.
The speaker, busy tallying birds for a survey, turns to simply watching after a wren comes close.
The speaker records the many different species of birds found at a frozen pond in a morning.
The speaker regrets joining the survey because counting disturbs the birds being observed.
items.explanation: In plain English: the speaker is carefully counting birds and keeping neat columns of numbers. Then a wren lands close by and seems to study the speaker, and 'only then' does the speaker stop writing and just watch. Choice B covers both the counting and that 'only then' turn at the end.

A.why: This reverses the tone. The speaker is absorbed, not bored, and stays at the pond to watch the wren. The poem never says the speaker leaves or loses interest.

C.why: This describes only the first three lines, the tallying. It misses the turn the poem ends on, where the speaker stops counting and simply watches.

D.why: You added a regret and a reason the poem never gives. Nothing says the survey bothers the birds or that the speaker wishes they hadn't volunteered.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Nalini Desrosiers's 2017 novel The Loom Room. In the 1840s, Abigail has recently started work at a cotton mill in Lowell, Massachusetts.

For her first week Abigail could not hear herself think. The looms shook the floorboards, and lint settled in her hair so thickly that the older girls called her Snowy. She broke three threads the first morning and wept over the third. By the second month, though, her hands had learned to find a slack thread before her eyes did, and she could tie a weaver's knot without looking. When the overseer placed a new girl at the loom beside hers, Abigail caught herself explaining the shuttle as though she had been born to it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Abigail remains so shaken by the noise of the mill that she cannot help the new worker.
Abigail is teased by older workers, who give her a nickname because of lint in her hair.
Abigail tries to impress the overseer so that she will be moved to a better-paying loom.
Abigail, at first overwhelmed by mill work, grows skilled enough to guide a newcomer.
items.explanation: Follow Abigail from start to end. In her first week she cannot think over the noise and cries over broken threads. 'Though' marks the change: by the second month she works by feel, and the last sentence shows her explaining the shuttle to a new girl 'as though she had been born to it.' Choice D covers both her early struggle and the confidence she grows into.

A.why: This reverses the direction of the passage. Abigail is overwhelmed at first, but by the end she is confidently teaching the new girl, not unable to help her.

B.why: The nickname is true, but it comes from one sentence. This choice is too narrow because it skips how Abigail changes from struggling to skilled.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. The overseer only places the new girl next to Abigail, and nothing suggests Abigail wants to impress anyone or move to another loom.

The following text is adapted from Miriam Okafor's 2019 novel *The Long Ward*. Adaeze, a nurse, is going door to door during a measles vaccination campaign.

The following text is from Tomasz Weller's 1931 poem "Observatory, Late."

All night I chart the cold and turning lights
and print their names in columns, ruled and neat;
I track each drifting point across the heights
and know the sky the way I know my street.
But when the dawn has washed the last star out,
I set my pencil down and feel how small
my careful columns are, and learn to doubt
that I had understood the sky at all.

The speaker celebrates having finally mapped the night sky as completely as a familiar street.
The speaker regrets choosing astronomy and decides to give up observing for a simpler kind of work.
The speaker's confidence from a night of charting stars gives way at dawn to a humbling sense of doubt.
items.explanation: In plain English: all night the speaker records the stars and feels they know the sky well. B.why: This reverses the ending. The speaker does say they know the sky "the way I know my street," but by the last line they doubt they understood it at all. You stopped reading before the turn.

C.why: The speaker feels humbled, but nothing in the poem suggests regret about the career or a plan to quit. You added a decision the poem never makes.

The following text is adapted from Ruth Calloway's 2008 memoir *A Year of Wings*. As a girl, Calloway kept a notebook of the birds she saw near her family's farm.

At first I wrote down only the birds that seemed worth the ink: a heron, once, and a pair of kestrels. The sparrows on the fence I ignored. That spring I sat by the fence every morning, and by May I had filled six pages with birds I had walked past my whole life.

choices: Prompted by her grandfather, the narrator learns to look closely at common birds she had always overlooked.
The narrator resents her grandfather's question and stops writing in her bird notebook that spring.
The narrator recalls once seeing a heron and a pair of kestrels from her family's farm.
The narrator sits by the fence each morning to avoid the farm chores her grandfather gives her.
items.explanation: Her grandfather's question shows the narrator she has been ignoring the sparrows. She responds by watching them every morning until she has filled six pages. Choice A covers the cause (his question) and the change (paying attention to ordinary birds).

C.why: The heron and kestrels are mentioned, but only as the birds she noticed before her change. You chose a true detail from the first sentence over the point of the whole passage.

D.why: The text never mentions chores or avoiding anything. You added a motive. She sits by the fence because the question made her curious.

The following text is from a short story. Marisol, an apprentice in a print shop, is pulling the first print from a woodblock she has carved.

Marisol peeled the paper back slowly, bracing for the worst. items.stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker is crossing a city bridge that the speaker's father inspected for many years.

Each morning the bridge takes the weight of the city:
trucks of lettuce, the school bus, a man with a cello.
It does not complain. It was built to flex,
to give an inch in August and take it back in frost.
My father checked its rivets for thirty years.
I used to think him rigid, a man of fixed numbers.
Only now, crossing it, do I see what he knew:
that holding firm means learning when to bend.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker realizes that the father, once thought rigid, understood the strength in bending.
The speaker lists the many vehicles and travelers that cross the city bridge each morning.
The speaker resents the years the father spent inspecting the bridge instead of being home.
The speaker admires the bridge's fixed design and wishes the father had been as unbending.
items.explanation: Put the poem into plain English first. A bridge carries the city's traffic and is built to flex with the seasons. The speaker's father inspected it, and the speaker once thought of him as rigid. items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. Anil, a graduate student in linguistics, is recording his grandmother, one of the last speakers of her village's dialect.

Anil had come with a list of four hundred words and a recorder charged overnight. His grandmother answered the first dozen patiently (water, smoke, the word for a younger brother) and then set the list aside. She wanted to tell him instead about the flood year, when the river took the mill. Anil glanced at the blinking red light, then at his unfinished columns. He let the list slide to the floor. Somewhere in her story, he realized, were words no list would have thought to ask for.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Anil drops his planned word list, sensing that his grandmother's story holds more of her language.
Anil grows impatient when his grandmother drifts away from the word list he has prepared.
Anil's grandmother refuses the word list because she distrusts the recorder he has brought.
Anil's grandmother describes a flood year in which the river carried away the village mill.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you the situation: Anil is recording a dialect that is disappearing. Follow what he does. He arrives with a long list, his grandmother sets it aside to tell a story, and he lets the list 'slide to the floor.' The last sentence names what he has realized: her story contains words his list would never have asked for. A matches both what he does and why he does it.

B.why: Anil does look at his unfinished columns, but he doesn't become impatient. He gives up the list and sees the value in her story. This choice reverses his reaction.

C.why: The grandmother does set the list aside, but the text gives her reason: she wants to tell a story. Nothing says she distrusts the recorder. You supplied a motive the passage never states.

D.why: This is accurate, but it is only the subject of the grandmother's story. It leaves out Anil's decision and what he realizes, which is what the passage as a whole is about. This is the too-narrow trap.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Mara Lindqvist's 2019 novel *The Grid*. Teodora, a city planner, is visiting a public square she designed ten years earlier.

Teodora had drawn every bench on this square herself, angling each one toward the fountain so that strangers would sit side by side and watch the water. Now she found the benches dragged into loose circles, turned toward one another, the fountain behind them ignored. A boy had chalked a hopscotch court across her careful paving. She had expected to feel slighted. Instead she stood a long while at the edge of the square and felt, absurdly, that she had been thanked.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Teodora resents that residents have ignored the layout she planned and rearranged the square without her approval.
Teodora finds that residents' changes to the square she designed leave her unexpectedly gratified rather than offended.
Teodora originally placed the benches facing the fountain so that strangers would sit together and watch the water.
Teodora decides that future squares she designs should leave residents free to arrange the benches however they like.
items.explanation: Follow Teodora's feeling from start to end. She sees her design undone and 'had expected to feel slighted', but the final sentence turns: 'Instead' she feels 'that she had been thanked'. Choice B gets both the situation (residents have changed her square) and the direction of the feeling (gratified, not offended). The last sentence adds up the scene, and B is the only choice that matches it.

A.why: You took the feeling Teodora expected to have and treated it as the one she actually has. The word 'Instead' tells you she did not feel slighted. She felt thanked.

C.why: This is true, but it only describes the first sentence. It says nothing about what Teodora finds now or how she feels about it, and that is what the passage is about. It's too narrow.

D.why: You gave Teodora a plan the text never mentions. She stands and reflects, but she never decides anything about future designs.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Jonas Okafor's 1958 short story "Piece Rate." Ruth works at a sewing machine in a shirt factory.

For eleven years Ruth had paid herself in shirts. Every collar she finished was worth a few cents, and by noon she could tell from the pile at her elbow whether the week's rent was safe. The new manager meant the hourly wage as a kindness, and the others welcomed it. But at her machine Ruth found that the pile meant nothing now. The clock paid her the same whether she hurried or not, and she could not decide whether that made her free or simply lost.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ruth joins her coworkers in welcoming the new hourly wage as a relief from years of anxious counting.
Ruth secretly keeps working at her old pace to protest the manager's decision to change the way she is paid.
Under the old system, Ruth's weekly pay depended on how many shirts she managed to finish at her machine.
Ruth is unsettled by the switch to hourly pay because her familiar way of measuring her work no longer applies.
items.explanation: The introduction places Ruth at a factory machine. The passage then follows her from confident counting ('she could tell... whether the week's rent was safe') to confusion after the change: 'the pile meant nothing now', and she feels perhaps 'simply lost'. Choice D matches both the situation (the change to hourly pay) and the direction of her feeling (unsettled).

A.why: The text says 'the others welcomed it.' Then 'But' separates Ruth from them. You applied the coworkers' feeling to Ruth and reversed her tone.

B.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Nothing suggests that Ruth is protesting or hiding anything. She simply can't tell what the new pay means for her.

C.why: This is accurate, but it only covers the background in the first two sentences. It leaves out the change and Ruth's reaction to it, which is where the passage is heading. It's too narrow.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Elena Varga's 2011 poem "Field Notes." The speaker is a linguist recording one of the last speakers of a language.

I came with a recorder and a list:
the word for river, for grandmother, for rain.
Old Ilona gave them gladly,
spelling each one twice into the hum.
I filed them by evening, neat as seeds.
Only when the tapes played in a quiet room
did I hear what the list had left out—
her laughing between the words,
the song she hummed while she thought—
and know I had kept the words and lost the talk.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker realizes that a careful record of individual words missed the living speech that surrounded them.
The speaker describes collecting and filing a list of everyday words given by an elderly speaker of a language.
The speaker celebrates having fully preserved Ilona's language so that future listeners can still hear it spoken.
The speaker resolves to return to Ilona and record her songs before they are forgotten by the next generation.
items.explanation: Put the poem into plain English first. The speaker collects words efficiently, and then, 'Only when' the tapes play back, notices the laughter and humming that the list left out. The last line, 'kept the words and lost the talk', is the turn the poem builds toward. Choice A states that realization and covers the whole poem.

B.why: This describes only the first five lines, the collecting and filing. It misses the reflection the poem turns to after 'Only when', which is the point of the poem.

C.why: This reverses the tone. The speaker says the language was not fully preserved: she 'lost the talk'. The ending is regret, not celebration.

D.why: You added a plan the poem never mentions. The speaker recognises what is missing but never says she will go back or do anything about it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a 2021 novel. Ines, a graduate student, is spending her first summer working at an archaeological excavation in southern Spain.

Before she came, Ines had pictured discovery as a flash of gold in the dirt, the kind of find that ends up behind museum glass. By August she had found no gold at all. What she found instead, on an ordinary Tuesday, was a shard of a cooking pot with a small thumbprint pressed into its rim, left by someone who had lifted it while the clay was still soft. She held it longer than she had held anything all summer. The gold she had imagined, she realized, would never have felt this close.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines is disappointed that her first summer has turned up nothing but ordinary cooking pottery.
Ines keeps the marked shard to herself so that she can study it without her supervisors.
Ines finds that a modest object moves her more deeply than the treasure she once imagined.
Ines notices that the cooking pot was handled by its maker while the clay was still soft.
items.explanation: Follow how Ines feels from start to finish. She begins by imagining gold, finds only a plain shard with a thumbprint, holds it 'longer than she had held anything all summer,' and ends by realizing the gold 'would never have felt this close.' The passage turns on the gap between what she expected and what she found, and that gap comes out in favor of the humble object. Choice C covers both halves of that comparison and the feeling the final sentence names.

A.why: You reversed the tone. Ines does find only a cooking pot and no gold, but the passage says the shard affects her more than gold would have. She is moved, not disappointed.

B.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Nothing in the passage says Ines hides the shard or wants to keep it from anyone. She simply holds it for a long time.

D.why: You chose a detail that is true but too narrow. The text does say the clay was soft when the thumbprint was made, but that is one sentence. It leaves out the comparison with the gold she imagined, which is the point of the passage.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a 2017 poem. The speaker describes a quilt made by the speaker's grandmother.

As a child I counted its squares for sleep:
the blue of a work shirt, a curtain's faded rose,
a yellow torn from some forgotten apron.
It was a blanket, and blankets were for warmth.
Years later, sorting her letters, I found the shirt
in a photograph, the apron at a wedding,
and then, only then, I understood
she had been writing her life in cloth
and I had slept beneath the pages.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker comes to see that a quilt once valued only for warmth records the grandmother's life.
The speaker recalls the colors of the quilt's squares and how counting them brought sleep in childhood.
The speaker is troubled to learn from the letters that the grandmother kept her past from the family.
The speaker discovers that the quilt's fabrics had little to do with anything in the grandmother's past.
items.explanation: First put the whole poem into plain English. As a child, the speaker thought of the quilt as just a blanket 'for warmth.' Years later, the speaker finds the same fabrics in old photographs and, 'then, only then,' understands that the grandmother had been 'writing her life in cloth.' The poem compares two ways of seeing the same object, and the main idea is the change between them. Choice A captures both the earlier view and the later one.

B.why: You described only the opening images. Counting the squares at bedtime is what the poem starts with, but it misses the 'then, only then' turn, where the speaker realizes what the quilt meant.

C.why: You added a motive the poem never gives. The letters and photographs show where the fabrics came from. Nothing suggests the grandmother hid her past, and the speaker is not troubled.

D.why: You reversed what the speaker finds. The shirt and apron show up in photographs from the grandmother's life, so the fabrics are tied directly to her past. That connection is the whole point of the ending.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a 2015 memoir. The author, a linguist, describes returning to the island where the author grew up to record the speech of older residents.

At university I learned to describe my grandmother's speech in the tidy terms of the field: a dropped final consonant, a vowel that rose where the mainland's fell. I could chart such features in an afternoon. Yet when I sat in Mrs. Doyle's kitchen with the recorder running, the charts seemed thin. She paused before certain words the way you might pause at a grave, and no column in my notes had room for that. I went home with forty hours of tape, convinced I had captured the sounds and missed the speech.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The author is pleased that years of academic training made a complete record of the island's speech possible.
The author learns that island speakers raise certain vowels in places where mainland speakers lower them.
The author abandons the study of linguistics after deciding that its methods are of no real use on the island.
The author realizes that the methods of the field capture the sounds of the dialect but not its deeper meaning.
items.explanation: Follow the author from beginning to end. At first the training seems powerful ('I could chart such features in an afternoon'). In Mrs. Doyle's kitchen the charts 'seemed thin,' and the last sentence sums it up: the author 'captured the sounds and missed the speech.' The passage is about the gap between what the methods can record and what the speech means to the people who use it. Choice D states both sides of that gap.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The author leaves feeling that the record is incomplete, not pleased with it. The final sentence says the 'speech' was missed even though forty hours of sound were recorded.

B.why: You picked a detail that is true but too narrow. The vowel difference is one example from the first sentence. It is not the author's realization about what the methods miss.

C.why: You went further than the text does. The author finds the methods incomplete, not useless, and nothing says the author gives up linguistics. The author leaves with forty hours of tape.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Marguerite Osei, a civil engineer, attends the opening ceremony for a railway viaduct she designed.

The mayor's speech ran long, the band played twice, and someone pressed a ribbon of ceremonial silk into Osei's hand. She held it without looking at it. When the first freight train eased onto the span, the crowd cheered; Osei did not. She had gone down to the riverbank, where she stood with one palm flat against the nearest stone pier. Through the stone she felt the load arrive, settle, and pass, exactly as she had known it would. Only then did she smile, and only then did she climb back up to the platform, where the applause had already ended.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although Osei is honored at the opening, the satisfaction she wants comes from feeling the viaduct carry its load as she planned, not from the public celebration.
Although Osei is honored at the opening, she slips away from the crowd because she fears the viaduct may not hold the weight of the first train.
Osei finds the opening ceremony tedious and resents the mayor for delaying the moment when the first train is finally allowed to cross the viaduct.
Osei is so moved by the crowd's cheering for the viaduct that she has to step down to the riverbank to compose herself before returning to the platform.
items.explanation: Start with the italic introduction: Osei designed the viaduct, and this is its opening. Then follow what she does from start to end. She holds the ceremonial ribbon without looking at it. She does not cheer. She goes down to the pier to feel the train cross, which happens "exactly as she had known it would." She smiles only after that, and by the time she climbs back up, the applause has ended. So her satisfaction comes from feeling the structure perform as she planned, not from the ceremony. Choice A covers the honor, where her attention goes, and why she smiles.

B.why: You correctly saw that Osei separates herself from the celebration, then explained it with the motive that seemed most likely: nerves. The text rules that out. She felt the load pass "exactly as she had known it would," so she had no doubt to resolve. The first half of this choice is right and the second half adds a fear the passage never gives her. Read every choice to the end.

C.why: You noticed that the speech "ran long" and that Osei ignores the ribbon, and you read her detachment as boredom and resentment. The text never says she is annoyed with the mayor or anyone else. Her attention is on the bridge, not against the ceremony. This choice adds a motive the text never gives.

D.why: This reverses the tone. The text says that when the crowd cheered, "Osei did not," and she goes to the riverbank to feel the train cross, not to recover from the cheering. She misses the applause altogether, so it cannot be what moved her.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker is an archaeologist excavating the remains of an ancient settlement.

I logged the sherds by depth and grid and hue,
bagged bone and charcoal, numbered every stone,
and wrote the site as something I could know
the way one knows a ledger or a map.
Then, under the lip of a broken jar,
a thumbprint, pressed in clay three thousand years
before my glove: some potter's careless mark.
I set my pencil down. The grid stayed true,
but I could not go back to counting what
I'd measured; someone's hand had measured me.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the careful methods used to record the site, from charting each find's depth to bagging bone and charcoal for later study.
A potter's thumbprint prompts the speaker to abandon the excavation grid, which now seems an inaccurate way to record the settlement's remains.
A potter's thumbprint shifts the speaker from treating the site as data to be logged to sensing the individual person who once lived there.
The speaker regrets a careless moment that left a mark on an ancient jar, realizing that the excavation has damaged what it meant to preserve.
items.explanation: Restate the poem in plain English. In the first four lines, the speaker records everything methodically and thinks of the site the way one thinks of "a ledger or a map." At "Then," the poem turns: the speaker finds a potter's thumbprint left in the clay three thousand years ago, puts the pencil down, and cannot go back to simply counting, because "someone's hand had measured me." The poem moves from data to a sense of one real person, and Choice C follows that whole movement.

A.why: This describes only the opening lines: the logging, bagging and numbering. It misses the turn at "Then" and the change in the speaker that the rest of the poem is about. It is true, but too narrow.

B.why: You correctly saw that the thumbprint changes the speaker, then guessed that the change is a rejection of the method. The poem says the opposite: "The grid stayed true." What the speaker can't go back to is treating the finds as mere counting, not the grid itself. The first half of this choice is right and the second half contradicts the text.

D.why: This misattributes the word "careless." The "careless mark" belongs to the ancient potter, pressed into the clay three thousand years before the speaker's glove. The speaker damages nothing and expresses no regret. The feeling is closer to awe at another person's presence.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. In the 1950s, Ruth Okafor works as a nurse in a rural vaccination campaign.

By Friday the ledger showed 412 children inoculated, more than any other district on the coast, and Dr. Mensah had written "Excellent" across the bottom in red. Ruth read the word several times on the bus home. Yet the number she kept arriving at was not 412 but one: the boy on the ridge road whose mother had stood in the doorway, arms folded, until Ruth closed her bag. The ledger had no column for him. She found herself wishing it did.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ruth takes quiet pride in her district's record, which her supervisor has praised as the best result anywhere on the coast.
Ruth worries that Dr. Mensah's praise will be withdrawn once he learns that a mother on the ridge road refused the vaccine.
Although her campaign has been officially praised, Ruth's thoughts keep returning to the one child she was unable to vaccinate.
Ruth is troubled that her ledger leaves out the boy, and she resolves to change how the campaign records families who refuse.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker describes a night spent at a backyard telescope.

I logged them as my father taught me:
magnitude, the hour, the patient drift
of Vega past the maple's highest limb.
I kept the columns neat, the pencil sharp.
It was near dawn, the eyepiece cold with dew,
before I looked down at the page and saw
the slant of every figure was his slant,
the night's whole log was in his hand
as much as mine.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the methodical way of recording the brightness and movement of stars that a father once taught.
The speaker comes to see that a night of careful stargazing has also been a way of carrying on a father's practice.
The speaker regrets spending a whole night filling columns with figures instead of simply looking up at the stars.
The speaker comes to see that a father's habits have kept the speaker from developing a way of observing of the speaker's own.
items.explanation: Restate the poem in plain English. I logged the stars the way my father taught me, and near dawn I saw that my handwriting was his, so the log was as much his as mine. The turn at 'before I looked down' is a recognition: the speaker's careful observing carries the father's practice forward. Nothing in the poem says this is a loss.

A.why: You summarized the opening lines and skipped the turn. The poem's point is what the speaker realizes near dawn, not the method of logging.

C.why: You added a regret the poem doesn't contain. The speaker keeps the columns 'neat' and 'sharp' with no sign of wishing the night had gone differently, and the ending is a discovery, not a complaint.

D.why: You caught the turn toward the father and then gave it the wrong meaning. Seeing his hand in the log is not presented as a limitation. Nothing says the speaker has been held back from an independent style.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a memoir. As a teenager, the narrator joined a volunteer bird survey on a coastal marsh.

I had come for herons, or at least an osprey, and by the third morning I had counted nothing but sparrows: brown, quick, maddeningly alike. Mr. Haskell, who ran the survey, handed me his own field guide without comment. I began to notice the streaked breast of one, the yellow fleck above the eye of another, the way a third flicked its tail twice before it flew. By the end of the week I had stopped looking up at the sky at all.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Disappointed at first by the lack of rare birds, the narrator gradually becomes absorbed in the differences among the common ones.
Disappointed at first by the lack of rare birds, the narrator grows too discouraged by the week's end to keep scanning the sky.
With the help of Mr. Haskell's field guide, the narrator learns to identify several species of sparrow found on a coastal marsh.
Resenting Mr. Haskell for assigning a newcomer to sparrows, the narrator spends the week counting birds without much interest.
items.explanation: Trace the emotion. It starts as frustration ('maddeningly alike') and moves into close, specific noticing: the streaked breast, the yellow fleck, the double tail flick. The final line confirms the change. The narrator stopped looking up for herons because the sparrows below had become absorbing.

B.why: You read the last sentence literally and stopped there. The narrator did stop looking at the sky, but out of absorption, not discouragement. The sentences right before it show growing attention, which reverses the tone this choice gives.

C.why: This is roughly true but too narrow. It names what the narrator learned and leaves out the change in feeling from disappointment to absorption, which is what the passage is about.

D.why: You invented a grievance. Mr. Haskell only hands over a field guide, and the narrator's interest grows. It doesn't stay low.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Archaeologist Lena Varga has spent eleven seasons searching for a ruler's tomb.

The trench opened not onto a burial chamber but onto a kitchen: a hearth ringed with soot, three cracked storage jars, a grinding stone worn into a shallow bowl. Her students were careful with her that evening, speaking softly, as one does around a loss. Lena let them. She did not explain that she had spent the afternoon with her palm pressed to the hollow of that stone, fitting her hand to the shape another hand had made, and that she had not wanted a king for hours.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although Lena hides her disappointment from her students, failing to find the tomb after eleven seasons weighs heavily on her.
Although Lena is moved by the find, she hides this from her students because she fears they will think her long search was wasted.
Although the trench held no tomb, it revealed a hearth, storage jars, and a grinding stone used by the valley's ordinary residents.
Although her students assume the find is a disappointment, Lena is deeply absorbed by the traces of ordinary life it reveals.
items.explanation: The students treat the evening 'as one does around a loss,' but the last sentence shows what Lena actually felt. She spent the afternoon fitting her hand to the worn stone and 'had not wanted a king for hours.' The passage turns on the gap between what the others assume and what she feels.

A.why: You took the students' view as Lena's. The final sentence shows she isn't grieving at all, so this reverses her feeling.

B.why: The first half is right. She is moved, and she doesn't tell her students. But the text never says why she stays silent. The fear that her search will look wasted is a motive you supplied.

C.why: This lists what the trench contained and leaves Lena out entirely. A literary main idea has to cover the character's response, and that response is the point of the passage.

The following text is adapted from a novel. Tomasz's textile mill has just stopped paying workers by the piece and begun paying them by the hour.

The new wage was, by the foreman's arithmetic and his own, eleven cents an hour more than he had ever averaged at the old rate. Yet on the first Monday Tomasz caught himself glancing at the tally board where his count used to climb in chalk, and finding it wiped clean, he worked the loom more slowly than he meant to, as if something had been taken from the hour along with the counting.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Though Tomasz earns more under the new system, he misses the higher pay he could reach on his fastest days at the old rate.
Though Tomasz earns more under the new system, he senses that something has gone out of his work now that it is no longer counted.

Tomasz checks the foreman's arithmetic and confirms that the new hourly wage is higher than his average at the old piece rate.
items.explanation: The first sentence settles the money question: he is better paid. items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker works in a laboratory that measures the nutrients in food.

All week I weigh the lentils into grams,
burn them to ash, and read what's left: the iron,
the zinc, a little magnesium, the sum
of what a body takes from what it eats.
My mother never weighed a thing. She fed us
by the fistful and the look on our faces.
And only on the Friday drive back home
did I think she had been measuring as well,
just not in any unit I was taught.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the laboratory process of reducing lentils to ash in order to measure the minerals they contain.
The speaker regrets that a mother who never weighed food could not give her children the nutrients a laboratory would advise.
The speaker comes to regard a mother's untrained way of feeding the family as its own kind of careful measurement.
The speaker comes to regard a mother's untrained way of feeding the family as more accurate than the laboratory's methods.
items.explanation: In plain English: at work I measure food precisely, my mother never measured anything, and on the drive home I realized she had been measuring too, just in units I wasn't taught. The 'only then' turn reframes the mother's feeding by eye as another form of measurement.

B.why: You reversed the tone. The speaker ends by crediting the mother ('measuring as well'), not by faulting her diet.

D.why: This gets the realization right and then ranks it. The poem calls her measuring different ('not in any unit I was taught'), not better. 'More accurate' is a comparison the speaker never makes.

The following text is adapted from a novel. Decades ago, Arturo Llosa was chief engineer on a bridge that his granddaughter is now driving him across.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Arturo cannot share his granddaughter's simple pride in the bridge until he has privately satisfied himself that it is still sound.
Arturo is indifferent to his granddaughter's pride in the bridge, having long since stopped caring about his earlier work.
Arturo hears a bearing beginning to seize as they cross, and he keeps this from his granddaughter so as not to spoil her pride.
Arturo shows his granddaughter how the bridge's expansion joints and bearings have kept it sound over many decades.

C.why: You noticed his anxiety and his concealment ('would not have admitted') and finished the thought the obvious way. But the text says 'There was none.' He finds no fault, so there is nothing to hide.

The following text is adapted from a novel. In 1931, Hester Crane is mapping a river valley that a new reservoir will soon flood.

choices: Hester records the valley's daily life beyond her official task, hoping the fuller map will persuade the commission not to flood it.
Hester resents the commission for flooding the valley and keeps her field copy as proof that the official map is inaccurate.
Hester gives the commission the contours and property lines it requires for a valley that will be under water by spring.
Hester records the valley's daily life beyond her official task and treasures that record even after it is cut from the map.

After those details are struck, she keeps her copy 'in the drawer where other people keep letters,' which tells you she treasures it as something personal. Only this choice covers both her going beyond the task and how she treats the result.

B.why: The text shows no resentment and never calls the official map inaccurate. It is only missing details. Keeping the copy among 'letters' points to attachment, not to gathering evidence.

The following text is adapted from Delia Marsh's 2011 novel The Quiet Needle. Ines, a newly hired technician, is spending her first night at a remote seismic monitoring station.

To portray Ines's growing fascination with work she had expected to find dull
To show Ines's regret at having accepted a job only for the salary it paid
To reveal how Ines first became interested in studying earthquakes as a child

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Varga's 1998 poem "For the Bridge Builders."

They say the river does not remember who tamed it,
that no plaque will ever carry your names.
But you who sink the pilings in the cold brown current,
who bolt the girders while the wind leans hard,
look up: each morning thousands cross the water
on the strength of what your hands have set.
Build on. The far bank is waiting,
and the span you raise will hold for years.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

To describe the materials and methods used to construct a bridge across a river
To criticize the public for failing to learn the names of the people who build bridges
To encourage the bridge builders by affirming the lasting value of their labor

B.why: You noticed the pilings and girders and took them to be the point. The poem mentions these details only to honor the people doing the work. It never explains how a bridge is built.

C.why: You read too much into the line about no plaque. The poem mentions that the builders go unnamed only so it can answer that worry. It never blames the public. The speaker's attention stays on the builders the whole time.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Priya Nandakumar's 2015 novel The Piece Rate. Jonah works at a garment factory where pay is about to change from an hourly wage to a set amount for each finished shirt.

The foreman announced the change as though it were a gift: from now on, every shirt would earn its own wage. Jonah, however, did the arithmetic in his head and felt his stomach tighten. He was careful, not fast, and he knew it. Around him, the younger workers were already grinning and flexing their fingers. Jonah bent over his machine and tried to make his hands move quicker, but every crooked seam he had to tear out seemed to cost him more than thread.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray the younger workers' excitement about earning more under the new system
To explain why the factory's owners decided to change how the workers would be paid
To convey Jonah's anxiety that the new pay system will leave him worse off
To show Jonah's relief that his careful work will finally be properly rewarded
items.explanation: The setup line names Jonah as the focus. The foreman presents the change as a gift, and 'however' turns to Jonah's reaction: his stomach tightens, he knows he is slow, and every mistake now 'cost him more than thread.' The following text is from Halvard Prete's 1998 poem "To a Young Forecaster."

C.why: You added a story the poem doesn't tell. The speaker says 'the wisest' have been fooled but never describes a forecast of their own. The rain that 'will go elsewhere' is the young forecaster's, and it is in the future.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Maren Holt's 2019 novel The Lower Terrace. Ines has joined an archaeological excavation in southern Portugal for the summer.

Ines had always pictured archaeology as a series of revelations: a trowel strikes bronze, someone shouts, a photograph is taken. For her first two weeks on the site, however, she found only soil. She scraped it away in layers thinner than a fingernail, poured it through screens, and wrote numbers on paper bags. Somewhere in the third week she stopped waiting for the shout. She began to notice how the earth changed color one shade at a time, and she found she could read those shades the way her grandmother had once read the sky.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray how Ines comes to value the slow, careful work she had not expected the excavation to involve
To describe the particular artifacts Ines uncovers once she learns to read the changing colors of the soil
To convey her grandmother's skill at reading the weather, which Ines has long tried to imitate on the site
To suggest that Ines regrets joining a project that has failed to produce any of the discoveries she hoped for
items.explanation: The setup line tells you the focus is Ines. The passage opens with what she expected (dramatic finds), turns at 'however' to what she actually does (scraping, sifting, labeling), and ends with her learning to read the soil's shades. The following text is from Ruth Calloway's 2016 novel Second Shift. In 1934, Della works at a cannery where workers are paid a fixed amount for each crate they fill.

To explain the reasons the cannery owner gives his workers for lowering the piece rate month after month
To suggest that Della deliberately slows her pace once she learns that the piece rate has been reduced
items.explanation: The excerpt follows the 'old belief, then the correction' pattern. Della has believed that speed pays. After 'But,' the rate keeps falling, she works even faster, and in the last sentence she understands that her speed is losing value. That realization is what the whole passage builds toward, so choice A is the answer.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Anika Sorel's 2018 poem "To My Son, Before His First Vaccination."

Hold still, small one. The needle is quick,
a bee that does not stay.
What it leaves is not a wound but a lesson:
a faint likeness of a danger,
too weak to harm you, strong enough to study.
Your blood will learn its face
and keep the drawing somewhere deep,
so that if the real thing ever knocks,
you will already know its name
and open no door.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

To warn a child that the needle carries a danger his body may not be strong enough to resist
To compare the quick sting of a needle to the sting of a bee that a child once felt in a garden

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Miriam Okafor's 2009 novel The Last Speaker. Ruth, a linguist, is recording Tessaly, an elderly woman who is one of the few remaining fluent speakers of her village's language.

Tessaly said the word for river again, slowly, so that Ruth could write it down. Ruth wrote it: four letters, neat and correct. But when Tessaly said it a third time, she was smiling, and the word seemed to carry the sound of water over stones, the cold of a morning crossing, the name of someone Ruth would never meet. Ruth looked down at her four letters. They were accurate, she thought, and they were almost nothing.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To convey Ruth's sense that her written record holds far less than Tessaly's spoken word
To portray Tessaly's frustration that Ruth keeps failing to write the word down correctly
To explain how Ruth worked out a spelling system for the sounds of the village's language
To show Tessaly's satisfaction that her language will finally be preserved in written form
items.explanation: The setup tells you Ruth is the focus. The excerpt sets two things against each other: Ruth's four letters, which are "neat and correct," and the spoken word, which carries water, cold, and a person's name. The last line, "accurate... and almost nothing," names the gap between them. So the text's purpose is to convey Ruth's sense of how much her record leaves out.

B.why: You assumed the repetition meant something was going wrong. The text says Ruth's letters are "neat and correct" and that Tessaly is smiling, so there's no failure and no frustration.

C.why: You read a process into the scene that isn't there. Ruth writes down one word, and the text never describes her designing a spelling system.

D.why: You moved the focus from Ruth to Tessaly and invented a feeling. The excerpt is about Ruth's reaction, and it suggests writing can't preserve the word. It doesn't celebrate that it can.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Hollis Brandt's 1998 poem "To a Young Diver." The speaker addresses a student about to make a first dive on a coral reef.

Up here the water is only a glare,
a flat gray sheet that hides its floor.
Go under. Let the noise of the boat fall away.
Below, the reef is a city that never sleeps:
parrotfish grinding coral into sand,
an octopus folding itself into a crack.
What looks like nothing from the deck

The following text is adapted from Dolores Vance's 2014 memoir Second Shift. In 1979, the narrator's mother has just started a job at a fish cannery.

C.why: You looked for a reason the text never gives. It says her pay was smaller but never explains why, and it gives no details about cannery work or pay rates.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Renata Villacorta's 2011 novel The Fourth Morning. Ines, a linguist, is recording Aldo, one of the last fluent speakers of a mountain dialect.

For three mornings Ines had arrived with her printed lists (every pronoun, every tense, every way to say carry), and for three mornings Aldo had answered each prompt with a story about his brother or a stubborn mule. She had begun marking those minutes in her notebook as lost. On the fourth morning, however, transcribing the tale of the mule, she found in it four tenses her lists had never thought to ask for. After that she left the lists in her bag and simply asked him what happened next.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray a speaker's reluctance to answer a researcher's questions until he comes to trust her
To show a researcher giving up her scholarly aims so that she can simply enjoy a speaker's stories
To depict a researcher realizing that what she had written off as a distraction was serving her purpose
To suggest that a researcher's printed lists were flawed because they misrepresented a dialect's grammar
items.explanation: The setup line puts the focus on Ines. Across the excerpt she treats Aldo's stories as wasted time (she marks those minutes "as lost"). Then, after "however," she finds in one story four tenses her lists never asked about, and she switches to asking for more stories. So the excerpt shows her coming to see that the supposed distraction was actually giving her the data she came for. Choice C names the right person and the right change.

A.why: You moved the focus from Ines to Aldo and added a motive the text never gives. Aldo answers every prompt, just with stories, and the excerpt never mentions trust. This is the subtype's main trap: it uses the right characters but makes the wrong person the subject.

B.why: You saw that Ines changes her approach, which is the key insight, but you misread why. She puts the lists away because the stories gave her four tenses her lists missed. The change serves her research goals. It doesn't abandon them.

D.why: The text says the lists never thought to ask for certain tenses, so they were incomplete. It never says they contained errors or misrepresented the grammar. On top of that, the excerpt is about Ines's realization, not about judging her materials.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Teodor Lisk's 2016 poem "Annealing." The speaker addresses a young apprentice in a glassworks.

You flinch when the oven door shuts on your bowl,
as if the waiting were a verdict. It is not.
Glass that is hurried from fire into air
keeps the fire inside it as strain,
and one day breaks for no reason anyone can see.
So we cool it by hours, a degree at a time,
and what comes out looks no different—
only able, now, to be dropped and stay whole.
You are being cooled the same way. Let it take its time.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To warn an apprentice that rushing her work will cause the glass she makes to crack and break
To explain the technical process by which glassmakers relieve the internal strain in their glass
To describe the speaker's lasting regret over the work she ruined when she was an apprentice
To reassure an apprentice that a period of waiting she dreads is what will make her resilient
items.explanation: The poem is addressed to the apprentice, so focus on what it says to her. She "flinch[es]" at the waiting, and the speaker answers right away: "It is not" a verdict. The description of slow cooling leads to the last line, "You are being cooled the same way," which turns the glass into a picture of her own slow training. Just as slow cooling makes the bowl able to "stay whole," the waiting she fears is making her stronger. The tone is comforting, which matches Choice D.

A.why: You noticed that hurried glass breaks, which is the key detail, but you finished the thought in the wrong tone. The apprentice isn't rushing anything. She is anxious about waiting, and the speaker calms her down ("It is not") instead of warning her. Turning an encouraging poem into a warning is this subtype's tone trap.

B.why: You described what most of the lines are about instead of what the poem does. The annealing process is there to set up the comparison in the last line about the apprentice. Someone who skipped that line could have written this choice, and that is a sign it misses the purpose.

C.why: The poem never mentions the speaker's own past failures or regrets. This choice invents a backstory and also moves the focus away from the apprentice the poem is speaking to.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Sofía Marend's 2015 poem "Field Recording." The speaker, a linguist, addresses an elderly woman who is the last fluent speaker of her language.

Say it again, the word for the river in spring—
the levels are right now; the red light holds.
The machine will keep your vowel, the small catch
before the final stop, exactly.
It will not keep the way you turned to the window
to find the word, as if the river told you,
or how you laughed when I said it back wrong.
Say it again. I am getting everything but you.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To express the speaker's awareness that the recording can capture the woman's words but not her presence
To celebrate the recording's power to preserve the woman's language exactly as she speaks it
To urge the woman to speak more clearly so that the recording of her language will be accurate
To apologize to the woman for having mispronounced her word for the river in spring
items.explanation: The poem turns on 'will keep' versus 'will not keep.' The machine records the sounds exactly. It misses her turn toward the window and her laugh. The last line says it directly: 'everything but you.' The purpose is the speaker's recognition of what a recording cannot hold.

B.why: You saw that 'exactly' praises the machine and stopped there. The next three lines list what it cannot keep, and the closing line makes that loss the point of the poem.

C.why: 'Say it again' is a recording request, not a complaint about her speech. The speaker says the machine already gets her vowel 'exactly,' so clarity is never the problem.

D.why: The mispronunciation is one remembered moment, and it is offered as something precious, her laugh. You took an incidental detail for the poem's purpose.

To argue that pteropods deserve more study from marine scientists
To describe a group of tiny snails that live in open water
To show that pteropods move in much the same way garden snails do
items.explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. Each one gives a fact about pteropods: how they swim, how small they are, how they feed and what eats them. items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Hydrologists call a river a "losing stream" when it feeds water into the ground beneath it instead of drawing water from it. Streams are not fixed in one category, though: a stream can shift between gaining and losing as the water table around it rises and falls. The Arroyo Pinto in northern Mexico is a case in point. During the summer rains, groundwater near its channel sits high enough to seep into the stream. By late winter, the surrounding aquifer has dropped so far that the arroyo's water drains downward, and the channel runs dry within a few kilometers.

To describe the summer rains that raise groundwater levels near the Arroyo Pinto each year
To argue that losing streams are more vulnerable to drought than hydrologists have assumed
To show that the Arroyo Pinto remains a losing stream during every season of the year
items.explanation: The text defines a 'losing stream,' states the general rule that streams can switch between gaining and losing, and then uses the Arroyo Pinto to illustrate that rule. Choice A covers the definition, the rule, and the example together.

B.why: You chose one real detail. The summer rains appear only as part of the example, and the text is about the stream's changing relationship to groundwater, not about the rains.

C.why: You read in an argument the text never makes. It says nothing about drought vulnerability or about what hydrologists have wrongly assumed. It only explains and illustrates.

D.why: You reversed the example. In summer, groundwater seeps into the Arroyo Pinto, so it is gaining then. It becomes a losing stream only in late winter.

items.stimulus: For decades, the fossil plant Velatophyllum, known only from scattered leaf impressions in Antarctic rock, was assumed to be a fern. items.stimulus: Metallic glasses are alloys cooled so quickly that their atoms freeze in a disordered arrangement instead of forming crystals, which makes them unusually strong and springy. To describe a class of materials, a long-standing obstacle to making them, and a recent advance

items.stimulus: Marine biologists once assumed that a whale carcass sinking to the deep-sea floor was a brief feast, stripped bare within a few months and then abandoned. Observations of such "whale falls," however, have revealed a far longer sequence. Hagfish and sleeper sharks do remove most of the soft tissue during the first year. Finally, bacteria digest the oils stored in the bones, releasing sulfide compounds that feed mussels and clams, sometimes for half a century.

To describe the succession of communities that a sunken whale carcass can support for decades
To illustrate how bacteria in whale bones release compounds that feed deep-sea mussels and clams
To explain why biologists expected sunken whale carcasses to be stripped bare within months

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Immunologists have traditionally divided the immune system into two branches: an adaptive branch that remembers specific pathogens and an innate branch that responds the same way to every threat. Yet innate cells, it turns out, can be primed by experience. Monocytes taken from people months after they received the BCG tuberculosis vaccine release more inflammatory signaling molecules when exposed to unrelated fungi and bacteria. The change traces to the bone marrow, where the vaccine alters how tightly DNA is packaged in the stem cells that produce new monocytes. Researchers call this nonspecific, long-lasting priming "trained immunity."
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how the BCG vaccine changes DNA packaging in stem cells within the bone marrow
To argue that innate cells remember particular pathogens much as adaptive cells do
To propose that the BCG vaccine be given to protect people against fungal infections
To describe a lasting but nonspecific priming in the branch long thought to lack memory
items.explanation: Track the structure. The text starts with the traditional view that only the adaptive branch has memory and the innate branch always responds the same way. 'Yet' then introduces a phenomenon: innate cells can be primed. The next sentences give an example (BCG-exposed monocytes react more strongly to unrelated microbes) and a mechanism (changes in the bone marrow), and the last sentence names the phenomenon and calls it 'nonspecific' and 'long-lasting.' Every sentence is there to present trained immunity, and the text informs rather than argues. Choice D covers the whole text and keeps the detail that the priming is nonspecific.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. The DNA-packaging mechanism really is in the text, but it is one supporting sentence. The text uses it to explain where the phenomenon comes from, not as its main subject. This choice leaves out the traditional view, the monocyte evidence, and the naming of trained immunity.

B.why: You correctly saw that the text revises the old view of the innate branch, and then took that revision too far. The text says the priming works against 'unrelated' microbes and calls it 'nonspecific.' Innate cells are not shown remembering particular pathogens the way adaptive cells do, which is the difference the text is careful to keep.

C.why: The text reports that BCG-exposed monocytes react more strongly to fungi, but it never recommends using the vaccine against fungal infections. 'Propose' needs an explicit recommendation, and this text only describes findings.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Economists have often described union hiring halls, where dockworkers once gathered each morning to be assigned shifts, as inefficient holdovers that slowed the matching of workers to jobs. Labor historian Inés Calderón's study of the hall at the Port of Tamsen complicates that picture. Assignment ledgers from 1952 to 1971 show that the hall rotated shifts by seniority within skill grades, so that crane operators rarely waited more than a day for work, and that ships unloaded there turned around faster, on average, than those at nearby nonunion piers.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To show that union hiring halls were, as a rule, more efficient than the arrangements economists preferred
To present evidence from one port that challenges a common view of how a labor institution performed
To explain the seniority system that one port's hiring hall used to assign shifts to crane operators
To trace how economists came to see union hiring halls as holdovers that slowed the matching of workers
items.explanation: The text opens with a common view (hiring halls were inefficient), says Calderón's study 'complicates that picture,' and then gives ledger evidence from a single port. Every sentence serves that purpose: one port's records push back on a widely held view. The verb 'challenges' matches the text's 'complicates,' and 'from one port' keeps the claim as narrow as the evidence.

A.why: You spotted the correction, which is the key insight, and then stretched it further than the text does. The evidence comes from one port, and the text never says what economists preferred. 'As a rule' turns one case study into a general law.

C.why: The seniority rotation really is in the text, but it is only one piece of the evidence. This choice leaves out the faster turnaround times and, more importantly, the view that the evidence challenges.

D.why: Only the first sentence is about the economists' view, and the text never traces how that view developed. This choice describes the setup and misses the evidence that makes up most of the passage.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Seismometers are expensive to install on the seafloor, so the ocean bottom is poorly monitored. Geophysicist Tomás Reyna has found a substitute already lying in place: the fiber-optic cables that carry internet traffic between continents. When a seismic wave stretches a cable, it slightly alters how laser pulses scatter inside the glass, and those alterations can be read as a record of ground motion every few meters along the line. Infrastructure built for one purpose can quietly serve another. Using a single 40-kilometer cable off Chile, Reyna's team detected hundreds of small offshore earthquakes that land stations had missed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that fiber-optic cables should replace seismometers on the seafloor
To explain why seismometers have been difficult to place on the seafloor
To describe a method that uses existing undersea cables to record earthquakes
To claim that most infrastructure could be adapted to serve scientific research
items.explanation: Each sentence fits under one heading: what the method is (cables as sensors), how it works (laser scattering), and what it achieved (hundreds of earthquakes detected). The text informs rather than argues, so the neutral verb 'describe' fits, and 'existing undersea cables' covers the whole account.

A.why: The word 'substitute' pulled you toward a recommendation the text never makes. The text says the cables can stand in where seismometers are scarce. It does not say they should replace seismometers, and 'argue' needs an opinion that isn't there.

B.why: The cost of seismometers is the opening background, given only to explain why a substitute matters. One clause of setup can't be the purpose of the whole text.

D.why: You noticed the one abstract sentence, which was a good thing to notice, and then treated it as the thesis and inflated it. The text says infrastructure 'can' serve another purpose, not that 'most' of it could. That sentence is a side comment on Reyna's method, not the point the passage builds toward.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: In the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, western hemlocks often stand in straight rows, their roots arching over empty space. Each row marks where a fallen tree once lay: seedlings sprouted on the rotting trunk, and when it decayed, the young trees were left standing on stilts. Ecologists call such trunks nurse logs. Why seedlings favor them was long unclear, but ecologist Mara Lindqvist found that seedlings planted on bare forest floor survived well when moss was cleared away, suggesting that logs help mainly by raising seedlings above smothering moss.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe a forest pattern and present a finding about what causes it
To explain how the roots of some hemlocks come to arch over empty space
To show that rotting logs give seedlings nutrients the forest floor lacks
To argue that clearing moss from forests would improve tree regeneration
items.explanation: The text first describes a pattern (rows of hemlocks on stilts, grown from nurse logs). It then raises an open question (why do seedlings favor logs?) and answers it with Lindqvist's finding (logs lift seedlings above the moss). The right purpose has to cover both halves.

B.why: The text does explain the stilt roots, but only in its second sentence. This choice covers the opening and leaves out the question and the study that take up the second half.

C.why: The name 'nurse log' suggests nourishment, but the study points the other way. Seedlings did well on bare ground once the moss was gone, so the benefit is height, not nutrients.

D.why: The finding is about why seedlings survive on logs, and the text recommends nothing. 'Argue' and a forest-management proposal go well past an explanation of one natural pattern.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: When the Orrin Street Viaduct opened in 1928, newspapers celebrated its length: at 1.4 kilometers, it was the longest concrete span in the region. As engineering historian Lena Okafor notes, however, the viaduct's lasting influence came from something few visitors noticed. Its designer, Ruth Calloway, divided the deck into short segments separated by joints packed with tarred felt, allowing the concrete to swell and shrink with the seasons without cracking. Within a decade, the approach had become standard on bridges across the country.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To report the length that made the viaduct the longest concrete span in its region
To argue that newspapers praised the viaduct for a feature engineers thought trivial
To explain how felt-packed joints let concrete swell and shrink without cracking
To describe a bridge and point to an overlooked feature behind its influence
items.explanation: The text turns on 'however.' The bridge's famous feature (its length) is set aside for the feature that actually made it influential (the segmented deck and its joints), and the last sentence confirms that influence. The right choice names both the bridge and the overlooked feature.

A.why: The length is the setup that the 'however' turns away from. You picked a true detail from the first sentence instead of the point the text moves to.

B.why: You caught the contrast, but the text never says engineers thought the length was trivial or that the newspapers were wrong. It says the bridge's lasting influence came from elsewhere. 'Argue' and 'trivial' make that contrast harsher than the text does.

C.why: This is how the joints work, which is one sentence of the passage. It leaves out the viaduct, the contrast with its fame, and the influence that is the reason the joints are mentioned at all.

items.stimulus: Most surviving records of eighteenth-century weaving were kept by mill owners, who noted output and wages but rarely the cloth itself. The pattern book of Agnes Muir, a handloom weaver in Paisley, Scotland, is a rare exception. Across 212 pages, Muir pasted a snippet of every cloth she wove beside the threading draft used to produce it, and she annotated failures as carefully as successes. A craft's knowledge often survives only where a practitioner chose to write it down. Historians now use Muir's book to reconstruct techniques that no mill ledger describes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To claim that craft knowledge survives only when practitioners write it down
To present a weaver's record and explain why it matters to historians of the craft
To describe how one weaver arranged cloth samples alongside her threading drafts
To argue that mill owners deliberately left weavers' techniques out of their records
items.explanation: The text sets out a gap (mill records ignore the cloth), introduces Muir's book as the exception, describes what the book contains, and ends with how historians use it. 'Present' a record and 'explain why it matters' covers each of those steps.

A.why: You picked out the one general sentence, but you changed its 'often' to 'only' and treated it as the main claim. In the passage it is a comment on Muir's book, not the claim the book is offered to support.

C.why: The text does say how the samples and drafts were arranged, but that is a description of the book's contents. It leaves out why the book matters, which the first and last sentences make the point.

D.why: The text says mill owners 'rarely' recorded the cloth. It says nothing about why. 'Deliberately' adds a motive, and 'argue' adds an accusation, and neither is in the text.

items.stimulus: For decades, archivists catalogued Henrik Dahl's 1868 map of the Vessa delta as an unfinished draft. Many of its channels are drawn only in dotted lines, and several islands appear twice, in slightly different positions. A reexamination by cartographic historian Priya Natarajan suggests the map is complete. Comparing it with Dahl's field notes, she found that the dotted channels hold water only during spring floods and that the doubled islands mark where sandbars stood in summer and in winter. Dahl, it appears, mapped a landscape that would not stay still.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To present a reinterpretation of a map's odd features as a record of seasonal change
To criticize archivists for carelessly cataloguing a complete map as an unfinished draft
To explain why the sandbars of a river delta shifted position between summer and winter
To urge that other maps catalogued as drafts be reexamined using surveyors' field notes
items.explanation: The text starts with an old belief (the map was unfinished), names the features behind that belief (dotted channels, doubled islands), and then gives Natarajan's correction: those features record seasonal change. The verb 'present' fits the text's measured tone ('suggests,' 'it appears').

B.why: You saw that the archivists were wrong, which is right, but the text never blames them. Being mistaken isn't the same as being careless, and 'criticize' needs an opinion that the text's neutral tone doesn't show.

C.why: The text says that the sandbars moved with the seasons, not why they did. The movement is the explanation for the map's features, not the subject of the passage.

D.why: The text deals with one map and makes no recommendation. Turning one reexamination into a call to review other maps adds a prescription the passage never makes.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Hydrologists have long known that a stream's flow rises after rain, but it has been unclear how much of that rise is new rainwater and how much is older groundwater pushed out by it. Hydrologist Daniel Osei set out to test this in a small Welsh catchment. Because rain and groundwater carry slightly different ratios of oxygen isotopes, he could track each source in the stream. During storms, he found, more than two-thirds of the water in the channel had been underground for weeks before the rain fell.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how oxygen isotopes distinguish rainwater from groundwater in streams
To argue that rainfall has little effect on the amount of water a stream carries
To show that in all catchments, storm water in streams is mostly old groundwater
To report a finding about where the water that swells a stream during storms comes from
items.explanation: The text poses a question (is storm flow new rain or old groundwater?), describes how Osei tested it, and gives the answer (mostly old groundwater). 'Report a finding about where the water comes from' covers the question, the method and the result without saying more than the single study shows.

A.why: The isotope method is only how the question was answered, and it takes up one sentence. This choice leaves out the question and the result.

B.why: Once you see that most storm water is old, it's tempting to conclude that rain doesn't matter. But the text starts by saying flow rises after rain. The rain still causes the rise; it does so by pushing out groundwater.

C.why: You read the result correctly, then spread it to 'all catchments.' Osei studied one small catchment in Wales, so the text can't support a universal claim.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Divers have long regarded the pistol shrimp as little more than a source of noise: the snap of its oversized claw, loud enough to interfere with sonar, crackles across warm reefs. Marine biologist Keiko Arai has documented a less obvious side of the animal. The shrimp dig burrows in reef sediment and share them with gobies, small fish that watch for predators while the nearly blind shrimp maintain the tunnels. In Arai's survey plots, the burrows also aerated sediment to a depth of half a meter, sustaining worms and clams that sheltered there.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how the pistol shrimp's claw makes a snap loud enough to disrupt sonar
To describe the partnership in which gobies stand guard while shrimp dig tunnels
To present overlooked ways in which an animal known for its noise supports reef life
To argue that the pistol shrimp does more good than harm to the reefs it inhabits
items.explanation: The text sets up the common view (the shrimp is mostly a noise), then turns to 'a less obvious side' and gives two examples: the shared burrows with gobies, and burrows that aerate sediment for worms and clams. 'Overlooked ways' covers both examples, and 'present' matches the informational tone.

A.why: The snap belongs to the old view that the text moves away from, and the text never explains how the claw produces it. You fixed on the first sentence.

B.why: The goby partnership is real and in the text, but it is only the first of two examples. The choice leaves out the aeration finding and the contrast with the shrimp's reputation, so it is too narrow.

D.why: You saw the shift from nuisance to benefit, then turned it into a verdict. The text never compares the shrimp's harms with its benefits, and the word 'argue' needs an opinion the text doesn't state.
