items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus: An ecologist counted the nesting pairs of a seabird on six islands. The counts were 14, 9, 22, 17, 11, and $x$, where $x$ is a whole number. The median of the six counts is 15.5, the range is greater than 13, and the mean is an integer less than 17.
items.stem: What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: In order, the known counts are 9, 11, 14, 17, 22. A median of 15.5 is the average of 14 and 17, so $x \geq 17$. If $x \leq 22$, the range is $22 - 9 = 13$, which is not greater than 13, so $x > 22$. For the mean to be an integer, $73 + x$ must be a multiple of 6, so $x$ could be 23, 29, and so on. Only $x = 23$ gives a mean less than 17: $\frac{96}{6} = 16$.

A.why: 16 is the mean of the six counts when $x = 23$. The question asks for $x$.

B.why: 17 meets the median condition and gives an integer mean of 15. But the range would then be $22 - 9 = 13$, and the range has to be greater than 13. You stopped before checking every condition.

items.stimulus: A linguist gave a list of borrowed words to speakers of two dialects and recorded how many of the words each speaker recognized. The 12 speakers of the coastal dialect recognized a mean of 30 words. The 8 speakers of the inland dialect recognized a mean of $x$ words. Across all 20 speakers, the mean was 34 words.
items.stem: What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Turn each mean into a total. All 20 speakers recognized $34 \times 20 = 680$ words in total. The coastal speakers recognized $30 \times 12 = 360$ of them. D.why: 320 is the total number of words the 8 inland speakers recognized together. You stopped before dividing by 8 to get their mean.

items.stimulus: A textile historian counted the threads per centimeter in five linen fragments from a 17th-century weaving workshop. The counts were 46, 52, 57, 63, and $x$. The mean of the five counts is 56.
items.stem: What is the value of $x$?

items.stem: What is the value of $x$?

D.why: 84 is the total for all six days. You still need to subtract the five known days, 60, to get $x$.

items.stem: What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Station P's total is $40 + 52 + 47 + 61 = 200$, so its mean is $200/4 = 50$. Station Q's mean is $50 + 4 = 54$, so its total over 5 readings is $54 \times 5 = 270$. The known readings at Q add to $38 + 55 + 49 + 63 = 205$, so $x = 270 - 205 = 65$.

A.why: You multiplied Q's mean by 4 instead of 5 ($54 \times 4 = 216$). You forgot that $x$ is one of Station Q's 5 readings.

B.why: You set Station Q's mean 4 below Station P's (46) instead of 4 above. That gives a total of 230 and $x = 25$.

C.why: You made the two means equal at 50 and dropped the condition that Q's mean is 4 greater. That gives a total of 250 and $x = 45$.

items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus: A marine biologist recorded how long each of 5 bottlenose dolphins stayed underwater on a single dive. Four of the dive times were 4, 7, 9, and 6 minutes, and the fifth was $x$ minutes. The mean of the 5 dive times is 7 minutes.
items.stem: Which of the following must be true about $x$?
choices: $x$ is equal to the mean of all 5 dive times.
$x$ is equal to the greatest of the other 4 dive times.
$x$ is less than the least of the other 4 dive times.
$x$ is greater than the sum of the other 4 dive times.
items.explanation: Turn the mean into a total first: the 5 dive times must add up to $7 \times 5 = 35$ minutes. The four known times add up to $4 + 7 + 9 + 6 = 26$, so $x = 35 - 26 = 9$. The greatest of the other four times is 9 minutes, so $x$ equals it.

A.why: You assumed the missing value has to be the mean, 7. Only the average of all 5 values is 7. The unknown value itself is 9.

C.why: You left the unknown out of the count and solved $26 + x = 7 \times 4 = 28$, which gives $x = 2$. There are 5 dive times, so the total must be $7 \times 5 = 35$.

D.why: You took the required total, 35, as the value of $x$. Thirty-five is the sum of all 5 times. You still have to subtract the 26 minutes already known.

items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus: Two survey teams digitized tiles for a coastal map. Team A digitized 12 tiles and averaged 30 minutes per tile. Team B digitized 8 tiles and averaged 40 minutes per tile.
items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The mean time for all 20 tiles is 35 minutes.
The mean time for all 20 tiles is 34 minutes.
The mean time for all 20 tiles is 36 minutes.
The mean time for all 20 tiles is 680 minutes.
items.explanation: Turn each mean into a total. Team A spent $12 \times 30 = 360$ minutes and Team B spent $8 \times 40 = 320$ minutes, so the two teams spent $680$ minutes altogether. Divide by all 20 tiles: $680 \div 20 = 34$ minutes.

D.why: You stopped at the combined total, 680 minutes. To get the mean, you still have to divide by the 20 tiles.

items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus: An archaeologist weighed 5 pottery shards from one dig site. Four of the masses were 12, 23, 15, and 20 grams, and the fifth was $x$ grams. The mean mass of the 5 shards is 17 grams.
items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The median mass of the 5 shards is 15 grams.
The median mass of the 5 shards is 17 grams.
The median mass of the 5 shards is 20 grams.
The median mass of the 5 shards is 12 grams.
items.explanation: The 5 masses must add up to $17 \times 5 = 85$ grams. The four known masses add up to $12 + 23 + 15 + 20 = 70$, so $x = 85 - 70 = 15$. Sorted, the masses are 12, 15, 15, 20, 23. The middle value is 15, so the median is 15 grams.

C.why: You used the total, 85, as $x$. Sorting 12, 15, 20, 23, 85 then puts 20 in the middle. You still had to subtract the 70 grams already known, which gives $x = 15$.

D.why: You left the unknown out of the count and solved $70 + x = 17 \times 4 = 68$, which gives $x = -2$ and a median of 12. There are 5 shards, so the total must be $17 \times 5 = 85$.

items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus: A paleobotanist measured five fossil fern leaves from one shale layer. Their lengths, in millimeters, are $42$, $47$, $51$, $58$, and $x$. The mean of the five lengths is $6$ millimeters less than $x$.
items.stem: What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: The four known lengths add to $42 + 47 + 51 + 58 = 198$. The mean of all five lengths is $x - 6$, so the total is $5(x - 6)$. That gives $198 + x = 5x - 30$, so $4x = 228$ and $x = 57$. Testing the choices is faster: with $57$, the total is $255$ and the mean is $255 \div 5 = 51$, which is $57 - 6$. It checks.

A.why: You treated the mean as 6 more than $x$, not 6 less. That gives $198 + x = 5x + 30$ and $x = 42$. Check it: with $42$, the mean is $240 \div 5 = 48$, which is more than $42$, not less.

B.why: $51$ is the mean of the five lengths when $x = 57$. You found the mean, not the missing length that the question asks for.

D.why: You divided by 4 because there are four known values, which leaves the unknown out of the count. Solving $(198 + x)/4 = x - 6$ gives $74$. Divide by all five lengths, and with $74$ the mean is $54.4$, not $68$.

items.stimulus: Pay records from an 1840s linen mill show that workshop A had $12$ weavers, and their mean weekly output was $30$ meters of cloth. Workshop B had $18$ weavers. The mean weekly output of all $30$ weavers in the two workshops was $39.6$ meters.

D.why: You swapped the group sizes and gave workshop A 18 weavers and B 12. That gives $540 + 12m = 1{,}188$, so $m = 54$.

items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus: A warehouse has 5 day-shift workers, with hourly wages of $\$18$, $\$20$, $\$21$, $\$25$, and $x$ dollars. It has 3 night-shift workers, with hourly wages of $\$24$, $\$27$, and $\$30$. The mean hourly wage of all 8 workers is $\$1.50$ greater than the mean hourly wage of the 5 day-shift workers.
items.stem: What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Let $S$ be the day-shift total, so $S = 84 + x$. The day-shift mean is $\frac{S}{5}$. The night-shift total is $24 + 27 + 30 = 81$, so the mean of all 8 workers is $\frac{S + 81}{8}$. Set up the condition: $\frac{S+81}{8} = \frac{S}{5} + 1.5$. Multiply both sides by 40 to get $5S + 405 = 8S + 60$, so $3S = 345$ and $S = 115$. Then $x = 115 - 84 = 31$. Check: the day-shift mean is $\frac{115}{5} = 23$, and the overall mean is $\frac{196}{8} = 24.5$, which is $1.5$ more.

A.why: You solved correctly but stopped at the day-shift mean, $\frac{115}{5} = 23$, which is not the missing wage $x$.

C.why: You found the overall mean by averaging the two shift means, $\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{S}{5} + 27\right)$, as if both shifts had the same number of workers. The day shift has 5 workers and the night shift has 3, so you have to combine the totals and divide by 8. Averaging the means gives $S = 120$ and $x = 36$.

D.why: You made the overall mean $1.50$ less than the day-shift mean instead of $1.50$ more. That gives $\frac{S+81}{8} = \frac{S}{5} - 1.5$, so $S = 155$ and $x = 71$.

items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus: A city planner recorded the number of new building permits issued in each of 8 neighborhoods. Listed from least to greatest, the counts are $5$, $9$, $a$, $13$, $b$, $21$, $24$, and $c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are integers. The median of the counts is $16$, the range is $30$, and the mean is an integer.
items.stem: What is the value of $a$?
items.explanation: There are 8 values, so the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values: $\frac{13 + b}{2} = 16$, so $b = 19$. The range is the maximum minus the minimum: $c - 5 = 30$, so $c = 35$. The sum is $5 + 9 + a + 13 + 19 + 21 + 24 + 35 = 126 + a$. For the mean to be an integer, $126 + a$ must be divisible by 8. Because the list is in order, $a$ must also be between 9 and 13, inclusive. Of 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13, only $a = 10$ makes the sum divisible by 8: the sum is 136 and the mean is 17. So $a = 10$.

A.why: $a = 2$ gives a sum of 128, which is divisible by 8, so the mean is an integer. But it breaks the order: $a$ comes after 9 in the list, so it must be at least 9. You checked divisibility but not the ordering.

C.why: You took the 5th value, $b$, to be the median and set $b = 16$. With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values, so $b = 19$. Using $b = 16$ makes the sum $123 + a$, which leads you to $a = 13$.

D.why: 17 is the mean of the 8 counts, $\frac{136}{8}$, not the value of $a$. You found the total but answered with the mean instead of solving for $a$.

items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus: A textile museum holds two collections of hand-woven samplers. Collection P has 14 samplers with a mean age of 120 years. Collection Q has a mean age of 150 years. The mean age of all the samplers in both collections is 130 years. After one sampler from collection Q is loaned out, the mean age of the remaining samplers is 128 years.
items.stem: What is the age, in years, of the loaned sampler?
items.explanation: Turn each mean into a total. Collection P totals $14 \times 120 = 1{,}680$ years. If Q has $n$ samplers, then $1{,}680 + 150n = 130(14 + n)$, so $20n = 140$ and $n = 7$. That makes 21 samplers with a total of $21 \times 130 = 2{,}730$ years. After the loan, 20 samplers remain with a total of $20 \times 128 = 2{,}560$ years. The loaned sampler is $2{,}730 - 2{,}560 = 170$ years old.

A.why: You kept the count at 21 after the loan and calculated $2{,}730 - 21 \times 128$. Once a sampler leaves, only 20 remain, so the new total is $20 \times 128$.

B.why: You assumed the loaned sampler was exactly as old as collection Q's mean. If that were true, the overall mean would rise above 130, not fall to 128.

D.why: You weighted the groups backwards and got 28 samplers in Q instead of 7. The overall mean of 130 sits closer to 120, so Q has to be the smaller collection.

items.stimulus: A city planner lists the one-way commute times, in whole minutes, for 7 neighborhoods in increasing order: $14$, $18$, $a$, $b$, $27$, $31$, $c$. No two times are equal. The median of the times is 24, the mean is 25, and the range is at most 24.
items.stem: What is the value of $c$?

D.why: 61 is $a + c$. You still needed to split that sum using the ordering and range conditions.

items.stimulus: A labour economist studies a firm with two departments. Department R has 30 workers with a mean hourly wage of $\$24$. Department S has a mean hourly wage of $\$33$, and the mean hourly wage of all workers in the firm is $\$27$. The firm then hires 5 new workers into Department S, each earning $\$39$ per hour.
items.stem: What is the new mean hourly wage of Department S?
items.explanation: Let Department S have $n$ workers. Then $30(24) + 33n = 27(30 + n)$, so $720 + 33n = 810 + 27n$ and $n = 15$. Department S's wage total is $15 \times 33 = 495$. Adding $5 \times 39 = 195$ gives 690 across 20 workers, so the new mean is $690 \div 20 = \$34.50$.

A.why: $28.20 is the new firm-wide mean, $1{,}410 \div 50$. The question asks only about Department S.

C.why: You averaged $33 and $39 as if the 5 new hires were as many as the 15 existing workers. You have to combine totals, not means.

D.why: You added the new workers' wages to the total but still divided by 15. The count has to go up to 20 as well.

items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus: A marine biologist measured 7 juvenile fish. Their lengths, in whole centimeters, are listed in increasing order: $11$, $14$, $p$, $18$, $q$, $25$, $27$. No two lengths are equal. The mean of the 7 lengths is 19, and the mean of the three shortest lengths is a whole number.
items.stem: What is the value of $q$?
items.explanation: A mean of 19 over 7 fish gives a total of 133. The known lengths add to 95, so $p + q = 38$. The ordering with no repeats means $15 \le p \le 17$. For the mean of 11, 14, and $p$ to be a whole number, $25 + p$ must be divisible by 3, and only $p = 17$ works. So $q = 38 - 17 = 21$.

A.why: 17 is the value of $p$. The question asks for $q$.

C.why: Using $p = 16$ fits the mean and the ordering, but $11 + 14 + 16 = 41$ is not divisible by 3, so the three shortest lengths do not have a whole-number mean.

D.why: You took the first candidate, $p = 15$, and stopped. It fits the mean and the ordering, but $11 + 14 + 15 = 40$ is not divisible by 3.

items.subtype_name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
items.stimulus:
A musicologist counted how often a recurring motif appears in each movement of two suites.
Suite A: $8$, $12$, $15$, $x$, $10$
Suite B: $4$, $6$, $8$, $2x$
The mean of the counts for Suite A is 3 less than the mean of the counts for Suite B.
items.stem: What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Write the equation using each suite's own count: $\frac{45 + x}{5} + 3 = \frac{18 + 2x}{4}$. Multiplying by 20 gives $180 + 4x + 60 = 90 + 10x$, so $6x = 150$ and $x = 25$. To check: Suite A's mean is $70 \div 5 = 14$ and Suite B's mean is $68 \div 4 = 17$, which is 3 more.

A.why: You added the 3 to the wrong side and made Suite A's mean 3 more than Suite B's. With $x = 5$, A's mean is 10 and B's is 7.

C.why: You divided Suite A's total by 4, which leaves the unknown movement out of the count. Suite A has 5 movements.

D.why: 50 is $2x$, the count for Suite B's last movement. The question asks for $x$.

items.subtype_name: Work backward to the original whole
items.stimulus: A linguist recording a regional dialect found that 48 of the words she recorded were borrowed from Spanish. These borrowed words make up 16% of all the words she recorded.
items.stem: What is the total number of words the linguist recorded?
items.explanation: The 48 borrowed words are the part, and the total is unknown. Write $0.16x = 48$. Then $x = \frac{48}{0.16} = 300$. The linguist recorded 300 words.

A.why: You found 16% of 48 ($0.16 \times 48 = 7.68$). But 48 is already the part. It is 16% of the unknown total, so you need to divide by 0.16, not multiply.

B.why: You added the percent to the count as if they were the same kind of number ($48 + 16 = 64$). A percent is a multiplier, so you have to solve $0.16x = 48$.

D.why: You set up the division correctly but wrote 16% as 0.016. Then $\frac{48}{0.016} = 3{,}000$. As a decimal, 16% is 0.16.

items.subtype_name: Work backward to the original whole
items.stimulus: After a restoration project, the number of nesting herons at a wetland increased by 25%. After the increase, there were 180 nesting herons at the wetland.
items.stem: How many nesting herons were at the wetland before the increase?
items.explanation: 180 is the count after the increase, so it equals 125% of the original. Write $1.25x = 180$. Then $x = \frac{180}{1.25} = 144$. Check: 25% of 144 is 36, and $144 + 36 = 180$.

A.why: You tried to undo the increase by taking 25% off 180 ($180 \times 0.75 = 135$). But the 25% was figured on the original count, not on 180. Divide 180 by 1.25 instead.

C.why: You applied the 25% increase to 180 again ($180 \times 1.25 = 225$). That goes forward in time, but the question asks for the count before the increase.

D.why: You divided by 0.75 ($\frac{180}{0.75} = 240$), which is the multiplier for a 25% decrease. For a 25% increase, the multiplier is 1.25.

items.subtype_name: Work backward to the original whole
items.stimulus: A museum conservator is studying a fragment of a woven tapestry from the 1600s. The fragment is 54 centimeters wide, which is 30% of the tapestry's original width.
items.stem: What was the original width, in centimeters, of the tapestry?
items.explanation: The fragment is the part, and the original width is the whole. Write $0.30x = 54$. Then $x = \frac{54}{0.30} = 180$. The original width was 180 centimeters.

A.why: You found 30% of 54 ($0.30 \times 54 = 16.2$). But 54 is already 30% of the whole, so you need to divide by 0.30.

B.why: You increased 54 by 30% ($54 \times 1.3 = 70.2$). The fragment is not 30% less than the original. It is 30% of the original, so solve $0.30x = 54$.

C.why: You found the original width correctly and then subtracted the fragment ($180 - 54 = 126$). That is the width that is missing, but the question asks for the full original width.

items.subtype_name: Work backward to the original whole
items.stimulus: Every fossil leaf in a paleobotany collection is classified as a fern, a cycad, or a conifer. Of these leaves, 45% are ferns and 35% are cycads. The remaining 60 fossil leaves are conifers.
items.stem: How many fossil leaves are in the collection?
items.explanation: First find the percent that is conifers: $100\% - 45\% - 35\% = 20\%$. The 60 conifers are 20% of the collection, so write $0.20x = 60$. Then $x = \frac{60}{0.20} = 300$.

A.why: You found 20% of 60 ($0.20 \times 60 = 12$). But 60 is the conifer count, which is 20% of the collection, so you need to divide by 0.20.

B.why: You used 80%, the share of ferns and cycads together, as if it were the conifers' share ($\frac{60}{0.80} = 75$). The conifers are the leftover group, which is $100\% - 80\% = 20\%$.

C.why: You found the total of 300 and then took 45% of it ($0.45 \times 300 = 135$). That is the number of ferns, but the question asks for the whole collection.

items.subtype_name: Work backward to the original whole
items.stimulus: A nutrition label shows that one serving of a yogurt contains 9 grams of protein. The label says this amount is 18% of the recommended daily value of protein.
items.stem: What is the recommended daily value of protein, in grams, used on the label?
items.explanation: The 9 grams are the part, and the daily value is the whole. Write $0.18x = 9$. Then $x = \frac{9}{0.18} = 50$. The daily value is 50 grams.

A.why: You found 18% of 9 ($0.18 \times 9 = 1.62$). But 9 grams is already 18% of the daily value, so you need to divide by 0.18.

D.why: You set up the division correctly but wrote 18% as 0.018. Then $\frac{9}{0.018} = 500$. As a decimal, 18% is 0.18.

items.subtype_name: Work backward to the original whole
items.stimulus: A public health clinic vaccinated 84 patients on Monday. This number is 35% of the patients scheduled to be vaccinated at the clinic that week.
items.stem: How many patients were scheduled for the week?
items.explanation: The 84 patients are the part, and the weekly total is the unknown whole. Write $0.35x = 84$, so $x = \frac{84}{0.35} = 240$ patients.

A.why: You took 35% of 84 ($0.35 \times 84$) when you should have divided by 0.35. The 84 patients are already 35% of the total, so the total has to be bigger than 84.

B.why: You found the total correctly but then subtracted the 84 Monday patients. That gives the patients still to be vaccinated, not the number scheduled for the week.

D.why: You multiplied 84 by 1.35 as if 84 had grown by 35%. In this question 84 is 35% of the total, so the equation is $0.35x = 84$.

items.explanation: An increase of 20% means the original amount was multiplied by 1.2. Write $1.2x = 270$, so $x = \frac{270}{1.2} = 225$ folktales.

D.why: You multiplied 270 by 1.2, which applies the increase a second time. You need to go backward to the starting amount, so divide by 1.2.

items.stimulus: A weather station recorded that a town's total rainfall in July was 25% less than its total rainfall in June. The town received 6 inches of rain in July.
items.stem: How many inches of rain fell in the town in June?
items.explanation: A 25% decrease means July's rainfall is 75% of June's. Write $0.75x = 6$, so $x = \frac{6}{0.75} = 8$ inches.

A.why: You took 25% off July's total ($6 \times 0.75$). June had more rain than July, so the answer has to be greater than 6.

B.why: You tried to undo the decrease by adding 25% of 6 ($6 \times 1.25$). The 25% is a percent of June's rainfall, not July's, so you need to divide 6 by 0.75.

D.why: You divided 6 by 0.25, which is the size of the decrease. July's 6 inches is the 75% that is left, so divide by 0.75.

items.subtype_name: Given the area or volume, find a dimension
items.stimulus: A luthier cuts a flat triangular brace to glue inside the soundboard of a concert harp. The brace has an area of $54$ square inches, and its base is $12$ inches long.
items.stem: What is the height, in inches, of the triangular brace?
items.explanation: The area of a triangle is $A = \frac{1}{2}bh$. Substitute what you know: $54 = \frac{1}{2}(12)h$, so $54 = 6h$ and $h = 9$. The height is $9$ inches.

A.why: You divided the area by the base, $54 \div 12 = 4.5$, without first doubling the area. That ignores the $\frac{1}{2}$ in the triangle formula.

C.why: You subtracted the base from the area, $54 - 12 = 42$. The base multiplies the height in the formula, so you have to divide, not subtract.

D.why: You doubled the area to get $2A = 108$ but stopped there. You still need to divide by the base: $108 \div 12 = 9$.

items.subtype_name: Given the area or volume, find a dimension
items.stimulus: In a portion-control study, nutrition researchers serve a sports drink in paper cups shaped like right circular cones. Each cup has a volume of $24\pi$ cubic centimeters, and the circular opening at the top has a diameter of $6$ centimeters.
items.stem: What is the height, in centimeters, of the cup?
items.explanation: The volume of a cone is $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$. The diameter is $6$, so the radius is $3$. Substitute: $24\pi = \frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2 h$, so $24\pi = 3\pi h$ and $h = 8$. The height is $8$ centimeters.

A.why: You used the diameter, $6$, as the radius. That gives $24\pi = \frac{1}{3}\pi(36)h$, so $h = 2$. Halve the diameter before you substitute.

B.why: You left out the $\frac{1}{3}$ in the cone formula and solved $24\pi = \pi(3)^2 h$, which gives $\frac{24}{9} = \frac{8}{3}$.

D.why: You used $r$ where the formula has $r^2$: $24\pi = \frac{1}{3}\pi(3)h$ gives $h = 24$. The radius has to be squared.

items.stimulus: A wildlife group builds wooden nest boxes for eastern bluebirds. Each box is a right rectangular prism with a square base. The box is $10$ inches tall, and its volume is $490$ cubic inches.
items.stem: What is the length, in inches, of each edge of the square base?
items.explanation: The volume of the prism is $V = s^2 h$, where $s$ is an edge of the square base. Substitute: $490 = s^2(10)$, so $s^2 = 49$. Take the positive square root: $s = 7$. Each edge is $7$ inches.

items.stimulus: A materials engineer tests how a new resin cures by casting a specimen in a mold shaped like a right circular cone. The cured specimen has a volume of $96\pi$ cubic centimeters and a height of $8$ centimeters.
items.stem: What is the diameter, in centimeters, of the base of the specimen?
items.explanation: The volume of a cone is $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$. Set it equal to the given volume and substitute the height: $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 (8) = 96\pi$. Divide both sides by $\pi$ to get $\frac{8}{3}r^2 = 96$. Multiply both sides by $\frac{3}{8}$ to get $r^2 = 36$. Keep only the positive root, so $r = 6$. B.why: $6$ is the radius. You solved the equation correctly but stopped there, and the question asks for the diameter, which is twice the radius.

D.why: $36$ is $r^2$. You stopped before taking the square root, so this value is in square centimeters and isn't a length at all.

items.explanation: Set the cone formula equal to the volume: $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2(25) = 300\pi$. Divide both sides by $\pi$ and multiply by 3 to get $25r^2 = 900$, so $r^2 = 36$ and $r = 6$. You can also test the choices: $\frac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(25) = 300\pi$.

A.why: You dropped the $\frac{1}{3}$ and solved $25\pi r^2 = 300\pi$, which gives $r^2 = 12$. A cone's volume is one third of a cylinder's, so you have to multiply by 3 when you undo the formula.

C.why: 12 is the diameter of the base. The question asks for the radius, which is half of that.

D.why: 36 is $r^2$. You stopped before taking the square root.

items.subtype_name: Given the area or volume, find a dimension
items.stimulus: A clinic puts up a triangular hand-washing reminder sign. The base of the triangle is 6 inches longer than its height, and the sign has an area of 216 square inches.
items.stem: What is the height, in inches, of the sign?
items.explanation: If the height is $h$, the base is $h + 6$, so $\frac{1}{2}h(h+6) = 216$, which means $h(h+6) = 432$. Testing the choices is faster than factoring: $18 \times 24 = 432$, so the height is 18 inches.

A.why: You solved $h(h+6) = 216$ and forgot to double the area to undo the $\frac{1}{2}$. Check it: $\frac{1}{2}(12)(18) = 108$, not 216.

C.why: 24 is the base of the triangle. The height is 6 inches shorter.

D.why: 432 is the product $h(h+6)$, which you get partway through. You still need the height that gives that product.

items.stimulus: A hydrology station stores runoff in a cistern shaped like a right circular cylinder. The cistern has an inside diameter of 6 meters and holds $72\pi$ cubic meters of water when full.
items.stem: What is the height, in meters, of the cistern?

D.why: You forgot to square the radius and wrote $3\pi h = 72\pi$, which gives 24. The formula has $r^2$, so you should get $9\pi h$.

items.stimulus: A materials scientist casts a ceramic test sample shaped like a right pyramid with a square base. The sample has a volume of 96 cubic centimeters and a height of 8 centimeters.
items.stem: What is the length, in centimeters, of one edge of the sample's base?
items.explanation: The volume of a pyramid is $V = \frac{1}{3}Bh$, and here the base area is $B = s^2$. Substitute: $\frac{1}{3}s^2(8) = 96$, so $s^2 = 36$. Keep the positive root, so $s = 6$ centimeters.

D.why: 36 is $s^2$, the area of the base. You stopped before taking the square root to find the edge.

items.stimulus: An ornithologist marks out two triangular plots to survey ground-nesting plovers. Both plots have a base of 12 meters. One plot has an area of 90 square meters, and the other has an area of 144 square meters.
items.stem: How many meters greater is the height of the larger plot than the height of the smaller plot?
items.explanation: Use $A = \frac{1}{2}bh$ for each plot. For the smaller plot, $90 = \frac{1}{2}(12)h$, so $90 = 6h$ and $h = 15$ meters. For the larger plot, $144 = 6h$, so $h = 24$ meters. The question asks for the difference, so the answer is $24 - 15 = 9$ meters.

A.why: You divided each area by the base without doubling it first, so you dropped the $\frac{1}{2}$ from the formula. That gives heights of 7.5 and 12, which are half the real heights, and their difference is 4.5.

D.why: 54 is the difference between the two areas in square meters. It is not a length, and the question asks for the gap between the heights.

items.stimulus: A sediment hopper at a river gauging station is a right circular cone with its vertex pointing down. The height of the cone equals the diameter of its circular top. When water fills the hopper to exactly half its height, the volume of water is $18\pi$ cubic feet.
items.stem: What is the radius, in feet, of the top of the hopper?
items.explanation: The water forms a smaller cone similar to the hopper, scaled by $\frac{1}{2}$. Volumes scale by $k^3$, so the water is $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{8}$ of the full volume. That makes the full volume $8 \cdot 18\pi = 144\pi$ cubic feet. items.stimulus: A quilter reproducing a 19th-century block pattern starts with a square of fabric that is 10 inches on each side. D.why: You set up $2x^2 = 32$ correctly but stopped at $x^2 = 16$. You still need the square root to get the leg length.

In a 2021 trial, cyclists who drank beetroot juice before a time trial finished an average of 11 seconds faster than cyclists who drank a placebo. Because beetroot is rich in nitrate, which can help muscles use oxygen more efficiently, the researchers concluded that nitrate produced the gap.

Text 2
Although the 11-second gap is real, the juice also delivered about 60 more calories of sugar than the placebo, which was artificially sweetened. Extra carbohydrate shortly before exercise could simply have produced the faster times, so it is difficult to credit nitrate alone.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: On average, the cyclists given beetroot juice finished the time trial faster than the cyclists given the placebo.
The 11-second gap between the two groups most likely came from errors in how the time trial was timed.
Nitrate improves the muscles' use of oxygen enough to account for the full 11-second gap between groups.
Extra carbohydrate before exercise does more to improve cycling times than nitrate from beetroot does.
items.explanation: Split Text 1 into what was observed and what was concluded. The observation is that the juice group finished 11 seconds faster. The conclusion is that nitrate caused the difference. Text 2 opens by granting the observation ("Although the 11-second gap is real") and then offers a different cause, the extra sugar. The faster average time for the juice group is the one point both authors accept.

B.why: You assumed Text 2 attacks the data. It doesn't. Text 2 calls the gap "real" and questions only what caused it. Neither author suggests the timing was faulty.

C.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, and Text 2 is written to challenge it. Text 2 says it is "difficult to credit nitrate alone," so its author would not accept this.

D.why: You went further than Text 2 does. Text 2 says only that sugar "could" explain the gap, not that it beats nitrate. Text 1's author would reject this outright.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In archives of tales gathered across Brittany in the 1890s, versions of the "sunken bell" legend from coastal parishes outnumber those from inland parishes by about three to one. Folklorist Anne Morvan argues that this imbalance shows the legend arose among fishing communities and spread inland only later.

Text 2
Morvan's count is accurate. But the collectors who compiled those archives traveled mostly by the new coastal railway and spent far more days in seaside parishes than inland ones. A three-to-one ratio could reflect where the collectors went rather than where the legend began.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The archives contain more recorded versions of the legend from coastal parishes than from inland ones.
The collectors misrecorded a large share of inland versions of the legend as coming from the coast.
The sunken bell legend most likely began in fishing communities before it spread to inland parishes.
The new coastal railway was the main route by which the legend traveled from the coast to inland areas.
items.explanation: Text 1 observes a three-to-one imbalance in favor of coastal versions and concludes that the legend began on the coast. Text 2 grants that "Morvan's count is accurate." It then names another possible source of the imbalance: collectors spent more time on the coast. Both authors accept that the archives hold more coastal versions than inland ones.

B.why: This is the trap of reading Text 2 as an attack on the data. Text 2 says the count is accurate. Its point is about where the collectors went, not about labeling mistakes.

C.why: This is Morvan's conclusion, which Text 2 is written to challenge. Text 2 says the ratio could reflect the collectors' movements "rather than where the legend began."

D.why: You picked up the railway because it appears in Text 2 but lost its role. In Text 2, the railway explains where the collectors traveled. Neither text says it carried the legend anywhere.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
On surviving charts of the Velna estuary, the shoreline drawn on charts made after 1650 lies about two kilometers seaward of the shoreline on charts made before 1600. Historian Pieter Aalst concludes that river sediment built the coast outward during that interval.

Text 2
The seaward shift on the later charts is plain. Yet most post-1650 surveyors traced the low-tide line, where broad mudflats are exposed, whereas earlier surveyors traced the high-water mark. On so flat a coast, that change in practice alone could move the drawn shoreline by kilometers.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Charts made after 1650 show the Velna shoreline farther seaward than charts made before 1600 do.
Surveyors before 1600 drew the Velna shoreline too far inland for their charts to be trusted.
River sediment pushed the Velna coast outward in the period between the two sets of charts.
Exposed mudflats at low tide make the Velna coast too difficult to chart with any accuracy.
items.explanation: Text 1 compares two sets of charts, finds a two-kilometer seaward shift, and concludes that sediment built the coast outward. Text 2 accepts the shift ("is plain") and gives another cause for it: surveyors switched from tracing the high-water mark to tracing the low-tide line. Both authors agree that the later charts place the shoreline farther seaward.

B.why: You took Text 2 to mean the early charts were wrong. Text 2 says only that early surveyors traced a different line, the high-water mark. It never says that line was drawn inaccurately.

C.why: This is Aalst's conclusion, the claim Text 2 is written to answer. Text 2 argues that a change in surveying practice alone could explain the shift, so its author wouldn't accept this.

D.why: This repeats Text 2's technical terms (low tide, mudflats) but leaves out its argument that a different cause could explain the shift. Neither author says the coast can't be charted accurately.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In a study of mouse lymph nodes, immunologist Rhea Okonjo's team counted germinal centers, the clusters where B cells refine the antibodies they produce. They found roughly half as many in aged mice as in young ones. Because B cells drive germinal-center formation, the team concluded that B cells lose this capacity with age.

Text 2
Using higher-resolution imaging, Tomas Lindqvist confirmed Okonjo's count. His images also showed that aged nodes contain far fewer follicular dendritic cells, which display the antigens B cells must encounter before forming germinal centers. A shortage of these cells could by itself limit germinal centers, Lindqvist notes, even if aged B cells remain fully capable.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The lymph nodes of aged mice hold fewer of the sites where B cells refine antibodies than those of young mice do.
B cells in aged mice are less able than B cells in young mice to start forming new germinal centers.
A shortage of follicular dendritic cells is the main reason that germinal centers decline in aged mice.
Imaging at lower resolution probably overstated how few germinal centers the aged mice actually had.
items.explanation: Split Text 1 into its observation and its inference. The observation is that aged mice have about half as many germinal centers. The inference is that aged B cells lose the ability to form them. Lindqvist 'confirmed Okonjo's count', so he accepts the observation and challenges only the inference by naming another possible cause: too few follicular dendritic cells. The one thing both authors hold is the observation. Choice A restates it, using Text 1's definition of germinal centers as the clusters where B cells refine antibodies.

B.why: This is Okonjo's inference, not something both authors accept. Lindqvist says aged B cells may 'remain fully capable', and that is exactly the conclusion he is questioning. You picked the claim Text 1 ends on without checking whether Text 2 accepts it.

C.why: You saw that Text 2 offers another cause and then made it stronger than it is. Lindqvist only says the shortage 'could' limit germinal centers, so he doesn't call it the main reason. Okonjo blames the B cells, so she wouldn't agree with this either.

D.why: This is the trap for this subtype: you treated Text 2 as an attack on the data. The higher-resolution imaging confirmed the count instead of correcting it. Lindqvist disputes what the count means, not the count itself.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
When engineer Priya Haddad repeatedly loaded 3D-printed titanium brackets, they cracked after far fewer cycles than forged brackets did. Microscopy showed a small pore at the origin of nearly every crack. Haddad therefore concluded that porosity left by printing is what shortens the brackets' fatigue lives.

Text 2
Re-examining Haddad's brackets with high-resolution x-ray tomography, Felipe Arce did find pores at the crack origins. Yet those pores sit where unusually coarse grains meet, and such boundaries concentrate stress on their own. It is difficult to exclude, Arce argues, that the grain boundaries start the cracks and the pores simply happen to lie nearby.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: In the printed brackets, fatigue cracks tended to begin at locations where pores were present.
The pores left by printing are what cause the printed brackets to crack after fewer cycles.
Coarse grain boundaries, not pores, are what cause the printed brackets to crack early.
Ordinary microscopy mistook features at the crack origins for pores that were not really there.
items.explanation: Text 1's observation is that a pore sat at the origin of nearly every crack. Its inference, marked by 'therefore', is that porosity causes the early failure. Arce's tomography 'did find pores at the crack origins', so he accepts the observation. He then names another possible source of the same pattern: coarse grain boundaries that concentrate stress, with the pores 'simply' nearby. Both authors therefore agree only that cracks began where pores were, which is choice A.

B.why: This is Haddad's 'therefore' conclusion, and it is the claim Text 2 was written to challenge. Arce suggests the pores may just be nearby while the grain boundaries start the cracks, so he wouldn't agree with it.

C.why: You spotted Arce's alternative cause and then stated it as settled fact. He says only that it is 'difficult to exclude', which raises a possibility without proving it. Haddad blames the pores, so she would reject this choice as well.

D.why: This is the subtype trap: you read the new imaging method as overturning the old data. Arce's tomography confirmed that the pores were really there. He questions what they mean, not whether they exist.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Comparing charts produced by a single Venetian workshop, historian Livia Morandi found that coastlines on its charts from after 1583 match modern surveys far more closely than those on its earlier charts. Because the improvement is abrupt rather than gradual, Morandi concluded that the workshop had begun receiving measurements taken by pilots on newly commissioned voyages.

Text 2
Morandi is right that the later charts are more accurate. But multispectral imaging reveals that their coastlines were redrawn over erased earlier outlines, and the new outlines match, inlet for inlet, those of a Genoese chart the workshop acquired in 1583. An abrupt gain in accuracy could simply reflect copying a rival's work.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The workshop's later coastlines were drawn from measurements its own pilots took at sea.
The workshop's later charts drew on information that it did not have before 1583.
The later charts seem more accurate only because their coastlines were redrawn.
The erased outlines under the later coastlines record the workshop's earlier survey methods.
items.explanation: Split Text 1 into its observation (the charts made after 1583 are abruptly more accurate) and its inference (pilots' new measurements caused this). Text 2 accepts the observation and offers a different source: a rival chart acquired in 1583. The two causes differ, but they share one feature. Both say the workshop got information after 1583 that it lacked before, whether from voyages or from a Genoese chart. Both authors would accept that statement.

A.why: This is Text 1's inference, and it is the very claim Text 2 calls into question. You picked a statement only one author holds.

C.why: You assumed Text 2 attacks the observation. Text 2 opens by saying 'Morandi is right that the later charts are more accurate.' It disputes only why they improved, not whether they did.

D.why: You were drawn by Text 2's technical detail about erased outlines. Neither text says what those outlines show about survey methods, so neither author makes this claim.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Indigo-dyed linen fragments excavated at a medieval market town grow markedly paler in layers dated after 1350. Because the soil chemistry is uniform across all layers, textile historian Hana Okafor ruled out fading in the ground and concluded that rising indigo prices had led local dyers to use weaker dye baths.

Text 2
Okafor's color measurements are sound, but under scanning electron microscopy the later fibers show the abrasion and alkali pitting produced by repeated washing in lye soap, which became common in the town around 1350. Cloth dyed at full strength could have faded through laundering alone.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Rising indigo prices after 1350 led local dyers to prepare weaker dye baths.
The color measurements exaggerate how much paler the later fragments are.
Lye soap became common in the town because indigo had grown too costly.
The later fragments had already become paler before they were buried.
items.explanation: Text 1 rules out fading in the ground and blames weaker dyeing, which happens before the cloth is ever used. Text 2 accepts the paleness and blames repeated laundering, which happens while the cloth is being worn. The two causes compete, but both act before burial. That shared timing is the one point both authors hold.

A.why: This is Okafor's conclusion. Text 2 argues that cloth dyed at full strength could have faded anyway, so it does not accept this claim.

B.why: You treated Text 2 as attacking the data. Text 2 calls Okafor's color measurements 'sound' and disputes only her explanation for them.

C.why: This joins a term from each text into a causal link that neither author makes. Neither text explains why lye soap spread.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Engineers embedded microcapsules of liquid monomer in a polymer, cracked the samples, and heated them to 80°C. The samples regained 90 percent of their original strength. The team concluded that heating had ruptured the capsules, releasing monomer that flowed into the cracks and bonded their faces.

Text 2
The recovery is well documented. Yet micro-CT scans of the same samples show that most capsules along the cracks remained intact. At 80°C, the polymer's own chains can soften and re-entangle across a crack face, so it is difficult to exclude heat alone as the cause of the healing.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Heating the cracked samples played a part in their regaining strength.
The heat ruptured the capsules, releasing monomer that bonded the crack faces.
The samples regained considerably less strength than the engineers reported.
The microcapsules contributed nothing to the strength the samples regained.
items.explanation: In Text 1, heat triggers the capsules. In Text 2, heat makes the polymer chains re-entangle. The two texts disagree about the mechanism, but in both of them heating is part of how the samples recovered. That is the shared ground.

B.why: This is Text 1's mechanism. Text 2's scans show that most capsules stayed intact, which casts doubt on this claim.

C.why: Text 2 says outright that 'the recovery is well documented.' It accepts the result and questions only its cause.

D.why: You took Text 2 further than it goes. It says that most capsules, not all, stayed intact, and that heat alone is 'difficult to exclude.' It does not say the capsules did nothing, and Text 1 would reject this claim anyway.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Recording blackbirds in Vienna and in nearby forests, ornithologist Mira Ahn found that city birds' songs had a minimum frequency about 160 hertz higher. Since traffic noise is concentrated at low frequencies, Ahn concluded that urban blackbirds raise their pitch so that their songs are not masked.

Text 2
Reanalyzing Ahn's recordings with calibrated microphones, Teo Brandt found that the city songs were also considerably louder, as birds strain to be heard over traffic. In songbirds, singing louder raises pitch as a physical byproduct, so the higher frequencies may be an incidental consequence of volume rather than a shift to escape masking.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: City blackbirds raise their pitch in order to keep traffic noise from masking their songs.
The city recordings overstate how much higher urban songs are than forest songs.
Traffic noise is ultimately behind the higher pitch of the city blackbirds' songs.
City blackbirds sing more loudly because raising their pitch increases their volume.
items.explanation: Text 1 says that birds shift pitch to escape traffic noise. Text 2 says that birds sing louder to be heard over traffic, and the higher pitch follows as a byproduct. The paths differ, but in both accounts traffic noise is the root cause. The authors disagree only about whether the pitch change is a strategy or a side effect.

A.why: 'In order to' is Text 1's claim that the shift is deliberate. Text 2 calls the shift 'incidental,' so it rejects this statement.

B.why: Text 2 reanalyzes the same recordings and builds on the pitch difference without disputing it. It challenges the explanation, not the measurement.

D.why: This reverses Text 2's causal chain. In Text 2, loudness raises pitch, not the other way around.

items.stimulus:
Text 1
After sea otters recolonized a stretch of the central California coast in 2016, divers recorded that purple sea urchin densities there fell by nearly 70 percent within two years. Ecologist Rosa Ibarra concluded that otter predation had driven the decline.

Text 2
Ibarra's survey counts are not in question. But when Jun Okada examined the empty urchin tests—the shells—that divers collected during those surveys, many bore the lesions of a wasting disease that swept the coast in 2017. Disease could have produced the same drop with or without otters.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Otter predation was the main cause of the drop in urchin densities after 2016.
The divers' surveys overstated how sharply urchin densities fell after 2016.
The lesions on the collected urchin tests were left by otters attacking urchins.
The drop in urchin densities came from urchins dying rather than moving away.
items.explanation: Text 1's cause is predation and Text 2's is disease, and they compete. However, both are ways urchins die. Neither author suggests that the urchins left the site, so both would accept that the decline came from deaths.

A.why: This is Ibarra's inference. Text 2 says that disease could explain the same drop, so it does not grant this claim.

B.why: Text 2 begins by saying that the survey counts 'are not in question.' You chose an attack on the data when Text 2 attacks only the conclusion drawn from it.

C.why: You were drawn by the technical word 'lesions.' Text 2 attributes them to a wasting disease, and Text 1 never mentions them.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Commercial piano recordings made between 1905 and 1925 present Chopin's nocturnes at tempos as much as 20 percent faster than modern performances. Since the recordings' pitch confirms they are being played back at the correct speed, musicologist Ilse Varga concluded that pianists of the period simply preferred brisker tempos.

Text 2
Varga's measurements hold up, but a disc side then held barely four minutes of music. Comparing the same pianists' discs with their piano rolls, which had no such limit, Paolo Ruiz found consistently slower tempos on the rolls. Pianists may have hurried to fit a nocturne onto one side.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The fast tempos on the discs reflect how quickly the pianists actually played.
Pianists of the period preferred brisker tempos than pianists do today.
The discs are played back too fast, which exaggerates the pianists' tempos.
Piano rolls preserve the period's tempos more faithfully than pitch analysis does.
items.explanation: Text 1 uses pitch to rule out a playback error and concludes that the pianists really played fast because they liked to. Text 2 accepts the measurements and says the pianists really played fast because they were short of time. Both agree that the speed is genuine and came from the pianists, not from the equipment. They differ only on why the pianists played that way.

B.why: This is Varga's conclusion. Ruiz's piano rolls show the same pianists playing slower when time was not limited, so Text 2 does not accept it.

C.why: Text 1 rules out a playback error by checking pitch, and Text 2 says that 'Varga's measurements hold up.' Neither author doubts the observation.

D.why: This sets two of the passage's technical terms against each other. Pitch analysis checks playback speed and is not a record of tempo, so the comparison answers a question neither text asks.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Twelve distance runners spent four weeks training at 2,400 meters, and afterward their 5,000-meter times at sea level improved by an average of 2 percent. Physiologist Dana Kerr attributed the gain to thin air stimulating the runners' bodies to produce more oxygen-carrying red blood cells.

Text 2
The runners did get faster. But carbon-monoxide rebreathing tests showed that half of them gained no measurable hemoglobin mass, yet they improved as much as the others. Since the camp also nearly doubled their weekly mileage, the extra training alone could account for the faster times.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The thin air raised the runners' production of oxygen-carrying red blood cells.
The runners' faster times after the camp reflect timing errors, not real gains.
Something about the training camp was responsible for the runners' faster times.
Training at altitude has no effect on the hemoglobin mass of distance runners.

items.subtype_name: Same evidence, different cause
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Of 64 versions of a Norwegian folktale collected in the 1890s, nearly every coastal version includes an episode in which the youngest son outwits a sea serpent; no inland version does. Folklorist Erik Haugen concluded that coastal storytellers had reshaped the tale around the hazards of their seafaring lives.

Text 2
Haugen's tally is accurate. Yet stylometric comparison shows that the coastal serpent episodes repeat, nearly phrase for phrase, a cheap chapbook that peddlers sold only in harbor towns in the 1870s. The episode may have entered through print, not through tellers' own invention.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

The collectors misrecorded the coastal versions, adding an episode the tellers omitted.
The chapbook's printer took the serpent episode from coastal storytellers' versions.

items.subtype_name: How sample size changes the margin of error
items.stimulus: Astronomers randomly selected 150 stars from a catalog of stars within 50 light-years of the Sun. They found that 32% of the selected stars have at least one known planet, with an associated margin of error of 6%. The astronomers then randomly selected 600 different stars from the same catalog and estimated the same percentage. The margin of error for the second sample was calculated the same way.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The second sample's margin of error is expected to be greater than 6%.
The second sample's margin of error is expected to be less than 6%.
The second sample's margin of error is expected to be about 6%.
The second sample's margin of error is expected to be about 1.5%.
items.explanation: Both samples come from the same catalog and use the same method. The only difference is size: the second sample has 600 stars instead of 150. A larger sample gives a smaller margin of error, so you should expect the second margin of error to be less than 6%. Because the sample is 4 times as large, the margin is divided by $\sqrt{4} = 2$, which gives about 3%.

A.why: You reversed the relationship. A larger sample gives a smaller margin of error, not a larger one.

C.why: You treated the margin of error as fixed for the catalog. You missed that the sample size changed from 150 to 600, and that change shrinks the margin.

D.why: You divided 6% by 4 because the sample is 4 times as large. The margin of error is divided by the square root of 4, so it comes to about 3%, not 1.5%.

items.subtype_name: How sample size changes the margin of error
items.stimulus: An immunology lab estimated the mean antibody level in a random sample of 50 vaccinated volunteers. The margin of error for the estimate was 8 units.
items.stem: If the lab instead used a random sample of 100 volunteers from the same population and computed the margin of error the same way, which of the following is the most plausible value for the new margin of error?
items.explanation: Going from 50 to 100 volunteers doubles the sample size, so the margin of error is divided by $\sqrt{2}$: $\frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 5.66$ units. That is smaller than 8 but not as small as 4, so it falls between 4 and 8 units.

A.why: You assumed that doubling the sample halves the margin of error. The margin is divided by $\sqrt{2}$, not by 2, so it shrinks to about 5.66 units, not 4.

C.why: You treated the margin of error as fixed. A larger sample from the same population gives a smaller margin, so it can't stay at 8 units.

D.why: You reversed the relationship. A larger sample makes the margin of error smaller, not larger.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate explanation for why the two margins of error differ?

The first survey was given to more users than the second survey was.
The second survey's estimate is closer to the true percentage of all users.
items.explanation: Both samples came from the same population, and both margins of error were computed the same way. So the margin of error depends on sample size: a larger sample gives a smaller margin. The second survey's margin (3 points) is smaller than the first survey's (6 points), so the second survey most likely used the larger sample.

items.subtype_name: How sample size changes the margin of error
items.stimulus: A city planning office surveyed a random sample of 500 residents about a proposed network of protected bike lanes. Based on the sample, it is estimated that 64% of residents support the proposal, with an associated margin of error of 4.4 percentage points. Before the city council votes, the office plans a second survey of a new random sample of 1,000 residents.
items.stem: If the second survey's margin of error is computed the same way, which of the following ranges is it most likely to fall in?

items.stimulus: An ecologist weighed a random sample of 50 wood frogs from a wetland preserve. Based on the sample, it is estimated that the mean mass of all wood frogs in the preserve is 22 grams, with an associated margin of error of 3.0 grams. The ecologist wants a new random sample from the same preserve with a margin of error of at most 1.5 grams, computed the same way. Assume the margin of error is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size.
items.stem: Which of the following is the least sample size that would give a margin of error of at most 1.5 grams?
items.explanation: To cut the margin from 3.0 to 1.5 grams, you need to divide it by 2. The margin is divided by $\sqrt{k}$ when the sample is multiplied by $k$, so you need $\sqrt{k} = 2$, which means $k = 4$. That requires $50 \times 4 = 200$ frogs.

B.why: You multiplied the sample by $\sqrt{2}$, which mixes up where the square root belongs. That only divides the margin by about 1.19, which leaves it near 2.5 grams.

C.why: You assumed doubling the sample halves the margin. Doubling only divides the margin by $\sqrt{2}$, which gives about 2.1 grams and is still above 1.5 grams.

items.stimulus: At an excavated Bronze Age settlement, archaeologists randomly selected 150 animal bone fragments from a storage pit and checked each one for butchery marks. Next season, the team will examine 300 more randomly selected fragments from the same pit and combine them with the original 150 into a single sample.
items.stem: If the new margin of error is computed the same way, which of the following ranges is it most likely to fall in?
items.explanation: The combined sample has $150 + 300 = 450$ fragments, which is 3 times the original 150. The margin of error is divided by $\sqrt{3}$: $6 \div \sqrt{3} \approx 3.5$ percentage points. That falls between 3.0 and 4.0.

items.stem: About how many adults should be in the new sample?
items.explanation: Going from 120 to 60 milligrams divides the margin of error by 2. Because the margin of error is divided by $\sqrt{k}$ when the sample size is multiplied by $k$, you need $\sqrt{k} = 2$, so $k = 4$. The new sample should have $150 \times 4 = 600$ adults.

C.why: You assumed doubling the sample halves the margin of error. Doubling divides the margin of error only by $\sqrt{2}$, to about 85 milligrams. To halve it, you need 4 times as many adults.

C.why: You used the right factor, $\sqrt{9} = 3$, but in the wrong direction. A smaller sample makes the margin of error larger, so you multiply by 3 instead of dividing.

D.why: You made two mistakes here. You shrank the margin of error when a smaller sample makes it grow, and you used the full factor of 9 when you should have used its square root.

items.subtype_name: How sample size changes the margin of error
items.stimulus: To check a new city map, a cartographer chose a random sample of $n$ street intersections and estimated the mean positional error to be $e$ meters, with an associated margin of error of $m$ meters. She then checked a random sample of $kn$ intersections on the same map, where $k > 1$, and calculated the margin of error the same way.
items.stem: Which of the following expressions best approximates the margin of error for the mean positional error estimated from the larger sample?
items.explanation: The sample size is multiplied by $k$. The margin of error depends on the square root of the sample size, so it is divided by $\sqrt{k}$. The new margin of error is about $\frac{m}{\sqrt{k}}$. It is smaller than $m$ because the sample is larger.

D.why: You scaled the estimate $e$ when you should have scaled the margin of error $m$. The sample size changes how precise the estimate is. It does not predict that the estimate itself will shrink.

items.stimulus: A folklore researcher wanted to estimate the percent of adults in one county who have heard a local legend about a ghost ferry. items.stimulus: An astronomer selected 200 galaxies at random from a sky catalog and classified each one by shape. items.stem: Which of the following must be true?

The new margin of error will be between 3.3 and 6.6 percentage points.
The new margin of error will be greater than 6.6 percentage points.
items.explanation: The sample size doubles from 200 to 400. When the sample size is multiplied by k, the margin of error is divided by $\sqrt{k}$. items.subtype_name: How sample size changes the margin of error
items.stimulus: A printmakers' guild wants to estimate the mean price of the woodblock prints sold at its annual fair. Plan 1 is to record the prices of 64 prints selected at random from the fair's sales. Plan 2 is to record the prices of 256 prints selected at random from the same sales. items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Plan 2's margin of error will be about one-half of Plan 1's.
Plan 2's margin of error will be about one-fourth of Plan 1's.
Plan 2's margin of error will be about twice as large as Plan 1's.
Plan 2's sample mean will be closer to the true mean than Plan 1's.
items.explanation: Plan 2 uses $\frac{256}{64} = 4$ times as many prints. When the sample size is multiplied by k, the margin of error is divided by $\sqrt{k}$, and $\sqrt{4} = 2$. So Plan 2's margin of error will be about one-half of Plan 1's.

items.stem: Which of the following sample sizes would most likely produce a margin of error of 3 percentage points?
items.explanation: To go from a margin of 6 to a margin of 3, you divide it by 2. That means $\sqrt{k} = 2$, so $k = 4$, and the sample must be $4 \times 250 = 1{,}000$. Check it: $\frac{6}{\sqrt{4}} = 3$.

D.why: You squared the target margin, 3, to get a factor of 9. The factor comes from squaring the ratio $\frac{6}{3} = 2$, and a 2,250-person sample would bring the margin down to 2.

items.subtype_name: How sample size changes the margin of error
items.stimulus: Two linguists each surveyed randomly selected adult residents of the same city to estimate the percent who speak more than one language at home. items.stem: Which of the following is the most plausible explanation for the difference between the two margins of error?
choices: Linguist A surveyed fewer residents than Linguist B did.
Linguist A found a lower percent than Linguist B did.
Linguist B surveyed more residents, so her estimate is exact.
Linguist A surveyed residents of a different city than B did.
items.explanation: When two samples come from the same population and the margins of error are computed the same way, the size of the sample decides how big the margin is. Linguist A's sample of 400 is smaller than Linguist B's sample of 1,600, so Linguist A's margin of error is larger. The percent each linguist found does not explain the difference.

B.why: You gave the credit to the estimate instead of the sample size. The percent found is a different number from the setup, and it is not what makes one margin larger than the other. Here the sizes are 400 and 1,600, and that gap is the reason.

D.why: The setup says both linguists surveyed residents of the same city. You worked from a detail the question never gave you.

items.subtype_name: Scale factor: lengths vs. areas
items.stimulus: An immunology lab counts white blood cells using a slide etched with square grids. On one slide, square $A$ is a small counting square. Square $B$ is a larger counting square whose side length is $3$ times the side length of square $A$.
items.stem: The area of square $B$ is $k$ times the area of square $A$. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: The scale factor for lengths is $k = 3$. Areas scale by the square of the length factor, so square $B$'s area is $3^2 = 9$ times square $A$'s area. To check, give square $A$ a side of $1$: its area is $1$, and square $B$ has side $3$ and area $9$.

A.why: You gave the ratio of the side lengths, $3$, as the ratio of the areas. Areas scale by $k^2$, not by $k$.

B.why: You doubled the scale factor ($2 \times 3$) when you needed to square it ($3 \times 3$).

D.why: You cubed the scale factor, which gives the ratio of volumes. A square is flat, so its area scales by $3^2$, not $3^3$.

items.subtype_name: Scale factor: lengths vs. areas
items.stimulus: An urban planning team is designing two triangular plazas, $P$ and $Q$, that are similar. Each side of plaza $Q$ is $\frac{1}{2}$ the length of the corresponding side of plaza $P$. The area of plaza $P$ is $96$ square meters.

items.explanation: The length scale factor from $P$ to $Q$ is $k = \frac{1}{2}$, so the area scale factor is $k^2 = \frac{1}{4}$. The area of plaza $Q$ is $96 \times \frac{1}{4} = 24$ square meters.

D.why: You applied the scale factor in the wrong direction and multiplied $96$ by $4$. Plaza $Q$ is the smaller plaza, so its area has to be less than $96$.

items.subtype_name: Scale factor: lengths vs. areas
items.stimulus: A printmaker carves a rectangular woodblock plate that measures $6$ centimeters by $10$ centimeters. She then carves an enlarged plate that is similar to the first one. The area of the enlarged plate is $4$ times the area of the original plate.
items.stem: What is the length, in centimeters, of the longer side of the enlarged plate?

items.subtype_name: Scale a sample up to the population
items.stimulus: An ornithologist estimates that 9,000 songbirds use a particular wetland reserve during spring migration. From mist nets set at random locations in the reserve, she examined a random sample of 250 songbirds and found that 35 of them carried at least one tick.
items.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the sample data?
choices: Exactly 1,260 of the songbirds in the reserve carry ticks.
About 1,260 of the songbirds in the reserve carry ticks.
About 7,740 of the songbirds in the reserve carry ticks.
About 14% of songbirds in every reserve carry ticks.
items.explanation: The sample fraction with ticks is $\frac{35}{250} = 0.14$. Multiply by the reserve's population: $0.14 \times 9{,}000 = 1{,}260$. A random sample supports an estimate for the population it came from, so the right wording is 'about,' not 'exactly.'

D.why: All of the birds were sampled from this one reserve, so the result says nothing about other reserves. Applying it to every reserve stretches it to a population that was never sampled.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Approximately 16% of the wheat plots at the station yielded more than 60 bushels per acre.
Approximately 16% of the Redfield plots at the station yielded more than 60 bushels per acre.
The Redfield plots at the station had a mean yield of about 60 bushels per acre.
Approximately 16% of the Redfield plots in the state yielded more than 60 bushels per acre.
items.explanation: The sample came at random from the station's Redfield plots only, so its 16% carries over, approximately, to the Redfield plots at that station. The other three varieties and other farms were not sampled.

A.why: You applied the result to all four wheat varieties. Only Redfield plots were sampled, so the sample says nothing about the other varieties.

C.why: You turned the percent of plots above 60 bushels per acre into a mean yield. A share above a cutoff doesn't tell you the average.

D.why: You extended the result beyond the one station. Redfield plots elsewhere in the state were never sampled, and they could grow under different soil and weather.

items.subtype_name: Which population can the sample speak for
items.stimulus: An economist randomly selected 400 warehouse workers from all warehouse workers in one state. Of the workers selected, 30% reported working more than 45 hours in a typical week.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Approximately 30% of all warehouse workers in the state work more than 45 hours in a typical week.
Approximately 30% of all workers in the state, in any job, work more than 45 hours in a typical week.
The warehouse workers in the state work a mean of approximately 45 hours in a typical week.
Approximately 30% of all warehouse workers in the state work 45 hours or fewer in a typical week.
items.explanation: The sample was drawn at random from the state's warehouse workers, so you can carry the 30% figure over to that group and no other. You keep the statistic the same (a percent above 45 hours stays a percent above 45 hours) and hedge it with 'approximately', because a sample gives an estimate, not an exact count.

B.why: You stretched the result to every worker in the state. Only warehouse workers were sampled, so the data say nothing about people in other jobs.

C.why: You turned a percent above a threshold into a claim about the average. Knowing that 30% work more than 45 hours tells you nothing about the mean number of hours.

D.why: You attached 30% to the wrong side of the threshold. The 30% worked more than 45 hours, so about 70% would work 45 hours or fewer.

items.stimulus: A linguist randomly selected 250 Welsh speakers from all Welsh speakers living in one county in Wales. Of those selected, 40% said they speak Welsh at home every day.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Approximately 40% of all residents of the county, whatever language they speak, use Welsh at home every day.
Approximately 40% of the Welsh speakers living in the county speak Welsh at home every day.
The Welsh speakers living in the county speak Welsh at home on approximately 40% of days.
Approximately 40% of the Welsh speakers living anywhere in Wales speak Welsh at home every day.
items.explanation: The random sample came only from Welsh speakers in this one county, so that is the only group the 40% can describe. Choice B keeps the same statistic (the share of people who speak Welsh at home daily) and hedges it with 'approximately'.

A.why: You widened the claim to every resident of the county. Only Welsh speakers were sampled, so residents who don't speak Welsh were never part of the data.

C.why: You changed what the percent counts. The 40% is a share of people who speak Welsh daily, not a share of days on which a typical speaker uses it.

D.why: You stretched the result from one county to the whole country. Welsh speakers in other counties were never sampled, and their habits could be different.

Approximately 15% of the plants of this variety in the greenhouse show signs of leaf blight.

items.stimulus: At an excavation site, archaeologists randomly selected 120 pottery shards from among all the shards recovered in the site's eastern trench. They found that 15% of the selected shards had a glazed surface.

choices: Approximately 15% of the pottery shards recovered at sites across the region are glazed.
Approximately 15% of the pottery shards recovered in the site's western trench are glazed.
Approximately 15% of the pottery shards recovered in the site's eastern trench are glazed.
Exactly 18 of the pottery shards recovered in the site's eastern trench are glazed.

D.why: 18 is the number of glazed shards in the sample of 120. You treated that count as the count for the whole trench, which holds more shards than were sampled, and you dropped the hedge by saying 'exactly'.

items.stem: In the figure, the boundary of the inequality is a dashed line. The shaded region shown represents the solutions to the inequality $y < mx + b$, where $m$ and $b$ are constants. What is the value of $b - m$?

A.why: You matched angle $PQS$ with angle $P$ instead of angle $R$, so you found $\cos P = \frac{3}{5}$.

C.why: You found $\tan(\angle PQS) = \frac{PS}{QS} = \frac{9}{12}$, which is opposite over adjacent, instead of the cosine.

D.why: You divided the two given segment lengths, but neither one is a side or the hypotenuse of a triangle containing angle $PQS$ in the right way for a cosine.

items.subtype_name: Similar right triangles: carry a ratio or a side across
items.stimulus: A cartographer marks three landmarks on a map as points $A$, $B$, and $C$, forming right triangle $ABC$ with its right angle at $C$. On the map, $AB = 17$ centimeters and $AC = 8$ centimeters. The three landmarks themselves form triangle $DEF$ on the ground, which is similar to triangle $ABC$, where $A$ corresponds to $D$, $B$ corresponds to $E$, and $C$ corresponds to $F$. On the ground, $DE = 6.8$ kilometers.
items.stem: What is the value of $\cos(E)$?
items.explanation: Because $B$ corresponds to $E$, angle $E$ is congruent to angle $B$, so $\cos(E) = \cos(B)$. Similar triangles have the same trig values, so you can ignore the 6.8 km. Do the work in triangle $ABC$, where you know two sides. First find the missing leg: $BC = \sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$. Measured from angle $B$, the adjacent leg is $BC$ and the hypotenuse is $AB$, so $\cos(B) = \frac{15}{17}$. That makes $\cos(E) = \frac{15}{17}$, or about 0.8824.

items.subtype_name: Similar right triangles: carry a ratio or a side across
items.stimulus: An archaeologist sets out a small survey grid shaped like right triangle $PQR$, with its right angle at $R$, where $\tan(Q) = \frac{12}{5}$. A larger excavation trench is shaped like triangle $STU$, which is similar to triangle $PQR$, where $P$ corresponds to $S$, $Q$ corresponds to $T$, and $R$ corresponds to $U$. The hypotenuse $\overline{ST}$ of the trench is 39 meters long.
items.stem: What is the length, in meters, of $\overline{TU}$?
items.explanation: Because $Q$ corresponds to $T$, $\tan(T) = \tan(Q) = \frac{12}{5}$. In triangle $STU$, the right angle is at $U$. Measured from angle $T$, the opposite leg is $SU$ and the adjacent leg is $TU$, so $SU : TU = 12 : 5$. The legs 12 and 5 go with a hypotenuse of $\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = 13$, which makes the sides $SU : TU : ST = 12 : 5 : 13$. Since $ST = 39 = 3 \times 13$, the scale factor is 3, and $TU = 3 \times 5 = 15$ meters.

items.stimulus: For a poster on daily nutrient intake, a nutrition scientist draws right triangle $JKL$ with its right angle at $K$, where $JK = 20$ inches and $KL = 15$ inches. A segment is drawn from $K$ perpendicular to $\overline{JL}$, meeting $\overline{JL}$ at point $M$.
items.stem: What is the value of $\sin(\angle JKM)$?
items.explanation: The altitude $\overline{KM}$ splits triangle $JKL$ into two smaller right triangles, and each one is similar to $JKL$. In triangle $JKM$, the angles at $J$ and $K$ add to $90^\circ$, and in triangle $JKL$, angles $J$ and $L$ also add to $90^\circ$. That means $\angle JKM$ is congruent to $\angle L$, so $\sin(\angle JKM) = \sin(L)$. In triangle $JKL$, the hypotenuse is $JL = \sqrt{20^2 + 15^2} = 25$. Measured from angle $L$, the opposite side is $JK$, so $\sin(L) = \frac{20}{25} = \frac{4}{5}$. To check: $JM = \frac{20^2}{25} = 16$, and in triangle $JKM$, $\frac{JM}{JK} = \frac{16}{20} = \frac{4}{5}$.

items.stimulus: A public health clinic is adding a wheelchair ramp. From the side, the ramp forms right triangle $ABC$: $\overline{AC}$ is level ground, $\overline{BC}$ is a vertical post at the high end, and the right angle is at $C$. items.stem: What is the length, in feet, of the ramp surface $\overline{AB}$?

items.stimulus: A seismologist draws right triangle $ABC$ to estimate the distance from a monitoring station to an earthquake's epicenter. In the diagram, angle $C$ is a right angle, $AB = 26$ kilometers, and $BC = 10$ kilometers. Triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$, where $A$, $B$, and $C$ correspond to $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. In triangle $DEF$, $DE = 13$ kilometers.
items.stem: What is the value of $\cos E$?
items.explanation: Angle $E$ corresponds to angle $B$, so the two angles are congruent and have the same cosine. In triangle $ABC$, the side next to angle $B$ is $BC = 10$ and the hypotenuse is $AB = 26$. So $\cos E = \cos B = \frac{10}{26} = \frac{5}{13}$. The length $DE = 13$ only tells you the scale factor. It doesn't change the ratio.

A.why: You mixed the two triangles. You divided triangle DEF's adjacent side, $EF = 5$, by triangle ABC's hypotenuse, 26. Because you treated the scale factor as if it changed the trig value, you put sides from different triangles in one ratio. Similar triangles have the same cosine, so take both sides from one triangle.

C.why: You found $\frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{10}{24}$. That is tan A, a different ratio at a different angle. Cosine is the adjacent side over the hypotenuse, and you need it at the angle that corresponds to E.

D.why: This is $\cos A = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{24}{26}$. You used the wrong angle. E corresponds to B, not A, so the side adjacent to the angle you need is BC = 10, not AC = 24.

items.stem: What is the value of $\sin(\angle PQS)$?
items.explanation: Triangle $PQS$ has a right angle at $S$, so $\angle PQS = 90^\circ - \angle P$. Triangle $PQR$ has a right angle at $Q$, so $\angle R = 90^\circ - \angle P$ too. C.why: Angle PQS sits at vertex Q next to side PQ, so you matched it to angle P and found $\sin P = \frac{20}{25}$. That matches angles by where they are in the picture. In the nested triangle, angle PQS is equal to angle R, not angle P.

D.why: You flipped the ratio and divided the hypotenuse by the opposite side, $\frac{25}{15}$. A sine is never greater than 1, so the hypotenuse belongs in the denominator.

items.stimulus: A nutrition scientist is designing triangular labels for two package sizes. On the smaller label, triangle $JKL$, angle $K$ is a right angle and $\sin J = \frac{15}{17}$.
