items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: Ecologists are mapping a restored wetland. Two straight boundary paths, line $j$ and line $k$, are both crossed by a straight drainage ditch, line $t$. Line $t$ meets line $j$ at point $A$ and meets line $k$ at point $B$, with $B$ below $A$. At point $A$, angle 1 is above line $j$ and to the right of line $t$, angle 2 is above line $j$ and to the left of line $t$, and angle 3 is below line $j$ and to the left of line $t$. At point $B$, angle 5 is above line $k$ and to the right of line $t$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $j$ is parallel to line $k$?
items.explanation: Angle 1 and angle 5 are in the same position at the two crossings: above their path and to the right of the ditch. That makes them corresponding angles. If corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel, so this fact is enough.

A.why: Angles 1 and 3 are vertical angles at the same crossing, and vertical angles are always equal whenever two lines cross. Because this is true whether or not $j$ and $k$ are parallel, it can't prove that they are.

B.why: Angles 1 and 2 form a linear pair along line $j$, so they always add to $180^\circ$. You used the supplementary rule, but it only proves parallel lines when it applies to same-side interior angles at two different crossings.

D.why: Saying angle 1 equals angle 2 only tells you that each is $90^\circ$, so the ditch is perpendicular to line $j$. It tells you nothing about line $k$, so it doesn't compare the two paths at all.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A marine biologist divides a kelp survey area into triangular sections. In triangle $ABC$ and triangle $DEF$, $m\angle A = 50^\circ$ and $m\angle D = 50^\circ$, where $A$ corresponds to $D$, $B$ corresponds to $E$, and $C$ corresponds to $F$.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$?
items.explanation: You already have one pair of equal angles, $\angle A$ and $\angle D$. A second pair, $\angle B = \angle E = 70^\circ$, completes Angle-Angle (AA) similarity.

B.why: For SAS similarity, the equal angle has to sit between the two proportional sides. Sides $AB$ and $BC$ meet at $\angle B$, not at $\angle A$, so this is side-side-angle, which doesn't prove similarity.

C.why: A single pair of equal sides plus a single pair of equal angles doesn't meet any similarity criterion. You still need a second angle or a second proportional side next to the equal angle.

items.stimulus:
A linguist uses triangles $JKL$ and $MNP$ to represent the vowel spaces of two related dialects. It is known that $\angle J \cong \angle M$. Each statement below is to be considered separately, on its own, alongside this given fact.

I. $\angle K \cong \angle N$
II. $\frac{JK}{MN} = \frac{JL}{MP}$
III. $\frac{JK}{MN} = \frac{KL}{NP}$
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $JKL$ is similar to triangle $MNP$?
items.explanation: Statement I gives a second pair of congruent angles, so the triangles are similar by AA. Statement II makes the sides on either side of angle $J$ proportional to the sides on either side of angle $M$, and the congruent angle lies between them, so the triangles are similar by SAS. Statement III pairs $JK$ with $KL$, but angle $J$ is opposite $KL$ rather than between the two sides. That is SSA, which does not prove similarity.

A.why: You saw that I works by AA but missed that II also works on its own. The given angle $J$ lies between $JK$ and $JL$, so proportional sides around it complete SAS similarity.

C.why: You ruled out I, probably because angles alone are never enough for congruence. Similarity is different: two pairs of congruent angles prove it by AA. You also accepted III, which is SSA.

D.why: Statement III gives proportional sides, but angle $J$ is not between $JK$ and $KL$. Proportional sides with a non-included angle (SSA) do not prove similarity, so III should be excluded.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: An immunologist sketches the crossing arms of two antibody fragments as segments $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BD}$, which intersect at point $E$. Triangles $AEB$ and $CED$ are formed on opposite sides of $E$. It is given that $AE = CE$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $AEB$ is congruent to triangle $CED$?
items.explanation: You already have $AE = CE$, and $\angle AEB \cong \angle CED$ because they are vertical angles. Adding $BE = DE$ gives two pairs of congruent sides with the included angle between them. That proves the triangles congruent by SAS.

A.why: These are vertical angles, so they are congruent whenever two segments cross. You already had this for free, so it adds nothing. One side and one angle is not a congruence criterion.

C.why: With the vertical angles, this gives two sides and an angle, but the angle at $E$ is not between $AE$ and $AB$. That is SSA, which does not guarantee congruence.

D.why: Angle $ABE$ corresponds to angle $CDE$, not angle $DCE$. Matching angles at non-corresponding vertices does not complete ASA or AAS. Check which vertex matches which before you use an angle pair.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: An ornithologist is building a flight cage for warblers, and two horizontal support rods lie along lines $\ell$ and $m$. A diagonal brace along line $t$ crosses both rods. Angle $A$ is formed where $t$ meets $\ell$, and angle $B$ is formed where $t$ meets $m$. Both angles lie between lines $\ell$ and $m$ and on the same side of line $t$, so they are same-side interior angles. The measure of angle $A$ is $(3x + 14)^\circ$, and the measure of angle $B$ is $(5x + 6)^\circ$.
items.stem: What value of $x$ would be sufficient to prove that lines $\ell$ and $m$ are parallel?
items.explanation: First, name the criterion. Angles $A$ and $B$ are same-side (co-interior) angles, and lines cut by a transversal are parallel exactly when their same-side interior angles add to $180^\circ$. They do not need to be equal. Set up $(3x + 14) + (5x + 6) = 180$, so $8x + 20 = 180$, which gives $8x = 160$ and $x = 20$. Check it: the angles are $74^\circ$ and $106^\circ$, and $74 + 106 = 180$.

You solved correctly but gave the measure of angle $A$, $3(20) + 14 = 74$, instead of $x$.
You solved correctly but gave the measure of angle $B$, $5(20) + 6 = 106$, instead of $x$.
You used $360^\circ$, the angle sum around a point, instead of $180^\circ$: $8x + 20 = 360$ gives $x = 42.5$.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A paleobotanist traces a triangle $PQR$ between three vein junctions on a fossil fern frond, where $PQ = 12$ millimeters, $PR = 18$ millimeters, and $QR = 15$ millimeters. On a second, smaller frond she traces triangle $STU$, where angle $S$ has the same measure as angle $P$ and $ST = 8$ millimeters.
items.stem: What length of side $SU$, in millimeters, would be sufficient to prove that triangle $PQR$ is similar to triangle $STU$, with $P$, $Q$, and $R$ corresponding to $S$, $T$, and $U$, respectively?
items.explanation: Start with what you already have: one pair of equal angles ($\angle P = \angle S$) and one side next to that angle in each triangle ($PQ$ and $ST$). To finish SAS similarity, the sides that enclose the equal angle must be in proportion. Those sides are $PQ$ and $PR$ in the first triangle and $ST$ and $SU$ in the second. Under the stated correspondence, $\frac{SU}{PR} = \frac{ST}{PQ}$, so $\frac{SU}{18} = \frac{8}{12}$ and $SU = 12$. Side $QR$ is not between the equal angles, so making $TU$ proportional to it would only be SSA, which proves nothing.
items.license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

common_errors.why: You scaled $QR$ by $\frac{8}{12}$ and got $10$, the length $TU$ would need. That side is not one of the two sides enclosing the equal angle (the SSA trap), and the question asks for $SU$ anyway.
You paired $ST$ with $PR$ instead of $PQ$, giving $SU = \frac{8 \cdot 12}{18} = \frac{16}{3}$. That ignores the stated correspondence $Q \leftrightarrow T$.
This is the decimal form of $\frac{16}{3}$, from pairing $ST$ with $PR$ against the stated correspondence.
You inverted the scale factor and computed $18 \cdot \frac{12}{8} = 27$, making the second triangle larger even though $ST < PQ$.
You treated similarity as additive: $ST$ is $4$ less than $PQ$, so you subtracted $4$ from $18$. Similar triangles scale by multiplication, not subtraction.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: An immunologist sketches the binding region of an antibody fragment as right triangle $ABC$, with the right angle at $C$, leg $AC = 10$ micrometers, and leg $BC = 24$ micrometers. A second fragment is sketched as right triangle $DEF$, with the right angle at $F$ and leg $DF = 10$ micrometers.
items.stem: What length of $DE$, in micrometers, would be sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$, with $A$, $B$, and $C$ corresponding to $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively?
items.explanation: You already have a right angle in each triangle and one matching leg ($AC = DF = 10$). Under the correspondence, $DE$ matches $AB$, which is the hypotenuse because it lies opposite the right angle. The hypotenuse-leg (HL) criterion finishes the proof if the hypotenuses are equal, so you need $AB$. By the Pythagorean theorem, $AB = \sqrt{10^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{676} = 26$. So $DE = 26$ is sufficient.

You added the legs, $10 + 24 = 34$, instead of using $\sqrt{10^2 + 24^2}$.
You stopped at $10^2 + 24^2 = 676$ and did not take the square root.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: An urban planner is checking whether two straight streets, Elm Street and Birch Street, are parallel. Both are crossed by Harbor Avenue. Where Harbor Avenue meets Elm Street, angle 1 measures $112^\circ$. Where Harbor Avenue meets Birch Street, angle 3 is the angle in the position that corresponds to angle 1, and angle 2 forms a linear pair with angle 3. The measure of angle 2 is $(2y + 8)^\circ$.
items.stem: What value of $y$ would be sufficient to prove that Elm Street and Birch Street are parallel?
items.explanation: The streets are parallel when corresponding angles are equal, so you need angle 3 to equal $112^\circ$. Angle 2 forms a linear pair with angle 3, so angle 2 must be $180 - 112 = 68^\circ$. Set $2y + 8 = 68$, so $2y = 60$ and $y = 30$. A linear pair adds to $180^\circ$ whether or not the streets are parallel, so it only works here as a route to angle 3. The parallel test is the corresponding-angle equality.

You found that angle 2 must be $68^\circ$ but solved $2y = 68$, dropping the $+8$.
You gave the required measure of angle 2 instead of the value of $y$.
You set $2y + 8 = 180$, treating angle 2 as a straight angle instead of one half of a linear pair.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: On a test farm, two irrigation channels run along lines $\ell$ and $m$, and a straight access road along line $t$ crosses both. Angles 1 and 2 lie between $\ell$ and $m$ on the same side of $t$. Angle 1 measures $112^\circ$ and angle 2 measures $(4x + 8)^\circ$.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A printmaker enlarges a triangular woodblock. In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 4$ centimeters, $AC = 7$ centimeters, $BC = 9$ centimeters, and $\angle A = 50^\circ$. In triangle $DEF$, $\angle D = 50^\circ$ and $DE = 10$ centimeters.
items.stem: What length of $DF$, in centimeters, would make these facts sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$, with $A$, $B$, and $C$ corresponding to $D$, $E$, and $F$?
items.explanation: You already have one pair of equal angles, $\angle A = \angle D$. For SAS similarity, the two sides that form those angles must be in proportion. Angle $A$ sits between $AB$ and $AC$, and angle $D$ sits between $DE$ and $DF$. The scale factor is $\frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{10}{4} = 2.5$, so $DF = 2.5 \times 7 = 17.5$. items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A marine biologist cuts two triangular net panels. In triangle $PQR$, $\angle P = 48^\circ$ and $\angle Q = 63^\circ$. In triangle $STU$, $\angle T = 63^\circ$ and $\angle S = (3x - 6)^\circ$. Also, $PQ = ST$.
items.stem: For what value of $x$ would these facts be enough to prove that triangle $PQR$ is congruent to triangle $STU$ by ASA?
items.explanation: ASA needs two angles and the side between them. Side $PQ$ lies between angles $P$ and $Q$, and side $ST$ lies between angles $S$ and $T$. You already have $PQ = ST$ and $\angle Q = \angle T$. The remaining condition is $\angle S = \angle P$, so $3x - 6 = 48$. Then $3x = 54$ and $x = 18$.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: In a wetland survey, two fence lines are crossed by a straight transect. Angles $a$ and $b$ are alternate interior angles formed by the transect and the two fence lines. Angle $a$ measures $(5x - 12)^\circ$ and angle $b$ measures $(3x + 20)^\circ$.
items.stem: For what value of $x$ would these facts be enough to prove that the two fence lines are parallel?

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A sports scientist models two ramp profiles as right triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, with right angles at $C$ and $F$. $AB = DE = 17$ feet, $BC = 8$ feet, and $AC = 15$ feet. In triangle $DEF$, $EF = (2k - 4)$ feet.

items.stimulus:

items.explanation: You already have one pair of equal angles, $\angle A = \angle D$. items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus:
A nutrition scientist designs two triangular food-label icons, triangle $PQR$ and triangle $STU$. In these triangles, $PQ = ST$ and $QR = TU$.

1. $\angle Q = \angle T$
2. $\angle P = \angle S$
3. $PR = SU$

items.stem: How many of the numbered statements, each on its own, are sufficient to prove that triangle $PQR$ is congruent to triangle $STU$?
items.explanation: You already have two pairs of equal sides. To finish, you need either the included angle (SAS) or the third side (SSS). Statement 5: if two pairs of angles are equal, the third pair must be equal too, because each triangle's angles add to $180^\circ$. So $\angle Q = \angle T$, SAS applies, and it is sufficient. items.stimulus: An ecologist lays out two straight survey trails, $\ell$ and $m$, across a meadow, and a straight fence line $t$ crosses both of them. items.stimulus: A marine biologist marks two triangular survey plots on a coral reef. In triangle $JKL$, $JK = 6$ meters and $KL = 9$ meters. In triangle $RST$, $RS = 4$ meters and $ST = 6$ meters.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: An archaeologist records two triangular sections of a mosaic floor as triangles $PQR$ and $XYZ$. Angle $Q$ and angle $Y$ are right angles, and $PQ = XY$.

items.stimulus: A printmaker carves two straight grooves, lines $\ell$ and $m$, into a linoleum block, then makes a straight diagonal cut, line $t$, that crosses both grooves. Angle 1 is formed where $t$ meets $\ell$, and angle 2 is formed where $t$ meets $m$. Angles 1 and 2 are same-side interior angles. The measure of angle 1 is $64^\circ$.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$?

D.why: You treated same-side interior angles as if they had to be equal. They need to add up to $180^\circ$. If angle 2 is $64^\circ$, the sum is $128^\circ$, so the lines are not parallel.

items.stimulus: An immunologist sketches two triangular regions of a cell-staining slide as triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$. In these triangles, $m\angle A = m\angle D = 40^\circ$ and $m\angle B = m\angle E = 75^\circ$.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$?

Side $BC$ is opposite $\angle A$, and side $EF$ is opposite $\angle D$, so they are corresponding sides. Adding $BC = EF$ gives Angle-Angle-Side, which proves the triangles are congruent.

D.why: The triangles are already similar by AA, so corresponding sides are automatically in proportion. This ratio is true for any scale factor, so it can't show that the triangles are the same size.

items.stimulus: A printmaker carves two straight grooves, $\ell$ and $m$, into a linoleum block, then carves a third straight groove, $t$, that crosses both. Where $t$ crosses $\ell$, the angle above $\ell$ and to the right of $t$ measures $64^\circ$.
items.stem: Which of the following additional pieces of information is sufficient to prove that groove $\ell$ is parallel to groove $m$?
choices: Where $t$ crosses $m$, the angle above $m$ and to the right of $t$ measures $64^\circ$.
Where $t$ crosses $\ell$, the angle below $\ell$ and to the left of $t$ measures $64^\circ$.
Where $t$ crosses $\ell$, the angle above $\ell$ and to the left of $t$ measures $116^\circ$.
Where $t$ crosses $m$, the angle above $m$ and to the left of $t$ measures $64^\circ$.
items.explanation: The angle above the line and to the right of $t$ sits in the same position at both crossings, so the two angles are corresponding angles. If corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel. Both measure $64^\circ$, so $\ell \parallel m$.

B.why: This angle is vertical to the given $64^\circ$ angle, and vertical angles are equal wherever two lines cross. It tells you nothing about $m$, so it can't prove anything about parallel lines.

C.why: This angle forms a linear pair with the given angle, so it must be $180^\circ - 64^\circ = 116^\circ$ no matter where $m$ is. A fact that is always true proves nothing.

D.why: You matched the right number to the wrong position. The angle in that position at $\ell$ is $116^\circ$, so for parallel lines this angle would also need to be $116^\circ$. A $64^\circ$ angle there actually shows the lines are not parallel.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A musicologist compares the triangular frames of two harps. In the larger frame, triangle $PQR$, $PQ = 6$ feet and $PR = 9$ feet. In the smaller frame, triangle $STU$, $\angle S \cong \angle P$.
items.stem: Which of the following additional pieces of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $PQR$ is similar to triangle $STU$?
items.explanation: $\angle P$ is the angle included between $PQ$ and $PR$, and $\angle S$ is included between $ST$ and $SU$. Since $\frac{6}{4} = \frac{9}{6} = 1.5$, the sides on either side of the equal angles are proportional, so the triangles are similar by SAS similarity.

B.why: The ratio $\frac{9}{6}$ matches, but $TU$ is opposite $\angle S$ and is not one of the sides that form it. Proportional sides with an angle that isn't between them (SSA) don't prove similarity.

C.why: You added $2$ to each length instead of multiplying them by the same factor. $\frac{8}{6}$ and $\frac{11}{9}$ are not equal, so the sides are not proportional.

D.why: This gives a second angle in triangle $PQR$, but nothing about triangle $STU$. For AA, the second pair of angles has to be equal across both triangles.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A materials scientist cuts two triangular test brackets from an alloy sheet. In triangle $ABC$, $\angle C$ is a right angle, and in triangle $DEF$, $\angle F$ is a right angle.
items.stem: Which of the following additional pieces of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$?
items.explanation: Both triangles are right triangles. $AB$ and $DE$ are the hypotenuses, and $AC$ and $DF$ are corresponding legs. With an equal hypotenuse and an equal leg, the triangles are congruent by HL.

B.why: Matching all the angles makes the triangles similar, but they can still be different sizes. Angles alone (AAA) never prove congruence without at least one pair of equal sides.

C.why: $\angle A$ corresponds to $\angle D$, not $\angle E$. An angle at a non-corresponding vertex doesn't complete ASA or AAS, so these two facts prove nothing together.

D.why: The right angles were already given, so this adds only the equal hypotenuses. A right angle and a hypotenuse still need an equal leg or another equal angle to prove congruence.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A nutrition science poster plots two guideline rows, line $\ell$ and line $m$, with $\ell$ above $m$. A diagonal line $t$ crosses $\ell$ at point $P$ and crosses $m$ at point $Q$. At $P$, angle 1 lies above $\ell$ and to the right of $t$, and angle 2 lies below $\ell$ and to the left of $t$. At $Q$, angle 3 lies above $m$ and to the right of $t$, and angle 4 lies below $m$ and to the right of $t$.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$?
items.explanation: Angle 1 and angle 3 are both above their lines and to the right of $t$, so they are corresponding angles. If corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel, so knowing $m\angle 1 = m\angle 3$ is enough to prove $\ell \parallel m$.

A.why: Angle 1 and angle 2 are vertical angles at $P$. Vertical angles are always equal wherever two lines cross, so this fact says nothing about line $m$ and can't prove the lines are parallel.

B.why: Angle 3 and angle 4 form a linear pair on line $m$, so they always add to $180^\circ$. A fact that is true however the lines are tilted can't prove they are parallel.

C.why: Angle 2 and angle 3 are alternate interior angles, which must be equal, not supplementary, to prove parallel lines. You applied the same-side interior rule to the wrong pair of angles.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A city planner sketches two triangular plazas, $ABC$ and $DEF$. In the sketch, $AB = 30$ meters, $AC = 45$ meters, $DE = 20$ meters, and $DF = 30$ meters.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$?
items.explanation: The given sides are proportional: $\frac{AB}{DE} = \frac{30}{20} = \frac{3}{2}$ and $\frac{AC}{DF} = \frac{45}{30} = \frac{3}{2}$. Angle $A$ is between $AB$ and $AC$, and angle $D$ is between $DE$ and $DF$. Two pairs of proportional sides with equal included angles prove similarity by SAS similarity.

A.why: Angle $B$ is not between sides $AB$ and $AC$, so this setup is side-side-angle. SSA does not prove similarity, because more than one triangle can fit those measurements.

C.why: Angle $F$ does not correspond to angle $A$. The angle between $DE$ and $DF$ is angle $D$, so you matched angle $A$ with the wrong angle in triangle $DEF$.

D.why: Angle $C$ is opposite $AB$ rather than between the two given sides. This is another side-side-angle setup, and that doesn't guarantee similarity.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: On a cartographer's survey map, triangles $PQR$ and $STU$ mark two land parcels. Angle $Q$ and angle $T$ are right angles, and $m\angle P = m\angle S$.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $PQR$ is congruent to triangle $STU$?
items.explanation: You already have two pairs of equal angles: the right angles at $Q$ and $T$, and angles $P$ and $S$. So the third angles, $R$ and $U$, are also equal by the $180^\circ$ sum. Side $QR$ lies between angles $Q$ and $R$, and side $TU$ lies between angles $T$ and $U$. Knowing $QR = TU$ completes ASA, so the triangles are congruent.

A.why: Equal third angles follow from what you were given, so this adds nothing new. Angles alone (AAA) prove only that the triangles have the same shape, not the same size.

B.why: $PR$ is the hypotenuse of triangle $PQR$, but $TU$ is a leg of triangle $STU$. These sides don't correspond, so setting them equal doesn't prove congruence.

D.why: Proportional legs prove only that the triangles are similar, which the angles already showed. It doesn't show the two triangles are the same size, so concluding congruence claims too much.

items.stimulus: On an archaeologist's site map, two straight trench walls lie along lines $\ell$ and $m$, and a survey line $t$ crosses both. Line $t$ intersects line $\ell$ at point $P$ and line $m$ at point $Q$. Points $A$ and $B$ lie on line $\ell$ on opposite sides of $P$. Points $C$ and $D$ lie on line $m$ on opposite sides of $Q$, with $A$ and $C$ on the same side of line $t$. Point $E$ lies on line $t$ so that $P$ is between $E$ and $Q$. The measure of angle $APQ$ is $64^\circ$.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$?
choices: Angle $EPB$ and angle $APQ$ have the same measure.
items.explanation: Angles $APQ$ and $CQP$ both lie between lines $\ell$ and $m$ and on the same side of $t$, so they are same-side interior angles. If angle $CQP$ is $52^\circ$ greater than $64^\circ$, it measures $116^\circ$. Then $64^\circ + 116^\circ = 180^\circ$. Same-side interior angles that add to $180^\circ$ prove that $\ell \parallel m$.

A.why: Angles $BPQ$ and $APQ$ form a linear pair on line $\ell$, so $BPQ$ is always $180^\circ - 64^\circ = 116^\circ$, which is $52^\circ$ more than $APQ$. That is true however line $m$ is tilted, so it can't prove anything about line $m$. You picked a fact that holds whenever the lines cross.

C.why: Angle $DQP$ is on the other side of $t$ from angle $APQ$, so the two are alternate interior angles. Parallel lines would make them equal, both $64^\circ$. If $DQP$ is $116^\circ$, the lines are not parallel. You used the supplementary rule on an alternate interior pair, which needs the equal rule.

D.why: Angles $EPB$ and $APQ$ are vertical angles at $P$, so they are always equal. That fact never involves line $m$, so it can't show that $m$ is parallel to $\ell$. You picked a fact that holds whenever two lines cross.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: An agricultural scientist marks out two triangular test plots, $JKL$ and $RST$, where $J$, $K$, and $L$ correspond to $R$, $S$, and $T$, respectively. In plot $JKL$, $JK = 30$ meters and $KL = 45$ meters. In plot $RST$, $RS = 20$ meters and $ST = 30$ meters.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $JKL$ is similar to triangle $RST$?
choices: Angle $J$ and angle $R$ have the same measure.
Angle $K$ and angle $S$ have the same measure.
Side $JL$ is $15$ meters longer than side $RT$.
Side $JL$ is $1.5$ times as long as side $KL$.
items.explanation: The ratios $\frac{30}{20}$ and $\frac{45}{30}$ both equal $1.5$, so two pairs of sides are already in proportion. For SAS similarity, you also need the angle between those sides to be equal in both triangles. That angle is $K$ in triangle $JKL$ (between $JK$ and $KL$) and $S$ in triangle $RST$ (between $RS$ and $ST$). If angle $K$ equals angle $S$, the triangles are similar.

A.why: Angle $J$ is not between sides $JK$ and $KL$, so this gives you side-side-angle (SSA), which is not a similarity criterion. SAS similarity needs the equal angle to be the one between the proportional sides.

C.why: Similarity depends on ratios, not differences. $JK$ and $RS$ differ by $10$, while $KL$ and $ST$ differ by $15$, but what matters is that both ratios are $1.5$. Knowing $JL - RT = 15$ doesn't pin down the ratio $\frac{JL}{RT}$, so it doesn't complete SSS similarity. You compared the gap instead of the ratio.

D.why: This compares two sides of the same triangle. It says nothing about side $RT$, so you still can't check the third ratio between the triangles. You need a ratio between corresponding sides of the two triangles.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A folklore archive's logo is made of two triangles, $ABC$ and $DEF$, that stand for paired versions of the same legend. In the triangles, $AB = DE$ and the measure of angle $A$ equals the measure of angle $D$.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$?
choices: The sum of angles $B$ and $C$ equals the sum of angles $E$ and $F$.
Angle $B$ is $30^\circ$ greater than angle $C$, and angle $E$ is $30^\circ$ greater than angle $F$.
Angle $B$ is $30^\circ$ greater than angle $C$, and angle $E$ is $30^\circ$ greater than angle $D$.
Side $BC$ is $9$ centimeters long, and side $EF$ is $9$ centimeters long.
items.explanation: Angle $A$ equals angle $D$, so the remaining angles in each triangle add to the same total: $B + C = E + F$. If the differences also match, with $B - C = 30^\circ$ and $E - F = 30^\circ$, then adding the sum and the difference gives $2B = 2E$, so $B = E$. Now you have angle $A$, side $AB$, and angle $B$ equal to angle $D$, side $DE$, and angle $E$. That is ASA, so the triangles are congruent.

A.why: This follows automatically from the 180° angle sum once angle $A$ equals angle $D$, so it adds nothing new. It is the first step of the correct solution. To show $B = E$, you also need the difference between the two remaining angles.

C.why: The second condition compares $E$ with $D$ rather than with $F$, so the two triangles aren't described in matching terms. It gives $B = 105^\circ - \frac{A}{2}$ and $E = A + 30^\circ$, which are generally not equal. No congruence criterion follows.

D.why: Side $BC$ is opposite the given angle $A$. That makes this side-side-angle (SSA), where the equal angle is not between the two equal sides. SSA can allow two different triangles, so it does not prove congruence.

items.stimulus: An archaeologist lays out two triangular excavation plots, $ABC$ and $DEF$. The plots satisfy $AB = 1.5(DE)$ and $BC = 1.5(EF)$. In plot $ABC$, $m\angle A = 50^\circ$ and $m\angle C = 60^\circ$.
items.stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$, with $A$, $B$, and $C$ corresponding to $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively?
items.explanation: You already know two pairs of sides are in proportion, $AB:DE = BC:EF = 1.5$. To finish with SAS similarity, you need the angles between those sides to be equal, which means $\angle B$ and $\angle E$. In triangle $ABC$, $m\angle B = 180^\circ - 50^\circ - 60^\circ = 70^\circ$. If $m\angle D + m\angle F = 110^\circ$, then $m\angle E = 180^\circ - 110^\circ = 70^\circ$. That gives $\angle B \cong \angle E$ with the proportional sides on either side of it, so the triangles are similar.

That triangle is not similar to $ABC$.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: An urban planner models three city roads as triangle $ABC$. A proposed connector road runs from point $D$ on $\overline{AB}$ to point $E$ on $\overline{AC}$.
items.stem: Which of the following additional pieces of information is sufficient to prove that $\overline{DE}$ is parallel to $\overline{BC}$?
items.explanation: With these lengths, $AB = 10$ and $AC = 15$, so $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{4}{10} = \frac{2}{5}$ and $\frac{AE}{AC} = \frac{6}{15} = \frac{2}{5}$. Angle $A$ is shared, and it is the angle between those two sides, so triangle $ADE$ is similar to triangle $ABC$ by SAS similarity. That makes $\angle ADE \cong \angle ABC$, which are corresponding angles, so $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$.

A.why: Points $A$, $D$, and $B$ lie on one line, so $\angle ADE$ and $\angle BDE$ form a linear pair. Their sum is $180^\circ$ wherever $E$ is, so this fact can't prove anything about parallel lines.

B.why: You noticed that $\frac{AD}{AC} = \frac{4}{8}$ and $\frac{AE}{AB} = \frac{5}{10}$ are equal, so triangle $ADE$ is similar to triangle $ACB$. But in that pairing, $D$ corresponds to $C$, not to $B$. For $\overline{DE}$ to be parallel to $\overline{BC}$, you need $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{AE}{AC}$, and here $\frac{4}{10} \neq \frac{5}{8}$.

D.why: Angle $A$ is not the angle between $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{DE}$. This is side-side-angle, which is not a similarity criterion: a second point on $\overline{AC}$ can also be $\frac{2}{5}BC$ away from $D$ without $\overline{DE}$ being parallel to $\overline{BC}$.

items.stimulus: A public health team maps two roads leading to a clinic as lines $\ell$ and $m$. Points $A$ and $B$ lie on line $\ell$, and points $D$ and $E$ lie on line $m$. items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A seismologist locating an epicentre sketches two triangles. In triangle $JKL$, $JK = 6$, $KL = 9$, and $m\angle K = 50^\circ$. In triangle $MNP$, $MN = 8$ and $m\angle M + m\angle P = 130^\circ$.
items.stem: Which of the following additional pieces of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $JKL$ is similar to triangle $MNP$?
items.explanation: From the angle sum, $m\angle N = 180^\circ - 130^\circ = 50^\circ = m\angle K$. With $NP = 12$, you get $\frac{JK}{MN} = \frac{6}{8} = \frac{3}{4}$ and $\frac{KL}{NP} = \frac{9}{12} = \frac{3}{4}$. B.why: You saw that $6$ became $8$ by adding $2$, so you added $2$ to $9$ as well. Similarity needs a common ratio, not a common difference: $\frac{9}{11} \neq \frac{3}{4}$.

C.why: You can already work out $m\angle N = 50^\circ$ from the given angle sum, so this adds nothing. Without the length $NP$, you have only one pair of angles and one pair of sides, which is not enough.

items.stimulus:

D.why: Statement II describes vertical angles. They are equal whenever two lines cross, whether or not $j$ and $k$ are parallel, so statement II proves nothing.

items.subtype_name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
items.stimulus: A civil engineer models a bridge truss as triangle $ABC$. Point $D$ lies on $\overline{AC}$ between $A$ and $C$, and $\overline{BD} \perp \overline{AC}$. In the model, $AB = 13$ and $AD = 5$.
items.stem: Which of the following additional pieces of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABD$ is congruent to triangle $CBD$?
items.explanation: If $AC = 10$, then $CD = 10 - 5 = 5 = AD$. Both triangles have a right angle at $D$ and share the side $\overline{BD}$. Leg $\overline{AD}$ equals leg $\overline{CD}$ and the right angles are between the matching legs, so the triangles are congruent by SAS.

A.why: $BD = 12$ already follows from the Pythagorean theorem in triangle $ABD$, since $13^2 - 5^2 = 144$. It is a step you can work out, and it tells you nothing new about triangle $CBD$.

D.why: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is always longer than either leg, so $BC > BD$ is true for any position of $C$. It puts no limit on the length of $\overline{BC}$.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: For decades, hydrologists have measured river discharge with gauging stations: permanent structures anchored to a riverbank that record water height around the clock. Building one can cost tens of thousands of dollars, so many small mountain streams have never been measured at all. Researchers in Nepal recently tested a cheaper approach. Volunteers filmed a stretch of stream with a phone, and software estimated flow speed from the movement of floating leaves and twigs. The estimates closely matched readings from a nearby station.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about gauging stations?
choices: They tend to give less accurate readings than phone-based estimates do.
Their high cost helps explain why many small streams have gone unmeasured.
They record water height during the day but not during the night.
They will soon be removed from rivers and replaced by volunteer videos.
items.explanation: The text says a station can cost tens of thousands of dollars and then uses 'so' to link that cost to the fact that many small streams have never been measured. Saying the cost helps explain the gap is exactly one step beyond what the text states.

A.why: You assumed the new method beat the old one. The text says the phone estimates closely matched the station's readings, so it never says the stations are less accurate.

C.why: You misread a detail. The text says stations record water height 'around the clock,' which includes the night.

D.why: You fell for the absolute claim. The text shows a cheaper method that works for unmeasured streams. It never says stations will be removed anywhere, let alone everywhere.

items.stimulus: Early collectors of folk songs usually wrote melodies down by ear, turning what a singer performed into standard musical notation. items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the handwritten transcriptions made by early folk-song collectors?

They are of no value to musicologists who study folk songs today.
They may not show exactly how the singers actually performed the songs.
They kept irregular rhythms but altered pitches that fell between piano keys.

items.stimulus: Paleobotanists often estimate the temperature of an ancient climate by finding the proportion of fossil leaves with smooth rather than toothed edges. The method rests on a pattern seen in living plants: smooth-edged leaves are more common in warm regions, and toothed leaves are more common in cool ones. However, a recent survey of modern forests found that trees growing along streams and lakeshores tend to have toothed leaves even where temperatures are warm.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the leaf-edge method of estimating ancient temperatures?
choices: It could give misleading results for fossils of plants that grew near water.
It cannot provide a useful estimate of temperature for any ancient climate.
It assumes that toothed leaves are more common in warm regions than cool ones.
It works most reliably for fossils found along ancient streams and lakeshores.
items.explanation: After 'However,' the text says streamside trees have toothed leaves even in warm places. Under this method, toothed leaves suggest a cool climate, so fossils from plants that grew near water could make a warm climate look cooler than it was.

B.why: You fell for the absolute claim. The survey points to a problem with one kind of site, not a failure of the method everywhere.

C.why: You reversed the pattern. The method assumes smooth-edged leaves are more common in warm regions and toothed leaves in cool ones.

D.why: You reversed the implication. Streamside sites are exactly where the method is likely to be least reliable.

items.stimulus: Forecasters have long measured conditions high in the atmosphere with weather balloons, which are launched twice a day. Each balloon records a single pass upward, so a storm that develops in the hours between launches may go unrecorded until the next one. Atmospheric scientist Lena Okafor is testing ground-based sensors that scan the air overhead every ten minutes.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about weather balloons?
choices: They provide no reliable measurements of conditions high in the atmosphere.
They can miss atmospheric changes that occur in the hours between launches.
They record conditions more often than Okafor's ground-based sensors do.
They cost more to operate than any network of ground-based sensors.
items.explanation: The text says each balloon records a single pass and that a storm forming between launches "may go unrecorded." Taking one step from that, you get that balloons can miss changes that happen between launches. That is the drawback Okafor's more frequent sensors are meant to fix.

A.why: You turned a limitation into a total failure. The text says balloons can miss changes between launches, not that their measurements can't be trusted at all. Forecasters have relied on them for a long time.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. Balloons go up twice a day and the sensors scan every ten minutes, so the sensors measure far more often.

D.why: The text never mentions cost. You brought in a common reason for replacing an old method that this passage doesn't give.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: In woodcut printing, an artist carves away every part of a wooden block that should remain blank, leaving raised areas to carry the ink. Once wood has been cut away, it cannot be put back. Printmaker Tomas Reyes therefore draws each design in pencil directly on the block and studies it for several days before he makes a single cut.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about Reyes's habit of studying his sketches for days?
choices: It lets him repair mistaken cuts before the block is ever inked.
It reveals that he values pencil drawing more than printmaking.
It helps him avoid making cuts that he could not later undo.
It ensures that none of his finished blocks ever contains an error.
items.explanation: The word "therefore" ties Reyes's careful study to the fact before it: wood that has been cut away cannot be put back. The one-step implication is that studying the sketch helps him avoid cuts he couldn't reverse.

A.why: The text says removed wood cannot be put back, so mistaken cuts can't be repaired. The careful study only matters because repair is impossible.

B.why: The pencil sketch is a step in making the print, not a rival to it. Nothing in the text compares how much Reyes values the two.

D.why: You took "helps avoid" and made it "guarantees." The text shows a careful habit, not a promise that he never makes a mistake.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: City officials in Brennick credited a new bus lane on Harlow Avenue with shortening downtown commutes. However, a review by urban planner Aisha Morrow found that travel times had fallen by a similar amount on nearby streets without bus lanes. The drop came during the same months in which a large employer moved its offices out of downtown.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the bus lane on Harlow Avenue?
choices: It may not have been the main reason that commutes became shorter.
It had no effect at all on travel times along Harlow Avenue.
It made commutes longer on the streets near Harlow Avenue.
It should be removed so that the employer will return downtown.
items.explanation: "However" introduces the real finding. Commutes got shorter on streets without bus lanes too, and a large employer left during the same months. So something besides the lane may explain the change, and the lane may not deserve the credit officials gave it.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap: you turned "may not be the main reason" into "no effect at all." Morrow's review raises doubt about the officials' claim but doesn't prove the lane did nothing.

C.why: The text says travel times fell on the nearby streets. They did not get longer.

D.why: The text recommends nothing, and it never connects the employer's move to the bus lane. You went several steps past what the passage implies.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: Nutrition researchers often ask study volunteers to list everything they ate the previous day. In a study led by Mei Tanaka, volunteers also photographed each meal and snack as they ate it. When the photographs were compared with the same volunteers' written lists, the photographs showed about 20 percent more snacks than the volunteers had recalled.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about asking people to recall what they ate?
choices: It tends to cause people to overstate how many snacks they ate.
It produces records too inaccurate to be of any scientific use.
It is less common among researchers than photographing meals.
It may cause people to leave out some of the snacks they ate.
items.explanation: The photographs and the written lists covered the same eating, and the photographs showed more snacks. One step beyond that, people working from memory may leave out some of what they ate.

A.why: You got the direction backward. The lists showed fewer snacks than the photographs, so people understated their snacks.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap: a gap in one category of food doesn't make recall records useless. The text shows a limitation, not a total failure.

C.why: The text says researchers "often" use recall. Photographing meals appears only as an extra step in one study.

items.stimulus: Hydrologists have traditionally measured river flow by wading into the water with a current meter and taking readings at points across the channel. During floods, when flow data are most needed, that work becomes too dangerous to attempt. At a station on the Velka River, engineer Rafael Duarte has mounted a radar unit on a bridge to measure the water's surface speed from above.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the radar unit on the Velka River?
choices: It can collect readings during floods, when wading would be unsafe.
It shows that current meters give inaccurate readings in any river.
It requires engineers to stand in the channel to take its readings.
It was installed mainly to protect the bridge from flood damage.
items.explanation: The text gives one drawback of the old method: wading is too dangerous during floods. The radar works from a bridge, above the water, so the one-step implication is that it can take readings when wading isn't safe.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. The old method has a safety limit during floods, but the text never says current meters are inaccurate, let alone in every river.

C.why: The radar is mounted on a bridge and measures from above. That is the point of it, since standing in the channel is what becomes dangerous.

D.why: The bridge is only where the radar is mounted. The text says the radar measures water speed and gives no sign that it protects the bridge.

items.stimulus: For much of the twentieth century, linguists documented endangered languages mainly in handwritten notes. Notes record words well, but they often fail to capture tone, the rise and fall of pitch that changes a word's meaning in many languages. Today, most field linguists also make audio recordings, which preserve tone along with the words themselves.
items.stem: Based on the text, what does it suggest about handwritten notes when they are used alone?
choices: They cannot be used to record a language in any useful way.
They may leave out details needed to tell some words apart.
They preserve tone more reliably than audio recordings do.
They are no longer made by most linguists working in the field.
items.explanation: The text names one drawback of notes: they often miss tone, and tone changes what a word means. Go one step further and you get B: notes alone may lose the detail that tells one word from another. That is the whole move behind the real 'most strongly suggests' questions. Find the stated drawback of the old method, then say what it implies, and stop there.

A.why: You turned a limitation into a total failure. The text says notes 'record words well' and miss one thing, tone. It never says they are useless. This is the trap this question type is built around: the passage implies a weakness, and the wrong choice claims something absolute.

C.why: You reversed the contrast. The text says recordings preserve tone and notes often fail to. If you go back to the line, it says the opposite of this choice.

D.why: You read 'also make audio recordings' as 'make recordings instead'. 'Also' means linguists add recordings alongside their notes, so the text implies they still take notes.

items.stimulus: Self-healing concrete contains bacteria that produce limestone when water seeps into a crack, gradually sealing it. In laboratory trials, small cracks closed within a few weeks. However, the bacteria have been tested mostly at mild temperatures, and engineers do not yet know whether they survive repeated freezing. The material's promise in harsher climates therefore remains an open question.
items.stem: Based on the text, what does it suggest about self-healing concrete in places with cold winters?
choices: It has been shown to seal cracks through repeated freezing.
It will fail in any region where the temperature drops.
Its performance there has not yet been clearly established.
Its bacteria produce limestone when water enters a crack.
items.explanation: After 'However', the text says the bacteria were tested mostly at mild temperatures and nobody yet knows whether they survive freezing. The one-step inference is C: in cold places, we do not yet know how well it works. Hedges like 'do not yet know' and 'open question' set how sure your answer can be. On real inference questions, the correct choice matches that level of certainty.

A.why: You took the lab success and applied it to the case the text says was not tested. The passage says engineers do not know whether the bacteria survive freezing, so nothing has been shown.

B.why: You turned 'we don't know yet' into 'it fails'. This is this question type's trap: an untested limitation becomes an absolute claim. The text leaves the question open and does not predict failure.

D.why: The sentence is true, but it repeats how the material works and says nothing about cold winters. The question asks what the text implies about cold climates, so this choice does not do the job.

items.stimulus: Nutrition labels can make a food look lighter than the way people actually eat it. For example, one cereal box lists its sugar content for a 30-gram serving. Yet when researchers asked adults to pour a normal breakfast, most filled their bowls with about 60 grams, twice the listed serving.
items.stem: Based on the example in the text, what does it suggest about the sugar figure printed on the cereal box?
choices: It is likely to understate the sugar many adults actually eat.
It matches the amount most adults pour into a breakfast bowl.
It is reported in grams rather than in cups or spoonfuls.
It is deliberately false and should be removed from the box.
items.explanation: The label is based on 30 grams, and most adults poured 60. If people eat twice the serving, they take in more sugar than the label shows, so the figure understates their intake. The passage opens with a general claim and then gives one example to support it. Spotting that pattern helps on the real questions, because the inference usually connects the example back to the opening claim.

C.why: You picked up an incidental detail, the unit. Grams appear in the passage, but the example is there to show a gap between the label and real portions, not to say anything about units.

D.why: You went two steps instead of one. The text says the figure is accurate for a smaller serving than people eat. It never says the label is false, intentional, or should be removed.

items.stimulus: Engineers once judged the condition of suspension-bridge cables mainly by eye, checking the surface for rust and broken wires. But corrosion often begins deep inside a cable, beneath layers of healthy-looking outer wire. Many agencies now attach acoustic sensors that detect the sharp sound of a single wire snapping within the bundle.
items.stem: Based on the text, what does it suggest about inspecting bridge cables by eye?
choices: It records the sound of wires snapping deep inside the bundle.
It never detects any damage at all on a suspension-bridge cable.
It finds hidden corrosion earlier than acoustic sensors can.
It can miss damage that has not yet reached the cable's surface.
items.explanation: 'But' brings in the real point: corrosion often starts inside the cable, under outer wire that looks healthy. An inspection that only looks at the surface can therefore miss that damage. That is D, exactly one step past the text. On harder inference questions, find the pivot word first. What comes after it is what the author wants you to conclude.

B.why: You turned a blind spot into total failure. This is the trap this question type is built around. The text says inspectors checked for rust and broken wires on the surface, so looking does catch some damage. It just misses damage inside the cable.

C.why: You reversed the contrast. The text says corrosion hides under healthy-looking wire, which is why agencies added sensors. That implies looking finds hidden damage later, not earlier.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: City planners have traditionally estimated pedestrian volume with manual counts: staff stationed at an intersection tally passersby for a few hours on a chosen weekday. In Valmont, planner Odile Marchetti compared such counts with a year of readings from sidewalk sensors installed along the Calder Street corridor. The two methods agreed closely on weekday mornings. However, the sensors recorded late-evening and weekend foot traffic on several blocks that was nearly double the weekday peaks the manual counts had captured, during hours that no scheduled count had ever covered.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about manual pedestrian counts?
choices: They fail to measure pedestrian volume accurately at any time of day, even during the hours they cover.
They can miss periods of heavy use on some blocks, since they cover only a few scheduled hours.
They can miss periods of heavy use on some blocks, since staff tend to miscount during busy hours.
They tend to overstate weekend foot traffic on blocks where weekday traffic is relatively light.
items.explanation: The pivot at 'However' tells you what the comparison found: the counts matched the sensors when they were taken, but the heaviest traffic came at evenings and weekends, 'hours that no scheduled count had ever covered.' Go one step past that and you get the implication: because manual counts sample only limited windows, they can leave out the busiest periods.

A.why: You turned a limitation into a total failure. The text says the two methods 'agreed closely on weekday mornings,' so the counts were accurate for the hours they covered. Their weakness is what they leave out.

C.why: You read the first half, which is correct, and stopped. The reason it gives is wrong: the counts matched the sensors during the hours they were taken, so miscounting isn't the issue. The issue is the hours they never covered.

D.why: This reverses the finding. No manual count covered weekends at all, and the sensors showed weekend traffic was higher than the counts suggested, so nothing was overstated.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: Purple sea urchins sometimes graze kelp forests down to bare rock, and the usual explanation credits the disappearance of predators such as sea otters. Biologist Tomas Reyna's team compared reefs off two islands where otters had been absent for decades. On one, urchins had stripped the kelp entirely; on the other, kelp persisted, and the team found that strong winter swells there regularly knocked urchins loose from the rock. Where swells were weak, barrens spread regardless of whether predatory fish were abundant.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the predator-loss explanation for urchin barrens?
choices: It is mistaken, because predators have no measurable effect on the size of urchin populations.
It is incomplete, because predatory fish appear to keep urchins in check where otters are absent.
It best accounts for kelp persisting on reefs where strong winter swells regularly occur.
It is incomplete, because physical conditions also appear to influence whether barrens form.
items.explanation: Otters were missing from both islands, yet only one island had a barren, and the difference was the swells. So predator loss can't be the whole story. The one-step inference is that the explanation is incomplete because physical conditions matter too. Nothing in the text says predators don't matter at all.

A.why: You went two steps instead of one. The study shows another factor is involved, not that predators have no effect. Neither reef had otters, so the study couldn't test what otters do.

B.why: The first half is right and the second half is wrong. The last sentence says barrens spread 'regardless of whether predatory fish were abundant,' so the fish didn't keep urchins in check.

C.why: This credits the predator explanation with a result that actually came from the swells. Otters were absent from that reef too. The kelp survived because waves knocked the urchins loose.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: Residents of the Breton village of Kerlouan have long described the dance tune "An Hini Kozh" as older than the parish church, and collectors who visited in the early 1900s dutifully recorded it as such. Musicologist Anaïs Le Goff notes, however, that the melody depends on a raised fourth scale degree common in printed quadrilles of the 1840s and absent from every earlier manuscript from the region. The villagers' account, she argues, may say more about the tune's place in local identity than about its actual age.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the early twentieth-century collectors who visited Kerlouan?
choices: They wrote down the villagers' claim about the tune's age without testing it against other evidence.
They deliberately exaggerated the tune's age in order to make their collections seem more valuable.
They accepted the villagers' account after comparing the tune with earlier regional manuscripts.
They were chiefly interested in how the tune expressed the village's sense of local identity.
items.explanation: Look at how the collectors are framed: they 'dutifully recorded' what residents said, and Le Goff then finds evidence the collectors apparently never checked. The ironic 'dutifully' implies they passed on local tradition without testing it. That is as far as the text goes.

B.why: You read uncritical recording as deliberate deception. The text suggests the collectors were too trusting, but it says nothing about motive or intent to mislead.

C.why: Le Goff's evidence comes from the earlier manuscripts, and the tune's feature is missing from all of them. If the collectors had made that comparison, they couldn't have accepted the villagers' claim.

D.why: This gives Le Goff's conclusion to the wrong people. The point about local identity is her modern reading of the claim. The collectors simply recorded the tune as old.

items.stimulus: Large studies of diet usually rely on food-frequency questionnaires, in which participants estimate how often they ate various foods over the past year. In a trial led by nutrition scientist Priya Haldar, 400 adults completed such questionnaires and also provided urine samples analyzed for nitrogen, a reliable marker of protein intake. For most participants, questionnaire estimates tracked the biomarker reasonably well. Adults with higher body weights, however, reported on average about 20 percent less protein than their samples indicated.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about food-frequency questionnaires?
choices: They cannot provide useful information about how much protein study participants eat.
They may skew results for some groups, because people forget foods eaten long ago.
They may underestimate protein intake for certain groups of participants in a consistent way.
They tend to overestimate protein intake among participants with higher body weights.
items.explanation: The questionnaires mostly worked, but one identifiable group under-reported protein by a similar margin on average. One step beyond that: the error isn't random. It runs in one direction for certain groups, so questionnaires may underestimate their intake consistently.

A.why: You took a limitation and made it absolute. For most participants the estimates 'tracked the biomarker reasonably well,' so the questionnaires do provide useful information.

B.why: The first half fits the text, but the cause doesn't come from it. The text never explains why the gap appears, and forgetting would affect everyone, not one weight group in particular.

D.why: This flips the direction. Those participants reported less protein than their samples showed, which is an underestimate.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: Reconstructions of ancient forests have relied heavily on fossil pollen, which accumulates in lake sediments in enormous quantities. Yet some trees, including larches, shed pollen grains that are fragile and seldom preserved. When paleobotanist Henrik Solvang examined needles and cones recovered from Norwegian lake cores, he found larch remains in layers dating to 9,000 years ago, a period for which the pollen record from the same cores shows almost no larch at all.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about forest reconstructions based on fossil pollen?
choices: They are too unreliable to show which tree species grew in ancient forests.
They may underrepresent tree species whose pollen rarely survives in sediment.
They may underrepresent larches, because pollen is scarcer in lake sediments than needles are.
They have overstated how common larches were in Norwegian forests 9,000 years ago.
items.explanation: The 'Yet' sentence names the weakness: some trees' pollen 'seldom' survives. The needles and cones then show larches were there when the pollen record says they weren't. The careful inference is that pollen records may undercount species with fragile pollen.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: Engineers often judge the health of a concrete bridge deck by inspecting its surface for cracks. In 2019, inspectors rated the deck of the Harlan River viaduct in good condition after finding only hairline surface cracking. Two years later, a ground-penetrating radar survey revealed that chloride from road salt had corroded the reinforcing steel across a third of the deck, beneath concrete that still looked sound. items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about visual surface inspections of concrete bridge decks?
choices: They can miss hidden deterioration that would have been less costly to repair if found sooner.
They are of no real value to engineers trying to assess the condition of a bridge deck.
They can miss hidden deterioration, since hairline cracks are usually too fine for inspectors to see.
They are designed mainly to detect the kinds of damage that road salt causes in concrete.
items.explanation: Each sentence adds a piece: inspectors saw a sound-looking surface, the corrosion was underneath, and the cost rose from $2 million to $9 million. Together they imply that surface inspections can miss internal damage, and that catching it late made it more expensive to fix.

B.why: You moved from 'can miss something' to 'useless.' One case of missed corrosion shows the method has a blind spot. It doesn't show the method has no value.

D.why: The text never says what surface inspections are designed for. If anything, salt damage was exactly what this inspection failed to catch.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: Nineteenth-century dealers in Japanese woodblock prints routinely advertised "first editions," assuring buyers that the brilliant blues of their impressions proved the prints came from the earliest runs, before the blocks had worn. Conservator Mei Tanabe's analysis of 120 impressions of a single Hiroshige design complicates that sales pitch. Blue intensity varied widely even among impressions with identical, crisply cut lines, and several of the most vivid examples came from late printings in which the block had visibly cracked.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the claims made by nineteenth-century print dealers?
choices: The dealers knowingly sold late impressions as early ones in order to charge higher prices.
Color was a less dependable sign, because blue pigments fade unevenly as prints age.
The most vivid impressions usually came from the earliest runs, just as the dealers maintained.
Color was a less dependable sign of an early impression than the dealers led buyers to believe.
items.explanation: The text reports the dealers' assurances without endorsing them. Calling them a 'sales pitch' signals the distance. Tanabe's data then show vivid blues in late, cracked printings. The one-step inference is that color was a weaker sign of an early impression than the dealers claimed.

A.why: You went from 'the claim was unreliable' to 'the dealers lied on purpose.' The text questions their evidence. It says nothing about what they knew or intended.

B.why: The first half is right, but fading is your own explanation. Tanabe found variation at the time of printing, including vivid late impressions, and the text never mentions pigments changing over time.

C.why: You took the dealers' claim as the author's view and missed the ironic framing. Tanabe found 'several of the most vivid examples' among late printings.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: Public health agencies typically gauge a city's flu activity by counting positive tests reported by clinics. Because many people with mild symptoms never see a doctor, epidemiologist Ruth Okafor's team began sampling wastewater in Dunmore, where material from every connected household reaches a single treatment plant. During the 2024 season, viral levels in the wastewater rose about ten days before clinic reports did. The team cautions that wastewater cannot show who is infected, but it may give officials an earlier signal that an outbreak is beginning.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about clinic-based reporting of flu cases?
choices: It fails to detect flu outbreaks and could therefore be replaced by wastewater sampling.
It registers a rise late, because clinics are slow to send their test results to agencies.
It tends to register a rise in flu activity some time after that rise begins in the community.
It identifies which individuals are infected less precisely than wastewater sampling does.
items.explanation: The wastewater rose 'about ten days before clinic reports did,' and the team calls it a possible 'earlier signal.' One step beyond that: clinic reports pick up an outbreak only after it has already started spreading. Notice the hedges, 'may' and 'cautions.' The text doesn't claim more than a lag.

A.why: This is the absolute trap. Clinic reports did detect the rise, just later. The team's caution that wastewater 'cannot show who is infected' also rules out replacing clinics.

B.why: The first half is supported, but the reason isn't. The text points to people with mild symptoms never seeing a doctor. It never says clinics are slow to send results.

D.why: This reverses the comparison. The text says wastewater 'cannot show who is infected,' so clinic testing is the more precise of the two for identifying individuals.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: For decades, forecasters have measured the lower atmosphere with radiosondes: instrument packages carried aloft by balloons twice a day from a few hundred stations worldwide. The readings are precise, but each balloon drifts with the wind and reports only once on its way up, so a thunderstorm that forms between launches can develop unobserved. Researchers in Oklahoma have therefore begun testing small drones that climb and descend over a fixed point every hour. In early trials, the drones' temperature and humidity profiles closely matched balloon data and revealed moisture building in the hours before several storms.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Drone trials in Oklahoma have shown that balloon radiosondes should no longer be used to forecast storms.
Hourly drone soundings may capture fast-changing conditions that twice-daily balloon launches tend to miss.
Drones can measure the lower atmosphere, but their readings have not yet matched the precision of balloons.
Radiosondes drift with the wind as they rise, so each balloon reports from a slightly different location.
items.explanation: The passage sets the old method against the new one: radiosondes are precise but infrequent, so storms forming between launches go unseen. The drones matched balloon accuracy and caught moisture building before storms. Take one step beyond what is literally said and you get B. Drones could fill the gaps in time that balloons leave. The word 'may' matches how sure the passage is, because these were early trials.

A.why: This is the trap this subtype is built around. The passage points to one limitation of radiosondes, the gaps between launches, and you turned it into a claim that they should be dropped entirely. The passage even calls their readings precise, and it never suggests replacing them.

C.why: This is a half-right answer. The opening is true, because drones do measure the lower atmosphere. But the second half reverses the passage, which says the drone profiles 'closely matched balloon data.' You probably recognised the topic and stopped reading.

D.why: This is true, but it only restates one detail from the second sentence. The passage goes on to bring in drones and report what the trials found, so this choice is too narrow to be the main idea.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: Museum catalogues usually credit a Japanese woodblock print to the artist whose signature appears in its corner. In the workshops of eighteenth-century Edo, however, an image passed through several hands: the artist supplied a brush drawing, a carver cut it into a block of cherry wood, and a printer decided how much pigment to load and how hard to press. As a result, two impressions from the same block can differ markedly in tone, and specialists now sometimes recognize individual printers by these habits even where no name was recorded.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Signatures on Edo woodblock prints are unreliable, since the signing artists did little of the actual work.
Edo workshops divided each print among several workers, so impressions from one block were nearly identical.
Crediting an Edo print only to its signing artist overlooks the craftsmen whose choices shaped its appearance.
Edo carvers cut each artist's brush drawing into a block of cherry wood before any printing could begin.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the usual view, that a print belongs to the artist who signed it. After 'however' comes what the author actually believes: carvers and printers made decisions that changed how the print looks, and their habits can be seen in the tone of each impression. The point left unstated is that the usual credit is incomplete. C says exactly that and nothing more.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. The passage suggests that crediting only the artist leaves people out, and you pushed that into an absolute claim that the signatures are unreliable and the artist did little. The passage never questions who made the drawing. It only adds the other contributors.

B.why: This is a half-right answer. It is true that the work was divided among several people, but the passage says impressions from one block 'can differ markedly in tone,' which is the opposite of nearly identical. Read every choice to the end.

D.why: This accurately describes one step in the workshop process, but the step is there only to show that several people shaped the print. It leaves out the passage's point about how the credit is given, so it is too narrow.

items.stimulus: Hydrologists have long estimated groundwater recharge by measuring how far the water in monitoring wells rises after a storm. The method works well in sandy aquifers, where rainwater drains downward within days. In clay-rich soils, however, water may take months to reach the water table, and by then pumping and evaporation have already shifted the levels in the wells. A team led by hydrologist Rosa Ibáñez instead traced chloride, a salt carried down by rain, through soil cores. This let them date water that was still moving toward the wells.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the well-measurement method of estimating groundwater recharge?
choices: It cannot give useful recharge estimates for any kind of aquifer.
It may give misleading estimates where water moves slowly through soil.
It is more dependable in clay-rich soils than in sandy aquifers.
It relies on tracing chloride through cores taken from the soil.
items.explanation: The text says the well method 'works well' in sandy aquifers. The problem comes after 'however': in clay soils, water arrives so slowly that pumping and evaporation have changed the well levels before the water gets there. One step beyond that is that the method's readings may be unreliable where water moves slowly. Choice B says exactly that and goes no further.

A.why: The text points to a limitation and you read it as total failure. The passage says plainly that the method works well in sandy aquifers, so 'any kind of aquifer' says far more than the text does.

C.why: You reversed the contrast. The text says the method works well in sandy aquifers and runs into trouble in clay-rich soils.

D.why: You gave the old method a feature of the new one. Tracing chloride through soil cores is what Ibáñez's team did instead of measuring wells.

They show that Wendt never improvised any music during her career.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: Living trees in cool climates tend to have leaves with toothed edges, so paleobotanists often use the share of toothed leaves at a fossil site to estimate ancient temperatures. A 2023 survey of Patagonian forests, however, found that streamside species had toothed leaves regardless of temperature, likely because wet soils favor that leaf form. Because many fossil leaf beds formed in river floodplains, the survey's authors argue that some of these temperature estimates may need revisiting.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about temperature estimates based on fossil leaves from ancient river floodplains?
choices: They should be abandoned because leaf shape reveals nothing about climate.
They may make those ancient environments seem cooler than they were.
They may make those ancient environments seem warmer than they were.
They are mostly drawn from tree species that grew in Patagonia.
items.explanation: This takes two steps. First, more toothed leaves lead to a cooler temperature estimate. Second, floodplain plants have toothed leaves whatever the temperature, so floodplain fossil beds probably contain extra toothed leaves. Put together, the estimates may come out too cool, and the ancient environments may have been warmer than calculated. The authors' hedges ('likely', 'some', 'may') fit B's 'may'.

A.why: The text says only that some estimates may need revisiting. You turned a limited problem into an absolute one. The text still treats leaf shape as linked to climate in general.

C.why: You took the right first step and then got the direction backwards. Extra toothed leaves point to a cooler climate, so the error would make sites look cooler, not warmer.

D.why: Patagonia is where the modern survey was done. Nothing in the text says the fossil beds themselves contain Patagonian species.

items.stimulus: Great tits living in cities sing at higher pitches than those in forests, and many researchers have attributed the difference to birds adjusting their songs to rise above traffic noise. To test this, ecologist Hana Morić collected eggs from both city and forest nests and raised the hatchlings in identical, quiet aviaries. As adults, the birds from city nests still sang at higher pitches than the forest birds, though none had ever heard traffic.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the higher-pitched songs of urban great tits?
choices: They have no connection to the noise levels found in cities.
They disappeared once urban birds were raised in quiet aviaries.
They are not explained only by each bird's own exposure to noise.
They help urban birds attract more mates than forest birds do.
items.explanation: Morić held one variable fixed: no bird ever heard traffic. The city-born birds still sang higher. So the difference can't come entirely from individual birds adjusting to noise they heard during their own lives. C makes exactly that one step.

items.stimulus: Histories of printmaking routinely credit the Dutch engraver Anneke Voorst (1612–1671) with inventing a waxy-ground etching method that lets a print imitate the grainy line of a pencil sketch. Voorst probably did not originate the method she is known for, though she may have helped it spread.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the official credit, and 'However' brings in evidence that undercuts it: plates with the same texture made before Voorst was born. B.why: This is an accurate detail, but it's only one sentence. The passage uses the date to question Voorst's credit, and this choice leaves that conclusion out.

items.subtype_name: What the text suggests about X
items.stimulus: City planners have traditionally judged a widened road by how much it eases congestion during its first year. Studies of highway widenings in several mid-sized cities, however, tracked traffic for longer and found that volumes on the widened roads climbed steadily over the next five years as drivers shifted their routes and new development clustered nearby. By the fifth year, rush-hour travel times on several of the roads had returned to roughly their pre-widening levels.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Judging a widened road by its first-year results may overstate how much it eases traffic over time.
Widening highways never reduces congestion, so city planners should stop approving such projects.
New development tends to cluster near roads in mid-sized cities soon after they have been widened.
Traffic on widened roads tends to fall over time as drivers grow used to the new road layout.
items.explanation: The conventional method (judging by the first year) is set against longer studies showing that the gains wore off by year five. The passage never says the old method is wrong outright. The one-step implication is that it gives too rosy a picture of long-term benefit, which is choice A.

B.why: You turned 'the benefit fades' into 'there is no benefit.' Congestion did ease at first, and the text gives no policy recommendation.

C.why: This is one of the two causes the passage lists for rising traffic. It's a supporting detail, not what the whole passage is about.

D.why: This reverses the finding. Traffic volumes rose over the five years, and they didn't fall.
