items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Streams with beaver dams often keep flowing through late summer, when nearby undammed streams run dry. One explanation is that the ponds behind the dams store surface water and release it slowly. Hydrologist Elena Sokolova proposes a different route: by spreading water across the floodplain, the dams raise the local water table, and groundwater then seeps back into the channel below the dam for weeks after inflow stops. Her team concluded that this groundwater pathway, not pond storage, is what sustains the late-summer flow.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's conclusion?
choices: In August, dammed streams were still flowing at most survey points, whereas nearby undammed streams had stopped flowing entirely.
Below dams whose ponds had already drained by August, flow continued wherever floodplain wells showed the water table was still raised.
Ponds behind the dams held more water in early July than the streams below them carried over the whole month of August.
Floodplain water tables stood higher along dammed streams than undammed ones, and the dams' ponds stayed full well into August.
items.explanation: The conclusion makes two claims: groundwater sustains the flow, and pond storage does not. Once a pond has drained, it has no stored water left to release, so pond storage can't explain flow below it. If flow continues there, and only where the water table is still raised, the flow is tied to groundwater and the rival explanation is removed.

A.why: You chose a restatement of the observed difference between dammed and undammed streams. Both explanations predict this result, so it can't favour one.

C.why: You chose evidence that the ponds hold enough water to supply August flow. That supports pond storage, the explanation the team rejects.

D.why: You noticed the raised water table but missed that full ponds were present too. With both possible sources in place, this finding can't show which one keeps the stream flowing.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Engineers sometimes embed capsules of dormant bacterial spores in concrete. When a crack lets in water, the spores revive and precipitate calcium carbonate, which seals the crack. But concrete can partly heal without bacteria: unreacted cement grains exposed in a crack also form calcium carbonate, and the capsules' cement-based shells could supply such grains. Materials scientist Ilse Vermeer tested samples that differed only in whether their capsules held live or heat-killed spores. She concluded that the bacteria, not the capsule shells, account for most of the sealing.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Vermeer's conclusion?
choices: Cracks in samples with live spores were filled with calcium carbonate along their full depth after four weeks in water.
Cracks in samples with live or heat-killed spores closed far more fully than cracks in samples containing no capsules.
Cracks closed more fully in samples kept submerged in water than in otherwise identical samples kept in dry air.
Cracks in samples with heat-killed spores closed little more than those in capsule-free concrete, while live-spore cracks closed fully.
items.explanation: The heat-killed samples have the same capsule shells but no working bacteria. If those samples barely outperform concrete with no capsules at all, the shells add little. If the live-spore samples seal fully, the bacteria account for the difference. This choice compares the two conditions the way the conclusion needs.

A.why: You matched calcium carbonate to the bacteria. The passage says unreacted cement grains form the same mineral, so finding it in the cracks doesn't show which process put it there.

B.why: You chose a result that holds for both capsule groups. If dead-spore capsules seal almost as well as live ones, the shells may be doing the work. That points away from Vermeer's conclusion.

C.why: Both healing processes need water, so better sealing under water fits either explanation. It doesn't separate bacteria from shells.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Volunteers were given one of two breakfast drinks matched in volume and calories. One was thickened with viscous guar gum, and the other contained an equal mass of non-viscous cellulose fiber. At lunch three hours later, volunteers ate less after the guar drink. Nutrition scientist Tomás Ferreira hypothesizes that guar reduced intake because its thick gel slowed the rate at which the stomach emptied, prolonging the stretch signals that suppress appetite.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's hypothesis?
choices: When given with a compound that speeds stomach emptying, the guar drink no longer reduced lunch intake relative to the cellulose drink.
Both the guar drink and the cellulose drink left the stomach more slowly than an equal volume of plain water did.
Volunteers ate less at lunch after the guar drink whether they had eaten a large or a small dinner the night before.
Volunteers who ate the least at lunch after the guar drink also rated it as the thickest and most filling drink.
items.explanation: Ferreira proposes a chain: guar leads to slower stomach emptying, which leads to eating less. If the middle link is that cause, removing it should remove the effect. Speeding emptying back up erases guar's advantage, so this finding isolates slow emptying as the cause.

B.why: You found the right mechanism but in both groups. If both drinks slow emptying, slow emptying can't explain why only guar reduced lunch intake.

C.why: You chose evidence that the result holds up across conditions. It confirms that guar reduces intake again but says nothing about why.

D.why: You linked perceived thickness to eating less. How thick or filling a drink feels is not how fast the stomach empties, so the proposed mechanism is never tested.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Summer afternoon storms drop more rain on the area east of Halvorsen, downwind of the city, than on similar countryside to its west. Two features of the city could explain this. Its pavement and buildings heat the air above them, driving stronger updrafts. Its traffic and industry also emit aerosol particles on which cloud droplets can form. After analyzing two decades of radar data, meteorologists concluded that the rainfall increase is driven mainly by the city's heat, not by its aerosols.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the meteorologists' conclusion?
choices: Over the two decades, summer afternoon rainfall east of Halvorsen exceeded rainfall west of the city by about a fifth.
Rainfall rose on hot afternoons both east and west of Halvorsen, and by similar amounts in the two areas.
On weekends, when the city's aerosol emissions fell sharply but its surface heating did not, rain east of the city stayed just as elevated.
The rainfall increase east of the city was largest on its hottest days, which were also the days when its air was most polluted.
items.explanation: To show that heat, not aerosols, drives the increase, you need conditions where one changes and the other doesn't. On weekends aerosols drop but heating stays the same. If downwind rain doesn't fall, aerosols aren't needed for the increase, which leaves heat.

A.why: You chose a figure for the observed increase. It confirms that the effect exists but doesn't say what causes it.

B.why: You chose a pattern that appears both east and west of the city. Something true of both areas equally can't explain why only the downwind area gets extra rain.

D.why: You noticed that the increase follows heat, which fits the conclusion. But the hottest days were also the most polluted, so aerosols rise with heat and the finding can't separate the two.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Ocean acidification slows shell growth in many bivalves, but a parent's experience may shape how its offspring cope. Marine biologist Akosua Mensah raised rock oysters in either acidified or normal seawater. She then reared the larvae of each group in both conditions. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mensah's conclusion?

Larvae of exposed parents outgrew those of unexposed parents in acidified water, but the two grew equally in normal seawater.
Larvae of both exposed and unexposed parents grew more slowly in acidified water than they did in normal seawater.
Adults kept in acidified water built thinner shells than adults kept in normal seawater over the same period.

Offspring of exposed parents should do better in acidified water, and that advantage should not appear in normal water, because an advantage everywhere would just be general vigour. Only this choice shows both: an advantage in acidified water and none in normal seawater.

A.why: You checked the acidified-water half and stopped. An advantage in both kinds of water is exactly the overall vigour that Mensah's conclusion rules out.

C.why: You chose a result that holds for both groups of larvae. It shows that acidification slows growth but doesn't compare offspring of exposed and unexposed parents.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Wheat planted along hedgerows often outyields wheat in the open centers of the same fields. Hedgerows slow the wind, which reduces water loss from the crop's leaves. They also house parasitoid wasps that lay eggs in aphids, killing these sap-feeding pests before their numbers build. Agronomist Priya Raman concluded that the yield gain in her study fields came chiefly from the wasps' suppression of aphids rather than from shelter from the wind.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Raman's conclusion?
choices: Wheat growing beside the hedgerows yielded more grain per hectare than wheat growing in the open centers of the fields.
Wind speeds over wheat beside the hedgerows were lower than wind speeds over wheat growing in the field centers.
Hedgerows netted so that wasps could not reach the wheat still cut wind speed over the adjacent wheat by about half.
Beside hedgerows netted so that wasps could not reach the wheat, the wheat yielded no more than wheat in the field centers.
items.explanation: Raman credits the wasps rather than the windbreak, so the evidence has to remove one and keep the other. Netting keeps the wasps out while the hedgerow still blocks wind. If the yield gain disappears under those conditions, wind shelter alone doesn't produce it, and the wasps do.

A.why: You chose the observed yield gain, which the passage already reports. Both explanations predict it, so it doesn't favour Raman's.

B.why: You chose evidence for the wind-shelter mechanism, the one Raman downplays. Calmer air near hedgerows fits the rival explanation, not hers.

C.why: You recognised the right experiment but chose its setup instead of its result. Knowing that netted hedgerows still block wind tells you nothing until you know what happened to the yield.

items.stimulus: Probate inventories from the Lowland towns show that the share of households owning printed cotton rose sharply in the 1780s, displacing woolen worsted. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Svensson's claim?

items.subtype_name: Conditional probability from a table ('given that…')
items.stimulus:
A museum of textile history catalogued its collection of woven fragments by fiber and by the century in which each fragment was made. The results are shown in the table.

Woven Fragments by Fiber and Century
Fiber | 17th century | 18th century | Total
Wool | 24 | 36 | 60
Linen | 16 | 44 | 60
Total | 40 | 80 | 120
items.stem: If one of the 18th-century fragments is selected at random, what is the probability that it is made of linen?
items.explanation: The condition is "one of the 18th-century fragments," so the 18th-century column is now your whole world. Its total, 80, is the denominator. The linen cell in that column is 44. The probability is $\frac{44}{80} = \frac{11}{20}$.

A.why: You divided the 44 linen 18th-century fragments by the grand total, 120. That gives the probability that a fragment from the whole collection is both linen and from the 18th century, not the probability among the 18th-century fragments only.

B.why: You used the right column but took the wool cell, $\frac{36}{80} = \frac{9}{20}$. That is the probability of wool, not linen.

D.why: You swapped the condition and the target and divided 44 by the linen total, 60. That answers "of the linen fragments, what fraction are from the 18th century?", which is a different question.

A gallery's printmaking exhibition includes 80 prints. Each print is classified by technique and by whether it was printed in black ink only or in multiple colors. The results are shown in the table.

Exhibition Prints by Technique and Color
Technique | Black ink only | Multicolor | Total
Woodcut | 14 | 21 | 35
Etching | 36 | 9 | 45
Total | 50 | 30 | 80
items.stem: If one of the multicolor prints is selected at random, what is the probability that it is an etching?
items.explanation: The condition is "one of the multicolor prints," so keep only the Multicolor column. Its total, 30, is the denominator. The multicolor etchings number 9. The probability is $\frac{9}{30} = \frac{3}{10}$.

A.why: You divided 9 by the grand total, 80. That is the probability that a print chosen from the whole exhibition is both multicolor and an etching, not the probability among multicolor prints only.

B.why: You swapped the condition and the target and divided 9 by 45, the etching total. That answers "of the etchings, what fraction are multicolor?"

D.why: You used the Multicolor column but took the woodcut cell, $\frac{21}{30} = \frac{7}{10}$. The question asks about etchings.

items.stem: If one of the observations made at Observatory South is selected at random, what is the probability of selecting a nebula observation?
items.explanation: The condition is "made at Observatory South," so your whole world is the Observatory South column, which has 60 observations. Of those, 40 are nebulae. The probability is $\frac{40}{60} = \frac{2}{3}$.

A.why: You used the galaxy cell in the Observatory South column, $\frac{20}{60} = \frac{1}{3}$. That is the probability of selecting a galaxy, not a nebula.

B.why: You divided the 40 South nebulae by the grand total of 100. That gives the probability that an observation is both from South and a nebula. The question only lets you choose from South's 60 observations.

D.why: You swapped the condition and the target. You divided 40 by the 50 nebulae, which answers "of the nebula observations, what fraction were made at South?"

items.stem: If one of the residents who prefer the bike lane is selected at random, what is the probability of selecting a resident from Hillcrest?

items.stimulus:
Fossil Leaves Collected at Two Dig Sites
Site | Fern | Cycad | Total
Site A | 6 | 14 | 20
Site B | 18 | 12 | 30
Total | 24 | 26 | 50
items.stem: A fossil is chosen at random from Site A. What is the probability that it is a fern?
items.explanation: The words "from Site A" mean only the Site A row matters. Cover the rest of the table. That row has 20 fossils in total, so 20 is your denominator. The fern cell in that row is 6, so the probability is $\frac{6}{20} = \frac{3}{10}$. This is the first step in every SAT question that says "given that" or "if the item chosen is…": find the one row or column that becomes your whole world, then divide inside it.

B.why: You divided 6 by 24, the total number of ferns. That answers a different question: of the ferns, what fraction came from Site A? The condition is Site A, so the Site A total of 20 belongs in the denominator.

D.why: You used the right row but took the cycad cell, 14, as your numerator. $\frac{14}{20}$ is the probability that a Site A fossil is not a fern. The question asks about ferns, which is 6.

Marine biologists recorded the species and habitat of 200 sea turtles sighted during a coastal survey. The results are shown in the table.

Sea Turtle Sightings by Species and Habitat
Species | Reef | Seagrass | Open water | Total
Green | 32 | 42 | 6 | 80
Loggerhead | 48 | 14 | 58 | 120
Total | 80 | 56 | 64 | 200
items.stem: If one of these turtles is selected at random, how much greater is the probability that it is a loggerhead observed on the reef than the probability that it is a green turtle observed on the reef?
items.explanation: The turtle is selected from all 200 sightings, so both probabilities use 200 as the denominator. The probability for a loggerhead on the reef is $\frac{48}{200}$, and for a green turtle on the reef it is $\frac{32}{200}$. The difference is $\frac{48 - 32}{200} = \frac{16}{200} = 0.08$.

B.why: You divided the difference of 16 by the Reef column total of 80 instead of by 200. That answers a question about turtles already known to be on the reef, which nobody asked.

C.why: $\frac{48}{200} = 0.24$ is only the loggerhead-on-reef probability. You didn't subtract the green-on-reef probability.

D.why: You divided 48 by the Loggerhead row total of 120, which gives $0.40$, the probability that a loggerhead is on the reef. That's a conditional probability, not the gap the question asks about.

items.subtype_name: Two-way table, probability out of everyone
items.stimulus:
An astronomy team classified 200 galaxies by shape and by whether each has an active nucleus.

Galaxies by Shape and Nucleus Type
Shape | Active nucleus | No active nucleus | Total
Spiral | 18 | 62 | 80
Elliptical | 12 | 48 | 60
Irregular | 10 | 50 | 60
Total | 40 | 160 | 200
items.stem: If one of these galaxies is selected at random, which of the following must be true?
choices: The probability that the galaxy is spiral and has an active nucleus is 0.225.
The probability that the galaxy is elliptical and has an active nucleus is 0.30.
The probability that the galaxy has an active nucleus is 0.20.
The probability that the galaxy is irregular and has no active nucleus is 0.24.
items.explanation: The galaxy is picked from all 200, so the denominator is the grand total, 200. Only one trait is named, an active nucleus, so the numerator is that column's total, 40. $\frac{40}{200} = 0.20$.

A.why: You divided 18 by the Spiral row total, 80. That gives the probability of an active nucleus among spiral galaxies only, which is a conditional question nobody asked. Out of all 200 galaxies the probability is $\frac{18}{200} = 0.09$.

B.why: You divided 12 by the Active nucleus column total, 40. That tells you what share of active galaxies are elliptical. Out of all 200 the probability is $\frac{12}{200} = 0.06$.

D.why: You used 48, the neighbouring Elliptical cell, when you should have used the Irregular cell, 50. The correct probability is $\frac{50}{200} = 0.25$.

A seismology station recorded 250 earthquakes in one year and sorted them by focal depth and by magnitude.

Shallow | 80 | 40 | 15 | 135
Deep | 50 | 55 | 10 | 115

items.stem: If one of these earthquakes is selected at random, which of the following must be true?
choices: The probability that the earthquake was shallow and had magnitude at least 4.0 is 0.22.
The probability that the earthquake had magnitude below 4.0 is 0.54.
The probability that the earthquake was deep but not below magnitude 4.0 is 0.20.
The probability that the earthquake was deep and had magnitude 6.0 or above is 0.40.
items.explanation: The earthquake is picked from all 250, so the denominator is 250. A shallow earthquake with magnitude at least 4.0 falls in either the 4.0 to 5.9 column or the 6.0 or above column, so the numerator is $40 + 15 = 55$. $\frac{55}{250} = 0.22$.

B.why: You read 135, the Shallow row total, when you needed 130, the Below 4.0 column total. The correct probability is $\frac{130}{250} = 0.52$.

C.why: You treated 'deep but not below 4.0' as 'deep and below 4.0', which is the 50 cell. 'Not below 4.0' means the other two columns, so the correct probability is $\frac{55 + 10}{250} = 0.26$.

D.why: You divided 10 by the 6.0 or above column total, 25. That gives the share of strong earthquakes that were deep. Out of all 250 the probability is $\frac{10}{250} = 0.04$.

C.why: You used the timber-and-good cell, 6. 'Not rated good' means the Fair and Poor cells, so the numerator is $10 + 4 = 14$ and the probability is $\frac{14}{200} = 0.07$.

items.stimulus:
A city planning office surveyed residents of three neighborhoods about a proposed protected bike lane. Each resident gave exactly one response. The table shows the results.

Responses to Proposed Bike Lane
Neighborhood | Supports | Opposes | Undecided
North | 34 | 18 | 8
Central | 52 | 20 | 8
South | 24 | 26 | 10
items.stem: If one of these residents is selected at random, what is the probability of selecting a resident who lives in South and opposes the bike lane?
items.explanation: No totals are printed, so you add all nine cells to get the whole group: $60 + 80 + 60 = 200$ residents. The resident must be both from South and opposed, which is the single cell where the South row meets the Opposes column: 26. The probability is $\frac{26}{200} = \frac{13}{100}$.

A.why: You used the neighbouring cell in the South row, 24 residents who support the lane, so you got $\frac{24}{200} = \frac{3}{25}$.

C.why: You counted every resident who opposes the lane, $18 + 20 + 26 = 64$, and ignored the requirement that the resident live in South: $\frac{64}{200} = \frac{8}{25}$.

D.why: You divided 26 by the South row total of 60. That is the probability of opposing *given that* the resident lives in South, which is a conditional question nobody asked.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Marine biologists have long assumed that the larvae of reef fish simply drift wherever ocean currents carry them before settling on a reef. Biologist Teresa Okafor, however, suspected that the larvae steer themselves. She placed larvae in a long tank with an underwater speaker at one end playing recorded reef sounds. <u>Most of the larvae swam steadily toward the speaker, even against a weak artificial current pushing them the other way.</u> Okafor concludes that the larvae are far more active navigators than once believed.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It describes the experimental setup Okafor used to test the larvae.
It presents a result that supports Okafor's suspicion about the larvae.
It explains why biologists believed that the larvae drift with currents.
It proves that currents have no effect on where the larvae settle.
items.explanation: Cover the underlined sentence and you lose what the larvae actually did in the experiment. The sentence before it sets up the tank, and the sentence after it draws the conclusion. The underlined sentence sits between them as the result, and that result backs up Okafor's suspicion that the larvae steer themselves.

A.why: You matched the words 'speaker' and 'current' to the experiment and called the sentence a method. The setup was described in the sentence before it. The underlined sentence reports what happened, which makes it a result.

C.why: You pointed the sentence at the wrong part of the text. The underlined sentence gives evidence against the old belief about drifting. It doesn't explain why anyone held that belief.

D.why: You chose a verb that is too strong. The larvae swam against a weak current in one tank. That supports active steering, but it doesn't prove that currents play no role at all.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Urban planners sometimes find that very small design changes alter how people use a street. In one midsize city, officials replaced two parking spaces outside a bakery with a narrow wooden platform holding benches and planters. <u>Within a month, foot traffic on that block had risen by roughly a fifth, and nearby shops reported that customers were staying longer.</u> Projects like this cost little, yet they can noticeably reshape the character of a street.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It describes how officials designed the platform outside the bakery.
It challenges the claim that small changes can alter street use.
It shows that such platforms raise business on every city street.
It gives a specific result that illustrates the text's opening claim.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim: small design changes can alter how people use a street. The underlined sentence gives a concrete outcome, more foot traffic and longer visits, from one such change. Its job is to illustrate that opening claim with a specific result.

A.why: You gave the sentence the wrong role. The platform's design (benches, planters) is described in the sentence before. The underlined sentence reports what happened afterward, so it is a result and not a description of the design.

B.why: You reversed the relationship. A rise in foot traffic supports the opening claim. It doesn't challenge it.

C.why: You generalized from a single block in a single city. The sentence reports one case and says nothing about every street.

On average, their times differed by less than a hundredth of a second.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It identifies a question that the study described afterward addresses.
It presents the finding that stretching barely affects sprint times.
It explains why many sprinters choose to stretch before a race.
It dismisses the belief that stretching helps sprinters as foolish.

C.why: You pointed to the wrong sentence. The first sentence gives the sprinters' reason for stretching. The underlined sentence raises a question about whether that belief holds up.

D.why: You chose a verb that is too strong. The sentence only says the answer is unclear. It doesn't call the belief foolish or reject it.

items.stimulus: Nutrition labels list a food's total fiber, but researchers increasingly distinguish between different kinds of fiber. <u>Fermentable fiber is the portion that bacteria in the large intestine can break down, producing compounds that nourish the lining of the gut.</u> In a recent trial, nutrition scientist Mei Arakawa found that volunteers who added fermentable fiber to their diets showed larger gains in beneficial gut bacteria than volunteers who simply ate more fiber overall.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It summarizes the results of Arakawa's trial on gut bacteria.
It argues that nutrition labels should stop listing total fiber.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Astronomers have generally assumed that the icy moons of the outer solar system formed alongside their planets. Observations of Neptune's moon Triton fit poorly with that account. <u>Triton orbits in the direction opposite to Neptune's rotation, a pattern almost never produced when a moon condenses from the disk of material around a young planet.</u> Many researchers therefore propose that Triton was once an object in the Kuiper belt that Neptune's gravity later captured.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains how moons condense from the disk of material that surrounds a young planet as it forms.
It provides evidence that most icy moons of the outer solar system were captured by their planets.
It presents an objection that researchers who favor the capture hypothesis for Triton must answer.
It identifies a feature of Triton that is difficult to reconcile with the usual account of how icy moons form.
items.explanation: The second sentence says Triton 'fit[s] poorly' with the usual view that icy moons formed alongside their planets. The underlined sentence says why: Triton's backward orbit is almost never produced by that kind of formation. The last sentence ('therefore') builds the capture hypothesis on this. Choice D names the role correctly: the sentence identifies a feature that conflicts with the standard account.

A.why: You matched the words 'condenses from the disk of material around a young planet' and took the sentence to be an explanation of moon formation. It mentions that process only to show that Triton's orbit does not fit it. It never explains how the process works.

B.why: You widened one moon into a rule for many. The sentence concerns Triton alone, and even the final sentence proposes capture only for Triton, not for most icy moons.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: When a language borrows a word, the borrowed form usually bends to the sounds the borrowing language already has. items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It offers a further example of Japanese speakers adapting English words to the sounds of Japanese.
It introduces an observation that runs counter to the pattern described in the first two sentences.
It explains the recording method Tanaka used to study the speech of younger residents of Tokyo.
It shows that Japanese as a whole has abandoned its long-standing restriction on consonant clusters.
items.explanation: The first two sentences set up a pattern: borrowed words are changed to fit the borrowing language's sounds, as in sutoraiku. 'However' marks the turn. items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: City planners have traditionally assumed that adding lanes to a congested road will ease traffic on it. Yet decades of data from widened highways suggest otherwise: congestion on such roads usually returns to its earlier level within five to ten years. <u>The new lanes draw drivers who had previously taken other routes, traveled at other hours, or skipped the trip entirely.</u> Transportation researchers call this effect induced demand, and many now argue that it should be weighed before any widening project is approved.

It describes a pattern that helps account for why widening roads has not eased congestion.

It states the text's recommendation that cities stop approving any new road-widening projects.
items.explanation: The text opens with an old belief (more lanes ease traffic) and then corrects it: congestion comes back within five to ten years. Without this sentence you would know that widening fails but not how. Choice B names that explaining role and ties it to the right idea.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Forecasters have long assumed that the lightning produced by a thunderstorm is concentrated near the storm's core, where updrafts are strongest. Yet when meteorologist Ana Ferreira mapped strikes from dozens of storms over the Brazilian plains, a different pattern emerged. <u>Nearly a third of the strikes she recorded landed more than 15 kilometers from a storm's center, beneath its trailing anvil cloud.</u> Ferreira argues that safety guidance based only on distance from the core may therefore underestimate the danger zone.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a finding that challenges the assumption described in the first sentence.
It explains the method Ferreira used to map lightning strikes across the plains.
It describes the conditions that make updrafts strongest near a storm's core.
It proposes a change to safety guidance that the final sentence then rejects.
items.explanation: The first sentence gives the old belief: lightning stays near the core. 'Yet' signals a correction, and the underlined sentence supplies the evidence: a third of strikes landed more than 15 kilometers away. Its job is to report a result that cuts against the assumption, and the last sentence builds on that result.

B.why: You matched 'strikes she recorded' to the word 'mapped' and called the sentence a method. The mapping is mentioned in the sentence before. The underlined sentence reports what the mapping found, so it is a result, not a method.

C.why: You picked up 'storm's center' and linked it to the updrafts in the first sentence. The underlined sentence is about strikes landing far from the core. It never explains updrafts, and it works against the core-focused view rather than describing it.

D.why: The underlined sentence proposes no guidance, and the final sentence doesn't reject anything. It draws on the finding to question existing guidance. You got both the role and the relationship wrong.

items.stimulus: Farmers who plant clover between rows of corn hope it will add nitrogen to the soil, but it has been unclear whether the clover also takes water the corn needs during dry summers. Agronomist Tomás Reyes grew corn with and without clover through two drought years. <u>In both years, corn grown with clover yielded about 4 percent less grain than corn grown alone, a much smaller gap than the 20 percent loss many growers had feared.</u> Reyes suggests that clover's cost to corn in dry years may be modest.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains the method Reyes used to compare corn grown with and without clover in drought years.
It reports a result that addresses the uncertainty raised in the first sentence of the text.
It shows that clover adds more nitrogen to the soil in drought years than it does in wet years.
It indicates that clover does not take any of the water that corn needs during dry summers.
items.explanation: The first sentence raises an open question: does clover take water the corn needs in dry summers? The second sentence sets up Reyes's trial. The underlined sentence gives the outcome: a small yield gap, much smaller than growers feared. That is a result that answers the opening question, and Reyes's suggestion in the last sentence is built on it. Choice B names that role and links it to the right part of the text.

A.why: You picked up the words 'with clover' and 'grown alone' and treated the sentence as the method. The method (growing corn with and without clover through two drought years) comes in the sentence before. The underlined sentence gives the numbers that trial produced.

C.why: You brought in a claim the text never makes. Nitrogen comes up only as farmers' hope in the first sentence, and the study measures grain yield in drought years only. Nothing compares nitrogen across wet and dry years.

D.why: You turned 'a smaller gap' into 'no gap.' Corn with clover still yielded about 4 percent less, so the text suggests some cost. Reyes calls that cost modest. He never says it is zero.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: In eighteenth-century Japan, a woodblock print passed through several hands: a designer drew the image, a carver cut it into cherry wood, and a printer inked and pressed each sheet. Collectors have usually credited the designer alone. <u>Yet when historian Mariko Sato compared early and late impressions from the same blocks, she found that the colors changed far more from one edition to the next than the drawn lines did.</u> Sato argues that printers, who chose those colors, shaped these works more than their anonymity suggests.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It introduces evidence that complicates the collecting practice described in the previous sentence.
It explains how a carver transferred a designer's drawing onto a block of cherry wood for printing.
It supports collectors' long-standing view that the designer alone determined how a print looked.
It proves that printers, rather than designers, were the true creators of most woodblock prints.
items.explanation: Sketch the structure: background on who made a print, the usual practice (credit only the designer), then 'Yet' and Sato's comparison, then her argument. The underlined sentence comes right after the pivot. The difference it reports, colors varying far more than lines, is evidence that someone besides the designer shaped the print. That complicates crediting the designer alone, which is what choice A says.

B.why: You described the first sentence, not the underlined one. Carving is mentioned only as background. The underlined sentence is about comparing impressions from different editions, and it says nothing about how a carver worked.

C.why: You missed the 'Yet.' It marks a turn against the collectors' view. If colors changed between editions while the designer's lines stayed the same, the designer did not decide everything about how a print looked.

D.why: You made the claim too strong. Sato says printers shaped the works more than people have recognized. She doesn't say they replaced designers as the creators, and 'proves' is stronger than one comparison of impressions can support.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Historians have long described the eighteenth-century calico trade out of western India as a story of finished cloth flowing west to European buyers. Historian Priya Raman's study of merchant records from the port of Surat complicates that account. <u>Ledgers kept by Surat traders between 1740 and 1760 list more shipments of raw indigo and madder root to Southeast Asia than of printed cotton to Europe.</u> For these traders, at least, dyestuffs rather than cloth appear to have been the more valuable export.
items.stem: Which choice does NOT accurately describe the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It provides evidence that complicates the account of the trade given in the first sentence.
It explains the method Raman used to date the ledgers kept by the Surat traders.
It offers an example of the merchant records mentioned in the preceding sentence.
It presents the specific data on which the final sentence's conclusion is based.
items.explanation: Sketch the passage first: an old view (cloth flowed west), a pivot (Raman's records complicate it), the underlined evidence (more dyestuff shipments than cloth), then a conclusion (dyestuffs mattered more). The underlined sentence reports what the ledgers show. It is a result, not a method, and it never says how the ledgers were dated. Choice B borrows the words 'ledgers' and 'Surat traders' but gives the sentence the wrong role, so it is the one description that fails.

A.why: You may have thought 'complicates' was too strong a verb. The text itself says Raman's records complicate the cloth-flowing-west account, and the underlined ledger figures are what do that work. The description is accurate, so it can't be the answer to a NOT question.

C.why: You may have decided this choice points to the wrong part of the text. The preceding sentence mentions Raman's study of merchant records, and the underlined ledgers are one of those records. The link is correct, so this description holds.

D.why: You may have read the final sentence as a separate point rather than one drawn from the underlined sentence. 'Dyestuffs rather than cloth' rests directly on the shipment counts in the ledgers, so this description is true.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Forecasters have generally treated hail size as a product of a storm's updraft strength alone. Meteorologist Tomás Ibarra set out to test whether the moisture of the air feeding a storm also matters. <u>Comparing radar records from 212 summer storms on the Great Plains, he found that storms with similar updraft speeds produced markedly larger hailstones when the low-level air was humid.</u> Ibarra argues that forecasts of hail size should therefore weigh humidity alongside updraft strength.
items.stem: Which choice does NOT accurately describe the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It reports the result of the comparison Ibarra made to address his question.
It presents a finding that qualifies the view described in the first sentence.
It supplies the basis for the recommendation Ibarra makes in the final sentence.
It refutes the idea that updraft strength has any effect on the size of hail.
items.explanation: The passage runs from an assumption (updrafts alone set hail size) to a question (does moisture matter too?), then the underlined result (at similar updraft speeds, humid air gave larger hail), then a recommendation. The finding adds humidity as a second factor. It holds updraft speed steady and doesn't deny that updrafts matter; the final sentence even keeps updraft strength in the forecast. 'Refutes' is too strong a verb, so choice D is the description that fails.

A.why: You may have taken the underlined sentence for a description of the question rather than its answer. It begins with the comparison Ibarra made and ends with what he found, which is a result that answers the question raised in the second sentence. The description is accurate.

B.why: You may have thought the finding contradicts the first sentence outright, which would make 'qualifies' too weak. The finding limits the 'updraft strength alone' view by adding humidity without dismissing updrafts, and that is exactly what qualifying means. The description is true.

C.why: You may have thought the final sentence stands on its own. It begins with 'therefore,' which shows it draws on the underlined finding. The description correctly names the part of the text the sentence supports.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Off the coast of Baja California, marine biologist Leah Okafor tagged juvenile yellowtail that had hatched near a single kelp bed. Years later, most of the tagged fish that were recaptured had returned to spawn within a few kilometers of that bed. <u>Such findings suggest that a fish's earliest surroundings can shape where it breeds long after it has left them.</u> Okafor now plans to test whether the pattern holds for species whose larvae drift much farther from home.
items.stem: Which choice does NOT accurately describe the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a finding that contradicts the recapture results reported in the preceding sentence.
It states a general principle that the tagging results described before it illustrate.
It draws a broader conclusion from the specific observations of the tagged yellowtail.
It offers the idea whose reach Okafor plans to test in the study the final sentence describes.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence is the abstract one among the specifics: no place names and no species, just a broad rule that early surroundings can shape later breeding sites. It grows directly out of the recapture results and agrees with them. It doesn't contradict them. Choice A gets that relationship backward, so it is the one description that fails.

B.why: You may have thought the principle comes before its example, so 'described before it' seemed to point the wrong way. Here the specific tagging results come first and the rule follows. They illustrate the rule, and the description is accurate.

C.why: You may have thought calling the sentence a 'broader conclusion' claims more than the passage supports. 'Such findings suggest' signals a generalization from the yellowtail data to fish in general, which is what this choice says. It is true.

D.why: You may have read the final sentence as introducing a new topic. 'The pattern' Okafor plans to test is the principle stated in the underlined sentence, now applied to species that drift farther. The description is correct.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Collared flycatchers time their spring return from Africa so that their chicks hatch when caterpillars, the chicks' main food, are most abundant. As springs warmed, ornithologists expected the birds to fall out of step with this food supply. On one Baltic island, the caterpillar peak did advance by roughly twelve days between 1990 and 2020. <u>Over the same three decades, the flycatchers' mean arrival date moved by less than two days.</u> Arrival, however, proved to be the wrong measure: females began laying eggs sooner after arriving, so hatching kept pace with the caterpillars.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains how the researchers determined that the caterpillar peak on the island had advanced.
It provides the evidence that overturns the ornithologists' expectation that the birds would fall behind.
It establishes that the flycatchers were unable to adjust their breeding to the earlier food peak.
It reports a result that seems to confirm the expected mismatch, which the final sentence then undercuts.
items.explanation: Follow the passage's structure. The ornithologists expect the birds to fall out of step, and the caterpillar peak does move twelve days earlier. The underlined sentence adds that arrival barely moved. Taken alone, that looks like exactly the mismatch they predicted, so the sentence seems to back up the expectation. Then the last sentence turns on 'however': arrival was the wrong thing to measure, because females shortened the gap between arriving and laying eggs, so hatching kept up. The underlined sentence therefore gives a result that appears to confirm the mismatch, and the final sentence undercuts it.

A.why: You matched on the dates and the talk of measurement and called the sentence a method. The underlined sentence gives a result about when the flycatchers arrived. It says nothing about how anyone measured the caterpillar peak, which the sentence before it reports.

B.why: You noticed correctly that the passage ends by overturning the expectation, but you gave that job to the wrong sentence. An arrival date that barely moved while the food peak moved twelve days fits the prediction that the birds would fall behind. The evidence against the prediction is the egg-laying finding in the last sentence.

C.why: You stopped reading at the underlined sentence. It only shows that arrival didn't shift. The final sentence says the females adjusted by laying sooner, so the text directly contradicts the claim that the birds couldn't adjust their breeding.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Employers have often defended noncompete clauses as harmless for hourly workers, who rarely hold trade secrets and are rarely sued for changing jobs. If that were true, banning the clauses for such workers should change little. Economist Rana Okafor studied a 2019 state law voiding noncompetes for anyone earning under $40,000 a year. Within three years, hourly wages in the affected jobs had risen about 4 percent. <u>In neighboring states, where the clauses remained enforceable, pay for the same jobs was essentially flat over that period.</u> The clauses, Okafor concludes, had been holding wages down.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It reports the main wage increase that Okafor attributes to the state's ban on noncompetes.
It indicates that the wage increase was not simply part of a broader regional trend in pay.
It suggests that the benefits of the ban were confined to workers within a single state.
It supports the employers' view that noncompete clauses have little effect on hourly pay.
items.explanation: The sentence before the underlined one gives the finding: wages in the affected jobs rose about 4 percent. That rise alone could have come from a regional economy that was lifting pay everywhere. The underlined sentence closes off that possibility. In neighboring states, where the clauses were still in force, pay for the same jobs stayed flat. That comparison is what lets Okafor tie the rise to the ban and conclude that the clauses had been holding wages down. Its job is to rule out a competing explanation for the finding.

A.why: You saw pay figures and called the sentence the main result. The 4 percent rise is in the sentence before it. The underlined sentence describes a comparison group, and it matters because it shows the rise belongs to the ban and not to the wider economy.

C.why: You took the mention of other states as a limit on the finding. The neighboring states are there as a comparison, not as evidence that the ban's effects stopped at the border. The text makes no claim about how far the benefits reached.

D.why: You may have linked the flat pay to the clauses and read it as harmless. But that flat pay is what the rise in the ban state is measured against, so it supports Okafor's conclusion that the clauses held wages down. That is the opposite of the employers' view.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Forecasters in northern Italy's Po Valley have traditionally blamed its dense winter fogs on still air: on windless nights the ground loses heat, and the chilled air near it condenses. Meteorologist Ilaria Benassi suspected that moisture from irrigated fields mattered more. Analyzing twelve winters of station records, she found that fog formed on many breezy nights that followed heavy irrigation. <u>Yet on windless nights that followed dry spells, fog was comparatively rare.</u> Benassi concludes that soil moisture, not calm air alone, best predicts the valley's fogs.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents an exception that Benassi concedes limits her conclusion about the role of soil moisture in fog.
It reports a finding showing that the condition forecasters emphasized was often not enough on its own.
It explains the method Benassi used to separate the effect of wind from the effect of irrigation.
It establishes that still air plays no part at all in the formation of the valley's winter fogs.
items.explanation: The previous sentence shows fog forming without still air (breezy nights after irrigation). The underlined sentence adds the other half: still air without moisture seldom produced fog. Together, the two findings show calm air was often not enough on its own, which sets up Benassi's conclusion. 'Yet' contrasts the two kinds of night. It does not contrast the sentence with Benassi's view.

A.why: You read 'Yet' as pushing back against Benassi. It actually contrasts the dry, windless nights with the irrigated, breezy ones, and both results support her. Benassi concedes nothing here.

C.why: You noticed that the sentence pulls wind apart from moisture and called that a method. The sentence reports what the records showed. That is a result, not a description of how she analyzed them.

D.why: You saw that the sentence weakens the still-air explanation and pushed that too far. Benassi says 'not calm air alone,' which leaves still air some role.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Astronomers monitoring the young star HD 31460 noticed that its light dipped irregularly, sometimes by a fifth, for days at a time. A planet passing in front of the star could not explain dips so deep and so uneven, since a planet blocks the same share of light on every pass. <u>A clump of orbiting dust, by contrast, can change its shape and density from one pass to the next.</u> The team therefore proposed that the dips come from debris left by colliding rocky bodies, a sign that the star's planetary system is still forming.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents an observation of HD 31460 that allowed the team to rule out a planet as the cause of the dips.
It offers a general contrast explaining why the cause the team proposes fits the uneven dips better than a planet.
It states the team's conclusion that the planetary system around HD 31460 is still in the process of forming.
It raises a possible objection to the team's proposal that orbiting debris is responsible for the dips.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence names no star, date, or measurement. It states a general property of dust clouds. Set against the previous sentence's point that a planet blocks the same light on every pass, it explains why dust can produce uneven dips when a planet cannot. 'Therefore' in the next sentence shows that the team's proposal rests on this contrast.

A.why: You saw that the sentence helps argue against a planet and assumed it was an observation of this star. It is a general statement about dust. The planet was already ruled out in the sentence before it.

C.why: You pointed to the wrong part of the text. The conclusion about a forming system comes in the final sentence. The underlined sentence supplies the reasoning that leads there.

D.why: You read 'by contrast' as a challenge to the team. The contrast is between dust and a planet, and it supports the team's proposal.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Fossil leaves are widely used to estimate ancient carbon dioxide levels, because many plants grow fewer stomata, or breathing pores, when the gas is plentiful. Paleobotanist Rhea Okafor asked whether this response holds for ferns, whose fossils are abundant in rocks too old for other methods. Growing twelve living fern species under varied carbon dioxide levels, she found that nine grew fewer stomata as levels rose. <u>The other three showed no consistent change, and all three belong to a lineage that grows in deep shade.</u> Okafor suggests that fern fossils can serve as gauges, provided their lineage is identified first.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It reports results that undermine Okafor's claim that ferns respond to carbon dioxide as other plants do.
It identifies a pattern among exceptions to the main finding that accounts for Okafor's stated condition.
It describes how Okafor chose which fern species to grow under the varied levels of carbon dioxide.
It explains why many plants grow fewer stomata when carbon dioxide is plentiful in the surrounding air.
items.explanation: The sentence before gives the main result: nine of twelve species responded. The underlined sentence covers the three that did not and notes what they share, a single shade-dwelling lineage. That shared trait is why Okafor's final suggestion comes with a condition: identify the lineage first. The sentence qualifies the finding. It does not overturn it.

A.why: You correctly saw that the sentence describes exceptions but chose a verb that is too strong. Okafor still endorses fern fossils as gauges, so the exceptions narrow her claim without undermining it.

C.why: You matched words like 'three' and 'lineage' to a description of species selection. The sentence reports how the species behaved, which is a result, not how they were chosen.

D.why: You went to the background in the first sentence. The underlined sentence is about ferns that did not respond. It gives no general explanation of the stomata response.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: After the Varne River was dammed in 1974, wells in the downstream farming town of Elsby began to fall, and residents blamed the reservoir for holding back water that once soaked into the ground. <u>Records show that well levels dropped fastest in the decade the dam was completed.</u> Hydrologist Tomas Reyes, however, notes that the same decade saw Elsby's farms triple their pumping to water newly planted orchards, and that wells upstream of the dam, beyond the reservoir's reach, fell just as quickly.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a pattern in timing that seems to back the residents' view but that Reyes shows fits another cause.
It provides the evidence that Reyes uses to show that the reservoir lowered the water table near Elsby.
It introduces Reyes's claim that increased pumping, rather than the dam, caused Elsby's wells to fall.
It establishes that the dam had no effect on groundwater levels anywhere along the Varne River.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence comes before 'however.' At that point, the decline lining up with the dam seems to support the residents. Reyes then points to a second change in the same decade, tripled pumping, and to upstream wells that fell just as fast. That shows the timing fits pumping equally well. The sentence sets up an apparent story that the rest of the text reframes.

B.why: You recognized the sentence as evidence but gave it to the wrong side. Reyes uses it to show that the timing points to more than one cause, not to blame the reservoir.

C.why: You pointed to the wrong part of the text. Reyes's alternative appears only after 'however.' The underlined sentence still belongs to the residents' account.

D.why: You took Reyes's doubt about the residents' explanation and made it absolute. Neither the sentence nor Reyes says the dam had no effect anywhere.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Folklorists long treated the many versions of a folktale as corruptions of a lost original, ranking each by how faithfully it seemed to preserve that source. Scholar Aino Reinikainen argues instead that tellers reshape tales on purpose to suit their listeners. <u>In fishing villages along the Gulf of Bothnia, the tale of the clever youngest daughter ends with her outwitting a sea spirit; told inland, the same tale gives that role to a forest troll.</u> Such shifts, she contends, follow the local landscape too closely to be lapses of memory.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It gives an example of variants whose differences Reinikainen treats as evidence that tellers adapt tales on purpose.
It gives an example of the corruptions that earlier folklorists measured against a tale's lost original version.
It describes the method earlier folklorists used to rank versions of a tale by their faithfulness to a source.
It shows that the tale of the clever youngest daughter first arose in the fishing villages of the Gulf of Bothnia.
items.explanation: The text sets up an old view (variants are corruptions) and then Reinikainen's view (variants are deliberate). The underlined sentence gives a concrete pair of variants. The final sentence shows how she reads them: the change follows the landscape too closely to be accidental. So the example serves her argument.

B.why: You correctly saw that the sentence is an example but placed it under the wrong view. The text offers it as evidence for Reinikainen's position, not as a case of corruption.

C.why: You linked a sentence about differing versions to the earlier practice of ranking versions. The sentence describes two tellings. It does not describe how anyone ranked them.

D.why: You read the coastal version, which is mentioned first, as the original. The text says nothing about where the tale began.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: When app-based delivery companies spread to midsize US cities, many observers predicted that restaurant kitchen workers would leave for the flexible new jobs, leaving restaurants short-staffed. Economist Dana Whitlock examined payroll data from 140 cities and found that kitchen employment barely changed after the platforms arrived. <u>What did change was turnover: workers quit and were replaced far more often, so restaurants spent more each year on hiring and training.</u> Whitlock argues that the platforms' main cost to restaurants was not fewer workers but a less stable workforce.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It reports a finding that identifies the actual effect on restaurants in place of the effect observers predicted.
It qualifies the preceding finding by indicating that kitchen employment did fall in some of the cities.
It presents evidence supporting the observers' prediction that restaurants would be left short-staffed.
It explains the method Whitlock used to measure kitchen employment across the 140 cities she studied.
items.explanation: Observers predicted fewer kitchen workers, and the sentence before shows that did not happen. The underlined sentence reports what did change: higher turnover and the costs that came with it. Whitlock's conclusion ('not fewer workers but a less stable workforce') rests on this finding. It replaces the predicted effect with the one actually observed.

B.why: You took 'What did change' as walking back the sentence before it. The underlined sentence accepts that employment held steady and points to a different measure.

C.why: You saw 'workers quit' and heard the observers' prediction. But quitting workers were replaced, so headcount held. The finding replaces the prediction rather than supporting it.

D.why: You treated the sentence's description of turnover as a description of method. It reports a result from the payroll data, not how Whitlock gathered or measured it.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Can small earthquakes warn of large ones? Foreshocks precede some major quakes, but they look like ordinary tremors until afterward. Seismologist Keiko Mori studied a different signal: tiny repeating quakes that strike the same patch of a fault at steady intervals. <u>In the two years before a magnitude 7.1 quake struck off the Kaminari coast, the intervals between those repeating quakes shrank by half.</u> Mori cautions that a single record cannot show the pattern is reliable, but she argues that repeating quakes deserve monitoring in a way ordinary foreshocks do not.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a finding that Mori treats as a reason for monitoring rather than as proof of a reliable warning sign.
It provides evidence that shrinking intervals reliably signal the approach of a major offshore earthquake.
It describes a foreshock pattern that, like other foreshocks, could be recognized only after the quake struck.
It explains how Mori identified the repeating quakes that struck the same patch of the fault at steady intervals.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question and introduces a new candidate signal. The underlined sentence gives a single result that looks promising. The next sentence sets limits on it: one record cannot show reliability, though it justifies monitoring. Getting this right means seeing both that the sentence supports Mori and that she limits how far it goes.

B.why: You correctly saw the sentence as evidence for Mori's signal but missed her caution. She says one record cannot show the pattern is reliable.

C.why: You lumped the repeating quakes in with the foreshocks from the second sentence. The text presents them as a different signal, which Mori says deserves monitoring in a way foreshocks do not.

D.why: You matched the phrase about repeating quakes to the sentence that introduces them. The underlined sentence reports what the intervals did, which is a result, not how Mori identified the quakes.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
items.stimulus: Farmers plant cover crops such as rye after harvest to protect the soil, and many assume the rye also raises the next crop's yield. Field trials have been mixed: in some, corn planted after rye outyielded corn on bare soil; in others, it did worse. Agronomist Priya Nandakumar noticed that the trials differed in spring rainfall. <u>Rye roots open channels that drain water deep into the soil, but the living rye also pulls moisture out before it is cut down.</u> Where spring rain was heavy, the drainage helped the corn; where rain was scant, the lost moisture hurt it.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It describes two opposing effects of rye that together account for the conflicting results of the trials.
It presents evidence confirming farmers' assumption that rye raises the yield of the following corn crop.
It reports the results of Nandakumar's trials comparing corn grown after rye with corn on bare soil.
It explains why the amount of spring rainfall differed among the field trials Nandakumar reviewed.
items.explanation: The text starts with a puzzle: trials disagree. Nandakumar's clue is rainfall. The underlined sentence gives the mechanism, one effect that helps (drainage) and one that hurts (lost moisture). The final sentence shows that rainfall decides which effect wins, which resolves the conflicting results.

B.why: You focused on the helpful effect and missed the 'but.' Rye can also hurt yields, so the sentence explains the mixed results instead of confirming the farmers' assumption.

C.why: You called an explanation a result. The trial outcomes are given in the second sentence, and Nandakumar reviewed those trials rather than running them. The underlined sentence explains why the outcomes differed.

D.why: You linked 'water' in the sentence to the rainfall differences. The sentence explains how rye responds to water. It never says why rainfall varied among the trials.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Ruth Okafor's 1998 memoir about her years as a vaccination nurse.

Every morning before dawn I packed the clinic cooler: vials of measles vaccine, boxes of syringes, ice packs wrapped in newspaper. When spring rains washed out the road to the hill villages, I walked the last mile with the cooler strapped to my back. <u>It always weighed more than anything inside it, because every name on my list was a child waiting at the end of that road.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains that the cooler was built of heavy materials that made it hard to carry.
It conveys the sense of responsibility the narrator felt toward the children she served.
It describes the narrator's conversations with families about the vaccination schedule.
It suggests that the narrator resented having to walk the last mile to the villages.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence says the cooler 'weighed more than anything inside it' and gives the reason: each name on the list was 'a child waiting.' That extra weight is figurative. It is the weight of knowing that children depend on her. So the sentence shows her sense of responsibility.

A.why: You read the image literally. The text never describes what the cooler is made of. The 'because' clause tells you the weight comes from the children waiting, not from the cooler's materials.

C.why: You added a scene the text doesn't contain. The narrator mentions a list of names but never says she talked with any family. Before you pick a choice, check that you can point to the words that support it.

D.why: You misread the tone. The sentence explains why the load felt heavy: children were waiting for her. That shows devotion, not resentment. Nothing in the text suggests she minded the walk.

The following text is from Lucía Ferrante's 2011 novel The Dry Field. Teodora has returned to her family's farm after a year at an agricultural research station.

Her father judged a field the way his own father had: he crumbled a handful of soil between his fingers, smelled it, and announced whether it was ready. <u>Teodora pushed a steel probe into the same ground and read the nitrogen level off a screen to the second decimal place.</u> Neither of them, she suspected, was entirely wrong.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains the scientific process by which the probe measures nitrogen in soil.
It shows that Teodora considers her father's method of judging soil useless.
It contrasts Teodora's way of assessing the field with her father's way.
It describes an argument Teodora and her father had about whether to plant.
items.explanation: The sentence before the underlined one shows the father testing soil by touch and smell. The underlined sentence shows Teodora testing 'the same ground' with a probe and a screen. Putting the two methods side by side sets up a contrast between the characters, and the last sentence comments on that contrast.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Harold Visser's 1987 short story "The Inspector."

For thirty years Marguerite had climbed beneath the river bridge with a flashlight and a small hammer. She tapped each rivet and listened for the dull note that meant rust. She recorded every hairline crack in a green notebook, and she knew which ones had widened since the winter before. <u>The bridge, in other words, had been the one long conversation of her life.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It sums up the earlier details by casting Marguerite's work as a lifelong relationship.
It reveals that Marguerite spoke aloud to the bridge while she inspected it.
It describes a repair Marguerite made after she discovered rust on a rivet.
It suggests that Marguerite found her years of inspections dull and repetitive.
items.explanation: 'In other words' tells you the sentence restates what came before it. Thirty years of tapping, listening, and tracking cracks are recast as a 'conversation,' which is a figure for a close, two-way relationship. The sentence summarizes the details and tells you what they meant to her.

B.why: You took 'conversation' literally. The tapping and listening are what make the image fit. The text never says Marguerite talked to the bridge.

C.why: You added an event. The passage covers inspecting and recording only: tapping, listening, and writing in a notebook. No repair is ever mentioned.

D.why: You probably caught the word 'dull,' but in the text it describes the sound that means rust, not her feelings. Calling the bridge 'the one long conversation of her life' shows close attachment, not boredom.

items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains why the earlier ceramic samples burst apart under the press.
It describes how Reyes gripped the final sample to keep it in the press.
It shows that Reyes had lost interest in her long series of experiments.
It marks the moment when Reyes's long string of failed tests finally ends.
items.explanation: The sentence before it describes four hundred samples that all burst. The underlined sentence reports that the next one 'held,' meaning it survived the press. B.why: You read 'held' as gripping something with a hand. The previous sentence uses 'held its shape,' which tells you 'held' here means the sample survived the load. Nobody holds anything.

C.why: You missed her reaction. Reyes stands 'very still, as if moving might undo it,' which shows intense investment in the result, not a lack of interest.

items.subtype_name: Function of the underlined line (fiction/memoir)
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Dara Whitcombe's 2019 memoir about years spent surveying wetlands.

Each spring I waded the same marsh with a clipboard, counting frogs by their calls. The first year, the chorus was so loud that I had to shout to my partner a few feet away. items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

To explain why a highway was built near the marsh and how its construction damaged the surrounding wetlands
To recount a disagreement between the narrator and a partner about the most reliable way to count frogs
To show that the narrator abandoned the survey because the marsh had grown too noisy to work in
items.explanation: Follow the change in sound. In the first year the frogs are so loud the narrator has to shout. By the fifth year a highway two miles away is audible, which means the frogs have gone quiet. The last sentence says the quiet 'told me what they would say': the narrator knows the count has dropped without writing it down. So the text exists to show a realization, and the change in what can be heard is how that realization arrives.

B.why: You took the highway as the topic. The text only says the highway could be heard. It never says when or why the road was built or that it damaged anything. The highway shows how quiet the marsh had become.

C.why: You made up a conversation. The partner appears only to show how loud the frogs once were, since the narrator had to shout. No one argues about counting methods anywhere in the text.

D.why: You got the sound backwards. The marsh grew quieter, not noisier. Hearing a distant highway means the frogs had faded. The narrator stops writing numbers because the quiet already gives away the result.

The following text is from a memoir by a nutrition researcher.

It shows that the parents often argued aloud about how much to eat.
It suggests that the father had no interest in his own health.
It introduces the narrator's later career in nutrition research.

D.why: You gave the job of the next sentence to the underlined one. The narrator's career comes in the final sentence. The underlined line looks back at the parents, not forward to the career.

D.why: You attached the underlined line to the earlier sentence about walking the shore. The underlined line takes place after she has gone home. It says nothing about her route.

The following text is from Tomas Eberle's 2008 memoir of his career as an archaeologist.

To express the narrator's resentment at being given dull work by the director of the dig
To explain how the narrator identified the remains of an old fire by the color of the soil
To show how one experience changed the narrator's sense of what counts as a discovery

To suggest that Duarte distrusted outsiders who came to his village to record local stories
To explain that the narrator's recording equipment failed during her very first interview

The following text is from Rafael Soto's 2017 memoir about his work as a materials scientist.

In graduate school, I was taught that every crack in a sample was a failure, something to log and discard. My grandmother, who mended pottery, would have disagreed. To show how a memory of his grandmother's craft shaped the narrator's view of damage in his work
To argue that self-sealing polymers are stronger than pottery that has been repaired with gold
To recount an argument the narrator had with his grandmother about his graduate training

The following text is from Marisol Okafor's 2017 memoir about her years as a reef surveyor.

For my first season I counted parrotfish the way I had been taught, as tally marks on a slate. To describe how one observation changed the narrator's view of parrotfish from tallies to shore builders
To argue that slate counts are an unreliable method that reef surveyors should stop using
To show that parrotfish harm reefs by grinding living coral into sand that washes away
items.explanation: The text moves from how the narrator first saw parrotfish ("tally marks on a slate") to one morning that changed that view ("After that, I could never again see the fish as a number"). The closing image of each fish as "a small mill making the shore" is figurative. It means the fish build the beach. So the text's purpose is to describe how one observation changed the narrator's understanding, which is what B says.

D.why: You took the "mill" image too literally and made it sound destructive. The fish grinds a dead branch, not living coral, and the sand builds the shore rather than being lost. The text presents the fish as a maker, not a threat.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Priya Lindqvist's 2015 memoir about her work as a nutrition researcher.

In graduate school I believed a food was simply the sum of its label: so many grams of fiber, so many of sugar. Then our lab fed two groups identical portions of the same apples, one served whole and one pureed. The pureed group grew hungry again within the hour. A label, I realized, could describe a meal without describing what that meal would do.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that pureed fruit should be removed from diets because it causes hunger to return quickly
To explain that whole apples contain more fiber and less sugar than the same apples once pureed
To describe the daily routine the narrator followed while working in a graduate research laboratory
To describe how a study led the narrator to doubt that a food's listed nutrients fully predict its effects
items.explanation: The text follows an old belief, then a correction. The narrator first believed a food was "simply the sum of its label." A study then gave two groups identical apples, and only the preparation differed, yet the groups grew hungry at different times. Her conclusion is that a label can describe a meal "without describing what that meal would do." The purpose is to show how the study changed her belief, which is D.

A.why: You turned one result into a dietary recommendation. The narrator draws a lesson about labels, not advice about what people should eat. Nothing in the text says pureed fruit should be removed from anyone's diet.

B.why: The groups ate "identical portions of the same apples," so their labels would read the same. That sameness is what makes the result surprising. A difference in nutrients would undo the narrator's point.

C.why: You pictured a setting the text barely touches. The lab appears only as the place where one study happened. The text describes no routine, only the experiment that changed the narrator's thinking.

It suggests that a fossil meant more to him than an ordinary rock did.
It shows that he resented the hours he spent splitting shale each day.
items.explanation: Read the sentences on either side of the underlined line. The line before shows him tossing empty slabs aside, and the line after names his 'patience for rare things.' Comparing his habit to reading the morning paper makes it sound routine, even comfortable. Choice D invents a feeling you can't point to in the text, so it is the one that fails.
